units.la: REVERENDISSIMO IN CHRISTO PATRI, Domino meo colendissimo, Georgio Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi, totius Anglia Primati, Magnæ Britanniæ Regi à secretiori consilio: vitam in Christo beatam, spiritum prudentiæ, fortitudinis, ac sanctificationis, & multiplicem à Domino gratiam, pacemq;.
units.tr: TO THE MOST REVEREND FATHER IN CHRIST, my most honoured lord, George, Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate of all England, and member of the Privy Council of the King of Great Britain: a blessed life in Christ, the spirit of prudence, fortitude and sanctification, and manifold grace and peace from the Lord.

units.la: QUum populus Dei ex Æ-gypto vocatus (Reuerendissime in Christo Pater, & vigilantissime in Ecclesia Præsul) per varia discrimina in terram promissam renderet per miraculosa in Ægypto ostenta, per rubri maris profunda, per desertum Sinæ, per medios hostes Amalachitas, per serpentes igneos, per versutias Balaam, per varia bella cum hostibus ex gigantea progenie, quorum species insolita, urbes vallatæ, ferrei & falcati currus formidinem populo incusserant: quæ videbantur impedimenta, totidem cesserunt credentibus fidei firmamenta, dum per ea diuina virtus, potentia & bonitas in populo suo liberando clarius eluceret. At infirmioribus atque ignauis animis totidem obstacula videbantur obiecta. Postquam vero idem Deus populum suum ex Antichristi iugo ac tyrannide vocauerit, ex seruitute illa duriori, quam fuit Ægyptiaca, ex captiuitate illa acerbiore, quam fuit Babylonica; quamuis multi Iosuæ & Calebo similes reperti sunt, qui populum ad fidem & constantiam adhortarint: plurimi tamen vel ex propria malignitate, animique angustiis obmurmurantes, vel per aliorum fraudem seducti, viam, quam Deus verbo suo tanquam digito demonstrauit, Spiritu suo ductore ac directore communiuit, sanctorum exemplis tanquam pedibus attritam & manifestatam proposuit, claram, regiam, antiquam deserunt, & semitas nouas atq; impeditas quærunt. Cogimur igitur antiquam viam à Tridentinis desertam indagare. Ad quod quidem studium sacræ nos literæ mirifice prouocant, & torpentes excitant. Iubet
units.tr: Since the people of God, called out of Egypt (most reverend Father in Christ and most vigilant prelate of the Church), made their way to the promised land through many dangers: through the miraculous signs in Egypt, through the depths of the Red Sea, through the desert of Sinai, through the midst of the Amalekite enemies, through fiery serpents, through the cunning of Balaam, and through various wars with enemies of the giant race, whose unusual appearance, walled cities and iron scythed chariots had struck fear into the people. These things which seemed to be hindrances became so many supports of faith for those who believed, since through them the divine power, might and goodness in freeing its people shone forth more clearly. But to weaker and more cowardly minds, the same obstacles seemed to be thrown in their way. But after the same God called his people out of the yoke and tyranny of Antichrist, out of that servitude harsher than the Egyptian, out of that captivity more bitter than the Babylonian, although many men like Joshua and Caleb were found who exhorted the people to faith and steadfastness, very many, either through their own malice and murmuring from narrowness of spirit, or seduced by the deceit of others, abandon the clear, royal and ancient way which God demonstrated in his word as with a finger, which his Spirit as guide and director has paved, and which the examples of the saints have set forth as trodden and made plain by feet. They seek instead new and obstructed paths. We are therefore compelled to search out the ancient way deserted by the Tridentines. Holy Scripture powerfully stirs us to this task and rouses us when we are sluggish. It bids

units.la: DEDICATORIA.
units.tr: DEDICATORY.

units.la: Moses dierum antiquorum meminiffe, singulas generationes cogitare, interrogare patres & maiores. & Ieremias iubet stare super vias, & videre, & interrogare de semitis antiquis, quae sit via bona, & in ea ambulare. Diuinis igitur oraculis admoniti, interrogamus patres, antiquitatem consulimus. Dum haec agimus, per Dei prouidentiam admirabilis sese [?]prodit consensus eorum, qui eandem [?]viam antiquam & bonam per diuersa secula tenuerunt, quam nos tenere cupimus; quos comites in hoc itinere habemus, quorum fidei ac conuersationis viua atque expressa vestigia obseruamus. Una est via, quam omnes tenent, qui veritatem quaerunt. Et ne erroris locus Deum quaeretibus relinquatur, Christus Dominus hanc viam, quam solus optime nouerat, quaerentibus & pulsantibus clarissime commonstrauit, his verbis:
units.tr: Moses bids us remember the days of old, consider the generations one by one, and ask our fathers and elders; and Jeremiah bids us stand upon the ways, look, and ask for the old paths, which is the good way, and walk in it. Admonished therefore by these divine oracles, we ask the fathers and consult antiquity. While we do this, by the providence of God there appears the remarkable agreement of those who have held to the same old and good way through different ages, the way we too desire to hold; we have them as companions on this journey, and we observe the living and clear traces of their faith and conduct. There is one way which all hold who seek the truth. And lest room for error be left to those who seek God, Christ the Lord, who alone knew this way perfectly, showed it most clearly to those who seek and knock, in these words:

units.la: Ego sum via, veritas, & vita, nemo venit ad patrem, nisi per me. Quaerimus primo exordium huius itineris, quod nos ad vitam perducat. Exordium, unde progredimur, est Christus veritas: quia veritas Prophetica & Apostolica est lux ad initium viarum nostrarum. Itaque à veritate, quæ est in Christo per Prophetas & Apostolos patefacta, tendimus per viam, quæ est in Christo per Spiritum sanctificationis, mon-stratam, ad vitam, quæ est in Christo gloriosa futura. Ex hac luce Tridenti-nos arguimus, qui Christum viam ic-circo non inueniunt, quia Christum veritatem [?non] tenuerunt. Vt hæc via [?manifestius constaret] nobis, quam vera Christi Ecclesia semper tenuit, disputauimus de regula fidei, de Ecclesia, de fide iustificante, de gratia. Hæc via expeditissima visa est demonstrandi Ecclesiam, scilicet, ex huius thesauri custodia, qui Ecclesiæ à Deo concreditus est, vt hæc oracula Dei in Ecclesia deposita, ipsa Ecclesia fide, industria, integritate conseruet vsque ad aduentum Domini nostri.
units.tr: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me. First we inquire into the beginning of this journey, which leads us to life. The beginning from which we set out is Christ the truth, because the prophetic and apostolic truth is the light at the start of our ways. Therefore from the truth, which in Christ has been made known through the Prophets and Apostles, we press on by the way which is shown in Christ through the Spirit of sanctification, to the life which is to be glorious in Christ. By this light we refute the Tridentines, who do not find Christ the way precisely because they have not held Christ the truth. So that the true Church of Christ's constant way might stand clearer to us, we have disputed about the rule of faith, the Church, justifying faith, and grace. This seemed the most convenient way of demonstrating the Church, namely, from the keeping of this treasure which was entrusted to the Church by God, so that the Church itself, by faith, diligence and integrity, may preserve these oracles of God deposited in her until the coming of our Lord.

units.la: Tuæ vero Amplitudini, Reuerendissime ac vigilantissime Præsul, hoc meum studium dicaui, non tam in meum priuatum, quam in publicum Ecclesiæ bonum. Cui enim Christi & Ecclesiæ causa magis erat commendanda, quam ei, qui ad Ecclesiæ clauum gubernandum à Christo vocatus, non in alium finem, quam in Chri-sti gloriam, in Ecclesiæ utilitatem, atq; ecclesiasticæ dignitatis patrocinium vivere se ac vigilare agnoscit. Hanc[?] tibi mentem Deus perpetuo confirmet, ut tuo exemplo alii complures in hoc deplorato seculo ad industriam & vi-gilantiam excitentur. Deus Opt. Max. te quamdiutissime incolumem ad Ecclesiæ suæ ædificationem & dignita-tem conseruet.
units.tr: To your Eminence, most reverend and vigilant Prelate, I have dedicated this my labour, not so much for my private good as for the public good of the Church. For to whom should the cause of Christ and the Church be more commended than to him who, called by Christ to govern the helm of the Church, acknowledges that he lives and keeps watch for no other end than the glory of Christ, the profit of the Church, and the defence of ecclesiastical dignity? May God continually confirm you in this mind, so that by your example many others in this despairing age may be roused to diligence and vigilance. May God, most good and most great, preserve you safe for a very long time for the building up and dignity of his Church.

units.la: Reuerendissimæ tuæ Amplitudinis obseruantissimus
units.tr: Of your Most Reverend Eminence the most devoted

units.la: Georgius Carleton.
units.tr: George Carleton.

units.la: PRÆFATIO AD VIROS CLA- RISSIMOS, LITERARVM, omniumque bonarum artium cultura præ- stantes, antiquæ virtutis cultores, Mertonensis Collegii socios.
units.tr: PREFACE TO THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MEN, EMINENT IN LETTERS AND IN THE CULTIVATION OF ALL THE GOOD ARTS, CHERISHERS OF ANCIENT VIRTUE, FELLOWS OF MERTON COLLEGE.

units.la: SI quis antiquioris Ecclesiæ historiam, cum turbis, deplorato hoc sæculo exortis, quotidieque orientibus, attentius conferat (viri Mertonenses mihi pluribus nominibus colendi) facile poterit de Ecclesiarum ruinis æstimare, & Ecclesiam Christi non magis luporum fraudibus, quam pastorum ignauia desolatam agnoscere. Trahunt enim secum suo vitio, vt homines singuli, ita & Ecclesia excidium suum. Duæ enim res, doctrinæ puritas, & vitæ integritas quamdiu coniunctæ atque unitæ retinentur Ecclesiam Dei propria & natiua luce ornatam, lucentemq; vel cæcis demonstrare possunt: qui vero hæc à se invicem avelli patiuntur, & tamen Ecclesiam retinere videri volunt, seipsos data opera fallere, atque in eam curam incumbere videntur, ut ruinam sibi machinentur, & suo se laqueo conficiant. Antiqua Ecclesia consensus luculenter hoc confirmat. Pulchre enim Augustinus {a}: Errat, quisquis putat, veritatem se posse cognoscere, quum adhuc nequiter viuat. Et Cyprianus {b}: Non remanere in Ecclesia Dei possunt, qui deificam disciplinam nec actus conuersatione, nec morum pace tenuerunt. Et Ambrosius {c}: Talibus decoctoribus ad Ecclesiam Christi non peruenitur. Et Gregorius {d}: Extra menstruas Ecclesiae sunt omnes reprobi, quamuis intra limitem fidei esse videantur. Et Bernhardus {e}: Charitas de Ecclesia non deficit.
units.tr: If anyone will carefully compare the history of the more ancient Church with the disturbances that have arisen in this deplorable age and keep arising every day (gentlemen of Merton, whom I must honour on many counts), he will easily be able to judge from the ruins of the churches, and to recognise that the Church of Christ has been laid waste not so much by the frauds of wolves as by the idleness of its pastors. For, just as individuals bring about their own destruction by their faults, so too does a Church. Two things, the purity of doctrine and the integrity of life, when they are kept joined and united, can show the Church of God adorned with its own native light, a light visible even to the blind. But those who allow these two to be torn apart from one another, and yet wish to seem to keep the Church, deceive themselves on purpose, and appear to devote their efforts to contriving their own ruin and to destroying themselves by their own noose. The consensus of the ancient Church confirms this clearly. For Augustine says well: {a}: He errs who thinks he can know the truth while he still lives wickedly. And Cyprian: {b}: They cannot remain in the Church of God who have not kept the divine discipline, either in the practice of their conduct or in the peace of their morals. And Ambrose: {c}: To such bankrupt men one does not come to the Church of Christ. And Gregory: {d}: All the reprobate are outside the bounds of the Church, although they seem to be within the limit of faith. And Bernard: {e}: Charity does not fail from the Church.

units.la: Rem nouam, & prisci temporibus inauditam referimus. De Ecclesia nobiscum decertant illi, qui reiecta vitae sanctitate, Ecclesiam apud se esse probaturos se sperant ex horrendis facinoribus, ex Regum & principum virorum homicidiis, ex regnorum ruinis, ex adulteriis & veneficiis Iesuiticis, ex antiquorum scriptorum depravationibus, ex salsariorum confictis monumentis: ex illis operibus cognoscimus illos. At Ecclesia ex talibus operibus non demonstratur. Itaque qui hæc velagunt, vel probant, ex Ecclesia Dei per flagellum ex suis sceleribus confectum præcipites eiiciuntur. Quamuis igitur ipsa vita impuritas Tridentinos ex Ecclesia Christi eiectos liquido demonstrat: si tamen hæc distinctius perpendantur, fateri cogi-mur, Ecclesiæ calamitates ultimas, ruinas, excidiaque, à doctrinæ depravatione exorta. Profecto tamdiu stare solent Ecclesiæ, quamdiu in illis locum habere potest cælestis doctrina veritas: tum demum ruere incipiunt, quum primum à veritate excidunt. Huius rei adumbratam demonstrationem, imo expressam imaginem continebat ignis ille cælitus à Deo missus in altare Domini: quem semel de cælo exceptum sacerdotes perpetuo conservabant, neque fas fuit, sacrificia Dei alio igne absumere: ac proinde Nadab & Abihu, quanquam ipsi sacerdotes, & Aaronis filii fuerint, à Deo igne percussi perierunt, quia ignem alienum obtulerant, quod Dominus non præceperat eis: quorum exitium tum demonstrat, sacerdotes non succes-sione, sed doctrina integritate Deo probari: tum vero hereticorum omnium iudicium illustre continet, qui doctrinas alienas audeant in Ecclesia Dei coram Domino offerre. Sine igitur officium spectemus eo-rum tum[?] sacerdotum, qui Deo placuerunt, sive[?] exitium transgressorum, constat, in Ecclesia successione doctrina puritatem, tanquam divinum thesaurum Ecclesiae ministris divi-nitus commissam, ab illis summa fide ac in-tegritate perpetuis temporibus conservan-dam. Atque vel hinc suspicere licet sapientissimum ab Apostolicis usque tempori-bus institutum, ut sint in Ecclesia tum pa-stores, qui populum in recta fide instituant, eiusq; vitam ac mores efforment, atque ad normam verbi flectant: tum etiam Episcopi, qui pastorum possent[?] & mores, & doctrinam inspicere, atque examinare, ut nascen-tia in Ecclesia errorum semina, velut inter aedificia occulte orientia incendia, vi-gilum providentia extinguantur. Quo ma-gis, qui ad Ecclesiarum clavum sedent, in hanc curam totis sensibus excubare debent, ut Ecclesiam Dei ab omni haeresi purgatam, integramque Christo Domino sistant. In hoc tam honorifico ac divino studio post Apostolos antiqui Episcopi cum summo Ecclesiae emolumento vigilarunt. His artibus Irenaeus Valentinianos, Cyprianus Novatianos, Athanasius Arianos, Basilius & Gregorius insignes Arii propugnatores Eunomianos, Cyrillus Alexandria Episcopus Nestorianos,
units.tr: We are reporting a new thing, one unheard of in earlier times. Those who have cast off holiness of life, and hope to prove that the Church is with them, dispute with us about the Church, drawing their proof from horrible crimes, from the murders of kings and princely men, from the ruin of kingdoms, from Jesuit adulteries and poisonings, from the corruptions of ancient writers, and from the forged records of the salsarii. "By their works we know them." But the Church is not shown by such works. Therefore those who wish to do or to defend these things are hurled headlong out of the Church of God by the scourge that their own crimes have fashioned. Although, then, the very impurity of their lives clearly shows that the Tridentines have been cast out of the Church of Christ, yet if these matters are weighed more carefully, we are compelled to confess that the last calamities, ruins and overthrows of the Church have arisen from the corruption of doctrine. Indeed, churches are wont to stand for as long as the truth of heavenly doctrine can have a place in them; they only begin to fall when they first fall away from the truth. That fire sent from heaven by God upon the altar of the Lord contained a shadowy demonstration, or rather a clear image, of this matter. The priests, having once received it from heaven, kept it perpetually, and it was not lawful to consume the sacrifices of God with any other fire. Therefore Nadab and Abihu, although they were priests and sons of Aaron, perished, struck down by the fire of God, because they had offered strange fire, which the Lord had not commanded them. Their destruction shows both that priests are approved by God not through succession but through integrity of doctrine, and it contains a notable judgment upon all heretics who dare to offer alien doctrines before the Lord in the Church of God. Let us then look at the office of those priests who pleased God, or at the destruction of the transgressors: it is established that in the Church the purity of doctrine, committed by God to the ministers of the Church as a divine treasure, is to be preserved by them through all times with the greatest faith and integrity, by succession. And from this one may also perceive the most wise arrangement instituted from apostolic times: that there should be in the Church pastors who instruct the people in the right faith, shape their life and manners, and bend them to the rule of the Word; and also bishops, who may inspect and examine both the morals and the doctrine of the pastors, so that the seeds of error beginning to sprout in the Church may be put out by the watchfulness of guards, like fires arising secretly among buildings. All the more, those who sit at the helm of the churches ought to keep watch with all their senses over this care, so that they may present to Christ the Lord a Church purged of every heresy and whole. In this so honourable and divine task, after the Apostles, the ancient bishops kept watch to the very great advantage of the Church. By these arts Irenaeus opposed the Valentinians, Cyprian the Novatians, Athanasius the Arians, Basil and Gregory the Eunomians, the notable champions of Arius, Cyril bishop of Alexandria the Nestorians,

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Augustinus Manichæos, Donatistas, Pelagianos, multosq; praeterea alios: hoc est, lucis ministri tenebrarum ministros profligarūt. Ita veteres illi Episcopi ad officium suum & ministerium inprimis spectare intelligebant, ut insurgentes in Ecclesia hæreses omni studio suo opprimerent: felices illos atq; emeri-tos milites labores sui atq; certamina sequuntur: manet interim eadem felicitatis occasio, eadem manet Ecclesia, eadem in Ecclesia manent certamina, eadem certantes expectat corona: nos vero non iidem manemus. Ita enim sumus plerique erga Christum & Ecclesiam Dei, quam suo sanguine acquisivit, affecti, ut Ecclesiarum cura egregie suscipi videatur scilicet, si res nostra crescant. Ita sumus omnes ad dominationem attenti, in eo adeo vigilanter omnes ingeniorum articulos versamus, ut regnum Dei, & gloria ipsius a primo in secundum aut tertium locum, aliquando in ultimum reiiciatur. Verum ne querimoniam hoc loco tollere possemus, optimi Regis imperium, & vigilantissimi Archiepiscopi regimen pastorale effecit: qui auctoritate, prudentia, studio, vigilis [?] improborum conatus confringunt, ut Ecclesia tranquillitati prospiciatur, ne errorum incendia Ecclesia intentata latius sese efferant: quorum sanctissimæ curæ, animos etiam torpentes ad industriam excitare possunt: hinc mihi quoque cura succreuerat, ut ad publicum incendium restinguendum, quod ab hareticis ingeniis est excitatum, nostram hanc aquæ situlam alacri manu porrigeremus. Patres vero Ecclesiasticos, quantum licet, adhortor, atque obtestor coram Deo, ac Domino nostro Iesu Christo (donec ab ipsis, qui autoritate, doctrina, & sanctimonia valent, legitima, libera, ac plena sanctarum Ecclesiarū Synodus coacta errores istos examinauerit, profligauerit, pacemque Ecclesiæ reddiderit) ut interim Ecclesiam Dei integram, & quantum in ipsis est, castam Christo exhibeant. Sciant rei Ecclesiastica male gesta Christo se rationem reddituros: industria vero sua fructum uberrimum, & apud Deum, & apud homines consecuturos: neque vero vel bruta illa Romani Pontificis fulmina[?], vel confœderatorum hostium adversus Christum & Ecclesiam vires quascunque metuendas putabimus, quamdiu si Ecclesia nostra integram doctrina cœlestis anitatem[?] conseruauerit. Quod si Ecclesia pastorum ignauia veritatem mutauerit in mendacium, quidnam deinceps expectandum iudicemus, nisi ruinam? Non enim nouum houum[?] in Ecclesia, aut mirum videri debet; si, qui Ecclesiis præficiuntur, derelicta veritate, in insigniores hæreses prolabantur, omnia secum in ruinam trahant. Sed quoniam Ecclesiam suam Deus velut arenam maximorum certaminum voluit esse, magno animo subeunda sunt, quæcunque ad excitandam seruorum suorum industriam in Ecclesia sua DEVS fieri præordina-verit[?].
units.tr: Augustine overthrew the Manichaeans, the Donatists, the Pelagians, and many others besides: that is, the ministers of light overthrew the ministers of darkness. So those early bishops understood that their office and ministry chiefly required them, with every effort, to suppress the heresies that arose in the Church. Those men followed the labours and struggles of those happy and veteran soldiers: the same opportunity for happiness remains, the same Church remains, the same contests remain in the Church, and the same crown awaits those who contend. But we do not remain the same. For most of us are so disposed towards Christ and the Church of God, which he acquired with his own blood, that the care of the Churches seems to be taken up splendidly, so to speak, only if our own affairs prosper. We are all so intent on domination, and we turn over every faculty of our minds so vigilantly toward it, that the kingdom of God and his glory are pushed from first place to second or third, and sometimes to last. Yet, lest we should have grounds for complaint here, the rule of an excellent King and the pastoral government of a most watchful Archbishop have brought it about that they, by authority, prudence, zeal and vigilance, break the attempts of the wicked, so that the tranquillity of the Church is looked after and the fires of error, which threaten the Church, do not spread more widely. Their most holy care can rouse even sluggish minds to diligence. Hence care for this too had grown in me, so that to put out the public fire kindled by heretical minds I might hold out this little bucket of water with a willing hand. I exhort the ecclesiastical Fathers, as far as is permitted, and I solemnly beseech them before God and our Lord Jesus Christ (until a lawful, free and full synod of the holy Churches, convened by those who excel in authority, learning and holiness, has examined and overthrown these errors and restored peace to the Church) that in the meantime they should present the Church of God whole and, so far as lies in them, chaste to Christ. Let them know that they will render account to Christ for any ill management of ecclesiastical affairs, but that by their diligence they will obtain a most abundant fruit, both before God and before men. Nor shall we think that the brutish thunderbolts of the Roman Pontiff, or the forces of his confederate enemies against Christ and the Church, are to be feared at all, so long as our Church preserves the integrity of the heavenly doctrine. But if the Church, through the sloth of its pastors, has turned truth into lie, what shall we judge is to be expected thereafter, except ruin? For it ought not to seem new or strange in the Church if those who are placed over the churches, having abandoned the truth, slip into more notable heresies and drag everything with them into ruin. But since God willed that his Church should be as a sand-field for the greatest contests, whatever God has ordained to be done in his Church to rouse the diligence of his servants must be undergone with a great spirit.

units.la: Quodsi quis diligentius consideret, qua variis temporibus hæreses in Ecclesia variæ exortæ fuerint, quarum quædam ipsam Trinitatem oppugnarint, quod fecerunt ante Arium hæreses fere omnes: quædam Spiritus sancti divinitatem, sicut Macedoniani: alia non minus Christi, quam Spiritus sancti divinitatem, ut Ariani: quædam Christi humanitatem negarint; quod fecit non minus Nestorius, dissolvendo Christum in duas personas; quam Eutyches, confundendo distinctas Christi naturas in unam: alia vero Christi officia (prophetiam dico, regnum & sacerdotium) eluserint; in quo luto totus fere Antichristianismus, vel ut alii vocant, Papismus volutatur: omnia profecto videntur mirifice à Deo ordinata, ut excitaretur industria seruorum Dei in Ecclesia
units.tr: If anyone considers more carefully how at various times various heresies have arisen in the Church, some of which assailed the Trinity itself (as almost all the heresies before Arius did), some the divinity of the Holy Spirit, as the Macedonians did, others no less the divinity of Christ than of the Holy Spirit, as the Arians did, some denied the humanity of Christ (which Nestorius did no less, by dissolving Christ into two persons, than Eutyches did by confusing the distinct natures of Christ into one), and others overthrew the offices of Christ (I mean his prophetic, royal and priestly offices), in which mud almost the whole of Antichristianism, or, as others call it, Papism, wallows: all these things surely seem to have been marvellously ordained by God, so that the diligence of God's servants might be roused in the Church.

units.la: PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: Ecclesia per singula secula, ut veritas magis magnā luceret. Nam quid tandem perfece-runt ista tam portentosa hæreses? & num sine voluntate Dei? num fortuito obrepse-runt? Imo vero ipsi veritatis Adversarii ad veritatem confirmandam inservire cogun-tur. Hoc enim quanquam inscii agunt, ut velut ex somno excitentur ad industriam atq; ad vigilias ministri lucis, ut omnes arti-culi firmentur, omnis doctrina retineatur pura puta, & sicut aurum per ignem purga-ta, ut sapientia justificetur à filiis suis. Ergo in ipsis haereticis excitandis, singularis Dei providentia apparet, eximium Dei in Eccle-siam beneficium, eximium ad veritatem promouendam studium in Ecclesia excita-tur. Hoc ipsum praemonuerunt Apostoli, ut qui ad messem domini à domino messis emit-tuntur, sciant, nec certamina, nec pericula unquàm defutura, neq; vero in laboribus suis ac periculis providentia Dei aliquando desu-turam. Jubet ergo nos magno animo in messe dominica versare, neq; occurrētibus periculis ac turbis frāgi, quia, quacunq; in Ecclesia excitatur turba, divina providentia adeo vigi-lanter regitur atq; ordinatur, ut nemo possit ad Ecclesiam turbandam accedere, qui non prius in aeterno Dei consilio ad hoc judicium, ac proinproinde ad iustam damnationem scriptus fuerit. Cohortatur ergo nos Apostolus Iudas, vt semper decertemus pro fide, quæ semel tradita est sanctis. Nam subrepserunt quidam homines prius iam olim descripti ad hoc iudicium, impii, Dei nostri gratiam transferentes ad luxuriam, & solum illum verum Deum, ac Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum negantes. Quid ergo restat aliud, quam vt in conspectu Christi Domini cum omni alacritate militemus? Atque hæc erat ratio, quæ nos in hanc arenam produxerit.
units.tr: The Church, through every age, so that the truth might shine the more brightly. For what, after all, have those so monstrous heresies accomplished? And did they creep in without the will of God, by chance? Nay rather, the very adversaries of the truth are compelled to serve in confirming the truth. For though they act unwittingly, they do so that the ministers of light may be roused, as if from sleep, to diligence and watchfulness, so that all the articles are strengthened, all doctrine kept pure and, like gold refined by fire, that wisdom may be justified by her children. Therefore, in the very stirring up of heretics, a singular providence of God appears, an extraordinary benefit of God to the Church, and an extraordinary zeal for promoting the truth is aroused in the Church. The Apostles foretold this very thing, that those who are sent by the Lord into the Lord's harvest should know that neither contests nor dangers will ever be lacking, and that God's providence will never fail them in their labours and perils. He therefore bids us labour in the Lord's harvest with a great spirit, and not be broken by the dangers and tumults that meet us, because whatever tumult is stirred up in the Church, divine providence is so watchfully governed and ordered that no one can come to disturb the Church who has not first been written down in God's eternal counsel for this judgement, and so for just damnation. Therefore the Apostle Jude exhorts us to contend always for the faith that was once delivered to the saints. For certain men crept in who were long ago marked out for this judgement, ungodly men, who turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness and deny the only true God and our Lord Jesus Christ (Jude 3–4). What then remains, but that we fight in the sight of the Lord Christ with all eagerness? And this was the reason that brought us into this arena.

units.la: Apud vos vero, viri doctissimi, ornatissimi, mihi plurimis nominibus colendi, hanc adhortationem depositam esse volui, vt intelligatis, vestram operam, industriam, eruditionem, ad causam Christi adiuuandam implorari, vestros labores ab Ecclesia Christi exspectari, vosq; velut nominatim à Christo Domino compellari. Quo enim alio pignore vel vestram in me singularem humanitatem excipere, vel meam in vos fidem atque amorem exprimere potui, quam vt vos ad Ecclesiam Christi vestris laboribus iuuandam, adificandam, erigendam prouocarem? Hanc à vobis operam antiquam Mertonensium nostrorum exempla postulant. Ex hoc enim Collegio principes in omni litelit[illegible, ~25 letters] Ti[illegible, ~25 letters] Ba[illegible, ~25 letters] du[illegible, ~25 letters] Vi[illegible, ~25 letters] Th[illegible, ~25 letters] tra[illegible, ~25 letters] ru[illegible, ~25 letters] De[illegible, ~25 letters] su[illegible, ~25 letters] ini[illegible, ~25 letters] Vt[illegible, ~25 letters] ter[illegible, ~25 letters] du[illegible, ~25 letters] hoc[illegible, ~25 letters] cur[illegible, ~25 letters] Th[illegible, ~25 letters] que[illegible, ~25 letters] the[illegible, ~25 letters] cre[illegible, ~25 letters] rep[illegible, ~25 letters] sia[illegible, ~25 letters] spe[illegible, ~25 letters] tan[illegible, ~25 letters] cer[illegible, ~25 letters] scie[illegible, ~25 letters] mu[illegible, ~25 letters] bus[illegible, ~25 letters] literarum genere viri, tanquam ex equo Troiano,ad veritatis defensionem, atque ad Babylonici Imperij incendium & ruinas per diuersa secula prodierunt. Hinc Iohannes VVicleuus, hinc Guilielmus Occham, hinc Thomas Bradvvarden, hinc alii multi contra pseudofratres bellum susceperunt, quo-rum clarissima monumenta apud Ecclesiam Dei etiam inter tenebras lucem fulgoremq; suum retinuerunt, sicut apud Israelitas lux inter tenebras Aegyptiacas resplenduit. Vt mittam vetera; arbitror equidem,orbem terrarum in hoc literato genere vix tales duos viros per multa secula tulisse, quales ex hoc Collegio habemus hodie in bonum publicum vigilantes, duos clarissimos equites, Thomam Badlaum, & Henricum Sauilium: quorum alter magnificis sumptibus Bibliothecam Oxoniensem instituit,adornauit, incredibili librorum multitudine & varietate repletam, tanquam splendidissimum Ecclesia ocellum inter rarissima orbis Christiani spectacula exornatam posuit. Alter ad innatatam prudentiam, ad ingenium summum, acerrimumque iudicium,incredibilem rerum scientiarumq; omnium cognitionem ascumulans, magnifico pariter apparatu omni-bus pene per orbem terrarum bibliothecis exquisitis, Gratam S. Iohannis Chrysostomi editionem iam consummauit. Ambo quasi duo Consules sortiti prouincias mirifico animorum consensu, quasi unico iugo connexi, regio plane animo in bonum publicum adui-gilantes, rarissima virtutis exempla omnibus, maxime vero Mertonensibus suis relinquunt. Equidem mihi de Ecclesia Christi pro meo modulo sollicite cogitanti, grande, nescio, quod bonum Deus misericors ad piorum consolationem, atque in Antichristi ruinam parare videtur, in eumque finem istorum duorum clarissimorum virorum animos ad magnifica opera excitasse, ut alii istorum laboribus quasi giganteis humeris sublevati, opus Domini maioribus animis suscipiant, susceptum industria ac fide perficiant. Hac est illa arena, quæ vos exspectat, viri mihi plurimum colendi: ut nihil iam vobis deesse videatur, non instrumenta ad labores, non magnifice extructa ac dotata Collegia, non bibliotheca ornatissima, non exempla praestantium virorum, non eximia causa bonitas, nec denique laborantibus praemium deerit.
units.tr: To you, learned and most distinguished men, whom I wish to honour in many ways, I have wished to address this exhortation, so that you may understand that your effort, diligence and learning are sought to aid the cause of Christ, that your labours are expected by the Church of Christ, and that you are, as it were, called by name by the Lord Christ himself. For by what other pledge could I either repay your singular kindness towards me or express my faith and love towards you, than by urging you to help, build up and raise up the Church of Christ by your labours? The examples of our ancient Mertonians demand this effort from you. For from this College, men of every kind of literary talent [illegible] came forth as leaders, as if from the Trojan horse, to defend the truth and to set fire to and overthrow the Babylonian empire through diverse ages. From here John Wycliffe, from here William Ockham, from here Thomas Bradwardine, and from here many others took up war against the false brothers, and their most famous monuments have kept their light and splendour among the Church of God even amid the darkness, just as the light shone among the Israelites amid Egyptian darkness. To pass over antiquity: I think the world has hardly borne two such men in this literary field through many ages as we have today from this College, vigilant for the public good: two most distinguished knights, Sir Thomas Bodley and Sir Henry Savile. The one, at great expense, founded and adorned the Bodleian Library at Oxford, filled with an incredible number and variety of books, and set it up as a most splendid jewel of the Church, adorned with the rarest sights of the Christian world. The other, heaping up with an uncommon judgement, the highest intellect and the keenest insight, an incredible knowledge of all things and sciences, and with magnificent equipment drawn from almost all the libraries of the world, has now completed the Greek edition of St John Chrysostom. Both, like two consuls who have drawn their provinces, bound together by a remarkable harmony of minds as if under a single yoke, watching for the public good with a truly royal spirit, leave the rarest examples of virtue to all, and above all to their Mertonians. Indeed, as I anxiously think about the Church of Christ, according to my small ability, it seems that God, in his mercy, is preparing some great good for the consolation of the godly and for the ruin of Antichrist, and to this end he has roused the minds of these two most distinguished men to magnificent works, so that others, lifted up by their labours as on giant shoulders, may undertake the work of the Lord with greater spirit and complete what has been undertaken with diligence and faith. This is that arena which awaits you, gentlemen whom I greatly honour: so that nothing now seems lacking to you, neither instruments for your labours, nor magnificently built and endowed colleges, nor a most splendid library, nor examples of outstanding men, nor the excellence of the cause; and finally, there will be no lack of reward for those who labour.

units.la: Restat, ut instituti mei rationem vobis aperiam. Delectatus olim ingenio & industria Mart. Buceri, praestantis Theologi, qui controuersias inter nostros & Pontificios compouere[?] studebat, omnesq; ad pacem & concor-diam, quantum fieri posset, revocare, existi-mabam, operam non inutilem futuram, si a-liqua concordia ineunde ratio excogitari po-tuerint. Sed quum res ipsas propius perspexe-rim, videbatur concordia quaerenda studium ex bono quidem animo proficisci[?], sed impossi-bilia tentare eos, qui post Decreta Tridentina reconciliationem aut concordiam cogitant. Ante Concilium illud Tridentinum facti-tius hoc negotium expediri potuisse videbatur. Quamuis enim in multis doctrina capitibus corruptela subintroducta fuerant à fraterculis, in praecipuis tamen articulis, & fundamentalibus videmus integritatem doctrina à multis mirifica Dei providentia conseruatam[?]: ita ut in dubio pendere videretur ante Concilium Tridentinum, quaenam fuerit Ecclesia Romana doctrina, illane, quam multi viri religiosi integram retinuerunt, an potius illa, quam pseudofratres induxerunt. Hinc ardor & studium animum meum invaserat, inquirendi huius mutationis origines. Animatus etiam fui ad hunc laborem à Reverendissimo Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi, qui, quum forte ante aliquot annos de origine errorum Tridentinorum sermo fuisset iniectus, operam illam difficilem quidem, sed vtilissimam Ecclesiam futuram spondebat. Itaque me in eam curam esset cohortatus, vt tentarem, si quid in ea re efficere potuissem: in quam curam ego pro mea mediocritate libenter incubui. Tandem vniuersum hoc malum deprehenditur à fraterculis inuectum, vt non male iam nobiscum agi videretur, si talem hodie Ecclesiam per omnes Europa partes retineremus, qualem ante fraterculorum ordines instituto patres nostri tenuerunt. Istas fraterculorum perniciosas tragœdias in Ecclesia antiqui Episcopi praesensisse videntur; maxime vero beatæ memoriæ vir, Gualterus de Merton, celeberrimus ille Collegii huius Mertonensis fundator, qui accurate cauisse videtur, ne quis eorum, qui religiones istas ordinesꝫ[?] intrasset, ex huius Collegii stipendiis aleretur: facile enim videbat vir prudentissimus, qui vixerat paulo post primos fraterculorum ordines institutos, malas istas bestias Ecclesiæ ruinam, quacunque grassarentur, secum tracturos. Nam quod Iohannes Wicleuus testetur, Episcopos olim pseudofratres tanquam Diabolos odiuisse: de his temporibus loquitur, quibus vixerat Episcopus ille, cuius memoriam veneramur, Gualterus de Merton, qui pseudofratres istos è suo Collegio decreto suo excludi curauit. Hoc vero libro demonstrare tentauimus in maximis articulis, & fundamentalibus doctrinam à fraterculis fuisse mutatam: nempe in doctrina de regula fidei, de Ecclesia de fide ac gratia: à multis tamen viris doctis piisq; veram fidem in istis omnibus conseruatam obseruauimus, usque ad tempora Concilii Tridentini. Qua igitur ex hac nostra disputatione velut corollaria sequuntur, haec sunt:
units.tr: It remains that I explain to you the plan of my undertaking. Once I was delighted by the talent and industry of Martin Bucer, an outstanding theologian, who laboured to settle the controversies between our people and the Papists, and to bring everyone back, as far as possible, to peace and concord; I thought that my effort would not be useless if some way of reaching agreement could be devised. But when I had looked more closely at the matters themselves, it seemed that the effort to seek concord, though it arose from a good mind, was an attempt at impossibilities for those who now, after the Tridentine decrees, think of reconciliation or agreement. Before that Council of Trent, this business seemed capable of being settled more easily. For although corruption had been introduced into many heads of doctrine by the little friars, yet in the chief and fundamental articles we see the integrity of doctrine preserved by the wonderful providence of God in the view of many; so that before the Council of Trent it seemed doubtful which was the doctrine of the Roman Church: that which many religious men kept whole, or rather that which the false brothers introduced. From this, a zeal and eagerness seized my mind to inquire into the origins of this change. I was also encouraged to this labour by the most reverend Archbishop of Canterbury, who, when a discussion about the origin of the Tridentine errors had by chance been raised some years ago, promised that this task, difficult indeed but most useful to the Church, would be undertaken; and so he urged me to that care, to see whether I could accomplish anything in this matter. To this care I gladly applied myself, according to my modest ability. At last this whole evil is found to have been brought in by the little friars, so that it would now seem we were not badly off if we kept in every part of Europe such a Church as our fathers held before the orders of the little friars were established. The ancient bishops seem to have foreseen these pernicious tragedies of the friars; and above all the man of blessed memory, Walter of Merton, that most famous founder of this Merton College, who seems to have taken care, by his careful precaution, that no one who had entered any of those religious orders should be supported from the stipends of this College; for that most prudent man, who had lived shortly after the first orders of friars were founded, easily saw that those wicked beasts would drag the Church into ruin wherever they rampaged. For what John Wycliffe reports, that bishops once hated the false brothers as devils, he speaks of those times in which that bishop whom we revere, Walter of Merton, lived, who by his decree took care to exclude those false brothers from his College. In this book we have attempted to show that in the greatest articles and fundamental doctrines the teaching was changed by the little friars: namely, in the doctrine of the rule of faith, of the Church, of faith and of grace; yet we have observed that the true faith in all these points was preserved by many learned and pious men up to the time of the Council of Trent. The conclusions which follow from this our discussion, as if by corollaries, are these:

units.la: 1. Consensus Ecclesia, quae unica est in patribus ac filiis, ante Concilium Tridentinum, in maximis doctrinae capitibus semper sibi constans observatur.
units.tr: 1. Among the Fathers and their sons, the consensus of the Church, which is one, is observed to remain constant in the greatest heads of doctrine before the Council of Trent.

units.la: 2. Vera Christi Ecclesia fletisse[?] probatur usque ad Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: 2. The true Church of Christ is shown to have flourished until the Council of Trent.

units.la: 3. Ecclesiae reformatae nihil aliud sunt, quam huius antiquae, verae, unicae Ecclesiae continuatio, quae ante Concilium Tridentinum perstiterit, & ad finem mundi est duratura.
units.tr: 3. The reformed Churches are nothing other than the continuation of this ancient, true and only Church, which persisted before the Council of Trent and will last until the end of the world.

units.la: 4. Separatio, quae facta est, est separatio, qua Rom. curia sese separabat ab Ecclesia, & qua Ecclesia Christi sese retraxerat ab illa curia; siue qua, secundum mandatum diuinum, Ecclesia exiuerat è Babylone.
units.tr: 4. The separation that has taken place is the separation by which the Roman court cut itself off from the Church, and by which the Church of Christ withdrew from that court; or, in accordance with the divine command, the Church went out of Babylon.

units.la: 5. Origines & occasiones errorum demonstrantur.
units.tr: 5. The origins and occasions of the errors are demonstrated.

units.la: 6. Patres, maioresq; nostri, qui in Romana Ecclesia vixerunt, & mortui sunt, media ad salutem necessaria habuerunt, quia vera doctrina praedicatio, quamuis multum impedita à fraterculis, permissa tamen retinebatur vsq; ad Concilium Tridentinum. At ex Decretis Tridentinis media ad salutem necessaria iam sublata sunt.
units.tr: 6. The Fathers and our ancestors, who lived and died in the Roman Church, had the means necessary to salvation, because the preaching of true doctrine, although greatly hindered by the friars, was nevertheless permitted and retained until the Council of Trent. But by the Tridentine decrees the means necessary to salvation have now been taken away.

units.la: Hæc sunt, quæ disputationis huius scopum continent. Hanc vero operam meam qualemcunque Deo & Ecclesiæ posuit[?]: qua, si nihil aliud effecerim, illud saltem me præstitisse confido, ut via vestris aliorumq;[?] maioribus ingeniis præstruatur, qua facilius veritas confirmari, & hypocrisis falsiloquorum retegi possit. Deus vestra studia in suam gloriam & Ecclesiæ suæ consolationem dirigat. Valete viri mihi plurimum colendi. E meo Musæo, 1612. Nouembris quinto, quem diem celebramus in memoriam diuinæ liberationis, quam misericors Deus Ecclesiam & Rempublicam nostram ex faucibus Antichristi, atque ex intentata nobis per puluerem tormentarium internecione liberauit.
units.tr: These are the matters which contain the aim of this disputation. I have offered this work of mine, such as it is, to God and the Church. If I have accomplished nothing else, I trust at least that I have achieved this, that a way may be prepared for your greater talents and those of others, by which the truth may more easily be confirmed and the hypocrisy of the liars be exposed. May God direct your studies to his own glory and to the comfort of his Church. Farewell, gentlemen whom I greatly esteem. From my museum, 1612, the fifth of November, which day we celebrate in memory of the divine deliverance by which merciful God freed our Church and commonwealth from the jaws of Antichrist, and from the destruction prepared for us by gunpowder.

units.la: Vobis in Christo deuinctissimus
units.tr: Most bound to you in Christ,

units.la: Georgius Carleton.
units.tr: Georgius Carleton.

units.la: Apocalyps. 20.
units.tr: Revelation 20.

units.la: vers.3. Coniecit[?] eum (Draconem) in abyssum, quam occlusit & obsignauit super eum, ut non seduceret amplius gentes, donec complerentur anni mille. Nam postea oportet eum solui ad exiguum tempus.
units.tr: Verse 3. He cast him (the Dragon) into the abyss, and shut it and sealed it over him, so that he should not deceive the nations any more until the thousand years were completed. For after that he must be loosed for a little time.

units.la: vers.7. Quum uero expleti fuerint anni mille, soluetur Satanas è carcere suo, exibit, ut seducat gentes.
units.tr: Verse 7. And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be loosed from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations.

units.la: UT sensum huius Scripturæ genuinum teneamus, obseruanda sunt ea, quæ Christus docuit, de eiectione Satanæ, Iohan.12. Postquam enim vox Patris de cœlo insonuit, dicens: Et glorificaui, & rursus glorificabo: vocem illam, Christus monuit, nō propter ipsum, sed propter astantes extitisse. Deinde hæc verba subiicit: Nunc iudicium adest huius mundi, nunc princeps ille huius mundi eiicietur foras, & ego si sublatus fuero è terra, omnes traham ad me. Iudicium huius mundi vocat, non quod in fine seculi futurum est, sed quod ipsius aduentu, & manifestatione, & morte factum est: non damnationis, sed discretionis, ut Augustinus & Cyrillus locum hunc explicant. Iudicium mundi, hoc est, quod pro mundo, siue hominibus huius mundi, tyrannide Diaboli oppressis, erat, tam per mortem ipsius, futurum contra Diabolum, suo in homines imperio, iusto Dei iudicio spoliandum. Vnde explicandi causa, quomodo hoc iudicium mundi fieret, subiecit: Nunc princeps huius mundi eiicietur foras. Nam princeps huius mundi, Diabolus, regnum suum inter gentes longe lateque tenebat ante Christum exhibitum. At quum filius Dei Ecclesiam suam, hoc est, regnum suum apud gentes Apostolorum ministerio dilatauerat: tum primum Satanas eiectus est è regno illo suo, quod antea in gentibus seductis tenuerat. Tempus illud, quando primum eiectus fuerat Satanas, verba Christi demonstrant: Et ego si sublatus fuero è terra, omnes traham ad me. Hoc dicebat, significans, qua morte moriturus effet, inquit Euangelista. Haec igitur eiectio Satanae numeranda est à Christo crucifixo. Et ego, inquit, si sublatus fuero e terra, omnes trahamad me. Omnes, non Iudaeos tantum, sed & gentes.
units.tr: IN ORDER TO hold to the genuine sense of this Scripture, we must observe what Christ taught about the casting out of Satan, John 12. For after the voice of the Father had sounded from heaven, saying, I have glorified it, and will glorify it again, Christ warned that this voice had come not for his own sake but for the sake of those standing by. Then he adds these words: Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to me. He calls it the judgment of this world not because it is to come at the end of the age, but because it has come about through his coming, his manifestation and his death: a judgment not of condemnation but of separation, as Augustine and Cyril explain this passage. The judgment of the world, that is, the judgment which was to take place for the world, or for the men of this world oppressed by the tyranny of the devil, was to come about through his death against the devil, so that by the just judgment of God the devil would be stripped of his dominion over men. Hence, to explain how this judgment of the world would come about, he added: Now the prince of this world will be cast out. For the prince of this world, the devil, held his kingdom far and wide among the nations before Christ was revealed. But when the Son of God had extended his Church, that is, his kingdom among the nations, by the ministry of the apostles, then for the first time Satan was cast out of that kingdom of his which he had previously held among the deceived nations. The words of Christ show the time when Satan was first cast out: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to me. He said this, signifying by what death he was about to die, as the evangelist says. This casting out of Satan, therefore, is to be reckoned from Christ crucified. And I, he says, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to me. All men, not only the Jews but also the nations.

units.la: Quando vero Satanas eiectus fuerat à Christo, ne seduceret gentes amplius: tunc ligatus intelligitur, & in abyssum coniectus, ne seducat gentes. Itaque docet Iohannes, draconem in abyssum coniectum, vt non seduceret amplius gentes, donec complerentur anni mille: quum vero expleti fuerint anni mille, tum demum soluendum Satanam è carcere suo, & exituram, vt seducat gentes. Satanas igitur post Christum crucifixum coniectus in carcerem, id est, Christi potentia ligatus & retentus, vt ne gentes seduceret, sicut antea seduxerat, soluendus fuerat post mille annos ad seducendum gentes. Seductio autem est in erroribus de fide; quanquam vero plurimi errores ante mille annos à Christo crucifixo expletos, exorti fuerint : à Patribus tamen & Episcopis, in Ecclesia Dei vigilantibus, adiuuantibus etiam Romanis Episcopis, errores ante annum millesimum ita fuerunt compressi, vt insignis illa gentium seductio non appareret; atq; in Ecclesiam Rom. ante illud tempus, non multos insignes errores irrepsisse, probari possit. At vero post annos mille à Christo crucifixo (qui principem huius mundi eiecit è regno illo suo (quod antea in genti-bus horrendâ idolomaniâ immersis tenuerat) soluto tandem Satana plurimi insignes errores in Ecclesiam, quæ nunc Romana dicitur, exundarunt. Errores vero, qui in hodiernam Ecclesiam Romanam, post solutum Satanam prorupere, quanquam plurimos deprehendimus, tamen præcipuos tantum hoc loco tractabimus, in quibus ipsa fundamentalia, & vitalia fidei, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ institituta, immutata, lapsaque apud Pontificios, & penitus extincta deploramus. Affirmamus igitur, probari non posse ex probatæ fidei autoribus, testimoniis perspicuis, disertis, solidis, quæq; sunt extra suspicionem plagii, quenquam ex istis erroribus, quos hic examinandos dosufcepimus[?], aut exortum in Ecclesia Romana, ab eaque approbatum ante annum Christi millesimum: aut receptum fuisse in Ecclesia Romana, tanquam dogma de fide, ante Concilium Tridentinum: qui quidem errores hodie in Ecclesia Pontificia habentur dogmata de fide.
units.tr: But when Satan had been cast out by Christ, so that he should no longer deceive the nations, then he is understood to be bound and thrown into the abyss, so that he may not deceive the nations. Thus John teaches that the dragon was cast into the abyss, so that he should not deceive the nations any more until the thousand years were completed; and when the thousand years are completed, then at last Satan is to be loosed from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations. Satan, therefore, having been cast into prison after Christ was crucified, that is, bound and restrained by the power of Christ so that he should not deceive the nations as he had before, was to be loosed after a thousand years to deceive the nations. Now deception consists in errors about the faith. Although very many errors arose before the thousand years were completed after Christ was crucified, nevertheless by the Fathers and bishops who watched over the Church of God, and also with the aid of the Roman bishops, the errors before the year one thousand were so suppressed that that notable deception of the nations did not appear; and it can be proved that before that time not many notable errors had crept into the Roman Church. But after a thousand years from the crucifixion of Christ, who cast the prince of this world out of that kingdom of his (which he had held among the nations, sunk in horrible idolatry), and after Satan was at last loosed, very many notable errors burst forth into the Church now called Roman. Yet although we find very many errors which broke forth into the present Roman Church after Satan was loosed, we shall treat in this place only the chief ones, in which the very fundamentals and vital points of the faith, and the institutions of the Catholic Church, we lament to have been changed and overthrown among the Papists and utterly extinguished. We therefore affirm that it cannot be proved, from authors of approved faith, from clear, explicit and solid testimonies, which are beyond suspicion of plagiarism, that any of those errors which we have undertaken to examine here arose in the Roman Church and were approved by it before the year of Christ one thousand; or that any of them was received in the Roman Church as a doctrine of faith before the Council of Trent; whereas these errors today are held as doctrines of faith in the Papal Church.

units.la: Quatuor controuersias hoc ordine sumus hic explicaturi. Primam, de regula fidei, siue de sacris Scripturis, vt constare possit primo loco, quænam sit, & in Ecclesia semper habita fuerint fidei regula. Hæc una probabitur ab Apostolicis temporibus, vsque ad Concilium Tridentinum in Romana Ecclesia conseruata, in eo tandem Concilio mutata, inde controuersiæ cum Tridentinis exortæ. Deinde secundum illam regulam reliquas tres controuersias examinabimus, de Ecclesia, de Fide iustificante, de Gratia. In istis controuersiis, quæ grauissimæ omnium intelliguntur, post regulam fidei, testimonia Ecclesiæ deducemus vsque ad Concilii Tridentini tempora: & privatas fratercu-lorum opiniones ab Ecclesiæ Romanæ iudicio separabimus: quæ quidem privatæ opiniones hodie inter Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ decreta habentur. Illud vero initio admonendum videbatur, vt sententia sensusque noster recte excipiatur, in iis, quæ dicturi sumus, Ecclesiam nunc Romanam, & Ecclesiam Pontificiam à nobis dici, quæ revera nec Romana Ecclesia est, nec omnino Ecclesia, sed tantum Romana Curia. Nam apud omnes æquos rerum[?] æstimatores, & veritatis cupidos, proba-turos nos per Dei gratiam speramus, errores istos post annum à Christo crucifixo millesimum à fraterculis, & Romanæ Curiæ adula-toribus introductos fuisse, in quibus Ecclesia Romana (in qua patres maioresque nostri vixerunt, religionemque susceperunt) in maximis ac præcipuis fidei negotiis, nempe in fundamentalibus veritatem contra Romanæ Curiæ adulatores integram atque immutatam conservaverat, usque ad Concilii Tridentini tempora.
units.tr: We shall explain four controversies here, in this order. The first, concerning the rule of faith, or the holy Scriptures, so that it may first be established what the rule of faith is and has always been held to be in the Church. This one will be shown to have been preserved in the Roman Church from apostolic times until the Council of Trent, and at that Council to have been changed, from which the controversies with the Tridentines arose. Then, according to that rule, we shall examine the remaining three controversies: concerning the Church, concerning justifying faith, and concerning grace. In these controversies, which are understood to be the most serious of all, after the rule of faith we shall adduce the testimonies of the Church down to the times of the Council of Trent, and we shall separate the private opinions of the friars from the judgment of the Roman Church; and these private opinions are today held among the decrees of the Papal Church. It seemed necessary, however, to admonish at the outset that our view and meaning be rightly understood in what we are about to say: that we call the present Roman Church and the Papal Church by a name which in truth is neither the Roman Church nor the Church at all, but merely the Roman Court. For we hope, by the grace of God, to show to all fair judges of affairs, and lovers of truth, that these errors were introduced after the year one thousand from the crucifixion of Christ by the friars and the flatterers of the Roman Court; and that in them the Roman Church (in which our fathers and ancestors lived and received their religion) had preserved intact and unchanged, against the flatterers of the Roman Court, the truth in the greatest and chief matters of faith, namely in its fundamentals, until the times of the Council of Trent.

units.la: CAPUT I. De modo disputandi, & de ratione se-cessionis nostra à iugo Romani Pontificis.
units.tr: CHAPTER I. On the method of disputing, and on the reason for our secession from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: INter notas illas, quas Cardinalis Bellarmi-nus ad probandam Ecclesiam adduxerat, unam esse voluit, conspirationem in doctrina cum Ecclesia antiqua. Magnam sine dubio integritatis opinionem conciliasset, si, quod ingenuè proposuit, perfecisset. Sed quod perficere se non posse videbat, ne tentare quidem voluit. Quare ergo proposuit? Manifesta videtur & veritatis confessio, & causæ obtinendæ desperatio, proponere, quod verum agnoveris, nec in agnita veritate acquiescere. Si hæc sit genuina disputandi ratio, quare non sic instituis disputationem? Subiicien-da sunt Bellarmini verba, quibus ostendit, se hanc disputandi methodum refugere, qua una doctrinæ conspiratio cum antiqua Ecclesia probari possit. sic enim scribit : Duobus modis possemus ex hac nota probare Ecclesiam nostram veram esse, non autem Aduersariorum. Primo, proferendo sententias veterum, quibus singula nostra dogmata confirmaremus, Aduersariorum refutaremus. Sed hic modus prolixissimus esset, & multis calumniis & obiectionibus obnoxius. Altera via est breuior & certior; nimirum, ostendendo primum ex confessione Aduersariorum, nostra dogmata esse doctrinam omnium veterum. Deinde, dogmata Aduersariorum habita fuisse in Ecclesia antiqua pro exploratis harefibus. Sic enim constabit, doctrinam nostram conspirare cum doctrina veterum Catholicorum : doctrinam vero illorum conspirare cum doctrina veterum hæreticorum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Among those marks which Cardinal Bellarmine put forward to prove the Church, he wanted one to be agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church. He would certainly have won a great reputation for soundness if he had made good on what he frankly proposed. But what he saw he could not achieve, he did not even try to attempt. Why, then, did he propose it? It is plainly both a confession of the truth and a despair of winning the cause: to put forward what you know to be true, and yet not rest in the truth once acknowledged. If this is the genuine way of disputing, why do you not conduct the disagreement this way? Bellarmine's own words must be set out, in which he shows that he shrinks from this method of disputing, the only one by which agreement of doctrine with the ancient Church can be proved. For he writes thus: We could prove from this mark that our Church is true and not that of our adversaries in two ways. First, by bringing forward the opinions of the ancients, by which we might confirm each of our doctrines and refute our adversaries. But this method would be very long and exposed to many calumnies and objections. The other way is shorter and surer: namely, by showing first, from the confession of our adversaries, that our doctrines are the doctrine of all the ancients. Then, that the doctrines of our adversaries were held in the ancient Church as proven heresies. For thus it will be clear that our doctrine agrees with the doctrine of the ancient Catholics, but their doctrine agrees with the doctrine of the ancient heretics. So far he.

units.la: Veritatis indagandæ methodum ex antiquorum sententiis, qua una conspiratio doctrinæ cum antiqua Ecclesia demonstrari potest, ut prolixam, & multis calumniis, & obiectionibus obnoxiam refugit. Breuior via, & facilior placuit, ut calumnias quasdam in nostras Ecclesias conficeret. Nam quid breuius aut facilius, quam calumniam proferre? Itaque vera via relicta, breuiorem & facilem illam calumniandi viam secutus est. Dumque ex nostrorum confessione hoc ostendere laborat, nihil adferre potuit præter calumnias. Negamus hoc ex nostrorum confessione colligi posse, negamus à Cardinali demonstratum, aut demonstrari posse; quamvis in paucis controuersiis[?], immutando, & obtruncando Calvini, aliorumq; nostrorum verba, illud ostendere conetur: sed frustrà.
units.tr: The method of inquiring into the truth from the opinions of the ancients, by which alone agreement of doctrine with the ancient Church can be demonstrated, he shuns as long, and exposed to many calumnies and objections. A shorter and easier way pleased him, so that he might fabricate certain calumnies against our Churches. For what is shorter or easier than to bring forward a calumny? So, abandoning the true way, he followed that shorter and easier way of calumniating. And while he labours to show this from the confession of our people, he could bring forward nothing but calumnies. We deny that this can be gathered from the confession of our people, we deny that the Cardinal has demonstrated it, or that it can be demonstrated; although in a few controversies, by altering and mangling the words of Calvin and others of ours, he tries to show it, but in vain.

units.la: Illud vero Lectoribus non abreptis præiudicio diiudicandum proponimus; an non ex hac Cardinalis confessione constet, si sententiæ veterum proferendæ sint, non posse Pontificios conspirationem doctrinæ suæ cum antiqua Ecclesia probare, quia hic modus disputandi multis calumniis & obiectionibus est obnoxius.Sic veritas extorsit confessionem ex ore Aduersariorum : nam qui hæc dicunt, plane confitentur, veterum doctrinam nostram esse. Qui enim ex veterum doctrina prolata, calumnias & obiectiones metuunt, atque hoc nomine prolationem & collationem antiquæ doctrinæ refugiunt, nonne manifestam produnt confessionem, sese, utcunq; verbis ludunt, reuera conspirationem in doctrina cum antiqua Ecclesia, ut rem sibi formidabilem, penitus à se reiicere, & nobis relinquere.
units.tr: Yet we put it to the readers, who have not been carried off by prejudice, to judge whether it does not follow from this confession of the Cardinal that, if the opinions of the ancients are to be brought forward, the Papists cannot prove the agreement of their doctrine with the ancient Church, because this method of disputing is exposed to many calumnies and objections. Thus truth has wrung a confession from the mouths of our adversaries: for those who say these things plainly confess that our doctrine is the doctrine of the ancients. For those who, fearing calumnies and objections from the ancient doctrine brought forward, shrink from its presentation and comparison on that account, do they not openly betray a confession, that they, however much they play with words, in fact wholly cast off from themselves, as a thing formidable to them, agreement in doctrine with the ancient Church, and leave it to us?

units.la: Quem igitur disputandi modum isti refugiunt, nos ut genuinum suscipimus: quia conspiratio doctrinæ nostræ cum antiqua Ecclesia nullo alio modo probari potest, quam proferendo sententias veterum, quibus singula nostra dogmata confirmemus, Aduersariorum refutemus. Neque vel calumniis, vel obiectionibus hæc via obnoxia esse potest: quia Ecclesia una est atque eadem per omnes generationes, unitatis autem vinculum est in fundamentalibus Ecclesiæ consensus. In fundāmentalibus probabimus, nos habere certissimum antiquæ Ecclesiæ consensum continuatum usque ad nostra tempora, atque adeo ad Concilium Tridentinum : quo tempore patres nostri discessionem fecerunt ab illo conciliabulo, & à Romani Pontificis Curia. Nam ad illa usque tempora Ecclesia, quamuis etroribus, & varia fraude oppugnata; tyrannide preffa, patienter tamen Romi Pontificis tyrannidem, & fraterculorum impudentiam pertulit: At postquam errores illi, qui primum ex priuatis fraterculorum opinionibus prodierunt; pro Ecclesiæ dogmatibus tandem in Concilio Tridentino sancita fuerunt: tum primum Ecclesia (quæ priuatas fraterculorum opiniones patienter tulerat, ac proinde communionem cum illa Ecclesiæ parte hactenus habuerat) diuina prouidentia, imo vero Dei brachio potenti, sicut Israel, ex seruitute Ægyptiaca, sic sese à iugo Pontificio subduxit.
units.tr: Therefore the method of disputing which they shrink from, we accept as the genuine one: because the agreement of our doctrine with the ancient Church can be proved in no other way than by bringing forward the opinions of the ancients, by which we confirm each of our doctrines and refute our adversaries. Nor can this way be open to calumnies or objections, because the Church is one and the same through all generations, and the bond of unity is consensus in fundamentals. In fundamentals we shall prove that we have the most certain consensus of the ancient Church continued down to our own times, and so even to the Council of Trent: at which time our fathers made their secession from that conciliabulum and from the Court of the Roman Pontiff. For up to those times the Church, although assailed by errors and various deceit, and pressed by tyranny, nevertheless patiently bore the tyranny of the Roman Pontiff and the impudence of the friars. But after those errors, which had first come out of the private opinions of the friars, were at last sanctioned as dogmas of the Church at the Council of Trent, then for the first time the Church, which had patiently borne the private opinions of the friars and so had hitherto kept communion with that part of the Church, by divine providence, indeed by the mighty arm of God, as Israel out of Egyptian bondage, thus withdrew itself from the Pontifical yoke.

units.la: Qua in re profani homines casum, nescio; quem & cotingentiam obseruant. Sunt etiam inter Episcopos Pontificios, qui hac receffionem à iugo Pontificio, ad cœlestes conftellationes referunt. Sic isti in Christi schola hospites & peregrini. Nos vero certi sumus, Ecclefiam à suo capite sic institui ac gubernari; vt quamuis malorum hominum fraude ac tyrannide sæpius oppugnata fuerit, ita vt nonnunquam oppressa videatur, nunquam tamen penitus interierit. Et Christum Dominum
units.tr: In this matter profane men observe a chance, I know not what, and contingency. There are also among the Papist bishops some who refer this withdrawal from the Pontifical yoke to heavenly constellations. Such men are guests and strangers in the school of Christ. But we are certain that the Church is so instituted and governed by its head, that although it has often been assailed by the deceit and tyranny of evil men, so that sometimes it seems to be overwhelmed, yet it has never utterly perished. And Christ the Lord,

units.la: bu[?] pro[?] ora[?] diel[?] igi[?] Rc[?] sat[?] ift[?] diu[?] ric[?] po[?] sic[?] du[?] ma[?] me[?] de[?] me[?] dia[?] vic[?] mi[?] rat[?] tue[?] mu[?] coe[?] po[?] ius[?] ta[?] rec[?] ha[?] tia[?] hac[?] hum[?] præsentem semper, & Ecclesiam suam promissione, Spiritusq; suo confirmantem adoramus. Ecce, inquit, ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus, usq; ad consummationem seculi. Utcunque igitur profani homines hanc secessionem à Romano Pontifice, ad contingentiam, aut ad fatum astrologicum referant, nos tamen, vt istos in insania sua relinquamus, veneramur diuinam potentiam, prouidentiam, & misericordiam, qui, quod promiserat, in tempore effecit. Et quamuis tyrannis illa Pontificia longius durasse visa fuerit, in ea tamen duratione, qua Ecclesiam ad patientiam armauerat Deus, videmus, quid peccata nostra meruerint.
units.tr: ...ever present, and confirming his Church by his promise and by his Spirit, we adore. Behold, he says, I am with you always, even to the end of the age. Therefore, however profane men may refer this secession from the Roman Pontiff to chance, or to astrological fate, yet we, leaving them in their madness, venerate the divine power, providence, and mercy, which, what it had promised, brought to pass in its time. And although that Papal tyranny seemed to have lasted rather long, yet in that duration, by which God had armed the Church for patience, we see what our sins have deserved.

units.la: At quod Christus ab hac tyrannide liberauerit Ecclesiam, non nostris illud meritis tribuendum est, sed solius misericordiae diuinae benignitas in eo lucet, & veritatis victoria: quia quod Deus promiserat, necinimicorum potens superbia, nec impotens tyrannis, nec veto[?] nostra peccata auertere potuerunt.
units.tr: But that Christ freed the Church from this tyranny must not be attributed to our merits; rather, the kindness of divine mercy alone shines in it, and the victory of truth: because what God had promised, neither the proud power of enemies, nor impotent tyranny, nor our sins could turn aside.

units.la: Secessimus igitur à Romano iugo, exiuimus è Babylone, sed mandato Dei: nam vox cœlestis sic populum euocauit: Exite ex ea, popule mi, ne participes sitis peccatorum eius, & ex plagis eius accipiatis: nam accumulata peccata eius pertigerunt usq; ad cœlum, & recordatus est Deus scelerū eius. Deus igitur hanc secessionem voce sua mandauit, potentia sua perfecit. Et quanquam sæpius antea de hac secessione Ecclesia cogitauerat, nunquam tamen perficere potuit, donec impletum suisset, quod Scripturæ prædixerant, vt Ecclesia intelligeret, non suis viribus, aut sapientia sua se liberationem suam efficere, sed Christum liberatorem adoraret, & corpus sequeretur suum caput. Illud enim negari non potest, Ecclesiam sæpius antea secessionem à Romano Pontifice vel tentasse, vel de ea re deliberauisse.
units.tr: We have therefore seceded from the Roman yoke, we have come out of Babylon, but by the command of God: for the heavenly voice thus called the people: Come out of her, my people, lest you be partakers of her sins, and receive of her plagues: for her accumulated sins have reached even to heaven, and God has remembered her crimes. God therefore commanded this secession by his voice, and by his power he accomplished it. And although the Church had often before thought about this secession, it could never bring it about, until what the Scriptures had foretold was fulfilled, so that the Church might understand that it does not effect its own liberation by its own strength or wisdom, but adores Christ as its liberator, and the body follows its head. For it cannot be denied that the Church had often before either attempted this secession from the Roman Pontiff or deliberated about the matter.

units.la: Quum Robertus Grosthead noster Episcopus Lincolniensis, impiis olim Romani Pontificis prouisionibus obsisteret, Papa non se capiens præ ira, inquit Matth. Parisiensis, grauius aliquid in Episcopum consulturus videbatur. Sed, vt idem autor refert, consilium dederunt Cardinales Domino Papæ, vt omnia hæc conniuentibus oculis sub dissimulatione transfire permitteret, ne super hoc tumultus excitaretur, maxime propter hoc, quia scitur, quod quandoque discessio fit ventura. Hæc ille. Hæc multo ante Martini Lutheri tempora scripta sunt. Metuebant igitur Cardinales, ne insignis ille pietate & eruditione Lincolniensis Episcopus secessionem hanc inchoaret. Itaque ipsorum iudicio apparet, eum, qui primum se huic secessioni ducem & antesignanum esset præbiturus, insignem futurum hominem, pietate & eruditione excellentem, qualis tum Robertus Grosthead habebatur. De hac secessione consultatio tenuit eos, qui eruditione & pietate maxime floruerunt in Concilio Constantiensi, vt ex Cardinalis Cu-fani, sani, & Iohannis Gersonis scriptis constat. Cusanus de hac re scribit ad Rodericum de Treuino, Regis Castiliae oratorem. Primum quidem secessionem hanc dicet esse vitandam, quantum fieri potest, propter schismatis scandalum: verum post longam disputationem, tandem his verbis sententiam suam profert: Quando sacer princeps contra sancto-rum Patrum statuta aliquid praesumit, ubi non constat, cum ex causa utilitatis, aut necessitatis motus, sed ex aliqua particulari indigna causa; tunc ipse in priora Petri mandata offendit, exiens vires potestatis suae, quapropter non esset inconveniens, si pertinaciter in hoc persisteret, ab eo recedi posse per Ecclesiam. Haec Cusanus.
units.tr: When our Robert Grosseteste, Bishop of Lincoln, once resisted the impious provisions of the Roman Pontiff, the Pope, not containing himself for anger, says Matthew Paris, seemed about to take some more serious step against the bishop. But, as the same author relates, the Cardinals gave the Lord Pope counsel that he should let all these things pass with eyes winked at, under pretence of not noticing, so that no tumult might be stirred up over this, chiefly because it was known that a secession would someday come. So far he. These things were written long before the times of Martin Luther. The Cardinals therefore feared that that bishop of Lincoln, outstanding for piety and learning, might begin this secession. Thus by their judgement it appears that the man who would first offer himself as leader and standard-bearer of this secession would be a notable person, excellent in piety and learning, such as Robert Grosseteste was then held to be. Concern about this secession occupied those who flourished most in learning and piety at the Council of Constance, as is clear from the writings of Cardinal Cusanus and John Gerson. Cusanus writes about this matter to Roderick of Trevino, orator of the King of Castile. At first he says this secession ought to be avoided as far as possible, because of the scandal of schism: but after a long discussion, at last he states his opinion in these words: When a holy prince presumes to do something against the statutes of the holy Fathers, where it is not evident that he acts from a motive of utility or necessity, but from some particular unworthy cause; then he himself offends against the former commands of Peter, going beyond the powers of his authority; wherefore it would not be inappropriate, if he persisted obstinately in this, that he might be withdrawn from by the Church. So Cusanus.

units.la: Ex quibus verbis constat, hanc disputatio-nem tum quidem in Ecclesia iactaram[?] fuisse, de secessione Ecclesiae ab iugo Rom. Pontificis. Itaq; Iohannes Gerson de eadem re scribens, testatur, plurimos viros bonos in ea rum fuisse sententia, quando gravissimum schisma Ecclesiam perturbasset, quod longo tempore duraverat, viuente iam Gersone; ut ex illo schismate opportunitatem arriperent, neam-plius Papa ad administrationem ac iurisdictionem Ecclesiae admitteretur: sed optimum futurum, si Ecclesiae status ad primitivae Ecclesiae conditionem reduceretur, ut Praesules singuli commissos sibi populos regerent, neque ratio ulla haberetur aut reservationum, aut exactionum, quas Romana Ecclesia introduxerat. Gersonis verba sunt hæc: Forte aliqui- bus videtur, quod expediens Ecclesiæ vniuer- sali, redire omnia ad pristinum starum[?] Eccle- siæ, seu illius, qui fuit tempore Apostolorum, quantum fieri congrue posset, ablectis talibus iurisdictionibus pro magna parte; quæreddi- derunt Ecclesiam totam brutalem & carna- lem, vel redeundum esset ad statum Ecclesiæ tempore beati Syluestri, & Gregorii, quando quilibet Prælatus demittebatur in sua iurif- dictione. Itaque idem Gerson sic libere pro- nuntiat in eo libro, quem inscripsit, de Au-feribilitate Papæ: Auferibilis est Papa per generale Concilium perpetuo, vel ad tempus, quoad ea omnia, quæ sunt iurisdictionis.
units.tr: From these words it is clear that this dispute was then indeed being raised in the Church, concerning the secession of the Church from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. Accordingly John Gerson, writing on the same matter, testifies that many good men were of this opinion when the most grievous schism had disturbed the Church, a schism which had lasted a long time, while Gerson was still alive; that they might seize the opportunity from that schism, so that the Pope would no longer be admitted to the administration and jurisdiction of the Church; but that it would be best if the state of the Church were restored to the condition of the primitive Church, so that the bishops each ruled the peoples committed to them, and no account were taken either of the reservations or of the exactions which the Roman Church had introduced. Gerson's words are these: "Perhaps it seems to some that it is expedient for the universal Church that everything be restored to the former state of the Church, or to that which existed in the time of the Apostles, as far as can suitably be done, with such jurisdictions largely removed; for they consider the whole Church to have become brutish and carnal, or that we must return to the state of the Church in the time of blessed Silvester and Gregory, when each prelate was left in his own jurisdiction." Accordingly the same Gerson pronounces thus freely in that book which he entitled On the Removability of the Pope: "The Pope can be removed by a general council, permanently or for a time, as regards all those things which belong to jurisdiction."

units.la: Nihil ergo nouum in Ecclesia fit; si hæc pars Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, quam ad Occiden- tem Dei prouidentia statuit, tandem aliquan- do illud perfecerit, quod diu antea cogitaue- rat, & de quo multum deliberauerat, vt se à iu- go Romani Pontificis subduceret. Nam plu- rimæ aliæ partes Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ad Ori- entem, & ad Austrum hanc Romanam tyran- nidem nunquam tulerunt. Pars autem hæc Ecclesiæ Catholicæ Occidentalis maxima est, & sine dubio nobilissima, quandoquidem quæcunque sacræ Scripturæ de Antichristo prædixerunt, hic impleta videamus. Secessi- mus igitur non ab Ecclesia Romana, sed à Romana Curia. Secessimus, vt diuino man- dato obtemperaremus. Deus enim iubet po- pulum suum è Mystica Babylone exire.
