Imo vero, qui hanc secessionem mandauerat, ipse potenti sua manu populum suum eduxit, vt, quod mandauit, ipse perficeret. In quo admirabilem Dei prouidentiam suspicimus & adoramus, qui Ecclesiam suam ita sub hac captiuitate exercuit, vt semper sibi reliquum fecerit. Vere igitur cum Esaia Propheta[?] exclamare possumus: Nisi Dominus exercituū reliquias nobis fecisset reliquias, vt tantillum[?], quasi Sodoma fuisse-mus, & similes Gomorrhae. Nam vera doctrina in fundamentalibus ab Ecclesiae exordio, ad Mart. Lutheri tempora, integra semper in mediis tenebris lucebat, vt neque ignis, neque gladijs, non vinculis, nō tormentis Pontificis, nō perfidia & errorib. fraterculorū extingui potuerit ignis hic e coelo missus. Quanquam enim nō semper eadē clarare[?] lucerer, atq; arderet, nunquam tamē est extinctus. At hoc solius diuinae prouidentiae beneficium agnoscimus, ꝗ in Ecclesia sua semper vigilans, per omnia secula quosdam resuscitauerit[?], qui veritate perfidia & superbia pontificia pene obruta, pene sepultam, studiose ac fideliter conseruarint; donec tandem veritas ipsa victrix velut effracto sepulchro resurgens, longe lateq; triumphare inciperet, quae diligentes se diligit, & conseruat, vt victores secum triumphare faciat.
units.tr: Nothing new therefore happens in the Church, if this part of the Catholic Church, which by the providence of God was established in the West, has at last accomplished that which it had long before contemplated, and about which it had deliberated much, namely to withdraw itself from the yoke of the Roman Pontiff. For many other parts of the Catholic Church in the East and in the South have never endured this Roman tyranny. Yet this part of the Western Catholic Church is the greatest and without doubt the most noble, since we see fulfilled here whatever the holy Scriptures foretold about Antichrist. We have seceded therefore not from the Church of Rome, but from the Roman Curia. We have seceded in order to obey the divine command. For God commands his people to come out of Mystical Babylon. Indeed he who had commanded this secession himself led his people out with his mighty hand, so that he himself might accomplish what he commanded. In this we marvel at and adore the admirable providence of God, who so exercised his Church under this captivity that he always left a remnant for himself. Truly, then, we can exclaim with the prophet Isaiah: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a remnant, we would have been as Sodom, and like Gomorrah." For the true doctrine in fundamentals, from the beginning of the Church down to the times of Martin Luther, always shone whole in the midst of darkness, so that this fire sent from heaven could be extinguished neither by fire, nor by swords, nor by chains, nor by the torments of the Pontiff, nor by the treachery and errors of the little friars. For although it did not always shine and burn with the same clarity, it was never extinguished. Yet we acknowledge this as a benefit of divine providence alone, which, ever watchful over his Church, through all ages raised up certain men who, when the truth had been almost overwhelmed and almost buried by Pontifical perfidy and pride, studiously and faithfully preserved it; until at last truth itself, victorious, rising as from a broken sepulchre, began to triumph far and wide, since he who loves and preserves those who love him makes them triumph with him as victors.

units.la: Ad eos[?] igitur, qui Ecclesiam nostra à Mart. Luthero exortam suggillare solent, coarguendos: Ecclesiae Catholicae consensum, & doctrinam integre conseruatam, tanquam ignem illum perpetuum, qui per omnes sacerdotum succesfiones in altari Dei ardere solebat, produci-mus. Et ne Aduersarii se lapsos, aut opiniones ipsorum à nobis confictas quærantur (quod quidem grauissimum crimen apud Pontificios familiare atq; usitatissimum invenimus) eorum errores verbis ipsorum primo loco præponemus. Prima igitur controuersia est de regula fidei, siue de sacris Scripturis, de quare sic docent Pontificii.
units.tr: Therefore, to those who are accustomed to disparage the Church that arose from Martin Luther, we must answer: we produce the consensus of the Catholic Church and its doctrine preserved whole, like that perpetual fire which through all the successions of priests used to burn on the altar of God. And lest our adversaries complain that we have fallen into error, or that their opinions have been invented by us (a most grievous charge, which we find to be familiar and very customary among the Papists), we shall first set down their errors in their own words. The first controversy, therefore, is concerning the rule of faith, or concerning the holy Scriptures; and concerning this the Papists teach as follows.

units.la: CAPUT II
units.tr: CHAPTER II

units.la: Quæstionis status succincte ponitur, & argumentum futuræ disputationis. THESES PONTIFICIÆ.
units.tr: The state of the question is briefly set out, together with the argument of the disputation to follow. THE PAPIST THESES.

units.la: Asserimus, in Scripturis non contineri expresse totam doctrinam necessariam, siue de fide, siue de moribus, & proinde præter verbum Dei scriptum requiri etiam verbum Dei non scriptum, id est, diuinas & Apostolicas traditiones. Bellarmin. lib. de verb. Dei non script. cap. 3.
units.tr: We assert that the whole doctrine necessary to be believed or practised is not expressly contained in Scripture, and that therefore, besides the written word of God, the unwritten word of God is also required, that is, divine and Apostolic traditions. Bellarmine, book on the unwritten word of God, chap. 3.

units.la: Omnes libros veteris & noui Testamenti, necnon traditiones ipsas, tum ad fidem, tum ad mores pertinentes, tanquam vel oretenus à Christo, vel à Spiritu sancto dictatas, & continua successione in Ecclesia Catholica conseruatas, pari pietatis affectu ac reve-rentia suscipit ac veneratur Tridentina Synodus. Concil. Trid. sess. 4 decret. 1.
units.tr: The Tridentine Synod receives and venerates all the books of the Old and New Testament, and likewise the traditions themselves, both those concerning faith and those concerning morals, as dictated either by Christ's own voice or by the Holy Spirit and preserved in the Catholic Church by continuous succession, with equal affection of piety and reverence. Council of Trent, session 4, decree 1.

units.la: Scriptura sine traditionibus nec fuerunt simpli-citer necessaria, nec sufficientes. Bellarmin. lib. de verb. Dei non script. cap. 4.
units.tr: Scripture without traditions was neither simply necessary nor sufficient. Bellarmine, book on the unwritten word of God, chap. 4.

units.la: Dico, Scripturam, etsi non sit facta praecipue, vt sit regula fidei, esse tamen regulam fidei, non totalem, sed partialem. Totalis enim regula fidei, est verbum Dei, siue reuelatio Dei Ecclesiae facta, quae diuiditur in duas regulas partiales, scripturam & traditionem.
units.tr: I say that Scripture, although it was not made chiefly to be the rule of faith, is nonetheless a rule of faith, not a complete one but a partial one. For the complete rule of faith is the word of God, or the revelation of God made to the Church, which is divided into two partial rules, Scripture and tradition.

units.la: Bellarm. ibid. cap. 12.
units.tr: Bellarmine, ibid., chap. 12.

units.la: Quæstiones de scripturis & traditionibus multas instituunt Pontifici, quæ profecto omnes, quia pendent ex illa controuersia, quæ regulam fidei pertractat, & Scripturarum perfectionem probat, hinc lucem accipiunt, & in huius controuersiæ explicatione illæ quodammodo definientur. Nam sine Scripturarum suggillatione traditionum humanarum autoritas in Ecclesia confirmari nunquam potuit. Sed si in Scripturas hominum calumnia semel permissa fuerit, aperitur statim fenestra, traditiones scilicet vel Apostolicas confingendi, & quicquid pro libidine fo[?]-mniantium arridet, quantumcunque Scripturis, & prioribus Patrum scriptis repugnet, Apostolica tamen traditio habebitur.
units.tr: The Papists raise many questions concerning Scripture and tradition. All of these, since they depend on that controversy which treats the rule of faith and proves the perfection of Scripture, receive their light from it, and in the explanation of this controversy they are in some measure settled. For the authority of human traditions could never be established in the Church without disparaging Scripture. But if once men's calumny is allowed against Scripture, a window is at once opened: the power to invent Apostolic traditions, and whatever pleases those who invent them at their whim, however much it conflicts with Scripture and with the earlier writings of the Fathers, will still be held to be an Apostolic tradition.

units.la: Cuius imperiosæ cæcitatis atq; impuden-tiæ luculentum testimonium continent ea, quæ in secunda Nicæna Synodo, de adoratione imaginum statuuntur: non enim erubuerunt Patres in eo Concilio illud figmentum, tum nuper in Ecclesia natum, inter Apostolicas traditiones numerare: sæpiusque verbis saltem contendunt, illud scilicet ab Apostolorum temporibus in Ecclesia fuisse visitatum.
units.tr: The clear evidence of this domineering blindness and impudence is found in what was decreed about the adoration of images at the Second Council of Nicaea. For the Fathers at that council were not ashamed to count that fiction, which had only lately arisen in the Church, among the Apostolic traditions; and they often contend, at least in words, that it had been practised in the Church from the times of the Apostles.

units.la: Quam Epiphanius disertissime, non de suo tantum seculo, sed de superioribus omnibus contrarium testetur. Scribit enim, se, quum forte per Palæstinam iter faceret, Ecclesiam intrasse, ut oraret; atque invenisse ibi velum pendens in foribus eiusdem Ecclesiæ tunc temporis atque depictum, habens imaginem quasi Christi, vel Sanctæ cuiusdam. Addit Epipha-nius, fuisse hoc contra autoritatem Scriptura-rum, contra religionem nostram, & scrupulo-sitatem fuisse indignam Ecclesia Christi. Hæc ille. Tanta tamen vecordia regnarit in hominibus, quibus Scripturarum simplicitas lordet[?], ut quæ terribili Scripturarum fulmine feriuntur, quæ Patrum iudicio contra autoritatem Scripturarum, contra religionem nostram, indigna Ecclesia Christi habentur: ea sub traditionum titulo revocare audeant, & veterum gigantum furorem imitantes Babylonis ruinas resarcire, & concussum superbiæ regnum reponere.
units.tr: Epiphanius most plainly testifies to the contrary, not only about his own century but about all earlier ones. He writes that when he happened to travel through Palestine he entered a church to pray, and found there a veil hanging across the doors of that church, painted at that time and bearing what looked like an image of Christ or of some saint. Epiphanius adds that this was against the authority of Scripture, against our religion, and was a thing unworthy of the Church of Christ, and that it was a matter of scruple. So far he. Yet such madness has reigned among men, to whom the plainness of Scripture is displeasing, that they dare to bring back under the title of tradition things which are struck by the terrible thunderbolt of Scripture and which, by the judgment of the Fathers, are held to be against the authority of Scripture, against our religion, and unworthy of the Church of Christ. Imitating the fury of the ancient giants, they set about repairing the ruins of Babylon and restoring the tottering kingdom of pride.

units.la: Quæstionem igitur inprimis necessariam hoc loco proponimus, de regula fidei: An praeter doctrinas & mysteria fidei, quæ in scripto Dei verbo continentur, alia sint ex traditione admittenda de fide? Nos, quia cum antiquis Patribus, tantummodo scripturis canonicis hanc ingenuam debemus servitutem, ut eas solas in summo autoritatis fastigio ponamus, quas iudicare omnino non audemus, sed secundum ipsas, de omnibus omnium aliorum scriptis & traditionibus liberè iudicamus; Quæstio-nem nem hanc sic tractandam instituimus: Primo ipsarum Scripturarum, hoc est, Dei, de suo verbo loquentis, vocem referemus. Reliqua ad Scripturas, tanquam ad Lydium [?] lapidem examinabimus. Itaque Ecclesiæ testimonium post Scripturas producemus, id est, antiquo-rum Patrum, ipsorumque adeo, qui in Ro-mana Ecclesia vixerunt, consensum obser-[?] uabimus. Interim vero respondebimus [?] ad obiectiones, quæ à Cardinali Bellarmino [?] ad-ducuntur. Deinde ex istis principiis, Scriptu-ratum, inquam, & Patrum consensu, Co-rollaria aduciemus de regula fidei, de iudi-ce controversiarum, & de traditionibus non scriptis. Postremo erroris originem ape-riemus.
units.tr: Therefore, the question which we put forward here, as necessary above all, concerning the rule of faith is this: Whether, besides the doctrines and mysteries of faith contained in the written word of God, other things are to be admitted from tradition as matters of faith? We, because together with the ancient Fathers we owe this sincere servitude only to the canonical Scriptures, namely that we place those alone at the summit of authority, which we dare not judge at all, but by which we freely judge all the writings and traditions of all others, have arranged to treat this question as follows. First, we shall bring forward the voice of Scripture itself, that is, of God speaking of his own word. The rest we shall test by the Scriptures, as by the Lydian touchstone. Then we shall bring forward the testimony of the Church after Scripture, that is, we shall observe the consensus of the ancient Fathers, and of those very men who lived in the Roman Church. Meanwhile we shall reply to the objections which are brought forward by Cardinal Bellarmine. Then, from these principles, namely the Scriptures and the consensus of the Fathers, I say, we shall draw corollaries concerning the rule of faith, the judge of controversies, and unwritten traditions. Lastly, we shall uncover the origin of the error.

units.la: De statu quæstionis non est opus, ut multis verbis disceptemus. Nam ex thesibus Pontifi-ciis, supra à nobis positis, constat, Adversarios in regula fidei una cum sacris Scripturis tradi-tiones etiam non scriptas ponere, quas vo-cant verbum Dei non scriptum. Nos ver-bum hoc Tridentinum, non scriptum, reici-mus, & fidei regulam docemus esse unicam Scripturas, si regulam plenariam intelligamus perfecte explicatam: sin vero regula summa-ria intelligatur, dicimus, Symbolum Apostolicum è sacris Scripturis desumptum, esse re-gulam fidei. Ita traditiones non scriptas, Pon-tificias, ab hac regula, sive totali, sive partia-li, omnino reiicimus. Unicam hanc fidei regulam, quam nos tenemus, eandem perperpetuo in Ecclesia permansisse affirmamus, nec mutatam ante Concilium Tridentinum. Et hanc regulam, dicimus, contineri in Ecclesiæ fundamento[?], per quod Ecclesia consistit, & ex quo optime cognoscitur: atque hinc semper antiquos Patres docuisse, & demon-strasse, se tenuisse Ecclesiam. Hinc nos etiam probamus, esse nos in Ecclesia Catholica, quia eandem regulam fidei cum Catholica tenemus. Ecclesiam autem nunc Romanam hinc probamus nec esse Ecclesiam Catholicam, nec cum Catholica communicare, postquam in Concilio Tridentino aliam regulam fidei excogitarint, aliud fundamentum posuerint.
units.tr: There is no need for us to argue at length about the state of the question. For it is clear from the Papist theses which we set down above that our opponents place in the rule of faith, alongside the holy Scriptures, unwritten traditions as well, which they call the unwritten word of God. We reject this Tridentine expression, "unwritten," and we teach that Scripture alone is the rule of faith, if we understand by rule the complete rule, perfectly set out; but if a summary rule is meant, we say that the Apostles' Creed, drawn from the holy Scriptures, is the rule of faith. Thus we entirely reject the Papist unwritten traditions from this rule, whether complete or partial. We affirm that this one rule of faith, which we hold, has remained the same in the Church forever, and was not changed before the Council of Trent. And we say that this rule is contained in the foundation of the Church, by which the Church stands and from which it is best recognised; and hence the ancient Fathers always taught and demonstrated that they held to the Church. Hence we also prove that we are in the Catholic Church, because we hold the same rule of faith as the Catholic Church. But we prove from this that the present Roman Church is neither the Catholic Church nor in communion with the Catholic Church, since after the Council of Trident they devised another rule of faith and laid down another foundation.

units.la: CAPVT III. E Scripturis ostenditur fundamentum & regula fidei, contra Tridentinos.
units.tr: CHAPTER III. From the Scriptures it is shown what the foundation and rule of faith is, against the Tridentines.

units.la: Scripturæ de Scripturis sic testantur{4}: Do-ctrina Dei integra est, restituens animam, testimonium Dei verax est, sapientiam afferens imperito. Quo loco Propheta Legem scriptam docet esse integram, veracem, perfectam, rectam, lætificantem cor, puram, illuminantem oculos. Atque hæc omnia ita docet Scripturas præstare, ut omnes alias creaturas ad hæc præstanda inefficaces esse demonstret. Quamvis cœli enarrent gloriam Dei, dies diem instituit, nox noctem: nihil tamen creatum potest animam lapsam in peccatum restirestituere, & lætificare cor; ( quod est regulæ morum ) sapientiam impartiri, & illustrare oculos ( quod est regulæ fidei ) præter vnicas Scripturas. {a}Quæcunque ante scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam ante scripta sunt, vt per tolerantiam & consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. Quæ verba Apostoli extant in modum scopuli, in quem impactum Bellarmini commentum dissilit. Nam scribit, {b}Scripturæ finem proprium & præcipuum non fuisse, vt esset regula fidei, sed vt esset commonitorium quoddam vtile. Hæc Bellarminus. At Apostolus Christi hunc Scripturarum finem proprium, & præcipuum, imo vnicum assignat, quum doce[?]ar, quæcunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta esse. Si omnis scriptura ad doctrinam nostram, tanquam ad suum finem scripta est, quod docet Apostolus, certe fides nostra, quæ ex doctrina nascitur & pascitur, hanc habet regulam, & hæc regula hunc habet finem. Nam fides ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Dei. Ac ne quis Tridentinum sophisma obiiciat Apostolo; fidem esse ex auditu, auditum per verbum Dei; verbum tamen Dei esse verbum etiam non scriptum in traditionibus: hanc vanilo-quentiam comprimit Apostolus, quum doctrinam nostram scripto verbo alliget, & verbum in hunc finem scriptum esse demonstret, vt esset regula doctrinæ, & proinde fidei nostræ: quia, quæcunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt. Vel, qui ausus erit contra Apostolum dicere, Scripturas non fuisse in hunc finem proprium & præcipuum conscriptas: oportuit illum alium nobis finem proprium & præcipuum è sacris literis demonstrasse; non autem ex Cardinalitio cerebro confictum protulisse. Num ita insaniunt isti, vt æquum esse putent, Ecclesiam Dei, contra diserta Apostoli verba, Cardinalis commentum suscipere debere?
units.tr: The Scriptures bear witness to themselves{4}: "The doctrine of the Lord is whole, restoring the soul; the testimony of the Lord is true, bringing wisdom to the unskilled." In this place the Prophet teaches that the written Law is whole, true, perfect, right, gladdening the heart, pure, and enlightening the eyes. He teaches that the Scriptures accomplish all these things, and he shows that all other creatures are powerless to accomplish them. Although the heavens declare the glory of God, and day unto day utters speech, and night unto night, yet nothing created can restore a soul fallen into sin and gladden the heart (which is the office of the rule of morals), or impart wisdom and enlighten the eyes (which is the office of the rule of faith), apart from the Scriptures alone. {a}"Whatever things were written before were written for our learning, that through the patience and comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope." These words of the Apostle stand like a rock against which Bellarmine's invention is dashed to pieces. For he writes that {b}the proper and chief purpose of Scripture was not that it should be a rule of faith, but that it should be a certain useful reminder. So Bellarmine. But the Apostle of Christ assigns this as the proper, chief, indeed the only purpose of the Scriptures, when he teaches that whatever things were written were written for our learning. If all Scripture is written for our learning, as the end to which it is directed, as the Apostle teaches, then certainly our faith, which is born and nourished from doctrine, has this rule, and this rule has this end. For "faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God." And lest anyone throw at the Apostle the Tridentine sophism, that faith comes from hearing, and hearing from the word of God, but that the word of God is also the word not written, found in traditions, the Apostle silences this empty chatter: he binds our teaching to the written word and shows that the word was written for this end, to be the rule of doctrine and therefore of our faith, because whatever things were written were written for our learning. Or, if anyone dares to say against the Apostle that the Scriptures were not written for this proper and chief end, he ought to have shown us from the sacred letters another proper and chief end, and not brought forward something invented from a Cardinal's brain. Are these men so mad that they think it fair that the Church of God should accept a Cardinal's invention against the plain words of the Apostle?

units.la: Sed videamus, quo tendat Cardinalis commentum: Scriptura finis proprius (inquit) & præcipuus non est, vt offet[?] regula fidei, sed vt esset commonitorium quoddam vtile, ad conseruandam, & fouendam doctrinam ex prædicatione acceptam. Hæc ille. Quærimus, unde sit hæc prædicatio? è solis Scripturis an etiam ex traditionibus? Si è solis Scripturis, sequitur, Scripturas esse regulam fidei completam, & conseruare doctrinam Ecclesiæ, quam vnicam prædicare debet Ecclesia. Sin ex traditionibus non scriptis, dicat Cardinalis, vbinam? in quo thesauro conseruata semper fuerit prædicatio illa? deinde, quid sit illud, quod hic prædicatur? At facile respondet, prædicatio illa, quæ in traditionibus non scriptis continetur, est Romani Pontificis primatus, Christi Vicarii potestas, continetur autem non in Scripturis expresse, sed in cerebro Papæ, qui errare non potest, dum hanc potestatem è Scripturis deducit. Nam hæc est illa Helena, pro qua obtinenda, hoc bellum contra sacras Scripturas excitatur.
units.tr: But let us see where the Cardinal's invention tends: "The proper and chief end of Scripture (he says) is not that it should be the rule of faith, but that it should be a certain useful reminder for preserving and fostering the doctrine received from preaching." So he. We ask: whence comes this preaching? From the Scriptures alone, or also from traditions? If from the Scriptures alone, it follows that the Scriptures are the complete rule of faith, and that they preserve the doctrine of the Church, which the Church ought to preach alone. But if it comes from unwritten traditions, let the Cardinal say where? In what storehouse has that preaching always been kept? Then, what is that which is preached here? He readily answers that the preaching which is contained in unwritten traditions is the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, the power of Christ's Vicar; and this is contained not expressly in the Scriptures, but in the brain of the Pope, who cannot err while he deduces this power from the Scriptures. For this is that Helen, for the winning of whom this war against the holy Scriptures has been stirred up.

units.la: Respondeant Tridentini Christo & Ecclesiæ. fiæ. In prædicatione Ecclesiæ quid quæritur? quis est huius instituti finis proprius & præcipuus? Christusne? an Antichristus? Sacræ Scripturæ unum nobis finem prædicationis, Iesum Christum demonstrant; præterea vullum. Nam fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id, quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. 4 Hoc autem fundamentum{a} appellat Apostolus Prophetarum & Apostolorum. Fundamentum ergo est Iesus Christus, quia solus Christus prædicatur; idemq; dicitur fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quia è solis scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis Iesus Christus prædicatur. Quæris fidem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ? Fundamentum hoc demonstrabit. Quæris in hoc fundamento finem prædicationis? Respondet Apostolus: Est Iesus Christus. Prædicatio igitur illa, quæ fundamentum tenet, deducit Ecclesiam sine errore ad veram Christi fidem. Quæris regulam huius fidei? In fundamento invenies. Nam fundamentum dicitur Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quia scriptura Prophetica & Apostolica est regula huius fidei. Quid Tridentini ad hæc? Distrumpamus vincula eorum, & proiiciamus à nobis iugum eorum, hæc intus sibi canunt [?]. Num negabunt finem prædicationis proprium, præcipuum, unicum esse Iesum Christum? At Apostoli verba saluberrima [?] sunt, manifestissima sunt; nemo potest aliud fundamentum ponere, præter id, quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Num negabunt, sacras ScriScripturas continere hanc regulam fidei? At Apostolus in eo non est minus disertus. Dicat omnis Tridentina cohors, quare idem fundamentum dicitur Iesus Christus, idem etiam dicitur fundamentum Prophetarum & Apostolorum, cuius angularis lapis est Iesus Christus: nisi quia unicum fundamentum sit Christus Iesus; unica fidei regula, sacra Scriptura?
units.tr: Let the Tridentines answer to Christ and to the Church. In the preaching of the Church what is sought? What is the proper and chief end of this office? Is it Christ, or Antichrist? The holy Scriptures show us one end of preaching, Jesus Christ, and no other. For "no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ." {a}The Apostle calls this foundation "of the Prophets and Apostles." Therefore Jesus Christ is the foundation, because Christ alone is preached; and the same is called the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, because Jesus Christ is preached from the Prophetic and Apostolic Scriptures alone. Do you ask for the faith of the Catholic Church? This foundation will show it. Do you ask for the end of preaching on this foundation? The Apostle answers: it is Jesus Christ. Therefore that preaching which holds the foundation leads the Church without error to the true faith of Christ. Do you ask for the rule of this faith? You will find it in the foundation. For it is called the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles because the Prophetic and Apostolic Scripture is the rule of this faith. What do the Tridentines say to this? "Let us break their bonds asunder and cast away their yoke from us," they sing among themselves. Will they deny that the proper, chief and only end of preaching is Jesus Christ? But the words of the Apostle are most wholesome and most plain: no one can lay any other foundation than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Will they deny that the holy Scriptures contain this rule of faith? But the Apostle is no less plain on this point. Let the whole Tridentine cohort say why the same foundation is called Jesus Christ, and the same is also called the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, whose chief cornerstone is Jesus Christ; unless it is because Christ Jesus is the one foundation, and holy Scripture the one rule of faith.

units.la: Neque vero hoc nobis sufficit, fundamentum hoc, id est, hunc prædicationis finem hanc fidei regulam nouisse: nisi firma etiam fide teneamus, quod firmissima autoritate docuit Apostolus, fundamentum hoc unicum esse, nec mutari posse: quia aliud fundamentum nemo potest ponere: qui vero mutat aliquid in fundamento, ponit aliud fundamentum.
units.tr: Nor is it enough for us to know that this foundation, that is, this end of preaching and this rule of faith, unless we also hold with a firm faith what the Apostle taught with the most firm authority: that this foundation is one and cannot be changed, because no one can lay another foundation; and whoever alters anything in the foundation lays another foundation.

units.la: Dicant iam nobis, quis ille sit, qui aliud fundamentum posuit? qui pro Christo, & sacris Scripturis, Papam nobis, & traditiones obtrudit. Dicunt, non se extrudere Christum, & Scripturas, sed una cum Christo in fundamento ponere vicarium Christi, & una cum Scripturis traditiones non scriptas locare. At hoc est ponere aliud fundamentum, si aliud quicquam præter Christum in fundamento, aliud quicquam præter sacras Scripturas in regula ponatur; Ecclesia ædificata est super hoc unicum fundamentum, per hanc unicam regulam. Et quia apud Tridentinos hæc fundamentalia mutantur, quibus Ecclesia Catholica semper constitit, & cognita fuit, sem-
units.tr: Let them now tell us who it is that has laid another foundation: who, in place of Christ and the holy Scriptures, thrusts upon us the Pope and traditions. They say that they do not thrust out Christ and the Scriptures, but that together with Christ they place in the foundation the Vicar of Christ, and together with the Scriptures they set unwritten traditions. But this is to lay another foundation, if anything other than Christ is put in the foundation, and anything other than the holy Scriptures is put in the rule. The Church has been built upon this one foundation, by this one rule. And because among the Tridentines these fundamental things are changed, on which the Catholic Church has always stood and by which it has been known, [...]

units.la: Cut-off fragments of the right printed page; the lines are truncated at the scan edge. per consistet, & cognoscetur vsque ad finem seculi, dicimus, Ecclesiam, quæ quondam Romana fuerat, degenerasse primum in Romanam Curiam, postremo in Antichristi cathedram, & Satanæ synagogam. Iam in Scripturis pergamus.
units.tr: ...will remain and be known until the end of the age. We say that the Church, which once was Roman, has degenerated first into the Roman Curia, and at last into the chair of Antichrist and the synagogue of Satan. Now let us go on to the Scriptures.

units.la: {a}Nonne propterea erratis, quod non sciatis Scripturas, neq; potentiam Dei? Ergo error & hæresis ex Scripturarum ignorantia prorumpit; sicut ex earum notitia, fides, spes, patientia, consolatio. {b}Scrutamini Scripturas, quia vos [?]videmini vobis, in ipsis vitam æternam habere, & illæ sunt, quæ testantur de me. Ergo Iesus Christus, & veritas, quæ in illo est, ex Scripturarum testimonio perfecte innotescit: & pejores inventi sunt Pontificii Iudæis ipsis, qui vitæ æternæ cognitionem Scripturis solis tribuebant: quum enim sibi viderentur vitam æternam in Scripturis habuisse, constat profecto, Iudæos plenitudinem Scripturarum ad vitam æternam agnouisse, atque in eo à Christo probatos: quam quum Pontificii non agnoscant, atrocioris damnationis iudicium expectent necesse est.
units.tr: {a}"Do you not therefore err, because you do not know the Scriptures, nor the power of God?" Therefore error and heresy break forth from ignorance of the Scriptures, just as faith, hope, patience and comfort come from knowing them. {b}"Search the Scriptures, for in them you think you have eternal life, and they are those which testify of me." Therefore Jesus Christ, and the truth which is in him, is perfectly made known from the testimony of the Scriptures; and the Papists have been found worse than the Jews themselves, who ascribed the knowledge of eternal life to the Scriptures alone. For since they seemed to themselves to have eternal life in the Scriptures, it is certain that the Jews acknowledged the fullness of the Scriptures for eternal life, and were on this point approved by Christ. Since the Papists do not acknowledge this, they must necessarily expect a judgment of more terrible damnation.

units.la: CAPUT IV. Idem ostenditur ex aliis scripturis, & obiectiones refutantur.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV. The same is shown from other Scriptures, and objections are refuted.

units.la: PRoferamus etiam alias Scripturas, eandem fidei regulam demonstrantes, & Aduersariorum aduersus veritatem collusiones obseruemus. {c}Licet nos, vel Angelus de cœlo euaneuangelizet vobis praeterquam euangelizauimus, a-nathema sit. Ergo praeter doctrinam Euangeli-cā quam ab Apostolis accepimus, nō est aliud verbū non scriptū suscipiendum in Ecclesia.
units.tr: Let us also bring forward other Scriptures, which demonstrate the same rule of faith, and observe the conspiracies of our opponents against the truth. "Though we, or an angel from heaven, preach to you anything other than what we have preached to you, let him be accursed" (Gal. 1). Therefore, besides the evangelical doctrine which we received from the Apostles, no other unwritten word is to be received in the Church.

units.la: Qui ad malam causam agenda conducun-tur, multas officias excitare solent, vt animos hominum atque aliqua a veritate auertant. Quas artes egregie exercet Cardinalis Bellarminus. Multa enim excogitat, vt hæc Apostoli verba eludat. Duplicem adfert solutionem, vtramq; votar[?] solidam. Prior est, quod Apostolus non loquatur de solo verbo scripto, sed de omni verbo, siue scripto, siue tradito. Hoc adfert, vt probet, omne verbum Dei non esse scriptum, sed traditiones Romanæ Ecclesiæ, quamuis non scriptas, esse verbum Dei.
units.tr: Those who are hired to defend a bad cause usually raise many tricks to distract men's minds and turn them away from the truth. Cardinal Bellarmine practises these arts with particular skill. For he devises many things in order to evade these words of the Apostle. He offers a double solution, both of which he calls solid. The first is that the Apostle is not speaking only of the written word, but of every word, whether written or handed down. He adduces this in order to prove that the whole word of God is not written, but that the traditions of the Roman Church, although unwritten, are the word of God.

units.la: Respondeo: Nugacissimum esse disputato-rem, qui semper sumit id, q; est in controuersia. Hæc est ipsa cōtrouersia: An traditiones non scriptæ sint verbū Dei. Affirmant Tridentini: ante Tridentinos nemo. Vnus ipsius Bellarmini testimonium addā[?] vt verinaris[?] extortum, quo finum[?] hoc commentū valide conuellit. Verba sunt huiusmodi: {a}Nihil est de fide, nisi quod Deus per Apostolos & Prophetas reuelauit, aut quod euidenter inde deducitur. Non enim nouis reuelationibus nunc regitur Ecclesia, sed in iis permanet, quæ tradiderunt illi, qui ministrii fuerunt sermonis, & propterea dicitur Eph.2. Ædificati super fundamentum Apostolorum & Prophetarum. Hæc Bellarminus. Quid potuit à quoquam disertius dici, vel contra traditiones non scriptas, vel pro regula fidei
units.tr: I answer: it is a most trifling disputant who always assumes what is in controversy. This is the very controversy: whether unwritten traditions are the word of God. The Tridentines affirm it; before the Tridentines, no one did. I will add the testimony of Bellarmine himself, wrung from him as it were against his will, which thoroughly overturns this contrivance. His words are these: Nothing is of faith, unless it is what God has revealed through the Apostles and Prophets, or what is evidently deduced from it. For the Church is not now governed by new revelations, but remains in those things which were delivered by those who were ministers of the word; and therefore it is said, Eph. 2: Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets. Thus Bellarmine. What could have been said more clearly by anyone, either against unwritten traditions or for the rule of faith

units.la: tri fuerunt sermonis. Constat igitur, hoc verbum non scriptum esse vanissimum commentum, quod nunquam agnouere antiqui Patres; & quod verum esse, Pontificii ipsi nunquam induci possunt, ut credant. Deinde respondemus, haec Apostoli verba de verbo scripto esse intelligenda ex Patrum consensu; quem quia viderat Bellarminus, ideo ad alteram confugit responsionem.
units.tr: It is clear, therefore, that this unwritten word is a most empty invention, which the ancient Fathers never recognised, and which the Papists themselves can never be induced to believe is true. Next, we reply that these words of the Apostle are to be understood of the written word, according to the consensus of the Fathers; and because Bellarmine saw this, he fled to another answer.

units.la: Altera, inquit, soluitur esse: Paulus anathema denuntiat evangelizanti praeter id, quod evangelizavit: Praeter Apostolum intelligit, contra: & proinde non prohibet nova dogmata & praecepta, modo non sint contraria iam tradita. Haec ille. Si tanta improbitas in sacris literis exponendis ferenda sit, quid iam integrum, quid sanctum atque inviolatum in Scripturis habe-
units.tr: The second answer, he says, is this: Paul pronounces anathema on anyone who preaches beside what he has preached. He understands "beside" to mean "against," and therefore he does not forbid new doctrines and precepts, provided they are not contrary to what has already been handed down. So he says. If such shamelessness must be tolerated in expounding the sacred letters, what in the Scriptures remains whole, holy and inviolate? What has been left untouched by these mockers?

units.la: habemus? quid ab istis irrisoribus intactum? Dicat Bellarminus eodem spiritu, quum scriptum fit: a Videte,quod ego sum[?], ego,inquam,& non est Deus praeter me. Respondeat, inquam, hic Pontificius commentator, illud, praeter me, significare, contra me: & proinde non prohiberi nouos Deos, modo non sint contrarii Deo vero. Si haec in manifestis Scripturis distorquendis impudentia non fit ferenda, Cardinalis commentum stare non potest. Nam par est plane atque eadem ratio vtriufq; commenti, quia par est atque eadem ratio vtriufq; praecepti: Nullus Deus, praeter Deum verum: Nullum Dei verbum, praeter verbum in Euangelio scriptum. Ex hoc intelligimus, quid metuendum fit ab istorum audacia atque impudentia, quia Papa conducti, ad Scripturas exponendas veniunt. In quibus impletum videmus, quod scriptum est: Ipsi acceptâ pecuniâ, dixerunt sicut erant edocti.
units.tr: Let Bellarmine say in the same spirit, when it is written: "See that I, I am he, and there is no God besides me." Let this Papist commentator answer, I say, that "besides me" means "against me," and so new gods are not forbidden, provided they are not contrary to the true God. If such impudence in distorting plain Scriptures is not to be tolerated, the Cardinal's invention cannot stand. For the reasoning for each invention is plainly the same as the reasoning for each precept: no God besides the true God; no word of God besides the word written in the Gospel. From this we understand what is to be feared from the audacity and impudence of these men, since Papists hired for the purpose come to expound the Scriptures. In them we see fulfilled what is written: "They, having received money, said what they had been taught."

units.la: Bellarminus tamen hanc suam inuerecundem expositionem variis modis confirmare tentat, vt praeter, fit contra. Patet hoc, inquit, primo, quia Apostolus ipse multa alia posteà docuit. Respondeo: Apostolum, scimus, alia docuisse, quoad numerum librorum, aut verborum, sed nihil praeter Euangelium traditum, non aliud Euangelium. Docet autem idem Apostolus, quicquid fit praeter Euangelium iam traditum, hoc esse aliud Euangelium. Oportuit ergo Sophistam vel tacuisse, vel ostendisse, Apostolum aliquid postea docuisse praeter EuanEu[?] no[?] nil[?] do f[?] liu[?] din[?] vnu[?] num[?] uer[?] ten[?] lio[?] per[?] inu[?] pof[?] ver[?] hæc[?] Sed[?] exp[?] baon[?] esse[?] con[?] digu[?] capt[?] cere[?] leis[?] prae[?] pof[?] esse[?] sunt[?] ang[?] ang[?] Euangelium. Respondemus igitur Bellarmi-no, quod Chrysostomus respondet Marcio-nitis: {a}Similes sint scriptores, qui scribunt, me-do scribant eadem, multa illa vnicum esse Euangelium: nec, quicquam obstare scribentium multitudinem, quo minus vnum sit Euangelium. Vt enim vnum sit Euangelium, aut non vnum, non æstimatur numero scribentium: sed hinc, eademne sint, an diuersa, quæ scribuntur. Hæc ille. In eandem sententiam Theodoretus: {b}Hæc relicto Euangelio, non aliud inuenieta. Non enim alia per nos, alia per Apostolos prædicat Dominus, sed idem prædicamus omnes, qui sumus amatores veritatis. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Nevertheless Bellarmine tries to confirm this shameless exposition of his in various ways, so that "besides" means "against." "This is shown," he says, "first, because the Apostle himself later taught many other things." I reply: we know that the Apostle taught other things, as to the number of books or words, but nothing beside the Gospel delivered, and not another Gospel. But the same Apostle teaches that whatever is beside the Gospel already delivered is another Gospel. The Sophist therefore ought either to have kept silent, or to have shown that the Apostle afterwards taught something beside the Gospel, which would be a different Gospel. We therefore answer Bellarmine as Chrysostom answers the Marcionites: {a}Let there be writers who write, provided they write the same things; the number of writers does not prevent there being one Gospel. For whether the Gospel is one or not is not judged by the number of writers, but by whether what is written is the same or different. So he. To the same effect Theodoret: {b}These men, having left the Gospel, found nothing else. For the Lord does not preach one thing through us and another through the Apostles, but all of us who love the truth preach the same. So he.

units.la: Itaque non bene respondet, qui dicit, Apostolum alia docuisse, quoad librorum aut verborum numerum; nisi probauerit, alia hæc esse diuersa ab iis, quæ iam tradita sunt.
units.tr: Therefore he does not answer well who says that the Apostle taught other things as to the number of books or words, unless he proves that these other things are different from those already handed down.

units.la: Sed pergit Bellarminus: Secundo patet, inquit, ex proposito Apostoli, agit enim contra eos, qui docebant, seruanda esse legalia, quum ipse docuisset, non esse seruanda. Igitur cum dicit præter, intelligit contra. Hæc ille. Num quis est otii sui ita prodigus, vt has nugas scribat, nisi qui præiudicia captat? Nec nos in istis refutandis moras faceremus, nisi propter incautas animas, quas ille istis aranearum telis irretire tentat. Probat, præter, esse hoc loco, contra. Quare? Quia Apostolus agit contra eos, qui docebant, legalia esse seruanda. At quærimus, quare legalia non sunt seruanda? Profecto quia sunt præter Euangelium. Quod ergo non continetur in Euangelio, & quod est præter Euangelium, & quod est aliud Euangelium; hæc omnia Apo-stolo sunt [illegible, ~2 words]. Et verum est, quicquid fit præter Euangelium, illud contra esse. Sicut enim Christus docuit: {a}Qui non est mecum, contra me est, & qui non congregat mecum, spargit. Sic in iis omnibus, quæ sunt de fide, verissi-mum est, quæcunq; non continentur in Scri-pturis, esse contra Scripturas. Et sicut Christus Dominus alibi dixerat: {b}Qui non est contra nos, est pro nobis. Ita in iis omnibus, quæ sunt ἀδιάφορα[?], in ritibus externis positâ, verissimum est, quod non prohibetur in Scripturis, non esse contra Scripturas.
units.tr: But Bellarmine goes on: "Secondly, it is clear, he says, from the Apostle's purpose; for he argues against those who taught that legal observances must be kept, when he himself had taught that they need not be kept. Therefore when he says 'besides,' he means 'against.'" So he says. Who is so prodigal of his leisure as to write such trifles, unless one who seizes upon prejudices? We would not waste time refuting these things, except for the unwary souls whom he tries to ensnare in these spiders' webs. He proves that "besides" here means "against." Why? Because the Apostle argues against those who taught that legal observances must be kept. But we ask, why are legal observances not to be kept? Surely because they are beside the Gospel. Therefore what is not contained in the Gospel, what is beside the Gospel, and what is another Gospel, are all, to the Apostle, [illegible]. And it is true that whatever is beside the Gospel is against it. For as Christ taught: {a}"He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters." So in all those things which pertain to faith, it is most true that whatever is not contained in the Scriptures is against the Scriptures. And as Christ the Lord said elsewhere: {b}"He who is not against us is for us." So in all those things which are indifferent [ἀδιάφορα], placed in external rites, it is most true that what is not forbidden in the Scriptures is not against the Scriptures.

units.la: Quoties igitur quæstio est de regula fidei, certum est, quicquid diversum fit à regula, esse contra regulam. Itaque nihil ineptius cogitari potuit, quam quod respondet Sophista noster, præter significare contra: ac proinde non prohiberi noua dogmata, ac præcepta, modo non sint contraria iam traditis. Nam omnia noua dogmata de fide sunt contra regulam fidei, quia sunt præter regulam. Quia, sicut Bellarminus ipse conuictus, veritatis vi fatetur: Nihil est de fide, quod non evidenter habetur in Scripturis, quia Ecclesia in iis permanet, quæ tradita sunt ab iis, qui fuerunt ministri sermonis. Quæramus igitur, quodnam sit illud verbum, quod tu ex Tridentino præscripto non scriptum vocas? Quo fit, ut Bellarminus alius atque alius nobis prodeat, tanquam Proteus? Vnus Bellarminus, qui docet, nihil esse de fide, nisi quod Deus per Prophetas & Apostolos revelavit, aut evidenter inde deducitur, quia novis revelationibus non regitur Ecclesia: alius autem Bellarminus, qui docuit, totam doctrinam necessariam de fide, non contineri expresse in Scripturis, ac proinde requiri etiam verbum non scriptum in traditionibus. At si traditiones illae non scriptae, sint de fide, & in Scripturis non continentur: sequitur certe, Ecclesiam nunc regi novis revelationibus. Nam novum est de fide, quicquid nec expresse in Scripturis continetur, nec evidenter inde deducitur, iudice vel ipso Bellarmino.
units.tr: Whenever, therefore, the question concerns the rule of faith, it is certain that whatever differs from the rule is against the rule. Hence nothing more absurd could be thought of than what our Sophist answers: that "besides" means "against," and so new doctrines and precepts are not forbidden, provided they are not contrary to what has already been handed down. For all new doctrines of faith are against the rule of faith, because they are beside the rule. For, as Bellarmine himself, convicted by the force of truth, admits: nothing is of faith which is not evidently contained in the Scriptures, since the Church remains in those things which were handed down by those who were ministers of the word. Let us ask, then, what is that unwritten word which you call unwritten, following the Tridentine prescription? Why does Bellarmine come forward to us now as one man and now as another, like Proteus? One Bellarmine teaches that nothing is of faith except what God revealed through the Prophets and Apostles, or what is evidently deduced from it, because the Church is not ruled by new revelations. Another Bellarmine taught that the whole necessary doctrine of faith is not expressly contained in the Scriptures, and so an unwritten word is also required in traditions. But if those unwritten traditions are of faith and are not contained in the Scriptures, it certainly follows that the Church is now ruled by new revelations. For whatever is not expressly contained in the Scriptures, nor evidently deduced from them, is new, by the judgment of Bellarmine himself.

units.la: Pergit tamen strenue. Tertio, inquit, hoc patet ex aliquibus locis, vbi Apostolus vtitur voce, praeter Nam Rom. primo: Obstringuntur, inquit, eos, qui dissensiones & offendicula, praeter doctrinam, quam acceperunt, faciunt. Quae loco adito clarum est aliud, praeter significare contra, vt Erasmus vertit, contra. In Graeco autem loco eodem est vox Graeca, [illegible, ~4 letters]. Haec illa.
units.tr: He presses on vigorously still. "Thirdly," he says, "this is clear from some passages where the Apostle uses the word 'besides'. For in Romans (chapter 16?) he says: 'They are to be warned, he says, who make dissensions and stumbling-blocks besides the doctrine which you have received.' In that passage it is clear that besides means against, as Erasmus translates it, against." In the Greek passage the same word is used, [illegible]. So he says.

units.la: Respondeo: Si demus, Erasmum alicubi vertisse, [illegible, ~4 letters], contra, nihil ex eo causae Bellarmini adiuvatur. Mirum est, Bellarminum Erasmum nobis obiecisse, quum Bezam etiam potuisset. Nam & Beza eodem loco [illegible, ~4 letters] vertit, contra. Recte utrumque, si sensum ipsorum, non verba vertisse. Illud enim tanquam rem certam, de qua constat inter Christianos, sumunt: Quicquid sit praeter doctrinam Apostolicam, esse contra eandem doctrinam; quia nihil potest esse præter regulam, aut paulum diuersum à regula; quod non sit contra regulam. Itaque Beza, qui vertit, [illegible, ~12 letters] contra doctrinam, sic sese exponit: {a}Significat Apostolum, quosdam pro disputandis autoribus habendi sint, qui nimirum aliquid quippiam docent ab Apostolica doctrina, quos alibi vocat [illegible, ~10 letters]. Hæc ille. Nugas igitur, & verborum lites imperitus vendere voluit, qui ex interpretibus eruere tentat; quod contra ipsorum mentem fuisse omnes norunt. At verus translatio habet, præter, & reliqui omnes Latini; de quibus nihil dicit.
units.tr: I reply: even if we grant that Erasmus somewhere translated the word as "against," nothing is gained thereby for Bellarmine's cause. It is strange that Bellarmine should have objected Erasmus to us, when he could have objected Beza too. For Beza also translates it in the same place as "against." Both are right, if they rendered the sense and not the words. For they take it as a settled matter, agreed among Christians, that whatever is beside apostolic doctrine is against that same doctrine; because nothing can be beside the rule, or differ slightly from the rule, without being against the rule. Thus Beza, who renders the phrase "against the doctrine," explains himself thus: {a}It signifies that the Apostle means certain men who are to be regarded as authors of disputes, who indeed teach something different from apostolic doctrine, whom he elsewhere calls [illegible]. So he says. Thus the unskilled man who tries to extract from the translators wished to sell trifles and wrangles over words, when all know that this was contrary to their meaning. But the true translation has "besides," as do all the other Latin versions, of which he says nothing.

units.la: Pergit adhuc: Quarto, inquit, idem patet ex Patrum expositione. S. Ambrosius exponit, si contra: Hieronymus, si aliter. Respondeo, quod Ambrosium adducit, nihil esse contra sententiam nostram. Nam Patres intelligunt, ea esse contra doctrinam Apostolicam, quæcunque in eadem non continentur, sicut deinceps probabimus. Quod Hieronymi verba adduxerit, mirum videtur. Nam qui dicit, contra doctrinam Apostolicam esse, quicquid aliter doceatur, sententiam Pontificiam plane diffi-pat, quia Pontificii noua dogmata de fide inducunt, quæ volunt esse diuersa à iam traditis, non tamen contraria. Eiusdem est insaniæ, quod sic addit: Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, & Theophylactus dicunt, Apostolum non dixisse, si contraria, sed, si præterquam quod, &c. ut indicarent, non solum eos anathematizari, qui aperte contraria toti doctrinæ docent, sed etiam eos, qui quomodocunque docunducunque, siue aperte, siue oblique quicquid labefa- ctant[?] ex doctrina tradita. Hæc Bellarminus.
units.tr: He goes on: Fourth, he says, the same appears from the exposition of the Fathers. S. Ambrose expounds "if against," Jerome "if otherwise." I reply that what he adduces from Ambrose is nothing against our position. For the Fathers understood that whatever is not contained in the Apostolic doctrine is against it, as we shall prove below. That he cited the words of Jerome is surprising. For whoever says that whatever is taught otherwise is against Apostolic doctrine plainly overthrows the Papist position, since the Papists introduce new dogmas of faith which they want to be different from those already handed down, though not contrary to them. It is the same madness that he adds: Chrysostom, Oecumenius and Theophylact say that the Apostle did not say "if contrary," but "if beside what," etc., so that they might show that not only are those anathematized who teach things openly contrary to the whole doctrine, but also those who in any way, whether openly or obliquely, weaken anything from the doctrine handed down. So says Bellarmine.

units.la: Num quis existimare potest, hunc hominem ex animo loqui, aut serio de his rebus cogitasse, qui non erubuit Patrum verba ad sententiam suam confirmandam producere, quæ causam ipsam jugulant, quam illi confirmare voluit. Anathema dicit Apostolus euangelizanti præter id, quod accepimus. Bellarminus ait, præter hic intelligi contra. At Patres ab eo producti clamant magno consensu: Apostolum non dicere, qui contraria annuntiauerint, sed qui aliquid vel oblique labefactant, hoc anathemate perstringi. Num quid apertius? Præter ergo, ex eorum consensu, non est tantum contra Euangelium, sed & præter Euangelium; quia, judice Bellarmino, hoc anathemate feriuntur, non tantum qui contra Euangelium, sed etiam, qui paulo aliter docent.
units.tr: Can anyone suppose that this man spoke sincerely, or thought seriously about these matters, when he was not ashamed to produce the words of the Fathers in support of his view, words which cut the throat of the very cause he wanted to defend? The Apostle says, "Let him be anathema who preaches to you beside what we have received." Bellarmine says that beside here means against. But the Fathers he cites cry out with one voice that the Apostle does not mean those who preach contrary things, but that those who weaken anything, even obliquely, are struck by this anathema. Can anything be plainer? So by their consensus, beside means not only against the Gospel but also beside the Gospel, since, in Bellarmine's judgment, those are struck by this anathema not only who teach against the Gospel but also who teach even slightly differently.

units.la: Eâdem[?] fronte Basilium & Augustinum adducit. S. Basilius Moral. 72. cap. 1[?] docet, ex hoc loco haberi, eos recipiendos, qui consona Scripturis tradunt, eos reiiciendos, qui aliena.
units.tr: With the same brazenness he cites Basil and Augustine. S. Basil, in Moral. 72, chapter 1, teaches that from this passage it is to be concluded that those who hand down things consonant with the Scriptures are to be received, and those who hand down things alien to them are to be rejected.

units.la: Respondeo: S. Basilius probat, Pontificios el-se homines profanos, qui ea de fide tradere audeant, quæ Scripturis non sunt consona, sed aliena. Mirificus videtur thaumaturgus, qui ex his verbis probabit, nova dogmata esse recipienda, quæ aliena sunt, non autem consona Scripturis. Sed Augustinum audiamus: Augustinus, inquit Bellarminus, lib. 17. contra Faustum, cap. 3. exponit, contra. Et tract. 89. in lohannem sic loquitur. Non ait, plus quam accepisti, sed praeterquam quod accepistis. Nam illud dicere, sibi ipsi praeiudicaret, [illegible, ~8 letters] ad Thessalonicenses, ut supplerent, quae illorum fidei defuerant. Sed qui supplet, quod minus erat, addit non, quod inerat, tollit. Qui autem praetergreditur regulam fidei, non accedit in via, sed recedit de via. Haec Augustinus.
units.tr: I reply: S. Basil proves that the Papists are profane men, who dare to hand down articles of faith that are not consonant with the Scriptures but alien to them. The wonder-worker seems a marvellous witness if from these words he proves that new dogmas which are alien to the Scriptures, and not consonant with them, are to be received. But let us hear Augustine: Augustine, says Bellarmine, in book 17 against Faustus, chapter 3, expounds it as against. And in tractate 89 on John he speaks thus: "He does not say, more than you have received, but beside what you have received. For to say that would prejudge himself ..." [here the text is corrupt; in the passage about the Thessalonians, that they should supply what was lacking to their faith]. "But he who supplies what was lacking adds, he does not remove what was there. But he who goes beyond the rule of faith does not come onto the way, but departs from the way." So Augustine.

units.la: Respondeo: Augustinum priore loco non exponere haec verba, ut praeter sit contra: neque unquam in animo Augustini aut cuiuspiam veterum venisse tale figmentum, ut diceret, praeter significare contra: sed indifferenter his vocibus utitur Augustinus, aliquè, ut praeter Euangelium, idem illis sit, quod contra Euangelium: quia nihil potest esse praeter regulam, quod non sit contra regulam. Alterum Augustini locum, quare adduxerit Sophista noster, non intelligo, nisi quia non potest erubescere. Nam qui supplet, quod minus erat, addit, non quod inerat, tollit. Quibus verbis refutat Augustinus vanitatem Pontificiorum, qui non verbis & explicationibus orthodoxis supplent, sed novo sensu mutant, & praetergrediuntur regulam fidei. Nam regula fidei est sacra Scriptura Augustino, sicut deinceps constabit. At hanc regulam in Concilio Tridentino mutarunt Pontifici, quum pro una parte huius regulae, traditiones suas substituerint. Quae Scriptura? Quis Patrum hanc regulae partem agnovit unquam?
units.tr: I reply: in the former passage Augustine does not explain these words so that beside means against. Nor did any such figment ever come into the mind of Augustine or of any of the ancients, that beside signifies against. Augustine uses these words indifferently, so that "beside the Gospel" means the same as "against the Gospel," because nothing can be beside the rule which is not against the rule. As for the other passage of Augustine, why our sophist cited it I do not understand, unless because he cannot blush. For whoever supplies what was lacking adds, he does not remove what was there. With these words Augustine refutes the vanity of the Papists, who do not supply by orthodox words and explanations, but change the sense by novelty, and go beyond the rule of faith. For the rule of faith, for Augustine, is holy Scripture, as will become clear below. But the Papist bishops in the Council of Trent changed this rule, when they put their own traditions in place of one part of it. Which Scripture? Which of the Fathers ever acknowledged this part of the rule?

units.la: Neque vero dissimulandum est, quod ex hoc loco, quem citauit Bellarminus, Augustinus quaedam habet contra causam Pontificiam, quae tamen dissimulatisse [?]. Sic enim scribit Augustinus: {a}Si quid intellexerit, quod non sit contra regulam fidei, ad quam, velut viam, ad patriam pervenisti, & sic intellexerit, ut inde dubitare omnino non audeat: adde aedificium, noli tamen relinquere fundamentum. Haec ille. Ponit Augustinus duo contra Pontificios. Primum, regulam fidei docet esse viam ad patriam, quam viam omnes antiqui ponunt in Scripturis. In traditionibus non scriptis nemo viam ad patriam fuisse docuit ante Concilium Tridentinum. Secundo docet Augustinus, universam Ecclesiæ doctrinam esse velut ædificium super fundamentum doctrinæ Propheticæ & Apostolicæ. Quod docuit etiam Apostolus: {b}Secundum gratiam Dei, quæ data est mihi, ut peritus architectus, fundamentum posui, alius autem superædificat. Porro quisque videat, quomodo superædificet. Nam fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere præter id, quod positum est, quod est IESVS CHRISTVS. Hoc autem fundamentum positum est à Prophetis & Apostolis, sicut idem Apostolus docet. {c}Fundamentum ergo Ecclesiæ est Ie-sus Christus, secundum doctrinam Propheticam & Apostolicam prædicatus. Quicunque ædificant Ecclesiam Dei, aliud docere non possunt, nec per aliam regulam ædificare. At Pontificii aliud fundamentum ponunt. Nam qui ad fundamentum Prophetarum tarum & Apostolorum, id est, ad fundamen-tum scriptum, aliud fundamentum non scri-ptum in traditionibus addiciunt, fundamen-tum mutant. Nec possunt Iesuitæ effugere, Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, praeter id, quod positum est per Prophetas & Apostolos, inquit Apostolus. Neque vero rabulæ isti respondere possunt, Apostolum, quum aliud fundamen-tum dixerat, intelligere non aliud quoduis, sed contrarium fundamentum. Nam hoc quid aliud esset, quam irrisio doctrinæ Apo-stolicæ? Quod tamen Cardinalis non minori inuerecūdia Apostolo obiicere potuit, quam quum dicit, praeter Euangelium, esse, contra Eu-angelium, ac proinde Apostolum non pro-hibere noua dogmata, modo non sint con-traria iam traditis. Et quid vetat, quo minus idem commentator sic excipiat Apostolum, vt dicat, aliud fundamentum nemo potest ponere, aliud, hoc loco intelligi contrarium: ac proinde Apostolum hoc loco non prohibere nouum fundamentum, modo non sit contra-rium iam posito. Hæc est sapientia Iesuita-rum, qui vel non intelligunt, vel intelligere nolunt, aliud fundamentum quodcunque es-se contrarium, & contra regulam esse, quic-quid est præter regulam. Ad alias Scripturas pergamus.
units.tr: Nor must it be concealed that from this passage which Bellarmine cited, Augustine has certain things against the Papist cause, which nevertheless they have dissembled. For Augustine writes thus: {a}If he has understood anything which is not against the rule of faith, to which you came as to a way, to the homeland, and has understood it so that he dares not doubt it at all: add the building, but do not leave the foundation. So he. Augustine sets down two things against the Papists. First, he teaches that the rule of faith is the way to the homeland, which way all the ancients locate in the Scriptures. No one before the Council of Trent taught that the way to the homeland lay in unwritten traditions. Second, Augustine teaches that the whole doctrine of the Church is like a building upon the foundation of prophetic and apostolic doctrine. The Apostle also taught this: {b}According to the grace of God which has been given to me, as a skilful architect I have laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is JESUS CHRIST. This foundation has been laid by the Prophets and Apostles, as the same Apostle teaches. {c}Therefore the foundation of the Church is Jesus Christ, preached according to the prophetic and apostolic doctrine. Whoever builds the Church of God cannot teach anything else, nor build by any other rule. But the Papists lay another foundation. For whoever adds to the foundation of the Prophets and Apostles, that is, to the written foundation, another unwritten foundation in traditions, changes the foundation. Nor can the Jesuits escape: No one can lay another foundation, besides that which has been laid through the Prophets and Apostles, says the Apostle. Nor can those wranglers reply that the Apostle, when he said "another foundation," meant not just any other, but a contrary foundation. For what would that be other than a mockery of apostolic doctrine? Yet the Cardinal could have objected this to the Apostle with no less shamelessness than when he says that beside the Gospel is against the Gospel, and so that the Apostle does not forbid new dogmas, provided they are not contrary to what has already been handed down. And what prevents the same commentator from so qualifying the Apostle as to say: no one can lay another foundation, "another" here to be understood as "contrary," and so the Apostle in this place does not forbid a new foundation, provided it is not contrary to the one already laid? This is the wisdom of the Jesuits, who either do not understand, or do not want to understand, that any other foundation is contrary, and that whatever is beside the rule is against the rule. Let us go on to other Scriptures.

units.la: Apostolus sollicitè hortatur eos, qui ad Ecclesiæ clauum sedent, prouidere, vt vna eademque doctrina semper in Ecclesia viuat; ac proinde denuntiare inferioribus doctoribus & pa mus diam prob cere, doct fa tr riam
units.tr: The Apostle earnestly urges those who sit at the helm of the Church to see to it that one and the same doctrine always lives on in the Church; and therefore to instruct the lesser teachers and pastors to test and prove the doctrine.

units.la: Iden doctr noftr doctr quaff diue conf riam uerf imp
units.tr: The same [Apostle] ... our doctrine ... of divine doctrine ... confirmed ... (the Latin is too garbled in the scan to render with certainty).

units.la: Nam dide acp
units.tr: For indeed, I [...]
