units.tr: From [...] he had learned [...] to the [...] Scripture, for [...] the [...]

units.la: Dei, crat lute ctri & pastoribus, μὴ [illegible, ~10 letters] Iam quæri-musab illis commentatoribus, vel in libris[?] diuinarum Scripturarum, quid illud sit, quod prohibetur, quum Apostolus vetat aliter docere, (ut vetus interpres habet) vel, ut omnis doctrina non contraria tantum, sed & diuersa tradatur? Quamquam verum sit, contrariam esse doctrinam, quæcunque diuersa sit. Idem repetit Apostolus: Si quis diuersam docet doctrinam, neq; acquiescit sanis sermonibus Domini nostri Iesu Christi, & ei, quæ secundum pietatem est doctrina, attinget, nihil sciens, sed insanum circa quæstiones, & verborum pugnas. Quibus verbis diuersa omnis doctrina prohibetur, quæ non consentit cum regula. Non igitur, qui contrariam tantum doctrinam inducunt, sed qui diuersam afferunt quamcunque, prohibitæ ἑτεροδιδασκαλίας crimine conuicti tenentur. Nam quicquid non est hoc ipsum, quod tradiderunt Prophetæ & Apostoli, illud est ψεῦδος[?], ac proinde prohibitum.
units.tr: ... of God, was taught ... pastors ... [Greek: μὴ ...] Here we may ask those commentators, either in the books of the divine Scriptures, what that is which is forbidden, when the Apostle forbids teaching otherwise (as the old translator has it), or that all doctrine be handed down not only contrary but also different? Although it is true that any doctrine which is different is contrary. The Apostle repeats the same: If anyone teaches a different doctrine, and does not consent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the doctrine which is according to godliness, he is puffed up, knowing nothing, but sick about questions and quarrels over words. By these words every different doctrine which does not agree with the rule is forbidden. Therefore not only those who introduce a contrary doctrine, but those who bring forward any different doctrine whatever, are held guilty of the forbidden crime of [ἑτεροδιδασκαλία]. For whatever is not that very thing which the Prophets and Apostles handed down is [ψεῦδος], and so forbidden.

units.la: Apostolus etiam sic docet: Maneto in iis, quæ didicisti &c. sciens, à quo didiceris, neq; à puero sacras literas nouisse, quæ te possunt sapientem reddere ad salutem, per fidem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Tota Scriptura diuinitus est inspirata, & utilis ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu, ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus. Si sacræ literæ possunt nos sapientes reddere ad salutem per fidem, certè expresse continent doctrinam salutis ac fidei. Quomodo enim sapientiam dare possunt de rebus, quas non expresse patefaciunt? Si vero sapientiae atque fidei credentium sit e sacris Scripturis petenda: quid aliud possunt Pontifici ex traditionibus suis non scriptis haurire, quam stultitiam illam, de qua Apostolus: Quum sapientes se professi sunt, stulti facti sunt. Si sacrae literae tantae perfectionis ac sufficientiae valeant, ut ad docendum, quae omnem fidei doctrinam continent, & confirmandum: 2. ad arguendum, quia omnes haereses & errores convellunt: 3. ad corrigendum, quia omnes morum pravitates corripiunt: 4. ad erudiendum, quia in pietatis[?] atq; obedientiae operibus perfecte erudiunt. Profecto extremae est caecitatis, atq; blasphemiae, sacras literas de imperfectione accusare, & Scripturis perfectionem suam addendam per traditiones, hoc est, Dei sapientiam per hominum stultitiam perficiendam iudicare. Si sacrae Scripturae perfectum sistunt hominem Dei, ad omne opus perfecte instructum: certe Scriptura non est partialis, sed totalis, copleta, & perfectissima regula fidei: quia homine Dei non ex parte tantum, sed plene & perfecte instituit ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructum. Deniq; si universa Scriptura est a Deo inspirata: traditiones autem partim ab hominibus excogitatae, partim a Diabolo per hypocrisin falsiloquorum subintroductae; sicut de traditionibus Pontificiis illis aperte praedixit Spiritus S. quibus matrimonium prohibent, & a ciborum quibusdam, religionis praetextu, abstinere iubent, quos Deus creauit [Left page, cut off at the scan edge; only word ends visible:] n ex- / ue fi- / ren- / rio- / ulri- / entes / tan- / l do- / ient, / ones / gen- / oiut: / lien- / o ex- / as li- / turis / ones, / riam / erfe- / per- / rtia- / gula / ium, / opus / ierfa / auté / im à / sub- / ficiis / atri- / reli- / Deus / eauit creauit ad participandum gratiarum actione ab iis, qui noverunt veritatem. Si, inquam, manifestum sit ex testimonio Spiritus S. in Apostolo loquentes Scripturas à Deo, traditiones illas Pontificias à Diabolo inspiratas esse: ecquae tandem Antichristi vox in Ecclesia unquam agnoscetur, si haec ... [illegible, ~12 letters] Scripturas ut imperfectas accusat, perficiendas autem suis traditionibus tradat? Quid Bellarminus ad haec? Multa commentitur, quibus Apostolum eludat.
units.tr: The Apostle also teaches this: Continue in the things you have learned, knowing from whom you learned them, and that from childhood you have known the sacred letters, which are able to make you wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction which is in Christ Jesus, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto all good works. If the sacred letters can make us wise unto salvation through faith, they certainly contain expressly the doctrine of salvation and of faith. For how can they give wisdom about things which they do not openly disclose? But if the wisdom and faith of believers is to be sought from the sacred Scriptures, what else can the Papists draw from their unwritten traditions but that folly of which the Apostle speaks: Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools? If the sacred letters are of such perfection and sufficiency that they (1) teach everything which contains the whole doctrine of faith, and confirm it; (2) refute, since they overthrow all heresies and errors; (3) correct, since they rebuke all moral corruptions; (4) instruct, since they perfectly train men in works of godliness and obedience, then surely it is the height of blindness and blasphemy to accuse the sacred letters of imperfection, and to judge that Scripture must be completed by traditions, that is, that the wisdom of God must be perfected by the folly of men. If the sacred Scriptures make the man of God perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work, then certainly Scripture is not partial but total, complete and most perfect rule of faith, since it instructs the man of God not partly but fully and perfectly, furnished for every good work. Finally, if all Scripture is inspired by God, but traditions are partly devised by men and partly secretly introduced by the Devil through the hypocrisy of liars, as the Holy Spirit clearly foretold concerning those Papist traditions which forbid marriage and command abstinence from certain foods under the pretext of religion, foods which God created to be partaken of with thanksgiving by those who know the truth [the left page is cut off at the scan edge, and much of this sentence is illegible]. If, I say, it is manifest from the testimony of the Holy Spirit speaking through the Apostle that the Scriptures are from God and those Papist traditions are inspired by the Devil, what voice of Antichrist will ever at last be recognised in the Church, if [illegible] accuses the Scriptures as imperfect and hands them over to be perfected by its own traditions? What does Bellarmine say to this? He invents many things by which he may elude the Apostle.

units.la: {a}Negat inde deduci, Scripturam sufficientem esse, quia vulgò dicitur, & sic deinde ratiocinatur: Si dicas, Scriptura utilis est ad hoc, sive huic habet usum, sive ad hoc refertur, & ornatur, sive quodlibet aliud simile, nunquam tamen significatur eam solam sufficere. Sicut enim, quoties cibus vitae est ad vivendum hominem, dicit quidem, cibum ad hoc esse institutum, vt nutriat, sed non dicit, sufficere solum cibum, nam si calor naturalis deficiat, aut aliquod infirmum corpus ad nutriendum nec sanum cibus non sufficit. Itaq; Apostolus non dicit, solam Scripturam sufficere ad doctrinam, argumentum, &c. & prorsus ad hominem perficiendum & absolvendum, sed tantum ad haec omnia profuisse & iuuare. Haec ille.
units.tr: He denies that it follows from this that Scripture is sufficient, because it is commonly said, and then reasons thus: "If you say that Scripture is useful for this, or has this use, or is referred and directed to this, or any other similar thing, you never thereby signify that it alone is sufficient. For just as whenever food is the life of a man for living, we say indeed that food is instituted for this, that it nourishes, but we do not say that food alone is sufficient; for if natural heat fails, or if the body is weak, food is not sufficient for nourishing even a healthy body. Therefore the Apostle does not say that Scripture alone is sufficient for doctrine, argument, etc., and altogether for perfecting and completing man, but only that it has profited and helps for all these things." So he says.

units.la: Credo equidem, si quis Daemonas loquentes audire potuisset, non aliter illos, quam Daemonas istas Tridentinos locutos esse. Nam quoties audio homines sacris Scripturis detrahentes, earum auctoritatem imminuentes, sufficientiam perstringentes, plenitudinem invidentes, figmenta hominum in eodem auctoritatis fastigio cum sacris Scripturis constituen-
units.tr: I believe indeed that if anyone could have heard demons speaking, they would have spoken no differently than these Tridentines do. For whenever I hear men who disparage the sacred Scriptures, who diminish their authority, who attack their sufficiency, who begrudge their completeness, and who set the fabrications of men on the same summit of authority as the sacred Scriptures,

units.la: cuentuentes ; non hominum , sed dæmonum vo-ces audire videor. In Ecclesia Dei huiusmodi voces ante Concilium Tridentinum, quas vnquam audiuit? Longe alia sunt voces Scripturarum & Patrum. Nobis sufficere videtur, si respondeamus, impias istas voces à nobis re-pudiari, quia antè istos nemo sic locutus est in Ecclesia.
units.tr: I seem to hear not the voices of men but of demons. In the Church of God, before the Council of Trent, when has anyone ever heard such voices? The voices of the Scriptures and of the Fathers are quite different. It seems enough for us to answer that we reject these impious voices, because no one spoke like this in the Church before them.

units.la: Sed videamus, qua ratione motus[?], voces suas contra vocem Dei attollere audeat. Audite, quomodo Apostolo obgannit[?]. Apostolus dicit, totam sacram Scripturam esse diuinitus inspiratam, & utilem ad docendum, arguendum, corrigendum, instituendum in iustitia, ut perfecta sit homo Dei ad omne opus bonum perfecte instru-ctus.[?] Audis Apostolum prædicantem Scripturarum sufficientiam, & perfectionem, ad perficiendum hominem Dei. Ab illo quære, quomodo Scriptura ita perfecta sit, vt hominem Dei reddat sine traditionibus non scriptis perfecte instructum ad omne opus bonum. Cardinalis Apostolum interroget, ab isto quærat, quod à nobis quæritur, & dicat: O tu, qui clamas, totam Scripturam diuinitus inspiratam, & utilem esse ad docendum, arguendum, corrigendum, instituendum, vt homo Dei perfectus sit ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus, quomodo hoc fieri potest? Nam siue dicas, Scriptura utilis est ad hoc, siue hunc habet usum, siue ad hoc referatur, & ordinatur, siue quidlibet aliud simile; nunquam tamen significabis, eam solam sufficere: nam cibus utilis est ad nutriendum, & tamen solus cibus non nutrit, & calor naturalis deficiat. Qui sic vocem suam contra vocem Apostoli obfirmat, certe non ille disputare, sed Apostolo oblatrare existimandus est.
units.tr: But let us see by what reasoning he dares to raise his voice against the voice of God. Listen to how he snarls at the Apostle. The Apostle says that all sacred Scripture is inspired by God, and profitable for teaching, for refuting, for correcting, for instructing in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto every good work. You hear the Apostle proclaiming the sufficiency and perfection of Scripture for perfecting the man of God. Ask him how Scripture is so perfect that it makes the man of God thoroughly furnished for every good work without unwritten traditions. Let the Cardinal question the Apostle; let him ask of him what is asked of us, and say: "O you who cry out that all Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching, refuting, correcting, instructing, so that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work, how can this be done?" For whether you say that Scripture is useful for this, or has this use, or is referred and directed to this, or any other similar thing, you will never signify that it alone is sufficient; for food is useful for nourishing, and yet food alone does not nourish, and natural heat fails. He who thus fortifies his voice against the voice of the Apostle is certainly to be thought not to dispute but to bark at the Apostle.

units.la: Quod vero Cardinalis dicit, non solum cibum nutrire, sed & calorem naturalem, quam futile sit, quis non videt? Verbum Dei dicitur cibus & panis, ex quo homo vivit. Est ergo, ut cibus ad vitam naturalem, sic sacra Scriptura ad vitam spiritualem. Cibus autem non nutrit sine calore naturali, nec Scriptura sine fide. Quis hoc negat? At quum solus cibus nutrire dicitur, non excluditur calor naturalis, qui per cibum, & una cum cibo operatur: sed omne illud, quod vel non est cibus, & tamen ventrem ingreditur, sicut medicamenta, aut venena: vel non nutriret, quamuis ingrederetur, ut lapides; vel omnino non ingreditur, quamuis aptum sit ad nutriendum. Nam cibus non potest nutrire, nisi sumptus. Itaque solus cibus nutrit: quia quod non est cibus, & tamen in ventrem sumitur, tanquam cibus, non potest nutrire. Sic dicimus, solam Scripturam sufficere, non ut fidem excludamus, sine qua ne Scriptura quidem sufficit ad salutem homini non credenti: sed ut traditiones non scriptas excludamus, quae non sunt cibus & panis, ex quo homo spiritualis vivit. Et si Cardinalis impostoris famam vivere voluisset, demonstrasset, traditiones illas non scriptas, esse cibum hominis credentis. Hoc vero ne
units.tr: As for what the Cardinal says, that not only food nourishes but also natural heat, who does not see how futile this is? The Word of God is called food and bread, by which man lives. Therefore, as food is for natural life, so sacred Scripture is for spiritual life. But food does not nourish without natural heat, nor Scripture without faith. Who denies this? But when it is said that food alone nourishes, natural heat is not excluded, which works through food and together with food. But everything that either is not food and yet enters the stomach, like medicines or poisons, or would not nourish though it entered, like stones, or does not enter at all though it is fit for nourishing. For food cannot nourish unless it is taken. Therefore food alone nourishes, because what is not food, and yet is taken into the stomach as food, cannot nourish. So we say that Scripture alone is sufficient, not to exclude faith, without which not even Scripture is sufficient for salvation to a man who does not believe, but to exclude unwritten traditions, which are not the food and bread by which the spiritual man lives. And if the Cardinal had wished to live on the reputation of an impostor, he would have demonstrated that those unwritten traditions are the food of the believing man. But this he has not attempted

units.la: leui digito tentauit. Quam est hæc supina su-perbia? Grauissima res agitur. De regula fidei quærimus: de ipso fundamento Ecclesiæ. In quibus tamen colludunt homines superbi, & contemptores, nec disputant.
units.tr: even with a light finger. What is this supine arrogance? A most weighty matter is at stake. We are inquiring about the rule of faith, about the very foundation of the Church. Yet in these matters proud men and contemners collude, and do not dispute.

units.la: Apostolus, ut Scripturarum diuinitus inspiratarum perfectionem offendant non dicit, Scripturas simpliciter esse viles; neq; nos sic ratiocinemur: Scriptura est vilis, ergo sufficit; sicut ille somniat [?] nos colligere: sed quod docet Apostolus, quod nos ex Apostolo colligimus, illud est: Scripturæ viles sunt ad perficiendum hominem Dei. Hæc autem vilitas, quæ hominis Dei perfectionem operatur, ut perfectus sit ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus, est sufficientia, & perfectio. Vilitas illa, quæ perficit, est vilitas & perfectio. Nihil enim requiritur ad perfectionem, quod non hæc vilitas præstet; qua & veritas omnis docetur, & error omnis refutatur, & mores instituuntur, & vitia omnia corriguntur, & sic homo Dei perficitur. Nonne egregie notatur, qui quum traditiones non scriptas in regula fidei, in ipso fundamento reponat, solam Scripturam non ad omnia sufficere dicit, quia nec cibus solus nutrit sine calore naturali? Atqui nos expectauimus, ut ostenderet, non tantum sacras Scripturas, sed etiam figmenta illa, & portenta de verbo non scripto in traditionibus, esse cibum, quo homo spiritualis nutriatur, esse panem Ecclesiæ, esse iustum sermonem, qui possit seruare animas nostras,
units.tr: The Apostle does not say, in order to take away the perfection of the divinely inspired Scriptures, that the Scriptures are simply worthless; nor do we reason in this way: Scripture is worthless, therefore it is sufficient, as that man dreams that we infer. What the Apostle teaches, and what we gather from the Apostle, is this: the Scriptures are worthless (or useful) for perfecting the man of God. This usefulness, which brings about the perfection of the man of God, so that he may be perfect, thoroughly furnished unto every good work, is sufficiency and perfection. That usefulness which perfects is usefulness and perfection. For nothing is required for perfection that this usefulness does not supply: by it all truth is taught, all error is refuted, morals are formed, all vices are corrected, and so the man of God is made perfect. Is it not admirably noted that he, who places unwritten traditions in the rule of faith, in the very foundation, says that Scripture alone is not sufficient for everything, because food alone does not nourish without natural heat? Yet we had expected him to show that not only the holy Scriptures but also those fictions and monstrosities about an unwritten word in traditions are the food by which the spiritual man is nourished, are the bread of the Church, are the just word that can save our souls.

units.la: Mihi vero Scripturarum perfectio, & sufficientia, vel hinc etiam maxime lucere videtur, quod homines improbos & superbos, qui contra ipsas obstrepere audent, ut maiestate sua percellant, ut ingeniosos alioquin, & doctos, quasi cæcos & bardos dimittant[?]. Quod accidit Cardinali nostro, qui multa nugando, & obiiciendo, tandem eandem Scripturarum sufficientiam concludit, quam nos profitemur. Nam post multas leuissimas nugas, tandem coleum reliquisse sibi videtur, quum dixerat, non solam Scripturam sufficere, quia nec solus cibus sine calore naturali sufficit ad nutriendum. Quibus verbis ostendit, se nihil habere contra Scripturarum sufficientem perfectionem; concedit, quod nos docemus. Sufficiunt ergo cibus, si calor naturalis adsit, & sufficiunt Scripturæ, si fides adsit.
units.tr: Indeed, the perfection and sufficiency of Scripture seems to me to shine out most clearly from this very fact: that wicked and proud men, who dare to rail against it, are so struck by its majesty that they leave even otherwise clever and learned men as blind and dull-witted. This happened to our Cardinal, who, after much trifling and objecting, at last reaches the same sufficiency of Scripture that we profess. For after many very trivial jests, he seems finally to have laid down his shield, since he had said that Scripture alone is not sufficient, just as food alone is not sufficient for nourishment without natural heat. By these words he shows that he has nothing against the perfect sufficiency of Scripture; he concedes what we teach. So food is sufficient if natural heat is present, and Scripture is sufficient if faith is present.

units.la: Neque refert, de universo corpore Scripturarum hoc intelligamus, an de quolibet libro sacro. Nam quod adfert, nondum eranuisse[?] Apocalypsin, & Euangelium Ioannis, quum hæc Epistola scriberetur, aut hæc de veteri Testamento intelligenda esse, quæ loquitur Apostolus ad Timotheum, ab infantia sacras literas novisti: id est, vetus Testamentum. Nam quum esset infans Timotheus, nondum extabat Testamentum novum: hæc nihil impediunt sententiam nostram; imo potius confirmant. Nam si tanta est perfectio veteris Testamenti, num negabunt de universa Scriptura verum esse, quod in parte concedunt? Fatemur, Scrippturas à Deo suo tempore reuelatas esse Ec-clesiæ, quando voluit, & quantum voluit. Ve-rum quum in Ecclesia Israelitica nihil de Scri-pturis extaret, præter quinque libros Mosis, certum est, Scripturas illas divinitus inspiratas fuisse in Ecclesia regulam fidei omnibus cre-dentibus: nec debuisse Ecclesiam aliter sapere, aut aliter Deum cognoscere, nisi secundum Scripturas illas divinitus inspiratas, in quibus voluntatem suam Deus patefecerat. Itaque frigidum est, quod de aliis libris postea con-scriptis, & in canonem relatis obloquitur, aut quod de veteri Testamento profert: nam Scripturæ postquam semel ad Ecclesiam dirigen-dam conscriptæ fuerunt, semper erant cibus Ecclesiæ, & semper hominem Dei perfectum ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructum reddere potuerunt. Nec librorum additione aliquid aliud docebatur, sed eadem regula, eadem Dei sapientia, non perfectior, sed plenior tradebatur. Hactenus Scripturas de Scripturis loquentes audivimus: audiantur deinceps Patres.
units.tr: It does not matter whether we understand this of the whole body of the Scriptures or of any single sacred book. For what he adduces, namely that the Apocalypse and the Gospel of John had not yet appeared when this Epistle was written, or that the words the Apostle addresses to Timothy, "from infancy you have known the sacred letters," must be understood of the Old Testament, these do not hinder our view; rather they confirm it. For while Timothy was an infant, the New Testament did not yet exist. If the Old Testament has such perfection, will they deny that what they concede in part is true of the whole Scripture? We confess that the Scriptures were revealed to the Church by God at his own time, when he willed and as much as he willed. But since in the Israelite Church nothing of the Scriptures existed beyond the five books of Moses, it is certain that those divinely inspired Scriptures were the rule of faith for all believers in the Church, and the Church ought not to have thought otherwise, or known God otherwise, than according to those divinely inspired Scriptures in which God had made known his will. Therefore it is feeble of him to carp at the other books written afterwards and received into the canon, or to bring forward what he says about the Old Testament; for once the Scriptures had been written to guide the Church, they were always the food of the Church and were always able to make the man of God perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Nor was anything else taught by the addition of books; the same rule and the same wisdom of God was handed down, not more perfect but fuller. So far we have heard Scripture speaking about Scripture; let us now hear the Fathers.

units.la: CAPVT V. Græcorum Patrum sententia referitur.
units.tr: CHAPTER V. The opinion of the Greek Fathers is set out.

units.la: CLemens Alexandrinus, de regula fidei, & de Scripturis contra traditiones non scriptas sic disserit: {a}Regula ecclesiastica est consensus & conspiratio veteris & novi Testamenti, quod per adventum Domini traditur. {b}Hanc al-
units.tr: CLEMENT of Alexandria, on the rule of faith and on Scripture against unwritten traditions, argues thus: {a}The ecclesiastical rule is the agreement and harmony of the Old and New Testament, which is handed down through the coming of the Lord. {b}This high-
