units.la: {a} Strom.lib.6.
units.tr: {a} Strom. lib. 6.

units.la: {b} ibid.lib.7. titudinem minimè assequuntur, qui non sequuntur Deum eos ducentem, duxit autem per Scripturas divinitus inspiratas. {a}Is nobis solus est cognitione praeditus, qui quum in ipsis Scripturis consenuerit, Apostolicam & ecclesiasticam servans dogmatum rectitudinem, recte vivit secundum Euangelium.
units.tr: {b} Ibid. lib. 7. They do not at all reach the height who do not follow God leading them, and he led them through the Scriptures inspired by God. {a}He alone among us is endowed with knowledge who, having grown old in the Scriptures themselves, keeps the apostolic and ecclesiastical correctness of doctrines, and lives rightly according to the Gospel.

units.la: Clemens igitur & dogmatum & morum regulam, sacras Scripturas docuit esse. De antiquorum Patrum naevis inviti loquimur. Sed ea est Pontificiorum improbitas, & importunitas, ut ex Patrum naevis errorum suorum patrocinium quaerant. Adducunt enim quaedam è Clemente, quae nec ipsos iuvant, & Clementem suis obnoxium infirmitatibus produnt. Haec vero non adducantur à Bellar-mino; credo, quia videbat ille, causam Pontificiam ex Clemente nihil adiuvari. Sed quia ab aliis afferuntur pro traditionibus non scriptis, nos etiam referemus. Sunt autem haec eius verba: {b}Operarius, qui in messem Domini emittitur, duplicem habet agriculturam, [illegible, ~6 letters], & [illegible, ~6 letters].
units.tr: Clement therefore taught that the holy Scriptures are the rule both of doctrines and of morals. We speak against our will about the blemishes of the ancient Fathers. But such is the impudence and importunity of the Papists that they seek a defence of their errors from the blemishes of the Fathers. For they adduce certain things from Clement which do not even help them, and which betray Clement as subject to the same weaknesses as others. Bellarmine does not cite these, I believe because he saw that the Papist cause gains nothing from Clement. But since others put them forward in support of unwritten traditions, we too shall report them. Now these are his words: {b}The labourer who is sent into the harvest of the Lord has a twofold husbandry, [illegible, about six letters], and [illegible, about six letters].

units.la: Respondemus, his verbis traditiones Pontificias non scriptas nihil promoueri. Nam Clemens per [illegible, ~6 letters] duo intelligit, sicut diversis locis sese explicat. Aliquando enim dicit, Graecos per philosophiam fuisse iustificatos; quod quia in Scripturis non habetur, idcirco [illegible, ~6 letters] vocat. Haec est manifesta sententia Clementis variis locis. Atque adeo hoc ipso loco post verba superius citato, sic scribit: {c}Sunt anima propria habentes nutrimenta, & alia quidem augentur per cognitionem & scientiam, alia vero per Græcam philosophiam. Itaque ex hoc loco nihil habent Pontificii, nisi forte inter traditiones suas non scriptas, Græcam philosophiam numerare velint. Hunc autem fuisse Clementis errorem, nobiscum agnoscunt Pontificii, ac proinde suo ipsorum iudicio refutantur, qui hæc ad traditiones non scriptas confirmandas producunt.
units.tr: We answer that Papist unwritten traditions gain nothing from these words. For Clement by [illegible, about six letters] understands two things, as he explains himself in different places. For at one point he says that the Greeks were justified through philosophy; since this is not found in the Scriptures, he therefore calls it [illegible, about six letters]. This is the clear opinion of Clement in various places. And indeed in this very place, after the words cited above, he writes thus: {c}Some souls have their own nourishment, and some are increased through knowledge and science, but others through Greek philosophy. So the Papists have nothing from this passage, unless perhaps they wish to count Greek philosophy among their unwritten traditions. The Papists themselves acknowledge with us that this was an error of Clement, and so they are refuted by their own judgement, since they bring these things forward to confirm unwritten traditions.

units.la: Alia est etiam Clementis sententia de agraphis, sed à plurimis non recte explicata. Quidam enim obiiciunt hæc verba Clementis, {a}Ut Philosophi quadam arcana de suis dogmatibus tradiderunt, ita etiam Apostoli, ut ait Paulus, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Scio, hæc verba viros aliquot doctos conturbasse, itaque inter nævos Clementis reponunt. Certe nullam causam video, quare viri docti & cordati his magnopere moveantur, in quibus nihil inveniunt Pontificii pro errore suo stabiliendo. Nam per universum librum illum quintum Stromatum, Clemens nihil omnino habet de traditionibus Pontificiis non scriptis. Et certe Adversariorum fraude, verba illa proxime citata è Clemente ponuntur. Nam illa verba Clemens non habet. Disputat eo libro Clemens, de mysticis scriptionibus. Testatur, apud Ægyptios plures esse scribendi rationes: primum [illegible, ~12 letters] : secundam esse sacerdotalem, qua utuntur [?]ἱερογραμματεῖς[?] : ultimam esse [?]ἐπιστολογραφικὸν[?]. Postremam hanc variam esse docet. Probat etiam multa apud Phi-
units.tr: Clement also has another opinion about the agrapha, but it has been explained incorrectly by many. For some object these words of Clement: {a}As the philosophers handed down certain secrets concerning their doctrines, so also the Apostles, as Paul says, We speak wisdom among the perfect. I know that these words have disturbed several learned men, and so they count them among Clement's blemishes. Certainly I see no reason why learned and sensible men should be greatly moved by them, since the Papists find nothing in them to establish their error. For throughout that whole fifth book of the Stromata, Clement has nothing at all about the Papists' unwritten traditions. And indeed, by the fraud of our opponents, the words just cited are put forward from Clement, for Clement does not have those words. In that book Clement discusses mystical writings. He testifies that among the Egyptians there are several ways of writing: the first [illegible, about twelve letters]; the second is the sacerdotal, which the hierogrammatists use [ἱερογραμματεῖς]; the last is the epistolographic [ἐπιστολογραφικὸν]. He teaches that this last is various. He also proves that many of the Philosophers, especially the Pythagoreans, did not write things down. {a} Strom. lib. 5.

units.la: {a} Strom.lib.5. Philosophos, præsertim Pythagoricos, non fuisse scripta. Atq; hæc suo more ad nostros et-iam retulit, vt probet, multa, quæ in sacris litteris traduntur, rerenta[?] fuisse apud gentes illas, in quibus naturæ lux non omnino extincta fuerat. Obseruat igitur, his similia in sacris litteris posita fuisse. Itaq; multa producit è veteri Testamento, quæ suas habent allegorias, non tamen scripta. Cuius generis enumerat arcam, imagines, Cherubim, alas, tintinnabula, pectorale, gemmas, & plura eius ordinis, quarum rerum non scriptam, sed mysticam habere interpretationem docet. Huc etiam refert illa Apostoli verba: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos: quibus verbis intelligit Clemens, reconditam illam sapientiam Propheticam in veteri Testamento. Sic enim scribit: a Hæc germana dicit sanctus quoque Apostolus Paulus, Propheticam & vere antiquam conseruans occultationem: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, &c.
units.tr: In his own manner he applies this even to our people, in order to prove that many things which are handed down in the sacred letters were also known among those nations in which the light of nature had not been wholly extinguished. He therefore observes that similar things were set down in the sacred letters. Accordingly he brings forward many things from the Old Testament which have their allegories, yet are not written down. Of this kind he lists the ark, images, Cherubim, wings, bells, the breastplate, gems, and several more of that sort, and he teaches that these things have not a written but a mystical interpretation. He also refers to this those words of the Apostle: We speak wisdom among the perfect. By these words Clement understands that hidden prophetic wisdom in the Old Testament. For he writes thus: a The holy Apostle Paul also says these true things, keeping the prophetic and truly ancient concealment: We speak wisdom among the perfect, etc.

units.la: Hæc fusius exponere volui, quia torporis videbatur non ferendi in hoc obstrepente seculo, non intelligere sensum antiquorum Patrum, & antiquos Scriptores ab Aduersariorum fraude & impostura non vindicasse. Habet Clemens suos nævos, quos mallem sepultos, quam prolatos: illud tamen constanter affirmo, ex Clementis sententia traditiones Pontificias non scriptas confirmari non posse. Docet Clemens, haberi quædam non scripta, sicut sunt allegoricæ & mysticæ interinterpretationes earum rerum, quæ in veteri Testamento typice ponuntur. Quasquidem omnes interpretationes ad Scripturæ analogiam reuocandas docet Clemens. Itaque aliud verbum Dei in traditionibus non scriptum nusquam agnoscit, imo vehementer abhorret. Itaque quoties de regula fidei, de Scripturis disputat, constanter docet, nullum esse aliud opus, præter sacras Scripturas, vt homo salvus fiat. Nam sic scribit: {a}Hanc doctrinam Apostolus quum sciret esse diuinam, Tu autem, inquit, ô Timothee, ab infantia sacras literas nosti, quæ te possunt instruere ad salutem per fidem in Christum. Sunt enim vere sacræ litteræ, quæ sacros faciunt, & deificant: ex quibus literis & sacris syllabis compositas scripturas & opera idem consequenter Apostolus appellat diuinitus inspiratas, vt quæ sunt vtiles ad docendum, ad arguendum, &c. Non adeo autem admirabitur quisquam aliorum sanctorum adhortationes, vt ipsum Dominum, qui est benignus ac humanus. Nullum enim aliud est ei, præterquam hoc solum opus, vt homo salvus fiat. Hæc ille. Quid à quoquam difertius dici potuit, quam quod hic docet, nullum esse aliud opus, quo hominibus salus quæratur, quam ex vnico hoc opere sacrarum Scripturarum? Ergo salus hominum non est in traditionibus non scriptis, sed in solis Scripturis. Itaque idem hanc regulam alibi explicans, {b} dicit, regulam cognitionis esse traditionem veritatis per veritatem. Et paulo post sic etiam disserit: {c}Eis etiam illud producimus, contra quod dici non potest, quod Deus Deus est, qui dicit, & de unoquoque, de quibus quæri-mus, traditum adduxit in scriptis. Hæc Clemens. Quibus verbis traditiones à verbo Dei penitus reiicit. Nam Deus est, qui loquitur, & in Scripturis loquitur. Contra hoc nihil dici po-test, Clemente iudice. At contra traditiones non scriptas multa dici possunt. Probent, Deum hæc protulisse, & Deum in Scripturis suis protulisse, tum demum ea proferent, contra quæ nihil dici possit. Proferamus jam alios.
units.tr: I wished to explain these things at greater length, because it seemed a disgrace, in this clamorous age, not to understand the sense of the ancient Fathers, and not to defend the ancient writers from the fraud and imposture of our opponents. Clement has his blemishes, which I would rather were buried than brought forth; yet this I affirm firmly: from Clement's opinion the Papist unwritten traditions cannot be confirmed. Clement teaches that there are certain things not written down, such as the allegorical and mystical interpretations of those things which are set down typically in the Old Testament. And Clement teaches that all these interpretations must be referred back to the analogy of Scripture. Therefore he nowhere acknowledges another word of God that is unwritten in traditions; indeed he greatly abhors it. Accordingly, whenever he disputes about the rule of faith and about the Scriptures, he consistently teaches that there is no other work, besides the holy Scriptures, by which a man may be saved. For he writes thus: {a}When the Apostle knew this doctrine to be divine, he says, But you, O Timothy, from infancy have known the sacred letters, which can instruct you to salvation through faith in Christ. For those are truly sacred letters which make and deify holy men; from these letters, and from the sacred syllables, the writings and works composed the same way the Apostle consistently calls divinely inspired, as being profitable for teaching, for refuting, etc. Nor will anyone admire the exhortations of other saints as much as the Lord himself, who is kind and humane. For he has no other work than this alone: that man may be saved. Thus he. What could be said more plainly by anyone than what he teaches here, that there is no other work by which salvation is sought for men than this one work of the holy Scriptures? Therefore the salvation of men lies not in unwritten traditions but in the Scriptures alone. Accordingly, the same Clement, explaining this rule elsewhere, {b} says that the rule of knowledge is the tradition of truth through truth. And a little later he argues thus: {c}We also bring forward this, against which nothing can be said: that God is the God who speaks, and who has handed down in writing about each of the things we inquire into. Thus Clement. By these words he utterly rejects traditions from the word of God. For it is God who speaks, and who speaks in the Scriptures. Against this, nothing can be said, by Clement's judgement. But many things can be said against unwritten traditions. Let them prove that God has put these forward, and that God has put them forward in his Scriptures; only then will they produce things against which nothing can be said. Let us now bring forward others.

units.la: Origenes sic docet: {a}Vide quam prope pe-riculis illis sunt, qui negligunt exerceri in divinis lite-ris, ex quibus solis examinationis huiusmodi agno-scenda dijudicatio est. Hæc ille. Qui ex solis Scri-pturis controversias explicandas esse docet, traditiones non scriptas refutat. Idemque sic etiam habet: {b}Necesse est nobis Scripturas sa-cras in testimonium vocare, sensus quippe nostri, & narrationes sine his testibus non habent fidem.
units.tr: Origen teaches thus: {a}See how near to those perils are those who neglect to exercise themselves in the divine letters, from which alone the judgement of such examination is to be recognised. Thus he. He who teaches that controversies are to be explained from the Scriptures alone refutes unwritten traditions. And he likewise says: {b}It is necessary for us to call the sacred Scriptures as witnesses, for our senses and our narrations have no credibility without these witnesses.

units.la: Priorem sententiam Origenis dissimulat Bellarminus, quia videt, nihil posse responde-ri. Ad postremum testimonium sic respon-det: {c}Loquitur Origenes de obscurissimis quæstionibus. Hæc ille. At hoc non est respondere. Quasi vero faciliora deberent absque Scripturis recipi. Atqui Origenes eodem loco idem affirmat de omni verbo. Quod etiam repetendo docet in Matth. cap.13. In ore, inquit, duorum, trium, aut plurium testium è Scriptu-ra citatorum fundamus & confirmamus omne ver-bum Dei. Hæc Origenes. Si omne verbum Dei Scripturarum testimonio fundatur, quomodo possint traditiones non scriptæ esse ver-bum Dei. Oportuit Cardinalem ad hæc re-spondisse, & non distinctiunculārum nugis Lectorem à mente Origenis avocasse. Idem igitur[?] Origenes dicit, Ecclesiæ dotem fuisse Euangelis[?] & Prophetarum volumina. In Cant. ho-mil. 1. Vnum Origenis testimonium adiiciam, quo velut præsagio quodam traditiones Pontificias Antichristi verbum futurum esse mo-net. Postquam enim templum & locum sanctum expositisset significare Scripturam, subiicit: {a}In hoc loco sancto omnium Scripturarum, tam veteris, quam novi Testamenti, Antichristus, quod est falsum verbum, stetit[?]: per hoc ipsum, quod stare videtur in Scriptura divina, ostendens se, quasi sit Deus, & sit quasi Christus Dei verbum. Et quemadmodum sic extollitur, ut etiam in templo Scripturarum sedeat, per ipsum templum, id est, per divinas Scripturas volens se ostendere, quasi ipse sit Deus. Semper ergo, qui divinas legit Scripturas, intelligat ea. Hæc ille. Quid autem dixisset, si nunc vi-veret, & legeret eorum scripta, qui Rom. Pontificem adorandum Christi Vicarium, caput Ecclesiæ, Scripturarum, & omnium de fide controversiarum iudicem statuunt? qui docent, verbum Papæ esse verbum Dei?
units.tr: Bellarmine passes over Origen's earlier statement, because he sees that no answer can be given to it. To the last testimony he replies: {c}Origen is speaking of the most obscure questions. So far Bellarmine. But this is not an answer. As if easier matters ought to be received without Scripture! Yet Origen says the same thing in the same place about every word. He teaches this again in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 13: On the testimony of two, three, or more witnesses cited from Scripture, we establish and confirm every word of God. So Origen. If every word of God is founded on the testimony of Scripture, how can unwritten traditions be the word of God? The Cardinal ought to have answered this, not diverted the reader from Origen's meaning with the trifles of his little distinctions. Origen also says, then, that the dowry of the Church was the Gospels and the volumes of the Prophets (Homily 1 on the Song of Songs). I will add one more testimony from Origen, which warns, as if by a kind of foreboding, that the Papal traditions will be the word of Antichrist. After explaining that the temple and the holy place signify Scripture, he goes on: {a}In this holy place of all the Scriptures, both of the Old and of the New Testament, Antichrist, who is a false word, has stood, showing himself by this very thing, that he seems to stand in divine Scripture, as if he were God and as if he were the Word of God, Christ. And just as he exalts himself in this way, so that he sits even in the temple of the Scriptures, he wishes to show himself through the temple itself, that is, through the divine Scriptures, as if he himself were God. Therefore let whoever reads the divine Scriptures always understand them with care. So Origen. But what would he have said if he were alive now, and read the writings of those who declare the Roman Pontiff to be the Vicar of Christ to be adored, the head of the Church, and the judge of Scripture and of all controversies of faith, who teach that the word of the Pope is the word of God?

units.la: Athanasius in eandem sententiam ait: {b}sufficiunt sancta & divinitus inspirata Scriptura ad instructionem veritatis. Respondet Bellarminus, Athanasium non habere ad omnem instructionem, sed tantum ad instructionem veritatis. Hæc ille. At qui dicit, sufficere Scripturas ad instructionem, necessario intelligit omnem: alioquin non sufficerent. Et Athanasius habet, αὐτάρκεις εἰσὶν, per se, & ex se sufficiunt. Si autem per se sufficiunt, falsum ostenditur esse, quod Bellarminus docuit: {a}a Scripturas sine traditionibus non esse sufficientes.
units.tr: Athanasius says to the same effect: {b}The holy and divinely inspired Scriptures are sufficient for the instruction of truth. Bellarmine replies that Athanasius does not say "sufficient for every instruction," but only "for the instruction of truth." So he. But whoever says that the Scriptures are sufficient for instruction necessarily means every instruction; otherwise they would not be sufficient. And Athanasius has αὐτάρκεις εἰσὶν [autarkeis eisin], that is, they are sufficient in themselves and of themselves. If they are sufficient in themselves, then what Bellarmine taught, that {a}the Scriptures are not sufficient without traditions, is shown to be false.

units.la: Nazianzenus vocat doctrinam non è Scri-pturis traditam, {b}πίστως ἀναπόδεικτος Φαν-τασίαν.[?]
units.tr: Nazianzen calls a doctrine not taken from Scripture a fancy that is believed without proof: {b}πίστως ἀναπόδεικτος φαντασία [pistōs anapodeiktos phantasia].

units.la: Basilius idem docuit: {c}Non est æquum, vt quæ apud ipsos (hæreticos) obtinuit consuetudo, pro lege ac canone habeatur rectæ doctrinæ. Si enim ad demonstrandam veritatem valeret consuetudo, licer & nobis parimodo illis respondere. Sed stemus arbitratui inspiratæ à Deo Scripturæ, & apud quos inuenta fuerint dogmata diuinis sermonibus consonantia, his omnino veritatis accedat suffragiū.
units.tr: Basil taught the same thing: {c}It is not right that a custom which has prevailed among them (the heretics) should be held as a law and rule of sound doctrine. For if custom were enough to prove the truth, we too could answer them in the same way. But let us stand by the Scriptures inspired by God, and wherever doctrines are found that agree with the divine words, let the support of truth be given to those alone.

units.la: Responder Bellarminus; {d}Omisit Chemnitius verba, quæ erant in medio, & contra illum faciebant. Nam quæstio erat: An dicendum sit, esse in Deo tres hypostases, & unā naturam: Aliqui dicebant, nō esse sic dicendum, & proferebant pro argumento consuetudinē suæ regionis. Responder Basilius: In aliis regionibus est consuetudo, vt dicãt, tres esse hypostases. Hæc Bellarminus nugando, & plura etiam verba addit. Deinde subiicit: Non hic agi de traditione in tota Ecclesia recepta, sed de particularibus consuetudinibus: Basilium autem ideo provocasse à consuetudine ad Scripturas, quia à consuetudinibus contrariis nihil certi statui poterat. Hæc ille. Sed quomodo hæc contra Chemnitium faciant, non ostendit, aut quomodo omiserit Chemnitius verba in medio. Certe integram sententiam retulit, nihil omisit. Itaque quum nihil haberet Cardinalis, quod responderet, ad verba confugit. Quod ad particulares traditiones, hæc refert, frigidum est, & falsum. Nam qui tres hypostases docuerunt esse in una natura, non secuti sunt particularem, sed universalis Ecclesiæ consuetudinem. Et tamen Basilius negat, hoc ex consuetudine sumendum esse: quia in controversiis de fide non consuetudinem, sed Scripturæ authoritatem sequi debemus. Hæc sunt, quæ Basilius tractat; ad quæ non respondet Cardinalis, sed verborum fumum excitat. Gregorius Nyssenus vocat Scripturas, κανόνα καὶ ἀσφάλειαν [?], orat.deiis, qui adeunt Hierosol.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies: {d}Chemnitz omitted the words that were in the middle and that went against him. For the question was whether one ought to say that there are three hypostases and one nature in God. Some said that this should not be said, and they brought forward the custom of their region as an argument. Basil answers: In other regions it is the custom to say that there are three hypostases. Bellarmine says this, adding more words in his usual trifling way. Then he adds: Here there is no question of a tradition received in the whole Church, but of particular customs; and Basil appealed from custom to the Scriptures only because nothing certain could be established from contrary customs. So he. But he does not show how these points tell against Chemnitz, or how Chemnitz omitted the words in the middle. Certainly he gave the whole sentence and omitted nothing. So, since the Cardinal had nothing to answer, he took refuge in words. As for the point about particular traditions, what he says is frigid and false. For those who taught three hypostases in one nature did not follow a particular custom but the custom of the universal Church. And yet Basil denies that this is to be taken from custom, because in controversies about faith we ought to follow not custom but the authority of Scripture. These are the matters Basil deals with, and the Cardinal does not answer them, but raises a smoke of words. Gregory of Nyssa calls the Scriptures {κανόνα καὶ ἀσφάλειαν} [kanona kai asphaleian], a rule and a safeguard, in his oration on those who go to Jerusalem.

units.la: Plura è Basilio proferamus: Nulli mortalium omnino licet aut facere quicquam prohibitum in Scripturis, aut prætermittere quicquam mandatum, quum Dominus semel pronunciaverit, Verbum, quod hodie mando tibi, observabis, neque ei apponès quicquam, neque auferes ex eo. Scribit etiam Basilius elegantem & solidam fidei suæ confessionem, in qua sic probat Scripturas esse unicam fidei regulam: Manifestum est à fide ipsus, & signum superbiæ certissimum, vel reiicere aliquid eorum, quæ scripta sunt, vel eorum, quæ non scripta sunt, introducere, dicente Domino nostro Iesu Christo: Christo: Oues meae vocem meam audiunt. Primū vtiq; dixerat: Alienum nequaquam sequentur, sed fugient ab eo, quia non norunt vocem alienorum. Apostolo quoq; sub exemplo humano vehementissime prohibente, ne quis Scriptura à Deo inspiratu vel addat quicquam, vel subtrahat, quum dicat: Humanum etiam testamentum ratum factum nemo reiicit, aut ei quicquam superaddit. Sic nos igitur & nunc, & semper fugere nonminus omnem & vocem, & cogitationem alienam à doctrina Domini nostri. Hactenus Basilius.
units.tr: Let us bring forward more from Basil: It is wholly unlawful for any mortal either to do anything forbidden in the Scriptures, or to omit anything commanded, since the Lord has once pronounced: The word which I command you today, you shall observe; you shall neither add anything to it nor take anything away from it. Basil also wrote an elegant and solid confession of his faith, in which he proves in this way that the Scriptures are the sole rule of faith: It is clear from the faith itself, and a most certain sign of pride, either to reject anything of what is written, or to introduce anything that is not written, since our Lord Jesus Christ says: My sheep hear my voice. First of all he had said: They will by no means follow a stranger, but will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers. The Apostle also, with a human example, most strongly forbids anyone to add anything to or take anything from the Scripture inspired by God, when he says: No one sets aside or adds to a human covenant that has been ratified. So we too, now and always, must flee no less every voice and thought that is foreign to the teaching of our Lord. Thus far Basil.

units.la: Quibus verbis mentem suam vir sanctus ita diserte demonstrauit, vt vel pertinacissimis rixatoribus, qualesfunt Iesuitæ, satisfacere videatur, ne amplius de eius sententia dubitare possint. At Bellarmino non persuadebit, etiamsi persuaseris[?]. Itaque respondet: {a}Lo-quitur Basilius de iis, qui addunt ad Scripturæ dogmata alia contraria, & aliena, Scripturisq; repugnantia. Hæc ille. Sed quia animus contra veritatem armatus non potest quiescere, dubitat, hæret, mutat, addit. Et quomodo potuit aliis satisfacere, qui suæ primum conscientiæ non satisfacit? Itaque post verba nonnulla sic infert: Addo etiam, de iis quoque Basilium loqui, qui non contenti vocibus scriptis, ex proprio capite inuenium[?] alias. Id enim superbiæ signum est certissimum. Itaque agit de traditionibus, quæ excogitantur à priuatis hominibus, non de iis, quæ ab Apostolis Ecclesia per successiones Episcoporum accepit. Hæc ille.
units.tr: By these words the holy man has so clearly shown his mind that he seems to satisfy even the most stubborn wranglers, such as the Jesuits, so that they can no longer doubt his opinion. But it will not persuade Bellarmine, even if you were to persuade him. So he replies: {a}Basil is speaking of those who add to the dogmas of Scripture other things that are contrary and foreign, and that conflict with Scripture. So he. But because a mind armed against the truth cannot rest, he doubts, hesitates, changes, and adds. And how could he satisfy others when he does not first satisfy his own conscience? So, after some words, he adds: I would add that Basil also speaks of those who, not content with what is written, find out other things from their own head. For that is a most certain sign of pride. So he is dealing with traditions that are devised by private men, not with those which the Church received from the Apostles through the succession of Bishops. So he.

units.la: Nescio, quomodo alii in hac responsione acquiescere possint, in qua nec Cardinalis ipse acquiescere videtur. Dicit, Basilium loqui de iis, qui addunt Scripturæ dogmata contraria & repugnantia. At hæc responsio inutilis est, quia Pontificii addunt dogmata Scripturis aliena, contraria, repugnantia, sicut in sequentibus demonstrabitur. Deinde supra iam docuimus ex Apostolo, in controversiis de fide omnia esse contraria & repugnantia, quæcunque non habentur in Scripturis: quia quæ sunt præter regulam, sunt etiam contra regulam. Hæc una Bellarmini responsio semper sine pudore ingeminatur ad verba Apostoli, ad verba Patrum: quia præterea nihil habet, miserum est, nec tacere posse, nec recte loqui.
units.tr: I do not know how others can rest content with this answer, in which the Cardinal himself does not seem to rest. He says that Basil is speaking of those who add to the dogmas of Scripture things that are contrary and conflicting. But this answer is useless, because the Papists add dogmas that are foreign, contrary, and conflicting to Scripture, as will be shown in what follows. Moreover, we have already shown above from the Apostle that in controversies of faith everything that is not found in Scripture is contrary and conflicting, because whatever is beyond the rule is also against the rule. This one answer of Bellarmine is repeated without shame against the words of the Apostle and against the words of the Fathers; since he has nothing else, it is wretched, and he can neither keep silent nor speak rightly.

units.la: Quod addit, Basilium loqui contra eos, qui non contenti vocibus scriptis, ex proprio capite inueniunt alias: qui magis potuit Cardinalis suo se telo cōfodere? Nam Pontificii sunt, qui non contenti vocibus scriptis, alias excogitarunt ex proprio capite. Hæret adhuc Cardinalis, nec responsionis exitum videt: Tandem igitur ait, agit de traditionibus, quæ excogitantur à priuatis hominibus, non de iis, quas ab Apostolis Ecclesia per successiones Episcoporum accepit. Neque hæc expedire possunt Cardinalem: Nam quænam quæso Ecclesia, quæ successio Episcoporum ante Cœcilium Tridentinum traditiones non scriptas in regula fidei posuit?
units.tr: As for his addition that Basil speaks against those who, not content with what is written, find other things from their own head: how could the Cardinal have stabbed himself more fittingly with his own weapon? For it is the Papists who, not content with what is written, have devised other things from their own head. The Cardinal is still stuck and does not see a way out of his answer. At last, then, he says that Basil is dealing with traditions devised by private men, not with those which the Church received from the Apostles through the succession of Bishops. Nor can this help the Cardinal. For I ask, what Church, what succession of Bishops, before the Council of Trent, placed unwritten traditions in the rule of faith?

units.la: Quid interim respondet ad grauissimam illam Basilii rationem, qua commotus iudicat, nihil
units.tr: What, meanwhile, does he answer to that most weighty argument of Basil, by which, moved by it, he judges that nothing is to be received concerning faith except what is found in the written Word, because Christ the Lord says: "My sheep hear my voice"?

units.la: mhil fcrip git: Scrip prob & qu fe ab Hæ elle, ccm ptur tion ftro de, Car firm ftol fup noft &al fpo not tam ptu inu lem qui quc not pot neg iam nihil recipiendum de fide, nisi quod in verbo scripto habetur: quia Christus Dominus di-cit: Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt. Ex qua Scriptura Basilius, Augustinus, aliique veteres probat, Scripturas esse vnicam Christi vocem; & quicquid in illis non legitur, fugiendum esse ab iis, qui se Christi oues esse profitentur. Hæc apud illos ratio dominatur: Fugiendum esse, quicquid non est vox pastoris nostri: Vocem pastoris nostri non esse, quicquid in Scripturis non habetur. Et nos etiam eadem ratione probamus, nos esse veros patrum nostrorum filios: Traditiones non scriptas de fide, vt vocem alieni refugimus. Ad hæc quid Cardinalis: Quid ad illam validissimam confirmationem, quam adduxit Basilius ex Apostolo à Humano testamento semel rato nihil superaddi posse: Ergo testamento Saluatoris nostri nihil est superaddendum. Sudabit hic, & aliquid excogitabit. Dicet, quod semper respondere solet, Pontificios non contraria, non repugnantia superaddere Scripturis, sed tamen docere multa, quæ non sunt in Scripturis. Atqui hoc commentum est prorsus inutile, & oportet ingeniosissimum Cardinalem nouum commentum exquirere. Nam qui humano testamento aliquid aliud addit, quod à testatore non erat positum; quamuis non contraria testamento, aut repugnantia posuerit; falsarius tamen iudicabitur. Certe negare non possunt, multa ab illis doceri, etiam ad regulã fidei multa apponi, quę nõ sunt in Scripturis posita. Itaque si illorum confessione sacra Scriptura sit testamentum Salvatoris nostri, certe negare non possunt, se ex Apostoli verbis, ex Patrum iudicio, falsarios, & sacrilegos iam convictos esse, qui in Christi Domini nostri testamento audent facere, quod in humano testamento, postquam ratum fuerit testibus, & morte testatoris, impium atque illicitum iudicatur. Et quia Dominus Cardinalis ad hæc non potuit respondere, libenter omnia dissimulat. Nec veretur tacitum iudicium doctorum & cordatorum hominum: maluitq; sophisticam artem quoquo modo exercere, quam à veritate vinci.
units.tr: Scripture proves this, and Basil, Augustine and other ancient writers prove from it that the Scriptures are the one voice of Christ, and that whatever is not read in them must be shunned by those who profess themselves Christ's sheep. This is the reasoning that prevails among them: whatever is not the voice of our shepherd must be shunned; whatever is not in the Scriptures is not the voice of our shepherd. And we too, by the same reasoning, prove that we are the true sons of our fathers: we refuse unwritten traditions concerning faith as the voice of a stranger. Against these arguments, what does the Cardinal say? What does he say to that most forceful confirmation which Basil drew from the Apostle, that to a human testament once ratified nothing can be added: therefore nothing is to be added to the testament of our Saviour? He will sweat over this and will devise something. He will say what he is always accustomed to say, that the Papists do not add to the Scriptures things contrary or repugnant to them, but still teach many things which are not in the Scriptures. But this pretext is entirely useless, and the most ingenious Cardinal must seek out some new pretext. For whoever adds to a human testament something that the testator did not set down, even if he adds nothing contrary or repugnant to the testament, will nevertheless be judged a forger. Certainly they cannot deny that many things are taught by them, and that many things not set down in the Scriptures are added to the rule of faith. Therefore, if by their own confession Holy Scripture is the testament of our Saviour, they certainly cannot deny that, by the words of the Apostle and the judgment of the Fathers, they are already convicted as forgers and sacrilegious men, who dare to do in the testament of Christ our Lord what, in a human testament, once it has been ratified by witnesses and the death of the testator, is judged impious and unlawful. And because the Lord Cardinal could not answer these things, he gladly dissembles them all. Nor does he fear the silent judgment of learned and sensible men; he preferred to practise sophistical art by whatever means, rather than be conquered by the truth.

units.la: In Synodo Nicena prima, Constantinum Imperatorem sic differentem refert Theodoretus: {a}Euangelici, & Apostolici libri, & veterum Prophetarum oracula, plene instruunt nos, quid oporteat sapere de voluntate & sensu Dei. Ponentes ergo contentionem ex diuinitus inspiratis oraculis, quaeramus solutionem eorum, quae proponuntur.
units.tr: In the First Council of Nicaea, Theodoret reports Constantine the Emperor speaking thus: The Gospel and Apostolic books, and the oracles of the ancient Prophets, fully instruct us what we ought to think concerning the will and mind of God. Therefore, setting aside the contention, let us seek the solution of the matters that are proposed from the oracles inspired by God.

units.la: Respondet Bellarminus: Constantinum fuisse magnum Imperatorem, sed non magnum Ecclesiae doctorem. Sic solent Iesuitae irridere, quum, quod respondeant, non habent. Atqui multos Papas inferiores fuisse Constantino, in cognitione veritatis, constat. Deinde Constantinus non suam tantum, sed Concilii sententiam hic retulit, quam à sanctissimis Episcopis & Doctoribus hauserat. Postremo, nihil habet Constantinus, quod non Ecclesiae magni Doctores omnium seculoculorum tradiderunt. Ita haec irrisio non in Constantinum solum, sed & in Concilium Nicenum, & in omnes Ecclesiae Doctores magnos recidit. Synodus Constantinopolitana Macedonium non traditionibus, sed Scripturis repressit. Itaque Athanasius de ea re sic scribit: a Ne interroges, sed solum ex sacris literis addiscas: sufficiunt enim, quae in illis reperies, documenta. De duobus insequentibus Conciliis, Ephesinum dico, & Chalcedonense (ut quatuor primorum generalium Conciliorum explorata de hac re iudicia retineamus) Euagrius sic restatur: Ex Evangelicis & Apostolicis de Domino vocibus, scimus viros illos divinos constituisse. Quatuor igitur prima Concilia generalia, quorum semper in Ecclesia celeberrima viguit autoritas, nihil ex traditionibus, omnia ex sacris Scripturis confirmarunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies that Constantine was a great Emperor, but not a great teacher of the Church. Thus the Jesuits are accustomed to mock when they have nothing to answer. Yet it is established that many Popes were inferior to Constantine in the knowledge of the truth. Moreover, Constantine here set out not only his own opinion but that of the Council, which he had drawn from the most holy bishops and teachers. Finally, Constantine has nothing that the great teachers of the Church in all ages have not handed down. So this mockery falls not on Constantine alone, but on the Council of Nicaea and on all the great teachers of the Church. The Council of Constantinople repressed Macedonius not by traditions but by the Scriptures. Therefore Athanasius writes on this matter thus: Do not ask, but learn only from the sacred letters: for the proofs that you will find in them are sufficient. Concerning the two following Councils, I mean Ephesus and Chalcedon (so that we may keep the established judgments on this matter of the four first general Councils), Evagrius reports thus: From the Gospel and Apostolic words of the Lord we know that those divine men established it. Therefore the four first general Councils, whose authority has always flourished most famously in the Church, confirmed nothing from traditions, but everything from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: Chrysostomus sic docet: {b}Magna adversus peccatum munitio est Scripturarum lectio, magnum praecipitium, profundum barathrum Scripturarum ignoratio. Et mox: Eares & haereses peperit, & vitam corruptam immisit, & sursum ac deorsum omnia miscuit. Idemque sic exponit verba illa Apostoli: Siego, vel Angelus de caelo annuntiaverimus, praeterquam quod accepistis, anathema sit. Non dixit (inquit Chrysostomus c.) si contraria annuntiaverint, aut totum Evangelium subverterint, verum si paulum evangelizaverint praeter Evangelium, quod accepistis, etiamsi quidam labefactarint, anathema sit. Pauca haec verba Chrysostomi, vsitatissimam Bellarmini responsionem in fumum sophisticum dissipant. Illud e-nim respondere solet Bellarminus: Praeter id, significare contra id: ac proinde Apostolum non prohibere nova dogmata, modo non sint contraria iam traditis. At Chrysostomus non patitur Apostolum sic eludi. Apostolus non dicit, si contraria[?], sed si quis[?] praeter Euange-lium docuerint. Praeter Euangelium, non est contra-ria, sed, praeter.
units.tr: Chrysostom teaches thus: A great defence against sin is the reading of the Scriptures; a great precipice and deep abyss is ignorance of the Scriptures. And soon after: It has brought forth heresies and admitted a corrupt life, and has thrown all things up and down. He likewise explains in this way those words of the Apostle: But though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything besides what you have received, let him be anathema. He did not say (says Chrysostom, chapter ...) if they preach things contrary, or overthrow the whole Gospel; but if they preach a little beside the Gospel that you have received, even if some are shaken, let him be anathema. These few words of Chrysostom dissipate into sophistical smoke Bellarmine's most usual answer. For Bellarmine is accustomed to answer this: "Beside" signifies "against", and therefore the Apostle does not forbid new dogmas, provided they are not contrary to those already delivered. But Chrysostom does not allow the Apostle to be eluded in this way. The Apostle does not say if contrary[?], but if anyone[?] teaches beside the Gospel. Beside the Gospel is not contrary, but beside.

units.la: Idem Chrysostomus, Scripturas esse regulam fidei, sic docet: {a}Quam habemus exactissimam trutinam, gnomonem, & regulam divinarum legum assertionem, oro vos omnes, ut relinquatis, quid huic vel illi videatur, & de his à Scripturis hæc omnia inquirite. Respondet Bellarminus: {b}Non loquitur de dogmatibus fidei aut morum obscuritatis, sed de opinione carnalium, qui anteponunt opes paupertati: quum Scripturæ apertissime docent, paupertatem esse longe utiliorem ad salutem. Itaque Chrysostomus nihil hic aliud dicit; quàm, magis credendum esse Scripturis, quam hominum opinioni. Hæc ille. Sed quid si hæc responsio non satisfaciat? aut quid est in hac responsione, quod Cardinalis putabat satisfacere posse? Chrysostomus eo loco multa vitia reprehendit, fornicationem, avaritiam, invidiam, crudelitatem, vanam gloriam: denique de pauperis & divitis compa-ratione agit. Sed quid hæc ad rhombum? Non quæro, de quibus disputet; sed quid dicat? Nam contra omnia vitia, contra omnes omnium hominum opiniones unam profert reguregulam, vnum gnomonem, vnam trutinam, sacram Scripturam. Noli mihi illud respondere, quod nec quæro, nec refert. Profero, quid dicat, quid doceat. Scriptura est, inquit, exactissima trutina & regula. Cur non igitur ad hanc regulam Pontificias traditiones non scriptas reuocemus. Monet Chrysostomus, ne opinionum vento circumferamur, sed Scripturarum regulam sequamur. Et quia locus hic luculentissime Pontificias traditiones conuellit, verba Chrysostomi fusius apponam, quia ferunt Pontificios: {a}Ne igitur multorum opiniones habeamus, sed res ipsas inquiramus. Quomodo autem non absurdum est propter pecunias aliis non credere, sed ipsas numerare, & supputare, pro rebus autem amplioribus [?] aliorum sententiam sequi simpliciter? Præsertim quam habeant omnium exactissimam trutinam & gnomonem, & regulam domesticarum [?], inquam, legum affer-tionem [?]. Ideo obsecro & pro vobis omnes, vt relinquatis, quid huic vel illi videatur, deq; his à Scripturis hac omnia inquirite. Hæc ille. Nos sedulo quidem facimus, quod iubet Chrysostomus. Pontificii traditiones non scriptas nobis obtrudunt quasi pecunias; imo quasi verbum Dei omni thesauro pretiosius. Quod igi-tur homines non omnino supini facere solent in pecuniis excipiendis, vt non aliis credant, nec excipiant pecunias, nisi supputatas, & numeratas; Num prohibebunt Pontificii, nos idem facere in re omnium pretiosissima, in fide suscipienda? in animæ thesauro excipiendo? Negamus, nos traditiones non scriptas de fide, id est, pecunias Pontificias, nisi prius numeratas & supputatas receptūros: quia ad hæc diiudicanda sacrarum Scripturarum habemus exactissimam regulam: ex qua regula pecunias istas Pontificias adulteratas cognoscimus. Sic nos docuit Chrysostomus.
units.tr: The same Chrysostom, teaching that the Scriptures are the rule of faith, says: We have a most exact balance, gnomon and rule, the assertion of the divine laws; I beg you all to leave aside what seems so to this one or that one, and to seek all these things from the Scriptures. Bellarmine replies: {b}He is not speaking of the dogmas of faith or of obscure morals, but of the opinion of carnal men, who prefer riches to poverty, whereas the Scriptures most plainly teach that poverty is far more useful for salvation. Therefore Chrysostom here says nothing other than that one must believe the Scriptures rather than human opinion. So he. But what if this reply does not satisfy? Or what in this reply is there that the Cardinal thought could satisfy? Chrysostom in that place rebukes many vices: fornication, avarice, envy, cruelty, vainglory; finally he deals with the comparison of the poor man and the rich man. But what has this to do with the matter? I do not ask what he disputes about, but what he says. For against all vices, against all the opinions of all men, he sets forth one rule, one gnomon, one balance, the Holy Scripture. Do not answer me with that, which I do not ask and which does not matter. I set forth what he says and what he teaches. Scripture, he says, is the most exact balance and rule. Why, then, do we not recall the unwritten Papist traditions to this rule? Chrysostom warns that we should not be carried about by the wind of opinions, but should follow the rule of the Scriptures. And because this passage most clearly overthrows the Papist traditions, I will set out Chrysostom's words more fully, because the Papists bring them forward: {a}Therefore let us not have the opinions of many, but let us examine the things themselves. Is it not absurd, on account of money, not to believe others but to count and reckon it oneself, while in weightier matters simply to follow the opinion of others? Especially when they have the most exact balance and gnomon of all, and the assertion, I say, of the laws [?]. Therefore I beg and entreat you all to leave aside what seems so to this one or that one, and to seek all these things from the Scriptures. So he. We indeed do diligently what Chrysostom commands. The Papists force unwritten traditions upon us as if they were money; nay, as if they were the Word of God, more precious than all treasure. Therefore, just as men are not wont to be utterly careless in receiving money, so as not to believe others, nor accept money unless it has been reckoned and counted; will the Papists forbid us to do the same in the most precious of all things, in receiving the faith, in receiving the treasure of the soul? We deny that we will receive unwritten traditions concerning faith, that is, Papist money, unless first counted and reckoned; because for judging these things we have the most exact rule of the Holy Scriptures, by which rule we recognise that those Papist coins are adulterated. Thus Chrysostom taught us.

units.la: Autor operis imperfecti in Matth. idem docet: {a}Quicquid quaeritur ad salutem, totum iam adimpletum est in Scripturis.
units.tr: The author of the Opus imperfectum on Matthew teaches the same thing: Whatever is sought for salvation has already been fully supplied in the Scriptures.

units.la: Respondet Bellarminus: Loquitur Chrysostomus de remediis vitiorum, & docet, nullum esse vitium, ad quod sanandum non inveniatur in Scripturis aliquod remedium. Sed quid haec valent contra traditiones. Hæc ille. Respondeo: Valent hæc maxime contra traditiones, quia traditiones istæ vitia sunt, ad quæ sananda remedium invenitur in Scripturis. Sed certum est, hæc verba non tantum esse de remediis vitiorum, nisi & infidelitatem inter hæc vitia reponas: nam loquitur hic scriptor de omnibus necessariis ad salutem, & ad omnia Scripturas sufficere docet, sive de fide sit quæstio, sive de moribus. Itaque eodem loco sic scribit: Prandium meum paravi: id est, ex omni lege, & ex omnibus Propheris[?] Scripturarum mensas paravi. Quid? Num Cardinalis dicet, hæc esse tantum de remediis vitiorum? Item sic subiungit: Sicut viscera agni, ita eloquia Christi homines non manducaverunt, nisi postquam occisus est. Nam post mortem eius Evangelia praedicata sunt, sunt, & credita, & in iis homines quotidie nutriun-tur. Num hæc etiam ad remedia vitiorum tan-tum referenda sunt, an non etiam ad regulam fidei? Ita igitur progreditur hic scriptor ad verba illa exponenda [omnia parata sunt.] & infert: Quicquid quaeritur ad salutem, totum iam adimpletum est in Scriptura. Quaeris ignarus, inquiet ibi, quod discat, &c. Qui igitur hæc ad re-media vitiorum tantum retulit, non ille solli-citus videbatur, quid efficeret, modo aliquo commento vim verborum eludere posset. Postremo, si nullum sit vitium, ad quod sa-nandum Scriptura iam habeat remedium: certe iam Cardinalis concessione, Scriptura est perfecta regula morum. Quæritur igitur à Domino Cardinali, quam rationem afferre possit, quare non sit eadem perfecta regula fi-dei, quam morum perfectam regulam conce-dit? Hæc semicruda reliquit, quæ concoque-re non potuit.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies: Chrysostom is speaking of remedies for vices, and teaches that there is no vice for which a remedy is not found in Scripture. But what do these words have to do with traditions? That is his reply. I answer: these words bear most strongly against traditions, because those traditions are the very vices for which a remedy is found in Scripture. But it is certain that these words are not only about remedies for vices, unless you also count unbelief among the vices. For the writer here speaks of everything necessary for salvation, and teaches that the Scriptures suffice for all things, whether the question concerns faith or morals. So in the same place he writes: I have prepared my meal: that is, I have prepared the tables from the whole law and from all the Prophets of Scripture. Well? Will the Cardinal say that these words too concern only remedies for vices? He also adds: As the entrails of the lamb, so men have not eaten the words of Christ until he was slain. For after his death the Gospels were preached, and are preached and believed, and men are nourished daily by them. Are these words also to be referred only to remedies for vices, or not also to the rule of faith? So this writer goes on to expound those words [all things are ready] and infers: Whatever is sought for salvation has been wholly fulfilled in Scripture. You, being ignorant, seek what you may learn there, etc. Whoever referred these things to remedies for vices alone did not seem concerned about what they would achieve, provided he could evade the force of the words by some contrivance. Finally, if there is no vice for which Scripture already has a remedy, then by the Cardinal's own concession Scripture is a perfect rule of morals. So we ask the Lord Cardinal what reason he can give why it should not likewise be a perfect rule of faith, since he concedes it is a perfect rule of morals. He has left these things half-digested, which he could not concoct.

units.la: Epiphanius etiam sic habet: {a}Quum talis sit ipsorum (haereticorum) doctrina, quam neque Prophetæ prædicaverant, neq; Dominus docuit, neq; Apostoli tradiderunt, quam de vniuersis tacuerunt [?], se plus aliis cognouisse, ex non scriptis legentes, quod dici solet, ex arena funiculos nectunt. {b}Nos vniuer-sa quæstione inuentionem non ex prophetis ratiocina-tionibus docere possumus, sed ex Scripturarum consequentia.
units.tr: Epiphanius likewise says: Since the doctrine of the heretics themselves is such that neither did the Prophets preach it, nor did the Lord teach it, nor did the Apostles hand it down, and since they were silent about it in all things, they claim to know more than others by reading unwritten things; as is commonly said, they weave ropes out of sand. In the whole question we can teach the discovery not from prophetic reasonings, but from the consequence of the Scriptures.

units.la: Huic postremo testimonio respondet Bel-larminus: Non dicit Epiphanius, ex Scripturarum consequentia solum: alibi autem clarissime[?] dicit, non omnia à Scriptura accipi posse, & ideo necessariam esse traditionem.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies to this last testimony: Epiphanius does not say from the consequence of the Scriptures alone; elsewhere, however, he says very clearly that not all things can be taken from Scripture, and therefore tradition is necessary.

units.la: Respondeo primo, qui inuentiones pro-prias excludit, qui omnia non scripta reiicit, vt Scripturis locum relinquat, certe solam Scripturarum consequentiam confirmat. Deinde ex variis Patribus adducimus ea verba; ex Scriptura solum; ex sola Scriptura; tantummodo ex Scriptura: ad quæ tamen mutos est Bellarminus.
units.tr: I answer first: whoever excludes private inventions, and rejects all unwritten things, so as to leave room for Scripture, certainly confirms the consequence of the Scriptures alone. Next, from various Fathers we adduce these words: from Scripture alone; from Scripture alone; only from Scripture. Bellarmine is nevertheless silent about these.

units.la: Sed Epiphanius, inquit Bellarminus, traditionibus non scriptis fauet. Itaque quæ producit Bellarminus ex Epiphanio, pro traditionibus non scriptis examinanda sunt. Duos profert locos. Primum hæresi 55. quæ est Melchisedecianorum. Termini, inquit Epiphanius, nobis positi sunt, & ædificatio fidei, & Apostolorum traditiones, & Scripturæ sanctæ, & successiones doctrinæ, & undique veritas Dei manifesta est, & nemo decipiatur variis fabulis.
units.tr: But Epiphanius, Bellarmine says, favours unwritten traditions. Therefore the passages Bellarmine produces from Epiphanius in support of unwritten traditions must be examined. He brings forward two places. The first is from heresy 55, that of the Melchisedecians. The boundaries, says Epiphanius, have been set for us: the building up of faith, and the traditions of the Apostles, and the holy Scriptures, and the successions of doctrine; and on every side the truth of God is made manifest, and no one should be deceived by various fables.

units.la: Respondeo: Epiphanii locus est maxime contra Pontificios. Nam disputat eo loco contra traditiones non scriptas de fide; ab hæreticis confictas, (quales sunt traditiones Pontificiæ, contra quas nos etiam disputamus) vt confirmet, traditiones scriptas ab Apostolis, quas vocat & Scripturas sanctas, & successiones doctrinæ. Nam traditio sæpe apud Patres dicitur doctrinæ veræ traditio, è Scripturis, in Ecclesia conseruata: sicut in traditionum di-stinctione dicturi sumus. Et hanc fuisse Epiphanii mentem, constat, quia eodem capite
units.tr: I answer: Epiphanius's passage bears most strongly against the Papists. For in that place he disputes against unwritten traditions of faith invented by heretics (of the kind the Papist traditions are, against which we too dispute), in order to confirm the written traditions handed down by the Apostles, which he calls both holy Scriptures and successions of doctrine. For tradition is often spoken of among the Fathers as the tradition of true doctrine, drawn from the Scriptures and preserved in the Church, as we shall say when we distinguish the kinds of tradition. And that this was Epiphanius's meaning is clear, because in the same chapter

units.la: maxime reprehendit traditiones illas quæ non habent testimonium Scripturæ. Nam contra hæreticos Melchisedecianos disputat: Qui, inquit, fingunt libros sibi ipsi commentitios, sæpe decipientes. Etenim omnibus receptis libris nusquam habentur horum Patres. Itaque contra eos, qui traditiones tales iactabant, subiungit hæc verba: Quid igitur dicemus? Numquid fundamenta sunt nostra? Imo absit. Terminos enim nobis posuerunt sancti et fundamenta, &c. [?] Itaque terminos nobis positos, & fundamenta, & ædificationem fidei, vocat Apostolorum traditiones, quæ sunt & sacræ Scripturæ, & successiones doctrinæ eadem Scripturis. Ac proinde dicit, veritatem Dei undique munitam, ne decipiamur nostris fabulis [?]. Veritas enim vere munita dicitur, & quasi triplici muro vallata, quam primo tradiderunt Apostoli, per prædicationem, deinde eandem in Scripturis tradiderunt, postremo eadem doctrina per successiones Ecclesiæ traditur. Ac proinde merito dicit, hanc veritatem esse undique munitam.
units.tr: he especially rebukes those traditions which have no testimony of Scripture. For against the heretical Melchisedecians he disputes: they, he says, invent books of their own, often deceiving. Indeed, none of their Fathers are found in any of the received books. So against those who boasted of such traditions he adds these words: What then shall we say? Are they our foundations? Far from it. For the holy men have set boundaries for us, and foundations, etc. So by the boundaries set for us, and the foundations, and the building up of faith, he calls the traditions of the Apostles, which are both the holy Scriptures and the successions of doctrine that are the same as the Scriptures. And accordingly he says that the truth of God is fortified on every side, lest we be deceived by our own fables. For the truth is rightly said to be truly fortified, and as it were walled in by a triple wall: first the Apostles handed it down by preaching, then they handed down the same in the Scriptures, and lastly the same doctrine is handed down through the successions of the Church. Accordingly he rightly says that this truth is fortified on every side.

units.la: Alium locum ex Epiphanio adducit Bellarminus, hæres. 61. Oportet & traditione uti; non enim omnia ex sacra Scriptura accipi possunt. Quapropter aliqua in Scripturis, aliqua in traditione sancti Apostoli tradiderunt.
units.tr: Bellarmine brings forward another passage from Epiphanius, heresy 61: It is necessary to use tradition too; for not all things can be taken from holy Scripture. Therefore the holy Apostles handed some things down in the Scriptures, and some in tradition.

units.la: Respondeo: Epiphanius nihil hoc loco dicit, quod nos non libenter agnoscimus. Disputat enim contra Apostolicos, qui nuptias prohibebant, & à cibis abstinebant. Iam quia orthodoxi etiam, ratione quadam, à nuptiis, & cibis abstiabstinebant: hæc intelliguntur inter ἀδιάφο-ρα[?], quibus vel bene, vel male vti possumus. Agnoscimus autem, in huiusmodi rebus traditionem Ecclesiæ valere, in quibus disciplina ecclesiastica continetur. Hæc quia à Scripturis accipi non possunt, idcirco traditionibus recte reiuncuntur[?]. Eodemque modo Epiphanius refutat Aërium, qui statis temporibus ieiunandum negabat. Probat Epiphanius ex traditione Ecclesiæ, quarta feria, & profabbato ieiunium fieri. {a}Assumpsit, inquit, Ecclesia, & in toto mundo assensu factus est, antequam esset Aërius, & qui ab illo appellantur Aëriani. Hæc ille. Recte quidem in huiusmodi opinionibus refutandis, quæ sunt in disciplina ecclesiastica, adhibetur traditio non scripta, id est, Ecclesiæ disciplina.
units.tr: I answer: Epiphanius says nothing in this place that we do not gladly acknowledge. For he disputes against the Apostolics, who forbade marriage and abstained from foods. Now since the orthodox also, for some reason, abstained from marriage and foods, these matters are understood to be among things indifferent [ἀδιάφορα], which we may use either well or badly. We acknowledge, moreover, that in matters of this kind the tradition of the Church has force, namely those in which ecclesiastical discipline consists. Since these cannot be taken from the Scriptures, they are rightly referred to traditions. In the same way Epiphanius refutes Aërius, who denied that fasting should be observed at fixed times. Epiphanius proves from the tradition of the Church that fasting is observed on Wednesday and Friday. The Church, he says, has taken it up, and has become agreed throughout the whole world, before Aërius existed, and before those who are called Aërians after him. So far he. Rightly, indeed, in refuting opinions of this kind, which belong to ecclesiastical discipline, unwritten tradition, that is, the discipline of the Church, is brought to bear.

units.la: Respondemus igitur, multa apud Patres de traditionibus disputantur, sicut deinceps observabimus. Illud autem affirmamus, non protulisse Bellarminum unum locum ex Patribus, qui non sit vel de tradita doctrina scripta, de qua non litigamus: vel de traditionibus non scriptis in disciplina ecclesiastica, quam non oppugnamus. Ac proinde dicimus, esse istos nugacissimos scriptores, qui plurimum laborant in earum rerum probatione, quæ à nobis conceduntur, ut probent traditiones non scriptas in disciplina. Nunquam autem probant, quod nos negamus, traditiones scilicet non scriptas recipiendas esse in doctrina & fide.
units.tr: We therefore answer that many things are disputed among the Fathers concerning traditions, as we shall observe in what follows. But we affirm this: Bellarmine has not produced a single passage from the Fathers that is not either about doctrine handed down in writing, which we do not dispute, or about unwritten traditions in ecclesiastical discipline, which we do not oppose. And so we say that those writers are most trifling who labour greatly to prove those things which we concede, namely that unwritten traditions exist in discipline. But they never prove what we deny, namely that unwritten traditions are to be received in doctrine and faith.

units.la: Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus sic docet: a Ne-cesse est de divinis & sanctis fidei mysteriis, neq; sine sacris Scripturis temere quicquam tradere, nec sim-plicis credulitate, & verborum apparatu circumferri. Neq; mihi haec docenti simpliciter credas, nisi demon-strationem annunciatorum ex sacris literis acceperis. Salus enim ipsa fides nostra non ex communi[?]tia dis-putatione, sed ex demonstratione divinarum Scri-pturarum est.
units.tr: Cyril of Jerusalem teaches thus: It is necessary concerning the divine and holy mysteries of faith not to hand down anything rashly, nor without the holy Scriptures, nor to be carried about by mere simple credulity and show of words. Nor should you believe me simply when I teach these things, unless you receive the demonstration of the things announced from the holy letters. For our faith itself is salvation, and rests not on common disputation but on the demonstration of the divine Scriptures.

units.la: Cyrillus Alexandrinus: b Haec, quae relata sunt, sufficiunt ad plenissimam fidem attente legen-tium. c Non omnia, quae Dominus fecit, conscripta sunt, sed quae scribentes, tam ad mores, quam ad do-[illegible, ~6 letters] parerent sufficere, ut rectae fide, & operibus [illegible, ~3 letters] virtute [illegible, ~3 letters] ad regnum coelorum perueniamus. d Necessarium habere est divinos sequi [?]mus, & in nullo ab earum praescripto discedere.
units.tr: Cyril of Alexandria: "What has been related is enough for the full faith of attentive readers. Not everything that the Lord did has been written down, but what the writers set down was sufficient, both for morals and for [illegible in the scan], so that, by right faith and works [illegible in the scan] by virtue, we may come to the kingdom of heaven. It is necessary to follow the divine Scriptures and in no way to depart from their prescription."

units.la: Ad haec postrema verba respondet Bellar-minus: e Non dicit, non licere aliquid dice-[?]re, quod in Scripturis non habeatur: sed non licere contra Scripturas dicere; hoc enim est non discedere à praescripto Scripturarum. Haec ille. At Cyrillus habet, in nullo debere nos à Scripturarum praescripto discedere: hoc est, inquit Bellarminus, nihil contra Scripturas dicere. Hanc responsionem Bellarminus, tanquam Achillis clypeum, ad omnia fere testimonia obuertit. Si vis huius responsi concidat, ruunt protinus omnia, quae à Bellarmino in hac controversia disputantur. At contra hanc responsionis umbram opponimus Apollinis verba diserta, prohibentis omnem ἐπο[illegible, ~9 letters] quæ non est contraria tantum, sed & diversa quæcunque; demonstrantis contra fas & jus esse apud homines, humanum vel testamentum, vel pactum rumpere, aut etiam aliquid addere: quanto magis impium esset. De testamento aliquid addere? Denuntiantis denique anathema iis omnibus, qui aliquid præter Euangelium afferunt. Opponimus Patrum consensum. Qui negant, in Ecclesia inducere licere doctrinam aliquam non tantum contra, sed præter Scripturas: non contrariam tantum, sed alienam etiam, extraneam, diversam ab ea, quam Ecclesiæ ab Apostolis, Apostoli à Christo acceperunt. Jam vero post diserta Apostoli verba, post clarissima Patrum suffragia, in tanta veritatis luce, in tanto antiquitatis consensu, tam sæpe, tam impudenter inculcare, Patrum sententiam esse contra Patrum expressa verba: quid hoc aliud est, quam palam profiteri, se non de veritate solliciturum, sed mercede conductum, Jesuitica fronte grassari?
units.tr: Bellarmine replies to these last words: "He does not say that it is not lawful to say anything that is not found in Scripture, but that it is not lawful to say anything against Scripture; for this is not to depart from the prescription of Scripture." So he says. But Cyril says that we ought not to depart in any way from the prescription of Scripture; this, says Bellarmine, means saying nothing against Scripture. Bellarmine turns this reply, like Achilles' shield, against nearly all the testimonies. If this reply is shattered, everything that Bellarmine argues in this controversy collapses at once. Against this shadow of a reply, however, we set the plain words of the Apostle, forbidding every [word illegible in the scan] that is not merely contrary but is any sort of different thing; declaring that it is contrary to divine and human law for men to annul a human will or covenant, or even to add anything to it, and how much more impious it would be to add something to a divine testament. Finally, he pronounces anathema on all who bring in anything besides the Gospel. We set against them the consensus of the Fathers, who deny that any doctrine may be introduced into the Church that is not merely against, but apart from, Scripture; not merely contrary to it but alien, foreign, and different from that which the Churches received from the Apostles, and the Apostles from Christ. Now, after the plain words of the Apostle, after the clearest suffrages of the Fathers, in such a light of truth and such a consensus of antiquity, to inculcate so often and so shamelessly that the opinion of the Fathers is against the express words of the Fathers: what is this but openly to profess that one is not going to care about the truth, but is a hired man, and rages with a Jesuitical brow?

units.la: Theodoretus quæst. in Levitic. quæritque, quomodo intelligi debeat ignis alienus? Et post quædam verba sic ait: Ex quibus docemur, non debere nos extinguere spiritum, sed accendere gratiam, quam accepimus: extraneum, nihil ad sacram Scripturam inducere, contentos esse doctrina Spiritus sancti, abominari omnes hereses: quarum fautores nonnulla verba divina fabulas addiderunt, alii suas commentationes impias sententiæ Scriptura præstulerunt. Hæc ille. Docer igitur Scripturam
units.tr: Theodoret, in his Questions on Leviticus, asks how "strange fire" ought to be understood. And after some words he says: From these things we are taught that we ought not to quench the Spirit but to kindle the grace which we have received; that we should not introduce anything foreign into Sacred Scripture, should be content with the teaching of the Holy Spirit, and should abhor all heresies, whose defenders have added certain divine words to fables, while others have preferred their own impious commentaries to the sentence of Scripture. So he. Scripture is therefore taught
