units.la: I Re ce con tem Apo doc clef esse regulam immutabilem, & [?]quaecunque, qui nihil extraneum admittere possit. Et Tridentinos veteratores probat esse imitatores Nadab & Abiud, qui ignem alium sacrificiis intulerunt; sic istos cum igne extraneo coram Domino apparere, quum extraneum quicquam ad sacram Scripturam vel inferunt, vel conferunt. Probat etiam, eosdem Tridentinos in eo consentire cum antiquis haereticis, quod traditiones suas, fabulas illas suas Tridentinas, Scripturis vel praeferunt, vel coaequant, non contenti doctrina Spiritus sancti. Atque hoc, Theodoreti iudicio, est extinguere spiritum.
units.tr: ...is a changeless rule, and whatever [illegible in the scan], which can admit nothing foreign. And he shows that the Tridentine old deceivers are imitators of Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire in their sacrifices; so that these men appear before the Lord with strange fire whenever they either bring in or join anything foreign to Sacred Scripture. He also shows that these same Tridentines agree with the ancient heretics in this, that they either prefer their own traditions, those Tridentine fables of theirs, to Scripture or make them equal to it, not content with the teaching of the Holy Spirit. And this, in Theodoret's judgement, is to quench the Spirit.

units.la: Theophylactus: {a}Nec a Scriptura verbis, quae Spiritus sanctus locutus est, illustratis, semper ad divina nos educunt veritatem, neq; nunquam opinionibus seducti, neq; mundanis vanitatibus inescari permittimur. Haec ille. Ita probat Scripturas esse regulam & fidei, & morum. Sic docuerunt Graeci: veniamus iam ab Ecclesia Graeca ad Latinam.
units.tr: Theophylact: {a} Nor, when the words which the Holy Spirit spoke are explained from Scripture, do they always lead us to the divine truth, nor are we ever permitted to be led astray by opinions or allured by worldly vanities. So he. Thus he proves that Scripture is the rule both of faith and of morals. So the Greeks taught. Let us now pass from the Greek Church to the Latin.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Latinorum Patrum testimonia referuntur.
units.tr: The testimonies of the Latin Fathers are cited.

units.la: IRenaeus tradit, Polycarpum, quum sub Aniceto Romam venisset, multos haereticos conuertisse ad Ecclesiam Dei. {b}annuntian- tem unam, inquit ille, & solam hanc veritatem, ab Apostolis accepisse se, quae & Ecclesia tradidit. {c}Hic docuit semper, quae ab Apostolis didicerat, quae & Ecclesia tradidit, & sola sunt vera. Haec Polycarpus
units.tr: Irenaeus relates that Polycarp, when he came to Rome under Anicetus, converted many heretics to the Church of God, proclaiming, he says, that the one and only truth he had received from the Apostles is what the Church also hands down. "He always taught what he had learned from the Apostles, which the Church also hands down, and which alone is true." So Polycarp, the Apostolic man.

units.la: Apostolicus. Hoc est ergo Apostolicum, nihil aliud Ecclesiæ tradere, quam quod ab Apostolis hauserit. Idem habet Irenæus ipse: {a}Audius, inquit, a quodam presbytero, qui audiuerat ab his, qui Apostolos viderunt, & ab his, quos didicerant, sufficere vateribus, de his, quæ sine consilio spiritus egerunt, eam, quæ ex Scripturis esset, correptionem. Hæc ille. Hic igitur habemus Apostolicam etiam traditionem, de regula fidei, & plenitudine Scripturæ.
units.tr: So it is Apostolic to hand down nothing in the Church except what has been received from the Apostles. Irenaeus himself says the same: "I heard from a certain presbyter, who had heard from those who had seen the Apostles, and from those whom they had taught, that the correction drawn from the Scriptures suffices for the elders, in regard to those things which were done without the counsel of the Spirit." Thus far Irenaeus. Here, then, we have an Apostolic tradition also concerning the rule of faith and the fullness of Scripture.

units.la: Idemque Irenæus sic docet: {b}Non per aliós dispositionem salutis cognovimus, quam per eos, per quos Euangelium peruenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc prædicauerunt, postea vero per Dei voluntatem in Scripturis nobis tradiderunt, fundamentum & columnam fidei nostræ futurum. Ad hoc testimonium respondet Bellarminus: {c}Irenæum non dicere, nihil Apostolos prædicasse, quam quod scripserunt: sed tantum scripsisse Euangelium, quod antea prædicauerunt. Quod verum est, inquit, & non contra nos.
units.tr: Irenaeus also teaches this: We have come to know the arrangement of salvation through no others than those through whom the Gospel has come to us; which indeed they first preached, and afterward, by the will of God, handed down to us in the Scriptures, to be the foundation and pillar of our faith. Bellarmine answers this testimony: Irenaeus does not say that the Apostles preached nothing except what they wrote, but only that they wrote the Gospel which they had preached before. This is true, he says, and not against us.

units.la: Verba igitur Irenæi sunt examinanda. Primum dicit, non per alios viam salutis nos cognoscere, quam per Apostolos. Si quis respondeat, traditiones etiam non scriptas esse ab Apostolis: affirmat Irenæus, dispositionem illam salutis esse in Euangelio, & ad nos peruenisse per eos, per quos peruenit Euangelium. Deinde dicit Irenæus, Apostolos hanc Euangelii doctrinam primum prædicasse, deinde in Scripturis tradidisse. Quid tradiderunt in Scripturis? illud ipsum, quod antea prædicauerunt. uerum ipsum & po tum & co bus [?]
units.tr: I must therefore examine the words of Irenaeus. First, he says that we know the way of salvation through no others than the Apostles. If someone replies that the Apostles also handed down unwritten traditions, Irenaeus asserts that this arrangement of salvation is in the Gospel and has reached us through those through whom the Gospel reached us. Next, Irenaeus says that the Apostles first preached this doctrine of the Gospel and afterwards handed it down in the Scriptures. What did they hand down in the Scriptures? The very same thing that they had preached before. The very truth itself [the remaining words of this unit are too garbled in the scan to translate reliably].

units.la: Etia mni reta inqui loct mus lige qua rum lute ritia not
units.tr: [This unit is too garbled in the scan to translate reliably.]

units.la: Sect Apo lior dan Hæ ade mu fec quo nan har etia pra gerunt. Postremo affirmat Irenæus, illud ipsum, quod Apostoli primum prædicarunt, & postea scripserunt, fidei nostræ fundamentum esse, & columnam. Ergo fundamentum & columna fidei nostræ non est in traditionibus non scriptis, sed in Scripturis Apostolicis.
units.tr: [The opening words of this unit are too garbled in the scan to translate reliably.] Lastly, Irenaeus affirms that the very thing which the Apostles first preached and afterwards wrote down is the foundation and pillar of our faith. Therefore the foundation and pillar of our faith is not in unwritten traditions but in the Apostolic Scriptures.

units.la: Sed attendite subterfugium Cardinalis. Etiamsi, inquit, dicerer Irenæos, Apostolos omnia scripsisse, quæ prædicarant; nihil dice-reraduersus[?] sententiam nostram. Sunt enim, inquit, duo diligenter notanda, tum ad hunc locum, tum ad alia multa intelligenda. Audiamus quæso, quæ Dominus Cardinalis tam diligenter notanda monet. Primum est, inquit, quædam in doctrina, tam fidei, quam morum esse simpliciter omnibus necessaria ad salutem, alia non simpliciter necessaria per notitiam explicitam, sed satis esse, si implicita sit notitia, suscipiendi ea, quæ Ecclesia proponit. Secundo, ea, quæ sunt simpliciter necessaria, Apostolos consuevisse omnibus prædicare: aliorum autem non omnia omnibus, sed quædam solis Prælatis, Episcopis, & Presbyteris. Hæc ille. Atque ad huius rei confirmationem adducit Apostoli verba, Sapientiam loqui-mur inter perfectos. Prælatos Pontificios perfectos illos esse affirmat Bellarminus, apud quos reconditam illam traditionum doctrinam reposuerint Apostoli: atque adversus hanc sententiam Irenæum nihil dixisse putat, etiamsi dicat, Apostolos omnia scripsisse, quæ prædicarunt.
units.tr: But notice the Cardinal's escape route. "Even if," he says, "Irenaeus were to say that the Apostles wrote everything they preached, he would say nothing against our view. For there are two things," he says, "which must be carefully noted, both for this passage and for understanding many others. Let us hear, I beg you, what the Lord Cardinal so carefully bids us note. The first is that some things in doctrine, both of faith and of morals, are simply necessary for all to salvation, while others are not simply necessary by explicit knowledge, but it is enough for salvation that the knowledge be implicit, so that one accepts what the Church proposes. Second, the things that are simply necessary the Apostles were accustomed to preach to all; but of the others not all things to all, but certain things only to the prelates, bishops and presbyters." Thus far he. And to confirm this he adduces the words of the Apostle: "We speak wisdom among the perfect." Bellarmine affirms that the perfect are the Papist prelates, among whom the Apostles stored up that hidden doctrine of traditions; and he thinks Irenaeus said nothing against this view, even though he says the Apostles wrote everything they preached.

units.la: Atqui si Apostoli omnia scripserunt, quæ prædicarunt, profecto scripta sunt ea etiam, quæ Prælatis, & Episcopis, & perfectis prædicarunt. Nam qui omnia dicit, nihil excludit. Sed sic oportuit Antichristi satellites patrum suorum mensuram implere, & in antiquorum hæreticorum vestigiis sine pudore insistere. Hanc enim, quam a profunditatibus Satanæ proponit Cardinalis doctrinam, vetustissimam fuisse antiquorum hereticorum cantilenam, sancti Patres produnt. Quum enim ex verbo scripto sua delira probare non possent, ad traditiones recurrere solere antiquos hæreticos, antiqui & sancti Patres tradunt. Idem sancti Patres narrant, antiquos hereticos Scripturas de imperfectione accusasse[?], & docuisse, in Scripturis non contineri totam doctrinam necessariam de fide ac moribus, ac proinde præter verbum Dei scriptum requiri traditiones: illas traditiones ab iis scilicet exceptas fuisse, qui perfecti habebantur. Probant iidem antiqui & sancti Patres, antiquos hæreticos in hanc sententiam Scripturæ locos rapuisse: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Et: Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed ea non potestis portare modo. Et: Tenete traditiones, quas tradidi per sermonem, sive per epistolam accepistis. Et: O Timothee depositum custodi: & reliquos eius generis, quos omnes Tridentini hodie ad eandem causam rapiunt, maxime Bellarminus lib. de verb. Dei non script. cap. 5. Et quia universa traditionis doctrina ex istis fundamentis subsistit, non erit inutile, Sicut ex antiquis Patribus eadem an- riquorum haereticorum artes obseruemus, quibus nunc Iesuitae Ecclesiam D[?]s[?]I oppu- gnant.
units.tr: But if the Apostles wrote everything they preached, then surely those things also were written which they preached to prelates, bishops and the perfect. For whoever says "everything" excludes nothing. But so it was necessary for the satellites of Antichrist to fill up the measure of their fathers and, without shame, to tread in the footsteps of the ancient heretics. For the Holy Fathers report that the doctrine the Cardinal puts forward, drawn from the depths of Satan, was the most ancient song of the old heretics. For the ancient and holy Fathers relate that when the heretics could not prove their deliriums from the written Word, they used to have recourse to traditions. The same holy Fathers tell that the ancient heretics accused the Scriptures of imperfection and taught that the whole doctrine necessary concerning faith and morals is not contained in the Scriptures, and that therefore, besides the written Word of God, traditions are required; and that those traditions were received by those who were held to be perfect. The same ancient and holy Fathers prove that the ancient heretics snatched these passages of Scripture for this opinion: We speak wisdom among the perfect. And: I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. And: Hold the traditions which I delivered by word or by letter. And: O Timothy, keep the deposit. And the rest of that sort, which all the Tridentines today drag to the same cause, especially Bellarmine in the book on the unwritten Word of God, chapter 5. And because the whole doctrine of tradition rests on these foundations, it will not be useless to observe, from the ancient Fathers, the same arts of the ancient heretics by which the Jesuits now assail the Church.

units.la: Irenæus sic scribit: argumentantur haeretici, in accusationem contrariarum Scripturarum, quasi non recte habeant, nec sint ex authoritate, & quia varie sint dictae, & quia non possit ex his veritas inueniri ab his, qui nesciunt traditionem. Non enim per literas tradita est illa, sed per viuam vocem. Ob quam causam & Paulum dicebat: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. (Audiat Dominus Cardinalis, eadem protulisse haereticos antiquos, quae profert ipse ad defensionem traditionum non scripturarum.) Addit Irenæus: Hanc sapientiam mutuo quidem ipsorum esse dicit, quam à semetipsis adinuenire fictionem. Haec Irenæus. Agnoscimus formam infinitorum verborum, quam ab antiquis haereticis mutuantur Iesuitae. Utrique in Scripturarum abrogatione pariter conspirant, utrique traditiones non scriptas pariter extollunt, utrique de suis perfectis pariter gloriantur, utrique eadem Apostoli verba pari blasphemia ad infamiam suam confirmandam arripiunt.
units.tr: Irenaeus writes thus: The heretics argue, in accusing the Scriptures, as if they were not rightly held or not authoritative, and because they are variously expressed, and because the truth cannot be found in them by those who do not know the tradition. For it was not handed down in writing, but by the living voice. For this reason Paul also said: We speak wisdom among the perfect. (Let the Lord Cardinal hear that the ancient heretics put forward the same things which he himself puts forward in defence of unwritten traditions.) Irenaeus adds: He says that this wisdom is indeed borrowed from one another, which they themselves have invented as fiction. Thus Irenaeus. We recognise the pattern of endless words which the Jesuits borrow from the ancient heretics. Both alike conspire in the abrogation of the Scriptures; both alike extol unwritten traditions; both alike glory in their perfect ones; both alike seize the same words of the Apostle with equal blasphemy to confirm their infamy.

units.la: Terrullianus similiter haereticorum ingenium ita depingit, quasi ipsos Iesuitas ex industria describeret, aut quasi Domini Cardinalis libros legisset. b Eadem, inquit, dementia & praesumptio confitentur (haeretici) Apostolos quidem nobis ignorasse, sed non omnia potuisse illas omnibus tradidisse, sed quaedam palam, & vniuersis; quaedam secreto & pauci[?].
units.tr: Tertullian likewise depicts the nature of the heretics in such a way as if he were describing the Jesuits themselves on purpose, or as if he had read the Lord Cardinal's books. The same madness and presumption, he says, the heretics confess: that the Apostles indeed were ignorant of some things, but could not deliver everything to everyone; some things openly and to all, others secretly and to a few.

units.la: b [?] Marginal mark "b" beside the Tertullian note, partly illegible in the scan. paucis demandasse, atque hac Paulum voluisse. [O Timothee depositum custodi.] Athanasius testatur, eadem ab Ario iactata fuisse. Sic enim Arius: {a}Ecclesiae Dei secundum fidem, per spiritum Dei, veritate, qui sanctum Dei Spiritum acceperunt, ego ita didici. Augustinus eandem haereticorum actes hoc modo aperit: {b}Omnes insipientissimi haeretici, qui se Christianos vocari volunt, sed actus fermentorum suorum, quos maxime exhorret sensus humanus, haec occasione Euangelica sententia colore colorare conantur, vbi Dominus ait: Adhuc multa habeo vobis dicere, sed ea non potestis portare modo. Haec Augustinus. Ita igitur sancti Patres narrant nobis, cum quibus haereticis certamen illis fuerit, nempe cum iis, qui pro traditionibus non scriptis pugnabant ex iisdem Scripturae locis, ex quibus Iesuitae eandem hodie contra nos eandem suscipiunt.
units.tr: [The Latin continues:] ...they committed to a few, and that Paul meant this: [O Timothy, keep the deposit.] Athanasius testifies that the same things were bandied about by Arius. For thus Arius: I have learned this in this way, from the Churches of God, according to faith, through the Spirit of God, by truth, who have received the Holy Spirit of God. Augustine reveals the same device of the heretics in this way: All the most foolish heretics, who wish to be called Christians, but who try to colour the deeds of their own leaven, which the human mind most abhors, with this Gospel saying on occasion, where the Lord says: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. Thus Augustine. So the holy Fathers relate to us with which heretics they had their contest: namely with those who fought for unwritten traditions from the same passages of Scripture from which the Jesuits today take up the same stance against us.

units.la: Restat, vt Apostoli verba illa, sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, breuiter aperiamus; ne aliqua haereticis latebra relinquatur. Perfectos non intelligit Apostolus Praelatos Pontificios, nec electos Arianos, nec perfectos Manichaeos; sed quicunque vere credunt, & ex Euangelii doctrina iustificationem & sanctificationem consequuntur in Christo Iesu, qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, iustitia, sanctificatio, & redemptio. Haec est sapientia nostra, & perfectio. Apostolus enim Epistola ad Colossenses ait: Quem (Christum) annunciamus, corripientes omnem hominem, & docentes omnem hominem in omni sapientia; vt exhibeamus omnem ἄν-θρωπον
units.tr: It remains that we briefly explain those words of the Apostle, we speak wisdom among the perfect, lest any hiding place be left to the heretics. The Apostle does not mean by "perfect" the Papist prelates, nor the elect of the Arians, nor the perfect of the Manichaeans; but whoever truly believes and, from the doctrine of the Gospel, obtains justification and sanctification in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. This is our wisdom and perfection. For the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Colossians: Whom (Christ) we proclaim, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man [ἄνθρωπον]

units.la: a Orat. 2. contr. Arian.
units.tr: a Orat. 2. contr. Arian.

units.la: b in Ioan. tract 97. [illegible, ~12 letters] omnem hominem perfectum in Christo. Isdem verbis vtitur Apostolus vtroqi loco. Docet, quænam sit illa sapientia, quam loquitur inter perfectos; doctrina scilicet Euangelii, quam annuntiat. Docet etiam, quinam sint perfecti illi, nempe quicunque vere credunt: Docentes, inquit, omnem hominem in omni sapientia, vt sistamus omnem hominem perfectum in Christo. Itaq; Chrysostomus sic interpretatur hæc verba: a Sapientiam autem prædicationem, & salutis modum, hoc est, per crucem salutem: perfectos vero, credentes appellat. Hæc ille. Cui assentiuntur Theodoretus, Oicumenius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Lyra in hunc modum. Quod igitur Apostolus affirmat de omnibus sanctis, qui Euangelicam sapientiam suscipiunt, quiq; fidem & Spiritum sanctum habent: id si cum Manichæis, & Arianis, ad electos suos, cum Valentinianis, Cerdonianis, Marcionistis, Pontificiis ad perfectos suos, & Præsulatos restringas, nonne manifestam vim intuleris Apostolo? Sic scilicet oportuit eos in stuporem corripi, qui propter traditiones Babylonicas Scripturis obgarniunt. Sanctificatio nostra est perfectio nostra, quam hæretici omnes, maxime vero Pontificii ignorant.
units.tr: b in Ioan. tract 97. [illegible] every man perfect in Christ. The Apostle uses the same words in both places. He teaches what that wisdom is which he speaks of among the perfect: namely the doctrine of the Gospel, which he proclaims. He also teaches who those perfect ones are, namely all who truly believe: "teaching," he says, "every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ." Accordingly Chrysostom interprets these words thus: "By wisdom he means the preaching and the manner of salvation, that is, salvation through the cross; but he calls the perfect those who believe." So he. Theodoret, Oecumenius, Ambrose, Jerome and Lyra agree in this way. If you restrict to the Manichaeans and Arians their "elect," to the Valentinians, Cerdonians and Marcionites their "perfect," and to the Papists their "perfect" and prelates, what the Apostle affirms of all the saints who receive the evangelical wisdom and have faith and the Holy Spirit, will you not have plainly done violence to the Apostle? Surely those who, on account of Babylonian traditions, cloud the Scriptures ought to be struck with astonishment. Our sanctification is our perfection, which all heretics, and especially the Papists, do not know.

units.la: Tertullianus (vt ad institutum nostrum redeamus) de Scripturis contra traditiones non scriptas sic disserit: b Ideo sibi damnatum dixit Apostolum hæreticum, quia & in quo damnatur, sibi elegit. Nobis vero nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere ducere licet, sed nec eligere, quod alius ex arbitrio suo induxerit. Apostolos Dominus habemus auctores, qui nec ipsi quisquam ex suo arbitrio, quod inducerent, elegerunt, sed acceptam à Christo disciplinam fideli-ter nationibus adnunciarunt. {a} Nobis non est opus in-quisitione post Evangelium, quam credimus, nihil de-siderare ultra credere, hoc enim primùm credimus, non esse, quod ultra credere debemus [?].
units.tr: Tertullian (to return to our purpose) argues about the Scriptures against unwritten traditions thus: "Therefore he said that the Apostle was condemned by himself as a heretic, because he chose for himself that in which he is condemned. But for us it is not permitted to bring in anything by our own judgment, nor to choose what another has brought in by his own judgment. We have the Apostles as our authors, who did not themselves choose anything by their own judgment to introduce, but faithfully proclaimed to the nations the discipline received from Christ." {a} We have no need of inquiry after the Gospel; having believed it, we want nothing further to believe, for this we believe first, that there is nothing else we ought to believe beyond it.

units.la: Unum pro traditionibus non scriptis testimonium obiiciunt nobis Pontificii è Tertulliano. {b} Horum, inquit, si legem ex apostolis Scri-pturarum, nullam haereticis traditio tam praeiudicet auctrix, consuetudo confirmatrix, fides observatrix [?].
units.tr: The Papists throw at us one testimony for unwritten traditions, from Tertullian: "Of these, if the tradition, the author of the Scriptures from the apostles, prejudges no heretic, custom confirms and faith observes..." {b}

units.la: Respondeo, haec non esse contra nos. Disputat de corona militis, quum iam ad Montani paracletum transisset. Quaerit, an traditio non scripta suscipienda sit? Deinde multas traditiones non scriptas profert, quod renuntiamus Diabolo in Baptismo, quod ter mergimur, quod amplius aliquid respondemus, quàm Dominus in Evangelio determinavit, quod lactis & mellis concordiam praegustamus, quod ad omnem progressum, ad omnem aditum, & exitum, fronte crucis signaculo terimus. Plura huius generis commemorat. Deinde, si quis idem sentiendum iudicet de corona, respondet, non esse eandem rationem harum traditionum, & coronae: quum illas natura defendat, quae prima omnium disciplina est. Coronam autem militum contra naturam esse contendit. Hinc magni ingenii pervertersitas in eo se prodit libro, quod unius militis repenti-num. num factum contra iudicium Ecclesiæ probauerit. Verum quicquid de traditionibus docuit, nec est contra antiquam Ecclesiam, nec contra nos. Nam traditiones non scriptas probas, quæ non in doctrina, sed tantum in disciplina ecclesiastica constituerint. Bellarminus, & Tridentini omnes pro traditionibus pugnant, vt dogmata fidei, quæ in Scripturis non habentur, per traditiones confirmentur. Vbicunque vero Patres de traditionibus non scriptis loquuntur, quæ ad disciplinam ecclesiasticam pertinent, ea omnia referunt isti, vt confirmens doctrinam aliquam, quæ non habetur in Scripturis. Hoc vero est contra sententiam, sensumque Patrum, imo vero contra eorum communem consensum.
units.tr: I reply that these words are not against us. He is discussing the soldier's crown, after he had already passed over to Montanus the Paraclete. He asks whether an unwritten tradition ought to be accepted. Then he brings forward many unwritten traditions: that we renounce the devil in baptism, that we are dipped three times, that we answer more than the Lord determined in the Gospel, that we taste in advance the harmony of milk and honey, and that at every going forward, every entering and leaving, we wear away the sign of the cross on the forehead. He mentions many more of this kind. Then, if anyone judges that the same should be thought about the crown, he answers that the reason for these traditions and for the crown is not the same, since he defends those by nature, which is the first discipline of all, whereas he contends that the soldier's crown is contrary to nature. Hence the perversity of a great intellect is revealed in that book, in that he approved the sudden act of one soldier against the judgment of the Church. But whatever he taught about traditions is neither against the ancient Church nor against us. For he approves of unwritten traditions which have been established not in doctrine but only in ecclesiastical discipline. Bellarmine and all the Tridentines fight for traditions so that doctrines of faith which are not found in the Scriptures may be confirmed through traditions. But wherever the Fathers speak of unwritten traditions that pertain to ecclesiastical discipline, those men refer all of them to the confirmation of some doctrine which is not found in the Scriptures. This, however, is contrary to the opinion and sense of the Fathers, indeed contrary to their common consensus.

units.la: Quod Tertullianum attinet; optimus ipse sui interpres, docet, ea, quæ in disciplina sunt, posse ab Ecclesia mutari, & admittere nouitatem correctionis: quæ autem de fide sunt, esse prorsus immobilia, nec mutari posse. Et quia de regula fidei pulcherrime disputat in eo libro, quem de præscriptionibus aduersus hæreticos inscripsit, inde nonnulla, quæ proposito nostro congruunt, annotabo. Primo testatur, qui ad regulam fidei adiecerit quicquam, non tantum contrarium, sed aliud, esse fidei negatorem, his verbis: {a}Attendim si quid delinquerendo, etc. didi, & aliud deinde pure requirendum, sicut vtique, & aliud esse [illegible, ~6 letters], [?] fidem meam deserent, negatur [?] iuncior. Hæc ille.
units.tr: As for Tertullian, he is his own best interpreter: he teaches that the things which belong to discipline can be changed by the Church and admit the novelty of correction, but the things which concern faith are altogether immovable and cannot be changed. And because he argues most beautifully about the rule of faith in the book he wrote against the heretics, On Prescription, I shall note from it some points which agree with our purpose. First, he testifies that whoever adds anything to the rule of faith, not only something contrary but something other, is a denier of the faith, in these words: "Attend, if through sinning... I have said, and then something else must be sought, just as surely something else is... they desert my faith, it is denied... more..." So he.

units.la: Deinde regulam fidei explicat: Regula est fidei, vt hinc, quid credamus, profiteamur; illa scilicet, quae creditur. Subiungit autem breuem Scripturae summulam, quam vocat fidei regulam; post-ea sic ait: {a}Haec regula à Christo instituta, nullas habet apud nos quaestiones, nisi quas haereses inferunt, & quae haereticos faciunt. Fides in regula posita est. Ac proinde alibi dicit: {b}Regula fidei vna omnino est, sola immobilis, & irreformabilis, credendi scilicet in vnicum Deum omnipotentem, &c. Deinde subiungit summam Symboli Apostolici: {c}Haec, inquit, lege fidei manente, cetera iam disciplina & conuersationis admittunt nouitatem correctionis. Haec ille. Quis nostram sententiam explicatius aut accuratius tradere potuit? Plura ex eodem connectamus: {d}Vnde autem extranei & inimici Apostolis haeretici, nisi ex diuersitate doctrinae, quam vnusquisque de suo arbitrio aduersus Apostolos aut prophetas, aut recepit? {e}Omnia Apostolis secundum Deum docuerunt, omnia euangelizare voluerunt. {f}Aufer haereticis, quae cum ethnicis sapiunt, vt de Scripturis solis sistant quaestiones, & stare non poterunt. Haec ille. Quis fortius aduersus doctrinas non scriptas? Pontificii deploratam caulam habentes, verba Patrum contra exploratam ipsorum sententiam sensumque proferunt. Patres docuerunt, quod & nos docemus, in disciplina ecclesiastica a traditiones admitti non scriptas, in doctrina nihil inducendum, nisi quod scriptum est: quia nihil ex nostro arbitrio inducere licet, nec eligere, quod alius ex arbitrio suo induxerit: quia
units.tr: Then he explains the rule of faith: "The rule of faith is that from it we profess what we believe; namely that which is believed." He then adds a brief summary of Scripture, which he calls the rule of faith, and afterwards says: {a} This rule, instituted by Christ, has among us no questions except those which heresies bring in and which make heretics. The faith is set in the rule. And therefore elsewhere he says: {b} The rule of faith is altogether one, alone immovable and unreformable, namely, of believing in the one God almighty, etc. Then he adds the sum of the Apostles' Creed: {c} This, he says, the rule of faith remaining, the rest, namely discipline and conduct, admit the novelty of correction. So he. Who could have set forth our opinion more clearly or accurately? Let us gather more from the same author: {d} Whence otherwise are the heretics strangers and enemies to the Apostles, except from the diversity of doctrine which each has received from his own judgment against the Apostles or the prophets? {e} All things the Apostles taught according to God, all things they wished to proclaim as good news. {f} Take away from the heretics what savours of the pagans, so that they may hold questions only from the Scriptures, and they will not be able to stand. So he. Who has argued more strongly against unwritten doctrines? The Papists, having a desperate cause, bring forward the words of the Fathers against their own well-known opinion and sense. The Fathers taught what we also teach: that in ecclesiastical discipline unwritten traditions are admitted, but nothing is to be introduced into doctrine except what is written, because it is not permitted to introduce anything by our own judgment, nor to choose what another has introduced by his own judgment; because whoever thinks something else must be sought, deserting the faith, is found to be a denier; because the rule of faith is one, immovable, unreformable, instituted by Christ; because the rule of faith ought always to remain the same, while the rest admit the novelty of correction; because heretics, strangers and enemies to the Apostles, are convicted by the diversity of doctrine; because the Apostles taught all things according to God; because if heretics hold questions from the Scriptures alone, they cannot stand. Thus Tertullian confirmed the Catholic opinion against the Tridentine novelties.

units.la: [Right page, cropped at the scan edge; visible line ends only: qui, nega, imm, quia, relic, quia, diue, post, quia, sistat, tent, dent, T, ciun, de Sc, R, ctius, co., ad h, clesi, Non, refut, mod, & eg, cont, Scrip, prau, solea, ptur, quir, ftian, num] qui aliud requirendum putat, fidem deserens, negator inuenitur; quia regula fidei est vna, immobilis, irreformabilis, à Christo instituta; quia regula fidei eadem semper manere debet, reliqua nouitatem correctionis admittere; quia hæretici Apostolis extranei & inimici, et diuersitate doctrinæ conuincuntur; quia Apostoli omnia secundum Deum docuerunt; quia si hæretici de solis Scripturis quæstiones sistant, stare non possunt. Ita Tertullianus sententiam Catholicam contra nouitates Tridentinas confirmauit.
units.tr: [Right page, cropped at the scan edge; the visible line ends only are garbled, but the sense is recoverable:] whoever thinks something else must be sought, deserting the faith, is found to be a denier; because the rule of faith is one, immovable, unreformable, instituted by Christ; because the rule of faith ought always to remain the same, while the rest admit the novelty of correction; because heretics, strangers and enemies to the Apostles, are convicted by the diversity of doctrine; because the Apostles taught all things according to God; because if heretics hold questions from the Scriptures alone, they cannot stand. Thus Tertullian confirmed the Catholic opinion against the Tridentine novelties.

units.la: Tridentini præterea è Tertulliano obiiciunt: {a}Hæreticos non esse admittendos ad illam de Scripturarum traditionem.
units.tr: Moreover, the Tridentines object from Tertullian: {a} Heretics are not to be admitted to that disputation about the tradition of the Scriptures.

units.la: Respondeo: Vt Tertulliani sententia rectius teneatur, cum ex ipso Tertulliano explico. 1. Hæreticos dicit non esse admittendos ad hanc disputationem. Non loquitur de Ecclesia, non de orthodoxis; sed de hæreticis. Non autem negat hæreticos ab orthodoxis refutandos esse solis Scripturis. Nam quomodo potest illud damnare, quod & docuit, & egregie præstitit. Nullâ enim aliâ armaturâ contra hæreticos ubique utitur, quam solis Scripturis: sed cum hæretici Scripturas depravare suis expositionibus, atque adulterare soleant, negat hæreticos admittendos ad Scripturarum expositionem: Quia, {b}vbi, in-quit, apparet, esse veritatem disciplinæ & fidei Christianæ, illic esse veritas Scripturarum, & expositionum, & omnium traditionum Christianarum: aperte loquitur de expositionibus Scripturarum. 1. Quum hæreticos non admittat ad Scripturas, non hoc agit, vt traditiones non scriptas admittendas probet. Itaque frustrantur Pontificii. Nam si Tertullianus Scripturas solus non admitteret, vt ostenderet, traditiones non scriptas de fide, esse admittendas, aliquid pro Tridentinis attulisset: Sed traditiones omnes non scriptas de fide, penitus repudiandas docet. Itaq; quicquid aliud intelligat, modo non hoc ipsum velit, quod Pontificii tantis clamoribus ingeminant, certe sententia Tertulliani Pontificiâ[?] causam nihil adiuuat. Illis probandum fuerat, Scripturarum auctoritatem ab illo minui, vt traditiones non scriptas in doctrina & fide stabiliat, quod nunquam probare possunt. 3. Rationem adfert Tertullianus, qua adductus, hæreticos nō admittendos iudicat ad disputationem de Scripturis: Quia, inquit, disputare debes, cui competat Scripturarum possessio, ne is admittatur ad eam, cui nullo modo competit. Vtitur verbis iuris: Si quis possessionem litigando obtinere contra ius conatur, nimirum esset[?], talem litigatorem ad possessionem admittere, quamuis multis verbis & clamoribus id peteret: sicut, hæreticos non admittendos esse ad hanc disputationem, quia possessio Scripturarum ad eos iure non pertinet, sed ad Ecclesiam Catholicam. Scripturæ ergo nō sunt hæreticorum possessio, sed Ecclesiæ possessio, & hæreditas. Itaq; Ecclesiam subinde hæreticos alloquentem inducit: Quid in meo agis? non mea[?] hæresium Anabaptistarum.
units.tr: I reply: so that Tertullian's opinion may be held more rightly, I explain it from Tertullian himself. 1. He says that heretics are not to be admitted to this disputation. He is not speaking of the Church, nor of the orthodox, but of heretics. Yet he does not deny that heretics are to be refuted by the orthodox from the Scriptures alone. For how could he condemn what he both taught and excellently practised? He uses no other armour anywhere against heretics than the Scriptures alone; but since heretics are accustomed to corrupt and adulterate the Scriptures by their own expositions, he denies that heretics are to be admitted to the exposition of the Scriptures, because, {b} as he says, where it appears that the truth of Christian discipline and faith is, there is the truth of the Scriptures, of their expositions, and of all Christian traditions; he plainly speaks of expositions of the Scriptures. 2. Since he does not admit heretics to the Scriptures, he is not doing this to prove that unwritten traditions are to be admitted. Therefore the Papists are mistaken. For if Tertullian alone did not admit the Scriptures, in order to show that unwritten traditions about faith are to be admitted, he would have brought something in favour of the Tridentines; but he teaches that all unwritten traditions about faith are to be utterly rejected. Therefore, whatever else he understands, provided he does not will this very thing which the Papists repeat with such great clamour, certainly Tertullian's opinion helps the Papist cause not at all. They ought to have proved that the authority of the Scriptures was diminished by him, so that he might establish unwritten traditions in doctrine and faith, which they can never prove. 3. Tertullian gives a reason by which he judges that heretics are not to be admitted to disputation about the Scriptures: because, he says, you must dispute to whom possession of the Scriptures belongs, lest one be admitted to them to whom they in no way belong. He uses the words of law: If anyone tries by litigation to obtain possession against right, surely one would not admit such a litigant to possession, however much he might seek it with many words and clamours: just as heretics are not to be admitted to this disputation, because possession of the Scriptures does not belong to them by right, but to the Catholic Church. The Scriptures therefore are not the possession of heretics, but the possession and inheritance of the Church. Accordingly he introduces the Church, addressing heretics from time to time: What are you doing in my house? It is not mine [the words of the Anabaptist heresies].

units.la: 4. Respondeo, multas fuisse rationes antiquis Patribus, quare hæreticos refutandos numquam aggrederentur, non tantum Scripturis, sed & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensu: qui ante solutum Satanam Ecclesiæ consensus ita vigebat in Ecclesia per omnes successiones, ut hic unus consensus sufficere videretur ad omnes hæreticos refellendos. a Ecclesia quid verisimile est, inquit idem Tertullianus, ut tot ac tanta Ecclesiæ unam fidem vsurparint? [?] variasse debuerat error doctrinæ Ecclesiarum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: 4. I reply that the ancient Fathers had many reasons for never undertaking to refute heretics by the consensus of the Catholic Church as well as by Scripture. Before Satan was loosed, the consensus of the Church was so firmly maintained in the Church through all successions that this one consensus seemed sufficient to refute all heretics. Tertullian says again: "Is it likely that so many and so great churches should have all arrived at one faith? The error of the churches' teaching would have had to differ from one church to another." So far he.

units.la: Et quamvis magnam rebus confusionem attulerit Satanas solutus, quemadmodum miserabilis rerum experientia, & desolatio Ecclesiæ demonstrat; ita utrobique eadem potiorum & antiquorum temporum ratio videatur: Idem tamen in hac re per Dei gratiam etiam contra Pontificios nos probaturos speramus, utcunque illi de Ecclesia gloriantur. Non enim veremur sic eos provocare, sicut Patres Ecclesiæ videmus antiquos provocasse hæreticos. Dicimus igitur, quamvis non admittamus Pontificios ad disputationem de Scripturis, quia Scripturas reiicimus, quia Scripturarum possessio non ipsis competat, sed Ecclesiæ Catholicæ; ut, inquam, contra ipsos nihil de Scripturis proferamus: tamen ex ipso Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consensu Pontificios luculentissime refutari posse. Hanc veritatem Deus suo tempore magis magisque quotidie patefaciet, & confirmabit. Atque hoc illud est, quod in his quæstionibus agimus: ut Adversarios non tantum Scripturis, sed & Eccle-fiæ consensu revincendos doceamus.
units.tr: Although Satan, once loosed, has caused great confusion, as the wretched experience of things and the desolation of the Church show, the same reason for the earlier and older times seems to apply in both cases. Still, we hope that, by God's grace, we shall prove this same point in this matter against the Papists as well, however much they boast about the Church. For we do not hesitate to challenge them as the Fathers of the Church are seen to have challenged the heretics of their day. We say, therefore, that although we do not admit the Papists to dispute about the Scriptures, since we reject their Scriptures, because possession of the Scriptures belongs not to them but to the Catholic Church, nevertheless we do not bring forward anything from Scripture against them. Still, the Papists can be most clearly refuted from the very consensus of the Catholic Church. God will reveal and confirm this truth more and more every day in his own time. And this is what we are doing in these questions: showing that our opponents must be refuted not only by Scripture but also by the consensus of the Church.

units.la: Cyprianus Tertullianum, quem magi-strum vocare solebat, sequitur, idemque do-cuit: {a}Unde est ista traditio? Virumne de Do-minica & Evangelica auctoritate desumens, an de Apostolorum mandatu atq; epistolis veniens? Ea enim sarienda[?] esse, quæ scripta sunt, Deus testatur, & proponit ad Iosue dicens: Non recedet liber legis[?] huius ab ore tuo[?]. Sequitur aut de Evangelio præcipitur, aut in Apostolorum epistolis & actibus continetur, observetur etiam hæc sancta traditio.
units.tr: Cyprian follows Tertullian, whom he was accustomed to call his master, and he taught the same thing: "Where does this tradition come from? Does it derive from the authority of the Lord and the Gospel, or does it come from the command and the epistles of the apostles? For God testifies that those things which are written ought to be followed, and he sets this down to Joshua, saying: 'This book of the law shall not depart out of your mouth.' Whatever is commanded by the Gospel, or is contained in the apostles' epistles and Acts, let this holy tradition also be observed."

units.la: Respondet Bellarminus, Cyprianum hæc scripsisse, quum errorem suum tueri[?] vellet, ideo mirum non esse, si more errantium tunc ratiocinaretur. Deinde ait, Augustinum refel-lere hanc Epistolam. Postremo inquit, etsi Cyprianus reiecerit traditiones, quas contra Scripturas esse putabat, non tamen omnes re-iecit, quæ in Scripturis non sunt, nec cum Scripturis pugnant. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies that Cyprian wrote these things when he wished to defend his own error, so it is no wonder if he then reasoned in the manner of those who err. Next, he says that Augustine refuted this epistle. Finally, he says that even if Cyprian rejected traditions which he thought were contrary to Scripture, he did not reject all those which are not in Scripture and do not conflict with it. So far he.

units.la: Quum dicat, Cyprianum more errantium hæc scripsisse, interrogemus hominem, num & reliqui Patres omnes, qui idem cum Cypriano profitentur, more errantium loquan-tur? Quod si verum esse concedat, Pontificii concidunt. Nam si Patres omnes missos faciamus, ut solis Scripturis causa agatur, quomo-do stare possunt Pontificii, qui cum Ethnicis sapiunt, si de solis Scripturis quæstiones fi-stant? Sed Augustinum dicit refutasse hanc Epistolam. At Augustinus non omnia refellit, quæ scripsit Cyprianus in illa Epistola, sed unicam tantum Cypriani opinionem de hæreticorum baptismo, reliqua omnia probat. Et quomodo potuit Augustinus ea refellere, quæ ipse etiam non minore fide ac diligentia docuit, quam Cyprianus? Quod vero Bellarminus de traditionibus contra Scripturas respondet, superius ex Apostolo Patribusque repressimus.
units.tr: Since he says that Cyprian wrote these things in the manner of those who err, let us ask the man whether all the other Fathers who profess the same thing as Cyprian also speak in the manner of those who err. If he grants that this is true, the Papists collapse. For if we set aside all the Fathers, so that the cause is argued from Scripture alone, how can the Papists, who think like the heathen, stand their ground, if the questions are settled from Scripture alone? But he says that Augustine refuted this epistle. Yet Augustine does not refute everything that Cyprian wrote in that epistle, but only Cyprian's single opinion about the baptism of heretics; he approves all the rest. And how could Augustine refute those things which he himself taught with no less faith and diligence than Cyprian? As for what Bellarmine answers about traditions contrary to Scripture, we have already refuted it above from the Apostle and the Fathers.

units.la: Atque vt Cypriani sententia illustrius constet, plura adiiciemus ex eodem testimonia, in quibus nec more errantium loquitur, nec ad ea Pontificii quicquam respondent; {a}Non enim, inquit, nisi Christum sequendum. Quod Christus solus audiri debeat: Pater etiam de cœlo commendat, dicens: Hic est filius meus dilectissimus, in quo bene sensi, ipsum audite. Quare si solus Christus audiendus est, non debemus attendere, quid alius ante nos faciendum putauerit, sed quid qui ante omnes fuit, Christus primo fecerit. Neq; enim hominis consuetudinem, sed Dei veritatem sequi oportet. {b}Sicut fontis aquam ducens, quæ copiosè prius & largiter fluebat, subito deficiat: nunc ad fontem pergitur, vt illic defectionis ratio noscatur, vtrum ex defectu venis in capite, vnde succreuerit, an vero integra inde & plena procurrens, in medio itinere deficiat: vt si vitio interrupti aut bibuli canalis effectum sit, quo minus aqua continua perseueraret ac ingiter fluceret, refecto & confirmato canali ad visum atque ad potum eiusdem aqua collecta eadem veritate atque integritate representetur, qua de fonte profecta fuerit.
units.tr: And so that Cyprian's opinion may appear more clearly, we shall add more testimonies from the same author, in which he neither speaks in the manner of those who err nor do the Papists make any reply to them. "For," he says, "we must follow none but Christ. Only Christ ought to be heard. The Father also commends him from heaven, saying: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.' Therefore, if Christ alone is to be heard, we ought not to attend to what another has thought should be done after us, but to what Christ, who was before all, did first. For we must follow not the custom of man, but the truth of God. When the water of a spring, which before flowed copiously and abundantly, suddenly fails, one goes to the spring to learn the reason for the failure: whether the defect is in the veins at the head, from which it grew, or whether it flowed whole and full from there and fails halfway along its course. If the flow of continuous water and its steady stream has been stopped by a fault in the channel, then once the channel has been repaired and made sound, the water collected is presented for sight and drink with the same truth and integrity with which it came from the spring."

units.la: Quod & nunc facere oportet Dei sacerdotes, præcepta divina servantes, si in aliquo mutaverit & vacillaverit veritas, ad originem Dominicam, Evangelicam & Apostolicam traditionem revertentur.{a} Verbo igitur non insistens, quaecunque docuit, & fecit, discere & facere debemus.{b} {b}Iuniam[?] haereses mul-tiplicantur[?] & schismata, quibus subverterent fidem, veritatem corrumperent, scinderent unitatem. Hoc eo fit, dum ad veritatis originem non redeunt, nec caput quaerunt, nec magistri caelestis doctrina servatur. Haec Cyprianus. Ad quae nihil habent, quod respondeant Pontifici. Solus Christus sequendus, solus audiendus: haereses nascun-tur, dum magistri caelestis doctrina non ser-vatur. Ubi sunt ergo traditiones non scriptae, quae doctrinam continent? Quo maior appa-ret Bellarminus vanitas, qui etiam e Cypriano quodam (de vocatione post baptismum, & de mixtura vini & aquae in calice, id est, de rebus, quae non sunt in doctrina, sed in disciplina ec-clesiastica, quae possunt novitatem correctionis recipere) profert, ad confirmandum verbum illud Tridentinum non scriptum.
units.tr: This is what God's priests must also do now, keeping the divine precepts: if truth has altered or wavered in any point, they must return to the Lord's, the Gospel's and the apostolic tradition as its origin. Therefore, not clinging to the word alone, we must learn and do whatever he taught and did. From this, heresies and schisms multiply, by which men overthrow the faith, corrupt the truth and tear apart the unity. This happens when men do not return to the origin of the truth, do not seek the head, and do not keep to the teaching of the heavenly Master." So far Cyprian. To these words the Papists have no answer. Christ alone is to be followed, Christ alone is to be heard; heresies arise when the teaching of the heavenly Master is not kept. Where, then, are the unwritten traditions which contain doctrine? All the more does Bellarmine's vanity appear, who brings forward from Cyprian some passages (about the call after baptism, and the mixing of wine and water in the chalice, that is, about matters which are not part of doctrine but of ecclesiastical discipline, and which can admit of a novel correction) to confirm that unwritten word of Trent.

units.la: Hilarus sic docuit: {c}Quaedam aut praesumpta, aut sacrilega, aut error. Apostolica doctrina [?]ndemutabilem constitutionem, partim fraudulenter conscissa est, partim audacter transgressa. Haec Hilarus. Regulam fidei vocat [?]ndemutabilem constitutionem doctrinae Apostolicae, quam, dum audacter transgrediuntur Tridentini, in eodem certe & criminis & damnationis consortio, cum antiquis haereticis vinctos teneri, probat Hilarus. Eodem libro Imperato-
units.tr: Hilary taught as follows: "Some things are either presumed, or sacrilegious, or error. The apostolic doctrine, [...] unchangeable constitution, has been partly torn apart by fraud and partly boldly transgressed." So far Hilary. He calls the unchangeable constitution of the apostolic doctrine the rule of faith, and Hilary proves that those who boldly transgress it, the men of Trent, are certainly held bound, in the same fellowship of crime and damnation, with the ancient heretics. In the same book the emperor...

units.la: rem d[?] uersi[?] a Fi[?] pta su[?] boc v[?] anath[?] fit A[?] lariu[?] das t[?] Mot[?] fui p[?] fucu[?] rum Sicu[?] uter[?] Scri[?] ptur[?] lis c[?] illo Qui[?] rim error rum ftri[?] tific[?] rian[?] ptar[?] lari[?] riar[?] pra[?] Qu[?] rem collaudat Hilarius, expetentem controversias fidei, tantum per Scripturas tractari {a}Fidem, inquit, tantum scripturarum, quae scripta sunt, desiderantem. Addit Hilarius: {b}Quo hoc repudiat, Antichristus est, & qui dissimulat, anathema est. Dicant nobis Pontificii, quis sit Antichristus ille, quem praemonstravit Hilarius, qui fidei controversias negat definiendas tantummodo per ea, quae scripta sunt. Monet etiam Hilarius, haereticos in errores sui patrocinium Scripturas praetendere, sed fucum illum haereticum genuino Scripturarum usu, & vera traditione disiectum esse. Sicut enim Diabolus, quum Scripturis abuteretur, à Christo tantummodo per Scripturas reiectus fuerat: sic haeretici Scripturis abutentes, à Patribus nullis aliis telis confossi sunt, nisi tantummodo gladio illo ancipiti è sacris Scripturis extracto. Quid est, inquit Hilarius, {c}fidelibus simul- rius, qui praeter contumaciam illam terrigenarum errorem etiam hoc adiungunt, ut dimina-rum Scripturarum eloquia, pravam sibi professa doctrinae carere ratione. Dicant nobis Pontificii, quinam sint, quos haec verba feriant?
units.tr: ...which Hilary praises, when he desires that controversies of faith be handled only through the Scriptures. "He desires the faith," he says, "only of the Scriptures, which have been written." Hilary adds: "Whoever rejects this is Antichrist, and whoever dissembles is accursed." Let the Papists tell us who that Antichrist is, whom Hilary foreshadowed, who denies that controversies of faith are to be settled only by those things which are written. Hilary also warns that heretics put forward Scripture as a pretext for their errors, but that this heretical disguise has been unmasked by the genuine use of Scripture and by true tradition. For just as the Devil, when he abused Scripture, was repelled by Christ only by means of Scripture, so heretics who abuse Scripture have been pierced by the Fathers with no other weapons than that two-edged sword drawn from the holy Scriptures. "What is it," says Hilary, "to the faithful..., who, besides that stubbornness of the earth-born, also add this, that the words of truncated Scriptures lack any reasonable ground for the doctrine they have professed?" Let the Papists tell us who are the men that these words strike.

units.la: Ex Hilario tamen doctrinam non scriptam probare voluit Cardinalis, quia Hilarius contra Constantium, obiicienti Arriano, Nolo, inquit, verba, quae non scripta sunt, legi: respondet: Haec tandem vestra? Quae Episcopi iubent? Quae Apostolus pradicationis veteri formam? Dic primo, si recte edici[?] pu-tas, nolo aduersus noua venena nouas medicamento-rum comparationes. Quibus verbis, inquit Bel-larminus, {a} duo indicat Hilarius: Unum, prædicationem consubstantialitatis, esse A-postolicæ prædicationis, licet expresse non sit scriptum, Filium esse Patri consubstantialem: Alterum, nomen ipsum, ὁμοούσιον[?], esse quidem nouum, sed tamen retinendum, licet non sit scriptum, quia conforme est prædicationi Apostolicæ. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Yet the Cardinal wished to prove unwritten doctrine from Hilary, because Hilary, against Constantius, when the Arian objected, "I do not wish words which are not written to be read," replies: "Is this finally yours? Is this what the bishops command? Is this the old form of the apostolic preaching? Tell me first, if you think it is rightly stated, I do not want new comparisons of medicines against new poisons." By these words, says Bellarmine, Hilary indicates two things. First, that the preaching of consubstantiality is of apostolic preaching, although it is not expressly written that the Son is consubstantial with the Father. Second, that the name itself, homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], is indeed new, but nevertheless must be retained, although it is not written, because it agrees with apostolic preaching. So far he.

units.la: Respondeo: Frigidissimum esse, & uanissimum, quod obicit. Producant enim Pontifi-cii nouum uocabulum, quod antiquam Scripturarum doctrinam retineat, & nos non erimus molesti: non enim de uerbis litigamus, sed de rebus, de doctrina, & fide. Obiiciebant Arriani, ὁμοούσιον[?] non fuisse totidem syllabis in Scripturis. Quid Patres? Num ad traditiones non scriptas recurrunt? Nusquam; sed ne latum quidem unguem a Scripturæ doctrina se auelli posse profitentur. Docent igitur, rem ipsam, & doctrinam ipsam in Scripturis expresse contineri. Sic Hilarius, Basilius, Augustinus: Doctrina consubstantialitatis expresse habetur in Scripturis. Bellarminus ipse fatetur, hanc rem esse Apostolicæ prædicationis, & conformem Apostolicæ prædicationi. Dormitabat igitur Cardinalis, quum hæc produceret, ut doctrinam non scriptam probaret.
units.tr: I answer that what they object is very cold and very empty. Let the Papists produce a new word that keeps the old doctrine of Scripture, and we will not be troublesome: we are not disputing about words but about things, about doctrine and faith. The Arians objected that homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] was not in Scripture in so many syllables. What did the Fathers do? Did they have recourse to unwritten traditions? Nowhere. They professed that they could not depart a finger's breadth from the doctrine of Scripture. So they taught that the thing itself and the doctrine itself are expressly contained in Scripture. Thus Hilary, Basil and Augustine: The doctrine of consubstantiality is expressly found in Scripture. Bellarmine himself confesses that this matter belongs to apostolic preaching and agrees with it. The Cardinal was asleep, then, when he produced these passages to prove an unwritten doctrine.

units.la: Ambrosius eandem doctrinam retinuit, sic enim docet: {b} Discimus, nihil vel cautionis gratia iungere debere nos mandare: Si quid enim vel adw das, vel detrahas, praeuaricatio quaedam videtur esse mandati. Docet igitur nos praesens series lectionis, neq; detrahere aliquid diminui debere mandatu, neq; addere. Nam si Iohannes haec indicaret de suis scriptis: Si quis apposuerit, inquit, ad haec, adiiciet ei plagas, quae scriptae sunt in libro isto: & qui dempserit de verbis huius prophetiae huius, delebit Deus partem eius de libro vitae: quanto magis nihil divinis mandatis est detrahendum.
units.tr: Ambrose held the same doctrine, for he teaches thus: We learn that we ought not to add anything to a command, even out of caution. For if you either add or take away anything, it seems to be a kind of breach of the command. So the present course of reading teaches us that nothing should be taken away from the command, nor anything added. For if John had indicated this about his own writings: "If anyone shall add to these things, God shall add to him the plagues written in this book, and whoever shall take away from the words of this prophecy, God shall take away his part from the book of life": how much more must nothing be taken away from the divine commands.

units.la: Hieronymus idem habet: {a}Ecclesia Chri-sti, quae habitat lene, & in toto orbe Ecclesias possidens, Spiritu vnitate coniuncta est, & habet vrbes Legis & Prophetarum, Euangelij & Apostolorum, non est egressa de finibus suis, id est, Scripturis sanctis. Ad hoc & plurima huiusmodi, quae nullam admittunt responsionem, prudenter Bellarminus dissimulando nihil omnino respondet. Nam si fines Ecclesiae sunt Scripturae, extra quos fines Ecclesia Christi non est egressa, profecto traditiones non scriptae sunt extra fines Ecclesiae. Idemque Hieronymus sic docet: {b}Hoc, quia de Scripturis non habes auctoritatem, eadem facilitate contemnitur, qua probatur. Haec ille.
units.tr: Jerome has the same: The Church of Christ, which dwells in peace and possesses churches throughout the whole world, is joined by the Spirit in unity, and has the cities of the Law and the Prophets, of the Gospel and the Apostles; it has not gone out of its boundaries, that is, the holy Scriptures. Along with this and many similar passages, which admit of no answer, Bellarmine prudently dissembles and answers nothing at all. For if the boundaries of the Church are the Scriptures, beyond which the Church of Christ has not gone, then certainly unwritten traditions lie outside the boundaries of the Church. And Jerome teaches thus also: Because you have no authority from the Scriptures for this, it is despised with the same ease with which it is asserted. Thus he.

units.la: Ad hoc testimonium respondet Bellarminus: Loquitur de particulari sententia, non vniuersaliter. Respondeo, verum esse, Hieronymum de particulari sententia loqui, sed tamen vniuersaliter, saltem indefinite. Sed nisi nugas ageret hic Sophista, ratio reddenda erat, quare, quum de vna particulari sententia affir-
units.tr: To this testimony Bellarmine replies: "He speaks of a particular opinion, not universally." I reply that it is true Jerome speaks of a particular opinion, but nonetheless universally, at least indefinitely. But unless this Sophist were talking nonsense, he ought to give a reason why, when Jerome affirms about one particular opinion,

units.la: affirmet, non de quauis etiam alia particulari idem sit iudicandum? Deinde non hic propositionum quaestitas[?], sed Hieronymi iudicium exquiritur. Grauissimum Hieronymi iudicium in quolibet particulari idem fuisse, quod in hoc fuerat, ratio conuincit, qua iudicat, Ecclesiam non esse egressam de finibus suis, id est, de sacris Scripturis. Hieronymus etiam Apostolicas confictas traditiones sic refellit: {a}Qua absq; auctoritate[?] & testimonio Scripturarum, quasi traditione Apostolica sponte repperunt, aut confingunt, percussa gladio Dei. Haec sententia Tridentinos perturbat.
units.tr: affirm, the same judgment should not be made of any other particular opinion? Moreover, the question here is not about propositions, but Jerome's judgment is being sought. Reason proves that Jerome's most serious judgment about any particular matter was the same as in this passage, where he judges that the Church has not gone out of its boundaries, that is, out of the holy Scriptures. Jerome also refutes the invented apostolic traditions in this way: Those who, without the authority and testimony of the Scriptures, invent or fabricate things as if they were apostolic traditions, are struck down by the sword of God. This sentence disturbs the Tridentines.

units.la: Sed Bellarminus, mirificus scilicet responsionum artifex, facile eludit: Patet, inquit, solutio: solum enim agit contra eos, qui confingunt aliquid, & tamen videri volunt figmenta sua esse Apostolicas traditiones. Cardinalis rem acu tetigit. Nam Pontificii traditiones confingunt, & tamen videri volunt, figmenta sua esse Apostolicas traditiones. Interea qui pro responsis tantas nugas affert, lectore quaerit[?], vel stupidum, qui inter verbum ut sonitum, rerumq; cognitionem non possit decernere: vel pertinacem in errore, atque ita praeiudicio obfirmatum, utcunq; responsionis umbrae ultro acquiescat. Neque enim pro veritate pugnare velle videtur, sed tantum pro mercede operam navare, ut eos in errore retineat, qui sponte & industria ad veritatem exeunt. Hieronymus praeterea in illa verba: Dominus narrabit in Scriptura populorum, & principum ho-rum[?], rum, qui fuerunt in ea. {a}Videte, inquit, quid di-cat, qui fuerunt, non qui sunt: ut exceptis Apostolis, quicquid posteà aliud docetur, non habeat auctoritatem. Hæc Hieronymus. Num etiam ad hoc pater responsio? Planè patet. Nam efferre aliquid sine verecundia & pudore, hoc Cardinalis est respondere. Respondet: Hieronymum eo loco reiicere ea, quæ sunt aliena à doctrina Apostolica, id est, contraria & repugnantia Scripturis. Hic est Achilleus ille clypeus, vel Delphicus gladius in manu Cardinalis, sine quo causa Pontificia in gravissimo Patrum Senatu stare non potest. Oportet Apostolum æquo hoc animo ferre, omnes Patres hoc libenter pati, scilicet ut eorum verba in alium sensum deflectat Dominus Cardinalis, contra notum & communem verborum sensum: ut præter Evangelium, non sit præter, sed contra: in nullo à præscripto Scripturarum discedere, non sit hoc ipsum, quod verba sonant, sed aliud, quod vult Dominus Cardinalis: exceptis Apostolis nihil aliud docetur, ut nihil aliud, non sit nihil aliud, quod verba sonant, sed contrarium & repugnans: nisi enim Apostolus Patresq; omnes sic sibi improbe illu-di patiantur, Dominus Cardinalis non potest respondere. Quale cor habeat Dominus Cardinalis, nescio; ego certe non possum existimare, hunc hominem serio ad scribendum accedere, atque ex animo hæc dicere, qui non erubescit ita palam Apostolo Patribusque illudere.
units.tr: But Bellarmine, that wonderful artificer of answers, easily evades it: "The solution is plain," he says, "for it deals only with those who invent something and yet want their fictions to be seen as apostolic traditions." The Cardinal has hit the mark indeed! For the Papists invent traditions, and yet want their fictions to be seen as apostolic traditions. Meanwhile, the man who brings such trifles as answers takes the reader for either a dullard, who cannot distinguish between a word as mere sound and the knowledge of things, or a man so obstinate in error, and so hardened by prejudice, that he will gladly accept any shadow of an answer. For he seems not to want to fight for the truth, but only to work for wages, so as to keep in error those who of their own accord and with effort come out to the truth. Moreover, Jerome, on those words: The Lord shall tell in the Scripture of the peoples and of these princes, of those who were in it: Note, he says, what he says: "who were," not "who are," so that, apart from the Apostles, whatever is taught afterwards has no authority. Thus Jerome. Does the Father's answer apply to this too? Plainly not. For to bring out something without shame or modesty is what the Cardinal calls answering. He answers that Jerome in that place rejects those things which are foreign to apostolic doctrine, that is, contrary and repugnant to the Scriptures. This is that Achilles' shield, or Delphic sword, in the Cardinal's hand, without which the Papist cause cannot stand in the most serious senate of the Fathers. The Apostle must bear it with an equal mind, and all the Fathers must gladly suffer it, namely that the Lord Cardinal bends their words to another sense, against the known and common meaning of the words: so that beyond the Gospel does not mean beyond, but against; that he departs in nothing from the rule of the Scriptures does not mean what the words say, but something else which the Lord Cardinal wishes; that apart from the Apostles nothing else is taught does not mean nothing else as the words sound, but contrary and repugnant. Unless the Apostle and all the Fathers allow themselves to be so shamelessly mocked, the Lord Cardinal cannot reply. What sort of heart the Lord Cardinal has, I do not know; I certainly cannot think that this man comes seriously to write, and says these things from his heart, when he is not ashamed so openly to mock the Apostle and the Fathers.

units.la: Ruffinus, enumeratis libris canonicæ Scripturæ: Hæc, inquit sunt, quæ Patres intra canonem concluserunt, ex quibus fidei nostræ assertiones confirmare voluerunt. Expofit.in Symbol.
units.tr: Rufinus, after listing the books of the canonical Scripture, says: These are the books which the Fathers enclosed within the canon, and from which they wished to confirm the assertions of our faith. Expofit.in Symbol.

units.la: Ad Augustinum veniamus. Augustinus sic docuit: {a}In iis, quæ aperte in Scripturis posita sunt, inveniuntur ea omnia, quæ continent fidem moresque viuendi. Hæc ille. Si omnia, quæ fidem moresque continent, aperte posita inveniuntur in Scripturis: aperte falsum est, quod Bellarminus è Tridentinis fontibus hausit: In Scripturis non contineri expresse totam doctrinam de fide & moribus. Imo vero, inquit Augustinus, non tantum expresse, sed & aperte in Scripturis inuenisse omnia.
units.tr: Let us come to Augustine. Augustine taught thus: In those things which are plainly set down in the Scriptures are found all those things which contain faith and the rules of living. Thus he. If all things which contain faith and morals are found plainly set down in Scripture, then it is plainly false what Bellarmine has drawn from Tridentine sources: that the whole doctrine of faith and morals is not expressly contained in Scripture. Indeed, says Augustine, they have found not only expressly but also plainly in Scripture all things.

units.la: Responder Bellarminus: Loqui Augusti-num de illis dogmatibus, quæ necessaria sunt omnibus simpliciter, qualia sunt, quæ habentur in Symbolo Apostolico, & Decalogo. Hæc Bellarminus. At hæc responsio non potest expedire Bellarminum à mendacio, si verum docear[?] Augustinus. Nam si omnia, quæ continent fidem moresque, inveniuntur aperte in Symbolo & Decalogo: multo magis inveniuntur hæc aperte in universis Scripturis. Non ergo requiritur verbum non scriptum in traditionibus. Imo vero, si nihil extaret præter Symbolum & Decalogum, tamen ex Augustini verbis, etiam à Bellarmino expositis, inutiles prorsus essent traditiones. Quem enim traditionibus Pontificiis locum relinquit, qui fatetur, omnia, quæ continent fidem moresque, aperte contineri in Symbo-lo & Decalogo : quod fatetur Cardinalis. Quod vero addit, deiis[?], quæ necessaria sunt omnibus, & simpliciter, vt doceat, alia tradita esse omnibus, alia perfectis & Prælatis, hoc figmentum refutauimus supra in testimonio Irenæi. Hoc loco Bellarminus male sentire videtur de illis occultis doctrinis, quæ perfectis & Prælatis tantum prædicata affirmat. Nam neque fidem, neque mores continent: siquidem ea omnia, quæ fidem moresque continent, aperte posita inueniuntur in Scripturis. Quid ergo est, quod in istis clancularis doctrinis quærunt Pontificij, in quibus, Bellarmini sententia, neque fides, neq; mores continentur?
units.tr: Bellarmine answers: "Augustine is speaking of those doctrines which are necessary for all people simply, such as those contained in the Apostles' Creed and the Decalogue." Thus Bellarmine. But this answer cannot save Bellarmine from falsehood, if Augustine teaches the truth. For if all things which contain faith and morals are found plainly in the Creed and the Decalogue, much more are these found plainly in the whole of Scripture. Therefore there is no need for an unwritten word in traditions. Indeed, if nothing existed except the Creed and the Decalogue, still, from Augustine's words, even as Bellarmine expounds them, traditions would be entirely useless. For what room does he leave for Papist traditions, who confesses that all things which contain faith and morals are plainly contained in the Creed and the Decalogue? And what he adds, that some things are necessary for all and simply, so as to teach that some things were handed down to all and others to the perfect and the Prelates, this fiction we have refuted above in the testimony of Irenaeus. Here Bellarmine seems to think ill of those hidden doctrines which he affirms were preached only to the perfect and the Prelates. For they contain neither faith nor morals, since all things which contain faith and morals are found plainly set down in Scripture. What then is it that the Papists seek in these secret little doctrines, in which, by Bellarmine's opinion, neither faith nor morals are contained?

units.la: Augustinus præterea sic docet: {a}Siue de Christo, siue de Ecclesia[?], siue de quacunq; aliare[?], quæ pertinet ad fidem, vtcunq; nostram, non dicam, sinos, nequaquam comparandi es[?], quos dixit, licet si-nos, sed omnino, quod secutum adiecit: Si Angelus de cœlo vobis annunciauerit, præterquam quod in Scripturis Legalibus & Euangelicis accepistis, anathema sit. Hæc Augustinus. Bellarmino facilis est responsio ad manum: Præterquam significat, inquit, contra quam: quasi dicat: Cui hæc responsio non placet, quærat, si potest, meliorem. At, si neque Augustinus, neque Apostolus ipse, neque Angelus de cœlo audiendus sit, nisi è Scripturis loquatur; facile nobis conflare potest, quo spiritu corripiantur, qui tam facile, tam pertinaciter vocem audiunt Angeli, non de cœlo, sed de puteo abyssi; non è Scripturis, sed è traditionibus suis loquentis.
units.tr: Augustine also teaches this: Whether concerning Christ, or concerning the Church, or concerning any other matter that pertains to faith in any way, if an angel from heaven should announce to you something other than what you have received in the Law and the Gospels, let him be accursed. Augustine says this. Bellarmine has an easy answer ready: præterquam, he says, means "contrary to what." It is as if he were saying: whoever does not like this answer should look for a better one, if he can. But if neither Augustine, nor the Apostle himself, nor an angel from heaven is to be heard unless he speaks from Scripture, we can easily see what spirit possesses those who so readily and so stubbornly listen to a voice, not from heaven but from the pit of the abyss, speaking not from Scripture but from their own traditions.

units.la: Amplius Augustinus: {a}Quid, inquit, amplius te doceam, quam id, quod apud Apostolum legimus? Sancta enim Scriptura nostræ doctrinæ regulam figit, ne audeamus sapere plus quam oportet. Non sit ergo mihi, aliud te docere, nisi verba tibi doctoris exponere, & de eo, quod Dominus dederit, disputare. Respondet Bellarminus: Loquitur Augustinus non de omni dogmate, sed solum de professione viduitatis. Bellarminus sic dixit: sed Augustinus negat, se sic intelligendum esse. Nam in eodem capite, adeoque etiam in eadem sententia exordium sumit Augustinus à generali sententia, & progreditur ad hanc particularem: {b}Quum in omni quæstione, inquit, quæ ad vitam moresq; pertinet, non sola doctrina, verum & exhortatio sit necessaria, quid amplius te doceam, quam id, quod apud Apostolum legimus? Sancta enim Scriptura nostræ doctrinæ regulam figit. Ita connectit hæc Augustinus ex generali propositione. Deinde ridicula est Cardinalis responsio: quia Augustinus ait; Scripturam figere regulam doctrinæ nostræ. Regulam autem quis unquam ante Cardinalem nostrum de uno particulari intellexit? Quum igitur hæc particularis professio viduitatis non habeat particularem hanc regulam, sed in hac communi regula cum aliis continetur: Quid magis Iesuiticum videri potest, quam si dicas, communem Scripturarum regulam esse intelligendam de unico viduitatis dono?
units.tr: Augustine again: What more, he says, shall I teach you than what we read in the Apostle? For holy Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching, so that we do not dare to be wiser than we ought. Let it not be mine to teach you anything else, but only to set out the words of the teacher for you and to discuss what the Lord has given. Bellarmine replies that Augustine speaks not of every dogma but only of the profession of widowhood. Bellarmine said this; but Augustine denies that he is to be understood in this way. For in the same chapter, indeed in the same passage, Augustine starts from a general statement and proceeds to this particular one: Since in every question, he says, which pertains to life and morals, not only teaching but also exhortation is necessary, what more shall I teach you than what we read in the Apostle? For holy Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching. Thus Augustine draws these words from a general proposition. Then the Cardinal's answer is absurd, because Augustine says that Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching. But who, before our Cardinal, ever understood a rule to refer to one particular matter? Since, then, this particular profession of widowhood does not have a particular rule of its own, but is contained under this common rule along with other things, what can seem more Jesuitical than to say that the common rule of the Scriptures is to be understood as applying only to the single gift of widowhood?
