units.la: curis; am- legi- regu- orter. bi do- it, dif- uitur olum ic di- gen- tiam agu- ur ad eftio- h sola quid olum iare- is ex a est air; ftræ. dina- exit? dui- lam, onti- otest, n re- ratis ono? dono? Videbat Cardinalis, hanc responsio- nem fuisse ridiculam; itaque addit hæc verba: Quod autem Augustinus generaliter ponit, Scriptura nostræ doctrinæ regulam sigit: con- tra illos dictum est, qui ex proprio iudicio sin- gunt nouas doctrinas, quæ Scripturis conso- næ non sunt. Hæc Cardinalis. Quomodo po- tuit Cardinalis inter flammas ambulare, vt non ambustus exiret? Pontifici doctrinas nouas confingunt, quæ Scripturæ consonæ non sunt. Nam vt alia dissimulem, hoc ipsum, de quo nunc agimus, confingunt; nouam fi- dei regulam excudunt, quam Ecclesia non nouerat ante Concilium Tridentinum. Hæc est doctrina Scripturis non consona, de regu- la fidei, atque de fundamento ipso. Hanc re- gulam esse vnicas Scripturas, Augustinus cum omnibus antiquis Patribus docuit. Scriptura doctrinæ nostræ regulam sigit: Nihil igitur docere possumus in Ecclesia, nisi quod in Scripturis continetur. Hæc torquent Cardi- nalem, necexitum[?] videt. Primo dicit, Augu- stinum generaliter hæc posuisse contra eos, qui confingunt nouas doctrinas: At hæc non expediunt Cardinalem à mendacio. Nam hoc si verum sit, fallere voluit, & mentiri, qui dixit, Augustinum non hic loqui de omni do- gmate, sed de professione viduitatis. Nam si generaliter ponit Augustinus, Scripturam fi- gere regulam doctrinæ nostræ, loquitur de o- mni dogmate. Sed si hoc generaliter ponatur ab Augustino: quomodo possunt esse traditiones non scriptæ in regula fidei ? Expediat hæc, qui potest.
units.tr: The Cardinal saw that this answer was ridiculous, and so he adds these words: What Augustine states in general terms, that Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching, was said against those who, by their own judgment, invent new doctrines that do not agree with the Scriptures. So the Cardinal says. How could the Cardinal walk among the flames and come out unscorched? The Papists invent new doctrines that do not agree with Scripture. To pass over other examples, they invent this very matter we are now discussing: they forge a new rule of faith, which the Church did not know before the Council of Trent. This is a doctrine not consonant with Scripture, concerning the rule of faith and the very foundation. That the Scriptures alone are this rule, Augustine taught together with all the ancient Fathers. Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching; therefore we can teach nothing in the Church except what is contained in the Scriptures. These statements torment the Cardinal, and he sees no way out. First, he says that Augustine stated these things in general against those who invent new doctrines. But this does not free the Cardinal from falsehood. For if that is true, he who said that Augustine was not speaking here of every dogma but of the profession of widowhood was trying to deceive and lie. For if Augustine states generally that Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching, he is speaking of every dogma. But if Augustine states this generally, how can unwritten traditions be part of the rule of faith? Let whoever can explain this do so.

units.la: {a}Excellentia canonicæ auctoritatis veteris & novi Testamenti (ut alia etiam ex eodem anne-ctamus, ad quæ nihil respondet Cardinalis) Apostolorum confirmata temporibus, per successiones Episcoporum, & propagationes Ecclesiarum, tanquam in sede quadam sublimiter constituta est, cui seruiat omnis fidelis & pius intellectus, inquit Augustinus. Quibus verbis probat, Tridentinum intellectum & spiritum nec fidelem, nec pium esse, qui huic auctoritati non seruiat: qui hanc regulam, & auctoritatis excellentiam per successiones Episcoporum, & propagationes Ecclesiarum ad Tridentinum usque Concilium in Ecclesia conseruatam; cum primum immutare auderet, & ad verbum Dei, verbum Papæ in eadem auctoritatis excellentia addere.
units.tr: The excellence of the canonical authority of the Old and New Testament (to add other things from the same passage, to which the Cardinal makes no reply), confirmed by the times of the Apostles, through the succession of bishops and the spreading of the Churches, is established as on a lofty seat, and to it every faithful and pious understanding should be subject, says Augustine. By these words he proves that the understanding and spirit that does not submit to this authority is neither faithful nor pious. Those at Trent, who dared to change first this rule and this excellence of authority, preserved in the Church through the succession of bishops and the spreading of the Churches down to the Council of Trent, and who dared to add to the Word of God the word of the Pope in the same authority, are such a spirit.

units.la: {b}Tantummodo scripturis canonicis, inquit Augustinus, hanc ingenuam seruitutem debeo. At Tridentini non solis canonicis scripturis, sed traditionibus non scriptis hanc seruitutem profitentur.
units.tr: To the canonical Scriptures alone, says Augustine, do I owe this free servitude. But those of Trent profess this servitude not only to the canonical Scriptures but also to unwritten traditions.

units.la: {c}Non afferamus, inquit Augustinus idem stateras dolosas, ubi appendamus, quod volumus, & quomodo volumus pro arbitrio nostro, dicentes, hoc graue, hoc leue est; sed afferamus divinam stateram de Scripturis sanctis, tanquam de thesauris Dominicis, & in illis, quid sit grauius, appendamus; imo non appendamus, sed a Domino appensa recognoscamus. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Let us not bring, says Augustine, the same deceitful scales, where we weigh what we want, and as we want, by our own judgment, saying, this is heavy, this is light; but let us bring the divine balance of the holy Scriptures, as of the Lord's treasures, and in them let us weigh what is heavier; or rather, we do not weigh them, but acknowledge them as weighed by the Lord. So he says.

units.la: Hæc igitur de Scripturis docuit Augustinus, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ doctrinam retinuit: huit: Omnia, quæ fidem moresq; continent, aperte in Scripturis inveniri: Anathema esse, qui quicquam annuntiat, præterquam quod in Scripturis legimus: Scripturas doctrinæ nostræ regulam figere: Scripturas esse stateram Dominicam, esse thesauros Dominicos. Respondeant Tridentini, & dicant nobis, quænam sint illæ staterae dolosæ, ubi appendi-mus, quod volumus, & quomodo volumus pro arbitrio nostro? Pergimus, & reliquorum assensum apponamus. In quibus nullum nobis negotium facessit Cardinalis, sed alto in-dormit silentio.
units.tr: Augustine therefore taught these things about the Scriptures and kept the doctrine of the Catholic Church: that all things that contain faith and morals are openly found in the Scriptures; that whoever announces anything other than what we read in the Scriptures is accursed; that the Scriptures fix the rule of our teaching; that the Scriptures are the Lord's balance and the Lord's treasures. Let the men of Trent answer and tell us what those deceitful scales are, where we weigh what we want and as we want by our own judgment. Let us go on and add the agreement of others. On these points the Cardinal makes us no trouble, but sleeps on in deep silence.

units.la: Saluianus: {a}Si scire vis, quid tenendum sit: habes literas sacras, perfecta vatio[?] est tenere, quod le-gerit. Leo primus: {b}Sacerdotum, & cunctorum fidelium, ita demum erit plena devotio, si in his, quæ per unicum Dei filium, Deum verbum, pro nostra redemptione sunt gesta, nihil aliud sentiatur, quam quod ipse prædicari de se iussit, & credi. {c}Ab Eu-angelica Apostolicaq; doctrina nec vno quidem verbo licet discedere, aut aliter de Scripturis divinis sapere, quam beatis Apostoli & Patres nostri didicere, atque docuerunt. Hæc Leo. Et quid ad hæc referat Cardinalis, non video: forte priorem sententiam, eâdem, qua Scripturas sacras, Patrumq; testimonia eluserat, audacia & inverecundia, excipere potuisset: ut diceret, nihil aliud, non esse nihil aliud, sed repugnans & contrarium. At in secundo testimonio hæc audacia inutilis est; nam Leonis Papæ cautela Cardinalis impudentiam vicisse viderut. Nam si nec vno verbo discedere licet à doctrina Prophetica & Euangelica, quomodo isti doctrinam nobis non scriptam obtrudere possunt? & verbum Dei non scriptum? Si forte obiiciat Cardinalis, temerarium fuisse Leonis iudicium, quod de unico verbo dixerat, quia verba quaedam non scripta recipiuntur, ut ὁμοούσιον, & reliqua eius generis: possumus grauissimum Leonis iudicium contra Cardinalem defendere: quia Leo non dixerat, non licere verba admittere, quae licet totidem syllabis non habeantur in Scriptura, tamen doctrinam Scripturæ continent: sed nec uno verbo a doctrina Prophetica & Apostolica discedere. ὁμοούσιον, quamuis non sit verbum scriptum in sacris literis, non tamen quicquam discedit à doctrina Prophetica & Apostolica.
units.tr: Salvian: If you wish to know what must be held, you have the sacred letters; it is a perfect safeguard to hold what they have read. Leo the First: The devotion of the priests and of all the faithful will then be complete, if in those things which were done for our redemption through the only Son of God, God the Word, nothing else is thought than what he himself commanded to be preached about himself and believed. It is not lawful to depart from the evangelical and apostolic teaching even by a single word, or to think about the divine Scriptures otherwise than our blessed Apostles and Fathers learned and taught. So Leo. What the Cardinal can say in reply to these, I do not see. Perhaps with the same audacity and shamelessness with which he dismissed the holy Scriptures and the testimonies of the Fathers, he could have dealt with the former statement by saying that nothing else does not mean nothing else, but contrary and opposed. But against the second testimony this audacity is useless; for the Cardinal's impudence has been overcome by the caution of Pope Leo. For if it is not lawful to depart from the prophetic and evangelical teaching even by a single word, how can they force an unwritten doctrine on us, and an unwritten word of God? If the Cardinal perhaps objects that Leo's judgment was rash when he spoke of a single word, because some words not written are accepted, such as homoousion [ὁμοούσιον] and others of that kind, we can defend Leo's very weighty judgment against the Cardinal: Leo did not say that it is not lawful to admit words which, though not found in Scripture in so many syllables, nevertheless contain the doctrine of Scripture; he said only that one must not depart from the prophetic and apostolic doctrine even by a single word. Homoousion [ὁμοούσιον], although it is not a word written in the sacred letters, nevertheless departs in no way from the prophetic and apostolic doctrine.

units.la: Gregorius etiam Magnus idem docuit: {a}In hoc volumine (sacrarum Scripturarum) omnia, quae erudiunt; cuncta, quae aedificant, scripta continentur. {b}Scriptura continet ea omnia, quae aedi-ficant: & omnis munitio nostra in sacro eloquio continetur. Hæc Gregorius. Nullum hic locum verbo Tridentino non scriptor reliquit. Et bene se res habet, quod loquentibus Romanis Episcopis, Cardinalis obmutuit. Quid fortius aut disertius contra Tridentinas fabulas afferri potuit, quam quod Romani Episcopi docuerunt?
units.tr: Gregory the Great also taught the same thing: In this volume (of the Holy Scriptures) all things that instruct and all things that build up are contained in writing. Scripture contains all those things which build up, and all our defence is contained in the sacred word. So Gregory. Here the writer leaves no room for the Tridentine word. It is well that, when the Roman bishops speak, the Cardinal falls silent. What could be said more strongly or plainly against the Tridentine fables than what the Roman bishops taught?

units.la: Gregorius de una fide ab omnibus pastoribus, per omnia secula seruanda, sicait[?]: Gra-tias omnipotenti Deo agimus, qui immutatis pastovibus gregu [?] sui fidem, quam semel sanctis Patribus tradidit, etiam post eos immutabilem custodit.lib 9. indict.4. Epist.40.
units.tr: Gregory, on the one faith to be kept by all ministers through all ages, says as follows: We give thanks to almighty God, who, though the flocks of his ministers change, keeps unchanged the faith which he once delivered to the holy Fathers, and keeps it unchanged even after them. Book 9, indiction 4, Epistle 40.

units.la: Haec est causae nostrae fiducia: Habemus indubitata Scripturae testimonia: habemus Ecclesiae consensum. nostri sunt Patres: nostri sunt Romani Episcopi: nostra est Ecclesia universa, usque ad Concilii Tridentini tempora. Haec enim veritas in ipsis etiam tenebris lucebat: nec Satanas ipse post annum millesimum solutus, hanc lucem extinguere potuit. Scriptores igitur post annum millesimum eandem veritatem integram conseruarunt. Gratianus in hanc sententiam multa collegit, distinct.8. ex Augustino, Cypriano, Gregorio.
units.tr: This is the confidence of our cause: we have the undoubted testimonies of Scripture; we have the consensus of the Church. The Fathers are ours; the Roman bishops are ours; the whole Church is ours, down to the time of the Council of Trent. For this truth shone even in the darkness itself, and Satan himself, loosed after the thousandth year, could not extinguish this light. Writers after the year one thousand therefore preserved the same truth whole. Gratian gathered many passages to this effect in Distinction 8, from Augustine, Cyprian and Gregory.

units.la: Bernardus sic docuit: a Beati, qui audiunt{a} verbum Dei, & custodiunt illud. Vultis nosse, quam beati? Primum, quibus sonans in auribus animae vox divina conturbat, terret, adjudicatque: sed continuo, si bene adierteris, vivificat, liquefacit, calefacit, illuminat, mundat. Denique & cibus est noster, & gladius, & medicina, & confirmatio, & requies, & resurrectio quoque, & consummatio nostra. Nec mirum, quod verbum Dei iam nunc invenitur omnia in omnibus, quantum spectat ad iustificationem: siquidem & futurum est, omnia in omnibus ad glorificationem. Haec Bernardus. Nec veremur, ne quis haec Iesuitica fronte rapiat ad verbum Dei, quod vocant non scriptum in traditionibus: nam quis narrabit nobis, quomodo traditiones istae non scriptae sint cibus noster, & gladius,& medicina,& confirmatio,& requies,& resurrectio,& consummatio? Quis docebit, quomodo verbum non scriptum Tridentinum viuificet mortuos in peccato? quomodo liquefaciat cor induratum? quomodo calefaciat inflammando,& ardorem immittendo? quomodo illuminet, vt lucerna pedibus,& lumen semitis nostris? quomodo mundet, vt nobis etiam dicat Christus: Vos mundi estis propter sermonem, quem locutus sum vobis? aut quomodo verbum hoc non scriptum Tridentinum nunc inueniatur omnia in omnibus, quantum spectat ad iustificationem? Si ad haec demonstranda Iesuitae cum suo illo verbo non scripto impares inueniantur,& sub hoc onere succumbant: restat, vt ex Patrum sententia concludatur: Sicut vnicum verbum scriptum deducit nos sine errore ad verbum aeternum, Iesum Christum: sic verbum hoc non scriptum in traditionibus deducere Tridentinos per varios errores, ad verbum falsum, nempe Antichristum, filium illum perditionis,& impium illum, quem Dominus conficiet Spiritu oris sui,& illustri aduentu suo abolebit.
units.tr: Bernard taught thus: Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it. Do you wish to know how blessed? First, those in whose ears the divine voice sounds, troubling, terrifying and judging them; but at once, if you attend well, it gives life, melts, warms, illuminates and cleanses. In short, it is both our food and our sword, our medicine, our strengthening, our rest, our resurrection too and our consummation. Nor is it surprising that the word of God is already now found to be all things in all, as far as justification is concerned, since it will also be all things in all for glorification. So Bernard. Nor do we fear that anyone will snatch these words, with Jesuitical brazenness, and apply them to the word of God which they call unwritten, in traditions. For who will tell us how those unwritten traditions are our food, and sword, and medicine, and strengthening, and rest, and resurrection, and consummation? Who will teach us how an unwritten Tridentine word makes alive the dead in sin? How it melts a hardened heart? How it warms by kindling and by pouring in ardour? How it illuminates, as a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths? How it cleanses, so that Christ may also say to us, "You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you"? Or how this unwritten Tridentine word is now found to be all things in all, as far as justification is concerned? If the Jesuits, with their unwritten word, are found unequal to demonstrating these things, and give way under this burden, it remains that we conclude from the judgment of the Fathers: just as the one written word leads us without error to the eternal Word, Jesus Christ, so this unwritten word in traditions leads the Tridentines, through various errors, to the false word, namely Antichrist, that son of perdition, that wicked one whom the Lord will destroy with the breath of his mouth and abolish by the brightness of his coming.

units.la: Bernardus etiam omnem doctrinam non scriptam reiiciendam docet: {a}Profecto, inquit, vnusquisque, quod a magistro suo didicit, hoc in medium profert. Num in Euangelio legisti has differentias, aut in Prophetis, aut litteris Apostolorum? Christi sum discipulus, Christi discipulus loquor. Ego, si peregrinum dogma inauxero, ipse peccaui. Ita Bernar[Right page, cut off at the scan edge: line beginnings only, fragments] Ber[?] &tri[?] Spec[?] ram[?] per.[?] cun[?] dus[?] aut[?] dem[?] cut[?] cle[?] nou[?] pra[?] Dod[?] dici[?] idea[?] que[?] spo[?] Pa[?] ca[?] Sic[?] est[?] ter[?] in e[?] reu[?] har[?] Sic[?] suff[?] Ha[?] nou[?]
units.tr: Bernard also teaches that all doctrine not written must be rejected: Indeed, each one brings forward before the assembly what he has learned from his master. Have you read these differences in the Gospel, or in the Prophets, or in the letters of the Apostles? I am a disciple of Christ; I speak as a disciple of Christ. If I should introduce a foreign dogma, I myself would have sinned. So Bernard. [The remainder of this page is cut off at the edge of the scan; only fragments of line beginnings remain, which are not legible enough to translate.]

units.la: Bernardus sacras Scripturas regulam sibi do-ctrinæ propositam profitetur.
units.tr: Bernard professes that the holy Scriptures are set before him as the rule of doctrine.

units.la: Pet. Lombardus sic docet: {a}Theologorum speculatio studiosa atq; modesta diutinam Scriptu-rarum, formam præscriptam in doctrina tenere adverter. Hæc ille. Itaque regulam fidei integram cum superioribus Patribus retinuit Lombardus. Idemque sic etiam habet: {b}Secundum autoritatem Scripturarum virum fides ita se habeat, demonstrandum est. Hæc Lombardus. Si vero secundum autoritatem Scripturarum fides Ecclesiæ demonstranda sit: certæ traditiones non scriptæ Lombardi seculo non erant receptæ in regulam fidei.
units.tr: Peter Lombard teaches thus: The careful and modest speculation of theologians keeps to the form of doctrine prescribed by the long-standing Scriptures. So he. Thus Lombard retained, together with the earlier Fathers, the whole rule of faith. And he likewise says: It must be shown how faith stands according to the authority of the Scriptures. So Lombard. But if the faith of the Church is to be demonstrated according to the authority of the Scriptures, then certain unwritten traditions were not received into the rule of faith in Lombard's age.

units.la: Aquinas etiam eandem veritatem retinuit: Doctrina, inquit, {c}Prophetarum & Apostolorum dicitur canonica, quia est regula intellectus nostri, & ideo nullus aliter debet docere. Hæc Thomas. Ad quod testimonium quid possunt Iesuitæ respondere? Doctrina Prophetica & Apostolica est regula intellectus & doctrinæ nostræ. Sic Aquinas Ecclesiæ doctrinam retulit. Ubi est ergo regula Tridentina? Ubi sunt, qui aliter intelligere, aliter docere audent? Idemque in eandem sententiam: {d}Innititur fides nostra revelationi Apostolo & Prophetis facta. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Aquinas also kept the same truth: The doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles is called canonical, because it is the rule of our understanding, and therefore no one ought to teach otherwise. So Thomas. What can the Jesuits reply to this testimony? The prophetic and apostolic doctrine is the rule of our understanding and of our teaching. Thus Aquinas referred the doctrine of the Church to it. Where, then, is the Tridentine rule? Where are those who dare to understand otherwise and teach otherwise? To the same effect he says: Our faith rests on the revelation made to the Apostles and Prophets. So he.

units.la: Scotus etiam, qui in aliis multa corruperat, hanc tamen veritatem integram conseruauit. Sic enim docet: {e}Patet, quod sacra Scriptura sufficienter continet doctrinam necessariam viatori. Hæc Scotus. Tridentinas igitur traditiones non agnouit Scotus. Qui sequuntur, Bonaventura, Nicolaus Lyra, Iohannes Gerson, Panormitanus, aliiq; hanc de regula fidei doctrinam integram ab Ecclesia antiqua exceptam, posteris tradidere. Quorum testimonia referre non videbatur necessarium, quia in illis non habemus Adversarios repugnantes. Ita ut in hac re nulla fuerit mutatio, usque ad tempora Concilii Tridentini.
units.tr: Scotus too, who corrupted many things elsewhere, nevertheless kept this truth whole. For he teaches thus: It is clear that holy Scripture sufficiently contains the doctrine necessary for the wayfarer. So Scotus. Scotus therefore did not acknowledge Tridentine traditions. Those who followed, Bonaventure, Nicholas of Lyra, John Gerson, Panormitanus, and others, handed down to posterity this doctrine of the rule of faith, received whole from the ancient Church. Their testimonies did not seem necessary to relate, because we have no opposing adversaries in them. So in this matter there was no change up to the time of the Council of Trent.

units.la: Alphonsus de Castro, quem Pontificii pro suo numerant, contra Tridentinos disertus est. Sic enim scribit: Quum sacra Scriptura sit mystica quaedam turris David, ex qua omnia armatu-ra fortium & Catholicorum virorum pendent: id-eo haeretici conantur sacras Scripturas minuere, ne arma habeamus, quibus eorum insanas doctrinas prosternere valeamus. Haec ille. Multa in hanc sententiam habet lib. 1. cap. 2. Nec aliter scripserunt, aut senserunt, quicunque ante Concilium Tridentinum scripserunt.
units.tr: Alfonso de Castro, whom the Papists count as their own, is outspoken against the Tridentines. For he writes thus: Since holy Scripture is a certain mystical tower of David, from which all the armour of brave and Catholic men hangs, therefore the heretics try to diminish the sacred Scriptures, so that we may not have the weapons with which we could overthrow their insane doctrines. So he. He has much to this effect in Book 1, chapter 2. Nor did anyone who wrote before the Council of Trent write or think otherwise.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Corollarium de Regula Fidei.
units.tr: Corollary concerning the Rule of Faith.

units.la: HActenus perpetuam ab Apostolis usque ad Concilium Tridentinum, atque immutatam Ecclesiae doctrinam observavimus. Ex istis principiis quaedam sequuntur, tanquam corollaria, a nobis proximo loco tra-ctanda. Nam ex hoc Scripturarum, atque universae Ecclesiae consensu, sequitur manifesta demonstratio, atque indubitata consequentia earum earun [?] xime [?] contr [?] Trad [?] Adu [?] iudic [?] Quo [?] farun [?] bus. [?] trou [?] V [?] anti [?] rion [?] quil [?] fuit [?] qua [?] got [?] ex [?] Scr [?] Cu [?] qu [?] ius [?] Qu [?] est [?] fid [?] ex [?] tal [?] Ec [?] in [?] fi [?] if [?] earum rerum, quæ hoc nostrum seculum maximè perturbant; de Regula fidei, de Iudice controversiarum in controversiis fidei, & de Traditionibus non scriptis. De quibus rebus Adversarii nostri longè ab antiquorum sensu iudicioque, pro arbitrio suo disputare solent. Quorum omnis cura cogitatioque in [illegible, ~4 letters] versatur, vt Papa sit in Ecclesia omnia in omnibus. Hic os Ecclesiæ, regula fidei, Iudex controversiarum, denique Ecclesia ipsa habeatur.
units.tr: So far we have followed the doctrine of the Church, which has been continuous and unchanged from the Apostles down to the Council of Trent. Certain consequences follow from these principles, like corollaries, which we shall take up next. From this agreement of the Scriptures and of the whole Church there follows a clear demonstration and an indubitable consequence concerning [several words are unreadable in the scan] of those matters which especially trouble this age: the rule of faith, the judge of controversies in matters of faith, and unwritten traditions. Our opponents are accustomed to dispute about these things at their own pleasure, far removed from the sense and judgment of the ancients. The whole care and thought of these men is occupied with making the Pope to be all in all in the Church. He is to be regarded as the mouth of the Church, the rule of faith, the judge of controversies, and, in short, the Church itself.

units.la: Universa hæc de regula fidei res est apud antiquos tam certa, tam explorata, vt posteriores de hac re dubitare non possint, nec quisquam ea de re dubitabat, ante exortos lesuitas. Isti sunt, qui primi in hoc negocio antiquam Ecclesiæ traditionem immutando negotium nobis facéssunt. Legimus apud unum ex istis Sophistis; Regulam fidei non esse Scripturas, sed doctrinam & fidem Ecclesiæ, Cuius propositionis quis est sensus? Nam quum de regula fidei quæratur, fides hæc, cuius regulam quærimus, est fides Ecclesiæ. Quum vero regula eius fidei quæratur, quæ estfides Ecclesiæ? Si quis respondeat, regulam fidei Ecclesiæ, esse fidem Ecclesiæ: num quis existimare possit, hunc hominem priùs cogitasse, quid deinceps loqueretur? Sed hæc ad Ecclesiam eo consilio referunt, vt ab Ecclesia in Papam transferantur omnia, qui est Ecclesia Iesuitis.
units.tr: Among the ancients the whole matter of the rule of faith is so certain and so well established that later writers could not doubt it, and nobody doubted it before the Jesuits arose. They are the first who, by altering the ancient tradition of the Church in this matter, have given us trouble. We have read, in the work of one of these Sophists, that the rule of faith is not the Scriptures but the doctrine and faith of the Church. What is the sense of this proposition? For when we ask about the rule of faith, the faith whose rule we seek is the faith of the Church. But when we ask for the rule of that faith, what is the faith of the Church? If someone answers that the rule of the Church's faith is the faith of the Church, could anyone think that this man had first considered what he was going to say next? These men, however, refer everything to the Church with this purpose: that all things may be transferred from the Church to the Pope, who for the Jesuits is the Church.

units.la: Ex hoc intelligimus, nullam esse regulam isti, qui Scripturas ex alto despiciunt; nullum finem loquendi, scribendi, garriendi. errandi. Quicquid enim ista [?] arriserit ( modo Romani Pontificis falsum contra Scripturas, & supra Ecclesiam extollar ) continuo fides Ecclesiæ habenda iudicabitur. Scribant contra Scripturas, contra Patrum traditionem, sibiipsis etiam contradicant, loquantur sine autoritate, sine ratione, ex ipsorum sensu, imo vel sine sensu : tamen Ecclesiæ doctrinam egregie tractare videbuntur, modo Romani Pontificis autoritatem offerant. Non puto quenquam alium præter Iesuitas, nec ex ipsis Iesuitis, præter hunc vnum, nescio quem, Anonymum, tam insulse de regula fidei disputasse, vt dicat, regulam fidei Ecclesiæ, esse fidem Ecclesiæ. Et tamen habet hic sequaces suos.
units.tr: From this we understand that those who look down from on high upon the Scriptures have no rule, and no limit to speaking, writing, babbling, or erring. For whatever pleases them (provided it is a falsehood of the Roman Pontiff set against the Scriptures and raised above the Church), is at once judged to be the faith of the Church. Let them write against the Scriptures and against the tradition of the Fathers, let them even contradict themselves, let them speak without authority, without reason, according to their own meaning, or indeed without any meaning at all: they will still seem to handle the doctrine of the Church admirably, so long as they put forward the authority of the Roman Pontiff. I do not think that anyone other than the Jesuits has disputed about the rule of faith so foolishly, and among the Jesuits no one but this one unnamed man, I know not who, who says that the rule of faith of the Church is the faith of the Church. Yet he has his followers.

units.la: Quanto doctius Cardinalis Bellarminus, qui de regula fidei sic scribit: {a}Regula fidei certa, notaq; esse debet. Nam si nota non sit, regula nobis non erit, si certa non sit, nec regula quidem. Hæc ille. Et mox subiicit: {b}At sacræ Scripturæ, quæ Propheticis & Apostolicis litteris continentur, nihil est notum, nihil certum, vt stultissimum esse necesse sit, qui illi fidem esse habendam neget. Hæc ille. Deinde Scripturam esse regulam fidei, multis confirmat testimoniis & rationibus. Hæc recte Bellarminus contra Schwenckfeldianos [?], qui priuatum spiritum iactabant. Bellarmino multi assentiuntur ; imo ipse multis. Nam & ante ipsum, & post ipsum, idem tradiderunt post Patres, de quibus diximus; Clemens Papa I. cuius verba sunt: {c}Non sensum, quem ex-trin-
units.tr: How much more learned is Cardinal Bellarmine, who writes about the rule of faith as follows: {a}A certain rule of faith ought to be both certain and known. For if it is not known, it will not be a rule for us; if it is not certain, it will not be a rule at all. So he writes. And soon after he adds: {b}But the sacred Scriptures, which are contained in the prophetic and apostolic writings, are nothing known and nothing certain, so that he must be utterly foolish who denies that they are to be believed. So he writes. Then he confirms, with many testimonies and arguments, that Scripture is the rule of faith. Bellarmine rightly argues this against the Schwenckfeldians, who boasted of a private spirit. Many agree with Bellarmine, indeed he agrees with many. For both before him and after him, the same thing was taught by the Fathers of whom we have spoken, and by Pope Clement I, whose words are: {c}One should not seek a sense that is brought in from outside, or alien and foreign, nor confirm it in any way by the authority of the Scriptures themselves; rather one should take the sense of truth from the Scriptures themselves, since one has received from the divine Scriptures a whole and firm rule of truth.

units.la: {a} Lib. de verb. Dei, cap 2.
units.tr: {a} Book On the Word of God, chapter 2.

units.la: {b} ibid.
units.tr: {b} Ibid.

units.la: {c} dist. 37 c. 14. dicitur hic apud Gratian. Clem. 1. vixit anno Christi 1047. trinsecus adulteretur[?], alienum, & extraneum debe-tu quaerere, aut quoquo modo ipsum Scripturarum autoritate confirmare, sed ex ipsis Scripturis sensum capere veritatis, quum ex divinis Scripturis integram quis & firmam regulam veritatis susceperit. Idem docuerunt[?] {a} Durandus, {b} Cardinalis Camer[?]ensis, {c} Gerson. {d} Conradus Clingius Scripturam vocat normam, ulnam, iudicem. {e} Ios. Acosta haec habet verba: Nihil perinde Scripturam mihi videtur aperire, atque ipsa Scriptura. Itaq; diligens, attenta, frequens q; lectio, tum meditatio, & collatio Scripturarum omnium, summa regula ad intelligendum mihi semper est visa. Itaq; quod in caelestium orbium motu fieri amat, ut suprema sphaera mobilis rapiat suo motu inferiores planetarum sphaeras, quae tamen suum habent obliquum & contrarium motum. Idem hic etiam usu venisse videmus, ut summus universalis Ecclesiae consensus, de regula fidei, inferiores & posteriores omnes (etiam ipsos Iesuitas) in offensum rapiat: quamvis isti obliquo suo & contrario motu, ex Antichristi schola nituntur. Nam quis contra Christum & summum Ecclesiae consensum agi se pateretur, nisi ex illa schola?
units.tr: {c} Distinction 37, chapter 14; this is cited here from Gratian. Clement I lived in the year of Christ 1047 [sic]. The same was taught by {a} Durandus, {b} Cardinal Cameracensis, {c} Gerson. {d} Conrad Clingius calls Scripture the norm, the measuring rod, and the judge. {e} Joseph Acosta has these words: "Nothing seems to me to open up Scripture so much as Scripture itself. Therefore a diligent, attentive, and frequent reading, together with meditation and the comparing of all the Scriptures, has always seemed to me the highest rule for understanding." And just as in the motion of the heavenly spheres the highest sphere, moving in its own motion, carries along the lower spheres of the planets, which nonetheless have their own oblique and contrary motion, so we see the same thing happening here: the highest consensus of the universal Church concerning the rule of faim carries away all the lower and later ones (even the Jesuits themselves) against their will. They, with their oblique and contrary motion, struggle out of the school of Antichrist. For who would allow himself to be driven against Christ and the highest consensus of the Church, unless he came from that school?

units.la: Hinc est, quod Bellarminus, tanquam levis autor, sententiam suam mutet in hac re. Illorum hominum levitas & inconstantia movere nos non debet; nec novum videtur, si Iesuitae contra Scripturas, contra Patres, contra seipsos scribant: addo, nonnunquam etiam contra conscientiam suam. Bellarminus contra Schwenckfeldium, regulam fidei nullam agnoagnoscit, præter unicas sacras Scripturas: Quum vero pro traditionibus non scriptis pugnat, docet, Scripturæ finem non fuisse, ut esset regula fidei: deinde dicit, esse Scripturas regulam fidei, sed partialem, non totalem: atque ita agit, ut qui ardentes prun[illegible, ~2 letters] manu collegit, quas nec dimittere voluit, nec retinere valuit.
units.tr: Hence it is that Bellarmine, like a lightweight author, changes his opinion on this matter. We should not be moved by the levity and inconstancy of these men, nor is it strange if the Jesuits write against the Scriptures, against the Fathers, and against themselves; I add that sometimes they write even against their own conscience. Against Schwenckfeld, Bellarmine acknowledges no rule of faith except the Holy Scriptures alone. But when he fights for unwritten traditions, he teaches that Scripture was not made to be the rule of faith; then he says that Scripture is a rule of faith, but a partial one, not a total one. And so he acts like a man who has gathered burning coals in his hands, which he is neither willing to let go of nor able to hold.

units.la: At si Scriptura sit regula fidei contra spiritum Schwenckfeldii, quare non est eadem regula tenenda contra spiritum Pontificium? Regula una est, nec mutari potest: non alia producitur ad hunc errorem, alia ad illum refutandum, sed una eademque ad omnia probanda. Quæro igitur, quomodo potest Iesuita refutare Schwenckfeldium? Ea probo, inquit Schwenckfeldius, quæ spiritus mihi dictat. Eas, inquit Iesuita, probo traditiones, quæ Papa mihi dictat. Ergo ut Iesuita Schwenckfeldium reuincat, de regula fidei, convenire oportet. Scriptura, inquit, est regula fidei contra Schwenckfeldium. Recte quidem. Sed quid si Schwenckfeldius tuo te telo verberet? Nam si Scriptura est regula fidei contra spiritum Schwenckfeldii, regula hæc una eademq; stabit contra traditiones. Nam traditiones istas tu quoq; iactas à spiritu profectas: quia & verbum Dei contendis esse traditiones tuas. Omne autem verbum Dei à Spiritu sancto est. Si traditiones tuæ à spiritu sint, tu spiritum tuum iactas non minus, imo multo magis, quam Schwenckfeldius suum. Et q cogu priua Sch nand Tu S Schv per q mina resili Scrip lem, dei,e nibus fia est verbi bas,v quam quam quibu nes su festar fidei mino ita on regul Vt suis re sit reg cogn per E nulla
units.tr: But if Scripture is the rule of faith against the spirit of Schwenckfeld, why should it not be the same rule to be held against the Papal spirit? The rule is one and cannot be changed: it is not one rule brought forward to refute this error and another to refute that one, but one and the same rule for proving all things. I ask, therefore, how the Jesuit can refute Schwenckfeld. Schwenckfeld says: "I approve those things which the spirit dictates to me." The Jesuit says: "I approve those traditions which the Pope dictates to me." Therefore, if the Jesuit is to refute Schwenckfeld, the two must agree on the rule of faith. Scripture, he says, is the rule of faith against Schwenckfeld. Quite right. But what if Schwenckfeld strikes you with your own weapon? For if Scripture is the rule of faith against the spirit of Schwenckfeld, this same rule will stand equally against your traditions. For you also boast that those traditions proceed from the Spirit, since you maintain that your traditions are the Word of God. But every Word of God is from the Holy Spirit. If your traditions are from the Spirit, you boast of your spirit no less, indeed far more, than Schwenckfeld boasts of his. [The remainder of this unit is too garbled in the scan to be recovered with certainty.]

units.la: Et quia tu spiritum iactas: quæro, quomodo cognoscam, vtrum hic sit spiritus Christi, an priuatus spiritus, qualis ille est, quem iactat Schwenckfeldius. Ad hunc spiritum examinandum, de regula fidei conuenire oportet. Tu Scripturam ponis regulam fidei, contra Schwenckfeldii priuatum spiritum: quæro, per quam fidei regulam traditiones tuas examinabimus, si non per Scripturas? Hic Iesuita resiliendo, nugando, commentando turbatur. Scripturam esse regulam concedit; sed partialem, non totalem: totalem autem regulam fidei, esse verbum Dei in Scripturis & traditionibus. Atqui de traditionibus istis controuersia est. Non credo, traditiones non scriptas esse verbum Dei. Per quam fidei regulam hoc probas, vt credam? num per Scripturam? nequaquam, inquit, sed per traditiones. Rem non æquam postulat Iesuita, vt traditiones suas, de quibus est controuersia, probet per traditiones suas. Nonne seipsi[?] fures & latrones manifestarios produnt, qui lucem fugiunt? Regula fidei certa, notaq; esse debet, vel iudice Bellarmino: traditiones nec certæ sunt, nec notæ: ita omnia apud istos incerta erunt, quibus nec regula certa est.
units.tr: And since you boast of the Spirit, I ask how I may know whether this is the Spirit of Christ or a private spirit, such as the one Schwenckfeld boasts of. To examine this spirit, we must agree on the rule of faith. You set Scripture up as the rule of faith against the private spirit of Schwenckfeld; I ask, by what rule of faith will we examine your traditions, if not by the Scriptures? Here the Jesuit, by backing off, trifling, and commenting, is thrown into confusion. He concedes that Scripture is a rule, but a partial one, not a total one; the total rule of faith, he says, is the Word of God contained in Scripture and in traditions. But the controversy is precisely about those traditions. I do not believe that unwritten traditions are the Word of God. By what rule of faith do you prove this, so that I may believe it? By Scripture? Certainly not, he says, but by traditions. The Jesuit demands an unfair thing: that he prove his traditions, which are the matter in dispute, by his traditions. Do not thieves and robbers, who flee the light, betray themselves as the manifest criminals they are? A rule of faith ought to be certain and known, even by the judgment of Bellarmine; but traditions are neither certain nor known. So with them everything will be uncertain, since for them there is no certain rule.

units.la: Vt igitur cæcos istos incertosq; in tenebris suis relinquamus; Quum quæritur: quænam sit regula fidei? hanc regulam duobus modis cognoscere possumus; vel per Scripturas, vel per Ecclesiam. Si per Scripturas quæratur, nulla alia inueniri potest, quam ipsa Prophetica & Apostolica doctrina in sacris literis descripta. Sin per Ecclesiam quaeratur; affirmamus, nullam aliam fidei regulam in Ecclesia conseruatam, praedicatam, traditam, manifestatam per omnia Ecclesiae Christianae secula, & successiones ab Apostolicis temporibus usque ad tempora Concilii Tridentini, quam illam unicam, Propheticam, & Apostolicam doctrinam in Scripturis descriptam. Non dico, Ecclesiae fidem esse regulam fidei: sed Ecclesiam conseruasse, praedicasse, fideliter & constanter tradidisse hanc unicam regulam, ut per testimonium Ecclesiae cognoscamus, quaenam illa sit.
units.tr: So let us leave those blind and uncertain men in their darkness. When we are asked what the rule of faith is, we can know it in two ways: through the Scriptures or through the Church. If we seek it through the Scriptures, no other can be found than the very prophetic and apostolic teaching described in the holy writings. If we seek it through the Church, we affirm that no other rule of faith has been preserved, preached, handed down and made manifest in the Christian Church through all the ages and successions from the apostolic times to the time of the Council of Trent than that one prophetic and apostolic doctrine described in the Scriptures. I do not say that the Church's faith is the rule of faith, but that the Church has kept, preached and faithfully and constantly handed down this one rule, so that through the Church's testimony we may know what it is.

units.la: Eligant Pontificii utrum velint, regulam fidei per Scripturas, an per Ecclesiam probari. Si dixerint, neque per Scripturas, neque per Ecclesiam, sed per traditiones suas: quid aliud referemus istis miseris, quam ut libenter miseros esse iubeamus, qui per Scripturas convicti, Ecclesiae etiam iudicium refugiunt? Si dicant, Ecclesiae se iudicio staturos, modo Romanam Ecclesiam intelligamus: Respondemus, universalis Ecclesiae sententiam a nobis quaeri, nec Romanam excipimus. Nam Romana Ecclesia ad nostra usque tempora, non aliam suscepit regulam fidei, quam sacras Scripturas. Proferant illi, si possunt, vel unicum testimonium, non dico antiquorum, sed vel ipsorum Pontificiorum, qui Scripturas canonicas negauerit esse totalem canonem, seu fidei regulam: vel qui ad defectum Scriptura-
units.tr: Let the Papists choose whether they want the rule of faith proved by the Scriptures or by the Church. If they say, neither by the Scriptures nor by the Church, but by their own traditions, what else shall we answer these wretched men than that we bid them gladly to be wretched, since they, being refuted by the Scriptures, also flee from the judgment of the Church? If they say that they will abide by the judgment of the Church, provided we understand the Roman Church, we answer that we are seeking the opinion of the universal Church, and we do not exclude the Roman. For the Roman Church, down to our own times, has received no other rule of faith than the holy Scriptures. Let them produce, if they can, even a single testimony, not of the ancients only, but even of their own Papists, who has denied that the canonical Scriptures are the whole canon, or the rule of faith; or who has had recourse to traditions as a supplement for the deficiency of the Scriptures.
