units.la: Nos[?] pturas [?] dicium [?] sibi au[?] Euang[?] thema [?] perfec[?] ftram [?] &trina [?] eo, qu[?] ftitutu[?] ras: qu[?] hoc est[?] tur: qu[?] guunt [?] pietat[?] opus [?] sectos [?] ftruct[?] Script[?] regula[?]
units.tr: [Largely illegible in the scan. Readable fragments suggest a passage on the Scriptures: that they have judgment and authority of their own, that they make the man of God perfect, and that they are the rule.]

units.la: Sin[?] quæ su[?] rum supplendum traditiones non scriptas, in fidei regula posuerit. Et quid magis insanum aut furiosum dici aut cogitari potest, quam si quis dixerit, regulam fidei in Ecclesia nunquam notam, agnitamque fuisse ante Concilium Tridentinum? Certum autem est, regulam istam, quam Iesuitae [illegible, ~7 letters] nunquam antea fuisse agnitam, nullo consensu probatam, nulla auctoritate firmatam.
units.tr: [Partly illegible.] …to be supplied by unwritten traditions, he has placed them in the rule of faith. And what could be said or thought more mad or frenzied than if someone should say that the rule of faith had never been known or recognised in the Church before the Council of Trent? It is certain, however, that this rule, which the Jesuits [illegible] had never been acknowledged before, approved by no consensus, and confirmed by no authority.

units.la: Nos vero, ut fidei regulam probemus, Scripturas primum, deinde Ecclesiae universae iudicium proferimus. Scriptura inprimis hanc sibi auctoritatem vendicat: quia qui praeter Euangelium quicquam aliud annunciat, anathema est: quia doctrina Dei integra est, & perfecta: quia quaecunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt: unde igitur doctrina nostra regulam habere potest, quam ex eo, quod ad nostram doctrinam à Deo est institutum? quia errant, qui nesciunt Scripturas: quia omnis [illegible, ~9 letters] prohibetur, hoc est, quicquid in Scripturis non continetur: quia Scripturae docent veritatem, redarguunt haereses, corripiunt vitia, erudiunt ad pietatem, ut homo Dei perfectus sit ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructus: quod perfectos nos ad omne opus bonum perfecte instructos reddit, est regula perfecta. Si ergo Scripturas consulamus, ipsae Scripturae sunt regula fidei nostrae perfectissima.
units.tr: But we, in order to prove the rule of faith, set forth first the Scriptures and then the judgment of the whole Church. Scripture above all claims this authority for itself: because whoever preaches anything besides the Gospel is accursed; because the teaching of God is whole and perfect; because whatever has been written was written for our instruction; whence, then, can our doctrine have a rule other than that which God has appointed for our doctrine? Because those err who do not know the Scriptures; because [illegible] is forbidden, that is, whatever is not contained in the Scriptures; because the Scriptures teach the truth, refute heresies, rebuke vices, and train us in godliness, so that the man of God may be perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work. That which makes us perfect, thoroughly furnished for every good work, is a perfect rule. If therefore we consult the Scriptures, the Scriptures themselves are the most perfect rule of our faith.

units.la: Sin Ecclesiae iudicium expectemus, in illis, quae superius à nobis producta sunt, testimo-niis, niis, certum habemus Ecclesiæ consensum, Sicenim Ecclesiæ doctores tradiderunt: Ec-clesiastica regula est consensus veteris & noui Testamenti: è solis Scripturis examinationes sunt petendæ: manifestus est à fide lapsus; & superbiæ signum, aliquid docere, quod non est scriptum: in nullo debemus à Scripturarum præscripto discedere: regula fidei est una, immobilis, irrefragabilis: constitutio fidei est indemutabilis[?]: controuersiæ fidei tractandæ sunt tantummodo per ea, quæ scripta sunt: Ecclesia non est egressa de finibus suis, hoc est, de sacris Scripturis: Scriptura doctrinæ no-stræ regulam figit: ab Euangelica, Apostoli-caque doctrina, nec uno uerbo discedere licet: in sacris Scripturis cuncta, quæ ædificant; omnia, quæ erudiunt, scripta continentur: omnis munitio nostra in sacro eloquio continetur: doctrina Prophetarum & Apostolorum ideo dicitur canonica, quia regula est intellectus nostri.
units.tr: If, on the other hand, we await the judgment of the Church, we hold, in those testimonies which we have produced above, that there is a certain consensus of the Church. For thus the teachers of the Church have handed down: the ecclesiastical rule is the agreement of the Old and New Testaments; examinations are to be sought from the Scriptures alone; a manifest lapse from the faith, and a sign of pride, is to teach anything that is not written; in nothing must we depart from the prescription of the Scriptures; the rule of faith is one, unchangeable, irrefutable; the constitution of the faith is unalterable; controversies of faith are to be handled only by those things which have been written; the Church has not gone beyond her limits, that is, the holy Scriptures; the Scripture fixes the rule of our teaching; it is not permitted to depart from the Gospel and apostolic doctrine by a single word; in the holy Scriptures are contained all things that build up, all things that instruct; all our defence is contained in the holy word; the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles is therefore called canonical, because it is the rule of our understanding.

units.la: Hæc omnia superius ex Ecclesiæ proceribus produximus. Pro regula fidei habeatur, quæ hactenus pro regula fidei in Ecclesia habita fuit: non autem noua ista, incerta, mutabilis, conficta nuper in Concilio Tridentino, excepta à Iesuitis (ecquis uero nobis præstabit, ut non reiecta ista, aliam denuo confingant?) quam isti sua tantum autoritate obtrudunt, sine Scripturæ autoritate, sine con-senstu Patrum, de qua ante nostra secula in Ecclesia nihil fuit auditum, quæq; in hunc finem {confecta} est, ut omnia ad unius Papæ arbitrium revocentur, quem in Ecclesia adorandum docent Iesuitæ. Quanquam autem Iesuitas superbum genus hominum cognovimus, hæc tamen incredibilis superbia cum pari stultitia coniuncta est, si putent de re longe gravissima, qualis est regula fidei, figmenta sua pro oraculis in Ecclesia habenda esse, quamvis nullum habeant antiquitatis consensum. Sic ergo præscribimus Tridentinis: Ecclesiæ officium & ministerium in eo versatur, ut regulam fidei unam, immobilem, integram conservet: quam tamen isti mutarunt: quid [?]iis igitur cum Ecclesia Christi? {a}Expedite præscribimur, inquit Tertullianus, adulterū nostrū; illam esse regulam veritatis, quæ venit à Christo transmissa per comites ipsius, quibus aliquanto posteriores diversi isti commentatores probabuntur. Eandem hanc regulam, {b}unam, immobilem, irre-formabilem vocat. Hæc igitur est illa regula aurea, quæ veritatem Pontificiis tenebris immersam restituit nobis. Hæc regula Ecclesiam ab istis obscuratam evidenter ostendet. Veritas est, quæ cum hac regula consentit: Ecclesia est, quæ hanc regulam immutatam conservaverit. Hæc succinctè de regula fidei diximus.
units.tr: All these things we have set forth above from the leaders of the Church. Let that be held as the rule of faith which has hitherto been held as the rule of faith in the Church, and not these new, uncertain, changeable, invented rules lately devised at the Council of Trent and accepted by the Jesuits (yet who will guarantee us that, once these are discarded, they will not devise yet another?). These the Jesuits impose by their own authority alone, without the authority of Scripture, without the consent of the Fathers, of which nothing was heard in the Church in our former ages; and which has been contrived for this purpose, that everything may be referred to the will of one Pope, whom the Jesuits teach is to be adored in the Church. Although we have come to know the Jesuits as a proud race of men, this incredible pride is nevertheless joined with equal folly, if they think that in a matter of by far the greatest weight, such as the rule of faith is, their fictions are to be held as oracles in the Church, although they have no agreement of antiquity whatever. So we prescribe to the Tridentines: the office and ministry of the Church consists in this, that it keep the one, unchangeable and whole rule of faith; which yet they have changed. What, then, have they to do with the Church of Christ? We are readily prescribed against, says Tertullian, our adversaries; that is the rule of truth, which comes from Christ, transmitted through his companions, to whom these diverse commentators will be shown to be considerably later. The same rule he calls one, unchangeable, irreformable. This, then, is that golden rule, which has restored to us the truth sunk in Papistical darkness. This rule will clearly show the Church, obscured by those men. That is the truth which agrees with this rule; that is the Church which has kept this rule unchanged. We have spoken briefly here about the rule of faith.

units.la: Dicamus eâdem brevitate de iudice controversiarum. Nam ex iis, quæ superius produximus, expeditior erit harum rerum tractatio.
units.tr: Let us say with the same brevity concerning the judge of controversies. For from what we have set forth above, the treatment of these matters will be more expeditious.

units.la: CAPVT VIII. Corollarium de Iudice controuersiarum.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII. Corollary on the Judge of Controversies.

units.la: DE iudice controuersiarum quoties disputant Pontificii, triumphus statim decernitur Romano Pontifici. Sine hoc iudice Ecclesiam esse mutam, imbellem clamitant, nec autoritatem habere, nec potestatem vllam, ne vocem quidem. Ac proinde nos miseros esse, qui controuersias religionis non possumus definire, quippe qui Papam, vnicum scilicet Iudicem non agnoscamus.
units.tr: Whenever the Papists dispute about the judge of controversies, they at once award the victory to the Roman Pontiff. Without this judge, they cry, the Church is mute and powerless, with no authority, no power, not even a voice. And so, they say, we wretches cannot settle questions of religion, since we do not acknowledge the Pope, the one and only Judge.

units.la: Respondemus, controuersias definiendi eandem apud nos remanere rationem, quae apud antiquam Ecclesiam valuit. Vel enim Episcopi conuocabant Synodos intra suas dioeceses, vel Metropolitani prouinciales. Et si Ecclesiae necessitas postulabat, plures Metropolitani in vnum cogebantur, non imperio coacti a quoquam, sed vnitatis & charitatis vinculo cohaerentes coibant. Loquor de primis Ecclesiae temporibus. Haec antiqua conuocandi Synodos ratio omnis apud Pontificios antiquata est. Concilia, inquit Bellarminus, Romana particularia exoleuerunt, & in eorum locum Consistoria Cardinalium successisse videntur. Cognoscite igitur, quinam sint, qui Conciliorum vim autoritatemque, ipsorum confessione, mutarunt, labefactarunt, & exoletam reddiderunt. Apud nos antiqua haec ratio viget, valetque. Si ergo de prouin-
units.tr: We reply that the same method of settling controversies that prevailed in the ancient Church remains in force among us. Either bishops summoned synods within their own dioceses, or provincial metropolitans did so. And if the needs of the Church required it, several metropolitans were gathered into one. They were not compelled to come by anyone's command, but came together, held by the bond of unity and charity. I am speaking of the earliest times of the Church. Among the Papists this ancient method of summoning synods has been wholly abolished. "Provincial councils," says Bellarmine, "have fallen into disuse, and the consistories of the Cardinals seem to have taken their place." Consider, then, who they are that, by their own confession, have changed, weakened and made obsolete the force and authority of councils. Among us this ancient method flourishes and holds good. So if the question concerns provincial synods,

units.la: uinci loqu tion antic null Nam gion uoca bus quo ueni mna sub man tant pisc rat lude tant non nec sum Ro quid ftian ualu rali Cor Ecc inte sed vincialibus Synodis quæstio sit; sine fronte loquuntur, & scribunt, nullam esse eius rei ra-tionem apud nos, quum tantum apud nos antiqua ratio valeat, quæ apud illos exoleuit.
units.tr: ...provincial synods is the question; they speak and write without shame that there is no such method among us, although the ancient method, which has fallen into disuse among them, holds full force among us.

units.la: Si de generalibus Conciliis loquantur, nullus in illis Romanus Iudex inuenietur. Nam antequam Romani Imperatores religionem susceperant, Concilia quædam conuocata sunt, quæ maiora erant prouinciali-bus; sicut erat Concilium Antiochenum, in quo Episcopi diuersarum prouinciarum conueniebant[?]: & Paulus ille Samosatenus damnatus est, inquit Eusebius, ab omnibus, quæ sub cælis sunt, Ecclesiis Christi. Num hic Romanus Pontifex Iudex sederat nequaquam; tantum re gesta, scripserunt ad Romanum Episcopum, sicut & ad Alexandrinum. Non erat hic locus Romano supra alios: quis ergo Iudex erat? De iudice mox dicemus: illud tantum hic monitum volumus, Romanum non alio fuisse loco, quam alios Episcopos: nec conuocasse, nec præfuisse; tantum assensum præbuisse cum reliquis. Quid enim iuris Romano esse potuit in Græcos Episcopos? quid in Asia & Oriente? At postquam Christiana religio apud Romanos Imperatores inualuit, autoritas conuocandi Concilia generalia, & potestate coactiua firmandi canones Conciliorum, ad Imperatores deferebatur ab Ecclesia, ab iisque exercebatur. Imperatores interea non erant iudices controuersiarum, sed sicut Romani Episcopi eos appellant, custodes[?] disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ. Quis est ergo iudex controuersiarum?
units.tr: If they speak of general councils, no Roman judge will be found in them. For before the Roman emperors had embraced the Christian religion, some councils were convened which were larger than provincial ones, such as the Council of Antioch, in which bishops of various provinces gathered. And that Paul of Samosata, says Eusebius, was condemned by all the Churches of Christ that are under heaven. Did the Roman bishop preside there as judge? By no means. They merely reported what had been done and wrote to the Roman bishop, as they also did to the bishop of Alexandria. The Roman had no place above the others here. Who, then, was the judge? We shall speak of the judge shortly. For now we wish only to point out that the Roman held no other position than the other bishops: he neither convened the council nor presided over it, but merely gave his assent with the rest. For what right could the Roman have had over the Greek bishops? What right over Asia and the East? But after the Christian religion prevailed under the Roman emperors, the authority to convene general councils, and the coercive power to confirm the canons of councils, was transferred by the Church to the emperors, and they exercised it. Meanwhile the emperors were not judges of controversies; rather, as the Roman bishops themselves call them, they were guardians of ecclesiastical discipline. Who, then, is the judge of controversies?

units.la: Ex antiquis regulam fidei supra deduximus: ea nos regula quæ manu ducet ad iudicem controuersiarum. Controuersias enim istas intelligimus, conuouersias[?] de fide. Fides autem Ecclesiæ vna est, non diuersa, constans, firmaque est, non dubia, non controuersa. Pulchre Tertullianus:{a} Regula fidei à Christo instituta, nullas habet apud nos quæstiones, nisi quas hæresis infert, & quæ hæreticos faciunt. Controuersiæ ergo, quæ oriuntur ab hæreticis excitantur. Et quia hæretici fidem vnam, perpetuam, constantem Ecclesiæ, conantur euertere, idcirco aduersus hæreticos Ecclesia discernit controuersias fidei secundum regulam fidei. Quid ergo? Num Ecclesiam dicimus esse iudicem controuersiarum? Non dicimus: quia ante nos nemo ita dixit. Ecclesia testis est, non iudex. Vos eritis mihi testes in Ierusalem, & in tota Iudæa, & Samaria, & víquead vltimas terras.{} Non iudices esse voluit, quos testes constituit. Ipsa igitur prædicatio testimonium dicitur. Prophetarum prædicatio quid est, nisi testimonium? Huic omnes Prophetæ testimonium dant, remissionem peccatorum accepturum per nomen eius, qui crediderit in eum.{} Apostolorum prædicatio quid est nisi testimonium? Non recipient testimonium tuum de me.{} Vniuersa prædicatio Euangelii quid est nisi testimonium Christi? Testimonium
units.tr: From the ancients we have drawn up the rule of faith above; this rule will lead us by the hand to the judge of controversies. For by controversies we mean controversies about the faith. The faith of the Church, however, is one, not divergent, constant and firm, not doubtful, not disputed. Tertullian says it well: "The rule of faith, instituted by Christ, has among us no questions except those which heresy brings in, and which make heretics." Controversies therefore arise and are stirred up by heretics. And because heretics strive to overthrow the one, perpetual and constant faith of the Church, for that reason the Church, against the heretics, distinguishes the controversies of the faith according to the rule of faith. What then? Do we say that the Church is the judge of controversies? We do not say so, because no one before us has said it. The Church is a witness, not a judge. "You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and Samaria, and even to the uttermost parts of the earth." He who appointed them witnesses did not will them to be judges. Preaching itself is therefore called testimony. What is the preaching of the prophets but testimony? To this all the prophets bear witness, that through his name everyone who believes in him will receive forgiveness of sins. What is the preaching of the apostles but testimony? "They will not receive your testimony concerning me." What is the whole preaching of the Gospel but the testimony of Christ? "The testimony of Christ," says the Apostle to the Corinthians, "was confirmed among you."

units.la: {a} lib. præscrip. cap.14. ergo duxiiudienim Fides conatrofidei quie haoriecun Ecerius arsiergo? connos udex. tota rras. tuit. itur. eltimoacceum. estiium dest ium isti. Christi, inquit Apostolus ad Corinthios; con- firmatum fuit in vobis. Praedicatio igitur Ecclesiae testimonium est, & Ecclesia testis. Testis autem nihil addit, nihil subducit, sed ex regn-la veritatis loquitur. Deinde in eadem causa quis potest esse testis & iudex? Iam vero quum vniuersa Ecclesia praedicet testimonium sit, & Ecclesia testis: Si quis inter Ecclesiae membra est [?]tacet, nam in maiori loco habendus erit, quam testis loco? Certe quicunque in Ecclesia excelluerunt, & columnae videbantur, testimonium tantum perhibebant, testes erant, non iudices. Itaque Iohannes Baptista, quo maior non est ortus inter natos mulierum, non venit vt iudex, sed venit ad dandum testimonium de luce. Petrus Apostolus nusquam dicitur iudex, sed tantum testis afflictionum Christi. Ita Apostoli omnes testes fuerunt, non iudices.
units.tr: Accordingly, the preaching of the Church is testimony, and the Church is a witness. A witness, moreover, adds nothing and takes nothing away, but speaks from the rule of truth. Further, in the same cause, who can be both witness and judge? Indeed, since the whole Church's preaching is testimony and the Church is a witness, if anyone among the members of the Church is silent, must he be held in greater esteem than a witness? Certainly those who excelled in the Church and seemed to be its pillars bore testimony only; they were witnesses, not judges. So John the Baptist, than whom there has not arisen a greater among those born of women, came not as a judge but to give testimony concerning the light. The Apostle Peter is nowhere called a judge, but only a witness of the sufferings of Christ. So all the apostles were witnesses, not judges.

units.la: Nullusne igitur iudex est controuersiarum? Est certe. Quis igitur ille est, cui testes isti seruiunt, cuius mandato testimonium perhibent, qui testimonium eorum examinat, & diiudicat. Nam quicunque est iudex controuersiarum fidei, erit iudex fidei: quia in controversiis de fide, vbi quaeritur, quid sit credendum: iudex est, qui possit dicere, hoc tibi mando, hoc credas, qui credentes remanerat, qui incredulos iudicat. Iudex ergo controversiarum de fide, est iudex fidei nostrae. Qui vero iudex est fidei nostrae, est dominus fidei nostrae. Dominus autem fidei nostræ non est Petrus , non Paulus. Non dominamur fidei vestræ, inquit Apo-ftolus. Atqui dominatur fidei,qui iudex est fi-dei. Ergo inter Ecclesiæ membra iudex inue-niri non potest , quia dominus fidei inueniri non potest in membris. Iudex igitur de fide Ecclesiæ,est caput Ecclesiæ. Hoc etiam Ponti-ficii videbant, ac proinde Papam constituunt & caput Ecclesiæ,& iudicem de fide.
units.tr: Is there then no judge of controversies? There certainly is. Who, then, is he whom these witnesses serve, by whose command they bear testimony, and who examines and decides their testimony? For whoever is the judge of controversies of faith will be the judge of faith: because in controversies about faith, where the question is what is to be believed, the judge is the one who can say, "This I command you, this you are to believe," who keeps the believers and judges the unbelievers. The judge of controversies about faith is therefore the judge of our faith. But he who is the judge of our faith is the lord of our faith. Yet Peter is not the lord of our faith, nor is Paul. "We are not lords over your faith," says the Apostle. But he who is judge of the faith does lord it over the faith. Therefore no judge can be found among the members of the Church, because a lord of the faith cannot be found among the members. The judge of the Church's faith is therefore the head of the Church. The Papists saw this as well, and accordingly they set up the Pope as head of the Church and judge of the faith.

units.la: Nos vero affirmamus, Ecclesiam Christi in controuersiis fidei non alium agnouisse iudi-cem, quam Christum in Scripturis suis lo-quentem. Clamitant hic Pontificii, Scriptu-ram esse obscuram, indigere interpretatione viva,& iudice visibili. Clament,quantum vo-lunt, ringantur, rumpantur : at non alium in-uenient iudicem in controuersiis fidei. Vide-te primo, quomodo illi, tanquam caeci & a-mentes in suos gladios ruant. {a}Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis nihil est, inquit Bellarminus, certius, nihil notius, vt stultissi-mum esse necesse sit, qui illis fidem habendam esse negat. Quod est certissimum & notissimum, quomodo est ita obscurum, vt non intelligatur, imo quomodo iudicem quaerit? vnde tot controuersiae? Sed vere dicitur Scriptura certissima & notissima. Et controuersiae excitantur ab haereticis; qui controuersias in-dustria induxerunt, & quotidie augent, vt ex eo iudicem etiam visibilem inducant. Sed in-telligite sophismatum artifices. Docemus nos, vel potius Ecclesiæ Catholicæ doctrinam referefer & m riis. Scrip Dei sma est o Ref fe. obsc inan caus loco loci cuit clef qua omn lexa lux e lu e rege qui vag uri e post nun Deo quo ad gel [illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: We, however, affirm that the Church of Christ, in controversies of faith, has acknowledged no other judge than Christ speaking in his Scriptures. Here the Papists cry out that Scripture is obscure, that it needs a living interpretation and a visible judge. Let them cry out as much as they like, let them burst their lungs and their bellies; they will find no other judge in controversies of faith. Notice first how they rush, like blind and mad men, upon their own swords. Bellarmine says: "Nothing is more certain or better known than the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, so that he who refuses to give them faith must of necessity be most foolish." If it is most certain and best known, how is it so obscure that it cannot be understood, or indeed how does it seek a judge? Whence then so many controversies? But Scripture is rightly called most certain and best known. The controversies are stirred up by heretics, who have brought them in by design and increase them every day, so that from this they may introduce a judge who is also visible. But understand these artisans of sophistries. We teach, or rather we set forth the doctrine of the Catholic Church...

units.la: CAPUT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: referimus, retinemus: Scripturas esse apertas & manifestas in omnibus ad salutem necessariis. Quid Iesuitæ?[?] Probant scilicet, multos Scripturæ locos esse obscuros. Et quis negat? Deinde ad incautos decipiendos tale sophisma struere solent: Scriptura in multis locis est obscura, ergo iudex visibilis est statuendus. Respondeo, consequentiam plane nullam esse. Nam quæ necessaria sunt ad salutem, non obscure, sed aperte posita sunt in Scripturis: inane igitur est hoc sophisma, ponens non causam pro causa, propter quosdam Scripturæ locos obscuros, iudicem esse statuendum de locis apertis. De summa Scripturarum perspicuitate in necessariis magnus est antiquæ Ecclesiæ consensus. {a}Ita[?] inquit Augustinus, quæ aperta in Scriptura posita sunt, inveniuntur ea omnia, quæ continent vitam moresque. Clemens Alexand. {b}Nulla, inquit, veritas est, quæ non lux est communis, omnibus illucescit hominibus, nullum est in verbo Dei tenebrarum, sed omnes ad salutem, ad regenerationem. {c}Chrysostomus, Apostoli, inquit, & Prophetæ omnia confecerunt manifesta, utraque, quæ prodiderunt. Exposuerunt omnium veteres communes arbitri doctores, ut per se quisq; discere possit ea, quæ discuntur è sola lectione. Et hoc ante prænuntians Propheta, dicebat: Erunt omnes docti à Deo, & non dicet quisque proximo suo: noscite Deum, quoniam omnes noscent me à minimo eorum usque ad maximum. Cur non manifesta, quæcunque in Evangelio scripta sunt?
units.tr: We hold and maintain that the Scriptures are clear and manifest in all things necessary to salvation. What do the Jesuits say? They undertake, of course, to prove that many passages of Scripture are obscure. And who denies it? Next, to deceive the unwary, they usually construct this sophism: Scripture is obscure in many places, therefore a visible judge must be appointed. I answer that the inference is entirely null. For what is necessary to salvation is set down in the Scriptures not obscurely but plainly, so this sophism is empty, putting a non-cause in place of the cause: because of some obscure passages of Scripture, a judge must be appointed over the plain ones. There is great agreement of the ancient Church on the overall clarity of Scripture in necessary matters. {a}Thus Augustine says: all the things that are set down plainly in Scripture are found to contain everything that concerns life and conduct. Clement of Alexandria: {b}There is no truth, he says, that is not a common light; it shines on all men; there is nothing of darkness in the Word of God, but all things are for salvation and for regeneration. {c}Chrysostom: The apostles and prophets, he says, made both of the things they handed down plain. The common teachers of old, as judges of all things, expounded them, so that each one might learn by himself those things that are learned from reading alone. The prophet, foretelling this beforehand, said: All shall be taught by God, and no one shall say to his neighbour, know the Lord, for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest. Why should not whatever is written in the Gospel be plain?

units.la: Respondeo secundo, non posse istos hoc sophisophismate probare, talem iudicem de Scrip-pturis statuendum in locis obscurissimis. Probat obscuritas, interpretes quidem esse necessarios, non autem iudicem: quia obscura & profunda Scripturarum eruuntur, non per potestatem aliquam, aut iurisdictionem iudicis alicuius, sed per industriam & scientiam interpretum. Sic semper fugiens caulae cognitionem, ut verbis maniobus[?] incautos fallant. Scriptura interpretatione indiget, Ecclesia igitur per omnia secula interpretes habuit, & habitura est, qui obscura loca exponant. Sed quid hoc ad iudicem? Nam neque interpretes ipsi iudices habiti sunt Scripturarum, quas exponant; neque Romanus Pontifex interpretum illorum iudex in Ecclesia unquam est habitus: multo minus ipsarum Scripturarum iudex: nemo enim potest esse iudex earum rerum, quas non recte cognoue-rit. Itaque per ipsos Pontificios canones distinguitur iurisdictio à scientia interpretandi; & iurisdictio Rom. Pontificibus, at interpretandi scientia interpretibus defertur. Quum igitur longe aliud sit, causas forenses audire, aliud sacras Scripturas tractare, canones ipsi Pontificii Romanos Pontifices cum iurisdictione sua, & dignitatis apice, quam vocant; ad causas forenses statuunt; ad sacras vero Scripturas exponendas non Romanos Pontifices, sed sacros interpretes assignant. De qua re Gratianus sic habet: a Dionysio Scripturarum tra-ctatores, etsi scientia Pontificibus eminentes, tamen quia dignitatis aut etiam apicem non sunt adepti, in sa-crarum quidem Scripturarum expositionibus ea-rum [?] praeponantur, intanto vero desinendum [?], sistendum post eam locum merentur. Haec Gratianus. Ex qui-bus verbis constare potest figmentum hoc Iesuiticum de Papa iudice in controversiis fi-dei, non fuisse excogitatum Gratiani seculo: tum quidem canones ad Romanam Curiam mitterentur, magno studio exsabatur, ut in illis capitulis Romanus Pontifex summus [?] sederet iudex. Ad hoc iudicem in controver-siis de fide tunc temporis ne somniabant quidem. Sed quin Rom. Pontifex ex una praesumptione in aliam subinde transire soleret, tandem etiam se iudicem interponere voluit in controver-siis fidei. Sed hoc figmentum sero innotuit, & novitate sua defensores perterrebat. Scripturas affirmant esse obscuras: at nihil promouerunt: nam quod nos docemus, ipsi etiam conse-dunt, Scripturas apertas esse in iis omnibus, quae fidem moresque continent, unde con-troversiae de fide sunt definiendae. Obscuritas autem Scripturarum, interpretes probant, non iudicem. Miserit ergo Pontifex, dum iudicem quaerunt, interpretes unum probant, in quo munere Papae est, ipsorum confessione, in-utilis & ineptus. Nos interpretes multos con-cedimus, iudicem istum repudiamus: nec quenquam alium iudicem, praeter unum Christum, in Scripturis sua loquentem, in Ecclesia controversiis de fide habitum fuisse affirmamus.
units.tr: I answer secondly that they cannot prove by this sophism that such a judge must be appointed over the most obscure passages of Scripture. The obscurity proves that interpreters are indeed necessary, but not a judge; for the obscure and deep things of Scripture are brought out not by any power or jurisdiction of some judge, but by the diligence and learning of interpreters. So they always avoid the question of the case, so that they may deceive the unwary with empty words. Scripture needs interpretation; the Church therefore has had, throughout all ages, and will have, interpreters who expound the obscure passages. But what does this have to do with a judge? For neither were the interpreters themselves regarded as judges of the Scriptures they expounded, nor was the Roman Pontiff ever regarded in the Church as judge of those interpreters, much less judge of the Scriptures themselves: for no one can be judge of things he has not rightly known. Thus, by the very Papist canons, jurisdiction is distinguished from the knowledge of interpreting; jurisdiction is granted to the Roman Pontiffs, but the knowledge of interpreting to the interpreters. Since it is one thing to hear lawsuits and another to handle the holy Scriptures, the canons themselves of the Papists assign the Roman Pontiffs, with their jurisdiction and what they call the pinnacle of dignity, to forensic causes; but for expounding the holy Scriptures they assign not the Roman Pontiffs but holy interpreters. On this matter Gratian says thus: From Dionysius, the handlers of the Scriptures, although eminent in learning above the Pontiffs, yet because they have not attained the dignity or even the pinnacle, are to be placed before them in the expositions of the holy Scriptures, but as to the pinnacle, they deserve to stop and stand after that place. So Gratian. From these words it can be established that this Jesuit fiction of the Pope as judge in controversies of faith was not devised in Gratian's age: at that time canons were sent to the Roman Curia, and with great zeal it was sought that the Roman Pontiff should sit as judge in those chapters. At that time people did not even dream of a judge in controversies of faith. But when the Roman Pontiff, passing from one presumption to another, at length wished to interpose himself as judge also in controversies of faith, this fiction came to light late, and by its novelty it frightened its defenders. They assert that the Scriptures are obscure, but they have advanced nothing: for what we teach, they themselves also concede, that the Scriptures are clear in all those things which contain faith and conduct, from which controversies of faith are to be decided. But the obscurity of Scripture proves interpreters, not a judge. Strangely, then, while they seek a judge, they prove only interpreters, in whose office the Pope is, by their own confession, useless and unfit. We concede many interpreters; that judge we reject; nor do we affirm that any judge other than Christ alone, speaking in the Scriptures, has been held in the Church in controversies of faith.

units.la: In Concilio Nicæno, Constantinus iudicem controuersiæ accurate descripsit his verbis: {a} In disputationibus rerum diuinarum habent (Episcopi) sanctissimi Spiritus doctrinam perscriptam. Euangelici enim, & Apostolici libri, necnon antiquorum Prophetarum oracula plene instruunt nos: proinde suarum ex dictis diuini Spiritus explicationes quæstionum. Hæc ille. Constantinus a Catholicis Episcopis edoctus, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ fidem ita proposuit, ut Tridentinas fraudes luculenter præuerterit. 1. In disputationibus rerum diuinarum docet sancti Spiritus doctrinam esse perscriptam. A quo igitur spiritu est doctrina Tridentina, & verbum hoc non scriptum? 2. Euangelici, & Apostolici libri, & Prophetarum oracula plene nos instruunt: Scriptura igitur Propherica & Apostolica est regula fidei totalis, non partialis, ut isti novatores obgannunt. Quod enim plene nos instruit, non tantum ex parte, est regula completa, non partialis. 3. Sumendas esse docet ex dictis divini Spiritus explicationes quæstionum; Divina igitur Scriptura, ut lex Christi dictata à Spiritu sancto, ad omnes fidei controversias decidendas sufficit: quia error potest esse in dictis omnibus, quæ non sunt dicta sancti Spiritus. Hæc est Catholicæ Ecclesiæ sententia, quæ per successiones Episcoporum conservata est, & retenta in Ecclesia, usq; ad Concilium Tridentinum. Ecclesia nec aliam regulam, nec alium judicem in controversiis de fide agnovit præter sacras Scripturas. Cyp bum, gia: & rum quicqu Op mo vel mines vtraq impea non pot micu hac ve rendu cum nost dicen inuid iudic ric, ta tame quam pron ha ru Papa quun fide sum Opta in ter fiar recen inau
units.tr: At the Council of Nicaea, Constantine accurately described the judge of the controversy in these words: {a} In disputations about divine things the bishops have the teaching of the most holy Spirit written down. For the Gospel and Apostolic books, and likewise the oracles of the ancient prophets, fully instruct us; therefore the explanations of our questions are to be drawn from the sayings of the divine Spirit. So he. Instructed by the Catholic bishops, Constantine set forth the faith of the Catholic Church in such a way that he brilliantly overturned the Tridentine frauds. 1. In disputations about divine things he teaches that the teaching of the Holy Spirit is written down. From what spirit, then, is the Tridentine doctrine, and this unwritten word? 2. The Gospel and Apostolic books and the oracles of the prophets fully instruct us: Scripture, therefore, both prophetic and apostolic, is the complete rule of faith, not a partial one, as those novelties snarl. For what fully instructs us, and not merely in part, is a complete rule, not a partial one. 3. He teaches that explanations of questions are to be taken from the sayings of the divine Spirit; the divine Scripture, therefore, as the law of Christ dictated by the Holy Spirit, is sufficient for deciding all controversies of faith, because error can be present in all sayings that are not sayings of the Holy Spirit. This is the opinion of the Catholic Church, which has been preserved through the successions of bishops, and retained in the Church up to the Council of Trent. The Church acknowledged neither another rule nor another judge in controversies of faith, except the holy Scriptures.

units.la: Cyprianus sic docet: a Legat hic vnum verbum, & in hoc mandato meditatur Christiana religio: & iuuenies ex hac Scriptura omnium doctrinarum regulam emanasse, & huc nasci, & hinc reuerti, quicquid Ecclesiasticè ventilatum disputata [?].
units.tr: Cyprian teaches thus: Read here one word, and in this command the Christian religion is meditated upon; and you will find that from this Scripture the rule of all doctrines has flowed forth, and springs from here, and returns here, whatever is ecclesiastically debated and disputed.

units.la: Optatus eandem doctrinam refulit: b Nemo vobis credas, nemo [?] sumus, omnes sententiosi homines sumus. Quaerendi sunt iudices. Si Christiani de utraque parte dari non possunt, quia sanguis veritas imputatur. De foro quae ratio est iudex: si paganus, non potest nosse Christiana mysteria; si Iudaeus, inimicus est Christiani baptismatis. Ergo in terris de hac re nullam potestis reperire iudicium: de caelo quaerendum est iudex. Sed ad quid cultum adeo ad caelum, cum habemus hic in Evangelio? Haec ille. Iesuitae nostri hunc sanctum Patrem vel caecum fuisse dicent, vel delirum senem, vel indoctum, vel invidum Papae detractatorem, qui quum de iudice controversiarum ex professo disputaret, tanto se labore fatigans quaerendo, nec tamen hunc iudicem in terris inuenerit. At quam facile Papam controversiarum iudicem pronunciare potuisset, si illum iudicem Ecclesia tunc agnouisset? Haec Iesuitas doler, quod Papam penitus exclauserit. Exclusit omnino, quum in terris iudicem controversiarum de fide inveniri nullum posse profiteatur. Sensum Ecclesiae illius saeculi magna fide refert Optatus, Papam non habitum fuisse Christi in terris Vicarium, non iudicem controversiarum, non caput, non os Ecclesiae. Haec sunt recentia fratrum figmenta, antiquis Patribus inaudita monstra.
units.tr: Optatus shone forth with the same doctrine: {b}Trust no one among you, no one... we are all men of opinion. Judges must be sought. If Christians cannot be found on either side, because the truth is imputed as blood... What reason is there for judgment from the outside? If he is a pagan, he cannot know Christian mysteries; if a Jew, he is an enemy of Christian baptism. Therefore on earth you can find no judgment in this matter; a judge must be sought from heaven. But why seek so far up to heaven, when we have here in the Gospel? So he. Our Jesuits will say that this holy Father was either blind, or a raving old man, or ignorant, or a jealous detractor of the Pope, since, when he disputed expressly about the judge of controversies, labouring so hard in his search, he nevertheless did not find this judge on earth. But how easily could he have pronounced the Pope judge of controversies, if the Church of that time had acknowledged such a judge? The Jesuits grieve over this, that he has altogether shut out the Pope. He has shut him out completely, since he professes that no judge of controversies of faith can be found on earth. Optatus reports with great faith the sense of that Church of his age: that the Pope was not regarded as the Vicar of Christ on earth, not as judge of controversies, not as head, not as mouth of the Church. These are recent fictions of the brethren, monstrous things unheard of by the ancient Fathers.

units.la: Augustinus eodem modo, quum de controuersiarum iudice disserit, nullam iudicem in Ecclesia agnoscit, praeter unicum Christum in Scripturis suis loquentem. {a}Ipsa, inquit, controuersia iudicem quaerit: iudicem ergo Christum. Et mox: Iudicet & [?] Apostolus, quae in Apostolo ipse loquitur Christus. Idem alibi sic scribit: {b}Neq. hinc cauendum mihi vigilantiae suae Ecclesiasticum est confirmatum [illegible, ~12 letters] ad quem scripti libri Prophetarum & Apostolorum pertinent, quae omnino iudicare non audemus, sed secundum quae de caeleri litera, vel fidelium, vel infidelium, libera iudicemus. {c}Nec aperte de eo fidelium eterum atque iudicare, neq. de ipso libro tam, et similiter [illegible, ~10 letters] submittamus mentem.
units.tr: Augustine likewise, when he discusses the judge of controversies, acknowledges no judge in the Church except Christ alone, speaking in his Scriptures. "The controversy itself," he says, "seeks a judge; therefore the judge is Christ." And soon after: "Let the Apostle judge what Christ himself speaks in the Apostle." He writes elsewhere in this way: "Nor is it for me, in my vigilance, to be cautious here, since the ecclesiastical [...] is confirmed, to which the written books of the Prophets and Apostles belong; these we dare not judge at all, but according to them we judge freely of the rest of the writings, whether of the faithful or of unbelievers." And again: "Nor do we openly submit our minds to judge of him [...] nor of the book itself in the same way [...]."

units.la: Haec Augustinus. Notanda sunt quae de controuersiarum iudice cum differre habet Augustinus. Diserte [?] affirmat Christum & Apostolicas literas, in quibus Christus loquitur, esse controuersiarum iudicem. Diserte affirmat Ecclesiasticum canonem in Scripturis Propheticis & Apostolicis constitutum, esse regulam illam fidei, secundum quam de omnium scriptis iudicat Ecclesia. Diserte negat, quemuis hominem esse iudicem, quamuis, ut eodem loco scribit, {d}spiritualis homo sit, & renovatus in agnitionem Dei, secundum imaginem eius, qui creavit eum. Quanto magis si hodie inter vivos esset, hunc locum negaturus fuisset carnalibus, & impuris Pontificibus?
units.tr: So far Augustine. What he sets out about the judge of controversies must be noted. He plainly affirms that Christ and the apostolic writings, in which Christ speaks, are the judge of controversies. He plainly affirms that the ecclesiastical canon, established in the prophetic and apostolic Scriptures, is that rule of faith by which the Church judges all writings. He plainly denies that any man is the judge, even though, as he writes in the same place, the man is spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of him who created him. How much more, if he were alive today, would he deny this place to carnal and impure Pontiffs?

units.la: Haec eadem [?] de iudice in controuere conadicen[?] ristum[?] inquit[?] Christum[?] in Apo[?] eribit[?] nam Ec[?] eis fra[?] mminu[?] de cale[?] indice[?] tatem[?] non in[?] ellam[?] e conAugupottoe, esse rmat, Prosse renium quemut eo& remagiagis li negancifintroner perfus[?] fidei confessum fuit in Ecclesia, nemi-ne contradicente, usque ad annum Christi millesimum. A quo tempore, soluto[?] iam Sa-tana, adulatores Romanæ Curiæ cœperunt Romani Pontificis[?] auctoritatem sine modestia efferre. At contra istos adulatores, fratercu-los[?] dico, & Canonistas, Ecclesia Romana egregie in hac re veritatem, & antiquam Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consuetudinem conserua-rat, usque ad Concilii[?] Tridentini tempora. Nam quum in Concilio Basiliensi quæstio orta fuisset de iudice controuersiarum, & Bohemi ad disputationem accedere nolent, nisi prius de iudice convenisset. Quid Basilienses? Num Papam iudicem agnoscebant de fidei controuersiis? Nusquam: sed antiquam Ecclesiæ Catholicæ sententiam de iudice retu-nuerunt. Sic enim statuunt: {a}Lex divina, praeeunte Christi Apostolis & primaeua Ecclesia, cum Concilijs, doctoribusque, iudicium se re-tractatur in eadem, pro verissima, & [?]te iudice in hac Basiliensi Concilio admitti-tur. Haec Basilienses. Quibus verbis Ecclesiæ Romanæ iudicium, & sententia referetur. Itaque ad illud tempus Ecclesia Catholica sententia immutata constituitur. Evolvant origines suas Iesuitæ, & Iesuitis pandunt antiquiores fraterculi, & invenient, [?]gmentum hoc de Papa iudice, vel ab ipsis confictum, vel cum ipsis natum, cum ipsis moriturum, in Ecclesia nunquam receptam.
units.tr: [Heavily garbled in the scan; the legible parts give the sense:] ...the confession of this faith stood in the Church, no one contradicting, until the year of Christ one thousand. From that time, Satan now being loosed, the flatterers of the Roman Curia began to extol the authority of the Roman Pontiff without restraint. But against those flatterers, I mean the little brothers and the Canonists, the Roman Church itself had admirably preserved the truth in this matter and the ancient custom of the Catholic Church, up to the times of the Council of Trent. For when at the Council of Basel a question arose about the judge of controversies, the Bohemians were unwilling to come to disputation unless they first agreed about the judge. What did the Baselians do? Did they acknowledge the Pope as judge of controversies of faith? Nowhere: rather they retained the ancient opinion of the Catholic Church about the judge. For they decree thus: "Divine law, following Christ's apostles and the primitive Church, with councils and teachers, [...] judgment is sought in the same, as most true, and [...] judge is admitted in this Council of Basel." So far the Baselians. By these words the judgment and opinion of the Roman Church is refuted. Thus up to that time the opinion of the Catholic Church stood unchanged. Let the Jesuits unfold their origins, and let the younger little brothers reveal them to the Jesuits, and they will find that this fiction about the Pope as judge was either invented by them or born with them, and will die with them, and was never received in the Church.

units.la: Iam quia Romana Curia controuersiam hanc contra Ecclesiam Catholicam suscepit (nam quod contra nostras Ecclesias pugnantes ferendum videretur, nisi & nostrae Ecclesiae in hac re cum Catholica communionem habe-rent: Itaque quicunque contra nos de iis re-bus controuersias instituunt, in quibus com-munionem habemus cum Catholica, non contra nos tantum, sed contra Catholicam etiam Ecclesiam pugnant.) Quia igitur hanc litem cum Ecclesia Catholica habet Romana Curia, & Pontificis mancipia Iesuitae in eo o-peram suam strenuè ponunt, vt Papa habea-tur Ecclesiae os, & Caput, & Rector, & Rex, & summus Iudex in fidei controuersiis: illud nobis non obseruatione tantum, sed & admi-ratione dignum videtur, quod isti, dum haec agunt, non sentiant, se Antichristum ipsis Ec-clesiae cerviciibus imponere. Quis enim non videt, hunc esse ἀντικείμενον[?], qui se in Eccle-siam, supra Ecclesiam, contra Ecclesiam, con-tra Scripturas statuit? Nam hoc vere est, quod dicit Apostolus, ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν θεοῦ, ὡς θεὸν καθίσαι. Apostolus dicit eum sessurum εἰς ναὸν θεοῦ, non in templo tantum, sed in tem-plum: non in Ecclesia tantum, sed in Eccle-siam, contra Ecclesiam, & tanquam Deum supra Ecclesiam. Quis enim est supra Eccle-siam, nisi vnus Deus? Nonne igitur hic, qui se supra Ecclesiam ostentat, sese tanquam Deum ostentat. Quem igitur locum Ecclesia Catholica vni Christo semper seruauit, vt sit Ecclesiae [illegible, ~1 letters] [illegible, ~10 letters] [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~9 letters] [illegible, ~9 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters]
units.tr: Now, since the Roman Curia has taken up this controversy against the Catholic Church (for what would seem tolerable against our churches, were it not that our churches have communion with the Catholic Church in this matter; so whoever raises controversies against us about those things in which we have communion with the Catholic Church, fights not only against us but also against the Catholic Church), and since the Roman Curia has this quarrel with the Catholic Church, and the Jesuits, the henchmen of the Pope, strenuously put their effort into making the Pope be regarded as the mouth, head, ruler, king and supreme judge of the Church in controversies of faith, it seems to us worthy not only of observation but also of wonder that they, while doing these things, do not perceive that they are setting Antichrist upon the very necks of the Church. For who does not see that he is the adversary, who sets himself in the Church, above the Church, against the Church, against the Scriptures? For this is truly what the Apostle says: "so that he sits in the temple of God, as God" [ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰς τὸν ναὸν θεοῦ, ὡς θεὸν καθίσαι]. The Apostle says that he will sit "in the temple of God," not merely in the temple but into the temple; not merely in the Church but into the Church, against the Church, and as God above the Church. For who is above the Church except the one God? Does not he, then, who sets himself above the Church, display himself as God? Therefore the place which the Catholic Church has always kept for the one Christ, that he be the head of the Church [...].

Ut nobis merito mirandum videatur, quomodo Iesuitæ contra Scripturas, contra Ecclesiæ consensum, tam sordide Romano Pontifici adulari possint, ut non conscientiæ suæ vim inferant, & videntes, viventesque in horrendam se præcipitare ruinam intelligant.
units.tr: [...] ... Head, and Ruler, and King, and Judge. The Roman Curia gives this honour of the passage [...] to the Roman Pontiff, against the Catholic Church. So it seems to us rightly astonishing how the Jesuits can flatter the Roman Pontiff so basely, against the Scriptures and against the consensus of the Church, without doing violence to their own conscience; and how, seeing and living, they can fail to understand that they are hurling themselves into a dreadful ruin. [Thess.; 1. Cor. ...]

units.la: CAPVT IX. Corollarium de Traditionibus non scriptis.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. Corollary concerning unwritten traditions.

units.la: HAbemus contra Pontificios vnanimem Ecclesiæ vocem, eamque non interrup-tam, de auctoritate Scripturarum. Quid Pon-tifici contra? Scripturas scilicet, & Patres ia-ctant. Sed miserica[?] est horum hominum Dia-lectica; non enim concludunt; neque illud magnopere curant: tantum Scripturas, non ad vincendi spem, sed ad ostentationem adducunt. Sic enim colludunt: Cætera, tam vero dissonam[?], 1.Cor.ii[?]. Tenete traditiones, quas ac-cepistis, sive per sermonem, sive per Epistolam, 2. Thessal. 2. Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, 1.Corin.2. O Timothee depositum custodi, 1.Tim.6. Ex quibus locis Bellarminus concludit, Scripturas non sufficere ad salutem, sed requiri traditiones non scriptas; hoc est, aliud verbum Dei non scriptum, quæ cum verbo scripto pro regulam fidei compleat. Alii ex iisdem lo-cis tis Missæ sacrificium, Romani Pontificis pri-matum, invocationem Sanctorum confirmant. Denique quicquid Tridentini viderent[?] se ex Scripturis probare non posse, luculenter confirmandum sumsisse[?] ex huiusmodi testimoniis: Caeca, tam variis, [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: We have against the Papists the unanimous voice of the Church, and one that has never been broken, concerning the authority of the Scriptures. What do the Papists set against it? They boast of the Scriptures and the Fathers. But wretched is the reasoning of these men; for their arguments do not conclude, and they do not greatly care that they do not. They bring forward the Scriptures, not in hope of winning, but for show. For they collude in this way: "Other things, so truly dissonant ... 1 Cor. 2. Hold the traditions which you have been taught, whether by word or by our epistle, 2 Thess. 2. We speak wisdom among the perfect, 1 Cor. 2. O Timothy, keep that which is committed to your trust, 1 Tim. 6." From these passages Bellarmine concludes that the Scriptures are not sufficient for salvation, but that unwritten traditions are required, that is, another unwritten word of God, which together with the written word completes the rule of faith. Others, from the same passages, confirm the sacrifice of the Mass, the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, and the invocation of the saints. In short, whatever the men of Trent saw they could not prove from the Scriptures, they took up to be confirmed brilliantly from testimonies of this kind: "blind, so various ..."

units.la: Hæc Scripturarum testimonia antiqui hæretici contra antiquos Patres producere solebant. Nuper vero Romanæ Curiæ adulatores eadem testimonia proferre cœperunt contra Ecclesiam. Quod offendiculum, inquit Iohannes Gerson, posterum[?] erat per multos, determinantes ex retrubus[?] grosse, & non ad regulam Evangelicam acceptis. Æneas Sylvius de huiusmodi Scripturæ testimoniis ab adulatoriis Romanæ Curiæ productis, sic scribit: Hæc bis hominis mire multa sustinuerunt, expositionis [illegible, ~8 letters] Patrum doctorum omnino possibilis. Nec considerant, miseri, quod quæ prædicant tantopere verba, [illegible, ~12 letters] Pontificum sunt, [illegible, ~10 letters].
units.tr: The ancient heretics were accustomed to bring these testimonies of Scripture against the ancient Fathers. Lately, however, the flatterers of the Roman Curia have begun to bring forward the same testimonies against the Church. This is an offence, says John Gerson, which for many has been a stumbling-block, since they decide matters from crude and unevangelical notions. Aeneas Sylvius, writing of such testimonies of Scripture produced by the flatterers of the Roman Curia, writes thus: "These texts have endured many strange things ... of the exposition of the holy doctors and Fathers entirely possible." And the wretches do not consider that the words which they so greatly proclaim ... are of the Popes ...

units.la: Has igitur artes adulatorias, & in sacris Scripturis pervertendis[?] impostu-ras, ab ipsis Pontificibus, imo vero ab ipsis Pontificibus explosas, nos quoque merito reiicimus.
units.tr: These flattering arts, then, and these impostures in perverting the holy Scriptures, which have been exploded by the Popes themselves, indeed by the Popes themselves, we too rightly reject.

units.la: Superius obseruauimus, istas antiquorum hæreticorum artes olim displosas ab Irenæo, Tertulliano, Athanasio, Augustino, in quibus tamen strenuè pergunt Pontificii[?]. Quia igitur è Scripturis nihil habent, (nam tecum Tertulliano loquamur, Scriptura negat, quod non norat: & insignis est impudentia, adeoq;
units.tr: We have observed above that these arts of the ancient heretics were once exploded by Irenaeus, Tertullian, Athanasius and Augustine, yet the Papists still persist vigorously in them. Since therefore they have nothing from Scripture (for, to speak with Tertullian, Scripture denies what it did not know; and it is a remarkable impudence, and so ...
