Nos vero, quanquam controuersiarum, quæ sunt de fide, Patres arbitros non admittamus; neque eo consilio hæc agimus, sed vt e Pontificiorum manibus omnia excutiamus arma, non possumus tamen admirabilem Dei prouidentiam non suspicere, qui Patrum animos & linguas ita gubernauit, vt in hac controuersia, sicut & in aliis pluribus, ne vnam quidem testimonium antiquorum adhuc vsque diem protulerint Pontificii, quo probare possint, in Scripturis non contineri expresse totam doctrinam de fide & moribus, ac proinde præter verbum Dei scriptum requiri etiam verbum Dei non scriptum in traditionibus. Huius sententiæ ratio constabit, si monstremus, quomodo Patres de traditionibus disputare soleant.
units.tr: ... it is peculiar to the antichristian Church to wish to produce unwritten traditions against the authority of Scripture; the Papists everywhere try to produce testimonies of the Fathers. We indeed, although we do not admit the Fathers as judges of the controversies that concern faith, nor do we act with that purpose, but so that we may wrest every weapon out of the Papists' hands, nevertheless cannot fail to acknowledge the wonderful providence of God, who has so governed the minds and tongues of the Fathers that in this controversy, as in many others, the Papists have not yet to this day produced a single testimony of the ancients by which they could prove that the whole doctrine of faith and morals is not expressly contained in Scripture, and therefore that, besides the written word of God, an unwritten word of God in traditions is also required. The reason for this opinion will be clear if we show how the Fathers are accustomed to discuss traditions.

units.la: Traditionis vox varie apud Patres sumitur. [?]1. Traditionem vocant doctrinam tradi-dinam[?], quæ eadem semper e Scripturis per omnes Ecclesiæ successiones seruanda est. Sicut enim perpetuus ille ignis altaris, qui de cœlo venerat, per sacerdotum successiones idem semper ante Dominum lucere debebat: sic vnam eandemque doctrinam semper in Ecclesia per omnes successiones permanere oportet, vt nihil extraneum ad sacram Scripturam addatur, inquit Theodoretus. Hæc doctrina vna eademque in Ecclesia conseruata, ab Ecclesiæ Patribus Ecclesiæ filiis tradita, traditio vocatur. Quo sensu Apostolus traditionem vocat doctrinam à Christo acceptam, Eccle-siæ traditam. Ego accepi à Christo, quod & vobis tradidi. Sic Irenæus: {a}Neque per alios dis-positionem salutis cognoscimus, quam per eos; per quos Euangelium pervenit ad nos, quod quidem tunc prædicauerunt, postea verò per Dei voluntatem in Scripturis tradiderunt. Hæc ille. Itaque prouo-cat Irenæus ad Episcoporum Romanorum successiones, qui hanc traditionem integram tum conseruabant. Sic enim ait: Traditione, quæ est ab Apostolis, sic se habente, & permanente apud nos. Permanebat igitur hæc traditio apud Ecclesiam. Apud quos autem hæc traditio A-postolicæ doctrinæ integra conseruata est, a-pud eos non dubia manebat Ecclesiæ nota: quam notam ponit Irenæus, non in traditio-ne simpliciter, sed in traditione Apostolicæ doctrinæ puræ, ab Episcopis orthodoxis in Ecclesia conseruatæ. Atque hinc fraudem eo-rum exploratam tenemus, quum ea è Patribus pro suis traditionibus proferant, quæ ab illis afferuntur pro doctrina Apostolica per mini-steria Episcoporum Ecclesiæ tradita. Hic er-ror animaduersus, plurima Patrum testimo-nia à Pontificiis prauè detorta ostender.
units.tr: The word tradition is used in various ways among the Fathers. (1) They call tradition the doctrine handed down, which must always be kept the same, drawn from Scripture, through all the successions of the Church. For just as that perpetual fire of the altar, which had come down from heaven, was through the successions of priests to shine always the same before the Lord, so one and the same doctrine must always remain in the Church through all successions, so that nothing foreign is added to holy Scripture, says Theodoret. This one and the same doctrine, preserved in the Church and handed down by the Fathers of the Church to the sons of the Church, is called tradition. In this sense the Apostle calls tradition the doctrine received from Christ and delivered to the Church: "I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you." So Irenaeus: "Nor do we come to know the arrangement of salvation through any others than those through whom the Gospel came to us, which they indeed then preached, but afterwards, by the will of God, handed down in the Scriptures." Thus Irenaeus appeals to the successions of the Roman bishops, who then kept this tradition entire. For he says: "The tradition which is from the Apostles, being thus, and remaining among us." This tradition therefore remained in the Church. But among those with whom this tradition of apostolic doctrine was kept entire, there remained an undoubted known mark of the Church; a mark which Irenaeus sets not in tradition simply, but in the tradition of pure apostolic doctrine, preserved in the Church by orthodox bishops. And from this we hold their fraud exposed, when they bring forward as their own traditions those things which the Fathers assert as apostolic doctrine handed down in the Church through the ministry of bishops. Noting this error shows that many testimonies of the Fathers are wrongly twisted by the Papists.

units.la: 2. Obseruandum prætereà est, traditiones à Patribus sæpius pro externis Ecclesiæ ritibus vsurpari. De qua traditione Augustini sententia celebris est huiusmodi: {b}Quæ non scripta, sed tradita custodimus, quæ quidem toto terrarum orbe obseruantur, datur intelligi, vel ab ipsis Apostolis, vel plenariis Conciliis, quorum est in Ecclesia saluberrima autoritas, commendata atq; statuta retineri: sicut quod Domini passio, & resurrectio, & ascensio in cœlum, & aduentus de cœlo Spiritus sancti anniuersaria solemnitate celebrantur. Alia sunt, quæ per loca terrarum regionesq; variantur. Hæc Augustinus. De quibus variantibus ceremoniis, quas ille traditiones vocat, grauissima est Augustini sententia, quæ contentionis funem præscindere poterat apud animos, veritatis & pacis cupidos. {a}Sensi, inquit Augustinus, sæpe dolens, & gemens, multas infirmorum perturbationes fieri per quorundam fratrum contentiosam obstinationem, vel superstitiosam timiditatem, qui in rebus huiusmodi, quæ nec Scripturæ sanctæ autoritate, nec vniuersalis Ecclesiæ traditione, neq; vitæ corrigendæ vtilitate ad certum possunt terminum peruenire (tantum quia subest qualiscunq; ratiocinatio cogitantur, aut quia in sua patria sic ipse consueuit, aut quia ibi vidit, vbi peregrinationem suam, quo remotiorem à suis, eo doctiorem factam putat,) tam litigiosas excitant quæstiones, vt, nisi quod ipsi faciunt, nihil rectum existiment. Hæc ille. Quæ igitur de ceremoniis Ecclesiasticis contra Episcopos nuper excitatæ fuerant controuersiæ, easdem olim suscitatas testatur Augustinus; qui nudioribus quidem verbis, non tamen vanis, affirmat hanc de ceremoniis contentionem, non à conscientia profecta, sed à contentiosa obstinatione, & superstitiosa timiditate. De ceremoniis eius generis Ambrosii responsum (quo profitebatur, sc. dum Romæ esset, Romanæ Ecclesiæ consuetudinem observare, quum Mediolani esset, aliter fecisse, ac proinde moneret, in quacunq; Ecclesia quis viuat, vt eius Ecclesiæ morem in ceremoniis sequeretur.) Augustinus fatetur, se tanquam ex cœ-lesti oraculo profectum suscepisse. {a} Ego, inquit, de hac sententia etiam atque etiam cogitans, ita semper habui, tanquam ex cœlesti oraculo susceperim. Insignem hanc modestiam viri, insigni pietate, acerrimoq; iudicio præditi, proposui, vt moneamur, & nostro, & publico bono, pacem Ecclesiæ præstare. Sed videte veritatem contentionibus immersam, & fere obrutam, velut scopulum inter repugnantes fluctus extantem. Pontificii traditionibus non scriptis eandem auctoritatem tribuunt, quam Scripturis def-rût[?]. Alij, vt ab hoc errore quam longissime refugiant, nullum prorsus locum traditionibus non scriptis in Ecclesia relinquunt. Errant utrique: neq; istorum perniciolior error, contentiosam horum obstinatione excusat. Patres media viam ingressi sunt, quam si nobiscum omnes etiam sequeretur, exoptatissima Ecclesiis pax redire potuisset.{b} In his rebus, inquit Augustinus, de quibus nihil certi statuit Scriptura divina, mos populi Dei, vel instituta maiorum pro lege tenenda sunt.
units.tr: (2) It must further be observed that the Fathers quite often use the word traditions for the external rites of the Church. Augustine's opinion about this kind of tradition is famous, and runs thus: "What we keep not written but handed down, and which is observed throughout the whole world, is understood to be either commended and enjoined by the Apostles themselves, or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary: such as that the Lord's passion, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven are celebrated with yearly solemnity. Other things vary in different lands and regions." Thus Augustine. Concerning these varying ceremonies, which he calls traditions, Augustine's judgment is most weighty, and it could cut the rope of contention in the minds of those who desire truth and peace. "I have felt," says Augustine, "often grieving and groaning, that many disturbances of the weak arise through the contentious obstinacy or superstitious timidity of certain brothers, who, in matters of this kind, which can be brought to no fixed end either by the authority of holy Scripture, or by the universal tradition of the Church, or by the usefulness of correcting life (only because some reasoning underlies them, or because one was accustomed to it in one's own country, or because one saw it where one thinks one's pilgrimage, the further from one's own, makes one more learned), raise such litigious questions that, unless they do what they do themselves, they think nothing right." Thus he. So the controversies about ecclesiastical ceremonies which had lately been stirred up against the bishops, Augustine attests were stirred up of old as well; he affirms, in rather plain but not idle words, that this contention about ceremonies arose not from conscience but from contentious obstinacy and superstitious timidity. Concerning ceremonies of this kind, there is Ambrose's answer (in which he professed that, while he was at Rome, he observed the custom of the Roman Church, and while at Milan he had done otherwise, and therefore advised that wherever a person lives, he should follow the custom of that Church in ceremonies). Augustine confesses that he received it as if it came from a heavenly oracle: "I, thinking on this opinion again and again, have always held it as if I had received it from a heavenly oracle." I have set forth this remarkable modesty of a man endowed with remarkable piety and very keen judgment, so that we may be admonished, for our own good and the public good, to secure the peace of the Church. But see truth buried in contentions and almost overwhelmed, like a rock standing up among clashing waves. The Papists give unwritten traditions the same authority as the Scriptures. Others, that they may flee this error as far as possible, leave no place at all for unwritten traditions in the Church. Both err; nor does the more pernicious error of these men excuse the contentious obstinacy of those. The Fathers took the middle way, which, if all would follow with us, the most desired peace could have returned to the Churches. "In those matters about which divine Scripture has laid down nothing certain," says Augustine, "the custom of God's people, or the institutions of our ancestors, are to be held as law."

units.la: Sed ne in domesticis nostris contentionibus lætentur inimici, attendite Pontificiorum imposturas. Patres non reiiciunt omnes traditiones non scriptas. Nam quæ in externis riti-
units.tr: But lest our enemies rejoice in our domestic quarrels, notice the deceptions of the Papists. The Fathers do not reject all unwritten traditions. For as to those things in external rites which...

units.la: bus[?] bus fi[?] omni[?] per re[?] pro le[?] citari[?] suis, quan[?] verbi[?] prod[?] nis i[?] dunt[?] 3. bus [?] Patri[?] Patri[?] dicio[?] perst[?] fidu[?] tra h[?] Scrip[?] uert[?] retic[?] ditio[?] (quo[?] tres [?] scier[?] faria[?] bus [?] spon[?] ptur[?] poss[?] doc[?] bus sunt, quæ toto terrarum orbe obseruantur, omnino retinendas iudicant. In iis vero, quæ per regiones variantur, cuiusq; Ecclesiæ more pro lege tenendum statuunt: nec vltra lites excitari volunt. Pontificij vero pro traditionibus suis, quæ doctrinam continent non scriptam, quam tamen Scripturis ipsis coæquant, & verbum DEI vocant: testimonia Patrum producunt, quæ de ritibus Ecclesiæ externis intelliguntur. Atque ita frustra colludunt.
units.tr: ...are observed throughout the whole world, they judge that they must be wholly retained. As to those things which vary from region to region, they hold that each church's custom is to be kept as law, and they do not want disputes stirred up beyond this. The Papists, however, for their traditions, which contain an unwritten doctrine that they nevertheless place on a level with Scripture itself and call the Word of God, produce testimonies of the Fathers that are understood of the external rites of the Church. And in this way they collude to no purpose.

units.la: 3. Obseruandum etiam est, in traditionibus Ecclesiæ discernendis alium fuisse apud Patres Ecclesiæ statum, alium apud nos esse. Patres enim, qui conseruabant Ecclesiæ traditiones, erant fideles, incorrupti, integri à superstitione. Itaque aliquando innocentiæ suæ fiducia provocant ad traditiones, nempe contra hæreticos, qui, vt ait Irenæus, quum ex Scripturis arguuntur, in accusationem conuertuntur ipsarum Scripturarum. Ad ristos[?] hæreticos conuincendos, qui Scripturas sine traditionibus insufficientes fuisse clamitabant (quod hodie etiam faciunt Pontificij.) Patres Ecclesiæ primitiuæ, ex fiducia bonæ conscientiæ, quod se dogmata Scripturæ necessaria per verbi ministerium tradita, cordibus suis fideliter retinuisse crederent: ita respondent nonnunquam, vt dicant, si Scripturæ nullæ extarent, tamen conuincere se posse hæreticos per traditionem, hoc est, per doctrinam à prædicatione acceptam, traditamque. Itaq; Irenæus sicait: {a}Quid autem, si neque Apostoli Scripturas reliquissent nobis, nonne oportet ordinem sequi traditionis, quem tradiderunt iis, quibus committebant Ecclesias? Cui ordinationi assentiuntur multæ gentes barbarorum, sine charactere, & atramento scriptam habentes per Spiritum in cordibus nostris salutem. In quam sententiam Tertullianus ait: {b}Non ad Scripturas provocandum esse, nec in his constituendum certamen cum hæreticis, sed disputandum esse, quibus competat fi-des, cuius sint Scripturæ, à quo, & per quos, & quando fit tradita disciplina, qua fiunt Christiani. Quibus verbis non contra Scripturas disputat, aut hic, aut ille: sed hæreticos etiam sine Scripturis convinci posse docent: quia si Scripturæ non extarent, tamen doctrina Scripturarum tam firmiter fidelium cordibus infixa erat, ut per eam hæretici facile convinci possent. Si tamen ab iis duobus quæras, quomodo ipsi solerent refutare hæreticos? nonne per Scripturas? Negari non potest, hoc ab iis diligenter semper per Scripturas agi. Non ergo qui hæc dicunt, Scripturas accusant quasi imperfectas; nam de Scripturarum perfectione nihil addi potest ad ea, quæ ab iis dicuntur: sed hæc dicta primitivi sæculi sanctimoniam fidemque probant. Illa enim cum virginis Ecclesiæ florebat pudicitia, ut hæretica figmenta nullum in Ecclesia locum invenire possent. At nunc fidelis illa civitas ab Antichristo oppressa, violata, & nonnulla ex parte meretrix facta non eandem retinet in traditionibus castimo-niam, niam, fidem, & sanctitatem. Huius rei ratio est etiam à veteribus perspecta & prodita. Itaque autor operis imperfecti in Matthæum, obseruat, non eundem futurum Ecclesiæ statum sub Antichristo, qui fuerat viuentibus Patribus. {a}Docet enim, Ecclesiam Christi quondam variis modis distingui solitam à gentilitate: sed regnante Antichristo, nullam aliam viam reliquam futuram cognoscendi Ecclesiam veram nisi tantummodo per Scripturas. Atque hæc etiam temporum ratio obseruata, ostendet, ex diuersitate temporis traditiones à Patribus receptas, quas propter venerandam ipsorum integritatem non habemus suspectas, longe alio habendas esse loco, quam Pontificias sub Antichristo excogitatas & extrusas, non tantum suspicionis, verum etiam superstitiosæ cæcitatis atque insaniæ plenas.
units.tr: 3. It must also be observed that in distinguishing the Church's traditions, the state of the Church was one thing among the Fathers and is another among us. For the Fathers who preserved the traditions of the Church were faithful, uncorrupted, and free from superstition. Therefore they sometimes appeal to tradition out of confidence in their innocence, namely against heretics who, as Irenaeus says, when they are refuted from the Scriptures, turn the accusation against the Scriptures themselves. To convict those heretics who kept claiming that the Scriptures were insufficient without traditions (which the Papists also do today), the Fathers of the primitive Church, trusting in a good conscience and believing that they had faithfully retained in their hearts the doctrines of Scripture necessary to salvation, delivered through the ministry of the Word, sometimes answer in such a way as to say that even if no Scriptures existed, they could still convict heretics by tradition, that is, by the doctrine received and handed down from preaching. Thus Irenaeus says: But what if the Apostles had left us no Scriptures? Ought we not to follow the order of tradition which they handed down to those to whom they committed the churches? To this order many nations of barbarians assent, having salvation written in their hearts by the Spirit, without paper and ink. To the same effect Tertullian says: One must not appeal to the Scriptures, nor contend with heretics on that ground, but must dispute about who has the right to the faith, whose the Scriptures are, from whom and through whom and when the discipline by which people become Christians was handed down. In these words neither one argues against the Scriptures; rather, they teach that heretics can be convicted even without Scriptures, because even if the Scriptures did not exist, their doctrine was so firmly fixed in the hearts of the faithful that heretics could easily be convicted by it. Yet if you ask those two how they were accustomed to refute heretics, was it not by the Scriptures? It cannot be denied that they always did this diligently by means of the Scriptures. Therefore those who say these things do not accuse the Scriptures as imperfect; for nothing can be added to the perfection of the Scriptures beyond what they say; rather, these sayings prove the holiness and faith of the early age. For when the Church was flourishing in her virgin chastity, heretical inventions could find no place in the Church. But now that faithful city, oppressed and violated by Antichrist and in some part made a harlot, does not keep the same purity, faith, and holiness in her traditions. The reason for this has also been observed and set out by the ancients. Thus the author of the unfinished work on Matthew observes that the state of the Church under Antichrist will not be the same as it was while the Fathers were living. For he teaches that the Church of Christ was once accustomed to be distinguished from the Gentiles in various ways, but under the reign of Antichrist there would remain no other way of recognising the true Church except through the Scriptures alone. And this observed difference of times will also show that the traditions received by the Fathers, which we do not regard as suspect on account of their venerable integrity, must be held in a very different place from the Papistical traditions devised and thrust forth under Antichrist, which are full not only of suspicion but of superstitious blindness and madness.

units.la: 4. Nec vero in traditionibus discernendis omnino negandum est, aliquas traditiones Apostolicas in Ecclesia reseruari. Dicam libere, quod sentio, paratus meliora monstranti libenter acquiescere. Sentio, quasdam traditiones Apostolicas conseruatas, semperque conseruandas in Ecclesia. Nec enim frustra Augustinus: {b}Quod vniuersa tenet Ecclesia, nec Concilijs institutum, sed semper retentum est, non nisi authoritate Apostolica traditum rectissime creditur. Hæc ille. Sic probat, baptismum paruulorum esse traditionem Apostolicam. Sicut & ante illum Origenes: Ecclesia, inquit Origenes, ab Apostolis traditionem suscepit, etiam paruulis iis[?] baptismum dare. Ab Apostolica etiam traditione suscepimus genuinum Scripturæ canonem, & genuinum canonis sensum per veram prædicationem, successionibus Ecclesiæ conseruatum[?]. Hinc etiamdiem Dominicam Ecclesia celebrat. Addam, quod Ecclesiæ patribus & filiis examinandum propono.
units.tr: 4. Nor indeed must it be altogether denied, in distinguishing traditions, that some apostolic traditions are preserved in the Church. I will speak freely what I think, ready to acquiesce gladly to anyone who shows something better. I hold that certain apostolic traditions have been preserved and must always be preserved in the Church. For Augustine rightly says: What the whole Church holds, which was not instituted by councils but has always been retained, is rightly believed to have been handed down by apostolic authority alone. So he says. In this way he proves that infant baptism is an apostolic tradition. So also before him Origen: the Church, he says, received from the Apostles the tradition of giving baptism even to infants. From apostolic tradition we have also received the genuine canon of Scripture and the genuine sense of the canon, preserved through true preaching and the succession of the Church. Hence also the Church celebrates the Lord's Day. I will add something which I put forward for the fathers and sons of the Church to examine.

units.la: Apostolus 2. Thessal. 2. hæc verba habet: Nonne meminissis, quod iam, quum apud vos essem, hæc dicebam vobis? Et nunc, quid obstat, nostis, ut suo tempore retegatur. Nam mysterium iam operatur iniquitatis, tantum qui nunc obstat, obstabit, donec de medio sublatus fuerit. Ex his verbis Apostoli, Patres magno consensu traditionem Apostolicam retinuerunt. Nam ubi quæruntur, quid sit, aut quis sit, qui e medio tollendus est, quod obstat, donec de medio tollatur, ne Antichristus retegatur, quam is de medio prius sublatus fuerit: ad hanc quæstionem Patres magno consensu respondent, hoc scilicet esse Romanum Imperium. Romanum dicunt Imperium esse, quod prius e medio tollendum est, quam Antichristus conspicuus esse possit. Ita sublato Imperio, Antichristum tandem, in eadem Imperii sede, sublimem extollendum, & vacantem Imperii sedem occupaturum.
units.tr: The Apostle in 2 Thessalonians 2 has these words: Do you not remember that when I was still with you I told you these things? And now you know what is restraining, so that he may be revealed in his time. For the mystery of iniquity is already at work; only he who now restrains will restrain until he is taken out of the way. From these words of the Apostle, the Fathers with great agreement retained an apostolic tradition. For when they ask what it is, or who it is, that is to be taken out of the way, which restrains, until it is taken away, so that Antichrist is not revealed before it is removed, the Fathers with great agreement answer to this question that it is clearly the Roman Empire. They say that the Roman Empire is what must first be taken out of the way before Antichrist can be seen openly. So, when the Empire has been removed, Antichrist will at last be raised up on high in the same seat of the Empire and will occupy the vacant seat of the Empire.

units.la: Hæc habent Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus, Chrysostomus, Oecumenius, Theophylactus, Tertullianus, Lactantius, Ambrosius, Hieronymus, Augustinus, Primasius. Qui omnes uno consensu exponunt locum illum Apostoli de Antichristo in Romana urbe Imperii loco sessuro. Ita hæc Apostolica traditio videtur, quam proximi ab Apostoli ore susceptam, aliis deinceps tradiderunt. Loquitur enim Apostolus tanquam de re nota: Nonne meministi? Iterumque: Et nunc, quid obstat, nostu. Ergo de re nota loquitur, quam voce tradiderat, scriptis vero supprimit. Si quis quæret, quare Apostolus non aperte dixerit, Romanum Imperium destruendum, ut Antichristus retegatur? Respondet Hieronymus: {a}Si aperte audaster q.[?] dixis-set, Non venient Antichristus, nisi prius Romanum deleatur Imperium, iusta causa persecutionis in orientem tunc Ecclesiam consurgere videretur. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Cyril of Jerusalem, Chrysostom, Oecumenius, Theophylact, Tertullian, Lactantius, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Primasius hold this. All of them with one agreement explain that passage of the Apostle as concerning Antichrist who will sit in the city of Rome as the seat of the Empire. So this apostolic tradition appears to be one which those nearest to the Apostle received from his mouth and then handed on to others. For the Apostle speaks as of a known matter: Do you not remember? And again: And now you know what restrains. Therefore he speaks of a known matter, which he had handed down by word of mouth, but in his writings he suppressed it. If anyone asks why the Apostle did not openly say that the Roman Empire must be destroyed so that Antichrist may be revealed? Jerome answers: If he had boldly said openly, Antichrist will not come unless the Roman Empire is first destroyed, a just cause of persecution would then seem to arise against the Church in the East. So he says.

units.la: Ratio igitur evidens & conspicua apparet, quare Apostolus scriptis noluit committi hoc, quod de Antichristi revelatione viva docuerat voce. Neque veremur, si quasdam concedamus traditiones Apostolicas, ne fenestram aperiamus Pontificiis figmentis. Neque enim quaslibet pro libidine hominum impositas agnoscit Ecclesia traditiones Apostolicas: sed quæ originis suæ nobilitatem monstrantes, in ipsis Scripturis radice sua inherent, deinde indubitata veteris Ecclesiæ confessione, & non interruptis, non litigiosis Patrum testimoniis confirmantur. Ostendant nobis Pontificii traditionem ex tam conspicuis Scripturæ vestigiis prodeuntem; tanto Patrum consensu exceptam, omnibus in unum consentientibus, nemine interim contradicente; tanta Ecclesiæ experientia, rerumque eventu com-
units.tr: The reason, therefore, is evident and clear why the Apostle was unwilling to commit to writing what he had taught about the revelation of Antichrist by the living voice. Nor do we fear, if we concede certain apostolic traditions, that we open a window to Papistical fictions. For the Church does not acknowledge as apostolic traditions whatever is imposed at the whim of men; rather, those traditions which show the nobility of their origin and cling to their root in Scripture itself, and which are then confirmed by the undoubted confession of the ancient Church and by uninterrupted, uncontentious testimonies of the Fathers. Let the Papists show us a tradition that proceeds from such clear traces of Scripture; received with such great agreement of the Fathers, all agreeing together, with no one contradicting in the meantime; confirmed by such great experience of the Church and by the outcome of events; supported by such common reasons...

units.la: comprobatam ; tantis rationibus communi- tam ; & nos Apostolicam fatebimur.
units.tr: ...then we will acknowledge it as apostolic.

units.la: 5. Fit etiam aliquando, vt Patres traditiones non scriptas nimium videantur extollere. Vt recte intelligantur, æquissimam rem postulabimus. Ita accipiantur Patrum verba, ne sibi ipsis contradicentia posuisse videantur : & quum diuersa dicere videntur, sententia genuina Patrum ex ipsorum verbis disertis agnoscatur, non ex nostris commentis. Hæc monui propter vnum Basilii locum. Nam quæ ex Epiphanio, Tertulliano, Augustino, aliisve adferunt Pontificii, omnia sunt vel de doctrina Scripturæ tradita, vel de ritibus externis, nec attingunt hanc quæstionem. Locus vero Basilii aliquid videtur in speciem continere, quo incauti possunt falli. Et quia Basilii verba acrius vrgent Pontificii, quasi traditionibus suis propensius fauentia, is locus erit nobis accuratius examinandus. Verba sunt huiusmodi: {a}Quæ in Ecclesia seruantur, & prædicantur instituta, partim ex conscripta doctrina habemus, partim ex Apostolorum traditione in mysterio ad nos delata recepimus: quæ vtrag;[?] parem ad pietatem vim habent. Hæc ille.
units.tr: 5. Sometimes it also happens that the Fathers seem to exalt unwritten traditions too highly. To understand them rightly, we ask for a very fair procedure: the Fathers' words should be taken in such a way that they do not seem to contradict themselves. When they seem to say different things, the genuine opinion of the Fathers should be recognised from their own clear words, not from our inventions. I have given this warning because of one passage of Basil. The passages the Papists bring from Epiphanius, Tertullian, Augustine and others all concern either the doctrine of Scripture or external rites, and do not touch this question. But the passage of Basil seems to contain something that could mislead the unwary, and because the Papists press Basil's words harder, as if they favoured their traditions more, that passage must be examined more carefully by us. The words are these: What is observed and taught in the Church is partly from the written teaching we have, and partly we have received from the Apostles' tradition, handed down to us in mystery; both have equal force for piety. So he says.

units.la: Respondemus, hunc locum nihil pro traditionibus Pontificiis facere ; quia loquitur Basilius tantum de externis ritibus. Quod quum obseruasset Chemnitius : Respondet Bellarminus, Basilium non solum ritus quosdam, sed etiam quasdam essentialia referre ; vt confessionem fidei, id est, Symbolum Apostolo- licum,
units.tr: We reply that this passage does nothing for the Papists' traditions, because Basil speaks only of external rites. Chemnitz observed this, and Bellarmine answers that Basil refers not only to certain rites but also to certain essentials, such as the confession of faith, that is, the Apostles' Creed,

units.la: licum vnctio[?] Hæc ... ftam ... & Sac ... Basili ... bum ... nein ... ipsi P ... lent ... quæ ... num ... Quo ... bolo ... mus ... Eccl ... nise ... to? ... doct ... larm ... doct ... quut ... tam ... quat ... quu ... ferr ... dei, ... net ... de ip ... est q ... loq ... quo ... licum, quod ex traditione habemus, & olei unctionem in Sacramento Confirmationis. Hæc Bellarminus. In quibus egregiè sophistam agit. Nam quod de oleiunctione habet, & Sacramento Confirmationis: Respondeo, Basilium de Confirmatione nec unum verbum facere: sed de Baptismo, {a} & de unctione in baptismo: Hanc autem unctionem nec ipsi Pontifici inter essentialia numerare solent. Certe Bellarminus ipse hanc unctionem, quæ est in Baptismo, inter externos ritus connumerat lib.1. de Sacrament. Baptism. cap.25. Quod vero de fidei confessione refert, & symbolo Apostolico, quod ex traditione habemus: Dicimus, conseruationem Symboli in Ecclesia esse: ipsum autem Symbolum ex manifestis Scripturis. Et quantum hoc à proposito? Nam in Symbolo non continetur aliqua doctrina, quæ in Scripturis non habetur. Bellarmino vero, nisi præuaricari voluisset, aliqua doctrina non scripta producenda erat, quæ quum in Scripturis non habeatur, suscipienda tamen sit, tanquam verbum Dei. Quod nusquam facit. Fallere ergo voluit Sophista, quum dicat, Basilium quædam essentialia referre, ut confessionem fidei. Nam confessio fidei, & Symbolum Apostolicum, non continet doctrinam aliquam non scriptam. Deinde ipsa fidei confessio, & Symbolum ipsum, est quidem inter essentialia fidei: At Basilius loquitur de Symboli recitatione in Baptismo; quod inter externos ritus numerandum esse,
units.tr: and the anointing with oil in the Sacrament of Confirmation. So Bellarmine. In this he acts the sophist with great skill. For as to what he says about the anointing with oil and the Sacrament of Confirmation, I answer that Basil says not a single word about Confirmation, but about Baptism, and about anointing in baptism. Yet even the Papists themselves do not usually count this anointing among the essentials. Bellarmine himself certainly reckons the anointing that is in Baptism among the external rites, in his book on the sacrament of Baptism, book 1, chapter 25. As for what he reports about the confession of faith and the Apostles' Creed, which we have from tradition: we say that the Creed is preserved in the Church, but the Creed itself is from plain Scripture. And how far is this from the point? For no doctrine is contained in the Creed that is not found in Scripture. Bellarmine, unless he wished to prevaricate, ought to have produced some unwritten doctrine which, since it is not found in Scripture, must nevertheless be received as the word of God. This he never does. The sophist therefore wished to deceive when he says that Basil refers to certain essentials, such as the confession of faith. For the confession of faith and the Apostles' Creed contain no unwritten doctrine. Moreover, the confession of faith itself and the Creed are indeed among the essentials of the faith; but Basil speaks of the recitation of the Creed in Baptism, which who does not know must be counted among the external rites,

units.la: quis nescit? quis negat? Denique quicquid intelligat Basilius per illa verba, πῶς ὁμολογίας τῆς πίστεως[?], Pontificij causa cadunt: nam vel ipsum Symbolum intelligit, vel Symboli recitationem. Si Symbolum nihil continet non scriptum. Quomodo igitur ex hoc loco probabunt Pontificii, verbum aliud non scriptum? Sin recitationem Symboli intelligat, de externis ritibus agit. Ita ex hoc loco nihil adiuuantur Pontificij.
units.tr: and who denies it? Finally, whatever Basil means by the words the confession of faith [πῶς ὁμολογίας τῆς πίστεως], the Papists' cause falls. For he means either the Creed itself or the recitation of the Creed. If the Creed contains nothing unwritten, how then will the Papists prove from this passage any unwritten word? But if he means the recitation of the Creed, he is speaking of external rites. So the Papists get no help from this passage.

units.la: Quoniam vero de Basilij sententia disputamus, ipse sui interpres optimus, exponat se, & mentem suam sensumq; aperiat. In Scripturæ autoritate vindicanda nemo constantior Basilio: in traditionibus non scriptis refutandis, quæ doctrinam continent a Scripturis alienam, nemo fidelior. Epistola octogesima docet, hæreticos obiicere Catholicis trium hy-postasewn[?] doctrinam non esse in Scriptura. Quid Basilius? Num traditionem urget? Minime. Atqui si quis alius, profecto hic locus maxime opportunus erat pro iactandis traditionibus. Sed Basilius traditionem reiicit, & consuledam monet divinitus inspiratam Scripturam. Et apud quos, inquit, inuenta fuerint in dogmata divino verbo consonantia, his accedat veritatis suffragium. Atq; hoc ipso lib. de Spiritu S. ad eos, qui Patrum traditiones iactabat, sic respondet: {a}Sicut dixerunt patres nostri, ita & nos dicimus: sed hoc non sufficit nobis, quod Patrum traditione habemus, nam & illi Scriptura sensum secuti sunt. Hæc Basilius. Illustrem ergo regulam hac de tradi-
units.tr: Since we are discussing Basil's opinion, let him be his own best interpreter: let him set out himself, and reveal his mind and meaning. No one was more steadfast than Basil in defending the authority of Scripture, and no one was more faithful in refuting unwritten traditions that contain doctrine alien to the Scriptures. In his eightieth letter he teaches that the heretics objected to Catholics that the doctrine of three hypostases is not in Scripture. What does Basil say? Does he press tradition? Not at all. And yet, if anyone else had been going to, this passage would surely have been the most suitable place to trumpet traditions. But Basil rejects tradition and advises us to consult Scripture, which is divinely inspired. "Among those," he says, "in whom are found doctrines agreeing with the divine word, let the witness of truth be added." And in the same book, On the Holy Spirit, he answers in this way those who were boasting of the traditions of the Fathers: "We say what our fathers said, but this is not enough for us, that we have it by the tradition of the Fathers, for they too followed the sense of Scripture." So far Basil. Therefore, the illustrious rule [...]

units.la: tionib[?] trum q[?] Basiliu[?] non q[?] tradu[?] quoti[?] quid E[?] pturas[?] Æqui[?] ftimo[?] nemu[?] nuina[?] bent[?] ptas s[?]
units.tr: [...] of the traditions [...] Basil [...] not [...] handed down [...] Scriptures. [...] equally [...] no one [...] the Scriptures [...]

units.la: Sec[?] spe&[?] sed à[?] terun[?] script[?] suitæ[?] ercue[?] persu[?] Patr[?] appe[?] tius[?] sunt[?] libri[?] filio[?] geni[?] tans[?] bet[?] per[?] tionibus Basilius fixit; secundum quam de Patrum omnium sententiis iudicandum censuit Basilius: ut agnoscamus Patrum traditiones, non quia ita tradunt illi, sed quia è Scripturis tradunt. Hæc Basilij regula incoccuffa maneat, quoties de fidei controversiis agitur. Ergo si quid Basilius ipse tradat non secundum Scri-pturas, reiiciendum erit, ipsius Basilij iudicio. Æquum profecto postulamus, ut Patrum testimonia secundum ipsorum regulas examinemus. Itaque quamvis hæc verba Basilij genuina esse concedamus, nihil tamen ex iis habent Pontificij, quo doctrinas suas non scriptas stabilire possint.
units.tr: [...] by traditions Basil laid down a rule, according to which Basil judged that the opinions of all the Fathers must be judged: so that we acknowledge the traditions of the Fathers not because they hand them down, but because they hand them down from the Scriptures. Let this rule of Basil remain unshaken whenever controversies of faith are debated. Therefore, if Basil himself hands down anything not according to the Scriptures, it must be rejected by Basil's own judgment. Surely we ask what is fair: that we examine the testimonies of the Fathers according to their own rules. Accordingly, although we concede that these words of Basil are genuine, the Papists have nothing in them by which they could establish their unwritten doctrines.

units.la: Sed hunc locum Basilij viri doctissimi suspectum habent, quod non sint Basilij verba, sed à quodam nebulone inserta. Nam quis veterum nefarias manus adulterantium antiqua scripta, effugere potuit? Neque enim soli Jesuitæ interpolatrices & expunctrices artes exercuerunt. In hoc libro Basilii, fraudem ex diversitate styli, olfecit Erasmus nasutissimus in Patrum scriptis censor. Et profecto quemvis appello lectorem cordatum, qui paulo attentius Basilii scriptis assuevit: non[?] ea, quæ sunt in medio huius capitis vicesimi septimi, libri de Spiritu sancto. conveniant vel Basilio, vel præsenti disputationi? Basilius ingenii acrimoniam iudicii gravitate temperans, nusquam aberrat à scopo, nihil habet incommodum, aut inconsequens: semper vigilat, semper sui similis decurrit.
units.tr: But learned men regard this passage of Basil with suspicion, because these are not Basil's words but were inserted by some scoundrel. For who among the ancients could escape the wicked hands of those who falsified ancient writings? Nor have the Jesuits alone practised the arts of interpolators and erasers. In this book of Basil, Erasmus, that most keen-nosed critic of the Fathers' writings, smelled fraud from the difference of style. And indeed I appeal to any sensible reader who has become somewhat familiar with Basil's writings: do the things that stand in the middle of this twenty-seventh chapter of the book On the Holy Spirit agree either with Basil or with the present discussion? Basil, tempering the sharpness of his wit with the gravity of his judgment, never strays from his aim, has nothing awkward or inconsistent, always keeps watch, and always runs on consistent with himself.

units.la: At hoc loco suscepta disputatio omnino perturbatur: aliud proponitur, aliud vero tractatur. Et quae propositam disputationem sequuntur[?], nihil ad rem faciunt. Primum medio, medium imo discrepat. Quae vero initio capitis proponuntur, optime cohærerent cum illis, quae in fine tractantur; media autem, quae inseruntur ὡς[?] ἐξ ἀγράφων, omnia impediunt, & initio, & fini plane contradicunt. Nam suscepta disputatio erat, ut ostenderet, quam vim habeat hæc vox σὺν : quum dicitur, σὺν τῷ πνεύματι: & quomodo congruat cum Scriptura: πᾶς σύμφωνός ἐςι τῇ γραφῇ: hæc diuersis verbis proponuntur. Statim sequitur illa disputatio, de agraphis; cui disputationi nullus erat hic locus. Deinde quum velut ad se rediit Basilius, probat optime disputationem initio suscep-tam. Docet enim in fine capitis, quum dicimus, σὺν τῷ πνεύματι, nihil nostrum dicere nos, sed loqui ex canone Christi. Probat etiam rem ipsam, sententiamq; esse Scripturæ: etsi verba non sint; certe verba esse, quæ eandem vim habeant. Probat postremo, verba ipsa esse in Scriptura, idque ex Apostolo. Ergo inutilis erat omnis illa disputatio σὺν ἀγράφων: ut, nisi hæc ab alio inserta intelligantur, Basilius sibi cohærere non posset; nec Basilius Basilio reconciliari. Nam qui grauissimum doctrinæ caput probandum è Scripturis susceperit (quod hoc loco suscepit Basi-lius, æqualitatem scilicet Spiritus sancti cum Patre & Filio) quid huic negotii erit cum agraveteri denti pris. flagiti interf no ftu gendi antiq videri corun palam denti mus. cunt: infert mend tecti Te Chalc prima ctetu ptam agraphis ? cum traditionibus non scriptis? Deinde disputat Basilius, non de ritibus externis, sed de grauissima fidei controuersia. Hæc autem, quæ inseruntur de non scriptis traditionibus, sunt omnino in ritibus externis: Quid hæc ad controuersiam fidei?
units.tr: But at this point the discussion undertaken is completely disturbed: one thing is proposed, another is treated. And what follows the proposed discussion does nothing to the point. The beginning disagrees with the middle, and the middle with the end. Indeed, what is set out at the beginning of the chapter would fit very well with what is treated at the end; but the middle parts, which are inserted as from the unwritten [ὡς ἐξ ἀγράφων], hinder everything and plainly contradict both the beginning and the end. For the discussion undertaken was to show what force this word with [σὺν] has when we say with the Spirit [σὺν τῷ πνεύματι], and how it agrees with Scripture [πᾶς σύμφωνός ἐστι τῇ γραφῇ]; these things are proposed in different words. Immediately there follows that disputation about unwritten things, for which there was no place here. Then, when Basil comes back, as it were, to himself, he proves very well the discussion undertaken at the beginning. For at the end of the chapter he teaches that when we say with the Spirit, we are not saying anything of our own but speaking from the canon of Christ. He also proves the matter itself, and that the sense is that of Scripture, even if the words themselves are not there; certainly there are words in Scripture that have the same force. Finally he proves that the very words are in Scripture, and this from the Apostle. Therefore all that disputation about unwritten things was useless; unless these things are understood to have been inserted by another, Basil could not be consistent with himself, nor Basil be reconciled with Basil. For he who undertook to prove from Scripture the weightiest head of doctrine (which Basil undertakes here, namely the equality of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son), what has that to do with unwritten traditions? Moreover, Basil is discussing not external rites but the most serious controversy of faith. But these things that are inserted about unwritten traditions are wholly about external rites. What have these to do with the controversy of faith?

units.la: Et ne cui forte mirum videatur, quod in Basilii scriptis verba quædam ab aliquo nebulone, improbo studio, sint interpolata: non erit abs re, si digressiuncula hoc loco referamus veterum hæreticorum audaciam, & impudentiam, in corrumpendis antiquorum scriptis. Ita facilius intelligemus Pontificiorum flagitiosas impostouras, artesque ab ipsis inferis inter fumum abyssi euocatas, quæ nunc insano studio à Tridentinis exercentur, in expungendis, resecandis, interpolandis scriptoribus antiquis & recentibus. Incredibile equidem videri poterat, quod de antiquorum hæreticorum improbitate legimus, nisi easdem artes palam à Tridentinis multo maiori cum impudentia atque audacia tractatas hodie videremus. Ita tandem intelligimus, qui sint, qui dicunt: Percussimus fœdus cum morte, & cum inferno fecimus pactum; quia posuimus mendacium spem nostram, & mendacio protecti sumus.
units.tr: And lest anyone be surprised that certain words in Basil's writings have been tampered with by some scoundrel with wicked zeal, it will not be out of place to digress briefly here on the audacity and shamelessness of the ancient heretics in corrupting the writings of the ancients. In this way we will more easily understand the shameful frauds and arts of the Papists, arts summoned up from the very pit of hell through the smoke of the abyss, which the Tridentines now practise with mad zeal in expunging, cutting out and interpolating ancient and recent writers. Indeed, what we read about the wickedness of the ancient heretics might have seemed incredible, had we not today seen these same arts openly practised by the Tridentines with far greater impudence and audacity. Thus at last we understand who they are who say: "We have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made a pact; because we have made lies our hope, and we are protected by falsehood."

units.la: Testatur Cyrillus Alexand. Epistola, quæ in Chalcedonensi Concilio habetur, actione prima, Athanasii Epistolam ad beatum Epictetum, rectam fidem continentem, corruptam tamen ab hæreticis; in eaque quædam esse inserta, atque immutata, ab Athanasii sententia aliena. In Concilio Florentino Græci hunc ipsum Basilii librum, de Spiritu sancto, corruptum quæruntur. Latini sic respondent: Ex vetustissimarum vestrarum Synodorum actis apparet, corrumpendorum librorum vitium & malignitatem apud vos, à nostræ religionis hostibus ortum fuisse. Præterea hæretici studium fuisse corrumpendi Basilii, constare potest ex quarta actione Concilii Niceni secundi. Nam Patres in illo Concilio hæretici, pro adoratione imaginum pugnantes, Basilium obtorto collo trahere laborabant in eam sententiam, ut scilicet libro de Spiritu sancto, cap. 30. dicat, honorem imagini exhibitum, ad prototypum referri: quum de imaginibus per totum illum librum nihil quicquam, vel vigilans, vel somnians protulerit Basilius. Hæc ideo protuli, ut qui dixerint Basilium corruptum alicubi ab hæreticis fuisse, nihil novi dixisse; imo vero cum magnis autoribus sensisse videantur. Et ratione maxima hucadducimur, quum manifestarios suppostores, velut in flagranti plagio deprehensos proferamus; neque novæ sunt istæ artes apud hæreticos. Narrat Ruffinus in Apologia pro Origene, incredibilem hæreticorum audaciam in istis criminibus deprehensam. Exempla nos quædam ex Ruffino subiiciemus. Clementis libro, qui Recognitio inscribitur, ea sunt ab Eunomianis insertæ, quæ Ecclesiastica regula omnino non recipit. Eadem de Clementis Alexandrini libris narrat. Eadem de Dio-nysii libris; propter quod Athanasius com-pulsus erat, apologeticum pro libris eiusdem Dionysii scribere. Maxime vero istæ hæretico-rum impostura in Origenis libros invalue-runt; unde & Pamphilus Martyr Apologeti-cum etiam edidit pro Origene. Origenis au-tem Epistolam profert Ruffinus querimoniæ plenam. Conqueritur enim Origenes, quod se vivente, libros suos corruptos edere aude-rent hæretici. Hilarius Pictaviensis vivens et-jam, vidensque, idem passus est. Inter Cypria-ni Epistolas librum Tertulliani reprehensibiliter scriptum, inquit Ruffinus, hæretici infe-ruerunt. Adiiciam, inquit Ruffinus, unius fa-cti[?] exemplum, quod est memoriæ recentio-ris, & quod omnes veterum fabulas vincat. Damasus Episcopus, quum de recipiendis A-pollinarianis deliberatio haberetur, fidei edi-tionem mandabat conscribendam cuidam presbytero, cui editioni subscriberent Apolli-nariani. Quum in ea hominem Dominicum legerent Apollinariani, offensi, novitatem verborum accusant. Sed quum in Athanasii libello eadem verba offenderentur uni eorum, ille, quasi iam persuasus, rogavit sibi dari codicem, quo & aliis ignorantibus, & contradicentibus, satisfaceret. Accepto codice, verba illa rasit, deinde eadem verba rursus scripsit, quæ raserat. Codex redditus, simpliciter receptus est. Movetur iterum de iisdem verbis quæstio; ad probationem codex profertur: inueniuntur verba, sed super liturā posita: fides Codici derogatur. Sed quoniam hæc uiuenti facta sunt. & à uiuente, fraus perspecta & nudata est,& infamia in sceleris autorem redundauit. Quod si tot ac tanta auderent hæretici in veterum scriptis adulterandis, quis Basilium intactum iudicabit? Imo uero, quis potest Patrum scripta tam impudenter ab hæreticis depravata, sine Basilii regula illa aurea suscipere : Patrum scilicet traditionem recipiendam, non quia Patres ita tradunt, sed quia e Scripturū tradunt.
units.tr: Cyril of Alexandria testifies, in a letter read at the Council of Chalcedon, in the first action, that the letter of Athanasius to the blessed Epictetus, which contains sound faith, was nonetheless corrupted by heretics, and that certain things had been inserted and altered in it, alien to the mind of Athanasius. At the Council of Florence the Greeks complained that this very book of Basil, On the Holy Spirit, had been corrupted. The Latins replied: "It appears from the acts of your most ancient synods that the fault and malice of corrupting books arose among you from the enemies of our religion." Moreover, that heretics made it their aim to corrupt Basil can be established from the fourth action of the Second Council of Nicaea. For the Fathers of that council, who were heretics fighting for the adoration of images, laboured to drag Basil by the neck into their opinion, namely that in his book On the Holy Spirit, chapter 30, he says that the honour paid to an image is referred to the prototype; yet Basil, whether awake or dreaming, never said anything at all about images throughout that whole book. I have brought these points forward so that those who have said that Basil was corrupted somewhere by heretics may be seen to have said nothing new, but indeed to have agreed with great authors. And we are led to this with the greatest reason, since we produce manifest forgers, caught as it were in the act of plagiarism; nor are these arts new among heretics. Rufinus, in his Apology for Origen, relates the incredible audacity of heretics caught in these crimes. We shall add some examples from Rufinus. Into the book called the Recognitions of Clement, the Eunomians inserted things which the ecclesiastical rule by no means admits. He tells the same of the books of Clement of Alexandria. The same of the books of Dionysius; on account of which Athanasius was compelled to write an apologetic defence of the books of that Dionysius. But these frauds of the heretics most of all grew strong against the books of Origen; whence also Pamphilus the martyr published an apologetic defence even for Origen. Rufinus brings forward a letter of Origen full of complaint. For Origen complains that heretics dared, while he was still alive, to publish his books corrupted. Hilary of Poitiers, while still living and seeing it, suffered the same. Among the Epistles of Cyprian, says Rufinus, heretics inserted a book of Tertullian written in a reprehensible manner. "I shall add," says Rufinus, "one example of a deed, which is within recent memory, and which surpasses all the fables of the ancients. Damasus, the bishop, when there was deliberation about receiving the Apollinarians, commissioned a certain presbyter to draw up a confession of faith, to which the Apollinarians were to subscribe. When the Apollinarians read in it 'the man of the Lord,' they took offence and accused the novelty of the words. But when one of them found the same words in a little book of Athanasius, he, as if now persuaded, asked that a manuscript be given to him, so that he might satisfy both those who were ignorant and those who objected. Having received the manuscript, he scraped out those words, and then wrote again the same words which he had scraped out. The manuscript was returned and was simply accepted. The question about the same words was raised again; the manuscript was produced as proof: the words were found, but written over the erasure. The credit of the manuscript was called into question. But since these things were done while the man was living, and the fraud was detected and exposed by a living witness, the infamy fell back upon the author of the crime." But if heretics dared to do so many and such great things in falsifying the writings of the ancients, who will judge Basil to be untouched? Indeed, who can receive the writings of the Fathers, so shamelessly depraved by heretics, without that golden rule of Basil: that the tradition of the Fathers is to be received, not because the Fathers so hand it down, but because they hand it down from the Scriptures?

units.la: Hæc diximus, ut Tridentinorum immanes imposturas in corrumpendis, expungendis, & interpolandis veterum monumentis obseruemus. Nam isti antiquos istos hæreticos,in mendacio magistros, sequuntur; imo Diabolum, mendaciorum patrem. Neque Basilium ideo respondemus corruptum esse, quia putemus, verba illa esse contra sententiam nostram, aut pro Tridentinis; sed quia verba illa Basilij non cohærent cum reliquo Basilio. Vera quidem sunt, quæ eo loco inseruntur; de ritibus externis non scriptis: verè sunt hæc, quis negat? Dicit Basilius, quæ in Ecclesia seruantur, & prædicantur instituta; vel ex doctrina conscripta, vel ex traditione esse. Quæ verba sic resolui possunt, vt quædam dicat esse, quæ seruantur, quædam quæ prædicantur. Quæ prædicantur, esse ex doctrina conscripta: quæ seruantur,ex traditione. Ita ex hoc loco nulla probatur doctrina non scripta. Si quis putet Basilium (ut demus hæc esse Basilii) non recte de externis ritibus docuisse, quum ritus illos ita cum doctrina contulerit, ut utraque dicat parem ad pietatem vim habere: Respondeo, non esse mirum, si ea nonnunquam Patribus excidant, quæ aliquando in scriptis nostrorum hominum inveniuntur, quamvis nec male sentientium, & ad doctrinæ puritatem plurimum vigilantium. Quis enim in hoc negotio Theodoro Beza vigilantior? qui tamen eodem modo disciplinam cum doctrina contulerat, quo Basilius hoc loco, vel quicunque hæc scripsit. Bezæ verba, Basilii verbis parallela, sunt hæc: {a}Si quis (hanc disciplinam) vel per se, ut malum, damnare, vel nobis eripere conetur; illam non minus, quam ipsius doctrinæ defensionem à nobis deseri posse profitemur. Hæc ille. Nimio fortasse affectu uterque de traditionibus non scriptis. Nam & disciplinam illam, quam Beza cum doctrina contulerat, inter traditiones non scriptas numerandam esse constat.
units.tr: We have said these things so that we may note the monstrous frauds of the Tridentines in corrupting, expunging and interpolating the monuments of the ancients. For they follow those ancient heretics, masters in lying; indeed they follow the devil, the father of lies. Nor do we answer that Basil was corrupted because we think those words are contrary to our opinion or favourable to the Tridentines; but because those words of Basil do not cohere with the rest of Basil. True, indeed, are the things inserted at that place, about unwritten external rites: they are true, who denies it? Basil says that the institutions observed and proclaimed in the Church are either from written doctrine or from tradition. These words can be so resolved that some things, he says, are observed, and some are proclaimed. What is proclaimed comes from written doctrine; what is observed, from tradition. So from this passage no unwritten doctrine is proved. If anyone thinks that Basil (granting that these are Basil's words) did not rightly teach about external rites, since he compared those rites with doctrine in such a way as to say that both have an equal force for piety, I reply: it is no wonder if things sometimes slip from the Fathers which are sometimes found in the writings of our own men, though these are not ill-minded and are very vigilant for the purity of doctrine. For who was more vigilant than Theodore Beza in this matter? And yet he compared discipline with doctrine in the same way as Basil does in this place, or whoever wrote these words. Beza's words, parallel to Basil's, are these: {a}If anyone tries either to condemn this discipline in itself, as an evil, or to snatch it from us, we profess that it may be abandoned by us no less than the defence of the doctrine itself. So he. Both, perhaps, spoke with too much feeling about unwritten traditions. For it is agreed that that discipline which Beza compared with doctrine must be numbered among unwritten traditions.

units.la: Eligant iam Pontificii, utrum velint; hæc ab alio inserta, vel genuina esse: si inserta sunt, quid urgent adulterata scripta? si Basilii sunt, nihil habent, quod nos negamus. Quis enim negat ritus disciplinæ externos non esse con-scriptos[?], aut in Scripturis expresse contineri? Quæcunq; autem de traditionibus non scriptis aliquando vel dixerit, vel scripserit Basilius, quæ incommodam sententiam continere videri possunt; ea retractat Basilius, tractatu de Fide; quo loco sic scribit: Manifestum est prolapsus à fide, & superbia certissimum argumentum, vel reiicere aliquid eorum, quae scripta sunt, vel quicquam, quod non est scriptum, introducere; Apostolus vehementissime hoc prohibens, exemplo humani testamenti, cui nec detrahere, nec quicquam superaddere licet. [?]Itaq;, & potens omnem, & cogitationem alienam à doctrina Domini nostri semper & ubique fugiendam, monet Basilius. Deinde subiicit haec verba: Proposita siquidem, quod nunc tractamus, plurimum discrepante ab iis casibus, in quibus aliter aliquando, vel scribendo, vel dicendo praecessi fummus: quia tunc refutare haeresis, & subvertere Diabolica fraudis agebatur, nunc vero sanae fidei confessio, & simplex ac genuina manifestatio proponitur.
units.tr: Let the Papists now choose whichever they like: either these words were inserted by another, or they are genuine. If they were inserted, why do they press the falsified writings? If they are Basil's, they have nothing that we deny. For who denies that the external rites of discipline are not written down, or expressly contained in the Scriptures? But whatever Basil at some time either said or wrote about unwritten traditions, which may seem to contain an inconvenient opinion, Basil retracts it in his treatise On Faith; in that place he writes thus: It is clear that to fall away from faith and pride is the most certain sign, either to reject any of the things that are written, or to introduce anything that is not written; the Apostle forbids this most vehemently, by the example of a human testament, to which nothing may be taken away nor anything added. [Basil therefore warns that a powerful mind and any thought alien to the teaching of our Lord must always and everywhere be avoided.] Then he adds these words: For the matter we are now treating is very different from those cases in which I have at another time gone before, either in writing or speaking in another way; for then it was a matter of refuting heresy and overthrowing the devilish deceit, but now a confession of sound faith and a simple and genuine exposition is set forth.

units.la: Haec Basilii verba, sive dicamus continuae retractationem superioris sententiae, sive ejusdem pleniorem, ac luculentiorem declarationem; illud certe constat, Basilium, utcunque in Polemicis contra haereticos, traditiones aliquando non scriptas adhibendas putarit, in controversiis tamen de fide, omnia penitus reiiciienda iudicare, quae non ex manifestis Scripturis sumuntur. Iam vero quum tam differe, tam accurate ipse mentem suam explicet; quis de Basilii sententia dubitare poterit, nisi qui veritate relicta, contentiosam obstinationem unicum sibi scopum proposuit? units.tr: These words of Basil, whether we call them a continued retraction of his earlier opinion or a fuller and clearer declaration of the same, this at least is certain: that Basil, however he may have thought that unwritten traditions were sometimes to be used in polemics against heretics, nevertheless judged that in controversies about faith everything which is not taken from plain Scripture must be wholly rejected. Now, since he explains his mind so clearly and so accurately, who could doubt Basil's opinion, unless someone who has abandoned the truth and made stubborn contention his sole aim? We have been longer in vindicating Basil, because while our opponents, for display and show, bring forward many names of the Fathers, that is, empty masks and straw images [...] [the remainder of this unit is illegible in the scan].

Indignum enim videri posset, si dolus & improbitas Aduersariorum in peruertendis Patribus plus valeret, quam industria nostra in eo, vt eosdem honoremus, intelligamus, & vindicemus ab infamia errorum illorum, à quibus ipsi se immunes, & inuiolatos, maxima sua cura & vigilantia praestiterunt. Hactenus de auctoritate Scripturarum, de regula fidei, de iudice controuersiarum, de traditionibus non scriptis disseruimus; restat, vt de erroris huius origine quaeramus.
units.tr: [Obscura: the opening words are too garbled to translate reliably.] ...of whom, to strike terror into the fearful and the weak, it seemed unbearable if, through our sloth, we allowed even one of the ancient writings to stand unanswered. For it might seem shameful if the trickery and wickedness of our opponents in distorting the Fathers were more effective than our diligence in honouring them, in understanding them, and in clearing them of the infamy of those errors from which they kept themselves free and unharmed by their own great care and vigilance. So far we have discussed the authority of Scripture, the rule of faith, the judge of controversies, and unwritten traditions. It remains for us to inquire into the origin of this error.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: De erroris origine.
units.tr: On the origin of the error.

units.la: DE origine errorum in controuersiis, quas tractandas suscepimus, co libentius disputabimus, quia Pontifici contra nos semper obicere solent religionem, sensumq; Patrum, & maiorum nostrorum: vt nos a vera Patrum nostrorum aberrasse, imo vt nostro iudicio omnes maiores nostros damnatos insimulent. Necessaria igitur videtur haec disputatio, vt postquam Ecclesiae Catholicae consensum aperuerimus, quum q; nostra cum Ecclesia superiori communio coiter cognoscamus, indem quinam sint, qui ab Ecclesiae tam penitus recepta doctrina defecerint, & quando hic defectus in noruerit [?]. Ita non solum nostra communio cum Ecclesia antiqua, sed & Pa-trum nostrorum communio cum Romana Ecclesia constabit. Quæ quidem Romana Ecclesia in maximis fidei negotiis, veritatem contra Romanam Curiam egregie confirmauerat, & conseruauerat. Quum igitur constiterit patres maioresque nostros in fide ac religione Romanæ Ecclesiæ, communionem retinuisse cum Ecclesia antiqua: Aduersarii nostri nihil contra nostram, nihil contra patrum nostrorum fidem producere possunt, nisi recentia quædam Romanæ Curiæ decreta, quæ quia in Ecclesia recepta non sunt, auctoritatem apud nos promereri nullam possunt. Nos igitur, ut & maiores nostri perpetuam Ecclesiæ doctrinam secuti sumus, quæ doctrina ab Ecclesiæ primordiis usque ad patrum nostrorum memoriam, cum antiquæ, tum vero Romanæ Ecclesiæ certissima testimonia habet. Aduersarios denique nostros, utcunque antiquorum nomina iactent, originem erroris sui non ab Ecclesia, sed à Romana Curia traxisse constabit.
units.tr: I shall discuss the origin of the errors in the controversies we have undertaken all the more willingly because the Papists are always accustomed to object against us the religion and opinion of the Fathers and of our forebears, as if we had strayed from the true faith of our fathers, and indeed as if, in their judgment, they had condemned all our ancestors. This discussion therefore seems necessary, so that, after we have set out the consensus of the Catholic Church, and have together recognised our communion with the ancient Church, we may see who are those who have fallen away from the doctrine so thoroughly received in the Church, and when this defection began. In this way it will be established not only that we are in communion with the ancient Church, but also that our fathers were in communion with the Roman Church. That Roman Church, indeed, had firmly upheld and preserved the truth against the Roman Curia in the greatest matters of faith. Since it is therefore clear that our fathers and forebears retained, in the faith and religion of the Roman Church, communion with the ancient Church, our adversaries can produce nothing against our faith, or against the faith of our fathers, except certain recent decrees of the Roman Curia, which, since they have not been received in the Church, can have no authority with us. We, therefore, following our forebears, have followed the perpetual doctrine of the Church, which doctrine, from the beginnings of the Church down to the memory of our fathers, has most certain testimonies both from the ancient Church and from the Roman Church. Finally, however much they boast of the names of the ancients, it will be plain that our adversaries have derived the origin of their error not from the Church, but from the Roman Curia.

units.la: Ut igitur erroris huius origo aperiatur, non est huius mali antiquitas altius quærenda. Ignobile monstrum est in ipso Conciliabulo Tridentino nuper natum. Quamuis enim has artes antiquas hæreticorum inveniamus, ut traditiones non scriptas, ex iisdem Scripturæ locis proferre consueverint, ex quibus hodie Pontifici eas colligunt: quia tamen nobis proprop qui in rorum facim [?] quur Eccl te Tr mus. prim men prob fiæ ti tuer habe è Scr qui vide con ebr tam fice rum ard gral Trac rion ptu uer latu ho fer pti propositum hoc loco est, originem eorum, qui in Romanam Ecclesiam subrepserunt, errorum obscuare; antiquos hæreticos missos facimus; & erroris[?] huius originem notamus, quum primum in Romana, quæ sic dicitur, Ecclesia, locum inuenerit: quod profecto ante Tridentini Concilii tempora frustra quæritamus. Nam Eccium, Prierium, reliquosque, qui primum contra Lutherum disputarunt, commentum hoc latebat. Nam quæ è Scripturis probare non potuerunt illi, ea tum sub Ecclesiæ titulo iactabant. Quæcunque Ecclesia statuerat, ita tum defendebantur, quasi parem haberent vim atque auctoritatem cum iis, quæ è Scripturis manifestis producta fuerant. At qui in hac acie deinceps successerunt[?], quum viderent causam suam[?] verbi diuini gladio confossam, illustribus Scripturæ testimoniis obrutam: vt inane Ecclesiæ nomen contra tam manifestas Scripturas non viderentur sufficere: hoc tandem commentum excogitarunt, vt, quia nouas scripturas condere, opus arduum videbatur, magis compendiaria via grassati, verbum Dei verbo Dei opponerent. Itaque duo postulata sumunt: Primum, traditiones Apostolicas esse verbum Dei non scriptum, ac proinde cum verbo scripto pari reuerentia ac fide suscipiendas. Alterum postulatum, quod sumunt itidem, non probant, hoc est, Quicquid Romana Ecclesia tenet, seruatque, quod non potest probari è Scripturis, illud pro Apostolica traditione habendum dum esse. Hocillud est, quod Bellarminus in quinta traditionum regula sic profert: Id sine dubio credendum est, ex Apostolica traditione descendere, quae pro tali habetur in ipsa Ecclesia, quae est integra, & continua successio ab Apostolis. Et subiungit: Quae defecit certa successio omnibus aliis Ecclesiis, praeterquam in Romana; ideo ex testimonio huius solius Ecclesiae sumi potest certum argumentum ad probandam Apostolicam traditionem. Hæc ille. Atque ut sensum istorum hominum certum teneamus, Petrus à Soto verba etiam in eandem sententiam audiamus: Infallibilis, inquit, effecta[?], & Catholica: Quaecunque tenet, credit, & sonat[?] Romana Ecclesia, & in Scripturis non habentur, illa ab Apostolis esse tradita. Et enumerat: Oblationem sacrificii diurni, invocationem Sanctorum, merita operum, primatum Romani Pontificis, consecrationem aquae in Baptismo, elementa, verba, & effectus Sacramentorum Ordi-nis, Matrimonii, & Extremae unctionis, orationes pro defunctis, enumerationem peccatorum sacerdoti faciendam, necessitatem satisfactionis. Hæc ille.
units.tr: So that the origin of this error may be laid open, its antiquity is not to be sought from further back. It is an ignoble monster, born recently in the Council of Trent itself. For although we find that the heretics of old used these same arts, namely that they were accustomed to bring forward unwritten traditions from the very passages of Scripture from which the Papists today gather them, nevertheless, since our purpose in this place is to obscure the origin of those errors which crept into the Roman Church, we set aside the ancient heretics, and we note the origin of this error only from the point at which it first found a place in the so-called Roman Church. This we vainly seek before the times of the Council of Trent. For Eck, Prierias and the rest, who first disputed against Luther, were not aware of this invention. For what they could not prove from the Scriptures, they then put forward under the name of the Church. Whatever the Church had decreed, they then defended as if it had equal force and authority with those things which had been drawn from plain Scriptures. But when those who came afterwards in this battle saw their cause pierced through by the sword of the divine Word and overwhelmed by the clear testimonies of Scripture, so that the empty name of the Church did not seem sufficient against such manifest Scriptures, they at last devised this invention: since writing new Scriptures seemed a difficult task, they proceeded by a shorter way and set the Word of God against the Word of God. Accordingly they assume two postulates. The first is that Apostolic traditions are the unwritten Word of God, and therefore are to be received with the same reverence and faith as the written Word. The second postulate, which they likewise assume and do not prove, is that whatever the Roman Church holds and keeps, which cannot be proved from Scripture, is to be regarded as an Apostolic tradition. This is what Bellarmine sets out in his fifth rule of traditions: That is without doubt to be believed which descends from Apostolic tradition, which is held to be such in the Church itself, which has an unbroken and continuous succession from the Apostles. And he adds: Where the certain succession has failed in all other Churches except the Roman, therefore from the testimony of this Church alone can a certain argument be drawn for proving Apostolic tradition. So he. And that we may hold the mind of these men with certainty, let us also hear Peter of Soto saying the same thing: The Church, he says, being infallible and Catholic, whatever the Roman Church holds, believes and proclaims, and which is not found in the Scriptures, that has been handed down from the Apostles. And he lists: the offering of the daily sacrifice, the invocation of the saints, the merits of works, the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, the consecration of the water in Baptism, the elements, the words and the effects of the Sacraments of Orders, Matrimony and Extreme Unction, prayers for the dead, the enumeration of sins to be made to the priest, the necessity of satisfaction. So he.

units.la: Videmus ergo quam necessaria Aduersa-rius[?] nostros sit hæc de traditionibus non scrip-turis contentio, quæ nullo negotio causam Pontificiam stabilitat, quæ omnem illas cogitationes, omnem illam sublimitatem, quæ extollitur aduersus cognitionem Dei, omnia deniqueistorum insomnia, tanta cum confidentia ac securitate recipienda docet, ac si in Scripturis exprimerentur omnia. Num quis magis insignem in Spiritum sanctum contumeliam excogitare potuit, quam ut quæcunque profanis hominibus placuerint, ea omnia tam sancta, tam veneranda autoritate in Ecclesia valere debere affirmet: ac si Spiritus san-ti[?] dogmata ab ore Dei profecta, & in sacris Scripturis depositora forent? Quo impudentius sese in hac re iactat Antichristus, verba & instituta sua verbo Dei conferens: quoq; magis revelatur homo ille peccati, & filius perditionis, opponens sese, atq; efferé aduersus Deum, adeo ut in templum Dei, supra Ecclesiam, tanquam Deus sedeat (nam qui verba traditionesq; suas ab Ecclesia recipiendas mādat, tanquā verbum Dei, nonne is supra Ecclesiā tanquam Deus sedet?) quo, inquā, fur ipsius[?] sese effert Antichristus: eo certe maiore nos fidem industriamq; adferre debemus, viri Academici, ne per nostram locordiam in hoc abbladen-re[?] seculo, veritate nobis erípi patiamur. De controuersiis Pontificiis aliter fortasse iudicat alii: Ego vero, ut q̃ sentio, fateor, nulla existimo, nec in regno Pontificio, nec apud quosc̃ubiq̃; alios hæreticos, tā perniciosam sentē jam, villo seculo innatuisse, quā ea est, q̃ hodie sub traditionū nomine proponitur. In qua Pōtifices[?] ꝑ traditionibus pugnāt, nos ꝑ Scripturis, illi pro verbo suo, nos pro verbo Dei; illi de honore Papæ solliciti, de eius fide auctoritate, amplitudine, potestate; nos de diuino honore. Neq; n. nobis cōcedi volum, q illis negam, tantū sacris scripturis honore suo vindicam. Itaq; vel apud peruicaces auditores facile constare potest, quinam sint, in quibus regnet amor veritatis, quinam sint etiam, quos spiritus erroris, & efficacia deceptionis transuersos abripiat, vt ludibrio[?] habeant sacras Scripturas, cum quibus sua etiam commenta comparanda existimant.
units.tr: We see, then, how necessary this contention about unwritten traditions is for our adversaries, since it establishes the Papist cause without any trouble, and teaches that all those notions, all that loftiness which exalts itself against the knowledge of God, in short all the dreams of these men, are to be received with such confidence and certainty as if everything were expressed in the Scriptures. Could anyone devise a more notable insult against the Holy Spirit than to affirm that whatever has pleased profane men must be held in the Church with such sacred and venerable authority, as if the doctrines of the Holy Spirit had proceeded from the mouth of God and were laid up in the holy Scriptures? The more shamelessly Antichrist boasts of himself in this matter, setting his words and institutions beside the Word of God, the more that man of sin and son of perdition is revealed, opposing himself and lifting himself up against God, so that he sits in the temple of God, above the Church, as if he were God. (For he who commands that his words and traditions be received by the Church as the Word of God, does he not sit above the Church as God?) By how much more, I say, Antichrist exalts himself in this way, by so much the greater faith and diligence we ought to bring, learned gentlemen, lest through our sloth we allow the truth to be snatched from us in this age. Others perhaps judge the Papist controversies otherwise; but I, as I think, confess that I hold that no more pernicious opinion has ever sprung up in any age, either in the Papal kingdom or among any other heretics anywhere, than that which is today put forward under the name of tradition. In this matter the Pontiffs fight through traditions, we through Scriptures; they for their own word, we for the Word of God; they are anxious for the honour, faith, authority, greatness and power of the Pope, we for the divine honour. For we do not wish to be granted what we deny to them; we only defend the honour of the sacred Scriptures. And so even before stubborn hearers it can easily be made clear who they are in whom the love of truth reigns, and who they are whom the spirit of error and the power of deception carry away perverse, so that they hold the sacred Scriptures in mockery, while they think their own inventions must be set alongside them.

units.la: Bellarminus, qui cum magnis antiquorum nominibus hanc aciem turbidus ingreditur, nihil nouum attulit: tantum profligatas quasdam cohortes recolligit, quas nostri multo ante dissiparunt: ad ea vero, quæ nostri poluerunt, nihil omnino respondet. Mart. Chemnitius, quum traditiones in certas quasdam classes distinctas reposuerint, quas Andradius, aliuq; Pontificii consulto confusas esse voluerunt, vt sub communi vocis significatione facilius fallerent, sicut sophistæ solent: Lepius[?] atque accuratius monuit Aduersarios, si sincere agere velint, non debere eos offendere è Patribus traditiones, quas illi vel doctrinam è Scripturis traditam intelligunt, vel in externis ritibus esse volunt: sed ostendant id, quod est in controuersia, nempe dogma aliquod fidei suscipiendum esse, tanquam verbum Dei, quod non contineatur in Scripturis. Agimus Deo gratias, quod posit aliquot secula in contentionis studio abrumpta[?], post tot volumina, tot clamores strepitusque, tot litigantium successiones, dum vnus contentionis finis trahitur, ac retrahitur: Aduersarii non potuerint ad hunc vsque diem vel vnam sententiam, vel vni-
units.tr: Bellarmine, who charges into this battle turbulently with the great names of the ancients, has brought nothing new; he merely gathers together some routed cohorts which our men had dispersed long ago, and to those arguments which our men have advanced he makes no reply at all. Martin Chemnitz, having arranged the traditions into certain distinct classes, which Andradius and other Papists have deliberately wished to be confused so that they might more easily deceive under the common meaning of the word, as sophists are wont to do, more often and more carefully warned the adversaries that, if they wish to act sincerely, they ought not to take offence from the Fathers' traditions, which they understand either as doctrine handed down from Scripture or wish to be external rites; rather, they should show what is in controversy, namely that some dogma of faith must be received as the Word of God which is not contained in the Scriptures. We thank God that, after so many centuries spent in the zeal of contention, after so many volumes, so many clamours and uproars, so many successions of disputants, while one end of the controversy is dragged this way and that, our adversaries have not been able up to this day to agree on a single opinion, or on one uni-
