Hoc illud est, quod iam per aliquot secula ab Aduersariis perimus. Prodeunt noui scriptores Iesuitæ, orbem terrarum voluminibus onerant. Clamores suos repetunt ranæ istæ, causam fugiunt. Quid Bellarminus? Egregius scilicet sophismatum artifex, semper in ambigua & communi verbi significatione sese abscondit, de traditionum distinctione horret audire. Ad ea copiosissimus est, quæ non sunt in controuersia. Illud vero, ad quod omnes Pontifices tam sæpe, tam sollicite reuocant nostri, ne leui quidem digito attigit. Clamoribus agunt. Antiquorum nominum iactatione, quasi uento omnia complent. Ad id, quod est in controuersia, muti sunt. Quid aliud facere possunt, qui mercede conducti, honorariis stipendiis illecti, io[?] præscriptam e-missi militiam, missi bellum contra sacras Scripturas concitare, missi ingenium, literas, neruos omnes in hoc conuertere, ut hoc, tanquam ex Pythio oraculo profectum, adorent. Quæcunque Romana tenet, creditque Ecclesia, quæ è Scripturis probari non possunt, ea esse Apostolicas traditiones, esse verbum Dei non scriptum, sed verbo scripto conferendum. Atque hoc nusquam probant, tantum tan-quam quam verbum Dei alieni adorant. Isti sane Dii rui, ô Roma. Deus hic magnus est: & Deus necessario. Quis enim negare potest Deum es-se, cuius verbum est verbum Dei? Jesuitae in eo mirifice sudant, ut dicant (non enim do-cent, non probant, dicunt tantum) verba, & traditiones, quaecunque e cathedra probat Romanus Pontifex, esse indubitatum Dei verbum. Nonne igitur Papa Deus? Certe, atque etiam adorandus. Adorandum, affir-mat Bellarminus, sed non ut Deum. Atqui adoratio soli Deo competit. Quum enim Diabolus adorari voluit à Christo, reiectus est, quia solus Deus est adorandus. Solus Deus est adorandus, non ergo Diabolus. Solus Deus est adorandus: non ergo Diaboli prae-cogenitus Antichristus. Et tamen Papa ado-randus est, inquiunt, sed non ut Deus. Re-ste. Nam non adoratur ut Deus verus, sed ut Deus vanus, ut Deus alienus. Papa adora-tur à Pontificibus: ergo Deus est adorantibus ipsum. Papae verbum est verbum Dei: Pa-pa igitur Deus est. Deum esse necesse est, cuius verbum est verbum Dei. Sed hic Deus non erat in principio, sicut nec hoc verbum huius Dei. Nam ante Concilium Triden-tinum traditiones Ecclesiae Romanae non e-rant verbum Dei. Nuper igitur factum est verbum Dei, quod antea non erat. Non-ne curas animas merito dixeris, & cae-lestium manes, quibus universa religio & fides in illis fictionibus consistit? Ad istos [illegible, ~3 letters] une Dit & Deus eum ef futur in im dorba, & probat m Dei Certe affec Atqui n enim eiectur s Deus Solum oli pre apaads. Ref us, sed adoraactibus i: Paffe est Deus erbum dentinon eum est Nom & corgio & d isto fcor scopulos traditiones non scripta insanos homines adegerunt.
units.tr: ...they cannot bring forward a single word from antiquity, a single one to prove once what they constantly press and repeat everywhere: that before the Council of Trent the Church of Christ had never heard that some doctrine of faith must be received in the Church which cannot be proved from Scripture. This is the thing we have been refuting in our adversaries for several centuries now. New Jesuit writers come forward and burden the world with volumes. These frogs repeat their clamours and flee the question. What of Bellarmine? He is a remarkable craftsman of sophisms, who always hides himself in the ambiguous and common meaning of a word, and shudders to hear about the distinction between traditions. He is most copious on matters that are not in dispute. But that point, to which all our opponents so often and so anxiously recall the Pontiffs, he has not touched even with a finger. They argue by clamour; by tossing about the names of the ancients they fill everything as if with wind. On the point at issue they are mute. What else can they do, men hired for pay, enticed by honours and stipends, sent to wage a war, as it were a prescribed campaign, against the sacred Scriptures, sent to turn their talent, their letters and all their sinews to this one end, that they may worship this as if it had come from a Pythian oracle: whatever the Roman Church holds and believes which cannot be proved from the Scriptures, that this is Apostolic tradition, the unwritten word of God, to be set on a level with the written word. And they nowhere prove this; they only worship it as the word of God, a stranger to it. Those gods, surely, are fallen, O Rome. Here God is great, and God is necessary: for who can deny that God exists, whose word is the word of God? The Jesuits sweat wonderfully over this, so that they may say (for they do not teach, they do not prove, they only say) that words and traditions, whatever the Roman Pontiff approves from the chair, are the undoubted word of God. Is not the Pope then God? Certainly, and even to be worshipped. To be worshipped, Bellarmine affirms, but not as God. Yet worship belongs to God alone. For when the devil wished to be worshipped by Christ, he was rejected, because God alone is to be worshipped. God alone is to be worshipped; therefore not the devil; God alone is to be worshipped; therefore not the Antichrist, the devil's forerunner. And yet, they say, the Pope is to be worshipped, but not as God. Nonsense. For he is not worshipped as the true God, but as a vain God, a foreign God. The Pope is worshipped by the Pontiffs; therefore he is God to those who worship him. The word of the Pope is the word of God; therefore the Pope is God. It must be God whose word is the word of God. But this God was not there at the beginning, nor was this word of this God. For before the Council of Trent the traditions of the Roman Church were not the word of God. Therefore the word of God has lately come into being, which was not before. Would you not rightly call these cares and heavenly spirits the spirits of souls, on which all religion and faith rest in those fictions? ...these insane men have driven traditions, unwritten, onto rocks.

units.la: Ut igitur traditionum abyssum inuenia-mus: Si invocatio Sanctorum, merita operum, Missæ sacrificium, Romani Pontificis primatus, reliquaque huius generis, quæ nullo Scripturæ testimonio nituntur, probanda fuerint: hæc probatio elegans, & expedita videtur, si dicant, [?]esse Apostolicæ traditiones. Quid quæris amplius?
units.tr: So then, to find the abyss of traditions: if the invocation of the saints, the merits of works, the sacrifice of the Mass, the primacy of the Roman Pontiff, and the rest of this kind, which rest on no testimony of Scripture, are to be proved, this proof seems elegant and easy: they need only say that they are Apostolic traditions. What more do you ask?

units.la: Atqui hic nobis magnum occurrit mysterium, mirumque videtur, quod, qui negant, hæc è Scripturis probari posse, sed tantum à traditione sumenda esse docent: Scripturas tamen adducunt, ut ea, quæ à Scripturis probari posse negant, è Scripturis tamen probare velint. Verbi gratia: Primatum Romani Pontificis, affirmant, non è Scripturis, sed ex traditione constare. At vero ad hanc rem confirmandam, Scripturas plurimas adducunt, nempe: Tu es Petrus, & super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam. Et: Pasce oves meas; & alias Scripturas eius generis. Si hoc non è verbo scripto, sed è traditionibus, id est, è verbo non scripto petendum sit; quare verbum scriptum adducunt? [?]Audire abyssum. Nam ut in mysterio Chr[?]isti, sic in mysterio Antichristi, abyssum invocat. Verus sensus, inquiunt, horum verborum: Tu es Petrus, aut eorum, Pasce oues meas, & ex traditione pera-dus [?] est. Traditio autem Romanæ Ecclesiæ verba illa ad Romani Pontificis principatum stabiliendum conuertit. Atque hoc satis est.
units.tr: But here there arises for us a great mystery, and it seems a wonder that those who deny that these things can be proved from Scripture, and teach that they must be taken only from tradition, nevertheless adduce Scriptures, so that they wish to prove from Scripture those things which they deny can be proved from Scripture. For example: they affirm that the primacy of the Roman Pontiff rests not on Scripture but on tradition. Yet to confirm this point they adduce very many Scriptures, namely: Tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam ["You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church"]; and: Pasce oves meas ["Feed my sheep"]; and other Scriptures of that kind. If this is to be sought not from the written word but from traditions, that is, from the unwritten word, why do they adduce the written word? ...they invoke an abyss. For as in the mystery of Christ, so in the mystery of Antichrist, they call on the abyss. The true sense, they say, of these words, Tu es Petrus, or of those, Pasce oves meas, has been derived from tradition. But the tradition of the Roman Church has turned those words to establish the principate of the Roman Pontiff. And this is enough.

units.la: Sed vt in aliam abyssum feramur: sensus hic Pontificius eorum verborum primum inuencus est in Decretalibus antiquorum Pontificum Epistolis, quas confictas fuisse, affirmant plurimi Pontifici scriptores: necauden[?] Bellarminus negare. Nam Patres, qui plurimi ista Scripturæ verba interpretantur, non istum verborum sensum, sed longe alium affirmant. Quod ergo ē Scripturis probari non potest, quod à Patribus Scripturæ sensum tradentibus reiicitur; quod ex Pontificum Epistolis primum producitur, vel ipsorum Pontificiorum iudicio, confictis fallarisque[?]: illud quia sic renet[?] Romana Ecclesia, erit Apostolica traditio, verbum Dei non scriptum, non minori reuerentia & autoritate suscipiendum, quam verbum scriptum. Hic Pontificii viri docti & saluti sue expediant. Sensus horum verborum, Pasce oues meas, aliorumque eius generis, sicut hodie est in Romana Ecclesia receptus, estne traditio Apostolica? Est plane, per infallibilem regulam, inquit Soto. Est sine dubio, inquit Bellarminus. Atqui hanc Apostolicam traditionem, id est, illum Scripturæ sensum, unde primum habuit Romana Ecclesia? Ex Decretalibus Epistolis. At Epistolas illas omnino confictas fuisse, restantur Pon-
units.tr: But that we may be carried into another abyss: this Papist sense of those words was first discovered in the Decretal Epistles of the ancient Pontiffs, which very many Papist writers affirm were forged, and which Bellarmine does not deny could be. For the Fathers, who very often interpret these words of Scripture, do not affirm this sense of the words but a quite different one. So what cannot be proved from Scripture, what is rejected by the Fathers who give the sense of Scripture, what is first produced from the Epistles of the Pontiffs, which, even by the judgement of the Papists themselves, are forged and false: if this is held by the Roman Church, it will be an Apostolic tradition, an unwritten word of God, to be received with no less reverence and authority than the written word. Here let the learned Papists look to their own salvation. Is the sense of these words, Pasce oves meas, and others of that kind, as it is now received in the Roman Church, an Apostolic tradition? It is plainly so, by an infallible rule, says Soto. It undoubtedly is, says Bellarmine. But this Apostolic tradition, that is, that sense of Scripture, from where did the Roman Church first get it? From the Decretal Epistles. But that those Epistles were altogether forged, the Pon-

units.la: Pontif[?] scriptu[?] Scriptu[?] anguis[?] nunqu[?] tur ; ve[?] traditi[?] quicqu[?] Scriptu[?] non di[?] rum n[?] compa[?]
units.tr: ...Pontifical writings... never... the tradition... anything... the written... not... (the text here is too corrupt to be recovered with certainty).

units.la: Der[?] prius m[?] reticor[?] inhære[?] conuin[?] ptur ar[?] derent[?] bant, Apost[?] moner[?] tulisse[?] stolis t[?] fte b [?] ciam[?] pres.
units.tr: ...first... they... cling to... were... held... the Apostles... admonish... they brought... to the epistles... (the text here is too corrupt to be recovered with certainty).

units.la: Basilid[?] opinio[?] mens[?] superi[?] no. At[?] Pontificii. At continent[?] verbum Dei non scriptum, traditionem Ecclesiæ Romanæ sacris Scripturis conferendas. Vel sese Romanus anguis in omnia convertat, sicut Proteus, nunquam tamen sophistica lubricitate elabe-tur: vel confiteatur, non esse Apostolicam traditionem verbo scripto conferendam, quicquid Romana tenet Ecclesia, quod è Scripturis probari non possit: vel concedat, non dico hominum scripta, sed nequissimorum nebulonum figmenta sacris[?] Scripturis comparanda esse.
units.tr: The opinion of Basilides... the Papists. But they hold an unwritten word of God, and the tradition of the Roman Church is to be set beside the sacred Scriptures. Or let the Roman serpent turn itself into all shapes, like Proteus, yet it will never slip away from the slipperiness of its sophistry; or let it confess that whatever the Roman Church holds which cannot be proved from the Scriptures is not an Apostolic tradition to be set beside the written word; or let it concede that not, I say, the writings of men, but the fabrications of the most wicked scoundrels, are to be compared with the sacred Scriptures.

units.la: Denique postremo loco reuocemus, quæ prius monuimus, Pontificios antiquorum hæreticorum filios, patrum suorum vestigiis inhærere. Quum olim à Patribus è Scripturis convincerentur hæretici, nec se posse Scripturarum testimoniis deliria sua probare viderent, ad sacrum illud ἀπαράδοτον[?] recurrebant, habere se sua dogmata ex traditione Apostolorum. {a}Eusebius testatur, Artemonem ad hæresis suæ confirmationem attulisse, eam scilicet antiquitus ab ipsis Apostolis traditam fuisse. Basilides hæresis suæ te-fte {b}Clemente, magistrum proferebat Glaucian, qui, sicut ipse gloriatur, fuit Petri interpres. Hæreses, quæ à Valentino, Marcione, Basilide appellatæ sunt, gloriantur, se Matthiæ opinionem adducere, inquit idem {c}Clemens Alexandrinus. Plura in hanc sententiam superius annotauimus ex Irenæo, Tertulliano, Athanasio, Augustino, qui hanc antiquam hærehæreticorum fraudem aperuerint, ut quæ à Scripturis probare non possent, ea ad Apostolorum traditiones non scriptas retulerint.
units.tr: Finally, let us recall in the last place what we said before: that the Papists, sons of the ancient heretics, cling to the footsteps of their fathers. When the heretics were once refuted from Scripture by the Fathers, and saw that they could not prove their follies by the testimonies of Scripture, they ran back to that sacred unhanded-down [ἀπαράδοτον]: they had their doctrines from the tradition of the Apostles. {a}Eusebius testifies that Artemon brought this forward to confirm his heresy, namely that it had been handed down from the Apostles themselves from of old. Basilides, by the testimony of {b}Clement, offered Glaucias as the teacher of his heresy, who, as he himself boasts, was an interpreter of Peter. The heresies which were named after Valentinus, Marcion and Basilides boast that they bring forward the opinion of Matthias, says the same {c}Clement of Alexandria. We have noted more to this effect above from Irenaeus, Tertullian, Athanasius and Augustine, who have uncovered this old fraud of the heretics, by which they referred to unwritten traditions of the Apostles whatever they could not prove from the Scriptures.

units.la: At omnes istos hæreticos, quamquam traditiones suas ad Apostolos referentes, se se [?] etiam verbum Dei non scriptum, sed traditum habere iactantes, Patres vero Scripturæ testimoniis refutabant. Quum igitur eundem abyssi puteum aperiat Romanus Pontifex, Angelus ille abyssi [?], ut locustas suas è traditionum fumo emittat, quæ [?] rex est locustarum. Utcunque locustæ illæ de traditionibus gloriantur, utcunque os in cœlum aperiant, lordes suas in sanctum sanctorum tiendent [?], traditiones Apostolicas ex confictis & corruptis lacunis hauriant, libros fallaces & supposititios non solum in lucem, sed & in cœlum efferant, Scripturas novas, & Sacramenta nova excudant, Patrum genuina scripta per Indices expurgatorios infringant, commutent, corrumpant ; utcunque tecta [?] cælo, & lucem tenebris immisceant. Nos tamen per viam regiam, quam ante nos sancti Patres tenuerunt, incedentes, Patrum nostrorum inhærentes vestigiis, nihil illas larvatas [?] locustas metuemus. Nec illorum hominum aut ferocia, aut insania, aut inanis confidentia impediet nos ; imo vero expeditos magis, ac vigilantes acuat, atque excitet, ut & Deo suam gloriam, & sacris Scripturis suum honorem, & Patribus suam reverentiam exhibeamus.
units.tr: But all these heretics, though they referred their traditions back to the Apostles and boasted that they possessed an unwritten word of God handed down to them, were refuted by the Fathers with the testimonies of Scripture. Since the Roman Pontiff therefore opens the same pit of the abyss, and that angel of the abyss sends forth his locusts from the smoke of traditions, he is their king. However much those locusts boast of traditions, however widely they open their mouths to heaven, and however they thrust their filth into the holy of holies, however they draw Apostolic traditions from fabricated and corrupt cisterns, bring forth false and spurious books not only into the light but even into heaven, coin new Scriptures and new sacraments, and break, alter and corrupt the genuine writings of the Fathers through expurgatory indexes, and however they cover heaven and mingle light with darkness, we, walking along the royal road that the holy Fathers before us have trodden and keeping to the footsteps of our Fathers, will fear nothing from those masked locusts. Neither the ferocity, nor the madness, nor the empty confidence of those men shall hinder us. Rather, it shall sharpen and rouse us, made lighter and more watchful, so that we may give God his glory, Holy Scripture its honour, and the Fathers their reverence.

units.la: Nec mouamur audaculas istas locustas, quan-quam fastigio[?] turgentes, capillis mulierum, ac dentibus leonum armatas, quae est eorum nota iam, & perspecta omnibus lasciuia cum sanguinaria crudelitate coniuncta. Utcun-que præ se ferant equorum speciem, qui iam ad bellum parantur: quae omnia furores istos præmonstrant, quos illi in sanctos quotidie excitant, coniurationes, bella, cædes, clades, quas per orbem terrarum, per singulas regiones, per oppida, per domos, armis, venefi-ciis, puluere tormentario, secretis conspirationibus meditantur, & concitant: utcunque libera[?] palam in furores ferantur, ut furentem ipsorum audaciam nec cohibere, nec dissimulare possint: Nos tamen in Christi aduen-tum spe atque expectatione propendentes, omnia pericula, quæ nobis propter veritatem intentantur, vel contemnendo, vel subeundo, magno animo, hoc est, Christiana tolerantia vincimus.
units.tr: Let us not be moved by those bold locusts, swollen with pride, though armed with women's hair and lions' teeth, which is by now their known mark, and a wantonness clear to everyone, joined with bloody cruelty. However much they display the look of horses already readied for battle, all of this foreshadows the frenzies they stir up daily against the saints: conspiracies, wars, slaughters and disasters, which they plot and incite across the whole world, in every region, town and house, by arms, poisonings, gunpowder and secret plots. However openly they are carried away into frenzy, so that they can neither restrain nor conceal their raging audacity, we, however, leaning forward in hope and expectation of Christ's coming, overcome every danger threatened against us for the sake of the truth, whether by despising it or by enduring it, with a great spirit, that is, with Christian endurance.

units.la: SECVNDA CONTROVERSIA, DE ECCLESIA: THESES PONTIFICIORUM.
units.tr: SECOND CONTROVERSY, CONCERNING THE CHURCH: THE THESES OF THE PAPISTS.

units.la: Nostra sententia est, Ecclesiam unam tantum esse, non duas, & illam unam & veram, esse cœtum hominum eiusdem Christianæ fidei professione, & eorundem Sacramentorum communione colligatum, sub regimine legitimorum pastorum, ac præcipue unius Christi in terris Vicarij, Romani Pontificis. Bellarm. lib. 3. cap. 2. de Ecclesia.
units.tr: Our view is that the Church is one only, not two, and that this one and true Church is the assembly of men bound together by the profession of the same Christian faith and by communion in the same sacraments, under the government of lawful ministers, and above all of the one Vicar of Christ on earth, the Roman Pontiff. Bellarm. lib. 3. cap. 2. de Ecclesia.

units.la: Vt aliquis[?] absolute dici possit pars vera Ecclesiæ, de qua Scriptura loquuntur, non putamus requiri vllam internam virtutem; sed tantum externam professionem fidei, & Sacramentorum communionem, quæ sensu ipso percipitur. Bellarm. ibid.
units.tr: So that someone may be called absolutely a true part of the Church, of which the Scriptures speak, we do not think any inward virtue is required, but only the outward profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses themselves. Bellarm. ibid.

units.la: CAPUT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Via quaerendi, ratio, inveniendi Ecclesiam demonstratur.
units.tr: The way of seeking, the method, and the finding of the Church are shown.

units.la: Quum Ecclesiæ Catholicæ nomine, & nudo titulo gloriẽtur Pontificii, erroresq; varios, tanquam sub Ecclesiæ velo[?] recondant, ut tenebras illas excutiamus, inprimis necessarium erit, è Scripturis Patribusq; exquirere, quid sit Ecclesia Catholica, cum qua ratione cognoscatur. Ita enim fucus omnis
units.tr: Since the Papists boast of the Catholic Church by name and by bare title, and hide their various errors as if under the veil of the Church, we must first of all, in order to tear away those shadows, seek from the Scriptures and the Fathers what the Catholic Church is and by what means it is recognised. For so every pretence will be laid bare, once they have confessed that by the Catholic Church something quite different is understood from what the Papists dream of.

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] n ef- n bo- r co- um, a v- Bel- efia, i vl- oro- em, , & ro- re- ori- que am cus nis omnis aperictur, quum confiterit, per Eccle-siam Catholicam longe aliud intelligi, quam quod somniant Pontificij.
units.tr: ...every pretence will be laid bare, since they must confess that by the Catholic Church something quite different is understood from what the Papists dream of.

units.la: Duo sunt; quæ Ecclesiam maxime ostendunt, Caput, & Membra: quorum ignorantia facit, vt plurimi hodie Ecclesiam quærentes errent. Ante ostium subito scotomate percussi, sicut viri Sodomitæ ante ostium Lot errarunt. Qui hæc duo recte nouerit, Ecclesiam ignorare non potest; qui hæc non recte tenuerit, Ecclesiam nunquam inueniet[?]. De his duobus inter Ecclesiam Catholicam, & partem Tridentinam, magna est hodie controuersia. Caput Ecclesiæ ponunt illi, Romanum Pontificem; nos vnicum CHRISTVM agnoscimus: Membra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ statuunt illi etiam homines malos, in quibus nulla est interna virtus; sed tantum externa professio fidei, & Sacramentorum communio, quæ sensu ipso percipitur; at Ecclesia Catholica semper docuit, membra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ non esse alios, quam homines iustificatos, & sanctificatos, in quibus est vera fides, & gratia Christi, quæ sensu non percipitur.
units.tr: There are two things which chiefly show the Church: the head and the members. Ignorance of these makes many who seek the Church today go astray, like men struck suddenly with blindness before the door, as the men of Sodom went astray before the door of Lot. Whoever knows these two rightly cannot be ignorant of the Church; whoever does not hold them rightly will never find the Church. On these two points there is today a great controversy between the Catholic Church and the Tridentine party. They make the Roman Pontiff the head of the Church; we acknowledge CHRIST alone. They hold that even wicked men, in whom there is no inward virtue but only an outward profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses itself, are members of the Catholic Church; but the Catholic Church has always taught that the members of the Catholic Church are none other than justified and sanctified men, in whom there is true faith and the grace of Christ, which is not perceived by the senses.

units.la: Hanc igitur controuersiam de Ecclesia, omnium grauissimam intelligunt Aduersarii. At in quærenda Ecclesia, præscriptionibus suis imperitos circumducunt, vt nisi Ecclesia Romæ quæratur, frustra quæri videatur. At nos Catholicam quærimus Romanæ Ecclesiæ matrem. Hinc enim habuit Romana, vt sit Ecclesia, si modo sit Ecclesia. Ipsam sponsam quærimus, non filias sponsæ, non ancillas. Respondent Tridentini, Romanam Ecclesiam esse ipsam sponsam, Papam vero sponsum. Sic Bellarminus. Sed non satisfaciunt. Nam Ecclesia Catholica non est adultera, sed vni tantum viro coniuncta, nempe Christo. Quæ igitur Romano Pontifici, id est, alteri viro coniuncta est, sponsa Christi quomodo potest esse? Neque enim sanctus Apostolus Paulus ausus est se sponsum dicere, sed servum sponsi, qui Ecclesiam sponso desponsarat, vt vni viro virginem castam sisteret Christo. Iohannes Baptista, quo maior non est ortus inter natos mulierum, nunquam se sponsum nominare ausus fuit, sed amicum sponsi. Et ne quis sit fallaciæ locus in quærenda Ecclesia, ille amicus sponsi (qui ad hoc præcurrit, vt ostenderet) ostendit, inquam, Christum per Ecclesiam, & Ecclesiam per Christum. Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi, qui stat, & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi; hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est. Quibus verbis tria docet: 1. Quis sit sponsus: 2. Quæ sit sponsa: 3. Qui sint amici sponsi, siue membra sponsæ. Sponsus est, qui habet sponsam, hoc est, vnus Christus est, qui habet Ecclesiam suam. Habet autem sponsam, quia peculiarem sibi, & propriam tenet, sicut vir vxorem propriam. Habet, quia diligit, ducit, regit: ita Christus cognoscitur per Ecclesiam. Nec minus Ecclesia per ChriChristum. Nam sponsa est, quæ habetur à sponso, id est, quæ ab uno viro tenetur, ab uno pendet, non se alteri prostituit: ab uno diligitur, ducitur, regitur. Sic Ecclesia cognoscitur per CHRISTVM. Amici etiam sponsi, & membra non minus innoscunt[?]: Amicus sponsi stat, & audit vocem sponsi, & gaudio magno gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Membra enim Ecclesiæ cognoscunt, se membra esse ex delectatione, quam habent in voce CHRISTI; quia oues Christi vocem eius audiunt; alienum autem fugiunt. Itaque ad regenda ac dirigenda Ecclesiæ membra, nulla alia restat via aut regula, quam vox & doctrina Christi in Scripturis sonans. Quantum hæc sunt omnia apud Pontificios murata? Pro Chri-sto substituunt[?] Romanum Pontificem. Imo, inquiunt, hos CHRISTI Vicarium agnoscimus in universa Ecclesia Romanum Pontificem. At viri isti boni intelligere nolunt, sponsum in lecto suo Vicarium non instituisse. Pro sponsa offerunt[?] isti nobis Romanam meretricem; pro amicis sponsi, homines impios, in quibus nulla est virtus; pro voce sponsi, verbum suum non scriptum. Dominus noster IESVS CHRISTVS peregre profectus, ut regnum suum accipiat, reliquit sponsam hîc illam, quam amicis suis commendavit. Romanus Pontifex, qui quondam erat unus ex amicis sponsi, qui-bus bus Christus sponsam suam dilectam commendauerat; fidem suam violauit, & non iam custodem, aut amicum se, sed adulterum ostentat. Pulchrè Augustinus: {a}Ponite, inquit, aliquem peregrè profectum commendasse amico suo sponsam. Vide, quaeso te charus meus es, ne forte me absente, pro me aliquis ametur. Qualis ergo ille, qui custodiens sponsam vel uxorem amici sui, dat quidem operam, ut nullus alius ametur, sed si se amari pro amico voluerit, quam detestandum vniuerso humano generi appareat. Hæc Augustini verba Romani Pontificis caput demulcent. Itaque pergit Augustinus: {b}Quare tibi ut arrogare, quod tuum non est? Vsq; adeo absens est, qui hic reliquit sponsam suam? Nescis, quia ille, qui à mortuis resurrexit, ad dexteram Patris sedet? Et mox de gaudio amici, propter vocem sponsi: {c}Non, inquit, gaudeo propter vocem meam, sed propter vocem sponsi gaudeo. Ego sum in audiendo, ille in dicendo: Ego sum illuminandus, ille lumen: Ego sum in aure; ille in verbo. Chrysostomus in eandem sententiam: {d}Sponsalia hæc sunt, per vocem sponsi videlicet, & doctrinam. Ita Ecclesia conciliatur Deo. Quamobrem Paulus inquit: Fides ex auditu, auditus autem per vocem Dei. Ambrosius etiam: {e}Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: hoc est, ipse solus est vir Ecclesiæ. Hæc ille. Videmus igitur ex Patrum iudicio, quàm se humano generi detestandum exhibuerit Romanus Pontifex, qui primus in Ecclesia se sponsum vocari voluit. Iohannes Baptista, & Apostoli, seruos se, ministros, & amicos sponsi profitentur, & nemo se [?] num [illegible, ~6 letters] tionis ia&at sponsi in Ecclesia mea sponsa vni viro gebant bant: cula sponsi cum perbi ris, ali oricn riem, a Sia pem nisi quae debes.
units.tr: Our adversaries regard this controversy about the Church as the most serious of all. Yet in seeking the Church, they lead the unlearned about with their prescriptions, so that unless the Church is sought at Rome, it seems to be sought in vain. But we seek the Catholic Church, the mother of the Roman Church. For the Roman Church has its being from her, if indeed she is a church at all. We seek the bride herself, not the bride's daughters or maidservants. The Tridentines reply that the Roman Church is the bride herself and the Pope the bridegroom. So Bellarmine. But they do not satisfy us. For the Catholic Church is not an adulteress, but joined to one husband only, namely Christ. How then can she who is joined to the Roman Pontiff, that is, to another husband, be the bride of Christ? Nor did the holy apostle Paul dare to call himself the bridegroom, but the servant of the bridegroom, who had betrothed the Church to the bridegroom so as to present a chaste virgin to Christ, her one husband. John the Baptist, than whom there has not arisen a greater among those born of women, never dared to name himself the bridegroom, but called himself the friend of the bridegroom. And lest there be any room for deceit in seeking the Church, that friend of the bridegroom (who went before for this very purpose, to show it) showed, I say, Christ through the Church and the Church through Christ. "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice; this my joy therefore is fulfilled." In these words he teaches three things: 1. who the bridegroom is; 2. what the bride is; 3. who the friends of the bridegroom, that is, the members of the bride, are. The bridegroom is he who has the bride, that is, Christ alone is he who has his Church. He has her because he holds her as his own and peculiar, as a husband holds his own wife. He has her because he loves, leads and rules her: thus Christ is known through the Church. And the Church is known no less through Christ. For the bride is she who is had by the bridegroom, that is, who is held by one man, depends on one, does not prostitute herself to another, is loved, led and ruled by one. Thus the Church is known through Christ. The friends of the bridegroom, too, and the members, are known no less: the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears the voice of the bridegroom, and rejoices with great joy at the bridegroom's voice. For the members of the Church know that they are members from the delight they have in the voice of Christ, because Christ's sheep hear his voice, but they flee from a stranger. Therefore, for ruling and directing the members of the Church, no other way or rule remains than the voice and teaching of Christ sounding in the Scriptures. How much of all this has been walled up by the Papists! In place of Christ they substitute the Roman Pontiff. "Nay," they say, "we acknowledge him as Christ's vicar over the whole Church." But these good men are unwilling to understand that the bridegroom appointed no vicar for his bed. In place of the bride these men offer us the Roman harlot; in place of the friends of the bridegroom, impious men in whom there is no virtue; in place of the voice of the bridegroom, their own unwritten word. Our Lord Jesus Christ, having gone abroad to receive his kingdom, left here his bride, whom he commended to his friends. The Roman Pontiff, who once was one of the friends of the bridegroom, to whom Christ had commended his beloved bride, has violated his trust, and no longer shows himself as her guardian or friend, but as an adulterer. Augustine says it well: {a}"Suppose someone, having gone abroad, had commended his bride to his friend. Take heed, I beg you, that you are my dear one, lest perhaps in my absence someone love her for me. What then of him who, guarding his friend's bride or wife, takes pains that no one else should love her, but if he wishes to be loved himself in place of the friend, how detestable he appears to the whole human race." These words of Augustine lay bare the Roman Pontiff's head. And so Augustine goes on: {b}"Why do you claim for yourself what is not yours? Is he who left his bride here so far away? Do you not know that he who rose from the dead sits at the right hand of the Father?" And soon after, on the friend's joy at the bridegroom's voice: {c}"I do not rejoice, he says, at my own voice, but I rejoice at the voice of the bridegroom. I am in hearing, he in speaking; I am to be illuminated, he is the light; I am in the ear, he in the word." Chrysostom to the same effect: {d}"These are the betrothals, namely through the voice and teaching of the bridegroom. Thus the Church is reconciled to God." Therefore Paul says: "Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the voice of God." Ambrose also: {e}"He who has the bride is the bridegroom: that is, he alone is the husband of the Church. Thus he." We see therefore from the judgement of the Fathers how detestable the Roman Pontiff has shown himself to the human race, he who first wished to be called the bridegroom in the Church. John the Baptist and the apostles profess themselves servants, ministers and friends of the bridegroom, and no one among them dared to call himself the bridegroom before the Roman Pontiff. Does that son of perdition, then, have any way of hiding, who boasts himself above the apostles? They professed themselves only ministers and friends of the bridegroom; but he proclaims thus in the Church: "I am the bridegroom, and the Church is my bride." They were eager to betroth her not to themselves but to one man, namely Christ, and they exulted in the voice and teaching of the bridegroom; but he puts forward his own voice as the oracles of the bride, and does not hear the voice of the bridegroom with joy, but lords it over the bride with pride and mockery. These things are alien to the Scriptures, alien to the judgement of the Fathers.

units.la: {a} tract. 13. in Iohan. mo se sponsum vocare ausus fuit ante Romanum Pontificem. Num ergo filius iste perditionis latere potest, qui se Apostolis maiorem iactat? Illi se tantum ministros & amicos sponsi professi sunt, iste autem sic proclamat in Ecclesia: Ego sum sponsus, & Ecclesia est mea sponsa. Illi non se habere sponsam, sed uni viro, nempe Christo, desponsare eam satagebant, & in sponsi voce ac doctrina exultabant: iste autem vocem suam, tanquam oracula sponsæ proponit, nec audit vocem sponsi cum gaudio, sed sponsæ dominatur cum superbia & ludibrio. Aliena sunt hæc à Scripturis, aliena à Patrum iudicio. S. Bernardus quasi orientem prospiciens hanc immanem barbariem, & superbiam, Eugenium sic admonuit:
units.tr: {a} Tract. 13 on John. Who ever dared to call himself the bridegroom before the Roman Pontiff? Can that son of perdition, who boasts himself greater than the apostles, therefore remain hidden? Those men professed only themselves ministers and friends of the bridegroom; but he proclaims thus in the Church: "I am the bridegroom, and the Church is my bride." They strove to betroth her to one man, namely Christ, and rejoiced in the bridegroom's voice and doctrine; but he sets forth his own voice as the oracles of the bride, and does not hear the bridegroom's voice with joy, but domineers over the bride with pride and derision. These things are alien to the Scriptures, alien to the judgement of the Fathers.

units.la: {a}Si amicus sponsi es, ne dixeris dilectam eius, principem meam, sed principem, nil tuum in illa vindicans, nisi quod pro ea, si oportuerit, etiam animam dare debes. Hæc Bernardus.
units.tr: {a}If you are a friend of the bridegroom, do not call her your beloved or my princess, but princess, claiming nothing of your own in her, except that for her, if it is necessary, you ought even to give your life. Thus Bernard.

units.la: Quærimus ergo Ecclesiam, hoc est, sponsam Christi, non Petri, non Pauli, non Iohannis Baptistæ, non Papæ, sed Christi sponsam. Si enim omnia Papæ tribuamus, quæ vel Apostolo Christi tribuenda sunt, hoc certe ei non debemus dare, quod negamus Apostolis, ut sit sponsus Ecclesiæ. Itaque inter alios Antichristi titulos hunc etiam sibi arrogare ausus est Romanus Pontifex, quem nemo Prophetarum aut Apostolorum arrogare potuit. Quomodo igitur inveniemus, quam quærimus dilectam illam, pudicam, castam, unicam columbam, hortum conclusum, son-tem signatum puteum aquæ viuæ, paradisum cum fructu pomorum. Ibis enim multis, ad nostros amores excitandos, ad nostram dili-gentiam obtinendam[?], in quærendo rem tanti pretii, sponsam suam insigniuit sponsus. Si lustremus loca illa, in quibus quondam hospitari solebat hæc Sancta Ecclesia, videmus omnia mutata: urbem quondam fidelem, factam nunc meretricem. Nec mi-ramur, si mortalia mutentur. Nam in istis[?] lo-cis non erat hæreditas sponsæ, in quibus ipsam videmus pressam, pulsatam, dere-ctam, & de immortali sua hæreditate suspi-rantem.
units.tr: We seek therefore the Church, that is, the bride of Christ, not of Peter, not of Paul, not of John the Baptist, not of the Pope, but the bride of Christ. For if we attribute to the Pope everything that is to be attributed even to an Apostle of Christ, we certainly ought not give him this, which we deny to the Apostles, that he should be the bridegroom of the Church. Therefore, among the other titles of Antichrist, the Roman Pontiff has dared to arrogate this one to himself, which no prophet or apostle could arrogate. How then shall we find that beloved, chaste, pure, unique dove, the enclosed garden, the sealed well of living water, the paradise with its fruit of apples? The bridegroom has marked out his bride, to stir up our love and to win our diligence in seeking a thing of such great price. If we survey those places in which this holy Church once used to dwell, we see everything changed: a city once faithful, now made a harlot. Nor do we wonder that mortal things should change. For in those places there was not the inheritance of the bride, in which we see her pressed down, beaten, driven out, and sighing for her immortal inheritance.

units.la: Sed quis nos melius adiuuare poterit in hoc scrutinio, in quo sponsam scrutamur, quam sanctus ille amicus sponsi, qui hanc nobis lucem præfert: Qui sponsam habet, sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi gaudio magno gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Quæris, quæ sit vera Christi Ecclesia? Respondet eam esse, quam habet Christus sibi uni, quæq; re-gitur & delectatur voce sponsi. Vox autem sponsi sunt sacræ Scripturæ. Ad hanc vocem Iohannes remittit[?] omnes, qui volunt esse amici sponsi, & membra sponsæ. Ecclesia igitur optime cognoscitur per Scripturas. At clamant Pontificii[?], Scripturas cognosci per Ecclesiam. Neq; illud negamus. Mutuas enim operas inter se præstant Scriptura & Ecclesia. Quæris, quænam sint canonicæ Scripturæ, atque ha-rum rum Scripturarum quis sit sensus, quæ intelli-gentia? Ecclesia hoc docet. Alias enim Scri-pturas suscipere non audeo, nisi quas Ecclesia demonstrauit canonicas esse. Quærimus, quæ-nam sit Christi vera Ecclesia? ubi quærenda? Scriptura nobis illud demonstrant. Aliam e-nim Ecclesiam non audeo agnoscere, nisi quam veram esse sacra probauit Scriptura. Sed pergunt utra contentiosi homines, & quærunt ex illis duabus rebus, cuius maior sit autoritas? Scripturane, qua Ecclesiam co-gnosco? an Ecclesiæ, per quam Scripturas agnosco? Magnum est, quod quæritur; sed si contentionis studium ponatur, via quæsi-tæ veritatis non magno sane labore ostén-det illis omnibus, qui cum humilitate quæ-runt, quod cum charitate retineant. Utrum-que est res Dei. Ecclesia, & Scriptura. Ec-clesia est regnum Dei. Scriptura est ver-bum Dei. Sed hoc regnum administratur per illud verbum. Ecclesia parit filios Dei, Scriptura sapientiam Dei continet, & isti filii sunt per hanc sapientiam. Quum vero sapientia illa autoritatem habeat in filios sa-pientiæ: certe verbum Dei, quæ est sapien-tia Ecclesiæ, autoritatem obtinet in Eccle-siam, atque in filios Dei, non autem illam hanc sapientiam. Mutuas ergo operas præ-stant Ecclesia, & Scriptura: sed autoritas est Scripturæ, ministerium vero Eccle-siæ. Ostendit Ecclesia Scripturas, sed mi-nisterio suo: Ostendit Scriptura Eccle-siam, siam, sed autoritate sua. Recte ergo faciunt, qui Scripturas, earumq; sententiam in Ecclesia quærunt, quia Ecclesia est columna, & stabilimentum veritatis, nempe quæ ministerio suo custodit, confirmat, & prædicat veritatem. Et recte faciunt, qui Ecclesiam in Scripturis quærunt, quia amici sponsi, vocem sponsi summo gaudio excipiunt: quia oves Christi vocem pastoris sui audiunt.
units.tr: But who can help us better in this search, in which we seek the bride, than that holy friend of the bridegroom, who holds out this light to us: "He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom rejoices with great joy because of the bridegroom's voice." Do you ask what the true Church of Christ is? He answers that it is the one which Christ has for himself alone, which is ruled and delights in the voice of the bridegroom. Now the voice of the bridegroom is the holy Scriptures. To this voice John refers all who wish to be friends of the bridegroom and members of the bride. The Church is therefore best known through the Scriptures. But the Papists cry out that the Scriptures are known through the Church. Nor do we deny this. For Scripture and the Church render mutual services to one another. Do you ask which are the canonical Scriptures, and what is the sense and understanding of these Scriptures? The Church teaches this. For I dare not receive any other Scriptures, except those which the Church has shown to be canonical. We ask what the true Church of Christ is, and where it is to be sought? Scripture shows us this. For I dare not acknowledge any other Church, except the one which holy Scripture has proved to be true. But contentious men press on, and they ask of these two things, which has the greater authority: Scripture, by which I know the Church, or the Church, through which I recognise the Scriptures? The question is a great one; but if the zeal for contention is set aside, the way of seeking the truth will, without any great labour, show all those who seek with humility what they may hold with charity. Both are the things of God, the Church and Scripture. The Church is the kingdom of God; Scripture is the word of God. But this kingdom is administered through that word. The Church bears the sons of God; Scripture contains the wisdom of God, and these sons are sons through this wisdom. Since indeed that wisdom has authority over the sons of wisdom, certainly the word of God, which is the wisdom of the Church, holds authority over the Church and over the sons of God, but not the other way round, that this Church holds authority over that wisdom. The Church and Scripture therefore render mutual services; but the authority belongs to Scripture, and the ministry to the Church. The Church shows the Scriptures, but by its ministry; Scripture shows the Church, but by its authority. Those therefore rightly act who seek the Scriptures and their meaning in the Church, because the Church is the pillar and stay of the truth, namely that which by its ministry guards, confirms and proclaims the truth. And those rightly act who seek the Church in the Scriptures, because the friends of the bridegroom receive the bridegroom's voice with the greatest joy, since the sheep of Christ hear the voice of their shepherd.

units.la: Quum vero Scripturæ prædicamus autoritatem, Ecclesiæ autem ministerium: non simpliciter negamus Ecclesiæ autoritatem. Ecclesia enim ministerio suo exercendo, habet autoritatem, & in filios suos, & contra omnes inimicos suos. Verum quoties inter Ecclesiam & Scripturas instituitur comparatio: autoritas est Scripturæ, ministerium tantummodo Ecclesiæ. Nam quæ autoritatem in suos habet, & contra inimicos, omnes hæreticos; non habet in Scripturas aliquam, sed a Scripturis habet omnem. Itaque quum in sacris Scripturis legimus[?]; Ecclesiam esse domum Dei viventis, columnam & stabilimentum veritatis, ministerium tantummodo intelligitur: quia fidem continet, & prædicationem, inquit Chrysostomus. Nam columna dicitur, & firmamentum veritatis, non a natura sua, sed ab officio suo. Ac proinde Apostolus de Ecclesia Israelitica differens, affirmat, illis concredita fuisse eloquia Dei. Atque hinc est, quod Ecclesia columna dicitur, & firmamentum, ab eloquiis Dei, quæ concredita Ecclesiæ esse docet Apostolus. Hæc omnia officium & ministerium demonstrant. Quoties igitur sancti Patres de autoritate Scripturarum loquuntur, solent dicere, autoritatem mirabilem, summum & cælestè autoritatis culmen, autoritatis fastigium. Hæc passim apud Augustinum aliosq; legun-tur. At idem Ecclesiæ demonstrantes ministerium, Ecclesiam proponere solent, Scriptu-ras legentem, Scripturas docentem, Scripturis credentem, Scripturas tanquam cælestes thesauros custodientem. Hæc omnia ministerium probant.
units.tr: But when we proclaim the authority of Scripture and the ministry of the Church, we do not simply deny the authority of the Church. For the Church, in exercising its ministry, has authority both over its own sons and against all its enemies. But whenever a comparison is drawn between the Church and the Scriptures, the authority belongs to Scripture, and the ministry only to the Church. For the Church, which has authority over its own members and against its enemies, all heretics included, has no authority over the Scriptures, but has all its authority from the Scriptures. Therefore, when in the holy Scriptures we read that the Church is the house of the living God, the pillar and stay of the truth, only the ministry is understood, because it holds the faith and its preaching, as Chrysostom says. For it is called a pillar and the firmament of the truth not by its nature but by its office. And so the Apostle, discussing the Israelite Church, affirms that the oracles of God were entrusted to them. Hence it is that the Church is called a pillar and firmament, from the oracles of God, which the Apostle teaches were entrusted to the Church. All these things point to office and ministry. Therefore, whenever the holy Fathers speak of the authority of the Scriptures, they are accustomed to say wonderful authority, the highest and heavenly summit of authority, the pinnacle of authority. These expressions are read everywhere in Augustine and the others. But when these same Fathers point out the ministry of the Church, they are accustomed to present the Church as reading the Scriptures, teaching the Scriptures, believing the Scriptures, and guarding the Scriptures as heavenly treasures. All these things prove the ministry.

units.la: Quia vero in hoc ministerio suo, autorita-tem habet in suos filios, & contra hæreticos: secundum autoritatem sacrarum Scripturarum, quæ summum retinent autoritatis fastigium; sanctæ Ecclesiæ autoritatem maxime veneramur, quam maiorem in hoc mundo non invenimus. Sive igitur quæramus Ecclesiæ ministerium ad Scripturas legendas, docendas, tractandas, aperiendas: sive autoritatem in nos, qui in hoc gloriamur, quod sumus filii matris Ecclesiæ: Ubinam vel utilius quæritur, vel certius invenitur hoc ministerium, hæc autoritas, quam in sacris Propheticis & Apostolicis Scripturis? Deinde post Prophetas & Apostolos, apud sanctos & venerandos Patres? in quorum ministerio, Ecclesiæ ministerium, in quorum autoritate, Ecclesiæ autoritatem magna ex parte constitutam videmus. Quid ergo, dicet[?] mihi quispiam, num quæris Ecclesiam in Ecclesia? Ego vero hoc ipsum ago. Et post diuinas Scripturas interrogabo matrem meam, vt sese offendat: & vbi quaerenda sit Ecclesia, ipsa doceat Ecclesia. Nec meruam fraterculorum clamores, nec me impediant noui isti turbatores, quo minus Ecclesiam Christi me certo inuenisse sperem, quum & certissima Scripturarum auctoritate, & fidissimo Ecclesiae ministerio, & confessione constiterit, quaenam [?] sit illa, quam quaerimus. Ecclesia Dei. Nam indubitatam Ecclesiae de se confessionem, indicabunt nobis Patres illi sancti, & venerandi, quos gloriosos filios suos Ecclesia Christi per diuersa [?] saecula peperit, atque educauit.
units.tr: But because in this ministry it has authority over its sons and against heretics, we most highly revere the authority of the holy Church, according to the authority of the holy Scriptures, which hold the highest summit of authority; and we do not find any greater authority in this world. Whether therefore we seek the ministry of the Church for reading, teaching, handling and opening the Scriptures, or its authority over us, who glory in this, that we are the sons of mother Church: where is this ministry and this authority sought more profitably or found more surely than in the holy prophetic and apostolic Scriptures? Next after the Prophets and Apostles, among the holy and venerable Fathers? In whose ministry we see the ministry of the Church, and in whose authority we see the authority of the Church largely established. What then? someone will say to me, do you seek the Church within the Church? Indeed, that is exactly what I am doing. And after the divine Scriptures I will question my mother, that she may show herself; and where the Church is to be sought, the Church itself will teach. Neither the clamours of little brothers nor the new disturbers shall hinder me from hoping that I have surely found the Church of Christ, since by the most certain authority of the Scriptures, by the most faithful ministry of the Church, and by its confession, it is established what that is which we seek: the Church of God. For those holy and venerable Fathers, whom the Church of Christ bore and reared as its glorious sons through the various ages, will show us the Church's undoubted confession about itself.

units.la: De notis Ecclesiae, quibus cognoscatur, multas turbas concitare solent, qui tenebras quaerunt. Bellarminus quindecim notas seu proprietates ponit. Alii alias. Nos vero, quia de re maxima, de Ecclesiae Catholicae possessione agitur, non sequemur turbulentam disputationem, sed praesidia certa causae nostrae ponemus in illis proprietatibus, quae sunt tam manifestae, tam claræ, tam apud omnes confessæ, rem ipsam, quam quaerimus, tam evidenter demonstrantes: ut eas nemo (qui de Ecclesia quicquam audierit) ambigat continere certissimam Ecclesiae descriptionem: quas tamen tam manifestas notas fugit Cardinalis Bellarminus, tanquam latro crucem. Qui igitur nos profitemur Christianos, credimus in Symbolo Apostolico, Ecclesiam sanctam, catholicam, Sanctorum communio-nem. nem. Alias notas, vt cuique placet adiiciat. Nos inprimis istas excutiemus; quae sine dubio Ecclesiam demonstrant: neque tam obscuras Ecclesiæ, quam ipsam rem euidentiam sequemur. Sed hanc formam erecta constituerit Ecclesia Romana, dabimus ei honorem reverentiamque matris, veram Dei Ecclesiam esse fatebimur, nos ipsos denique accusabimus, quod ab hac Ecclesia discessimus: Sin vero Romana haec Curia, quam Pontifices quidam Romanam Ecclesiam vocant, tantum abest ab hac forma, quam e Symbolo traditam tenemus; vt nulla in re conueniat: defectionis & separationis crimen in illos recidet, qui ab ea, defecerunt Ecclesia, quam in Symbolo profitemur omnes Christiani, quam solam veram esse credimus. Quid si ipsorum Pontificiorum confessione probauerimus. Ecclesiam nunc Romanam, nec esse sanctam, nec catholicam, nec sanctorum in ea esse communionem?
units.tr: Those who love darkness are accustomed to stir up many quarrels about the marks of the Church, by which it is recognised. Bellarmine sets down fifteen marks or properties; others set down different ones. But we, since the matter at issue is of the greatest importance, namely the possession of the Catholic Church, will not follow a turbulent disputation, but will place the sure defences of our cause in those properties which are so manifest, so clear, and so generally acknowledged, demonstrating the thing we seek so plainly, that no one (who has heard anything about the Church) can doubt that they contain the most certain description of the Church. Yet Cardinal Bellarmine avoids these so manifest marks as a thief avoids the cross. Therefore we who profess ourselves Christians, believe in the Apostles' Creed: the holy, catholic Church, the communion of saints. Let anyone add other marks as he pleases. We will first examine these, which without doubt demonstrate the Church, and we will follow the thing itself, which is more evident than the obscure marks of the Church. But if the Roman Church, having set up this form, shall honour it and revere it as a mother, we will confess that it is the true Church of God, and we ourselves will finally accuse ourselves of having departed from this Church. But if this Roman Curia, which some Pontiffs call the Roman Church, is so far from this form, which we hold as handed down from the Creed, that it agrees with it in no respect, then the crime of defection and separation will fall back upon those who have fallen away from that Church which all Christians profess in the Creed, and which we alone believe to be true. What if we prove, from the very confession of the Papists themselves, that the Roman Church now is neither holy, nor catholic, nor has the communion of saints in it?

units.la: Numquid causa est, quod litem nobis coram vero & iusto Ecclesiæ iudice vlterius intentent, qui istas notas, quae sunt Ecclesiæ proprietates, prorsus inseparabiles, ita à seipsis reiiciunt, vt nihil ad se pertinere arbitrentur?
units.tr: Is it perhaps the case that they bring a suit against us before the true and just judge of the Church, when they so completely reject from themselves those marks, which are the properties of the Church and wholly inseparable from it, that they think none of them belongs to them?

units.la: Quæstio agebatur inter Booz & illum agnatum eius, coram senioribus populi; vt ex illis vindicaret agrum Elimelechi. Agnatus ille, sibi debere clamabat, seque vindicaturum dicebat. Esto, inquit Booz: sed possessio illa hanc habet legem annexam, vt vna cum agro illo, Ruthām etiam Moabitidem vxorem accipias. cipias: quo audito, agnatus ille renuntiat agro. Quæstio iidem coram senioribus Ecclesiæ hodie agitur, inter nos, & Pontificios, de Ecclesiæ possessione. Clamant Pontificii, possessionem illam ad se pertinere. Respondemus illis, si ius suum offendere velint, intelligant vna cum hac possessione, sponsam Christi se vindicare debere, sanctam, catholicam, sanctorum communionem. Quod si huic sponsæ renuntiant, profecto Ecclesiæ possessionem tenere non possunt. Nos igitur singulas istas notas Ecclesiæ examinabimus ordine. Prima Ecclesiæ proprietas est, vt sit sancta.
units.tr: A dispute once arose between Boaz and that kinsman of his, before the elders of the people, over whether he would redeem the field of Elimelech from them. That kinsman cried out that the right of redemption was his and said he would claim it. "Very well," said Boaz, "but that possession carries this condition attached: that together with the field you must also take Ruth the Moabitess as wife." On hearing this, the kinsman renounced the field. The same dispute is today being argued before the elders of the Church between us and the Papists over the possession of the Church. The Papists cry out that the possession belongs to them. We reply that if they wish to assert their right, they must understand that together with this possession they must also claim the bride of Christ, holy, catholic, and the communion of saints. But if they renounce this bride, they certainly cannot hold possession of the Church. Therefore we shall examine these individual marks of the Church in order. The first property of the Church is that it be holy.

units.la: CAPVT II
units.tr: CHAPTER II

units.la: Credo Ecclesiam sanctam.
units.tr: I believe the Church is holy.

units.la: Sanctam credimus Ecclesiam, cuius omnes sordes Christus suo sanguine abstersit: vt sanctificaret eam, & mundaret lavacro aquæ per verbum: vt sisteret eam sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam, aut rugam, aut quicquam huiusmodi, sed vt esset sancta & inculpata. Hæc autem sanctitas est à Capite in membra, vt membra omnia adolescant in eum, qui est caput, nempe Christus: ex quo totum corpus congruenter coagmentatum, per omnes commissuras, ex vi intus agente, pro mensura vnius cuiusque membri, incrementum capit corporis conueniens, ad ipsius ædificationem per charitatem.
units.tr: We believe the Church is holy, since Christ has washed away all her filth with his own blood, so that he might sanctify her and cleanse her with the washing of water by the word, and present her to himself as a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and blameless. This holiness flows from the Head into the members, so that all the members grow up into him who is the Head, namely Christ, from whom the whole body, fitted together and joined through every joint by the working of its inner power, according to the measure of each single member, receives its growth, building itself up in love.

units.la: Ex istorum locorum collatione facile con-stat, stat, Ecclesiam sanctam esse duobus modis. Primo imputatiue, deinde incboatiue. Imputatiue, cui sanctificatio Christi imputatur: atque hoc modo Christus sistit sibi gloriosam Ecclesiam, inculpatam, sine macula aut ruga, nempe imputatione sanctitatis ipsius, quæ vna est, & sola sine macula & ruga. Itaque docet Apostolus, Christum à Deo nobis factum sa-pientiam, iustitiam, sanctificationem, & redemptionem. Nam sapientia illa, atque illa iustitia, illa sanctificatio, quæ Deo placeat, & satisfaciat, perfecta est: nihil enim imperfectum Deo placere aut satisfacere potest. Nostra autem sapientia stultitia est, nempe sapientia car-nis, quæ inimica est Deo; Legi enim Dei non est subiecta, nec subiici potest. Nostra iustitia est quasi pannus menstruatæ. Vt igitur coram Deo nostro sistamur, sanctificemur oportet sanctificatione perfecta: quod quia nostra inhærente sanctitate fieri non potest; Idcirco ex Dei concilio & beneplacito, Christus factus est nobis à Deo sanctificatio. Hæc est illa perfecta nostra sanctificatio, sanctitas Christi nobis credentibus imputata. Deinde Ecclesia est etiam sancta inchoatiue, propter renoua-tionem, & novam obedientiam, quam Spiritus sanctus, qui datus est credentibus, operatur in ipsis, & quotidie auget per charitatem. Hoc est quod docet Apostolus, omnia Eccle-siæ membra incrementum accipere à Capite, ad ipsorum ædificationem per charitatem. Ecclesia ergo est corpus Christi: membra ve-
units.tr: From a comparison of these passages it is easy to establish that the Church is holy in two ways: first imputatively, and then inchoatively. Imputatively, the holiness of Christ is imputed to her, and in this way Christ presents to himself a glorious Church, blameless, without spot or wrinkle, namely by the imputation of his own holiness, which alone is one and sole, without spot or wrinkle. So the Apostle teaches that Christ was made by God our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption. For that wisdom, that righteousness and that sanctification which please God and satisfy him are perfect, since nothing imperfect can please or satisfy God. Our own wisdom, however, is foolishness, namely the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the law of God, nor can it be. Our righteousness is like a filthy rag. So if we are to stand before our God, we must be sanctified with a perfect sanctification; and since this cannot be done by the holiness inherent in us, therefore, by God's counsel and good pleasure, Christ was made sanctification for us by God. This is that perfect sanctification of ours, the holiness of Christ imputed to us who believe. Then the Church is also holy inchoatively, on account of the renewal and the new obedience which the Holy Spirit, who is given to believers, works in them and increases daily through love. This is what the Apostle teaches, that all the members of the Church receive growth from the Head, to build themselves up in love. The Church, therefore, is the body of Christ: the members

units.la: ꝓ Ecclesiæ[?], hoc est, membra huius corporis, cuius caput est Christus, accipiunt virtutem & sanctificationem à Capite, & in hoc corpore consistunt per charitatem. Sic nos docuit verbum Dei; vox sponsi, quæ nec fallit, nec sponsam fallere potest.
units.tr: [of the Church], that is, the members of this body whose Head is Christ, receive power and sanctification from the Head, and in this body they hold together through love. So the word of God has taught us; it is the voice of the Bridegroom, which neither deceives nor can deceive the bride.

units.la: Ex hoc initio statim exclusos ab initio videmus omnes Pontificios hodiernos, & suaquidem confessione exclusos. Nos sanctam Ecclesiam credimus: negant illi, hanc sanctitatem requiri in Ecclesia sua. Num igitur quicquam proferre possunt, quare non reiecti habeantur ab Ecclesia sancta, qui in Ecclesia, quam unam profitentur, sanctitatem non requiri contendunt? Neque vero nos hæc dicimus in eorum mores profanos, impudicos, sanguinarios, ne conuicium protulisse nos insimulent: quanquam hæc omnia sine conuitii suspicione, orbi iam valuerunt cõstent[?]. Verum ipsorum professionem doctrinamque proferimus. Publice enim hoc profitentur, habere se Ecclesiam, in cuius membris non requiritur sanctitas. Bellarminus, postquam docuit Ecclesiam esse cœtum hominum sub regimine Romani Pontificis: ad Capitis formam membra subiungit hoc modo: ut aliquis absolutè dicatur pars vera Ecclesiæ, non requiritur illa interna virtus, sed tantum externa professio fidei, & Sacramentorum communio, quæ sensu ipso percipitur. Videte, quomodo Bellarminus seiungat ac separet Ecclesiam illam, cuius caput est Romanus Pontifex.
units.tr: From this very beginning we see that all the Papists of today are excluded at the outset, and excluded by their own confession. We believe the Church is holy; they deny that this holiness is required in their Church. Can they therefore produce any reason why those who maintain that holiness is not required in the Church, which they alone profess to be one, should not be regarded as rejected from the holy Church? Nor do we say these things in order to attack their profane, shameless and bloodthirsty morals, lest they accuse us of abuse, although all these things have long been known to the world without any suspicion of abuse. Rather, we set forth their own profession and doctrine. For they openly profess that they have a Church in whose members holiness is not required. Bellarmine, after teaching that the Church is an assembly of men under the rule of the Roman Pontiff, adds to the form of the Head the members in this way: that someone may be called absolutely a true part of the Church, the inner virtue is not required, but only the external profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses themselves. See how Bellarmine separates and sets apart that Church whose head is the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: B[?] Chri[?] fursu[?] fursu[?] natu[?] sunt[?] clesia[?] Chri[?] bet c[?] sanc[?] Agni[?] Apo[?] quit[?] Pont[?] inqu[?] sanc[?] adhi[?] & m[?] mnil[?] temp[?] sex, ab illa Ecclesia, cuius caput est Christus. Necimmerito. Nam membra illius Ecclesiæ, cuius caput est Christus, sine interna virtute esse non possunt; quia membra huius Eccle-siæ incrementum capiunt à Capite, sicut & v-niuersum hoc corpus pro mensura vniuscu-iusque membri, incrementum capit corporis conueniens, ad ædificationem sui per charita-tem: quod docet Apostolus. Ac membra illius Ecclesiæ, cuius caput est Romanus Pontifex, possunt esse, sicut illud caput est, sine omni virtute interna.
units.tr: [Partly illegible in the scan.] ... from that Church whose Head is Christ. And not without reason. For the members of that Church whose Head is Christ cannot exist without inner virtue, because the members of this Church receive their growth from the Head, just as the whole body too receives its growth, according to the measure of each single member, to build itself up in love; this the Apostle teaches. But the members of that Church whose Head is the Roman Pontiff can exist, just as that head does, with no inner virtue at all.

units.la: Ecclesia Catholica dicitur sancta, & corpus Christi, & mater omnium nostrûm, & quæ sursum est Hierusalem, Gal. 4. 26[?]. Sed ea, quæ sursum est, Hierusalem, nihil habet coinquinatum, aut abominandum, sed qui scripti sunt in libro vitæ Agni, Apoc. 21. 27[?]. Ergo Ecclesia Catholica, quæ est sancta, quæ est corpus Christi, & mater omnium nostrûm, nihil habet coinquinatum, aut abominandum, sed sanctos tantum, & conscriptos in libro vitæ Agni. Huius syllogismi propositio est Pauli Apostoli: assumptio Iohannis Apostoli. Sequitur itaque, Ecclesiam Romanam, quæ Pontificiorum confessione multos habet coinquinatos, abominandos, reprobos, non esse sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam. Frustra hic adhibebitur distinctio, Ecclesiæ triumphantis, & militantis: nam Ecclesia vna est, vna in omnibus mundi partibus, vna in omnibus temporum successionibus, vna in cælo, & in terterris. Ecclesiæ status & conditio alia est in mi-litante parte, alia in triumphante: non autem alia Ecclesia, sed vna semper, & vbique. Nec est aliqua particularis Ecclesia, in terris militans; (sit modo vera Ecclesia) quæ non vnitatem hanc retineat[?] cum reliquo corpore. At qui nullam habent internam virtutem, non pos-sunt hanc vnitatem retinere cum reliquo Ec-clesiæ corpore.
units.tr: The Catholic Church is called holy, and the body of Christ, and the mother of us all, and the Jerusalem which is above (Gal. 4. 26). But that which is above, Jerusalem, has nothing defiled or abominable in it, but only those who are written in the book of life of the Lamb (Rev. 21. 27). Therefore the Catholic Church, which is holy, which is the body of Christ and the mother of us all, has nothing defiled or abominable in it, but only the saints, enrolled in the book of life of the Lamb. The major premise of this syllogism is the Apostle Paul's; the minor is the Apostle John's. It follows, then, that the Roman Church, which by the Papists' own confession has many defiled, abominable and reprobate members, is not the holy Catholic Church. The distinction between the Church triumphant and the Church militant will be brought in here in vain: for the Church is one, one in all parts of the world, one through all successions of times, one in heaven and on earth. The condition and state of the Church is different in the militant part and in the triumphant, but it is not a different Church; it is always and everywhere one. Nor is there any particular Church, militant on earth (provided it is a true Church), that does not retain this unity with the rest of the body. But those who have no inner virtue cannot retain this unity with the rest of the body of the Church.

units.la: Nam ad memoriam subinde revocandum est, nos hic Ecclesiam quærere Catholicam, matrem nostram. Ego vero nego, illam Eccle-siam esse matrem meam, quæ filios parit sine omni interna virtute. Mater mea est illa, quæ ex femine viri sui parit filios Deo: & fratres mei illi sunt, qui sanctificantur a fratre maio-re. Nam & qui sanctificat, & qui sanctifican-tur, ex uno sunt omnes. Quam ob causam non erubescit eos vocare fratres; dicens: An-nuntiabo nomen tuum fratribus meis, in me-dio Ecclesiæ tibi hymnos canam. Itaque Chri-stus Dominus dicit: Eorum causa ego sancti-fico me ipsum, ut sint & ipsi sanctificati in ve-ritate. Viderint ergo illi, in qua Ecclesia sint, qui non sunt fratres sanctificati, nec cohærent cum eo, qui sanctificat. Si quæramus Caput Ecclesiæ sanctæ, is est, quem Pater gloriæ se-dere fecit à dextra sua in cœlis, supra omnes principatus, & Potestates, & virtutes, & do-minationes, & super omne nomen, quod no-minatur non solum in hoc sæculo, sed & in su-turo, & omnia subiecit sub pedibus eius, cumq; eumq; super omnia dedit Caput Ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus, & complementum eius, qui omnia in omnibus complet. Sed quis est caput Ecclesiæ eius, cuius membra non sunt sancta? Certe quorum caput non est Christus, eorum caput Diabolum esse, vel Antichristum, necesse est. Eligant Pontificii, & agnoscant patrem ex istis duobus, quem velint, non enim subterfugere possunt. Sancti omnes & iustificati habent Christum pro capite, reliqui omnes Diabolum, ex Scripturarum Patrumque consensu: id est, ex Dei & Ecclesiæ sententia. Iam viderint isti, quænam sit illa Ecclesia, quæ non est Ecclesia Christi, sed Satanæ synagoga. Nam quis negare poterit, eam esse Satanæ synagogam, cuius membra non sanctificantur; quique Christum non habent pro capite. Clamat Bellarminus, in Ecclesiæ suæ membris non requiri internam virtutem & sanctitatem. Clamant Scripturæ Patresque: Qui non habent internam virtutem & sanctitatem à capite Christo, esse membra Diaboli. Num quis firmius aut evidentius probare poterit, Romanam hodiernam Ecclesiam esse Satanæ synagogam, quam faciunt isti, qui se Ecclesiæ quidem Romanæ membra esse iactant, ita tamen, ut illis liceat virtutibus eis renuntiare, per quas Ecclesia Christo capiti coniungitur?
units.tr: For it must be recalled from time to time that we are here seeking the Catholic Church, our mother. I, indeed, deny that that Church is my mother which bears children without any inner virtue. My mother is she who bears children to God from the seed of her husband, and those are my brothers who are sanctified by the greater Brother. For both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all of one. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: "I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing your praises" (Ps. 22. 22). So Christ the Lord says: "For their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth" (John 17. 19). Let those, then, see in what Church they are who are not sanctified brothers and do not cohere with him who sanctifies. If we seek the Head of the holy Church, it is he whom the Father of glory set at his right hand in the heavens, above all principalities, powers, virtues and dominions, and above every name that is named not only in this age but also in the age to come, and subjected all things under his feet, and gave him, as head over all things, to the Church, which is his body and the fullness of him who fills all in all. But who is the head of a Church whose members are not holy? Surely, those whose head is not Christ must necessarily have the devil, or Antichrist, as their head. Let the Papists choose, and acknowledge which of these two fathers they will have, for they cannot escape. All the saints and justified have Christ as their head; all the rest have the devil, by the agreement of Scripture and the Fathers, that is, by the judgment of God and the Church. Now let them see what that Church is which is not the Church of Christ but the synagogue of Satan. For who can deny that it is the synagogue of Satan, whose members are not sanctified and who do not have Christ as their head? Bellarmine cries out that inner virtue and holiness are not required in the members of his Church. Scripture and the Fathers cry out: those who do not have inner virtue and holiness from Christ the Head are members of the devil. Who could prove more firmly or more clearly that the present Roman Church is the synagogue of Satan than do those who boast that they are members of the Roman Church, yet in such a way that they are free to renounce those virtues by which the Church is joined to Christ the Head?

units.la: Hic mihi audire videor eorum murmura, qui me, velut iniecta manu revocant. Quid ergo? Num malos bonosque hic in Ecclesia permissos negas? Num zizania una cum tritico, non vis hic crescere? Ego vero illud liben-ter concedo. Zizania cum tritico in agro Dominico vna in hoc seculo crescere vsque ad tempus messis; bonos malosq; pisces simul in reticulo Dominico comprehensos: hoc est, in Ecclesia praesenti, bonos malosque simul colle&os permistosque; atq; ita permistos, vt nos lateant saepenumero. Hoc autem discrimen inter bonos malosq; diiudicare, non est meum. Mihi satis est, verbis Capitis mei admonito, vt patienter expectem vsque ad tempus messis. Itaque si mali, auari, raptores, foeneratores, aliíq; huiusmodi Ecclesiae praepo-nantur, modo sedeant[?] in cathedra Christi: quaecunq; agunt in Christi & Ecclesiae nomine, sine omni haesitatione suscipio: siue baptizauerint, siue ordinationem contulerint, siue quod aliud Ecclesiae munus peregerint: tam sunt apud me salua, & sana, quaecunq; hac au-toritate effecerint, ac si vel sanctissimi homines, vel ipsi Apostoli, vel Angeli de coelo eadem praestitissent: quia Ecclesiae instituta non à dignitate ministrorum, sed à Christo pendent. Haec omnia, sicut apud Ecclesiam firmata constant, ita sine controuersia suscipimus.
units.tr: Here I seem to hear the murmurs of those who, as if a hand had been laid on me, call me back. What then? Do you deny that good and bad are both tolerated in the Church here? Do you not want tares to grow here along with the wheat? I readily concede that. Tares and wheat grow together in the Lord's field until the harvest, and good and bad fish are caught together in the Lord's net. That is, in the present Church the good and the bad are gathered and mixed together, and so mixed that they often escape our notice. But it is not my task to distinguish between the good and the bad. It is enough for me, mindful of the words of my Head, to wait patiently until the time of harvest. Accordingly, if bad men, greedy men, robbers, usurers and others of that kind are set over the Church, provided they sit in the chair of Christ, I accept without any hesitation whatever they do in the name of Christ and the Church. Whether they baptize, or confer ordination, or perform any other office of the Church, I hold it as sound and valid, just as if the most holy men, or the Apostles themselves, or angels from heaven had done the same. For the institutions of the Church depend not on the dignity of the ministers but on Christ. All these things, as they stand established in the Church, we accept without controversy.

units.la: Sed attendite quaeso, in quo huius disputationis controuersia consistat. Contendimus hic de Ecclesiae Catholicae membris. Pontificii docent, Ecclesiam Catholicam vnam esse, nō duas, non plures. Huius autem vnius Ecclesiae Catholicae membra esse clamitant, impios sine fide, sine charitate: nam aliter nullum sibi in Ecclepen- Do- e ad ul in e est, imul os,vt fcri- n est iad- em- fœ- po- siti: omi- npti- fiue tam au- omi- ea- non pen- ma- us. uta- mus ficii nó esiæ sine i in cleEcclesia locum relictum verentur. Nos pen- tus negamus, impios & profanos homines esse membra Ecclesiæ huius, quę una est, & sancta, & corpus Christi, & catholica. Non negamus, malos esse permissos in Ecclesia, sed Ecclesiæ huius partes aut membra esse negamus: quia Ecclesia est sancta, & corpus Christi, & comple- mentum eius, qui omnia in omnibus complet. Sunt in Ecclesia, non vt membra, aut partes in corpore, sed vt palea in frumento, vt zizania in tritico. Atq; de hac re prouocabimus ad o- mnes Patres, imo ad omnes Scriptores Eccle- siasticos, qui ante annum Christi millesimum scripserunt, nec vnum excipiemus. Quicunq; enim de hac re disputant, non aliter docent. Atq; vt de Pontificiorum sententia in hac re certi simus: Bellarminus pluribus verbis hoc agit, lib 3. de Eccles. militante, cap. 2. reprehe- dit Confessionistas, & Philippum, & Brentium, reliquosque: quod malos docent non esse partes veræ Ecclesiæ. Et proinde, inquit Bel- larminus, caute Philippus nō dicit, Ecclesiam constare ex bonis malisque: sed dicit, malos admisceri Ecclesiæ: & Brentius dicit, malos esse aliquo modo in Ecclesia, sed non de Ec- clesia. Hæc Bellarminus. Atq; hoc eos nomi- nè reprehendit. Deinde docet, malos esse Ec- clesiæ partes. Credimus igitur Ecclesiam esse sanctam. Num hoc negant Pontificii? Certe de Ecclesia sua in[?] disputant, quasi non de san- cta Ecclesia Dei, sed de profano impiorum cœ[?]u[?] loquerentur.
units.tr: But please pay attention to where the controversy of this dispute lies. We are contending here about the members of the Catholic Church. The Papists teach that the Catholic Church is one, not two and not many. They insist that the members of this one Catholic Church are impious men without faith and without charity; for otherwise, they fear, no place would be left for them in the Church. We, on the contrary, utterly deny that impious and profane men are members of this Church, which is one, and holy, and the body of Christ, and catholic. We do not deny that bad men are tolerated in the Church, but we deny that they are parts or members of this Church, because the Church is holy, and the body of Christ, and the fullness of him who fills all things in all. They are in the Church not as members or parts of the body, but as chaff is in the wheat, as tares are in the wheat. And on this matter we appeal to all the Fathers, indeed to all the ecclesiastical writers who wrote before the year of Christ one thousand, and we will except not one. For whoever discusses this question teaches nothing different. And so that we may be certain of the Papists' opinion on this point: Bellarmine treats this at length in book 3 of On the Militant Church, chapter 2. He rebukes the Confessionists, Philip, Brenz and the rest, because they teach that the bad are not parts of the true Church. And therefore, says Bellarmine, Philip cautiously does not say that the Church consists of good and bad, but says that bad men are mixed into the Church; and Brenz says that the bad are in the Church in some way, but not of the Church. So says Bellarmine, and he rebukes them by name for this. Then he teaches that the bad are parts of the Church. We therefore believe the Church to be holy. Do the Papists deny this? Certainly they dispute about their own Church as if they were speaking not of the holy Church of God but of a profane assembly of the impious.

units.la: Imo, inquiunt, Ecclesia nostra sancta est. Audiamus ergo. Nam si vel professionem eo-rum saltem audiremus, aliquid viderentur vel praestitisse, vel tentasse ad hanc invidiam amoliendam: sed ita alte in hac re dormitant, ut cauere videantur, ne nos existimemus, vitae sancti-moniam quicquam ab iis citari. Bel-larminus enim, quum Sanctitatem Ecclesiae notam[?] posuisset, ita ut omnium exspectationem excitasse videretur, aliquid certe hoc lo-co de Ecclesiae sanctitate dicturum eum; sic e-labitur; {a}Octaua nota, inquit, est sanctitas doctrinae. Vera enim Ecclesia non solum est Catholica, sed etiam sancta, ut habet Symbo-lum Constantinopolitanum.
