Constat autem, sanctam dici Ecclesiam, quia professio eius sancta est, nihil continens falsum quoad fidei doctrinam, nihil iniustum, quoad doctrinam morum. Haec ille. Quae verba admiratione digna videbantur: videmus enim, vitae sancti-moniam, ut rem inutilem, nihil ad Ecclesiam pertinentem, plane repudiatam. Constat, in-quit, sanctam dici Ecclesiam, propter doctri-nae sanctitatem. Quomodo hoc constat? Ex qua traditione? Certe apud antiquos Patres constat, Ecclesiam non aliter sanctam dici, quam qua ratione vnumquodque Ecclesiae membrum sanctum dicitur. {b}Sancti omnes sunt, inquit Chrysostomus, qui fidem rectam sanctitari vitae communitatem habent, etsi signa non faciant illi, neq; ejiciant daemonia, sancti sunt. {c}Sancti sunt, inquit Augustinus, qui in terra viuen-tium rium spem suam posuerunt ciues Hierusalem cœlestis, quorum conuersatio spiritalis per ancboram spei in illa patria figitur, quæ recte Dei terra nominatur, quamuis adhuc & in hac [?] terra carne versentur.
units.tr: Indeed, they say, our Church is holy. Let us hear it, then. For if we heard at least their profession on this point, they might seem to have done or attempted something to remove this odium. But they slumber so deeply on this matter that they appear to take care lest we should think any holiness of life is claimed by them. For Bellarmine, when he had set down the holiness of the Church as a mark, so that he seemed to have aroused the expectation of everyone, that he would certainly say something on the holiness of the Church at this point, slips away thus: "The eighth mark," he says, "is holiness of doctrine. For the true Church is not only catholic but also holy, as the Constantinopolitan Creed has it. Now it is established that the Church is called holy because her profession is holy, containing nothing false as to the doctrine of faith, nothing unjust as to the doctrine of morals." So he says. These words seemed worthy of wonder, for we see that holiness of life, as something useless and having nothing to do with the Church, is plainly rejected. "It is established," he says, "that the Church is called holy on account of the holiness of doctrine." How is this established? From what tradition? Certainly among the ancient Fathers it is established that the Church is not called holy in any other way than that in which each member of the Church is called holy. "All are holy," says Chrysostom, "who have right faith and fellowship in a holy life, even if they do not work signs, nor cast out demons; they are holy." "They are holy," says Augustine, "who have placed their hope in the land of the living, the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose spiritual conversation is fixed by the anchor of hope in that homeland, which is rightly called the land of God, although they still dwell in this earthly land in the flesh."

units.la: Quibus verbis probat, membra omnia Ecclesiæ militantis, dum in carne versantur, esse ciues cœlestis Hierusalem. Plura non profero, quia non est necesse. Quis enim ante Iesuitas, fraterculosque natos, sanctitatem vitæ ab Ecclesia & Ecclesiæ membris reiecit? Deinde: Sancta, inquit, est Ecclesia, sicut habet Symbolum Constantinopolitanum. Nonne quis miretur, quod Symbolum Constantinopolitanum adducat, quum idem habeatur in Symbolo Apostolico? nisi quod sacræ literæ, & Symbolum Apostolicum iamdudum sordere cœpissent Pontificiis. Sed illud maxime admiratione dignum videtur, quod, quum Ecclesiæ sanctitas quærenda proponitur, doctrinæ sanctitas concluditur. Ecclesiæ proprietas est, ut sit sancta. Quæro ex te, Domine Cardinalis, estne Ecclesia illa sancta, cuius caput est Papa, cuius tu es illustrissimum membrum? sanctáne est Ecclesia? Quo fugis? quid tergiuersaris? Dic aliquid certum. Doctrina, inquit, est sancta. Quum de Ecclesiæ sanctitate quæsierit, & respondeat de sanctitate doctrinæ, nonne profitetur, se nihi habere, quod de vita sanctitate proferat? At quum Ecclesia sancta dicitur, non doctrinæ puritas, sicut hic nugatur, sed vitæ nouitas demonstratur. Videmus interea, quales nobis circulos faciunt
units.tr: By these words he proves that all the members of the militant Church, while they dwell in the flesh, are citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem. I bring forward no more, because there is no need. For who before the Jesuits and their little friars ever banished holiness of life from the Church and from the members of the Church? Next: "The Church is holy," he says, "as the Constantinopolitan Creed has it." Would not anyone wonder why he cites the Constantinopolitan Creed, since the same is found in the Apostles' Creed? Unless the Holy Scriptures and the Apostles' Creed had already begun to be despised by the Papists. But this seems most worthy of wonder: that when the holiness of the Church is what is being sought, the conclusion is holiness of doctrine. Holiness is a property of the Church, that she be holy. I ask you, Lord Cardinal, is that Church holy whose head is the Pope, and of which you are the most illustrious member? Is the Church holy? Where are you fleeing? Why do you dodge? Say something definite. "Doctrine," he says, "is holy." Since he has asked about the holiness of the Church and answers with the holiness of doctrine, does he not confess that he has nothing to offer about holiness of life? Yet when the Church is called holy, what is shown is not the purity of doctrine, as he trifles here, but the newness of life.

units.la: circulatores isti. Quum enim de doctrina impugnantur, ad Ecclesiam confugere solent. At quum de Ecclesiae sanctimonia contenditur, ad doctrinae sanctitatem se conferunt. Quid enim facere possunt, qui spem nullam certam habere se demonstrant? de meritis gloriantur: de vitae autem sanctimonia ne cogitant quidem.
units.tr: Meanwhile we see what sort of circles these tricksters run in. When they are attacked on doctrine, they are accustomed to take refuge in the Church. But when the holiness of the Church is contended about, they betake themselves to the holiness of doctrine. For what can those do who show that they have no certain hope? They boast of merits, but of the holiness of life they do not even think.

units.la: Ad eandem carnalis suae nuditatis confessionem, imo confusionem pertinet, quod in decima nota dicit: {a} Decima, inquit, nota est, sanctitas vitae autorum, sive primorum Patrum nostrae religionis. Inter hos autores numerat ordinum religiosorum Institutores, Dominicum & Franciscum. Miseram Ecclesiam narrat, quae sanctitatem suam mutuat, non a sancto sanctorum, sed a sanctulis, nescio, quibus, Dominico & Francisco. Hanc igitur sanctimoniae notam, vel ad Romani Pontificis res gerendas incommodam, vel ad fratercu-loruin[?] ministeria inutilem, vel, vt rem, carnis viribus, & mundi sapientia, qua regitur Romana Curia, maiorem: ab Ecclesia sua, ac proinde se ab Ecclesia sancta reiiciunt.
units.tr: To the same admission, or rather confession of their carnal nakedness, belongs what he says in the tenth mark: "The tenth mark," he says, "is the holiness of life of the authors, or of the first Fathers of our religion." Among these authors he counts the founders of the religious orders, Dominic and Francis. He describes a wretched Church which borrows its holiness not from the Holy of Holies but from little saints, I know not whom, Dominic and Francis. This mark of holiness, therefore, either inconvenient for the conduct of the affairs of the Roman Pontiff, or useless for the ministries of the little friars, or, to put it another way, greater by the strength of the flesh and the wisdom of the world by which the Roman Curia is governed, they cast off from their Church, and so separate themselves from the holy Church.

units.la: At alibi {b}etiam sanctam docet Ecclesiam dici propter tria. Primum, propter baptisma, quod sanctum esse, nemo negare potest. Secundo, propter professionem Christianam. Tertio, propter vnionem membrorum inter se, & cum Capite, saltem externam. Hæcille.
units.tr: But elsewhere he teaches that the Church is also called holy for three reasons. First, because of baptism, which no one can deny is holy. Second, because of the Christian profession. Third, because of the union of the members with one another and with the Head, at least an external union. So far he.

units.la: Respondeo, primum & secundum nihil esse ad se ad rem : Quæstionem non esse de Sacra-mentis, & professione, de quarum rerum san-ctitate non dubitamus, sed de membris Eccle-siæ. Quod autem tertio loco refert, de unione membrorum inter se, & cum capite ; hic rem tenet; sed addit, unionem hanc esse ex-ternam : quibus verbis omnia conturbat. Nam in unione externa, Papam intelligit Ca-put: in cuius capitis membris, ipse Bellarmi-nus docet, sanctitatem non esse quærendam. Quod igitur de sanctitate membrorum dixerat, sub hoc Capite, inanis est sine re verborum fo-nitus; merę nugę. Sed addit ibidē, Ecclesiam etiam sanctam dici posse, quia caput eius est Christus, sanctus sanctorum. Hic randem[?] ali-quando profert, quod res est: inuitus quo-dammodo, & reluctans, quasi Cerberus ad lu-cem, ad hæc verba protrahitur. At hæc verba uno velut ictu iugulant causam Pontificiam: quia Christus est sanctus sanctorum, ideoque Caput Ecclesiæ. Hæc verba numero pau-cissima (Sanctus sanctorum) admirabili ne-xu coniungunt caput, & membra Ecclesiæ. Christus igitur habet suos sanctos, quos sanctificat ; Sancti habent suum Christum, à quo vitam & sanctitatem accipiunt. Hic sanctus, & illi sancti : sed hic sanctus sanctorum, illi sancti sanctificati : hic sanctum caput, illi sancta Ecclesia, sancta membra : hic sanctus, qui sanctitate membris suis largitur; illi sancti, qui sanctitatem suam ab eo omnem mutuan-tur, qui propter ipsos sanctificauit seipsum. Christus ergo est sanctus sanctorum. At qui fatetur, Christum Ecclesiæ suæ caput, esse sanctum sanctorum: quomodo is dicere potuit, in membris huius sancti Capitis sanctitatem non esse quærendam? Imo vero, quia Christus, qua caput est Ecclesiæ suæ est sanctus sanctorum; sequitur non esse membra huius capitis, qui non sunt sancti. Christus igitur non est caput eorum, qui nullam habent internam virtutem.
units.tr: I answer that the first and second reasons have nothing to do with the question. The question is not about the sacraments or the profession, whose holiness we do not doubt, but about the members of the Church. As for the third reason, the union of the members with one another and with the Head, here he hits the mark, but he adds that this union is external, and by these words he overturns everything. For by the external union he means the Pope as Head, and Bellarmine himself teaches that holiness is not to be sought in the members of this Head. So what he had said about the holiness of the members under this Head is an empty sound of words, mere trifling. But he adds there that the Church can also be called holy because its Head is Christ, the Holy One of holies. Here at last, somewhat unwillingly and reluctantly, he is dragged out, like Cerberus into the light, and states what is the truth. Yet these words cut the throat of the Papist cause at one blow, because Christ is the Holy One of holies and therefore the Head of the Church. These few words, "the Holy One of holies," join the Head and the members of the Church in a wonderful bond. Christ therefore has his holy ones, whom he sanctifies; the saints have their Christ, from whom they receive life and holiness. Here is the Holy One, and there the saints: but he is the Holy One of holies, they are the saints made holy; he is the holy Head, they are the holy Church and holy members; he is the Holy One who bestows holiness on his members, they are the saints who borrow all their holiness from him who sanctified himself for their sake. Christ, then, is the Holy One of holies. But whoever confesses that Christ is the Head of his Church and the Holy One of holies, how could he say that holiness is not to be sought in the members of this holy Head? Indeed, because Christ, as Head of his Church, is the Holy One of holies, it follows that those who are not holy are not members of this Head. Christ, therefore, is not the Head of those who have no inward virtue.

units.la: Deinde unde est Ecclesia vocata? De mundo. Mundus autem quid est, nisi mali in mundo, in quibus nulla est interna virtus. Ecclesia igitur vocata est ex illis, in quibus nulla est interna virtus, ut iidem illi homines ex regno Satanæ in regnum Christi, & sortem sanctorum ducantur. Cardinalis autem in sanctis rebus tractandis, & cum sanctis ludere voluit. Mediam enim viam quærit, antea incognitam, qua Christum & Belial coniungat, lucem cum tenebris, fideles cum infidelibus societatis & concordiæ vinculo colliget. Nam & Ecclesiam retinere voluit, nec tamen mundum dimittere, ex quo vocata est Ecclesia. At Christus de Ecclesia sua, quæ est & regnum ipsius, sic respondet: Regnum meum non est ex hoc mundo. Ecclesia Christi, est regnum Christi: non est autem ex hoc mundo, id est, non consistit ex malis illis, in quibus nulla est interna virtus. Ita ut si verba hæc resoluas interpretando in suum proprium sensum: quid aliud volunt, quam ut dicat aliis verbis: Ecclesia mea non consistit ex hominibus, qui sunt c[?]-[?]mnino huius mundi, in quibus nulla est inter-na virtus? Nam alioqui regnum Christi est in hoc mundo, id est, viuit, & versatur in hoc mundo, & inter malosistos tempore militiæ suæ; quia Dominus dicit: Non rogo, ut tol-las eos de mundo, sed ut serues eos à Malo. Ecclesia igitur per orationem Christi seruatur à Malo. Atqui[?], in quibus nulla est interna virtus, non seruantur à malo: non sunt igitur Ecclesia Christi, aut Ecclesiæ huius membra. Nam Ecclesiæ huius membra seruantur à Malo, & Spiritu Dei reguntur. Sic enim docet Apostolus: Qui Spiritum Christi non ha-bet, hic non est eius. Membrum igitur Christi esse non potest, qui nullam habet virtutem internam. Apostolus etiam in eandem sententiam alibi docet: In vno Spiritu nos omnes in vnum corpus baptizati sumus. Est ergo Spiritus Christi, qui nos in hoc Ecclesiæ corpus incorporauit: ac proinde, qui Spiritum Christi non habent, in quo statu sunt omnes illi, in quibus nulla est interna virtus, Christi membra esse non possunt.
units.tr: Next, from where has the Church been called? From the world. But what is the world, except the wicked in the world, among whom there is no inward virtue? The Church, therefore, has been called out of those in whom there is no inward virtue, so that these same men might be led from the kingdom of Satan into the kingdom of Christ and the lot of the saints. But the Cardinal, in handling holy matters, wished to play with holy things. For he seeks a middle way, hitherto unknown, by which he may join Christ and Belial, light with darkness, and gather the faithful and the unbelievers into a bond of fellowship and concord. For he wished to keep the Church, yet not to leave the world from which the Church was called. But Christ, speaking of his Church, which is also his kingdom, answers thus: "My kingdom is not of this world." The Church of Christ is the kingdom of Christ; it is not, however, of this world, that is, it does not consist of those wicked people in whom there is no inward virtue. So if you unfold these words by interpreting them in their own proper sense, what else do they mean than that he says in other words: "My Church does not consist of men who are altogether of this world, in whom there is no inward virtue"? For otherwise the kingdom of Christ is in this world, that is, it lives and moves in this world, and during the time of its warfare it dwells among the wicked; for the Lord says: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the Evil One." The Church, therefore, is kept from the Evil One through the prayer of Christ. But those in whom there is no inward virtue are not kept from evil; they are not, therefore, the Church of Christ, or members of this Church. For the members of this Church are kept from evil and are ruled by the Spirit of God. So the Apostle teaches: "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his." Therefore one who has no inward virtue cannot be a member of Christ. The Apostle teaches the same sentiment elsewhere: "In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body." It is therefore the Spirit of Christ who incorporated us into this body of the Church; and consequently those who do not have the Spirit of Christ, in which state are all those in whom there is no inward virtue, cannot be members of Christ.

units.la: Ante Bellarminum, qui scripserunt Pontificii, communiter concedere solebant (istis forte atque huiusmodi rationibus permoti) impios homines, qui nullam haberent internam virtutem, non fuisse membra Ecclesiæ, nisi æquiuoce. Quæ sententia certe catholica est. Qui autem docuerunt, homines malos non esse Ecclesiæ membra, nisi æquiuoce, de-
units.tr: Before Bellarmine, the Papists who wrote were accustomed to concede in common (perhaps moved by such arguments as these) that impious men who had no inward virtue were not members of the Church, except equivocally. That opinion is certainly Catholic. Those, however, who taught that wicked men are not members of the Church except equivocally, denied

units.la: mitionem membri istis competere posse nega-bant. Improbi igitur Cardinalis audacia de-prehenditur, qui contra communem Ecclesiæ sententiam, definitionem membri Ecclesiæ mutare ausus fuit. Hanc autem prius fuisse communem Ecclesiæ sententiam, fatetur Bel-larminus his verbis: A multis solet con-cedi, malos non esse membra vera, nec sim-pliciter corporis Ecclesiæ, sed tantum secun-dum quid, & æquiuoce. Ita Iohannes de Tur-recremata, lib. 1. cap. 57. vbi id probat ex Ale-xandro de Hales, Hugone, & B. Thoma. Idem docent Petrus à Soto, & Melchior Canus, & alii: qui tamen, etsi dicant, malos non esse membra vera, dicunt nihilominus, vere esse in Ecclesia, siue in Corpore Ecclesiæ. Neq; enim sola membra sunt in corpore, sed etiam hu-mores, dentes, pili, & alia, quæ non sunt mem-bra. Hæc ille. Hanc igitur fuisse antiquorum sententiam, fatetur Bellarminus. Itaque de membris Ecclesiæ sententia nostra est, quam Bellarminus ante ipsum, communem fuisse Ecclesiæ sententiam concedit. Quare igitur Dominus Cardinalis non sequitur hanc sen-tentiam, quam Ecclesia communiter ante ipsum sequuta est? Quia scilicet Tridentina sapientia antiquam Ecclesiæ sapientiam con-temnit, & noua quotidie monstra ex Satanæ profunditatibus exorientia colligit, & am-plectitur. Operæ pretium videtur, obseruare rationem illam, qua permotus Cardinalis, an-tiquam Ecclesiæ doctrinam, de membris Ec-clesiæ clesiæ ecclesiæ communicant. Nam postquam antiquorum sententiam retulisset, contra eam sic disputat:{a} At si ita esset, sequitur, Pontificem malum non esse caput Ecclesiæ, & alios Episcopos, si mali sint, non esse Capita Ecclesiarum suarum. Hæc ille. Deinde respondet, malum doctorem esse membrum mortuum, & proinde non verum, quantum attinet ad rationem membri, tamen esse verum membrum, ratione instrumenti. Quibus verbis tacita confessio contineri videtur, si quidem non tantum consensu Ecclesiæ, sed & ratione omnino victum, pertinacem tamen in opinione, nec Ecclesiæ consensui, nec rationibus cessurum. Nam qui dicit, malum hominem sine interna virtute non esse membrum Ecclesiæ, ratione membri, sed tantum ratione instrumenti: dicit, non esse membrum, sed instrumentum: quod neminem existimo negare. Membrum mortuum, non est membrum, nisi æquivoce. Malum doctorem esse membrum mortuum concedit; definitio igitur membri in eum competere nullo modo potest. At quod membrum non est, potest esse instrumentum: quis negat? Ergo nugacissimus deprehenditur Cardinalis, qui post longam disputationem de membris Ecclesiæ; quæ definiuerat esse membra, tandem aliquando veritate victus, concludit, non esse membra, sed instrumenta.
units.tr: that the definition of a member could apply to them. So the audacity of the wicked Cardinal is exposed, for against the common opinion of the Church he dared to change the definition of a member of the Church. That this was formerly the common opinion of the Church, Bellarmine confesses in these words: "It is often conceded by many that the wicked are not true members, nor simply members of the body of the Church, but only in a certain respect and equivocally. So John of Turrecremata, book 1, chapter 57, where he proves it from Alexander of Hales, Hugh, and Blessed Thomas. Peter à Soto and Melchior Canus teach the same, and others, who nevertheless, although they say the wicked are not true members, say nonetheless that they are truly in the Church, or in the body of the Church. For not only members are in the body, but also humours, teeth, hairs, and other things which are not members." So far he. Bellarmine therefore confesses that this was the opinion of the ancients. Our view about the members of the Church is, then, the one which Bellarmine himself concedes was the common opinion of the Church before him. Why, then, does the Lord Cardinal not follow this opinion, which the Church commonly followed before him? Because, plainly, Tridentine wisdom despises the ancient wisdom of the Church, and gathers up and embraces new monsters rising daily from the depths of Satan. It seems worth while to observe the reasoning by which the Cardinal, moved to abandon the ancient doctrine of the Church concerning the members of the Church, set himself against it. For after he had related the opinion of the ancients, he argues against it thus: "But if it were so, it would follow that the Pope, if he is wicked, is not the head of the Church, and other bishops, if they are wicked, are not heads of their churches." So far he. Then he replies that a wicked teacher is a dead member, and therefore, as far as the nature of a member goes, is not a true member, yet is a true member by reason of an instrument. In these words a tacit confession seems to be contained: he is conquered not only by the consent of the Church but also by reason, yet remains obstinate in his opinion, yielding neither to the consent of the Church nor to arguments. For whoever says that a wicked man without inward virtue is not a member of the Church by the reason of a member, but only by the reason of an instrument, says that he is not a member but an instrument; and I think no one would deny this. A dead member is not a member except equivocally. He concedes that a wicked teacher is a dead member; therefore the definition of a member cannot apply to him in any way. But that which is not a member can be an instrument: who denies it? So the Cardinal is shown to be most trifling, who, after a long disputation about the members of the Church, having defined them as members, at last, overcome by the truth, concludes that they are not members but instruments.

units.la: Nec valet Bellarmini ratio, quod malus doctor propterea Ecclesiæ membrum sit; quia ratione instrumenti potest esse vtilis ad Ecclesiæ ædiædificationem. Nam ad membrum Ecclesiæ constituendum, requiritur charitas, sine qua non possunt consistere in hoc corpore, nec adolescere in eum, qui est caput, nempe Christus; nec incrementum capere corpori conueniens, ad ædificationem sui per charitatem. Quæ quidem omnia in Ecclesiæ membris necessaria esse, docet Apostolus. At qui non est membrum Ecclesiæ, potest esse vtilis ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem; sicut qui malus est vir, potest esse vtilis architectus; sicut mali illi architecti, qui arcam Noë ædificarunt, etiamsi vera fide Deo non seruiebant, vtiles tamen ad arcam construendam fuerunt. Et sicut in veteri Testamento Prophetica reuelatio nonnunquam malis hominibus à Deo concessa fuerat, quemadmodum Prophetæ illi seni, qui habitabat in Bethel; atque etiam Balaamo.
units.tr: Nor does Bellarmine's argument hold, that a bad teacher is for that reason a member of the Church, because in the manner of an instrument he can be useful for building up the Church. For to constitute a member of the Church, charity is required, without which men cannot remain in this body, nor grow into him who is the head, namely Christ, nor receive an increase fitting for the body, for its edification through charity. The Apostle teaches that all these things are necessary in the members of the Church. But one who is not a member of the Church can be useful for the building up of the Church, just as a wicked man can be a useful architect; as those wicked builders who constructed Noah's ark, although they did not serve God in true faith, were nevertheless useful for building the ark. And just as in the Old Testament prophetic revelation was sometimes granted by God to wicked men, as to that old prophet who dwelt in Bethel, and also to Balaam.

units.la: Prophetia enim, inquit {a}Nicolaus Lyra, respicit actum intelligendi; charitas autem, quæ facit hominem bonum, est actus voluntatis; prius potest esse sine posteriori, & ideo reuelatio Prophetica potest esse sine charitate: ita etiam in Ecclesia mali homines per doctrinam & intelligentiam possunt esse vtiles ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem, qui tamen Ecclesiæ membra non sunt. Nam administratio Ecclesiæ vel est interna per Spiritum, vel externa per disciplinam. Per internam administrationem fiunt homines filii Dei, & membra Ecclesiæ. At hoc non fit per externam administrationem in disciplina. Quanquam enim externa administratio ad internam referatur, tanquam ad suum finem: tamen mali homines, auari, superbi, ambitiosi, qui Spiritu Dei non regun-tur, subsistunt hic, & omnino commorantur in externa administratione, nec ad internam attingunt. Ea autem, quæ mali faciunt in ex-terna administratione, prorsus nihil differunt ab iis, quæ in externa administratione boni & fideles faciunt: quia sancti in externa admi-nistratione nihil plus conferre possunt, quam mali homines in eadem administratione: faciunt utrique, quod servi facere possunt: reliqua ex interna Spiritus administratione pen-dent.
units.tr: For prophecy, says Nicolaus Lyra, relates to the act of understanding; but charity, which makes a man good, is an act of the will; the former can exist without the latter, and therefore prophetic revelation can exist without charity. So also in the Church, wicked men through teaching and understanding can be useful for the building up of the Church, and yet they are not members of the Church. For the administration of the Church is either internal, through the Spirit, or external, through discipline. Through the internal administration men become sons of God and members of the Church. But this does not happen through the external administration in discipline. For although the external administration is referred to the internal as to its end, yet wicked men, the covetous, the proud, the ambitious, who are not governed by the Spirit of God, remain here and altogether dwell in the external administration, and do not reach the internal. Moreover, the things that the wicked do in the external administration differ in no way at all from those things that good and faithful men do in the external administration; for the saints can contribute nothing more in the external administration than wicked men can in the same administration: both do what servants can do; the rest depends on the internal administration of the Spirit.

units.la: Itaque sicut in Regni terreni admini-stratione non tantum Regum filii, sed & famuli in regimine statuuntur: ita fit in Eccle-sia, vt non tantum filii Dei ad externam admi-nistrationem vocentur, sed & servi nonnun-quam impii. Externa autem administratio non facit aliquem membrum Ecclesiæ, sed interna, qua membra cohærent cum Capite, ad ædificationem sui per charitatem.
units.tr: Therefore, just as in the administration of an earthly kingdom not only the sons of kings but also servants are placed in government, so it happens in the Church that not only the sons of God are called to external administration, but sometimes also ungodly servants. External administration, however, does not make anyone a member of the Church; the internal does, by which the members cohere with the Head, for their edification through charity.

units.la: Colligimus iam, quæ hactenus disputaui-mus. Ecclesiæ verè genuina proprietas est, vt sit sancta: Ecclesia nunc Romana, non est sancta: Ergo Ecclesia illa non est vera Ecclesia. Ecclesiam autem nunc Romanam, non ef-se sanctam, probant ipsi Pontificii, qui in membris huius Ecclesiæ nullam internam virtutem quærendam docent. Quæ quidem execranda sententia à fraterculis primum inuecta, à Tridentinis nuper publice promul-gata, gata, murat Ecclesiam sanctam, in Ecclesiam sceleratam. Si enim ideo sancta dicitur tantummodo, quia una pars eius est sancta: certè idcirco etiam sceleratà dici potest, quia una pars, imo & maior pars sceleratà esset. Nec valet responsio, denominationem fieri à meliori parte: quia nulla ratio reddi potest, quare maiór pars, quæ sæpenumero vincit & dominatur, non etiam aliquando denominet, seu homen tribuat. Restat nunc, ut de sanctitate membrorum Ecclesiæ antiquorum Patrum testimonia referamus.
units.tr: We now gather what we have argued so far. It is the true and genuine property of the Church that it be holy: the Church now at Rome is not holy: therefore that Church is not the true Church. That the Church now at Rome is not holy, the Papists themselves prove, since they teach that no internal virtue is to be sought in the members of this Church. This execrable opinion, first brought in by the little friars and lately published openly by the Tridentines, walls in the holy Church and turns it into a wicked Church. For if it is called holy only because one part of it is holy, then certainly it can also be called wicked, because one part, indeed even the greater part, would be wicked. Nor does the reply hold, that the denomination is taken from the better part: for no reason can be given why the greater part, which very often prevails and rules, should not sometimes also give the name, or lend its character. It remains now that we set out the testimonies of the ancient Fathers concerning the holiness of the members of the Church.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Continet Patrum testimonia, demonstran-tia, Ecclesiæ membra non esse alios, nisi sanctos.
units.tr: Containing the testimonies of the Fathers, showing that the members of the Church are none but the holy.

units.la: DE Theologorum sententia habemus Cardinalis confessionem, sicut superius observauimus, Alexandrum de Hales, Thomam Aquinatem, aliosque docuisse, malos non esse membra Ecclesiæ. Hoc loco antiquorum Patrum sententiam de hac re proferemus.
units.tr: Concerning the opinion of the theologians, we have the Cardinal's own confession, as we noted above: Alexander of Hales, Thomas Aquinas and others have taught that the wicked are not members of the Church. Here we shall set out the view of the ancient Fathers on this matter.

units.la: Origenes sic docet: {a}Ipsi, qui non habent maculam, aut rugam, aut aliquid huiusmodi, sunt vera Ecclesia. Atque alibi: {b}Ecclesia sancta & immaculata dicitur; non quod à principio immaculata fuerit; hoc enim [illegible, ~3 letters] ab homine non potest, quia: sed quod repa[illegible, ~8 letters] sincera. Hæc ille. Ira[?] Ecclesiæ sanctitatem à sancto Capite mutuatam, atq; imputatam, docuit Origenes.
units.tr: Origen teaches as follows: {a}Those who have no spot, or wrinkle, or anything of the kind, are the true Church. And elsewhere: {b}The Church is called holy and spotless; not because it was spotless from the beginning, for this cannot be true of any man, but because it is made sincere by repentance. So he says. Thus Origen taught that the holiness of the Church is derived and imputed from its holy Head.

units.la: Bas[illegible, ~2 letters] Ba lumba benefa hædus; Ch non su & fi dinem Quippe gneum corpus rugam phyla Re locum esse in ut sin Card non i sub fo Card butie quon gues rum dicit rat. esse v Eccl go, ba it ceret
units.tr: Basil, the dove, the one and perfect... The Church is the body without spot or wrinkle; the Cardinal says that it is not necessary that the wicked be in the Church, and that the Church has no need of them... (The Latin of this unit is too garbled in the scan to be recovered with certainty; its sense is the same as the passages of Basil and Chrysostom quoted below.)

units.la: Basilius: a Ecclesia, inquit, vna, perfecta co-lumba, quae in dextram Christi locum eos accipit, qui benefaciendo sunt exercitati, ac velut pastor oues ab hædis, probos separat ab improbis.
units.tr: Basil: The Church, he says, is one, a perfect dove, which receives into the right hand of Christ those who are practised in doing good; and, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats, so it separates the upright from the wicked.

units.la: Chrysostomus in illa verba: In magna domo non sunt tantum vasa argentea & aurea, sed ligneā[?] & fictilia, sic scribit: b Non referam[?] similitu-dinem ad Ecclesiam, sed ad mundum universum. Quippe in Ecclesia nullum est vas fictile, aut ligneum, sed argentea omnia, & aurea. Ibi enim est corpus Christi, casta virgo, non habens maculam aut rugam. Idem habent Theodoretus & Theophylactus.
units.tr: Chrysostom, on those words, In a great house there are not only vessels of silver and gold, but also of wood and earth, writes thus: {b}I will not apply the likeness to the Church, but to the whole world. For in the Church there is no earthen or wooden vessel, but all are of silver and gold. For there is the body of Christ, a chaste virgin, having no spot or wrinkle. Theodoret and Theophylact have the same view.

units.la: Respondet Bellarminus ad Chrysostomi locum: § Non negat Chrysostomus, malos esse in Ecclesia, sed dicit, nō esse necessarium, vt sint in Ecclesia. Et subiungit Dominus Cardinalis egregiam rationem, quia Ecclesia non indiget malis. Hæc ille. Antiquos Patres sub ferula sua castigandos revocat Dominus Cardinalis, atque eos, tanquam pueros balbutientes instituit, monetque, quid dicere, & quomodo debuissent: quasi vero Patres elingues essent, nisi hic magister elocutionis morum formator adesset. At Chrysostomus non dicit, quod eum dicere Cardinalis affinxerat. Scribit enim diserte, in Ecclesia nullum esse vas ligneum. Et rationem reddit: quia Ecclesia est corpus CHRISTI, casta virgo, sine macula. Bellarminus haec verba ita sub ferula sua transmutat, quasi diceret, non esse necessarium, vt sint mali in Ecclesia: & Ecclesiam non indigere malis. Quantæ ineptiæ? quasi vero mundus indigeat malis. Pergamus.
units.tr: Bellarmine replies to the passage of Chrysostom: Chrysostom does not deny that there are wicked people in the Church, but he says that it is not necessary for them to be in the Church. And the Lord Cardinal adds an excellent reason: because the Church has no need of the wicked. So he says. The Lord Cardinal calls the ancient Fathers back under his rod and corrects them, and instructs them as if they were stammering children, telling them what and how they ought to have said; as if the Fathers were tongue-tied unless this master of eloquence and teacher of manners were present. But Chrysostom does not say what the Cardinal pretends he said. For he writes plainly that there is no wooden vessel in the Church, and he gives the reason: because the Church is the body of Christ, a chaste virgin, without spot. Bellarmine, under his rod, so alters these words as if Chrysostom said that it is not necessary that the wicked be in the Church, and that the Church does not need the wicked. What great absurdity! As if the world needed the wicked. Let us proceed.

units.la: Cyrillus Alexand. {a}Quum Ecclesiam dicimus, non circuitu murorum vim huius dictionis accommodamus, sed potius in ea sanctissimam multitudinem significamus. Sic docuerunt Græci, audiamus etiam Latinos.
units.tr: Cyril of Alexandria: {a}When we say Church, we do not apply the force of this word to the circuit of walls, but rather we signify in it the most holy multitude. Thus the Greeks taught; let us hear the Latins too.

units.la: Irenæus ait: {b}Ecclesia est semen Abraha per Christum, cui adoptio redditur, & hereditas, quæ Abrahæ promissa est. Idemque: Ubi Ecclesia, ibi Spiritus, & ubi Spiritus Dei, ibi Ecclesia, & omnis gratia. Spiritus autem veritas. Hæc ille. Si adoptio, hereditas, gratia, Spiritus, veritas, sunt proprietates & dotes veræ Ecclesiæ, fallum docent, qui affirmant, nullam hic internam requiri virtutem.
units.tr: Irenaeus says: {b}The Church is the seed of Abraham through Christ, to whom adoption is given, and the inheritance which was promised to Abraham. And again: Where the Church is, there is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and all grace. The Spirit, moreover, is truth. So he says. If adoption, inheritance, grace, the Spirit and truth are the properties and endowments of the true Church, then those are wrong who affirm that no inward virtue is required here.

units.la: Cyprianus etiam sic docuit: {c}Ecclesia in Episcopo & Clero, & in omnibus staribus[?] est constituta. Absit enim, nec Domini misericordia & potestas eius multa[?] patiatur, ut Ecclesia esse dicatur lapsorum numerus. Hæc ille. Quod si lapsorum numerus non potest dici Ecclesia, profecto nec numerus eorum, qui nullam habent virtutem internam. Idemque Cyprianus sic docet: {d}Nec in Ecclesia Dei remanere possunt, qui Deificam & Ecclesiasticam disciplinam, nec actus sui conversatione, nec morum pace tenuerunt. Atque iterum: {e}Ecclesiam, id est, plebem in Ecclesia constitutam, fideliter & firmiter in eo, quod credidit, perseverantem, nulla res separare potest a Christo. Atque alibi: {f}In Ecclesia non nisi concordes & unanimes habihabitant, loquente in Psalmis Spiritu sancto, & dicente: Deus; qui habitare fecit vnanimes in domo.
units.tr: Cyprian also taught thus: {c}The Church is constituted in the bishop, the clergy, and in all who stand firm. Far be it, and may the mercy and power of the Lord not suffer it, that the number of the fallen should be called the Church. So he says. But if the number of the fallen cannot be called the Church, certainly neither can the number of those who have no inward virtue. Cyprian likewise teaches: {d}Those who have not kept the divine and ecclesiastical discipline, neither in the conduct of their acts nor in the peace of their morals, cannot remain in the Church of God. And again: {e}Nothing can separate from Christ the Church, that is, the people constituted in the Church, who persevere faithfully and firmly in what they have believed. And elsewhere: {f}Only those who are of one mind and one heart dwell in the Church, the Holy Spirit speaking in the Psalms and saying: God, who makes those of one mind to dwell in a house.

units.la: Aliis testimoniis missis, & dissimulatis, ad hoc postremum testimonium respondet Bel-larminus, {a}loqui Cyprianum non de quacunque concordia, sed de illa, quae opponitur schismati proprie dicto: agit enim ibi de Novatianis schismaticis. Haec ait Bellarminus, vt probet, malos homines esse membra Ecclesiae, schismaticos autem non esse.
units.tr: Setting aside and passing over the other testimonies, Bellarmine answers this last testimony by saying that Cyprian speaks not of any concord whatever, but of that which is opposed to schism properly so called: for he is there dealing with the schismatic Novatians. Bellarmine says this in order to prove that wicked men are members of the Church, but schismatics are not.

units.la: Respondeo, S. Augustinum longe aliud colligere ex iisdem Cypriani verbis. Nam Augustinus citat hunc ipsum locum Cypriani, vt probet, malos non esse Ecclesiae membra. Ait enim Cyprianus: Alienus fiat, & profanus Domi-nicae pacis, ac Dominicae vnitatis inimicus, non habitans in domo Dei; id est, in Ecclesia Christi, in qua non nisi concordes atq; vnanimes habitant. Haec Cyprianus. Subiungit Augustinus: {b}Sim Ecclesia Christi non nisi concordes & vnanimes habitant, procul dubio nō habitabant in Ecclesia Christi, quam-uis intus esse viderentur illi, qui per invidiam & contentionem, sine charitate Christum annunciabant: quos ipse intelligit, non haereticos aut schismaticos, sed Paulo Apostolo commemoratos, sed falsos fratres, cum illo interim commorantes. Haec Augustinus.
units.tr: I reply that St Augustine draws quite a different conclusion from the same words of Cyprian. For Augustine cites this very passage of Cyprian in order to prove that the wicked are not members of the Church. For Cyprian says: {g}Let him become a stranger and profane to the peace of the Lord, and an enemy of the Lord's unity, not dwelling in the house of God; that is, in the Church of Christ, in which only those of one mind and one heart dwell. These are Cyprian's words. Augustine adds: {b}If in the Church of Christ only those of one mind and one heart dwell, then undoubtedly those who preached Christ through envy and strife, without charity, did not dwell in the Church of Christ, although they seemed to be inside it: those whom he understands not to be heretics or schismatics, but the false brethren recalled by the Apostle Paul, who meanwhile lived together with him. So Augustine.

units.la: Deinceps ad Augustini sententiam deuenimus. Haec retuli hoc loco ex Augustino, vt Cypriani sententia constare possit contra Bellarmini responsum. Eundem Cypriani locum exponunt Augustinus & Bellarminus. Dicit Bellarminus, Cyprianum non de malis Chriftianis[?], sed de schismaticis loqui: Cardinalis egregie refutatur ab Augustino. Augustinus sensum Cypriani ex ipsis verbis, ex perpetuo Ecclesiae iudicio deducit. Bellarminus ex suo ingenio, ex libidine corrumpendi, torquet ea-dem verba, ut recentem Tridentinam blas-phemiam confirmet. Quod Bellarminus tan-tum de schismaticis dictum vult, Augustinus probat de falsis fratribus dici.
units.tr: We now come to the opinion of Augustine. I have cited these things from Augustine here so that Cyprian's view may stand firm against Bellarmine's reply. Augustine and Bellarmine both expound the same passage of Cyprian. Bellarmine says that Cyprian speaks not of wicked Christians but of schismatics: the Cardinal is excellently refuted by Augustine. Augustine deduces Cyprian's meaning from the words themselves and from the constant judgement of the Church. Bellarmine, from his own wit and from a desire to corrupt, twists the same words in order to confirm the recent blasphemy of Trent. What Bellarmine wants said only of schismatics, Augustine proves is said of false brethren.

units.la: Bellarminus etiam e Cypriano verba pro-ducit, quo probet, malos esse membra Eccle-siae. Verba Cypriani sunt lib.3. Epist.3. Impe-diri non debet, aut fides, aut charitas nostra, ut, quoniam Zizania esse in Ecclesia cernimus, ipsi de Ecclesia recedamus.
units.tr: Bellarmine also brings forward words from Cyprian to prove that the wicked are members of the Church. The words of Cyprian are in book 3, letter 3: {h}Neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered, so that, because we see tares in the Church, we should withdraw ourselves from the Church.

units.la: Respondeo, haec producendo Bellarminus ostendit, se nihil proferre posse. Zizania sunt in Ecclesia, sicut in tritico: non ut partes tritici; ergo nec ut partes aut membra Ecclesiae, {a} a Mater viventium Ecclesia est, inquit Ambrosius, quam aedificat Deus ipso summo angulari lapide de Iesu Christo.
units.tr: I reply that by producing these words Bellarmine shows that he can produce nothing. Tares are in the Church as they are in the wheat, but not as parts of the wheat; therefore neither are they as parts or members of the Church. {a}The Church is the mother of the living, says Ambrose, which God builds upon the very highest cornerstone, Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ambrosius etiam loquens de iis, qui nullam habent internam virtutem, sic ait: Non talibus decoctoribus ad Ecclesiam Christi perveni-tur, ad quam tendebat Iacob. lib.1.Epist.4.
units.tr: Ambrose, also speaking of those who have no inward virtue, says thus: Men of that sort, who are like dyers, do not come to the Church of Christ, toward which Jacob was heading. Book 1, letter 4.

units.la: Hieronymus in illa verba: Ecclesia est subiecta Christo; sic scribit: {b} Ecclesia Christi gloriosa est, non habens maculam, aut rugam, neque aliquid huiusmodi; Qui ergo peccator est, aut aliqua sorde maculatus, de Ecclesia Christi non potest appellari, nec Christo subiectus dici. Respondet Bellarminus, Hieronymum significat non posse malos de ea parte Ecclesiæ appellari, quæ solos perfectos continet. Hæc ille. Deinde hoc figmentum suum de his duabus Ecclesiæ partibus, ex Hieronymo probare contendit: quia Hieronymus in cap. 1. ad Galat. exponens illud, Ecclesiæ Galatiæ: dicit, Ecclesiam dupliciter accipi. Interdum enim tribuit Scriptura toti Ecclesiæ id, quod est proprium perfectorum, vt caeteræ macula, &c. Interdu id, quod est proprium imperfectorum, vt peccare. Hæc Bellarminus. Atq; hinc duas partes observasse se existimat. Respondeo, Hieronymum nusquam dicere, partes esse, aut membra Ecclesiæ, qui nullam habent virtutem internam: quod huic probandum fuerat. Dicit Hieronymus, a {a}Ecclesiam duplicitèr posse dici, & eam, quæ non habet maculam, aut rugam, & vere corpus Christi sit, & eam, quæ in Christi nomine, absq; plenis perfectisq; virtutibus, congregatur. Hæc Hieronymus. Deinde explicat se Hieronymus: Minus perfectam Ecclesiam vocari, quæ nondum ad perfectionem peruenit, sed tamen ad eam contendit. Fieri enim potest, sicut idem Hieronymus alibi docet, {b}vt pec-cator currat ad medicum; qui[?] non habent opus sani medico, sed male habentes, & curentur vulnera ipsius, & fiat de Ecclesia, quæ est corpus Christi. Hæc ille. Loquitur ergo Hieronymus de imperfectis, qui sunt, vt ipsius verba habent, absque plenis & perfectis virtutibus, qui tamen suo tempore ad plenas & perfectas virtutes acceaccedunt. Cardinalis disputat de illis, in quibus est nulla interna virtus. Quantum hæc sententia ab Hieronymi sententia differat, quis non videt?
units.tr: Jerome, on those words, The Church is subject to Christ, writes thus: {b}The Church of Christ is glorious, having no spot, or wrinkle, or anything of the kind. Therefore whoever is a sinner, or stained with any filth, cannot be called of the Church of Christ, nor be said to be subject to Christ. Bellarmine replies that Jerome means that the wicked cannot be called part of that Church which contains only the perfect. So he says. Then he sets out to prove from Jerome this figment of his about two parts of the Church: because Jerome, expounding in chapter 1 to the Galatians the words the churches of Galatia, says that the Church may be understood in two ways. For Scripture sometimes attributes to the whole Church what belongs to the perfect, such as being without spot, and so on; and sometimes what belongs to the imperfect, such as sinning. So Bellarmine says; and from this he thinks he has observed two parts. I reply that Jerome nowhere says that those who have no inward virtue are parts or members of the Church, which was what had to be proved. Jerome says: {c}The Church can be called in two ways: both that which has no spot or wrinkle and truly is the body of Christ, and that which is gathered in the name of Christ without full and perfect virtues. These are Jerome's words. Then Jerome explains himself: the Church is called less perfect when it has not yet attained perfection but still strives toward it. For it can happen, as Jerome teaches elsewhere, {d}that a sinner runs to the physician, who has no need of a healthy physician, but who is ill, and his wounds are healed, and he becomes part of the Church which is the body of Christ. So he says. Jerome therefore speaks of the imperfect, who are, as his own words have it, without full and perfect virtues, yet who in their time attain to full and perfect virtues. The Cardinal disputes about those in whom there is no inward virtue at all. Who does not see how far this opinion differs from the opinion of Jerome?

units.la: Ad Augustinum deuenimus. Augustinus hanc controuersiæ partem de membris Ecclesiæ diligentissime atque accuratissime tractauit. Quicunque non sunt sancti, qui sunt sine fide & charitate, non esse Ecclesiæ membra demonstrat, quamuis in Ecclesia esse videantur. Nos, quæ diuersis locis obseruauit de hac re, unā colligemus. Hæc igitur habet Augustinus: {a}Ecclesia est corpus eius, sicut Apostolica doctrina commendat, quæ etiam coniux[?] eius dicitur. Corpus ergo suum multis membris diuersa officia gerentibus, nodo unitatis & charitatis, tanquam sanitatis astringit. {b}Diabolus est caput impiorum, qui sunt eius quodammodo corpus, ituri cum illo in supplicio æterni ignis: sicut Christus est Caput Ecclesiæ, quæ est corpus eius futurum cum illo in regno & gloria sempiterna. Ad illam quæstionem: Utrum Baptisma hereticorum generet filios Deo? respondet Augustinus: {c}Quasi vero ex hoc generet, unde separata est, & non ex hoc, unde coniuncta est. Separata est enim à vinculo charitatis & pacis, sed adiuncta est in uno baptismate. Itaque est una Ecclesia, quæ sola Catholica nominatur, & quicquid suum habet in communionibus diuersorum, à sua unitate separatus, per hoc, quod suum in eis habet, ipsa utique generat, non illa. Neque enim separatio istarum generat, sed quod secum de ista tenuerunt: quod si & hoc dimittant, omnino non generant. Hac itaque in omnibus hub[?] generat, cuius Sacramenta retinentur, unde pos-sit tale aliquid ubicunq; generari, quamuis non o-mnes, quos generat, ad eius pertineant unitatem, qua vsq; in finem perseuerantes saluat. Neq; enim ÿ[?] soli ad eam non pertinent, qui separationis aperto sacri-legio manifesti sunt, sed etiam illi, qui in eius unitate corporaliter mixti, per vitam pessimam separantur. Hæc ille. Hæc plenius retuli, vt Augustini sen-tentia melius agnoscatur. Quod si ad Ecclesiam hanc Catholicam non pertinent, qui per vitam pessimam separantur, quomodo pot[?] vitam [?] leparantur, quomodo pol-sunt esse Ecclesiæ membra ? Iterumque Au-gustinus: {a}Non sunt in illa Ecclesia, de qua dicitur, vna est columba, vna eius matri suæ: ipsa est enim sine macula, aut ruga. Aut afferat, qui potest, huius columbæ membra esse, qui sæculo verbis, non factis re-nuntiant. Afferat, qui potest, inquit Augustinus: Potuit Bellarminus, possunt hodie Iesuitæ al-ferere [?], quod Augustinus credidit, neminem potuisse. Sed pergat Augustinus in inchoato sermone. {b}Nos, inquit, secundum id, quod in præsenti est, quærimus, utrum in illis Ecclesiæ membris, quæ vna columba dicta est, & sponsa Christi sine macula aut ruga, hodie deputandi sint, de quibus di-cit Cyprianus, quod viam Domini non tenerent. Quod si illos in suis membris nec illa columba agnoscit, & talibus, si in eadem peruersitate [?] permanserint, dicturus est Deus: Recedite à me, qui operamini iniquitatem. Videntur esse in Ecclesia, sed non sunt: imo & contra Ecclesiam faciunt. {c}Quodenim in libro Canticorum Ecclesia sic describitur, Hortus conclusus, soror mea, sponsa, fons signatus, puteus aquavitæ, paradisum cum fructu pomorum: hoc in-telligere non audeo, nisi in sanctis & iustis: neminem a-uaru & fraudatoribus, & raptoribus, & fœneratori-bus, & ebriosis, & immundis, quos tamen cum iustis ba-ptismum habere confitentur, cum quibus commu-nem non habebant charitatem.
units.tr: We come now to Augustine, who treated this part of the controversy, concerning the members of the Church, most diligently and accurately. He shows that those who are not holy, who lack faith and charity, are not members of the Church, although they seem to be in it. We will gather into one what he observed on this matter in various places. Augustine says this: {a}The Church is his body, as apostolic doctrine commends, and is also called his spouse. So he binds his body, whose many members perform diverse offices, with the knot of unity and charity, as with the sinews of health. {b}The devil is the head of the wicked, who are in a sense his body, destined to go with him into the punishment of eternal fire; just as Christ is the Head of the Church, which is his body, destined to be with him in the everlasting kingdom and glory. To the question Whether the baptism of heretics begets sons to God? Augustine replies: {c}As if it begot from that which it is separated from, and not from that to which it is joined! For it is separated from the bond of charity and peace, but it is joined in the one baptism. Therefore there is one Church, which alone is called Catholic; and whatever it has of its own among the communions of various people, separated from its unity, it certainly begets through that which it has of its own among them, and not through them. For the separation of those does not beget, but what they have held of this Church with them; and if they abandon even this, they beget nothing at all. Thus the Church begets in all cases, the Church whose sacraments are retained, from which something of this kind can be begotten anywhere, although not all whom it begets belong to its unity, by which it saves those who persevere to the end. For those who are manifestly guilty of open sacrilege of separation do not belong to it alone, but also those who, mixed in body within its unity, are cut off by a most wicked life. Thus he. I have related these things more fully so that Augustine's opinion may be better recognised. But if those who are cut off by a most wicked life do not belong to this Catholic Church, how can they be members of the Church? And again Augustine: {a}They are not in that Church of which it is said, one is my dove, one for her mother: for she is without spot or wrinkle. Let whoever can, show that those are members of this dove who renounce the world in words but not in deeds. Let whoever can show it, says Augustine. Bellarmine could; today the Jesuits could assert what Augustine believed no one could. But let Augustine continue his unfinished sermon. {b}We ask, he says, according to what is present, whether those who are to be counted today among those members of the Church which is called one dove and the bride of Christ without spot or wrinkle, of whom Cyprian says that they did not keep to the way of the Lord. But if that dove does not acknowledge them as its members, and if they persist in the same perversity, God will say to such: Depart from me, you who work iniquity. They seem to be in the Church, but they are not; indeed they act against the Church. {c}For what the Song of Songs describes the Church as, a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, a sealed fountain, a well of living water, a paradise with an orchard of fruit, I dare not understand this of anyone except the holy and just: not of the covetous, the defrauders, the robbers, the usurers, the drunkards, and the unclean, whom they nonetheless confess to have the baptism together with the just, but with whom they did not have common charity.

units.la: Hæc disputat Augustinus contra Donatistas, atque hæc est eius communis & vsitatissima responsio, per illos septem libros de baptismo Donatistarum, quibus refutat Cypriani opinionem, de Baptismo hæreticorum: in eoque totus est, vt doceat, eandem prorsus rationem esse hæreticorum extra Ecclesiam, & male viuentium in Ecclesia: nec membra Ecclesiæ esse, vel hos, vel iistos[?], donec conuertantur: tum demum membra fieri, quum vera fide & charitate ita inserantur in Corpus Christi, vt cum Capite connectantur: non tamen iterum esse baptizandos, quia ipsa reconciliatione ac pace præstatur, vt ad remissionem peccatorum, eis in vnitate iam prodesse incipiat Sacramentum, quod acceptum in schismate prodesse non poterat. {a}Siverum est, inquit, (quod obiicit Cyprianus) propterea filios Dei generare non potest hæresis per Christum, quia Christi sponsa non est: nec turba illa malorum intus constitutorum potest; quia & ipsa Christi sponsa non est. {b}Mali Catholici, & hæretici non pertinent ad sanctam Ecclesiam Dei, quamuis intus esse videantur; quia isti sunt auari, raptores, fœneratores, immundi, maleuoli: & cetera huiusmodi. Illa autem columba, unica, pudica, & casta sponsa, sine macula aut ruga, hortus conclusus, fons signatus, paradisus cum fructu pomorum, & caetera, quae de illa dicta sunt, quod non intelligitur, nisi in bonis & sanctis: id est, non tantum secundum operationes muneris Dei, bonum & malum communes, sed etiam secundum intimam & supereminentem charitatem, Spiritum S. habentibus, quibus Dominus dicit: Si tui[?] dimiseritis peccata, dimittentur ei, & si cui tenebitis[?], tenebuntur, Hæc Augustinus. Quid plura congerā ex Augustino vel certe hæc, quæ produximus, euin-cent homines, qui nullā habent internā virtu-tem, sed tantum externā professionem, & Sa-cramentorum communionem, quæ sensu ipso percipitur, non esse partes & membra Eccle-siæ, vel omnis autoritas & fides Augustini[?] est prorsus repudianda.
units.tr: Augustine argues this against the Donatists, and this is his common and most usual reply, throughout those seven books on the baptism of the Donatists, in which he refutes Cyprian's opinion on the baptism of heretics. In these books his whole aim is to teach that the reason is exactly the same for heretics outside the Church and for the badly living within it: neither these nor those are members of the Church until they are converted. Then at last they become members, when, joined to the Body of Christ by true faith and charity, they are connected with the Head. Yet they are not to be baptized again, because it is by reconciliation and peace itself that the sacrament, which when received in schism could not profit them, begins now to profit them in unity for the remission of sins. {a}It is true, he says, (as Cyprian objects) that heresy cannot beget sons of God through Christ because it is not the spouse of Christ; nor can that crowd of evil men standing within, because they too are not the spouse of Christ. {b}Evil Catholics and heretics do not belong to the holy Church of God, although they seem to be within; because they are covetous, robbers, usurers, unclean, malicious, and the like. But that dove, one, chaste, and pure bride, without spot or wrinkle, a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain, a paradise with an orchard of fruit, and the other things that are said of her, are not understood except of the good and holy: that is, not only according to the workings of God's gift, which are common to good and bad, but also according to the inward and surpassing charity of those who have the Holy Spirit, to whom the Lord says: If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; and if you retain any, they are retained. Thus Augustine. Why should I heap up more from Augustine? Either these things we have brought forward will convince people who have no inward virtue, but only outward profession and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses alone, that they are not parts and members of the Church; or the whole authority and faith of Augustine must be utterly rejected.

units.la: Atqui ex Augustino etiam sententiam suam probare voluit Cardinalis. Audiamus quomodo. Augustinus, inquit, tract.6.in Iohan. Nos, aut, fatemur, in Ecclesia Catholica & bonos, & malos esse, sed tanquam grana, & paleas. Hæcille. Impudentia excæcauit Cardinalem: quid enim non audet iste affirmare, qui ad tam manifesta Augustini verba, qualia sunt, quæ su-fius ex eo superius produximus, nihil omnino respondere voluit; & tamen ex eodem Augustino suam sententiam confirmare sperauit: quia in Ecclesia sunt boni & mali, sed sicut grana & paleæ. Quæ verba probant, malos non esse membra Ecclesiæ; quod & expressius Augustinus eodem tractatu docuit, his verbis: {a}Quæro, utrum ad huius columbae memibrapertineant[?] auari, raptores, subdoli, ebriosi, flagi-tiosi? Membra sunt columbæ huius? Absit, inquit, & revera, fratres, quis hoc dixerit? Hæc Augustinus. Per Columbam autem, Catholicam in-telligit; nam eodem loco hæc habet verba: O Catholica, tibi dictum est, una est Columba mea, una est matri suæ. Deinde de raptoribus, auaris, ebriosis loquens; sic pungit Iesuitas: {a}Anifti[?] omnes membra columbæ sunt? sic dehonestatis columbam vestram, ut ei membra vulturina faciatis. Hæc Augustinus. De membris Ecclesiæ quæstio est. Augustinus docet, malos bonosque esse in Ecclesia, malos autem non esse membra Ecclesiæ, sed tamen in Ecclesia esse, sicut paleæ[?] inter grana. Dominus Cardinalis, homo duræ auris, hæc ipsa verba Augustini adducit, ut probet, malos esse membra Ecclesiæ. Certe Dominum Cardinalem hæc malo animo tractasse, vel Papaiudice, vincam. Pergamus ad alios.
units.tr: But the Cardinal wanted to prove his own opinion also from Augustine. Let us hear how. "Augustine," he says, "in tractate 6 on John: We confess that in the Catholic Church there are both good and bad, but as grains and chaff." Thus he. Impudence has blinded the Cardinal. For what will this man not dare to affirm, who wanted to make no answer at all to such clear words of Augustine as those we have brought forward above from him, and yet hoped to confirm his own opinion from the same Augustine, namely that in the Church there are good and bad, but as grains and chaff? These words prove that the bad are not members of the Church; and Augustine taught this more plainly in the same tractate, in these words: {a}I ask whether the covetous, robbers, deceivers, drunkards, and the shameless belong to the members of this dove. Are they members of this dove? Far from it, says he; and indeed, brethren, who would say so? Thus Augustine. By the dove he means the Catholic Church; for in the same place he has these words: O Catholic, it has been said to you, one is my dove, one for her mother. Then, speaking of robbers, covetous men, and drunkards, he thus pricks the Jesuits: {a}Are all those you name members of the dove? You dishonour your dove so much as to make vulture's members of her. Thus Augustine. The question concerns the members of the Church. Augustine teaches that there are bad and good in the Church, but the bad are not members of the Church, though they are in the Church, as chaff is among the grain. The Lord Cardinal, a man hard of hearing, quotes these very words of Augustine in order to prove that the bad are members of the Church. Certainly I will be content to let the Pope judge whether the Lord Cardinal handled these things in bad faith. Let us go on to others.

units.la: Prosper sic docet: {b}Ecclesia Catholica est in electis præcognitis a Deo, filijs promissionis, membris corporis Christi. Fulgentius: {c}Hæc Ecclesia una, vera, catholica, sponsa est, quia inhæret Christo: mater est, quia fœcundatur a Christo: virgo est, quia incorrupte perseverat in Christo.
units.tr: Prosper teaches thus: {b}The Catholic Church is, in the elect foreknown by God, the sons of promise, the members of the body of Christ. Fulgentius: {c}This one, true, catholic Church is a spouse, because she cleaves to Christ; she is a mother, because she is made fruitful by Christ; she is a virgin, because she perseveres uncorrupted in Christ.

units.la: Iam Gregorium Magnum audiamus. Sic ille: {d}Sanctam Ecclesiam ille veraciter videt, cuius testatur vita, quia videt. {e}Neque enim sancta Electorum[?] Ecclesia solos sibi adversarios deputat, qui ab eius fide positi extra dissentiunt: sed eos quoque, qui vitam illius male vivendo, interim premunt. {a}Intra mensuras Ecclesiæ sunt omnes electi, extra has mensuras omnes reprobi, etiamsi intra fidei limitem esse videantur. Hæc Gregorius. Num qua arte possit Dominus Cardinalis hæc Episcopi Romani verba eludere? Si extra mensuras Ecclesiæ sint omnes reprobi, quamuis intra limitem fidei esse videantur, profecto externa fidei professio, & Sacramentorum communio, quæ sensu ipso percipitur, non facit membrum Ecclesiæ; quod improbe docent Iesuitæ. Sed pergit Gregorius: {b}Infideles quosque extra Ecclesiam, peccati sui unda perimit, & fideles suos in fide atque in charitate sanctæ Ecclesiæ unitas, quasi arca compago custodit. Gregorius his verbis satis liquido demonstrat, male viuentes ad Ecclesiam Christi non pertinere. Audiamus, quomodo sanctus hic vir Iesuitas nostros multis ante seculis, suis coloribus depinxerit, quasi prænuntians hæc tempora: {c}Sicut incarnata veritas, inquit, in prædicatione sua pauperes, idiotas, & simplices elegit: sic è contrario, damnatus ille homo, quem in fine mundi apostata Angelus assumet, ad prædicandam falsitatem suam, astutos, ac duplices, atque huius mundi scientiam habentes, electurus est. Hæc ille: tanquam penicillo depingens Papales istos prædicatores, qui relicta veteris Ecclesiæ syncericitate[?], abiecta veteris doctrinæ puritate, conculcata Ecclesiæ sanctitate, dum tanquam immundi sues in cœno volutantur, dum contempta Dei sapientia, sapientiam mundi in Ecclesiam sectantur[?], ita palam Deo & Ecclesiæ illudunt, ut in suis sordibus sanctam Dei Ecclesiam quærant. Hinc est, quod membra, & partes Ecclesiæ sanctæ, statuant homines impuros & profanos, qui nullam habent internam virtutem, sed tantum externam professionem, & Sacramentorum communionem, quæ sensu ipso percipitur. Non dubito, quin intelligant, se hæc mouere contra Scripturas, & vnanimem Patrum consensum. Neque enim ignorantiæ crimen sibi à nobis obiici, æquo patiuntur animo. Quia igitur videntes, & scientes peccant, viderint, quam horrendum bellum susceperint in Deum, & in Christum, & in Ecclesiam. Hæc omnia maiorem in nobis vigilantiam, & veritatis amorem accendere debent, vt tanquam filii lucis, in Christi & sanctæ Ecclesiæ institutis, cum bona conscientia ambulemus, contra istos, quos Spiritus Dei venturos prædixerat, habituros formam pietatis, sed virtutem eius abnegantes.
units.tr: Let us now hear Gregory the Great. He says: {d}He truly sees the holy Church whose life bears witness that he sees it. {e}For the holy Church of the elect does not count as enemies only those who stand outside her faith and dissent from it, but also those who, by living badly, press upon her from within. {a}All the elect are within the bounds of the Church; all the reprobate are outside these bounds, even if they seem to be within the boundary of the faith. So Gregory. By what art can the Lord Cardinal evade these words of the Bishop of Rome? If all the reprobate are outside the bounds of the Church, even though they seem to be within the boundary of the faith, then surely an outward profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses, does not make a man a member of the Church. The Jesuits teach this wickedly. But Gregory goes on: {b}The flood of their sin destroys all unbelievers outside the Church, while the unity of the holy Church, like an ark joined together, keeps her believers in faith and charity. By these words Gregory demonstrates quite plainly that those who live wickedly do not belong to the Church of Christ. Let us hear how this holy man, many centuries ago, painted our Jesuits in their own colours, as if foreseeing these times: {c}Just as the Truth made flesh, he says, chose poor, unlearned and simple men for his preaching, so on the contrary that condemned man, whom the apostate angel will take up at the end of the world to preach his falsehood, will choose the crafty and the deceitful, who have the wisdom of this world. So he says, as if painting these Papal preachers with a brush. They have abandoned the purity of the old Church, cast off the purity of the old doctrine, trampled the holiness of the Church, and while they wallow like filthy swine in the mire, and while, having despised the wisdom of God, they pursue the wisdom of the world into the Church, they so openly mock God and the Church that they seek the holy Church of God in their own filth. Hence it is that they declare to be members and parts of the holy Church men who are impure and profane, who have no inward virtue but only an outward profession and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses. I do not doubt that they understand that they are moving against the Scriptures and the unanimous consent of the Fathers. Nor do they bear calmly the charge that they sin through ignorance. Since therefore they sin while seeing and knowing, let them see how dreadful a war they have undertaken against God, against Christ and against the Church. All these things ought to kindle in us greater vigilance and love of the truth, so that, as children of the light, we may walk with a good conscience in the institutions of Christ and of the holy Church, against those whom the Spirit of God had foretold would come, having a form of godliness but denying its power.

units.la: De membris Ecclesiæ sanctis Gregorius sic etiam docet: {a}Omnes nos, qui in eius fide nati sumus, eius proculdubio Corpus existimus: quia igitur in varia dispensatione pietatis, membrorum suorum dominus caput factus est, repulsa reproborum multitudine, solus est etiam nobiscum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Gregory also teaches this about the holy members of the Church: {a}All of us who have been born in her faith are without doubt considered her body; therefore, since in the varied dispensation of godliness the Lord has been made head of his members, the multitude of the reprobate having been cast out, he alone is also with us. So he says.

units.la: Pergamus ad reliquos Scriptores, qui in sequentibus sæculis docuerunt, qui, quia communem superiorum sententiam secuti sunt, succinctius à nobis sunt commemorandi. Rabanus sic docuit: {b}Ex omnibus gentibus sancta congregatur Ecclesia, quæ electa Christi hæreditas est. est. Hæc ille. Arlefuitæ[?] docent hodie, quod nemo veterum somniauit: impios homines sine interna virtute esse Christi hæreditatem. Smaragdus etiam sic scribit: {a}a Domus spiritualis Ecclesia est iustorum, de lapidibus vivis, & animabus adificata sanctarum. Rupertus: Vniuersalis Ecclesia sanguine Christi mundata est ab omnidelic-to. Bernardus etiam hanc doctrinam de Ecclesiæ membris à Patribus traditam, magna fi-de, atque integritate suscepit, posterisque tra-didit. Sic enim docet: {b}b Ipsa sponsa est Ecclesia electorum, de quibus Apostolus, Omnia, inquit, propter electos. c Et, quid sponsa? nisi congregatio iustorum: quid ipsa? nisi generatio quærentium Dominum, quærentium faciem sponsi. Idemque sic etiam: d Non deficit haritas[?] de Ecclesia. Funda-ta est Ecclesia super petram: petra autem est Christus. Itaque nec verbositate Philosophorum, nec cavillationibus hæreticorum, nec gladiis persecutorum potuit ista, aut poterit aliquando separari à charitate Christi. Idem docuit Nicolaus de Lyra, in illa verba: Super petram hanc ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non prævalebunt adversus eam. e Ex quo patet, inquit Lyra, quod Ecclesia non consistit in hominibus ratione potestatis, aut dignitatis Ecclesiasticæ, vel secularis, quia multi principes & summi Pontifices, & alij inferiores inventi sunt apostatasse à fide. Propter quod Ecclesia consistit in illis personis, in quibus est notitia vera, & confessio fidei ac veritatis. Hæc Lyra. Quam apposite, quam ingenue inter densas tenebras lucem secutus est? contra quam isti tenebriones faciunt, qui in clarissima Euangelii luce executiunt. Lyræ igitur iudicio, Ecclesia non consistit ex iis, in quibus nulla est interna vir-tus. Iohannes Wiclefus Mertonensis noster, hanc opinionem, quæ improbos, etiam da-mnatos homines, Ecclesiæ Catholicæ membra esse finxerat, primum inter priuatas opiniones fraterculorum inuectam refert. Referam verba eius Anglice, sicut scripta sunt: a Friars destroyen this article of Christian mens faith, Iheleine o common or generall Churche[?]. For they teachen that tho men that shalbe damned be members of holy Churche. And thus they vvedden Christ, and the deuil together: id est, Fratres hunc articulum fidei Christianæ destruunt: Credo Ecclesiam Catholicam. Docent enim, homines damnandos membra esse Ecclesiæ sanctæ: & sic Diabolum cum Christo connubio coniungunt. Ita Wiclefus originem erroris huius notat, quam à fraterculis primum inuectam demonstrat: quos testatur horrendo coniugio Christum cum Diabolo copulasse: quam absurditatem nullo modo effugere possunt, qui membra Ecclesiæ, qui sunt & membra Christi, docent esse sine omni interna virtute: ita enim & membra Diaboli Christo coniungunt. Gratianus in hanc sententiam quædam etiam ex veteribus Scriptoribus colligit, ut probet, impios ab Ecclesia separari per vitam malam. Agnoscit Gratianus, longe aliam fuisse Romanæ Ecclesiæ doctrinam (illo quo scripsit ipse seculo,) quam hodie promulgant Iesuitæ, de membris Ec-clesiæ. elesia te, E mem Capi nulla ædific[?] mam mus camu D nos. Bella Eccl gior quar subi a plecti natio quid comm quit mnib Dabo tuam da, mu. sap. [?]lesiæ. Diximus de prima Ecclesiæ proprieta-te, Ecclesia sancta est. Sanctitas hæc est in membris, qua omnia sanctificantur à sancto Capite. At membra Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quæ nullam habent internam virtutem, non sanctificantur à sancto Capite. Non ergo Romana Ecclesia illa, quam in Symbolo crediRefeint: a faith, r they membrift, rticusiam andos cum origiculis tatur bolo modo qui e oDiananc Scrilesia atiadouam Ecsiæ. [illegible, ~6 letters]mus sanctam. Reitat, vt de proxima nota vi-[?]camus.
units.tr: Let us pass on to the other writers who taught in the following centuries. Since they followed the common opinion of those before them, they must be mentioned more briefly by us. Rabanus taught thus: {b}Out of all nations the holy Church is gathered, which is the elect inheritance of Christ. So he. The men of Arles teach today what no one of the ancients ever dreamed: that impious men without inward virtue are the inheritance of Christ. Smaragdus also writes thus: {a}The spiritual house is the Church of the righteous, built of living stones and of holy souls. Rupert: The universal Church has been cleansed from every sin by the blood of Christ. Bernard also received this doctrine about the members of the Church, handed down by the Fathers, with great faith and integrity, and handed it on to posterity. For he teaches thus: {b}The Church herself is the bride of the elect, of whom the Apostle says, "All things for the sake of the elect." And what is the bride? Only the assembly of the righteous; what is she? Only the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the bridegroom. And again, thus: Charity does not fail from the Church. The Church is founded upon the rock, and the rock is Christ. Therefore neither the wordiness of philosophers, nor the cavils of heretics, nor the swords of persecutors could or ever can separate them from the love of Christ. Nicholas of Lyra taught the same on those words: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. {e}From this, says Lyra, it is clear that the Church does not consist of men by reason of power, or of ecclesiastical or secular dignity, since many princes and supreme pontiffs, and others of lower rank, have been found to have apostatized from the faith. Therefore the Church consists of those persons in whom there is true knowledge and confession of the faith and of the truth. So Lyra. How aptly, how ingenuously has he followed the light amid thick darkness, unlike these dim-witted men who go astray in the clearest light of the Gospel! Therefore, in Lyra's judgment, the Church does not consist of those in whom there is no inward virtue. John Wycliffe, our Merton man, reports that this opinion, which had imagined that wicked, even damned, men are members of the Catholic Church, was first introduced among the private opinions of the friars. I will give his words in English, as they were written: Friars destroy this article of Christian men's faith, I believe in the holy catholic Church. For they teach that men who shall be damned are members of the holy Church. And thus they wed Christ and the devil together. That is, the friars destroy this article of the Christian faith, "I believe the holy catholic Church." For they teach that men who are to be damned are members of the holy Church, and so they join the Devil to Christ in marriage. Thus Wycliffe marks the origin of this error, which he shows was first brought in by the friars, whom he testifies to have joined Christ to the Devil in a horrible marriage. Those who teach that members of the Church, who are also members of Christ, are without any inward virtue cannot escape this absurdity in any way; for in this way they join the members of the Devil to Christ too. Gratian, in support of this opinion, also gathers certain passages from the ancient writers, to prove that the impious are separated from the Church by a wicked life. Gratian acknowledges that the doctrine of the Roman Church was far different in the age in which he wrote from what the Jesuits now promulgate about the members of the Church. We have spoken of the first property of the Church: the Church is holy. This holiness is in the members, by which all things are sanctified by the holy Head. But the members of the Roman Church, which have no inward virtue, are not sanctified by the holy Head. Therefore that Roman Church is not the one which we profess in the Creed to be holy. It remains that we consider the next mark.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Credo Ecclesiam Catholicam.
units.tr: I believe the Catholic Church.

units.la: DE Catholica Ecclesia controuersia est inter Catholicam Ecclesiam, & Tridentinos. Vt veritas illustrius appareat, apponemus Bellarmini verba, quæ catholicam Catholicæ Ecclesiæ descriptionem continent. Verba longiora sunt, sed quia doctrinam Tridentinam, quam stabilire volunt, maxime subuertunt, subiungenda sunt. Sic enim scribit:
units.tr: The controversy over the Catholic Church lies between the Catholic Church and the Tridentines. To make the truth clearer, we will set out the words of Bellarmine, which contain his description of the Catholic Church. The passage is rather long, but since it greatly undermines the Tridentine doctrine they wish to establish, it must be quoted in full. He writes as follows:

units.la: {a}Ecclesia vere Catholica non solum debet amplecti omnia tempora, sed etiam omnia loca, omnes nationes, omnia hominum genera. Sic enim explicat, quid sit, esse Catholicum, Vincentius Lirinensis in suo commonitorio: ubi dicit, eos proprie esse Catholicos, qui tenent id, quod semper, quod ubique, quod ab omnibus creditum est. Et sic prædictum erat Psalm.
units.tr: {a}The Church that is truly Catholic ought to embrace not only all times, but also all places, all nations, and all kinds of men. For Vincent of Lérins, in his Commonitorium, explains what it means to be Catholic in this way: he says that those are properly Catholic who hold that which has been believed always, everywhere, and by all. And so it was foretold in the Psalm,

units.la: 2. Dabo tibi gentes hereditatem tuam, & possessionem tuam terminos terræ. Sunt autem aliqua observanda, antequam ex hac nota argumentum deprompamus. Primum est ex Augustino, de veritate Ecclesiæ, sap.6.[?] & Beda, cap.6. Cant. Vt Ecclesia sit Catholica, impri-
units.tr: 2. "I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession." But there are some things to be observed before we draw an argument from this mark. The first comes from Augustine, On the Truth of the Church, chapter 6, and from Bede on Canticles, chapter 6: that for the Church to be Catholic, it must first be required that it exclude no times, places, or kinds of men.

units.la: inprimis requiri, vt non excludat vlla tempora, loca, vel hominum genera. In quo distinguitur à synagoga, quæ erat Ecclesia particularis, non catholica, quia erat all[?]gate vni tempori, id est, vsque ad aduentum Messiæ: item vni loco, id est, templo Solomonis, & vni familiæ, id est, filijs Iacob.
