Secundo, nota ex Augustino, Epist. 80. vt sit Ecclesia Catholica, non requiri, vt sit in omnibus hominibus totius mundi: sed tantum, vt innotescat omnibus prouincijs, & in omnibus fructificet: ita vt in omnibus prouincijs aliqui sint de Ecclesia. Tertio, ex Driedane, lib. 4. cap. 2. par. 2. Eccles. dogm. nota, non requiri, vt hoc fiat simul, ita vt uno tempore in omnibus provincijs necessario esse oporteat aliquos fideles; satis est enim, si fiat successiuè. Ex quo id sequitur, quod si sola vna prouincia retineret veram fidem, adhuc vere & proprie diceretur Ecclesia Catholica, dammodo clare offenderetur, eam esse vnam & eandem cum illa, quæ fuit aliquo tempore, vel diuersis in toto mundo. Quemadmodum nunc quælibet diœcesis dicitur catholica, quia est continuata cum aliis, quæ faciunt vnam Ecclesiam Catholicam. Vltimo nota, quod, etsi Ecclesia non necessario debuit simul esse in omnibus locis, tamen hoc tempore debet necessario vel esse, vel fuisse in maiori parte orbis terrarum: quia Ecclesia iam senuit. Hactenus Bellarminus.
units.tr: In this it is distinguished from the synagogue, which was a particular Church and not a Catholic one, because it was bound to one time, that is, until the coming of the Messiah; likewise to one place, that is, the temple of Solomon; and to one family, that is, the sons of Jacob. Second, note from Augustine, Letter 80, that for a Church to be Catholic it is not required that it be among all the men of the whole world, but only that it become known in all provinces and bear fruit in all of them, so that in every province there are some who belong to the Church. Third, from Driedo, On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, book 4, chapter 2, part 2: it is not required that this happen all at once, so that at one time there must necessarily be believers in all provinces; it is enough if it happens successively. From this it follows that if only one province kept the true faith, it would still be truly and properly called the Catholic Church, just as it is clear that it is one and the same with the Church that existed at some time or at different times throughout the whole world. In the same way, every diocese is now called catholic because it is joined with the others, which together make up one Catholic Church. Lastly, note that although the Church did not necessarily have to be in all places at once, nevertheless at this time it must necessarily be, or have been, in the greater part of the world, since the Church has now grown old. So far Bellarmine.

units.la: Si hanc Catholicæ Ecclesiæ delcriptionem recipiamus, Ecclesia nunc Romana nullo modo Catholica erit: quia tenet id, quod nec semper, nec vbique, nec ab omnibus creditum est: quia non retinet veram fidem: quia deniq in tot agnof
units.tr: If we accept this description of the Catholic Church, the present Roman Church will in no way be Catholic: because it holds that which has not been believed always, nor everywhere, nor by all; because it does not retain the true faith; because, finally, in so many ...

units.la: De mus, vnitatis de ho Ecclesiæ Boemiam, piam. Hæc bane licam per o tur. Nec tholi credi atq; qua Ecclesia na, a Vnit nis h quæ que latit pon rum net omn
units.tr: [Units of this passage are badly garbled in the scan; the sense can only be guessed: the author continues to argue, with reference to the unity of the Church, Bohemia and the Bohemian brethren, that the Roman Church is not Catholic, and that the consensus of the Church is not found in the Roman party.]

units.la: Et deniq; non est vna atq; eadem cum illa, quam in toto mundo Catholicam fuisse, omnes agnoscimus.
units.tr: And finally, it is not one and the same with that Church which, as we all acknowledge, was Catholic throughout the whole world.

units.la: De Romana antiqua Ecclesia non dubitamus, quin cum Catholica consensum atque vnitatem retinuerit. Omnis controuersia est de hodierna Romana Ecclesia, a Catholica Ecclesia, inquit Bellarminus, praeter Italiam, Hispaniam, Galliam, Germaniam, Angliam, Poloniam, Boëmiam, Hungariam, Graciam, Syriam, Æthiopiam, Ægyptum, in ipso nouo orbe habet Ecclesias. Hæc ille. Putat Bellarminus, sufficere ad probandum, Ecclesiam nunc Romanam Catholicam esse, si Iesuitæ, & Tridentina pars aliqua per omnes istas prouincias dispersi inueniantur. Nos etiam in omnibus istis prouinciis Catholicam vel esse, vel fuisse, vel futuram esse credimus; sed non nisi in illis, qui consensum atq; vnitatem retinent cum illa Ecclesia antiqua, quam Catholicam fuisse constat. Nam Ecclesia vna est, atq; eadem, quia vna doctrina, atque eadem fidei regula perpetuo manet. Vnitas autem Ecclesiæ non consistit in personis hominum, qui mutantur, sed in doctrina, quæ semper vna eademque permanet. Itaque Ecclesia Catholica dicitur non tantum à latitudine sua, quia nec locis certis, nec temporibus alligata est, sicut erat synagoga, verum etiam, & maxime à doctrina, quia tenet id, quod semper, quod vbique, quod ab omnibus creditum est, inquit Vincentius. Et Tertullianus de Marcione & Valentino scri-
units.tr: Concerning the ancient Roman Church we do not doubt that it kept the consensus and unity of the Catholic Church. The whole controversy concerns the present-day Roman Church. "The Catholic Church," says Bellarmine, "apart from Italy, Spain, France, Germany, England, Poland, Bohemia, Hungary, Greece, Syria, Ethiopia, and Egypt, has churches even in the New World." So he writes. Bellarmine thinks it is enough to prove that the present Roman Church is Catholic if Jesuits and some part of the Tridentine party are found dispersed through all those provinces. We too believe that the Catholic Church is, or was, or will be, in all those provinces; but only among those who keep consensus and unity with that ancient Church which is known to have been Catholic. For the Church is one and the same, because its doctrine and the rule of faith remain one and the same forever. The unity of the Church does not consist in the persons of men, who change, but in doctrine, which remains always one and the same. Therefore the Church is called Catholic not only from its breadth, because it is bound neither to fixed places nor to fixed times, as the synagogue was, but above all from its doctrine, because it holds that which has always, everywhere, and by all been believed, as Vincent says. And Tertullian, writing about Marcion and Valentinus, says:

units.la: scribens, sic ait: {a}a Constat, illos Catholicos primum doctrinam credidisse apud Ecclesiam Romanensem. Non vocat Tertullianus Romanam Ecclesiam, Catholicam, sed Ecclesiam quidem Romanensem, doctrinam autem catholicam. Quanquam verum sit, Ecclesiam esse, & dici Catholicam, quæcunque fidem Catholicam profitetur; quia singulæ Ecclesiæ ad Catholicam pertinent, quatenus vnitatem fidei cum Catholica tenent. Eligant iam Pontifices, quocunque velint sensu Catholicam dici, & Ecclesia nunc Romana non erit Catholica.
units.tr: "It is established that those Catholics first believed the doctrine in the Church of the Romans." Tertullian does not call the Roman Church Catholic, but calls it the Church of the Romans, and the doctrine Catholic. Although it is true that whatever church professes the Catholic faith is a Church and is called Catholic, since each church belongs to the Catholic Church insofar as it keeps unity of faith with the Catholic Church. Let the Pontiffs now choose in whatever sense they wish that it be called Catholic, and the present Roman Church will not be Catholic.

units.la: Ecclesia igitur vel catholica est, vel particularis. Catholica est, quæ in Symbolo describitur, sancta catholica, sanctorum communio. Hæc est, quæ ædificatur super petram, Matth. 16 18. super doctrinam Prophetarum & Apostolorum, Ephes. 2.20. Est corpus Christi, & complementum eius, qui omnia implet in omnibus, Ephes. 1.23. Quæ sursum est Hierusalem, quæ est mater omnium nostrum, Gal. 4. 26. Sancta ciuitas, Hierusalem noua, descendens de cælo, à Deo parata, vt sponsa ornata viro suo: in qua nihil intrat coinquinatum, aut abominandum, sed qui scripti sunt in libro vitæ agni: Apocalyp. 21. 2. 27. Ita Catholicam describunt Scripturæ.
units.tr: A Church is therefore either catholic or particular. The catholic Church is that which is described in the Creed: "the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints." This is the Church which is built upon the rock (Matt. 16:18), upon the doctrine of the Prophets and Apostles (Eph. 2:20). It is the body of Christ and the fullness of him who fills all in all (Eph. 1:23). It is the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all (Gal. 4:26). It is the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband, into which nothing unclean or abominable enters, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life (Rev. 21:2, 27). Thus the Scriptures describe the Catholic Church.

units.la: Particularis Ecclesiæ (siue vnius ciuitatis siue prouinciæ, siue vnius integræ sit gentis) descriptio peti potest ex Rom. 1. 2. quo loco Apostolus Ecclesiam Iudaicam breuiter de-
units.tr: A description of a particular Church (whether of one city or of one province, or of one whole nation) can be drawn from Rom. 3:2, where the Apostle briefly describes the Jewish Church,

units.la: ferib[?] Dei. Dei tum. Tali men Eccl rum de d lum ritat sibi, dita nes, fia la ba p lis q irrit dit, les fi cieta re, c 3. E mut diui xam lum quia quia bom infe mm [?]scribit, vbi docet, illis credita fuisse eloquia Dei. Non dicit, creditum illis fuisse verbum Dei tantum, λόγον [?]: nec Sacramenta tantum, τὰ μυστήρια: sed oracula Dei, τὰ λόγια Θεοῦ. Tali verbo utitur, quod & verbum & Sacramenta comprehendat. Ita Apostolus docet, Ecclesiam esse cœlestis thesauri, verbi nimirum & Sacramentorum custodem. Ac proinde docet idem Apostolus, Ecclesiam esse columnam, & firmamentum veritatis, quia veritatem in verbo & Sacramentis concreditam sibi, firma fide custodit. Huius igitur fidei credita sunt, non humana dogmata aut traditiones, sed divina oracula. De particulari Ecclesia loqui Apostolum, ac non de catholica, verba proxime sequentia euincunt: Quid si in illis quidam non crediderunt, num fidem Dei irritam reddiderunt? Quibus verbis ostendit, 1. In omni externo cœtu malos & infideles fidelibus commissos esse. 2. Malorum societatem externam non posse fidelibus nocere, qui in divinis promissionibus recumbunt. 3. Ecclesiam veram, id est, vere credentes in mundo consistere, non humana politia, sed divina virtute, fidei Dei, hoc est, veritati innixam. Fides autem Dei commendatur, non solum, quia Deus fidelis est, qui promisit, sed quia promisit fidem Ecclesiae. a Promisit, Inquit Augustinus, quasi se facturus erat, non quod homines erant facturi, quando Abrahae promiserat, in semine eius fidem Genitum. Quia etsi faciunt boni, ipse tamen facit, ut faciant, quae praecipit.
units.tr: ... (the rest of the sentence is lost in the scan) ... writes, where he teaches that the oracles of God were entrusted to them. He does not say that only the word of God [λόγον] was entrusted to them, nor only the sacraments [τὰ μυστήρια], but the oracles of God [τὰ λόγια Θεοῦ]. He uses a term that embraces both the word and the sacraments. So the Apostle teaches that the Church is the keeper of the heavenly treasure, namely of the word and the sacraments. And accordingly the same Apostle teaches that the Church is the pillar and ground of the truth (1 Tim. 3:15), because it guards with firm faith the truth committed to it in the word and sacraments. Therefore what was entrusted to this faith was not human dogmas or traditions, but divine oracles. That the Apostle is speaking of a particular Church, and not of the catholic one, is shown by the words that immediately follow: "What if some did not believe? Will their unbelief make the faith of God without effect?" By these words he shows, first, that bad and unbelieving men are committed to the faithful in every external assembly; second, that the external fellowship of the wicked cannot harm the faithful, who rest on God's promises; third, that the true Church, that is, those who truly believe, stands in the world not by human polity but by divine power, resting on the faithfulness of God, that is, on truth. Now the faithfulness of God is commended not only because God is faithful who has promised, but because he has promised faithfulness to the Church. "He promised," says Augustine, "as if he himself were going to do it, and not because men were going to do it, when he promised Abraham that in his seed the nations would be blessed. For even if good men act, it is he himself who makes them act in the things he commands."

units.la: a lib. 1. de praedestin. sanct. pit, alioquin, vt Dei promissa compleantur[?], non in Dei, sed in hominum esse potestate. Hæc Augustinus. Hæc est fides Dei, per quam Ecclesia consistit: quæ fides Dei irrita esse non potest, quamuis multi homines vani, superbi, auari, fraudulenti, inueniantur in cœtibus Ecclesiasticis omnibus, quales sunt particulares Ecclesiæ.
units.tr: From Augustine, On the Predestination of the Saints, book 1: "Otherwise, so that God's promises may be fulfilled, the matter would lie in the power of men, not of God." Thus Augustine. This is the faithfulness of God, through which the Church stands. This faithfulness of God cannot be void, although many men who are vain, proud, greedy and deceitful are found in all Church assemblies, such as the particular churches.

units.la: Itaque describi potest Ecclesia particularis, quod sit cœtus hominum visibilis, qui per externam verbi prædicationem, & Sacramentorum administrationem, ad internam communionem sanctorum ducitur. Hæc descriptio succincte continet ea omnia, quæ in aliorum descriptionibus fusius ponuntur. Nam communio sanctorum necessaria videtur in Ecclesiæ descriptione. 1. Quia ponitur in Symbolo: neque enim particularis Ecclesia vera Christi Ecclesia dici, aut esse potest, nisi quatenus cum Catholica vnitatem retinet. Vnitas autem, quam particulares Ecclesiæ cum Catholica habent, est vnitas Capitis, vnitas Corporis, vnitas doctrinæ, vnitas spiritus: sicut ostendemus eo loco, quo de vnitate Ecclesiæ Catholicæ disputabitur. Hæc vero omnia paucissimis verbis collecta, communio sanctorum continet. Ac proinde sine hac communione sanctorum non commode potest particularis Ecclesia ita describi, vt hæc vnitas cum Catholica retineatur, sine qua vnitate Ecclesia esse non potest. 2. Quia fallax illa Ecclesiæ descriptio per partem Tridenti-nam nam posita, paucissimis illis verbis facillime, & vere refellitur. Vident enim, in Ecclesiæ definitione exprimendam esse connexionem membrorum cum Capite, itaque communionem sanctorum reiiciunt, & pro ea novam atque inauditam communionem habituunt cum Romano Pontifice, tanquam cum Ecclesiæ Capite. At connexionem hanc, quam habet Ecclesia cum Capite, perfecte continet, atque optime explicat communionem sanctorum. 3. Quia hæc duo verba Pontificiorum exceptiones tollunt. Quanquam enim verum sit, quod docent nostri, id est, Catholici veteres ac recentes, Ecclesiam constare ex electis: quia tamen Pontifices exclamant, Ecclesiam in terris militantem, esse visibilem certum: ut offendiculis obturemus, & tamen Catholicorum omnium sententiam retineamus, communionem sanctorum in hac descriptione ponamus: ita idem efficitur, ac si electos solos posuissemus, quia non est hæc communio, nisi inter electos. Et Pontificis rixandi ansa præripitur: quia enim fronte ab Ecclesiæ descriptione reiicere possunt ea verba, quæ ad Ecclesiæ descriptionem illustrandam in Symbolo Apostolorum retinentur. Iam vero videamus, quantum errent Pontifices in Ecclesia describenda.
units.tr: A particular Church may therefore be described as a visible assembly of men, which is led by the external preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments to the inward communion of saints. This description briefly contains all the things that other descriptions set out at greater length. For the communion of saints seems necessary in the description of the Church, for three reasons: (1) it is set down in the Creed, for a particular Church cannot be called, or be, a true Church of Christ unless it retains unity with the Catholic Church. The unity that particular churches have with the Catholic Church is the unity of the Head, the unity of the Body, the unity of doctrine and the unity of the Spirit, as we shall show in the place where the unity of the Catholic Church is discussed. All these things, gathered together in very few words, the communion of saints contains. Therefore without this communion of saints a particular Church cannot fitly be described in such a way that this unity with the Catholic Church is retained, and without that unity the Church cannot exist. (2) The false description of the Church given by the Tridentine party is very easily and truly refuted by these few words. For they see that the connection of the members with the Head must be expressed in the definition of the Church, and so they reject the communion of saints and in its place invent a new and unheard-of communion with the Roman Pontiff, as though with the Head of the Church. But the connection that the Church has with its Head is fully contained in, and best explained by, the communion of saints. (3) These two words remove the Papists' exceptions. For although it is true, as our people teach (that is, the Catholics, both ancient and recent), that the Church consists of the elect, yet because the Pontiffs cry out that the Church militant on earth is visible, in order to block their stumbling-blocks and still keep the opinion of all Catholics, we set the communion of saints in this description. Thus the result is the same as if we had put only the elect, because this communion exists only among the elect. And the Pontiff's occasion for quarrelling is taken away, since they can openly reject from the description of the Church those words which are retained in the Apostles' Creed to illustrate the description of the Church. Now let us see how greatly the Pontiffs err in describing the Church.

units.la: Bellarminiana itaque definitio illa erronea est in plurimis. 1. Quia quum Catholicam definire profitetur, particularem descriptit.
units.tr: Bellarmine's definition is therefore erroneous in many respects. (1) Although he professes to define the Catholic Church, he describes a particular one.

units.la: 2. Quia, quam ille describit, [illegible, ~10 letters] vnicam esse affirmat, quæ errare non possit; quum particularis omnis errare possit. 3. Quod Christianæ fidei professionem requirat, & Sacramentorum communionem, suscipimus quidem hanc sententiam, modo recte explicetur. Professionem autem intelligit Bellarminus, quamcunque probat Romanus Pontifex: at vero fidei professionem, & Sacramentorum communionem, ad verbi diuini normam, non ad Romani Pontificis nutum revocandam credimus. 4. Quod membra Ecclesiæ externa tantum professione designet, & Sacramentorum communione, quæ sensu ipso percipitur. Nam docuimus è Scripturis, atque Ecclesiæ consensu, membra Ecclesiæ esse sanctos homines, qui veris virtutibus lucent. 5. Quod in Ecclesia Catholica Romani Pontificis regimen statuat. Si de particulari Ecclesia Romana loquatur, concedimus in ea regimen Romani Pontificis, quamdiu ille in verbi & Sacramentorum administratione erectus consistit. Catholica autem Romani Pontificis regimen non agnoscit. 6. Quod Romanum Pontificem Christi in terris Vicarium affirmat. Hæc sunt in Ecclesia definienda Pontificiorum postulata, quæ somniando optare solent, disputando probare non possunt.
units.tr: (2) The one he describes he affirms to be the only one that cannot err, whereas every particular church can err. (3) In requiring a profession of Christian faith and communion in the sacraments, we indeed accept this opinion, provided it is rightly explained. But Bellarmine understands by profession whatever the Roman Pontiff approves; we, however, believe that the profession of faith and the communion in the sacraments must be referred to the norm of the divine Word, not to the nod of the Roman Pontiff. (4) He designates the members of the Church only by external profession and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses. For we have taught from Scripture and from the consensus of the Church that the members of the Church are holy men who shine with true virtues. (5) He posits in the Catholic Church the government of the Roman Pontiff. If he speaks of the particular Church of Rome, we concede in it the government of the Roman Pontiff, for as long as he stands upright in the administration of the Word and sacraments. But the Catholic Church does not acknowledge the government of the Roman Pontiff. (6) He affirms the Roman Pontiff to be Christ's Vicar on earth. These are the demands of the Papists for defining the Church: they are accustomed to wish for them in their dreams, but they cannot prove them in debate.

units.la: De particularibus loquitur Scriptura, 1. Cor. 1. 2. Ecclesia, quæ est Corinthi. Sic Ecclesiæ Galatæ memorantur, Gal. 1. 2. & Ecclesia Thessalonicensium, 1. Thess. 1. 1. Huiusmodi erant septem illæ Ecclesiæ in Asia, de quibus 1. & 2. Apocal. Talis erat Ecclesia Romana, Rom.1.6.7. Quia vero in qualibet particulari Ecclesia boni sunt malis commixti, huiusmodi cœtus à Christo assimulantur agro, in quem quum bonum semen iactum fuerat, hominibus dormientibus zizania ab inimico seminantur, & verriculo in mare coniecto, atque omne genus piscium attrahens. Matth.13.
units.tr: Scripture speaks of particular churches: the Church which is at Corinth, 1 Cor. 1.2. So the churches of Galatia are mentioned, Gal. 1.2, and the Church of the Thessalonians, 1 Thess. 1.1. Such were the seven churches in Asia of which Rev. 1 and 2 speak. Such was the Church at Rome, Rom. 1.6-7. But because in any particular church good men are mixed with bad, Christ compares such assemblies to a field in which, when good seed had been sown, tares were sown by the enemy while men slept; and to a dragnet cast into the sea, gathering every kind of fish. Matt. 13.

units.la: Hæc distinctio inter catholicam & particularem Ecclesiam, e Scripturis manifestis confirmata, adeo illustris est, ac necessaria, ut eam Bellarminus ipse non potuerit non probare. {a}Aliud est, inquit, errare, & parum esse ad discendum, & quum didicerit ad obediendum: aliud nolle discere, & quum audierit veritatem, nolle acquiescere. Neutrum esse potest in Ecclesia universali, in Ecclesia autem particulari potest esse illud primum, in neutra autem illud secundum, sed solum in synagogis[?] Satanæ, & Ecclesia malignantium. Hæc ille. Agnoscimus distinctionem universalis & particularis e Scripturis exceptam, à Patribus traditam, ab ipsis Aduersariis approbatam, accelebratam. Neque vero duas, aut diuersas Ecclesias ponimus, sed vnicam tantum. Nam omnes particulares Ecclesiæ sunt Ecclesiæ, quatenus cum Catholica communicant; non aliter. Ad hanc formam examinabimus Ecclesiam nunc Romanam. De membris Ecclesiæ diximus: de communione membrorum cum capite, & inter se, deinceps est dicendum, in Communione sanctorum. Hoc autem loco ex Patribus partim Catholicae Ecclesiae, partim Romanae Ecclesiae descriptionem quaeremus. Sive enim Catholicam per orbem ubique dispersam, sive Romanam suis [finitibus?] comprehensam describant Patres: illud facile constabit, nec Romanam esse Catholicam, nec Catholicam Romanam. Catholicam igitur sic describere solent Patres.
units.tr: This distinction between the catholic and the particular Church, confirmed from manifest Scriptures, is so clear and so necessary that Bellarmine himself could not help but prove it: "It is one thing, he says, to err, and to be too little taught, and when taught, to obey; it is another to be unwilling to learn, and when one has heard the truth, to be unwilling to assent. Neither of these can be in the universal Church; in a particular Church the former can be, but in neither the latter, but only in the synagogues of Satan and the church of the evildoers." Thus he. We acknowledge the distinction between universal and particular, drawn from Scripture, handed down by the Fathers, and approved and celebrated even by the adversaries themselves. Nor do we posit two or different Churches, but only one. For all particular churches are Churches insofar as they communicate with the Catholic Church, and not otherwise. By this standard we will now examine the Church of Rome. We have spoken of the members of the Church; of the communion of the members with the Head and with one another, we must speak next, under the communion of saints. In this place, however, we shall seek from the Fathers a description, partly of the Catholic Church and partly of the Roman Church. For whether the Fathers describe the Catholic Church dispersed everywhere throughout the world, or the Roman Church contained within its own bounds, it will easily be established that the Roman Church is not Catholic, nor the Catholic Church Roman. So the Fathers are accustomed to describe the Catholic Church thus.

units.la: CAPUT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Continet testimonia Graecorum Patrum, de Ecclesia Catholica.
units.tr: Contains the testimonies of the Greek Fathers concerning the Catholic Church.

units.la: GRaeciae docente Origenes {a}Sol institia Christus est, huic si Luna, id est, Ecclesia sua, quae lumine ipsius repletur, multis fuerit, & penitus ei adhaeserit, tum festinuit atem Neomeniae agnus. Et mox: Tunc demum, scilicet, quando Ecclesia neque videri, neque comprehendi humanis affectibus potest. Sic Origenes Ecclesiam Catholicam descripsit. Quaerunt Pontifici ex Origene, reliquisque Patribus, quare Ecclesiam Catholicam dicant esse invisibilem: neque videri, neque comprehendi humanis aspectibus: & vel Patrum iudicia reiciant, vel nobis aequiores sint, qui Patrum doctrinam illibatam custodimus. Eusebius: {b}Per totum orbem terrarum Christi Ecclesia unius domus Dei locum obtinet. Basilius, qui de Catholica Ecclesia nunquam quaerebatur, graviter de Romana Ecclesia conqueritur: {c}Nullum eorum malo auxilium speran[?]ferendum ab Occidentali superciliō. Et quem locum Romano Pontifici nusquam concedit, cum facile S. Ambrosio concedit, vt Basilius, in primaria Apostolorum sede consulat, [illegible, ~12 letters] Quæ verba Basilii ad Ambrosium oblecnandō, quia probant primariam sedem in Ecclesia Catholica, non iure aliquo, aut prærogativa vni concessam, sed ex mutua charitate honorem hunc aliquando Romanis Episcopis, aliquando etiam aliis collarum.
units.tr: Origen, teaching in Greece, says: Christ is the Sun of righteousness; if the Moon, that is, his Church, which is filled with his light, is in many places and has clung to him closely, then the Lamb has hastened to the feast of the new moon. And soon after: Then at last, namely when the Church can be neither seen nor grasped by human senses. In this way Origen described the Catholic Church. Let the Papists and the other Fathers be asked why they call the Catholic Church invisible, one that cannot be seen or grasped by human senses. Either they must reject the judgments of the Fathers, or they must be more fair to us, who keep the Fathers' teaching unimpaired. Eusebius: Throughout the whole world the Church of Christ holds the place of one house of God. Basil, who was never questioned about the Catholic Church, complains bitterly about the Roman Church: None of them can hope for help to be brought to the evil from the Western haughtiness. He nowhere grants this to the Roman Pontiff, yet he readily grants it to Saint Ambrose, that Basil should consult him as the chief see of the Apostles. These words of Basil, when weighed carefully, prove that the primacy in the Catholic Church was not granted to one man by any right or prerogative, but that this honour was sometimes given to the Roman bishops out of mutual charity, and sometimes to others as well.

units.la: Cyrillus Hierosolymitanus: {b}Catholica vocatur, quia per vniuersum sit orbem terrarum dif-fusa, à finibus terræ vsque ad extrema: & quia docet catholicè, & quia in vniuersum curat omne genus peccatorum. Et mox: Hoc proprium nomen sanctæ huius, & nostræ omnium matris, quæ est sponsa Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Cyril of Jerusalem: The Church is called Catholic because it is spread throughout the whole world, from the ends of the earth to its farthest limits; and because it teaches universally, and because it heals every kind of sin. And soon after: This is the proper name of this holy Church, which is our mother of all, the bride of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Chrysostomus multa habet de Catholica, ex quibus constat, Romanam non esse Catholicam. Quædam subnectam ex Homilia de Pentecoste, vbi sic habet: {c}Multum Deo Ecclesia chara est, non maris circundata, sed fide circumsepta. Propter Ecclesiam namque extensum est cœlum, diffusum est mare, extensus aer, terra fundata est, paradisus plantatus est, mensuratur [?]tempo-rum qualitate, sed Spiritus eam fouet, gubernat gratia. Et ideo non senescit, non contrahitur, & multis impugnantibus, non opprimitur. Et tamen quidem, quum vndecim essent Apostoli, nullus eos superare potuit, sed pauci homines totum ceperunt mundum: & nunc, quando terra, & mare, & orbis terrarum, & inhabiles regiones, & civitates, & omnes fines terræ pietate replensi[?] sunt, putas eam te posse la-dere? Super hanc petram adificabo Ecclesiam meam, & portæ inferorum non pravalebunt adversus eam. Super hanc petram, non dixit, super Petrum: non enim super hominem, sed super fidem aedificavi Ecclesiam suam. Quid autem erat fides? Tu es Christus filius Dei vivi: Petram vocans Ecclesiam, stabilem suscipientem, & non titubantem. Etenim Ecclesia tot suscipit tentationes, non tamen vincitur. Quid est super petram? Hoc est, super confessionem, super sermones pietatis. Ubicunq; terr. ad Indos, ad Mauros, ad Britannos, ad Hispanos[?], usq; ad ultimum finem terrarum, inuenies Ecclesiam. Hæc Chrysostomus. Quæ subius[?] transcribenda censui, quia iuculenter[?] probant, Chrysostomi iudicio Romanam Ecclesiam non fuisse Catholicam: Ecclesiam Catholicam super petram ædificatam dicit, non super Petrum, super fidem, super confessionem veritatis fundatam, non super hominem, contra Tridentinos, qui nihil nisi Petrum & Papam sonare solent.
units.tr: Chrysostom has much about the Catholic Church, from which it is clear that the Roman Church is not Catholic. I shall add some passages from his homily on Pentecost, where he says: The Church is very dear to God; she is surrounded not by the sea but by faith, which fences her in. For the heaven was stretched out, the sea spread wide, the air extended, the earth founded, and paradise planted for the sake of the Church. She is measured by the quality of the times, but the Spirit cherishes her and grace guides her. Therefore she does not grow old, she is not diminished, and though many attack her, she is not overwhelmed. And indeed, when there were only eleven Apostles, no one could overcome them; yet a few men took hold of the whole world. And now, when land and sea and the whole circuit of the earth, and the uninhabitable regions and cities, and all the ends of the earth are filled with piety, do you think you can harm her? Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. He did not say "upon this rock," meaning upon Peter; for he did not build the Church upon a man but upon faith. And what was the faith? "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Calling the Church a rock, he meant that she is steadfast and does not waver. For the Church endures so many temptations and yet is not conquered. What is "upon the rock"? It means upon the confession, upon the words of piety. Wherever you go, to the Indians, to the Moors, to the Britons, to the Spaniards, to the farthest end of the earth, you will find the Church. So far Chrysostom. I have thought fit to transcribe these words in full, because they plainly prove that in Chrysostom's judgment the Roman Church was not Catholic: he says the Catholic Church is built upon a rock, not upon Peter; founded upon faith and the confession of the truth, not upon a man. This is against the Tridentines, who are accustomed to sound nothing but Peter and the Pope.

units.la: Sed obiiciunt ex Chrysostomo verba quædam Pontificii, quæ huic Chrysostomi loco contradicere videntur. Verba, quæ obiiciunt, sunt huiusmodi: {a}Ut Ecclesia tot tantùg; fluctibus impetu irrumpentibus immobilis maneat, cuius pastor & caput piscator homo, atq; ignobilis terrarum orbe reluctante, adamantu naturam firmitate superet. Et ad Hieremiam dicebat: Sicut columnam ferream, & sicut murum æneum posuite. Sed ipsum quidem gentis uni pater, hunc autem universo terraterrarum orbi Christus præposuit. Hæc ille. Ex quibus verbis colligunt, Petrum vocari caput Ecclesiæ, & vniuerso orbi præponi. Inde etiam Romani Pontificis prærogatiuam concludunt.
units.tr: But the Papists object to certain words of Chrysostom which seem to contradict this passage of his. The words they object are of this kind: That the Church may remain unmoved amid so many and such great waves rushing upon her, whose minister and head is a fisherman, a man of no rank, while the world of the earth strives against him, and who by his firmness surpasses the nature of adamant. And to Jeremiah he said: "I have made you a column of iron and a wall of bronze." But the one is the father of a single nation, while this man Christ placed over the whole world of the earth. That is what he says. From these words they gather that Peter is called the head of the Church and is set over the whole world. From this they also infer the prerogative of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Respondeo: Vt concedamus, hæc fuisse genuina Chrysostomi verba, non tamen attingunt Romanum Pontificem. Nam quæ Petro concessa erant à Christo, non solum omnibus æque Apostolis, sed in Petro etiam omnibus æque Episcopis concessa fuisse intelligunt antiqui Patres, sicut euidentibus constabit in testimonio Cypriani, omnibus etiam Ecclesiis, sicut habet Chrysostomus. Sed obseruato, quæso, insignem impudentiam istorum hominum, qui in [?] poluerunt spem suam. Nam in Latina Chrysostomi interpretatione homines nefarii verba illa interpolarunt [cum pastor & caput, piscator homo] vt probent, Petrum Ecclesiæ caput dici, Græca Chrysostomi verba nihil habent huiusmodi. Locus hic Græce sic legitur: καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἁλιέων ἐπέτρεψε πάσης ἀφορίζων τῆς οἰκουμένης πολέμους ἀπολειας, τοῦτο δὲ αὐτῷ ἐπαγγέλλεται [?]. Hæc Chrysostomus. In quibus verbis, nec caput Ecclesiæ, nec pastorem Ecclesiæ invenies; nec vniuersum terrarum orbem Petro subiectum. Atque hic est Pontificius candor, vt Patrum scripta nefariis manibus corrumpant, deinde ex corruptis & confictis scriptis simpliciores conturbent.
units.tr: I answer: even if we grant that these were Chrysostom's genuine words, they do not touch the Roman Pontiff. For the things that Christ granted to Peter were understood by the ancient Fathers to have been granted equally to all the Apostles, and in Peter equally to all bishops, as will be evident from the testimony of Cyprian, and to all the Churches, as Chrysostom also says. But, I beg you, notice the remarkable impudence of these men, who have placed their hope in corrupting the Fathers. For in the Latin translation of Chrysostom, wicked men have interpolated those words whose minister and head is a fisherman, a man, so that they may prove that Peter is called the head of the Church. The Greek words of Chrysostom contain nothing of this kind. The passage is read in Greek thus: [καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἁλιέων ἐπέτρεψε πάσης ἀφορίζων τῆς οἰκουμένης πολέμους ἀπολειας, τοῦτο δὲ αὐτῷ ἐπαγγέλλεται]. So Chrysostom says. In these words you will find neither a head of the Church nor a pastor of the Church, nor the whole world of the earth subjected to Peter. And this is Papist sincerity: they corrupt the writings of the Fathers with wicked hands, and then with corrupted and invented writings they disturb the simpler sort.

units.la: Theodoretus refert sententiam Constan-tini timi Magni, in hæc verba: {a}Unum Saluator noster universalem voluit esse Ecclesiam, quæ esset partibus in multas ac diversas loca distributa sic, nno tamen Spiritu, id est divino consilio fungitur[?]. Idemque Theodoretus verba refert Alexandri, Episcopi Alexand. huiusmodi: {b}Confitemur unam & solam Ecclesiam universalem, quam non totius mundi oppugnatio posset subvertere, perpetuo victricem seditiosa impietatis adversarium dogmatum. Hæc ille.
units.tr: Theodoret reports the opinion of Constantine the Great, in these words: Our Saviour willed that there should be one universal Church, which, though distributed into many and diverse places in its parts, is nevertheless governed by one Spirit, that is, by the divine counsel. Theodoret also reports the words of Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, of this kind: We confess one and only universal Church, which the assault of the whole world could not overthrow, always victorious over the seditious adversaries of impious doctrines. So he says.

units.la: Ita igitur docuerunt Græci Patres. Quum vero Græci Scriptores Catholicam matrem omnium nostrūm celebrent, num Romanam designant? Nihil minus. Orientales enim Ecclesiæ a Romana religionem ac fidem non acceperunt, sed Romanæ dederunt: nec quisquam Pontificiorum tantum unquam arrogare potuit, ut Romanam Ecclesiam diceret matrem Ecclesiarum in Oriente. Si autem Romana Ecclesia non sit illarum Ecclesiarum mater, profecto non est Catholica. Illæ enim Catholicam agnoscunt matrem suam. Nos vero eandem cum illis matrem agnoscimus Catholicam. Hactenus Græci; audiamus Latinos.
units.tr: Thus the Greek Fathers taught. But when Greek writers celebrate the Catholic mother of us all, do they mean the Roman Church? Least of all. For the Eastern Churches did not receive their religion and faith from the Roman Church; rather they gave theirs to Rome. Nor has any of the Papists ever been able to claim so much as to call the Roman Church the mother of the Churches in the East. If, then, the Roman Church is not the mother of those Churches, it certainly is not Catholic, for those Churches acknowledge the Catholic Church as their mother. We, indeed, acknowledge the same Catholic Church as mother together with them. So far the Greeks; let us hear the Latins.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Continet testimonia Latinorum Patrum, de Ecclesia Catholica, & de Ecclesia Romana.
units.tr: Contains the testimonies of the Latin Fathers concerning the Catholic Church and the Church of Rome.

units.la: Quatus[?] de Ecclesia Catholica sic disputat: {c}Ubi erit proprie Catholicæ nominis? Quum [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~4 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] [illegible, ~3 letters] [illegible, ~2 letters] Quum inde dicta sit Catholica, quia sit rationabilis, & vbique diffusa. Haec ille. Quum Donatistae in-[?]clarent Ecclesiam apud se fuisse, quod hodie faciunt Pontifici, interrogat eos Optatus. Si ergo voluntate vestra in angulum contracta Ecclesia, si vnius esse subducta gentibus, vbi rem illud quod Filius Dei mentit? [?] Tibi illam donaverit terra, cum gentibus totius orbis Christo, vnde possessio ... [illegible, ~12 letters] Haec ille. Probat, Ecclesiam Catholicam Christi haereditatem esse, non Romani Pontificis. Supra docuimus ex Optato, iudicem controversiarum in terris non esse quaerendum, sed Christum in Scriptura, iudicem in Ecclesia agnosci. Cyprianus etiam de Catholica sic scribit: {b} Non pauperum, nec Ecclesia vnius, aut vnius provinciae, sed totius orbis haec sanae est. Haec ille. At quicunque antiquitus de Romana Ecclesia scripserunt, vnius provinciae terminis eam claudere solebant. Alia est ergo Ecclesia Romana vnius provinciae, alia totius orbis.
units.tr: Quatus[?] disputes thus concerning the Catholic Church: {c} Where will the name "Catholic" properly be found? It is called Catholic because it is reasonable and spread everywhere. Thus he. When the Donatists claimed that the Church was with them, as the Papists do today, Optatus questions them: If therefore the Church has been drawn into a corner by your will, if it has been withdrawn to one people alone, where is that which the Son of God promised? ... the earth has given it to you, together with the nations of the whole world to Christ, whence the possession ... Thus he. He proves that the Catholic Church is the inheritance of Christ, not of the Roman pontiff. Above we showed from Optatus that the judge of controversies is not to be sought on earth, but that Christ is to be acknowledged in Scripture and the judge in the Church. Cyprian also writes thus about the Catholic Church: {b} This Church is sound, not of the poor, nor of one congregation or one province, but of the whole world. Thus he. But whoever wrote about the Roman Church in antiquity used to confine it within the bounds of a single province. The Roman Church of one province is therefore one thing, and the Church of the whole world another.

units.la: E Cypriano etiam adducunt Pontificii quaedam pro primatu Romani Pontificis, & Romanae Ecclesiae auctoritate. Sed quae adducuntur, aliud spectant. Negamus prorsus, vel primarum Romani Pontificis, vel auctoritatem Romanae Ecclesiae in alias concessam fuisse a Cypriano. Et quia Pontifices ex illis putant se probare, Ecclesiam suam Catholicam esse, examinanda sunt, quae producunt. Afferunt inprimis e Cypriano locum illum: {c}Nam enim aliunde haereses ortae sunt, aut natae schismata, quam inde, quod sacerdoti[?] Dei non obtemperatur, nec unus in Ecclesia ad tempus sacerdos & ad tempus Iudex vice Christi cogitatur. Hæc Cyprianus. Quæ quidem verba rapiunt Pontificii ad Romanum Pontificem, quem unum in Ecclesia Iudicem, unum sacerdotem intelligi volunt. Sed frustra: quia certissimum est, Cyprianum loqui non de Cornelio, ad quem scribit, sed de seipso, qui contemptus erat à Novatianis: & per totam Epistolam illam dolorem suum profert, quod criminarentur hæretici[?]: & quod hæreticorum calumniæ etiam apud Cornelium locum habere viderentur. Sic etiam a-pertissime de seipso scribit Epistola ad Pup-pianum, ubi eadem etiam verba refert: {a}In-decenter sibi fumata & horrida, inquit, obortæ sunt, & ornantur: dum Episcopus, qui unus est, & Ecclesiæ præest, superba quorundam præsumptione contemni-tur. Hæc Cyprianus non de Romano Pontifice, sed de seipso scribit, qui à Puppiano contemnebatur. Qui nostrum[?], inquit ibidem, longe est ab humilitate? Ego, qui quotidie fratribus inseruio, & venientes ad Ecclesiam, singulos benigne, & cum voto & gaudio suscipio: an tu, qui te Episcopum Episcopi, & Iudicem Iudicis ad tempus à Deo datis constituis? Quæ verba superioribus similima exponunt locum superiorem, & liquido demonstrant, Cyprianum seipsum vocare iudicem vice Christi ad tempus in Ecclesia. Quod autem de se in sua provincia sentit, idem etiam de quovis alio Episcopo (non de Romano tantum) in sua provincia iudicat. {b}Nam Episcoporum vnum est, inquit, Episcoporum multo-rum, concordi numero stirare[?] diffusum. Et: a Episco-{a}patu vnum est, cuius à singulis in solidum pars tenetur. Itaque eodem libro, de vnitate Ecclesiæ, Vnitatem, inquit, firmiter tenere & vindicare debemus, maxime Episcopi, qui in Ecclesia præsidemus, vt Episcopatum quoq; vnum atq; indivisum præbe-mus. Ac proinde eodem libro vnam[?] cathedram constituì, docet, & vnitatis eiusdem originem ab vno incipientem. Quem locum Pontificii magno applausu ad Romani Pontificis primatum stabiliendum rapere solent: sed frustra.
units.tr: The Papists also bring forward certain passages from Cyprian in support of the primacy of the Roman pontiff and the authority of the Roman Church. But what they adduce concerns something else. We utterly deny that Cyprian conceded either a primacy to the Roman pontiff or authority to the Roman Church over the others. And because the pontiffs think they prove from these passages that their Church is Catholic, what they produce must be examined. First they bring up that passage of Cyprian: {c} For heresies have arisen from elsewhere, and schisms have been born, than from this, that the priest of God is not obeyed, nor is one priest in the Church thought of for the time, and one judge in the place of Christ. Thus Cyprian. The Papists snatch these words for the Roman pontiff, whom they want to be understood as the one judge and one priest in the Church. But in vain: for it is most certain that Cyprian is not speaking about Cornelius, to whom he writes, but about himself, who was despised by the Novatians. Throughout that letter he expresses his grief that the heretics slandered him, and that the calumnies of the heretics seemed to have a place even with Cornelius. Likewise, most plainly, he writes about himself in the letter to Puppianus, where he also repeats these same words: {a} Indecently, he says, smoky and horrid things have arisen, and they are adorned, while the bishop, who is one and presides over the Church, is despised by the arrogant presumption of certain people. Cyprian writes this not about the Roman pontiff but about himself, who was despised by Puppianus. Who among us, he says in the same place, is far from humility? I, who daily serve the brethren, and receive those coming to the Church, each one kindly, and with prayer and joy; or you, who make yourself bishop of bishops and judge of a judge, for a time given by God? These words, very like the preceding ones, explain the earlier passage and clearly show that Cyprian calls himself a judge in the place of Christ for a time in the Church. What he thinks of himself in his own province, he judges equally of any other bishop (not only the Roman) in his province. {b} For the episcopate is one, he says, of many bishops, spread out in a harmonious number. And: the episcopate is one, of which a part is held in full by each individual. So in the same book, On the Unity of the Church, he says: we ought firmly to hold and defend unity, especially we bishops who preside in the Church, so that we may show the episcopate also to be one and undivided. And accordingly in the same book he teaches that one chair has been established, and that the origin of this same unity begins from one. The Papists are wont to snatch this passage with great applause to establish the primacy of the Roman pontiff, but in vain.

units.la: Nam: hoc, inquit, erant cæteri Apostoli, quod fuit Petrus, pari consortio prædití, & honoris, & potestatis, sed exordium ab vnitate proficiscitur. Primatus Petro datur, vt vna Christi Ecclesia, & cathedra una monstretur. Ad hæc verba exultant Pontificii, & se[?] primatum Romani Pontificis hinc certo probasse confidunt.
units.tr: For: "The other apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership both of honour and of power, but the beginning proceeds from unity. A primacy is given to Peter so that one Church of Christ and one chair may be shown." At these words the Papists exult, and they confidently believe that they have surely proved the primacy of the Roman pontiff from them.

units.la: Respondeo: Cyprianus ex his verbis probat vnitatem Episcoporum omnium; non primatum vnius: neque magis[?] ad Romanum Episcopum pertinent hæc verba, quam ad quemvis alium Episcopum. Nam quæ Petro dicta sunt à Christo, non ad vnum Romanum, sed ad omnes æque Episcopos dicta contendit Cyprianus: ita vt non plus Romanus Episcopus à Petro habuerit, quam Cyprianus, aut quiuis alius Episcopus: non hic commentum meum, sed Cypriani sententiam explico: & nisi hanc sententiam ex ipsius Cypriani verbis euincam, reiiciendam iudicabo.
units.tr: I reply: from these words Cyprian proves the unity of all bishops, not the primacy of one; nor do these words pertain to the Roman bishop any more than to any other bishop. For Cyprian contends that what was said by Christ to Peter was said equally to all bishops, not only to the Roman, so that the Roman bishop had no more from Peter than Cyprian or any other bishop. I am not presenting my own invention here but explaining Cyprian's opinion; and unless I establish this opinion from Cyprian's own words, I shall judge it to be rejected.

units.la: {a} lib. de vnit. Eccles.
units.tr: {a} From the book On the Unity of the Church.

units.la: Cyprianus ergo sic scribit: a Dominus noster, unius praecepta metuere, & observare debemus, Episcopi honorem, & Ecclesiae suae[?] rationem disponens, in Evangelio loquitur, & dicit Petro: Ego tibi dico, quia tu es Petrus, & super istam petram aedificabo Ecclesiam meam, &c. Inde per temporum & successionum vices Episcoporum ordinatio, & Ecclesiae ratio decurrit, vt Ecclesia super Episcopos, & omnis actus Ecclesiae per eosdem praepositos gubernetur. Haec Cyprianus. Quibus verbis armatura omnem è Pontificiorum manibus valida manu extorquet, & quem locum Scripturae isti adducere solent, ad Romani Pontificis primatum stabiliendum, Cyprianus differre ad omnes aeque Episcopos pertinere probat: omnes aeque Petro succedere in hoc, nec quicquam supra reliquos Romanum Pontificem à Petro habere. Non dicit Cyprianus, istis verbis Dominum Romani Episcopi honorem, sed Episcopi honorem, & Ecclesiae rationem disponere: neque inde Romani Episcopi ordinationem, sed Episcoporum omnium ordinationem, & Ecclesiae rationem decurrere: nec vt inde super Romanum Episcopum, sed super omnes Episcopos actum Ecclesiae, & praeposituram probari. Est ergo vnus Episcopus, vnus iudex, vnus Episcopatus[?], vna Cathedra. Ex verbis autem Christi ad Petrum, nihil omnino Cypriani iudicio probari potest, nisi vnitas, & aequalitas Episcoporum omnium. Haec Episcoporum vnitas mirifice demonstrat communionem sanctorum, quae tunc huic[?] in Ecclesia viguit: nunc vero per Rome-[?]ni Pontificis factum, proh dolor, conculcatur. Idem enim egit primatus Pontificis, ut hæc unitas Ecclesiæ, & communio inter Episcopos, penitus ab Ecclesia exulet.
units.tr: Cyprian therefore writes thus: Our Lord, whose precepts we ought to fear and observe, disposing the honour of the bishop and the order of his Church, speaks in the Gospel and says to Peter: I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, etc. From this, through the succession of times and of successors, the ordination of bishops and the order of the Church descend, so that the Church is governed over the bishops, and every act of the Church by the same appointed leaders. Thus Cyprian. With these words he wrests from the hands of the Papists, with a strong arm, every weapon, and he proves that the passage of Scripture which they are wont to bring forward to establish the primacy of the Roman pontiff pertains equally to all bishops: that all alike succeed Peter in this, and that the Roman pontiff has nothing above the rest from Peter. Cyprian does not say that by these words the Lord disposes the honour of the Roman bishop, but the honour of the bishop and the order of the Church; nor that from this the ordination of the Roman bishop descends, but the ordination of all bishops and the order of the Church; nor that by this an act of the Church and a pre-eminence are proved over the Roman bishop, but over all bishops. There is therefore one bishop, one judge, one episcopate, one chair. From Christ's words to Peter, in Cyprian's judgment, nothing whatever can be proved except the unity and equality of all bishops. This unity of the bishops wonderfully demonstrates the communion of the saints which then flourished in the Church; but now, alas, through the deed of the Roman pontiff it is trampled underfoot. For the primacy of the pontiff has done the same thing, namely that this unity of the Church and communion among bishops has been utterly banished from the Church.

units.la: Primatum Petro quidem concedit Cyprianus: at ut inde Romano etiam Episcopo primatum tribuat, quinquiam a Cypriano extorquebis. {a}Nam nec Petrum, inquit, quem primum Dominus elegit, & super quem aedificaret Ecclesiam suam, nam sicut Paulus de circumcisione postmodum disceptaret, vindicavit sibi aliquid insolenter, aut arroganter assumpsit, ut diceret, se primatum tenere, & obtemperari sibi a nouellis[?] & potius sibi patrem oportere. Hæc ille. Quibus verbis Romani Pontificis insolentiam & arrogantiam vellicat, qui primatum sibi iam tum affectabat. Itaque innuit, Romanum Pontificem hoc sibi insolenter vindicasse, & arroganter assumpsisse. Sententiam igitur suam satis accurate explicat Cyprianus. Nam quum primatum concesserat Petro, & videret, Romanos Pontifices primatum inde sibi arroganter assumere, negat profecto illis primatum, quem sibi supra reliquos vindicabant, quo cogerent alios sibi obtemperare.
units.tr: Cyprian indeed concedes a primacy to Peter; but that from this he attributes a primacy also to the Roman bishop, you will in fact wrest from Cyprian in vain. For he says: "Peter, whom the Lord first chose, and upon whom he would build his Church, when afterwards Paul disputed with him about circumcision, did not claim anything for himself insolently or arrogantly, so as to say that he held the primacy, and that he ought to be obeyed by newcomers, and that they ought rather to regard him as their father." Thus he. In these words he pricks at the insolence and arrogance of the Roman pontiff, who was already then aspiring to a primacy. Thus he hints that the Roman pontiff claimed this for himself insolently and assumed it arrogantly. Cyprian therefore explains his own opinion quite accurately. For since he had conceded a primacy to Peter, and saw that the Roman pontiffs were arrogantly assuming a primacy for themselves from this, he plainly denies them the primacy which they claimed above the rest, by which they would compel others to obey them.

units.la: Firmilianus ad Cyprianum scribens, sic ait: {b}Ego in hac parte iuste indignor, cum hanc tam a- pertam & manifestam Stephani stultitiam, quod sic de Episcopatu suo loco gloriatur, & se successorem Petri, tenere contendit. Hæc ille. Ipse etiam CyCyprianus insolentiam Romani Pontificis gravissimis verbis redarguit. {a}Neq; enim, inquit, quisquam nostrum Episcopum se Episcoporum constituit, aut tyrannico terrore ad obsequendi necessitatem, collegas suos adigit, quando habeat omnis Episcopus pro licentia libertatis & potestatis suae arbitrium proprium, tamen [?] iudicari ab alio non potest, quam nec ipse potest alterum iudicare. Haec ille. Dicant Pontificii, quem feriunt illa verba? & quisnam sit, qui tyrannico terrore jamdudum adegit collegas ad obsequendi necessitatem, & quisnam ille sit, qui se jam Episcopum Episcoporum constituit? Haec è Cypriano observavimus, quia Pontificii per fraudem, locum unum aut alterum arripere solent: quem extra Cypriani sententiam sensumq; torquent, ad probandum Romani Pontificis primatum. Si quis per insciitiam [?] aut fraudem locum aliquem luxatum rapiat, & veluti membrum de suo corpore avulsum ostentet, non negamus, hoc modo simplicioribus imponi posse: Sed si quis cordatus lector Cyprianum totum evoluat, negamus, per omnia eius opera verbulum unum reperiri, quo Romani Pontificis primatus ex Cypriani sententia stabiliatur. Ad reliquos pergamus.
units.tr: Firmilian, writing to Cyprian, says: "I am justly indignant in this matter, that Stephen should boast of his episcopate in such a place, and contend that he holds the succession of Peter, a folly so open and manifest." So he speaks. Cyprian himself also rebukes the insolence of the Roman Pontiff in very severe words: "For none of us makes himself the bishop of bishops, or drives his colleagues by tyrannical terror into a necessity of obeying him. Since every bishop has, by the liberty and power that are his, his own judgment, he cannot be judged by another, just as he cannot judge another." So he speaks. Let the Papists say whom these words strike, who it is that long ago drove his colleagues by tyrannical terror into a necessity of obeying him, and who it is that has now made himself the bishop of bishops. We have noted these things from Cyprian because the Papists are wont to snatch at one passage or another by fraud, and twist it beyond Cyprian's meaning and sense, to prove the primacy of the Roman Pontiff. If someone through ignorance or fraud seizes some dislocated passage and displays it like a limb torn from its body, we do not deny that this may deceive the simpler sort. But if any discerning reader will read through Cyprian as a whole, we deny that one word can be found in all his works by which the primacy of the Roman Pontiff is established by Cyprian's judgment. Let us go on to the rest.

units.la: Hieronymus: {b}Nec altera Romana urbis Ecclesia, altera totius orbis existimanda est. Et Gallia, & Britannia, & Africa, & Persis, & Oriens, & India, & omnes barbara nationes unum Christum adorant, unam observant regulam veritatis, si auctoritas quaeritur, orbis maior est urbe. Haec ille. Quo loco disputat Hieronymus contra quendam, qui ( vt ipsius verbis vtar ) in tantam eruperat vecordiam, vt Diaconos Presbyteris anteferret. Hanc ordinis Ecclesiastici confusionem Romana Ecclesia iam tum fouebat. Quam opinionis nouitatem sic refutat Hieronymus. Primo distinctionem adhibet Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, & Romanæ: vt Romana sit Ecclesia vnius prouinciæ aut vrbis: Catholica sit totius orbis Ecclesiæ. Et quia omnes particulares vnam catholicam constituunt, si catholicam vnitatem spectes, non est altera Romana, altera totius orbis Ecclesia; quia Ecclesia vna est in omnibus gentibus. Sed si vna aliqua particularis Ecclesia per se consideretur, maior est authoritas Catholicæ, quam vnius. Qui maiorem authoritatem Catholicæ Ecclesiæ affirmat esse, quam Romanæ: Romanam non potuit Catholicam intelligere.Hæc liquido demonstrant, Romanam Ecclesiam non fuisse Catholicam Hieronymo; quia Romana est vnius vrbis, Catholica totius orbis: Romanæ Ecclesiæ minor est authoritas, Catholicæ maior: Romana Ecclesia peruersum istum morem tulit, & confusionem ordinis Ecclesiastici, quem non tulit Catholica. Non ergo Romana erat Catholica.
units.tr: Jerome: "Nor should the Church of the city of Rome be thought one church, and the Church of the whole world another. Gaul, and Britain, and Africa, and Persia, and the East, and India, and all the barbarian nations worship one Christ and observe one rule of truth. If authority is sought, the world is greater than the city." So he speaks. In this place Jerome disputes against a certain man who (to use his own words) had broken out into such madness as to set deacons above presbyters. The Roman Church was already then fostering this confusion of ecclesiastical order. Jerome refutes this novelty of opinion as follows. First he draws a distinction between the Catholic Church and the Roman Church: the Roman Church is that of one province or city, the Catholic Church is the church of the whole world. And since all the particular churches together constitute one Catholic church, if you look at Catholic unity there is not one Church of Rome and another of the whole world, because the Church is one among all nations. But if one particular church is considered by itself, the authority of the Catholic Church is greater than that of any one church. Whoever affirms that the authority of the Catholic Church is greater than that of the Roman Church could not have understood the Roman Church as Catholic. These points clearly show that, for Jerome, the Roman Church was not Catholic: the Roman Church belongs to one city, the Catholic to the whole world; the authority of the Roman Church is less, that of the Catholic greater; the Roman Church tolerated that perverse custom and the confusion of ecclesiastical order, which the Catholic Church did not tolerate. Therefore the Roman Church was not Catholic.

units.la: Augustinus etiam inter Catholicam & Romanam comparationem instituit, qua quidem ita confirmat, Romanam non esse Catholicam, vt nulla distinctio Iesuitica suffugium præstet, etiamsi mare magnum Scoticarum rum speculationum euoluant. Vrbicus quidam Romanæ Ecclesiæ consuetudinem in Sabbati ieiunio aliis Ecclesiis imponere fata-gebat. Huic respondet Augustinus, {a}varios-que errores istius Romani Vrbici refutat, nempe istos:
units.tr: Augustine too drew a comparison between the Catholic and the Roman Church, and he confirms it so firmly that the Romanists' Jesuitical distinction offers no refuge, even if they turn over the great sea of Scotist speculations. A certain Urbicus of Rome was trying to impose on other churches the Roman custom of fasting on the Sabbath. Augustine replies to him, and refutes the various errors of this Roman Urbicus, namely these:

units.la: Quod ieiunium errores & peccata abluat.
units.tr: That this fast washes away errors and sins.

units.la: In ieiunio meritum esse.
units.tr: That there is merit in the fast.

units.la: Ad peccatum cogi homines, quia prandetur.
units.tr: That men are driven to sin because they dine.

units.la: Regnum Dei non esse in cibo & potu, sed in ieiunio.
units.tr: That the kingdom of God is not in food and drink, but in fasting.

units.la: Prandium esse malum & tenebras, &c.
units.tr: That dinner is evil and darkness, and so on.

units.la: Hæc Romanæ Ecclesiæ mysteria de ieiunio iam tum propalabat Romanus iste Vrbicus. Simon Petrus, inquit Romanus iste Vrbicus, Apostolorum caput, cœli ianitor, & Ecclesiæ fundamentum, extincto Simone Mago, qui fuerat Diaboli; non nisi ieiunio vincendi figura, idipsum Romanos edocuit. Hæc Augustinus irridet, & refutat, & diserte ait, Vrbicum hunc, {b}toto terrarum orbe diffusam, exceptis Romanis, & paucis adhuc Occidentalibus, blasphemare Ecclesiam. Hæc Augustinus. Ex quibus verbis constat, Ecclesiam Romanam Augustino non esse Catholicam, quia Vrbicus iste, qui Romanam collaudabat, blasphemaret Catholicam.
units.tr: These mysteries of the Roman Church concerning fasting were already then being proclaimed by this Roman Urbicus. "Simon Peter," says this Roman Urbicus, "head of the Apostles, doorkeeper of heaven, and foundation of the Church, after Simon the Magician, who had been of the devil, was overcome, taught the Romans this very thing, that fasting is the figure of victory." Augustine mocks and refutes these things, and plainly says that this Urbicus, "spread throughout the whole world of lands, except for the Romans and a few Westerners as yet, blasphemes the Church." So Augustine speaks. From these words it is clear that the Roman Church was not Catholic to Augustine, because this Urbicus, who praised Rome, blasphemed the Catholic Church.

units.la: Ex hoc loco duo sunt diligenter notanda: Primum, de moribus Ecclesiæ Romanæ, ex disputatione Vrbici: Alterum, de mori-
units.tr: From this passage two things are to be carefully noted: first, concerning the customs of the Roman Church, from the dispute of Urbicus; second, concerning

units.la: tiones Ecclesiæ Romanæ.
units.tr: the customs of the Roman Church.

units.la: cum Pontifice Carthaginiensi. bus Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, ex responso Augustini. Nam ex Urbici verbis intelligimus Romanæ Ecclesiæ ingenium. Romani Pontifices affectabant semper ceremonias suas aliis Ecclesiis, tanquam jugum, imponere. Et veteratorias artes prodit iste Urbicus. Nam traditiones, quas nulla alia ratione probare possunt, scilicet ad Apostolicas traditiones referunt. Sic Urbicus iste traditionem Romanam de jejunio, ad Petrum Apostolum referre ausus est. Itaque in hoc uno facto Romanæ Ecclesiæ ingenium & mores expressos habemus. Nec minora studio ex Augustini verbis Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ingenium moresque observare debemus, contra istas Romanorum artes. Nam Augustinus contra Romanæ Ecclesiæ consuetudinem opponit Catholicæ Ecclesiæ judicium. Hæc refutatio antiquis sufficiens videbatur, ut contra particularem aliquam Ecclesiam auctoritatem Catholicæ obicerent. Eodemque modo refutabant Patres Africani impudentiam Romanorum Pontificum, Zozimi, Bonifacii, & Cælestini. Etenim Ecclesia Romana potestatem in alias Ecclesias vindicare tentabat, vivo Augustino, & Appellationes ab aliis Ecclesiis ad Romanum Episcopum fieri voluerunt. Ad eam rem conficiendam, confictum Niceni Concilii canonem jactabant Romani Pontifices. Canon ille fictitius extat Concil. Carthag.6.cap.5. Augustinus, aliique Patres Africani, etsi imposturas Romanas satis intelligebant, satisque fuisse videretur fictionem simpliciter reiecisse: tamen ad posteritatis memoriam publico Ecclesiæ iudicio hanc impudentiam refutari voluerunt. Missa igitur legatione ad Episcopos Alexandriæ, & Constantinopolis, ab illis exemplaria Niceni Concilii authentica receperunt. Atque ita ex publico Ecclesiæ iudicio vanitatem Romanorum Episcoporum reiiciunt.
units.tr: concerning the customs of the Catholic Church, from Augustine's reply. For from the words of Urbicus we understand the character of the Roman Church. The Roman Pontiffs always aimed to impose their ceremonies on other churches as a yoke. And this Urbicus reveals the crafty arts of the Romans. For they refer to the Apostolic traditions those traditions which they cannot prove by any other means. So Urbicus dared to refer the Roman tradition about fasting to the Apostle Peter. Thus in this one fact we have the character and customs of the Roman Church expressed. Nor ought we to observe with no less zeal the character and customs of the Catholic Church from Augustine's words, against these Roman arts. For Augustine opposes to the custom of the Roman Church the judgment of the Catholic Church. This refutation seemed to the ancients sufficient to set the authority of the Catholic Church against any particular church. In the same way the African Fathers refuted the impudence of the Roman Pontiffs Zosimus, Boniface and Celestine. For the Roman Church was attempting, while Augustine was still alive, to claim power over other churches, and wanted appeals to be made from other churches to the Roman bishop. To support this claim the Roman Pontiffs boasted of a forged canon of the Council of Nicaea. That fictitious canon exists in the Council of Carthage, canon 5 of the sixth council. Augustine and the other African Fathers, although they understood the Roman impostures well enough, and although it might have seemed sufficient simply to reject the fiction, nevertheless wished this impudence to be refuted by public judgment of the Church, for the memory of posterity. Therefore, after sending a legation to the bishops of Alexandria and Constantinople, they received from them authentic copies of the Nicene Council. And so by the public judgment of the Church they rejected the vanity of the Roman bishops.

units.la: Quod igitur antiqui Patres facere solebat, hoc nos etiam sedulo facimus. Romanæ Ecclesiæ mores ex Catholicæ Ecclesiæ moribus iudicamus: nec Catholicam ad Romanam, sed Romanam ad Catholicam revocandam, & instituendam censemus. Numquid autem a quoquam difertius affirmari potuit, quam est ab istis duobus grauissimis Patribus, Hieronymo & Augustino constanter contestatum, Romanam Ecclesiam non esse Catholicam? quum ab utroque Catholica & Romana opponantur, tanquam universalis, & particularis. De primatu, quem tanta ambitione Romanus Episcopus affectabat; grauissima extat Augustini sententia, qua sententiam sensumque Ecclesiæ veteris diserte declarat:{a} Primatus, inquit, non est, nisi in sancta conuersatione, & vita bona. Iis addamus grauissimum Ambrosii iudicium. Exiis, quæ ex Hieronymo atque Augustino adduximus, facile constat, Ecclesiam Romanam iam tum aliis Ecclesiis innouationes quasdam obtrudere voluisse, fuisse, quibus isti egregie restiterunt. Huic Romanæ ambitioni, viuo etiam Ambrosio, in Mediolanensi Ecclesia locus non erat. Ambro-fius enim disputans de ceremonia illa, quæ erat in lotione pedum, sic ait: {a}In omnibus se-qui cupio Ecclesiam Romanam, sed tamen & nos homines sensum habemus: ideo quod alibi rectius seruatur, & nos recte custodimus. Hæc Ambrosius. Quum igitur dissentiret à Romana Ecclesia, se sensum habere non dubitabat Ambrosius: quod de Catholica Ecclesia nunquam dixisset, aut cogitasset. Romana igitur Ecclesia non erat Catholica Ambrosio.
units.tr: Therefore what the ancient Fathers used to do, we also diligently do. We judge the customs of the Roman Church by the customs of the Catholic Church, and we do not judge the Catholic Church by the Roman, but think the Roman should be brought back to and instructed by the Catholic. Indeed, could anything have been affirmed more plainly by anyone than what was constantly attested by those two most weighty Fathers, Jerome and Augustine, namely that the Roman Church is not Catholic? Since both of them set the Catholic and the Roman against each other, as universal and particular. Concerning the primacy, which the Roman bishop sought with such ambition, there is a most weighty judgment of Augustine, by which he plainly declares the sentiment and sense of the ancient Church: "Primacy," he says, "does not consist except in holy conduct and a good life." To these let us add the most weighty judgment of Ambrose. From what we have adduced from Jerome and Augustine it is easily established that the Roman Church already then wished to force certain innovations upon other churches, and that these men resisted them admirably. To this Roman ambition there was no place in the Church of Milan, even while Ambrose was living. For Ambrose, discussing that ceremony which was in the washing of feet, says: "In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church, but we men also have our own judgment, because elsewhere it is observed more rightly, and we keep it rightly." So Ambrose says. Since he therefore dissented from the Roman Church, Ambrose did not hesitate to say that he had his own judgment, which he never would have said or thought of the Catholic Church. The Roman Church therefore was not Catholic to Ambrose.

units.la: Veniamus ad Gregorium. Gregorius sic habet: {b}Vniuersæ Ecclesiæ, quæ vnam Catholicam faciunt, adolescentula vocantur, non iam veru-steper[?] culpam, sed nouellæ per gratiam. Hæc ille. Non ergo Romana Ecclesia Catholica est Gregorio, quia Catholicam vocat, quæ ex vniuersis particularibus constat. Particularem Ecclesiam sic describit: {c}Præsens Ecclesia bonos simul malosque colligit, nec eligit, quos trahit, quia quos eligere possit, ignorat. Iterumque: {d}Sicut inhonesta membra in corpore, ita quædam sunt intra sanctam Ecclesiam potentes, & proterui. Sic ille de Ecclesia præsente, quam vocat, siue particulari. De particulari Romana Ecclesia Gregorius, quod res est, fatetur; {e}Ex amore quippe fidelium, inquit, huius sedis rectoribus, mos vltra meritum erupit. Sicille de moribus quibusdam inuerecundis Ecclesiæ Romanæ, quos sanctus ille vir remouere cur,bat; alii vero post ipsum retinere, atque augere certarunt. De primatu Romani Pontificis nota est, & celebri Gregorii censura, ex contentione contra Iohannem Constantinopolitanum, & Iohannis successorem Cyriacum: qui œcumenici Episcopi titulum affectabant, quem Gregorii successores deinceps obtinuerunt. {a}Certe, inquit, Petrus Apostolus primum membrum sanctae vniuersalis Ecclesiae est: Paulus, Andreas, Iohannes, quid aliud quam singularum sunt plebium capita? & tamen sub vno capite omnes membra sunt Ecclesiae. Et mox: Sancti ante legem, sancti sub lege, sancti sub gratia, omnes hi perficientes corpus Domini, in membris sunt Ecclesiae, & nemo se vniuersalem vocari voluit. Haec Gregorius. Si Petrus, & Paulus, Iohannes, Andreas, sunt tantum singularum plebium capita, membra vero vniuersalis Ecclesiae: quis est hic, qui se post Gregorium Caput vniuersalis Ecclesiae vocari vult? Si demus Pontifici quantum vel Petro Gregoriusdederat, Caput Ecclesiae Catholicae non erit, quia nec Petrus erat. Gregorii humilitas, & synceritas[?] Antichristi superbiam confodit. Beda de Catholica sic docuit: {b}Omnes Ecclesiae per orbem vnam Catholicam faciunt. Haec ille. Non ergo vna Romana, sed omnes per orbem hoc praestant. Idem docent {c}Eucherius, {d}Rupertus, aliique, vsq; ad Bernardum.
units.tr: Let us come to Gregory. Gregory has this: "All the churches which make up one Catholic church are called a young girl, not now for fault of the old, but a newcomer through grace." So he speaks. Therefore the Roman Church is not Catholic to Gregory, because he calls Catholic that which consists of all the particular churches. He describes the particular church thus: "The present Church gathers good and bad together, nor does it choose whom it draws, because it does not know whom it could choose." And again: "As dishonourable members are in the body, so there are some powerful and insolent ones within the holy Church." So he speaks of the present Church, which he calls particular. Concerning the particular Roman Church, Gregory confesses what is the case: "Out of the love of the faithful," he says, "for the rulers of this see, a custom has broken out beyond merit." So he spoke of certain shameless customs of the Roman Church, which that holy man strove to remove, but which others after him strove to retain and increase. Concerning the primacy of the Roman Pontiff there is a well-known censure of Gregory, from the contention against John of Constantinople and John's successor Cyriacus, who aspired to the title of ecumenical bishop, which Gregory's successors afterwards obtained. "Surely," he says, "the Apostle Peter is the first member of the holy universal Church; Paul, Andrew, John, what else are they than heads of single peoples? And yet all are members under one head of the Church." And soon after: "The saints before the law, the saints under the law, the saints under grace, all these, making up the body of the Lord, are members of the Church, and no one wished to be called universal." So Gregory. If Peter, Paul, John and Andrew are only heads of single peoples, and the members of the universal Church, who is this man who after Gregory wishes to be called the Head of the universal Church? If we grant the Pontiff as much as Gregory had granted even to Peter, he will not be the Head of the Catholic Church, because neither was Peter. The humility and sincerity of Gregory pierces the pride of Antichrist. Bede taught about the Catholic Church thus: "All the churches throughout the world make up one Catholic church." So he speaks. Therefore it is not the one Roman Church, but all churches throughout the world, that accomplish this. The same is taught by Eucherius, Rupert, and others, down to Bernard.

units.la: Bernardus quaedam diuersa à superioribus Patribus docuit: sed tamen egregie de Ecclesia sensit; quam coetum electorum, & con-gre-
units.tr: Bernard taught some things that differ from the earlier Fathers, yet he judged the Church admirably. He calls her the assembly of the elect and the gathering of the righteous, as we observed above.

units.la: gre ler fide nup mer Ref Ber cap rem fuit fide
units.tr: Bernard, faith, ... Papists ... (the surrounding text is too garbled in the scan to recover)

units.la: F tos tot fuit fun clef cati Cat las Pap den Cat At mir
units.tr: ... Catholics ... Papists ... (the surrounding text is too garbled in the scan to recover)

units.la: I mal om est Cy liiq gregationem iustorum vocat, vt supetius obseruauimus. De aliis etiam articulis summa fide atque integritate docuit contra ea, quæ nuper statuit pars Tridentina. Gloriantur tamen Pontificii, Bernardum Papistam esse. Refert Bellarminus Caluini censuram de Bernardo. 4 Caluinus, inquit ille, Institut.{a} cap.10. §.17. vocat Bernardum pium scriptorem. Subiungit Bellarminus: At certe Papista fuit Bernardus, & nemo est pius sine vera fide.
units.tr: He also taught, with the highest faith and integrity, other articles against what the Tridentine party has lately laid down. Yet the Papists boast that Bernard was a Papist. Bellarmine reports Calvin's judgement on Bernard. Calvin, he says, in the Institutes, chapter 10, section 17, calls Bernard a pious writer. Bellarmine adds: "But surely Bernard was a Papist, and no one is pious without true faith."

units.la: Respondemus, vtinam tales Papistas multos, imo vel vnum talem hodie haberemus in toto regno Pontificio, qualem Bernardum fuisse constat. Ita sane, ita solide disputat ille de summis fidei capitibus, de Scripturis, de Ecclesia, de hominis miseria, de gratuita iustificatione, de gratia, de noua obedientia, cum Catholica Ecclesia contra Tridentinas fabulas, vt nihil solidius quæri possit. Num ergo Papista fuerat, qui contra Iesuitas, contra Tridentinos, in maximis fidei articulis, Ecclesiam Catholicam, & Patrum consensum sequitur? At certe Papista fuit Bernardus, inquit Bellarminus.
units.tr: We reply: would that we had many such Papists, or even one such today, in the whole Papal kingdom, as Bernard is known to have been. He argues so soundly and so solidly about the chief heads of faith, about Scripture, the Church, the misery of man, justification by free grace, grace, and new obedience, in agreement with the Catholic Church against the Tridentine fables, that nothing more solid can be sought. Was he then a Papist, when against the Jesuits and the Tridentines he follows the Catholic Church and the consent of the Fathers on the greatest articles of faith? Yet, says Bellarmine, "Bernard was surely a Papist."

units.la: Dicam aperte, quod res est.Bernardus Romani Pontificis iurisdictionem longe supra omnes superiores Patres extulit. Atque hinc est, quod Papista vocetur à Bellarmino. Nam Cyprianus, Augustinus, Ambrosius, aliique superiores, Romani Pontificis iurif[?]dictionem cohibuerunt. Bernardus autem incidit in fatalia illa tempora, vltra annum millesimum, Satana iam soluto. Itaque quod cohibere non potuit, tulit, vt potuit. Nam post annum millesimum multi viri sancti Romani Pontificis iurisdictionem in spiritualibus quum cohibere non possent, patienter tulerunt. Atque in hunc vsque diem forte Ecclesia Dei eandem patientiam praestitisset, si non obstitissent res duae: manifesta doctrinae mutatio in Concilio Tridentino, & iurisdictioni nouus gradus additus, inauditus antiquis, Papae scilicet principatum in temporalibus. Non enim Papistas, aut damnandos homines censemus, quicunque aliquam Papae iurisdictionem in spiritualibus agnosci volunt: sed qui ita in obsequium Papae flectuntur, vt cum doctrinae immutatione iurisdictionem Papae in temporalibus, vel directe, vel indirecte prositeantur: quiq; professionem hanc ad perniciem Principum, & Rerumpublicarum ruinam sequuntur: seque Papistas ostendunt, hoc est, non per patientiam ferentes spiritualem Papae iurisdictionem, sed pro temporali iurisdictione digladiantes, seque in eadem causa audaces, rebelles, nefarios, sanguinarios, parricidas praestant, vt hanc iurisdictionem in temporalibus stabilire possint. Qui haec vel agenda docent, vel acta probant, vel agunt ipsi, Papistas vocamus. Talis autem non fuit Bernardus. Sententia Patrum de Catholica Ecclesia à fraterculis primum immutata est; at à viris piis & eruditis iq[?] Romana Ecclesia egregie propugnata est antiqua sententia contra fraterculos. Picus Mirandula,lib.de fide & ordine credendi, Ecclesiae sententiam longe aliam refert, quam Iesuitae proponunt. Probat solius Papae determinationem in iis, quae sunt fidei, neminem obligare: ex sententia Gerfonis, Scoti, Panormitani, Cardinalis Cameracensis, Theorem.8.
