For he teaches that the Church of Christ could once be distinguished from the Gentile world in various ways, but that when Antichrist reigns, no other way will remain for knowing the true Church, he says, except only through the Scriptures, because Antichrist has in schism all those things that properly belong to Christ in truth: likewise the churches, likewise the divine Scriptures themselves, likewise the bishops and the other orders of clergy, and the sacraments. Therefore, wishing to know what the true Church of Christ is, from what could he know it amid such great confusion of likeness, except only through the Scriptures? So he.

units.la: Ad hoc testimonium Pontificii respondere non possunt, itaque elevatur auctoritatem eius. Respondet Bellarminus, librum illum non esse Chrysostomi. Facilis responsio. At non refert, cuius sit, neque in eo contendimus. Quæremus, quænam fuerit doctrina illa, quæ in antiqua Ecclesia conseruata fuit à Patribus. Hunc autem unum ex antiquis fuisse, non negant Pontificii. Quum de antiquitate conueniat inter nos, de autore non moramur. Sed Bellarminus obiicit etiam, autorem huius libri fuisse Arianum[?].
units.tr: The Papists cannot answer this testimony, and so they attack its authority. Bellarmine replies that this book is not Chrysostom's. An easy reply. But it does not matter whose it is, and we do not contend about that. We ask what doctrine was preserved in the ancient Church by the Fathers. The Papists do not deny that this author was one of the ancients. Since we agree about his antiquity, we do not linger over the author's name. But Bellarmine also objects that the author of this book was an Arian.

units.la: Respondeo, neq; hoc testimonii huius au-toritatem minuit. Nam hinc sequetur, (vt de-mus hunc fuisse Arrianum) nihil tunc in Ec-clesia auditum fuisse contra hanc sententiam (qua veteris Ecclesiæ antistites Ecclesiam per Scripturas probare solebant) contra hanc, in-quam, sententiam nihil tum temporis audi-tum, nihil scriptum, nihil fictum erat, quia cum orthodoxis Patribus ipsi etiam hæretici in hac re consentiebant. Deinde respondeo, si omnes Patres reiiciendi sunt, qui in aliquibus videntur Arrianismum sapere, actum erit de Origene, & de magna parte Græcorum Patrum. Postremo frustra obiicitur, non fuisse Chrysostomi sententia. Paulo enim supra adduximus è Chrysostomo, Ecclesiam ministe-rio suo fidem continere, & prædicationem veritatis. Quod si veritatem è sacris Scripturis prædicatam continet Ecclesia, certe Ecclesia optime cognoscetur ex hoc ministerio. Docet etiam Chrysostomus, {a}Scripturas esse exactissimam trutinam, gnomonem, & regulam. Hæc igi-tur regula exactissima, Ecclesiam nobis, & Ecclesiæ dogmata demonstrabit. Itaque idem affirmat, Scripturas esse ostium illud, quod ducit nos ad Deum, & oues Christi facit. {b}Ecce, inquit, latronis signa. Primum palam non ingreditur, neq; audet: inde non per Scripturarum testimonium, quod per ostium significatur. Hic, & qui fuerunt, & qui futuri sunt, notat, & Antichristum, & falsos Christos. Merito autem ostium Scripturas appellat, quoniam nos ad Deum duxint[?], & eum nobis cognitionem aperiunt, ipsæ omnes faciunt, & custo-diunt. Hæc ille. Quod si Scripturæ sint ostium, quo ducimur ad Deum, si Scripturæ omnes Christi faciunt, & custodiunt: Ecclesia certe optime ex iisdem Scripturis cognoscetur: quia Ecclesiam Scripturæ faciunt, & custodiunt, ex Chrysostomi sententia. Dicant autem nobis Pontificii, quisnam sit Antichristus ille, qui (sicut Chrysostomus docet) aliunde in Ecclesiam ingressurus est non per Scripturas? qui Scripturas horret, sicut latro crucem?
units.tr: I reply that this does not diminish the authority of this testimony either. For it follows from this (granting that he was an Arian) that nothing was then heard in the Church against this opinion, by which the bishops of the ancient Church were accustomed to prove the Church through Scripture. Against this opinion, I say, nothing was then heard, nothing written, nothing invented, since even the heretics themselves agreed with the orthodox Fathers on this point. Next, I reply that if all the Fathers who seem in some points to savour of Arianism are to be rejected, it will be all over with Origen and with a great part of the Greek Fathers. Lastly, it is vainly objected that this was not Chrysostom's opinion. For a little above we quoted from Chrysostom that the Church holds the faith and the preaching of the truth through her ministry. If the Church holds the truth preached from the holy Scriptures, then certainly the Church is best known from this ministry. Chrysostom also teaches that the Scriptures are the most exact balance, the gnomon and the rule. This most exact rule, therefore, will show us the Church and the doctrines of the Church. Accordingly he likewise affirms that the Scriptures are that door which leads us to God and makes us the sheep of Christ. Behold, he says, the signs of a thief. First he does not enter openly, nor does he dare; then he does not enter through the testimony of Scripture, which is signified by the door. This refers both to those who have been and to those who will be, and marks both Antichrist and false Christs. Rightly he calls the Scriptures a door, since they lead us to God and open to us the knowledge of him, and they themselves make and guard all things. So he. But if the Scriptures are the door by which we are led to God, if the Scriptures make and guard all the sheep of Christ, then surely the Church will be best known from those same Scriptures, because, according to Chrysostom's view, the Scriptures make and guard the Church. Let the Papists tell us, then, who that Antichrist is who (as Chrysostom teaches) is going to enter the Church from elsewhere, not through the Scriptures: who abhors the Scriptures as the thief abhors the cross?

units.la: Hactenus Græcos Patres audiuimus, sequuntur Latini.
units.tr: So far we have heard the Greek Fathers; the Latin Fathers follow.

units.la: Irenæus: {a}Prædicatio Ecclesiæ constans & aqualiter perseuerans, testimonium habet à Prophetis & Apostolis. Hæc ille. Ecclesia igitur non debet prædicare traditiones non scriptas, quæ non habent testimonium à Prophetis & Apostolis. Ita Ecclesia cognoscitur per prædicationem doctrinæ Propheticæ & Apostolicæ.
units.tr: Irenaeus: The preaching of the Church, constant and steadily persevering, has its testimony from the Prophets and the Apostles. So he. Therefore the Church ought not to preach unwritten traditions, which have no testimony from the Prophets and Apostles. Thus the Church is known through the preaching of Prophetic and Apostolic doctrine.

units.la: Tertullianus: {b}Apostoli in orbem profecti, eandem doctrinam eiusdem fidei nationibus promulgarunt, & proinde Ecclesias apud vnamquamq; ciuitatem condiderunt, à quibus traducem fidei, & semina doctrinæ, cæteræ exinde Ecclesiæ mutuatæ sunt, & quotidie mutuantur, vt Ecclesiæ fiant. Hæc ille. Quibus verbis docet, Ecclesias fieri quotidie per prædicationem eiusdem doctrinæ. Fides igitur Ecclesiam constituit, non autem Ecclesia fidem. Idemq; sic docet: {c}Constat, omnem doctrinam, quæ cum illis Ecclesiis Apostolicis, matricibus, & originalibus fidei conspirat, veritati deputandam tandam, id sine dubio tenentem, quod Ecclesia ab Ap-postolis, Apostoli a Christo, Christus a Deo suscepit. Reliquam vero omnem doctrinam de mendacio praeiudicandam, quae sapiat contra veritatem Ecclesiarum, & Apostolorum, & Christi, & Dei. Ad hanc igitur formam provocabuntur ab illa Ecclesia, quae licet nullum ex Apostolis, vel Apostolicis[?] auctore suum proferant, ut multo posteriores, quae denique quotidie instituuntur: tamen in eadem fide consentientes, non minus Apostolica deputantur, propter consanguinitatem doctrinae. Haec Tertullianus. Huius ergo iudicio, Ecclesia habet a doctrina Apostolica, ut Apostolica fiat, imo ut sit Ecclesia.
units.tr: Tertullian: The Apostles, going out into the world, proclaimed the same doctrine of the same faith to the nations, and accordingly founded churches in each city, from which the other churches afterwards borrowed the shoot of faith and the seeds of doctrine, and daily go on borrowing them, so that they may become churches. So he. In these words he teaches that churches are made every day through the preaching of the same doctrine. Faith, therefore, constitutes the Church, not the Church the faith. He likewise teaches thus: It is agreed that every doctrine which accords with those Apostolic churches, the mothers and originators of the faith, must be counted as truth, plainly holding that which the Church received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God. But all other doctrine must be condemned as falsehood, which savours against the truth of the Churches, of the Apostles, of Christ, and of God. Therefore, by this standard, those churches will be challenged which, though they bring forward no founder from among the Apostles or Apostolic men, being far later, and indeed instituted every day, nevertheless agree in the same faith, are counted no less Apostolic on account of the kinship of doctrine. So Tertullian. By his judgment, therefore, the Church has from Apostolic doctrine that she may be Apostolic, indeed that she may be a Church at all.

units.la: Hieronymus: {b}Ecclesia non in parietibus consistit, sed in dogmatum veritate. Ecclesia ibi est, ubi est vera fides. {c}Ego intrare cupio in domum tuam, id est, in Ecclesiam, & volo intrare per viam tuam rectam. Quae est ista via? Lectio Scripturarum.
units.tr: Jerome: The Church does not consist in walls but in the truth of doctrines. The Church is where the true faith is. I wish to enter your house, that is, the Church, and I wish to enter by your straight way. What is that way? The reading of the Scriptures.

units.la: Augustinus Ecclesiam e Scripturis demonstrandam sic docet: In Scripturis didicimus Christum, in Scripturis didicimus Ecclesiam. Quae-stio inter nos versatur, ubi sit Ecclesia? Quid ergo facturi sumus? In verbis nostris eam quaesituri, an in verbis Capitis sui? Puto, quod potius in illius verbis eam quaerere debemus, qui veritas est, & optime novit corpus suum. Haec ille. Augustinus igitur Ecclesiam in Christi verbis, id est, in Scripturis quaerendam iudicat. Sed num quis veterum produci poterit, qui docuerit, Ecclesiam in Papae verbis, vel in traditionibus non scriptis quaerendam? Idem Augustinus sic ha-bet: bet: {a}Nolo humanis documentis, sed divinis oraculis Ecclesiam demonstraris.
units.tr: Augustine teaches that the Church is to be demonstrated from the Scriptures in this way: We have learned Christ from the Scriptures; we have learned the Church from the Scriptures. The question between us is where the Church is. What then shall we do? Shall we seek her in our own words, or in the words of her Head? I think we ought rather to seek her in the words of him who is the truth and knows his own body best. So he. Augustine therefore judges that the Church is to be sought in the words of Christ, that is, in the Scriptures. But can any of the ancients be produced who taught that the Church is to be sought in the words of the Pope, or in unwritten traditions? The same Augustine also says: I do not want you to demonstrate the Church by human teachings, but by divine oracles.

units.la: Cardinalis Bellarminus, qui diutius in hoc argumento obmutuit, tandem ita respondet ad illa Augustini loca: {b}Ex Scriptura probari, vbi sit Ecclesia, non tanquam ex nota Ecclesiae, sed quia Scriptura docet, quae sint notae, dum docet, qualis illa sit, vbi coeperit, quando creuerit. Haec ille. Subtilis esse voluit Dominus Cardinalis: Ecclesia demonstratur ex Scriptura, non tanquam ex nota Ecclesiae, sed quia docet notas Ecclesiae. At hoc illud est, quod affirmat Augustinus, quod nos vrgemus, quod vbique ingeminamus: ad quod Iesuitae nihil habent, quod respondeant: Ecclesiae notas doceri in Scripturis. Si hoc concedant Iesuitae, quid vltra litigamus? Scriptura, inquit Bellarminus, docet Ecclesiae notas. At Scriptura notas illas non docet, quas nobis obtrudunt Pontificii: neque enim agnoscit Scriptura Ecclesiam illam, cuius Caput sit Romanus Pontifex, cuius membra sint homines impii, sine omni interna virtute, cuius regula vnica non sint Scripturae, sed & traditiones non scriptae. Si Ecclesiae notas Scriptura docet, Ecclesia certe apud Pontificios non est, quia Scriptura notas Ecclesiae Pontificiae non docet.
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine, who for a long time kept silent on this subject, at last replies to those passages of Augustine as follows: "That the Church is shown from Scripture, where it is, not as from a mark of the Church, but because Scripture teaches what its marks are, while it teaches what kind of Church it is, where it began, and when it grew." So he says. The Lord Cardinal wanted to be subtle: the Church is shown from Scripture, not as from a mark of the Church, but because it teaches the marks of the Church. But this is exactly what Augustine affirms, what we press, and what we constantly repeat, and to it the Jesuits have no answer: that the marks of the Church are taught in Scripture. If the Jesuits concede this, why do we go on quarrelling? Scripture, says Bellarmine, teaches the marks of the Church. But Scripture does not teach those marks which the Papists thrust upon us. For Scripture does not recognise that Church whose head is the Roman Pontiff, whose members are wicked men without any inward virtue, and whose one rule is not Scripture but also unwritten traditions. If Scripture teaches the marks of the Church, then certainly the Church is not among the Papists, since Scripture does not teach the marks of the Papist Church.

units.la: Sed quid est, quod Iesuita ad pauca respon-det? (quanquam non respondeat: haec enim eius verba non continent responsionem, sed tacitam confessionem veritatis, ad quam respondere non potuit ) in reliquis mutus fit ? Probant Patres, Ecclesiam Catholicam esse in unitate fidei, fidem vero esse in duobus testamentis: Doctrinam Ecclesiae esse muniendam regulis Euangelicis, & Apostolicis: Legis & Prophetarum volumina fuisse Ecclesiae doctrinam: Ecclesiam seipsam ædificare, legendo, & examinando Scripturas: Ecclesiam veram cognosci non posse, nisi tantummodo per Scripturas: Scripturas omnes Christi facere, & custodire, hoc est, Ecclesiam facere, & custodire. Ad hæc muti sunt Pontificii. Ad pauca vero Augustini loca, dum responsionem parat Iesuita, sic sudat, sic frangitur, ut facile prodat, bonitatem caulæ, pudoremque defuisse. Plura ex Augustino proferamus, ad quæ obmutescit Bellarminus.
units.tr: But why does the Jesuit reply to only a few points? (Although he does not really reply even to these, for his words contain not an answer but a tacit confession of the truth, to which he could find no reply.) Why does he fall silent on the rest? The Fathers prove that the Catholic Church is in unity of faith, that faith is in the two Testaments, that the doctrine of the Church is to be fortified by the evangelical and apostolic rules, that the volumes of the Law and the Prophets were the doctrine of the Church, that the Church builds itself up by reading and examining the Scriptures, that the true Church cannot be known except only through the Scriptures, and that all the Scriptures make and keep Christ, that is, make and keep the Church. To these the Papists are mute. At the few passages of Augustine, however, while the Jesuit prepares a reply, he sweats and breaks down so badly that he easily betrays that the goodness of his cause was lacking, and shame with it. Let us bring forward more from Augustine, at which Bellarmine grows mute.

units.la: {a}Si Christi Ecclesia canonicarum Scripturarum diuinus & certissimus testimonys in omnibus gentibus designata est, quicquid attulerint, quid dicunt, ecce hic est Christus, ecce illic. Audiamus potius, si omnes eius sumus, vocem pastoris nostri, dicentis: Nolite credere. {b}Habeo manifestissimam vocem pastoris mei, commendantis mihi, & sine vllis ambagibus exprimentis Ecclesiam. Mihi imputabo, si ab eius grege, quod est Ecclesia, per verba hominum seduci, atque aberrare voluero, quum me præsertim admonuerit, dicens: Quae sunt oues mea, vocem meam audiunt, & sequuntur me. Ecce vox eius clara & aperta. Hac audita, qui eum non sequitur, quomodo se ouem eius dicere audebit? Nemo mihi dicat, o quid dixit Donatus, aut quid dixit Parmenianus, aut Pontius, aut quilibet illorum: quia nec Catholicus Episcopis consentiendum, sicubi forte fallantur, ut contra canonicas Dei Scripturas aliquid sentiant. Hæc ille. Si nec Catholicis Episcopis, profecto nec Romano Episcopo consentiendum est contra Scripturas. Itaque nos etiam istis responde-mus, quod Augustinus Donatistis: {a}Ecce sunt Scripturæ Dei, ecce sunt in eis Ecclesiæ, & universalis totius orbis nomine, & nominatim designata, & expressa. Si aliunde clamas, vel recitas, non post[?] vocem pastoris nostri, per ora Prophetarum, per os proprium, per ora Evangelistarum nobis apertissime declaratam, voces vestras non admittimus, non credimus, non accipimus. {b}Credit Ecclesia Scripturis sanctis, & veteribus, & novis, quas canonicas appellamus, unde fides ipsa concepta est, ex qua iustus vi-vit, per quam sine dubitatione ambulamus, quamdiu peregrinamur a Domino. Ita docuit Augustinus, Ecclesiam fidem concipere ex Scripturis. Fides igitur est Ecclesiæ regula Augustino, fidei autem regula Scripturæ.
units.tr: If the Church of Christ is marked out by the divine and most certain testimony of the canonical Scriptures among all nations, then whatever they bring forward, whatever they say, "Behold, here is Christ; behold, there," let us rather listen, if we are all his, to the voice of our shepherd saying: "Do not believe." I have the most manifest voice of my shepherd, commending to me, and setting forth the Church without any circumlocution. I shall impute it to myself if I wish to be led astray and to wander from his flock, which is the Church, through the words of men, especially since he has warned me, saying: "My sheep hear my voice, and follow me." Behold, his voice is clear and open. Having heard this, how will he who does not follow him dare to call himself his sheep? Let no one say to me, "What did Donatus say, or what did Parmenian say, or Pontius, or any of them?" For neither must we agree with Catholic bishops, if perchance they are mistaken, so as to think anything against the canonical Scriptures of God. So he. If we must not agree with Catholic bishops, certainly we must not agree with the Roman bishop against the Scriptures. And so we answer these men too, as Augustine answered the Donatists: Behold, there are the Scriptures of God; behold, the Churches are in them, designated and expressly set forth under the name of the whole world. If you cry out or recite anything from elsewhere, we do not admit, do not believe, and do not accept your voices, which have been most openly declared to us through the mouths of the Prophets, through his own mouth, through the mouths of the Evangelists, the voice of our shepherd. The Church believes the holy Scriptures, both the old and the new, which we call canonical, from which the faith itself is conceived, by which the righteous lives, and through which we walk without doubt as long as we are pilgrims from the Lord. Thus Augustine taught that the Church conceives its faith from the Scriptures. Faith, then, is the rule of the Church for Augustine, but the rule of faith is the Scriptures.

units.la: Vincentius Lirinensis eandem antiquorum sententiam retinuit. {c}Christi, inquit, Ecclesia sedula & cauta, depositorum apud se dogmatum custos, nihil in iis unquam permutat, nihil minuit, nihil addit, non amputat necessaria, non apponit superflua, non amittit sua, non usurpat aliena. Hæc ille. Ad quod testimonium muti sunt omnes Pontificii. Sæpius diximus,autoritatem esse Scripturarum,ministerium vero Ecclesiæ: quod quidem Ecclesiæ ministerium accuratissime descripsit hic Lirinensis. In hoc ergo ministerio vigilat Ecclesia, non vt nouam fi-dei regulam procudat, sed vt vnicam illam, eandem, immutatam perpetuo conseruet. In-telligite interim, qualis sit Tridentinorum in re certissima, vel caecitas, vel obstinatio asse-ctata. Clamant Patres, fidem Ecclesiæ esse ex propriis testamentis: Ecclesias traducem fidei habere ab Apostolica doctrina, Ecclesiam esse omnes, quæ vnicam pastoris sui vocem audiunt, non vocem alieni: in Ecclesiam intrari non posse, nisi per Scripturas: Ecclesiam fidem suam concipere è Scripturis: Ecclesiam, regnante Antichristo, cognosci tantummodo per Scripturas: Ecclesiam esse sacrorum dogmatum custodem, in quibus nihil permutat, nihil immutauit[?], nihil addit, nihil ampu-tat, nihil suum amittit, nihil alienum vsurpat. Et tamen post tam mirificum Patrum consensum, de Ecclesiæ ministerio, ranæ istæ Pontificiæ, ad raucedinem cantilenam suam recinunt, de fide innouanda, mutanda, & ex arbitrio Romani Pontificis componenda. Nam ait Cardinalis Bellarminus: {a}Concilia condere posse, seu condidisse, vel edidisse nouas sententias, quas voluerunt haberi tanquam articulos fidei. Cardinalis vero Baronius apertius: {b}Ex arbitrio Romani Pontificis pependisse, decreta fidei sancire, & sancita mutare. Hæc est noua Cardinalium doctrina, contra Ecclesiæ antiquæ consensum. Ecclesia enim antiqua constanter docuit, Ecclesiæ CHRISTI hoc esse munus, & ministerium, ex quo opti-me me cognoscatur, vt sit sacrorum dogmatum sedula & cauta custos, nihil permutans, nihil nouum, aut non suum vsurpans. Atque vt idem Vincentius habet: Ecclesia ni-hil aliud Conciliorum decretis emissa est, nisi vt, quod antea simpliciter credebatur, hoc idem postea diligentius crederetur, instantius praedicaretur, &c. Nihil ergo nouum sancit Ecclesia CHRISTI, nihil de fide mutat: quae vero noua fidei dogmata & decreta sancit, & sancita mutat, non est Ecclesia CHRISTI.
units.tr: Vincent of Lérins held the same opinion as the ancients. The Church of Christ, he says, careful and cautious, the guardian of the dogmas deposited with her, never changes anything in them, diminishes nothing, adds nothing, does not cut off what is necessary, does not add what is superfluous, does not lose what is her own, does not usurp what is another's. So he. To this testimony all the Papists are mute. We have often said that authority belongs to the Scriptures, but the ministry to the Church, and this Lirinensis has described the ministry of the Church with the greatest precision. In this ministry, then, the Church keeps watch, not to forge a new rule of faith, but to preserve that one and the same rule, unchanged for ever. Understand meanwhile what kind of blindness or wilful obstinacy the Tridentines display in a matter so certain. The Fathers cry out that the faith of the Church is from its own testaments; that the Churches have their faith as a transmission from apostolic doctrine; that the Church consists of all who hear the one voice of their shepherd, and not the voice of a stranger; that one cannot enter the Church except through the Scriptures; that the Church conceives its faith from the Scriptures; that under the reign of Antichrist the Church is known only through the Scriptures; that the Church is the guardian of holy dogmas, in which it changes nothing, has changed nothing, adds nothing, cuts off nothing, loses nothing of its own, and usurps nothing of another's. And yet after so wonderful a consensus of the Fathers about the ministry of the Church, those Papist frogs repeat their tune until they are hoarse, about renewing and changing the faith and composing it at the will of the Roman Pontiff. For Cardinal Bellarmine says: that councils can establish, or have established or published, new opinions which they wished to be held as articles of faith. Cardinal Baronius says more openly: that the power of sanctioning decrees of faith, and of changing what has been sanctioned, depends on the will of the Roman Pontiff. This is the new doctrine of the Cardinals, against the consensus of the ancient Church. For the ancient Church constantly taught that this is the office and ministry of the Church of Christ, by which it is best known: to be the careful and cautious guardian of holy dogmas, changing nothing, claiming nothing new or not its own. And, as the same Vincent says: The Church has issued nothing by the decrees of Councils other than that what was before believed simply should afterwards be believed more diligently and preached more insistently, and so on. Nothing new, then, does the Church of Christ sanction, and it changes nothing of the faith; but whoever sanctions new dogmas and decrees of faith, and changes what has been sanctioned, is not the Church of Christ.

units.la: Gregorius in hanc sententiam multa habet: {a}Vna, inquit, fides est praecedentium & sequentium populorum. Haec ille. Qui vnam omnium fidem docet esse, certe noua de fide dogmata tollit. Quomodo enim vna Ecclesiae fides posset esse, si noua nobis condatur, quae antiquos latuit? Idemque sic docet: {b}Vniuersa nostra munitio in sacro eloquio continetur. Haec ille. Qui vniuersam munitionem nostram in Scripturis posuit, Scripturas certe regulam fidei totalem, non partialem affirmat. Idem sic habet in illa verba Iob: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia. {c}Quia haeretici sic de eloquij sui nitore superbiunt, vt nulla sacrorum librorum auctoritate solidentur, qui libri ad loquendum nobis quasi quaedam argenti venae sunt, quia ex ipsis loquutionis nostrae originem trahimus: eos ad sacra auctoritatis paginam vocat Iob, vt si vere loqui desiderent, inde sumere debeant, quod loquantur, & ait: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia: ac si aperte dicat, qui ad veræ prædicationis verba se præparat, necesse est, ut causarum origines à sacris paginis sumat: ut omne, quod loquitur, ad divinæ autoritatis fundamentum revocet, atq; in eo ædificium locutionis suæ firmet. Sic Beda etiam: {a} Fundamentum Ecclesiæ est in soliditate fidei Apostolorum, & Prophetarum. Hæc ille. Beda noster non ponit Ecclesiam fundamentum fidei, sicut faciunt hesterni Theologi: sed contra, Ecclesiæ fundamentum, fidem. Fidemque hanc non reuocat cum Iesuitis ad Ecclesiæ placita, vel ut apertius Baronius sese suosque explicat, ad arbitrium Romani Pontificis: sed ad doctrinam Propheticam & Apostolicam. Bernardus etiam: {b}Vbinam quæso est vera prudentia, nisi in Christi doctrina? {c}Vnusquisque, quod à magistro suo didicit, hoc in medium profert. Num in Euangelio legisti has differentias, aut in Prophetis, aut in literis Apostolorum? Caro & sanguis revelavit hanc sapientiam, non Spiritus Patris. Hæc ille. Si quicquid in Euangelio, aut scriptis Propheticis & Apostolicis non legitur, est carnis sapientia, non Spiritus: quomodo dicunt isti, Ecclesiam quædam docere posse, quæ non sunt in Scripturis?
units.tr: Gregory has much to the same effect: One faith belongs to the preceding and the following peoples. So he. Whoever teaches that there is one faith of all certainly removes new dogmas of faith. For how could there be one faith of the Church if something new were established for us which was hidden from the ancients? And he likewise teaches: Our whole defence is contained in the sacred word. So he. Whoever has placed our whole defence in the Scriptures certainly affirms that the Scriptures are the complete rule of faith, not a partial one. He says the same on those words of Job: He has the silver its veins' beginnings. Because the heretics boast so of the polish of their own eloquence that they are not strengthened by any authority of the sacred books, which books are for us, in speaking, like veins of silver, since from them we draw the origin of our speech, Job calls them to the sacred page of authority, so that if they truly wish to speak they must take from there what they speak. And he says: He has the silver of its veins' beginnings, as if to say plainly: whoever prepares himself for the words of true preaching must necessarily take the origins of his matter from the sacred pages, so that he may refer whatever he says to the foundation of divine authority, and strengthen the building of his speech upon it. So too Bede: The foundation of the Church lies in the solidity of the faith of the Apostles and Prophets. So he. Our Bede does not place the Church as the foundation of faith, as the theologians of our own day do, but on the contrary the foundation of the Church is faith. Nor does he recall this faith, with the Jesuits, to the decisions of the Church, or, to explain more openly how Baronius and his followers understand it, to the will of the Roman Pontiff, but to the prophetic and apostolic doctrine. Bernard too: Where, I ask, is true prudence, except in the teaching of Christ? Each one brings forward what he has learned from his master. Have you read these distinctions in the Gospel, or in the Prophets, or in the writings of the Apostles? Flesh and blood has revealed this wisdom, not the Spirit of the Father. So he. If whatever is not read in the Gospel or in the prophetic and apostolic writings is the wisdom of the flesh and not of the Spirit, how do these men claim that the Church can teach certain things which are not in the Scriptures?

units.la: Denique hæc doctrina conseruata est in Ecclesia, vsque ad tempora Concilii Tridentini. Quamuis enim fraterculi Romanæ Curiæ assecla, profanas subinde vocum, rerumq; nouitates induxerant, Ecclesia tamen Romana (illam intelligo, quæ in occiduis istis orbis partibus in variis nationibus collecta cum Roma-
units.tr: Finally, this doctrine was preserved in the Church right up to the time of the Council of Trent. For although the little brothers, the followers of the Roman Curia, had from time to time introduced profane novelties of words and things, the Roman Church (I mean that which was gathered in various nations in those western parts of the world together with Rome)

units.la: [right page, cut off at the scan edge; visible line beginnings only: Ro[?], mat[?], mu[?], Ecc[?], dic[?], cor[?], pug[?], bir[?], cis,[?], leb[?], pof[?], Co[?], iis a[?], fia t[?], trac[?], cen[?], Ioh[?], run[?], har[?], præ[?], fiæ[?], que[?], pro[?], Lat[?], & [?], vnu[?], regi[?], rati[?], petr[?], Leg[?], ta,[?], &[?]] Romana Ecclesia, tanquam cum originali, & matrice Ecclesia, sicut nonnullis fuerat, communionem habebant; qua quidem ratione Ecclesia ex istis nationibus collecta, Romana dici potest) hæc, inquam, Romana Ecclesia contra istos tenebriones veritatem hanc propugnavit. Ita ut ipsi etiam fraterculi, qui ad arbitrium Romanæ Curiæ, & Romani Pontificis, antiqua mutare, & novitates inducere solebant, in hac tamen re cohibiti videantur, ne possent venenum suum latius spargere ante Concilii Tridentini tempora. Multi igitur ex iis antiquam doctrinam cum Romana Ecclesia retinebant. Quicunque enim regulam fidei tradunt esse Scripturas canonicas, sicut docent Petrus Lombardus, Thomas Aquinas, Iohannes Scotus, aliique, idem etiam indicarunt, ministerium Ecclesiæ in hoc vigilasse, ut hanc fidei regulam custodiret immutatam, prædicaret, & unice conservaret. Hanc Ecclesiæ sententiam retulerunt Lyra, Gerson, aliique. Gerson sic habet: a Non sumitur Ecclesia{p} pro templo materiali, quod edificare melius potest Latomus, quam Theologus: nec pro solis proventibus, & iurisdictionibus, &c. Sic enim posset secularis unus expertus oeconomus iudicari utilior in Ecclesiæ regimine, quam Theologus, aut Iurista. Sed consideratur Ecclesia, ut instituta est à Christo super firmam petram fidei, ad finem supernaturalem, secundum Legem Euangelicam, & Scriptura divinitus revelata, secundum quam debet regulari iudicium de fide, & moribus. Hæc ille. Nihil hic dicit, nisi quod superius à Patribus dictum fuisse ostendimus. Sed illud obseruandum inprimis est, quod in mediis tenebris antiquam doctrinam integram immutataque conseruari videamus. 1.[?] Docet, Ecclesiam esse institutam à Chri-sto, super petram fidei: Fides ergo est Ecclesiæ regula, & fundamentum. 2. Iudicium Ecclesiæ regulari debere secundum Legem Euangelicam, & Scripturas: Non igitur erat in potestate, vel unius hominis, vel totius Ecclesiæ, noua decreta fidei sancire, & sancita mutare. 3. Secundum hanc Legem regula-ri debere iudicium de fide: Fidei igitur regula est sacra Scriptura. 4. Secundum eandem hanc Legem regulari debere iudicium de fi-de ac moribus.
units.tr: [right page, cut off at the scan edge; visible line beginnings only: Ro[?], mat[?], mu[?], Ecc[?], dic[?], cor[?], pug[?], bir[?], cis,[?], leb[?], pof[?], Co[?], iis a[?], fia t[?], trac[?], cen[?], Ioh[?], run[?], har[?], præ[?], fiæ[?], que[?], pro[?], Lat[?], & [?], vnu[?], regi[?], rati[?], petr[?], Leg[?], ta,[?], &[?]] the Roman Church, as with its original and mother Church, as some have said, kept communion with them; for which reason the Church gathered from those nations may be called Roman) I say, this Roman Church defended this truth against those dark-minded opponents. So much so that even the little brothers themselves, who were accustomed to change ancient teachings and introduce novelties at the will of the Roman Curia and the Roman Pontiff, seem in this matter to have been restrained, so that they could not spread their poison more widely before the time of the Council of Trent. Many of them therefore retained the ancient doctrine together with the Roman Church. For all who teach that the rule of faith is the canonical Scriptures, as Peter Lombard, Thomas Aquinas, John Scotus and others teach, have also indicated that the ministry of the Church has watched over this, so that it guards this rule of faith unchanged, proclaims it, and preserves it alone. Lyra, Gerson and others have related this opinion of the Church. Gerson thus states: "The Church is not taken for the material temple, which Latomus can build better than a theologian; nor for the revenues and jurisdictions alone, etc. For a secular and experienced steward could thus be judged more useful in the government of the Church than a theologian or a jurist. But the Church is considered as it was instituted by Christ upon the firm rock of faith, for a supernatural end, according to the Evangelical Law and Scripture divinely revealed, according to which the judgment concerning faith and morals ought to be regulated." Thus he. He says nothing here except what we have shown above was said by the Fathers. But this must be observed above all, that in the midst of darkness we see the ancient doctrine preserved whole and unchanged. (1) He teaches that the Church was instituted by Christ upon the rock of faith: faith therefore is the rule and foundation of the Church. (2) The judgment of the Church ought to be regulated according to the Evangelical Law and the Scriptures: it was therefore not within the power of one man, or of the whole Church, to sanction new decrees of faith and to change what has been sanctioned. (3) The judgment concerning faith ought to be regulated according to this Law: the rule of faith is therefore holy Scripture. (4) The judgment concerning faith and morals ought to be regulated according to this same Law.

units.la: Obseruandum est, hunc librum Gersonis, de Potestate Ecclesiastica, in Concilio Con-stantiensi fuisse recitatum, & ab universo Concilio approbatum. Ex quo constat, hanc tum fuisse Ecclesiæ Romanæ sententiam. Ità ad illum usque diem antiqua Ecclesiæ doctrina remanserat immutata.
units.tr: It must be observed that this book of Gerson, On Ecclesiastical Power, was read out at the Council of Constance and approved by the whole Council. From this it is clear that this was then the opinion of the Roman Church. Thus the ancient doctrine of the Church had remained unchanged down to that day.

units.la: Euicimus igitur contrà Tridentinos, hanc fuisse communem Ecclesiæ doctrinam, per omnes Ecclesiæ successiones conser-uatam, usque ad tempora Concilii Tri-dentini
units.tr: We have therefore proved against the Tridentines that this was the common doctrine of the Church, preserved through all the successions of the Church, right up to the time of the Council of Trent.

units.la: CAPVT XI. De Successione.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI. On Succession.

units.la: Hactenus de Ecclesia disputauimus, sancta, catholica, de sanctorum communione, de vnitate; denique docuimus: Ecclesiam demonstrari per canonicas Scripturas, sine per regulam fidei. In qua regula integra & incorrupta conseruanda, Ecclesiæ ministerium cernitur. Proximo loco de successione agetur. Quia enim de successione Romanæ Ecclesiæ tantum gloriantur Pontifici, vt hinc lumi argumentum euidentissimum, adeoque plane insolubile affirmet Bellarminus: non erit inutile successionis succinctam pertractationem hoc loco interponere.
units.tr: Hitherto we have disputed about the Church: that it is holy and catholic, about the communion of saints, and about unity. Finally we have taught that the Church is demonstrated by the canonical Scriptures, and not by a rule of faith. The ministry of the Church is seen in keeping that rule whole and uncorrupted. Next we shall treat of succession. Since the Papists boast of the succession of the Roman Church alone, so that Bellarmine affirms this gives a most evident argument, and one that is plainly insoluble, it will not be useless to insert here a brief treatment of succession.

units.la: Concedimus ii[?] apud Patres Ecclesiam aliquando demonstrari per successionem Romanorum Episcoporum in fide vera: quia illis temporibus constabat, non fuisse mutatam fidem in Ecclesia Romana: at nunc contrarium constat. Neque est hæc nostra tantum responsio, est antiquorum traditio. Sicolim[?] docebant: {a} Antea multis modis offendebatur, quæ esset vera Christi Ecclesia, quæ gentilitas[?]. At regnante Antichristo, nullo modo cognosceretur, quæ sit vera Ecclesia, nisi tantummodo per Scripturas. Ita Patrum sententia iudicio; successio, quæ quondam potuit esse Ecclesiæ nota, nunc non erit.
units.tr: We concede that among the Fathers the Church was sometimes shown by the succession of the Roman bishops in the true faith, because in those times it was clear that the faith in the Roman Church had not been changed. But now the contrary is clear. Nor is this only our answer; it is the tradition of the ancients. They once taught: Formerly the true Church of Christ was recognised in many ways, which was the gentile church. But under Antichrist, the true Church can be known in no way except only through the Scriptures. So by the judgment of the Fathers' opinion, a succession which once could be a mark of the Church will not be one now.

units.la: Dicimus 2. successionem illam à Patribus commemoratam, non fuisse localem, quam nunciant Pontifices, sed doctrinæ. Veteres enim successionem distinguunt, in doctrinæ & localem. Localis illa nullius unquam momenti fuit apud veteres. Doctrinæ successionem maxime vrgent in veritate positam, & gratia docendi veritatem, quam vocat Irenæus charisma veritatis. Nam Romanorum Episcoporum successionem contra hæreticos profert, sed quam intelligat ille successionem, demonstrat his verbis: {a}Iu[?], qui in Ecclesia sunt, presbyteris, obaudire oportet, his[?], qui successionem habent ab Apostolis, qui cum Episcoparus[?] successione charisma veritatis certum, secundum placitum Patris acceperunt. Reliquos vero, qui absistunt à principali successione, quocunque loco colliguntur, suspectos habere, vel quasi hæreticos, &c. Addit Irenæus: Omnes enim decidunt à veritate. Quibus verbis docet Irenæus, duplicem esse successionem: alteram in doctrina principalem; localem alteram: qui localem habent sine principali successione, à veritate eos decidere, quocunque loco colliguntur. In eandem sententiam Tertullianus Ecclesiam aliquam demonstrat Apostolicam esse, & haberi, non ex successione hominum ab Apostolis: sed, sicut ille loquitur, ex doctrinæ consanguinitate cum Apostolica. {b}Licet, inquit, Ecclesia nullum ex Apostolis, vel Apostolicis autorem suum proferant, vt multo posteriores, quæ deniq; quotidie instituuntur, tamen in eadem fide conspirantes, non minus Apostolica deputantur, propter consanguinitatem doctrinæ. Successio igitur personarum ab Apostolis non est semper veræ Ecclesiæ nota, quum vera &c ra ét pe stra mi sic stol nium cor cle na cle ten stol est cess nec Pon doc uer fate tem sanc diue cum P buit non legu local mnia ofter ra & Apostolica Ecclesia esse possit,quæ in doctrina cum Apostolicis consentiat, quamuis personarum successionem non possit demonstrare. Ita Ecclesiæ fiunt,non à successione hominum, sed à doctrina Apostolica. Idemque sic habet: {a}Communicamus cum Ecclesiis Apostolicis,quod nulla doctrina diversa: hoc est testimonium veritatis. Hæc Tertullianus. At si hinc communionem nostram probamus cum Ecclesiis Apostolicis, quia nulla nobis est doctrina diversa, conspirante nempe doctrina Ecclesiæ nostræ cum Apostolicis, ut id sine dubio teneamus, quod Ecclesiæ ab Apostolis, Apostoli à Christo,Christus à Deo suscepit: si hoc est unicum veritatis testimonium, certè successio personalis nō est veritatis testimonium, nec communionem inde probare possunt Pontificii cum Apostolicis Ecclesiis, quum doctrina eorum diversa sit ab Apostolica. Diversam esse doctrinam suam,diversam fidem, fatenturipsi, quiaffirmant, apud se autoritatem esse,qua nova fidei dogmata sanciant, & sancita mutent. Mutata fides est diversa fides, diversa non potest communionem habere cum Apostolicis Ecclesiis.
units.tr: Second, we say that the succession recorded by the Fathers was not local, as the Pontiffs proclaim it, but a succession of doctrine. For the ancients distinguish succession into doctrinal and local. The local kind was never of any weight among the ancients. They strongly press the succession of doctrine, which consists in truth and in the grace of teaching the truth, which Irenaeus calls the charism of truth. For he brings forward the succession of Roman bishops against the heretics, but he shows what sort of succession he means in these words: It is necessary to obey the presbyters who are in the Church, who have the succession from the Apostles, who with the succession of the bishops have received the sure charism of truth, according to the good pleasure of the Father. But as for the rest, who stand apart from the principal succession, wherever they are gathered, they are to be regarded with suspicion, or as heretics, etc. Irenaeus adds: For all of them fall away from the truth. By these words Irenaeus teaches that there is a twofold succession: one principal, in doctrine; the other local. Those who have a local succession without the principal succession fall away from the truth, wherever they are gathered. To the same effect Tertullian shows that a certain Church is apostolic and is held to be so not by a succession of men from the Apostles, but, as he puts it, by a kinship of doctrine with the apostolic. Although, he says, the Churches cannot point to any author among the Apostles or apostolic men, as those much later ones which are daily founded, yet, agreeing in the same faith, they are reckoned no less apostolic, on account of the kinship of doctrine. Therefore a succession of persons from the Apostles is not always a mark of the true Church, since a Church can be apostolic, if it agrees with the apostolic Church in doctrine, even though it cannot demonstrate a succession of persons. Thus Churches come to be, not from a succession of men, but from apostolic doctrine. And he says the same thus: We communicate with the apostolic Churches, because there is no diverse doctrine; this is the testimony of truth. So Tertullian. But if from this we prove our communion with the apostolic Churches, because we have no diverse doctrine, since the doctrine of our Church agrees with the apostolic, so that we undoubtedly hold what the Churches received from the Apostles, the Apostles from Christ, and Christ from God; if this is the sole testimony of truth, then certainly a personal succession is not a testimony of truth, nor can the Papists prove from it their communion with the apostolic Churches, since their doctrine differs from the apostolic. That their doctrine is different, their faith different, they themselves confess, since they affirm that there is among them an authority which sanctions new dogmas of faith and changes what has been sanctioned. A changed faith is a different faith, and a different faith cannot have communion with the apostolic Churches.

units.la: Pontificiis forte occasionem gloriandi præbuit Cathedræ Petri nomen, apud veteres nonnunquam usurpatum. Nam ubicunque legunt isti Cathedram, aut Petri Cathedram, localem successionem in Ecclesia Romana somniant. Quod utistis excutiamus somnium, ostendemus,vereres[?],quoties de Cathedra, vel Petri Cathedra loquuntur, semper intelligere successionem doctrinæ. Loquendi formula sumpta est ab iis Scripturæ verbis, Matth.23 2. In Cathedra Mosis sedent Scribæ & Pharisæi. Ubi per Cathedram Mosis, doctrinam Legis intelligit Christus. Itaque Origenes sic ha-bet: {a}Ante Christi adventum super Cathedram Mosis sederunt, qui bene, & secundum rationem dicta Mosis interpretabantur, post adventum Christi sedent super Cathedram Ecclesiæ, quæ est Cathedra Christi, & thronus. Hæc Origenes. Quibus verbis demonstrat, per Cathedram intelligi doctrinam. In more enim positum fuit apud antiquos, ut in Ecclesiis locus excelsior erigeretur, unde docebat Episcopus: is locus dicebatur Cathedra. De qua re Eusebius sic narrat: {b}Iacobi Cathedra in Hierosolymis usque in hodiernum diem conservatur, atque in ea sedent omnes, qui usque ad præsens tempus sedis illius sacerdotium sortiuntur.
units.tr: Perhaps the name "Chair of Peter," sometimes used by the ancients, gave the Papists an occasion for boasting. For wherever they read of the Chair, or the Chair of Peter, they dream of a local succession in the Roman Church. To refute this dream, we will show that the ancients, whenever they speak of the Chair or the Chair of Peter, always mean a succession of doctrine. The form of speech was taken from the words of Scripture, Matt. 23:2: The scribes and Pharisees sit in the chair of Moses. Where Christ understands by the Chair of Moses the doctrine of the Law. So Origen says: Before the coming of Christ, those sat on the chair of Moses who interpreted the sayings of Moses well and according to reason; after the coming of Christ they sit on the chair of the Church, which is the chair and throne of Christ. So Origen. By these words he shows that by the chair is understood doctrine. For it was the custom among the ancients that in the churches a higher place was raised, from which the bishop taught; this place was called the chair. Concerning this matter Eusebius thus narrates: The chair of James in Jerusalem is preserved to this day, and in it sit all those who up to the present time obtain the priesthood of that see.

units.la: Cyprianus monet: {c}Episcopo conservandum honorem sacerdotij sui, & Cathedræ. Atque alibi Cornelii Romani Episcopi facilitatem perstringens, qui ad se transfugientes schismaticos, & profanos homines nimia leuitate exceperat, sic ait: {d}Nauigare audent, & ad Petri Cathedram, atq; ad Ecclesiam principalem, unde unitas sacerdotalis exorta est, & à schismaticis & profanis literas ferre, nec cogitare, eos esse Romanos, quorum fides, Apostolo prædicante, laudata est, ad quos perfidia non possit habere accessum.
units.tr: Cyprian warns: The bishop must keep the honour of his priesthood and of his chair. And elsewhere, censuring the easiness of Cornelius, bishop of Rome, who had received with excessive levity schismatics and profane men who had fled to him, he says: They dare to sail to the chair of Peter, and to the principal Church, whence the unity of the priesthood arose, and to carry letters from schismatics and profane men, not considering that these are Romans, whose faith was praised when the Apostle preached it, to whom perfidy could not have access.

units.la: Cathedra[illegible, ~10 letters] hunc locum, & pauca huiusmodi, tri- folent Pontifici, sed frustra. Quid e- it Cyprianus, quod nos negamus? nia nos etiam antiquæ Romanæ Ec- ibuimus, quæ concedit Cyprianus. Sic elint, Romana Ecclesia Petri Cathe- l hac conditione, quam adscribit Cy- quamdiu perstiterit, talis, qualem ille t: Quorum fides ab Apostolo laudata d quos perfidia non possit habere ac- Basilius Ambrosium, Mediolanensem um constituturum, ait, fuisse{a} [?] ἀπὸ τῶν ἐν τῶν ἀποστόλων [?]. Augustinus ait: {b}V dicuntur, quæ etiam viliter non agunt, sua rere studeant, sed sua docere non audent: de et superiori sedu Ecclesiastica, quem sanæ constituit. Ambrosius {c}Non habent editatem, qui Petri fidem non habent. Hie- s: {d}Per Cathedram doctrinam Legis in- Chrysostomus: {e}Super Cathedram derunt sacerdotes, eum enim doctrinam ac- Cyrillus Hierolol. {f}Super Cathe- ederunt Scriba & Pharisei, nō hic ligneam m, sed doctrina significat potestatem. ibus testimoniis concludimus, Pa- tenere Cathedram Petri. Qui enim laborat in verbo, & doctrina, vel do- tegritatem non seruat, non sedet in Ecclesiastica, ex Patrum sententia. ui neutrum præstat, Petri Cathe- tá, excelsus erigitur, & regnat in pestilentiæ. Per successionem igitur,& Cathedram, constat, veteres non privilegium alicuius loci, sed doctrinae Aposto-licae integritatem in Ecclesia traditam, ab Episcopis conseruatam, intelligi voluisse.
units.tr: Cathedra[...] These passages, and a few others of this kind, the Pontiff's party usually presses, but in vain. For what does Cyprian say that we deny? We too acknowledge the ancient Roman Church, which Cyprian concedes. Thus, he says, the Roman Church holds the Chair of Peter, under this condition, which Cyprian adds: as long as it remains such as he describes: whose faith was praised by the Apostle, and to whom perfidy could not have access. Basil says that Ambrose of Milan was to constitute ... from the ... of the Apostles. Augustine says: Those are called ... who do not even act basely, yet are eager to teach their own things rather than the things of Christ, and do not dare to teach their own things; and of the higher seat of the ecclesiastical ... which he established sound. Ambrose: They do not have the Church, who do not have the faith of Peter. Jerome: By the Chair is meant the doctrine of the Law. Chrysostom: Upon the chair the priests sat, for they taught the doctrine... Cyril of Jerusalem: Upon the chair the Scribes and Pharisees sat; here chair signifies not a wooden seat but doctrine and authority. From these testimonies we conclude that the Fathers, with one voice, hold that the chair of Peter is kept by those who labour in the word and doctrine, and who keep the integrity of doctrine. For one who does not keep the integrity of doctrine does not sit in the Church's chair, according to the opinion of the Fathers. Whoever does neither does not hold the chair of Peter but is raised up on high and reigns in pestilence. Therefore, by succession and chair, it is clear that the ancients wished to understand not the privilege of any place, but the integrity of apostolic doctrine handed down in the Church and preserved by the bishops.

units.la: Redeamus iam ad illud insolubile argumentum Bellarmini. {a}Hinc argumentum, inquit ille, insolubile sumitur, hoc modo: Ecclesia non potest esse sine Episcopis: Apud Lutheranos non sunt Episcopi: nam non habent ordinationem, & successionem ab Apostolis. Ergo apud vos non est Ecclesia.
units.tr: Let us now return to that insoluble argument of Bellarmine. {a}"From this," he says, "an insoluble argument is drawn, in this way: The Church cannot exist without bishops. Among the Lutherans there are no bishops, for they do not have ordination and succession from the Apostles. Therefore among you there is no Church."

units.la: Respondeo, satis est, ad demonstrandam Ecclesiam, ex Patrum iudicio & consensu, ut successio sit in doctrina. Nam per illam successionem probant Patres, Ecclesiam vere Apostolicam dici, & esse, quamuis localem successionem non possit ostendere. Quum igitur apud Ecclesias nostras sit doctrinae consanguinitas, & conspiratio cum doctrina Apostolica, hoc sufficit ad demonstrandam Ecclesiam veram. Bellarminus producit etiam Brentii responsum. Respondet Brentius: Nos legitime vocati sumus a populo & Magistratu, & ab iis Episcopatum accepimus, & non nos intrusimus. At contra Bellarminus sic disputat: Hic non disputamus de electione Episcopi, quam scimus varie variis temporibus celebratam, &c. Caeterum quomodocunque fuerit electio, semper fuit necessaria ordinatio, quam non populus, sed soli Episcopi, & quidem tres ut minimum, regulariter conferebant.
units.tr: I reply: to demonstrate the Church, according to the judgment and consensus of the Fathers, it is enough that there be succession in doctrine. For by that succession the Fathers prove that a church is truly called and is Apostolic, even though it cannot show a local succession. Since our churches share the same doctrine and agree with apostolic teaching, this is sufficient to demonstrate that they are the true Church. Bellarmine also cites Brenz's reply. Brenz answers: we were lawfully called by the people and the magistrate, and we received the episcopate from them; we did not thrust ourselves in. But Bellarmine argues against this: "We are not disputing here about the election of a bishop, which we know was carried out in various ways at various times, etc. However the election was made, ordination was always necessary, and it was conferred not by the people but by bishops alone, and regularly by at least three of them."

units.la: Respondeo 1. Hoc argumentum non at-tingit Ecclesias nostras, & Episcopos nostros, qui canonicè ordinantur. Nam vt de successione Episcoporum nostrorum pauca dica-mus, facilè probabimus, Episcopos nostros multo magis regulariter instituros, quam Ro-manos. De successione Episcoporum nostræ Ecclesiæ nihil certum proferri potest ante Gregorii tempora, qui huc Augustinum Mo-nachum misit. Augustinus ille Monachus Româ profectus est, ordinatus autem Episco-pus est, non à Gregorio, sed à Virgilio, Arela-tensi Archiepiscopo, ad quem scripsit Grego-rius. {4}[?] Beda etiam testatur, Augustinum hunc ab Arelatensi Archiepiscopo ordina-tum fuisse, & renersum in Britanniam, misisse continuo Romam Laurentium Presbyterum, & Petrum Monachum, qui Gregorio referrent, gentem Anglorum fidem Christi accepisse, ac se Episcopum factum fuisse. Successio igitur Cantuariensium Archiepiscoporum, ac proinde reliquorum omnium Episcoporum huius gentis, non erat ab Ecclesia Romana, sed ab Arelatensi. Erat Arelatensis Ecclesia mater omnium Ecclesiarum Gallicarum, & Episcopus Arelatensis Primas omnium Episcoporum Galliæ, sicut ex pluribus Gregorii Epistolis constat, maximè Epistola 52. lib.4. indict.13. Arelati autem Trophymum Pauli discipulum, Christum docuisse narrant multi. Inter quos Perrus Cluniacensis probat hoc testimonio Papæ Zozimi. Cluniacensis verba sunt hæc: {a}Numquid apud Arelatem, quam nec, dū per Dei gratia vester sordidus error infecit, Pauli Apostoli discipulus Trophymus, de cuius fonte ut Papa Zozimus scribit, omnes Galliæ Ecclesiæ fidei vi-stulos[?] acceperunt, semper in campo, aut in foro prædi-cauit, baptizauit, orauit, & nunquam domum oratio-nis vel ipse habuit, vel alios habere instituit. Hæc ille. Legimus etiam in tomis Conciliorum, Concilio Arelatensi 2. cap.18. hæc verba: Ad Arelatensis Episcopi arbitrium synodum congregan-dam, ad quam urbem, ex omnibus mundi partibus, præcipue Gallicanis, sub sancti Martini tempore, legimus celebratum fuisse Concilium, atque conven-tum, si quis commonitus infirmitatis causa defuerit, personam vice sua dirigat. Hactenus verba Concilii. In hoc Concilio, Restitutus, Episcopus Londinensis, subscripsit inter Episcopos. Unde constare potest, etiam ante Archiepiscopi Cantuariensis institutionem, quam antiqua, quam concors fuerit animorum conspiratio, inter Arelatenses, & Britannos Episcopos.
units.tr: Answer 1. This argument does not touch our churches or our bishops, who are ordained canonically. To say a few words about the succession of our bishops, we can easily show that our bishops regularly ordain far more carefully than the Romans do. Nothing certain can be produced about the succession of the bishops of our church before the time of Gregory, who sent Augustine the monk here. This Augustine set out from Rome, but he was ordained bishop not by Gregory but by Virgilius, archbishop of Arles, to whom Gregory wrote. {4}[?] Bede also testifies that this Augustine was ordained by the archbishop of Arles, and that, on returning to Britain, he at once sent Laurence the presbyter and Peter the monk to Rome to report to Gregory that the English nation had received the faith of Christ and that he himself had been made bishop. Therefore the succession of the archbishops of Canterbury, and consequently of all the other bishops of this nation, came not from the Roman church but from Arles. The church of Arles was the mother of all the Gallic churches, and the bishop of Arles was primate of all the bishops of Gaul, as is clear from many letters of Gregory, especially Epistle 52 of book 4, indiction 13. Many relate that Trophimus, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, taught Christ at Arles. Among them Peter of Cluny proves this by the testimony of Pope Zosimus. Peter of Cluny's words are these: {a}Was it not at Arles, which your filthy error had not yet infected through the grace of God, that Trophimus, a disciple of the Apostle Paul, from whose source, as Pope Zosimus writes, all the churches of Gaul received the faith, always preached in the fields or the marketplace, baptized, prayed, and never himself had a house of prayer nor set one up for others? So he. We also read in the volumes of the Councils, in the Second Council of Arles, chapter 18, these words: To convene a synod at the discretion of the bishop of Arles, to which city, from all parts of the world and especially from the Gallic lands, we read that a council was celebrated and gathered in the time of St Martin; if anyone, warned, is absent because of sickness, let him send a representative in his place. So far the words of the Council. In this council Restitutus, bishop of London, subscribed among the bishops. From this it can be established that, even before the institution of the archbishop of Canterbury, the agreement of minds between the bishops of Arles and the Britons was both ancient and harmonious.

units.la: Nostræ igitur Ecclesiæ, ut & omnes Galliæ, successionem suam ab Arelatensi sumunt. Jam si quis à præsenti Archiepiscopo Cantuariensi, Georgio, Reverendissimo ac vigilantissimo Ecclesiæ Christi pastore, usque ad Virgilium illum, qui Augustinum ordinauerat, deinde à Virgilio, usque ad Trophymum, vel quemcunque alium virum Apostolicum, qui primus Ecclesiam illam plantauerat, universam successionem, & singulas propagines percurrat, non inveniet in tota hac successione nostronostrorum Episcoporum, vel fœminam, sicut Romana Ecclesia habuit Iohannem VIII. vel puerum, sicut erat Benedictus IX. vel alium quempiam, per quem formale successionis impedimentum fiat, sicut in Romana Ecclesia sæpius fit. Ita de nostra successione ratio constat, quæ de Romanorum Episcoporum successione constare non potest. Miseri ergo Pontificii de successione, nescio quid, obiicere nobis audent, & in angulis contra vocationem Episcoporum nostrorum, & presbyterorum susurrant[?], eaque tela in nos coniiciunt, quæ nec nostros lædunt, & retorta in auctores ipsos, ossibus ipsorum, & præcordiis penitus infixa hærent. Quod vero Niceni Concilii canonem 4. iactant, de Episcopo à tribus Episcopis ordinando, frustra nostris obiicitur Episcopis, qui semper canonice à tribus Episcopis, vt minimum ordinati sunt. Nihil igitur contra nostros Episcopos ab Adversariis proferri potest.
units.tr: Therefore our church, like all the Gauls, derives its succession from Arles. Now if anyone runs through the whole succession and each line, from the present archbishop of Canterbury, George, most reverend and most vigilant pastor of Christ's Church, back to that Virgilius who ordained Augustine, and then from Virgilius back to Trophimus, or whatever other apostolic man first planted that church, he will not find in this entire succession of our bishops either a woman, as the Roman church had John VIII, or a boy, as Benedict IX was, or any other person through whom a formal impediment to succession arises, as often happens in the Roman church. Thus the reckoning of our succession is established, which cannot be established for the succession of the Roman bishops. Wretched Papists therefore dare to object to us something about succession, I know not what, and whisper in corners against the calling of our bishops and presbyters. They hurl at us weapons which do not harm us, but which, turned back on their authors, stick deep in their bones and hearts. As for what they boast of, canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea, that a bishop must be ordained by three bishops, it is in vain objected to our bishops, who have always been ordained canonically by at least three bishops. Nothing therefore can be produced by our adversaries against our bishops.

units.la: Quod si obiiciant, se non Ecclesias illas accusare, in quibus certa Episcoporum successio constat: sed in quibusdam reformatis Ecclesiis non esse Episcoporum successionem.
units.tr: But if they object that they are not accusing those churches in which a certain succession of bishops is established, but that in some reformed churches there is no succession of bishops,

units.la: Respondeo 2. Vt omittam de meo iudicio aliquid dicere, certe non possunt Pontificii Pontificios authores reiicere. Solent ipsi Pontificii locum Ambrosii frequenter adducere, quem ex Gratiano citant: 4 Episcopi & Presbyteri vnam esse ordinationem, quia vterq; sacerdos est, sed Episcopum Primum esse. Habet igitur Episcopus ordinandi potestatem, quam non habet presbyter, ordinationem aliam non habet. Itaque Bellarminus de hac re sic habet: Etsi Episcopus & Presbyter distinguuntur, tamen quantum ad sacrificium, idem omnino ministerium exhibent, proinde unum ordinem, non duos faciunt. Hæc Bellarmin. lib.1. cap.11. de Clericis. Quod ex communi Scholasticorum sententia desumptum videtur. Capreolus in 4.sent.dist.2.q.1. concludit, Episcopatum non esse alium ordinem distinctum à sacerdotio. Quo loco inducit argumentum Aureoli, in quo acquiescit. Quia, inquit, omnis forma, quæ est in actu, videtur, quod possit se communicare in eadem specie. Ergo quicunque sacerdos poterit ordines celebrare. Ergo si potestas illa non sit impedita, sicut est de facto, & impedimentum removeatur per hoc, quod sit Episcopus, non datur ei nova potestas, sed tantummodo pristina potestas prius impedita expeditur, impedimento remoto. Et reductio illius potestatis ad visum, dicitur ampliatio potestatis. Hanc sententiam sequuntur Cameracens. in 4.sent. dist.44. Armacan.lib.10.q. Arm. cap.7. Gontarenus lib.de Sacram.
units.tr: Answer 2. To leave aside saying anything of my own judgment: the Papists certainly cannot reject their own authors. The Papists themselves often cite the passage of Ambrose which they quote from Gratian: "Bishops and presbyters have one ordination, because both are priests, but the bishop is first." Therefore the bishop has the power of ordaining, which the presbyter does not have; he has no other ordination. Thus Bellarmine on this matter says: "Although bishop and presbyter are distinguished, yet as regards the sacrifice they perform altogether the same ministry, and so they make one order, not two." So Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 11, on clerics. This seems to be taken from the common opinion of the Scholastics. Capreolus, on the Sentences book 4, distinction 2, question 1, concludes that the episcopate is not a distinct order from the priesthood. In that place he brings in the argument of Aureolus, in which he rests: "Because, he says, every form which is in act seems able to communicate itself within the same species. Therefore any priest will be able to celebrate ordinations. Therefore, if that power is not impeded, as it is in fact, and the impediment is removed by his being a bishop, no new power is given to him, but only his earlier power, previously hindered, is released once the impediment is removed; and the restoration of that power to act is called an enlargement of power." Cameracensis on Sentences book 4, distinction 44, Armachanus book 10, question Arm., chapter 7, and Gontarenus in his book on the sacraments follow this opinion.

units.la: Respondeo 3. Novum hoc esse, atque inauditum in Ecclesia, si quis dicat, Ecclesiam omnino periisse, nullamque esse, si forte canon quispiam Ecclesiasticus non servetur. Ecclesia enim non est, nec unquam fuit sine EpiEpiscopis, vel iis, qui locum supplent Episco-porum: sed Episcopi vere esse possunt, quamuis non seruetur Ecclesiasticus ille canon. Fatentur, antiquum esse canonem illum, in Concil. Nicen. can. 4. Sed ante Concilium Nicenum Episcopi constituti sunt, qui Ecclesias gubernabant. Neque vero idcirco Eccle-sia nulla erat antea, quia haec res originem à Concilio Niceno traxit. Euagrius Episcopus Antiochiae ab antiquis habebatur, à Socrate {a}, ab Hieronymo {b}: & tamen Theodoretus {c} scribit, cum Episcopum factum fuisse contra hunc canonem: quia à Paulino solo, non adhibitis aliis Episcopis, creatus erat. Quod si Bellarminus de sententia cedere noluit, nisi Romani Pontificis auctoritate reprimatur: en producimus Romani Episcopi sententiam.
units.tr: Answer 3. It is a new and unheard-of thing in the Church if someone says that the Church has utterly perished and does not exist because some ecclesiastical canon happens not to be observed. For the Church is not, and never was, without bishops, or those who fill the place of bishops; and bishops can truly exist even though that ecclesiastical canon is not observed. They admit that this canon is ancient, citing canon 4 of the Council of Nicaea. But before the Council of Nicaea, bishops were appointed who governed the churches. Nor was there therefore no church before, merely because this practice took its origin from the Council of Nicaea. Evagrius was regarded by the ancients as bishop of Antioch, according to Socrates {a} and Jerome {b}; yet Theodoret {c} writes that he was made bishop contrary to this canon, because he had been created by Paulinus alone, without other bishops being called in. If Bellarmine is unwilling to change his opinion unless he is restrained by the authority of the Roman Pontiff, then behold, we produce the judgment of the Roman bishop.

units.la: Nam Gregorius Primus Augustino Cantuariensi sic scribit: {d} In Anglorum Ecclesia, in qua tu solus adhuc Episcopum inueniris, ordinare Episcopum non aliter potes, nisi sine Episcopis. Haec Gregorius ad quæstionem Augustini. Quærebat enim Augustinus, utrum debeat Episcopus ordinari sine aliorum Episcoporum præsentia, quum longinquitas itineris [?] magni interiaceret, ut Episcopi non facile possent convenire: Respondet Gregorius, Episcopos illos, qui primi ordinandi erant in Anglia, non potuisse aliter ordinari, nisi sine Episcopis. Probat igitur Gregorius, ordinationem sine tribus Episcopis legitime fieri posse. At quod hoc idem ad Apostolorum canones refert Bellarminus, prorsus inane est, quum do illis apud Gratianum sic legamus: a Canones, qui dicuntur Apostolorum, nec sedes Apostolica recipit, nec sancti Patres illis assensum præbuerunt, pro eo, quod ab hæreticis sub nomine Apostolorum compositi dignoscuntur. Hæcille. Atqui sine istis falsariorum sigmentis non possunt Iesuitæ progredi.
units.tr: For Gregory the First writes thus to Augustine of Canterbury: {d} In the church of the English, in which you alone as yet find a bishop, you cannot ordain a bishop otherwise than without bishops. So Gregory, in answer to Augustine's question. For Augustine asked whether a bishop ought to be ordained without the presence of other bishops, since the great distance of the journey lay between them, so that bishops could not easily come together. Gregory answers that those bishops who were first to be ordained in England could not be ordained otherwise than without bishops. Gregory therefore proves that ordination without three bishops can be lawfully performed. But that Bellarmine refers this same matter to the canons of the Apostles is utterly empty, since in Gratian we read of those canons thus: The canons which are called the Apostles', neither the apostolic see accepts, nor have the holy Fathers given their assent to them, because they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles. So he. Yet without those forgeries of counterfeiters the Jesuits cannot make any progress.

units.la: Si importunius in hoc nodo hæreant Pon-tificii, apud quasdam reformatas Ecclesias non esse Episcopos. Respondeo: Si non sint Episcopi, ex necessitate erat: quia Episcopi, qui Ecclesias Pontificias tenebant, ordina-re noluerunt; recedendum erat ab Antichristo, & per consequens, à Romana illa Cu-ria, quæ nunc à Iesuitis Romana Ecclesia di-citur. Illud enim nos per Dei gratiam facile probaturos speramus, non posse eos cum Ecclesia Catholica communicare, qui per omnia cum Romana ista Ecclesia communi-cant. Ergo necessitas erat recedendi à Romana Curia, si cum Ecclesia Catholica communicare vellent. Et quia in quibusdam locis aliter fieri non potuit, presbyteris suis contenti erant. Minus enim malum videbatur, non habere Episcopos, quam veritatem, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ communionem amittere.
units.tr: If the Papists cling more stubbornly to this knot and object that some reformed Churches have no bishops, I answer: if they have none, it was a necessity. The bishops who held the Papist churches refused to ordain, so it was necessary to withdraw from Antichrist and, consequently, from that Roman Curia which the Jesuits now call the Roman Church. For we hope, by the grace of God, to prove easily that those cannot communicate with the Catholic Church who communicate in everything with that Roman Church. Therefore there was a necessity of withdrawing from the Roman Curia, if they wished to communicate with the Catholic Church. And since in some places this could not be done otherwise, they were content with their presbyters. For it seemed the lesser evil to have no bishops than to lose the truth and communion with the Catholic Church.

units.la: Atqui hic ulterius obiicient Pontificii rixatores, simplices presbyteros non posse ordinare, quia munus ordinandi, semper ad Episcopos spectauit.
units.tr: But here the Papist brawlers will object further that simple presbyters cannot ordain, because the office of ordaining has always belonged to bishops.
