units.la: Sentio, quam lubrico loco versetur haec disputatio. Nam quum semotis personis, de rebus ipsis disputamus, sunt, qui rapiunt orationem nostram, ad nescio quorum hominum contumeliam. Sed conscientiae bonae testimonio fre[?]rus, inter Aduersariorum minas, & amicorum querelas non impedior, a querenda veritate, quia inquisitionis huius finis est veritas, regula charitas. Qui se laedi sentiunt, quia forte ad opinionem ipsorum non omnia revoco, intelligant non hominum placita, non partium studia, sed veritatem quæri. Non omnis, qui parcit, amicus, nec omnis, qui verberat, inimicus est. Meliora sunt vulnera amici, quam oscula inimici. Melius est cum seueritate diligere, quam cum lenitate decipere. Itaque non metuam, ne viri boni in suam contumeliam rapiant haec, quae dicam, quum DEVM habeam conscientiae testem, scopum disputationis huius esse veritatem, regulam, quam maxime tenere cupimus, esse charitatem.
units.tr: I feel how slippery the ground is on which this dispute stands. For when we set persons aside and dispute about the matters themselves, there are some who twist our argument to the insult of I know not whom. But relying on the testimony of a good conscience, I am not held back from seeking the truth by the threats of adversaries or the complaints of friends, since the end of this inquiry is truth and its rule is charity. Those who feel themselves wounded, because perhaps I do not revoke everything to their opinion, let them understand that it is not men's opinions or party zeal that is being sought, but the truth. Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor is everyone who strikes an enemy. The wounds of a friend are better than the kisses of an enemy. It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. So I shall not fear that good men will twist what I say into their own insult, since I have God as witness of my conscience, that the aim of this disputation is truth, and that the rule which we most earnestly desire to keep is charity.

units.la: Post sacrarum Scripturarum autoritatem, Ecclesiae Catholicae consensus tantum apud me semper valuit, ut quaecunque ab hoc consensu confirmata videam, mihi sacrosancta & immutabilia videatur. At in eo habemus Ecclesiae antiquae consensum, Episcopos ordinare, & Presbyteros ab Episcopis ordinationem suá habere: Apostolos in hunc usum Ecclesias commisse Episcopis: Apostolos successores suos statuisse Episcopos: ac proinde extraor-dinariam Apostolorum potestatem cum ipsis finem habuisse, nec in Ecclesia locum deinceps reperisse: ordinariam vero Apostolorum potestatem Episcopis commendatam fuisse, atque in illis permansisse: ex hoc fundamento Episcopos semper ordinasse: non fas,aut licitum fuisse, ut inferior maiorem ordinaret, quia nemo tribuit,quod non accepit: Presbyteros quidem posse facere, quæcunq; faciunt Episcopi, excepta ordinatione: itaque presbyteros ordinare non potuisse. Hæc apud antiquam Ecclesiam magno consensu firma & fixa fuerunt.
units.tr: After the authority of the holy Scriptures, the consensus of the Catholic Church has always carried such weight with me that whatever I see confirmed by this consensus seems to me sacrosanct and unchangeable. Now in this matter we have the consensus of the ancient Church: that bishops ordain, and that presbyters receive their ordination from bishops; that the Apostles committed the Churches to bishops for this purpose; that the Apostles appointed bishops as their successors; and that therefore the extraordinary power of the Apostles ended with them and found no place in the Church thereafter, but that the ordinary power of the Apostles was entrusted to bishops and remained in them. On this foundation the bishops always ordained; it was not lawful or permitted for an inferior to ordain a superior, because no one gives what he has not received; presbyters indeed could do whatever bishops do, except ordination, and so presbyters could not ordain. These things were held firm and fixed in the ancient Church with great consensus.

units.la: Obiiciunt quidam Hieronymi sententiam, eundem esse Presbyterum & Episcopum: Nos, ut Hieronymi sententiam examinemus, locum integrum subiiciemus. Idem est, inquit, Presbyter, qui Episcopus, & antequam Diaboli instinctu studia in religione fierent, & diceretur in populis: Ego sum Pauli, ego autem Cephæ, communi presbyterorum Concilio Ecclesia gubernabantur. Postquam vero unusquisq; eos, quos baptizauerat, suos putauerat esse, non Christi, in toto orbe decretum est, ut unus de presbyteris electus, superponeretur caeteris, ad quem omnis Ecclesia cura pertineret, & schismatum semina tollerentur. Concludit tandem: Sicut ergo presbyteri sciunt, se ex Ecclesia consuetudine ei, qui sibi præpositus fuerit, esse subiectos, ita Episcopi noverint, se magis consuetudine, quam dispositione Dominica veritate presbyteris esse maiores, & in commune debere Ecclesiam regere. Hæc Hieronymus. Ex quo loco colligunt, hanc Episcopi dignitatem super presbyteros, fuisse in generali aliquo Concilio concessam. Deinde adiiciunt Augustini locum, quæst. ex utroque testam. q. 101. In Alexandria, & per totam Ægyptum, si desit Episcopus, consecrat presbyter. Ex iis verbis Hieronymi & Augustini hic[?] interrogat vir quidam doctus: Quis credat, si ante illud tempus vniuersali Concilio res fuisset definita, hæc fuisse Alexandrinos, & Ægyptios illo tempore futuros?
units.tr: Some object the saying of Jerome, that presbyter and bishop are the same. That we may examine Jerome's opinion, we shall set out the whole passage. Presbyter is the same as bishop, he says, and before, at the instigation of the Devil, parties arose in religion, and it was said among the peoples: I am of Paul, but I am of Cephas, the Church was governed by the common council of the presbyters. But after each man began to think that those whom he had baptized were his own and not Christ's, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and set over the rest, to whom the whole care of the Church should pertain, and the seeds of schisms should be removed. Finally he concludes: Just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to him who has been set over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters by custom rather than by the Lord's arrangement, and that they ought to rule the Church in common. So far Jerome. From this passage they gather that this dignity of bishops above presbyters was granted by some general council. Then they add the passage of Augustine, in the book Quaestiones ex utroque Testamento, question 101: In Alexandria, and throughout all Egypt, if a bishop is lacking, a presbyter consecrates. From these words of Jerome and Augustine a certain learned man asks: who would believe that, if the matter had been defined by a universal council before that time, the Alexandrians and Egyptians would have acted in this way at that time?

units.la: Respondeo: Primum nego, hanc rem ex vniuersali aliquo Concilio definitam. Hieronymi verba hoc non probant. Dicit Hieronymus, decretum toto orbe. Hoc non fuit ex Concilio generali, sed ex ordinatione Apostolica. Nam certum est, Hieronymum loqui de regesta, viuentibus Apostolis, quum iam diceretur, Ego sum Pauli, ego autem Cephæ; quod certum est fuisse viuentibus Apostolis.
units.tr: I answer: first, I deny that this matter was defined by any universal council. Jerome's words do not prove this. Jerome says it was decreed throughout the whole world. This did not come from a general council but from an apostolic ordinance. For it is certain that Jerome is speaking of something done while the Apostles were still living, since it was already being said: I am of Paul, but I am of Cephas; and it is certain that this was while the Apostles were alive.

units.la: Certe Hieronymi verba [illegible, ~6 letters] Certe Hieronymi verba viterius extendi non possunt. Hoc igitur institutum ex Apostolis fluxit, ex eorum vsu & consuetudine. Verum est, Presbyterum & Episcopum quondam eundem fuisse in primis Ecclesiarum plantationibus, vt constat ex locis ab Hieronymo adductis. Sed postea (viuentibus adhuc Apostolis) quum Ecclesiae perpetuo duraturae vsus postularet, vt vnus aliquis ex presbyteris supra reliquos constitueretur ad haec officia, sine quibus Ecclesia nec bene esse, necesse omnino potuit: nempe ad schismata tollenda; 1. Tim. 1. 4. Et ad ordinandos presbyteros, Tit.1. Dico Episcopos ab Apostolis constitu-tos supra presbyteros ad hæc officia. Hoc Apostolorum factum Hieronymus vocat consuetudinem Ecclesiæ, non autem Dominicam dispositionem. Nisi hæc ita intelligantur, nec Hieronymus sibi ipse constare poterit, nec superiora Scripturæ loca componi possunt.
units.tr: Certainly Jerome's words cannot be extended further. This practice, therefore, flowed from the Apostles, from their use and custom. It is true that presbyter and bishop were once the same in the first plantings of Churches, as is clear from the passages Jerome cites. But afterwards, while the Apostles were still living, since the use of a Church meant to last forever required that one of the presbyters be set above the rest for those offices, without which the Church could not well exist, and indeed could not exist at all: namely, to remove schisms (1 Tim. 1. 4.) and to ordain presbyters (Tit. 1.). I say that bishops were appointed by the Apostles above the presbyters for these offices. Jerome calls this act of the Apostles the custom of the Church, not the Lord's arrangement. Unless these things are understood in this way, Jerome cannot be consistent with himself, nor can the earlier passages of Scripture be reconciled.

units.la: At, inquiunt, nisi hæc res definita fuisset post illa tempora, de quibus loquitur Augustinus, non est credibile, Alexandrinos ordinare voluisse sine Episcopis. Quibus verbis probare contendunt, hoc institutum fuisse in generali Concilio, & hoc Concilium fuisse post Augustini tempora.
units.tr: But, they say, unless this matter had been defined after those times of which Augustine speaks, it is not credible that the Alexandrians would have wished to ordain without bishops. By these words they strive to prove that this practice was established in a general council, and that this council was held after the time of Augustine.

units.la: Respondeo : Loquitur Augustinus de re, quæ apud Alexandrinos in vsu fuerat, viuen-te iam Augustino. ( Si tamen liber ille sit Augustini, quod ne Pontificii quidem censores agnoscunt.) Sed vt demusfuisse. Loquitur de re, quæ in vsu fuerat Augustino viuente. At Hieronymus Augustino antiquior, loquitur de antiqua Ecclesiæ consuetudine, quæ multis ante ipsum seculis duraverat. Et ante Hieronymum Cyprianus & Irenæus testantur, Episcopos ab Apostolis instituto s, & in Ecclesia regenda, esse Apostolorum successores. Videte, in quantas angustias viri docti se coniiciant? Nam si hæc res definita fuerat in Concilio generali post Augustini tempora, quomodo potuit esse antiqua Ecclesiæ consuetudo ante Hieronymi tempora? Si interrogent, rogent, quare ergo Alexandrini hoc fecerint? Respondeo: Hæc verba ( si defit Episcopus, presbyter consecrat, ) non necessario intelligenda esse de ordinatione, quia frequenter etiam usurpantur apud veteres in consecratione Sacramentali. Deinde, ut concedamus, de ordinatione dicta fuisse: dicimus, Alexandrinos fecisse hoc ex necessitate, quùm Episcopus adesse non poterat. Nam melius est ordinare sine Episcopis, quam ut Ecclesia omnino careat presbyteris: Atque hanc fuisse Augustini mentem, ut, quando Ecclesiæ usus necessarium presbyterorum ministerium postulasset, & Episcopus adesse non poterat, crearentur presbyteri sine Episcopis: nunquam autem hoc fiebat extra hanc necessitatem. Sic enim ait Augustinus, Si defit Episcopus, consecrat presbyter. Hic certe mos antiquus excusare potest factum earum Ecclesiarum, qui presbyteros ex necessitate consecrarunt, ubi Episcopi adesse vel noluerunt, vel non potuerunt.
units.tr: I answer: Augustine speaks of a practice which was in use among the Alexandrians while Augustine himself was still living (if indeed that book is Augustine's, which not even the Papist censors acknowledge). But grant that it was so: he speaks of a practice in use while Augustine was living. Jerome, however, who is older than Augustine, speaks of the ancient custom of the Church, which had lasted for many centuries before his own time. And before Jerome, Cyprian and Irenaeus testify that bishops were instituted by the Apostles and are the successors of the Apostles in ruling the Church. See into what straits learned men throw themselves! For if this matter had been defined in a general council after the time of Augustine, how could there have been an ancient custom of the Church before the time of Jerome? If they ask, why then did the Alexandrians do this? I answer: these words (if a bishop is lacking, a presbyter consecrates) need not necessarily be understood of ordination, since they are often used by the ancients of sacramental consecration. Next, even if we grant that they were said of ordination, we say that the Alexandrians did this out of necessity, when a bishop could not be present. For it is better to ordain without bishops than for the Church to be wholly without presbyters. And this was Augustine's meaning: that when the use of the Church required the necessary ministry of presbyters, and a bishop could not be present, presbyters were created without bishops; but this was never done outside this necessity. For Augustine says thus: If a bishop is lacking, a presbyter consecrates. This ancient custom can certainly excuse the deed of those Churches which made presbyters out of necessity, where bishops either would not or could not be present.

units.la: Si omnia Ecclesiæ secula lustremus ab Apostolicis temporibus, usque ad Patrum nostrorum memoriam, nō alia ordinandi ratio invenietur, nisi per Episcopos. Quam igitur sacram ceremoniam Ecclesia ab Apostolis accepit, & per tot secula constanter coleruit: quis potest reiicere, qui Ecclesiæ Catholicæ auctoritatem nō reiiciat? Neq; hæc in cōtumeliam aliarum Ecclesiarum accipi velim, sed potius in admonitionē. Quid enim magis decet Ecclesias Christi, quā charitas, & unitas? quia una est EcEcclesia omnes ad vnitatem contendere debemus; charitas autem est vnitatis vinculum. Itaque Episcoporum officium ex sacris literis, & Ecclesiae consensu, probatur esse huiusmodi. Vt Episcopi inseruiant primo, ad ordinandos presbyteros: quod constat ex Tit. 1.5. quae quidem ordinatio, quamuis praesentibus aliis presbyteris fieri solebat, manus suas vna etiam cum Episcopo imponentibus, sicut haec traditio optime declaratur Concil. Carthag.[?] 4. cap.3. nunquam tamen sine Episcopo facta est in Ecclesia: quia potestas ipsa ordinandi in Episcopo fuisse semper intelligebatur. Simplex enim presbyter nunquam solebat ordinare. 2. Deinde inseruiunt etiam in hoc ministerium Episcopi, vt haereses, & alienas omnes doctrinas autoritate sua atque industria extirpari curent, quod constat ex 1. Tim. 1.3. quo loco iubet Apostolus, vt Timotheus mansionem suam Ephesi figat, vt denuntiare possit quibusdam, ne alienam doctrinam doceant. Ad haec ministeria Episcopos in Ecclesia constituerunt Apostoli, sicut partim ex Scripturis, partim ex Patrum consensu probatur. Quum igitur ex sacris literis, & Ecclesiae consensu Episcoporum officium probetur, debent omnes Ecclesiae reformatae ad hanc Ecclesiae vnitatem accedere, & spes est, accessuras omnes, quum posito contentionis studio, & pertinaci obstinatione, veritas, & Ecclesiae vnitas quaeritur. Spes est, inquam, quod ex necessitate pro tempore constitutum fuerat, rat, maturo consilio, & deliberatione, ex charitate, ad pristinam Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consuetudinem reducendum fore.
units.tr: If we survey all the centuries of the Church from the time of the Apostles down to the memory of our fathers, we find no method of ordination other than through bishops. Who, then, can reject a sacred ceremony that the Church received from the Apostles and kept constantly through so many centuries, unless he also rejects the authority of the Catholic Church? I do not wish this to be taken as an insult to the other Churches, but rather as an admonition. For what befits the Churches of Christ more than charity and unity? The Church is one, and we must all strive for unity, and charity is the bond of unity. Accordingly, the office of bishops is shown, from Holy Scripture and the consent of the Church, to be of this kind. First, bishops serve to ordain elders, as is clear from Titus 1:5. Although this ordination was usually performed in the presence of other elders, who laid their hands on with the bishop, as the Council of Carthage 4, chapter 3, plainly records, it was never performed in the Church without a bishop, because the power of ordaining was always understood to reside in the bishop. A mere elder never ordained. (2) Second, bishops also serve in this ministry, that they take care, by their authority and diligence, to root out heresies and all strange doctrines, as is clear from 1 Timothy 1:3, where the Apostle bids Timothy to remain at Ephesus so that he may charge certain people not to teach strange doctrine. The Apostles appointed bishops in the Church for these ministries, as is shown partly from Scripture and partly from the consent of the Fathers. Since, then, the office of bishops is proved from Holy Scripture and the consent of the Church, all the reformed Churches ought to come to this unity of the Church, and there is hope that they will all come, when, the zeal for contention and stubborn obstinacy being set aside, truth and the unity of the Church are sought. There is hope, I say, that what had been established for a time out of necessity will, by mature counsel and deliberation, and out of charity, be brought back to the ancient custom of the Catholic Church.

units.la: Quod si obstrepant Pontificii turbatores, atque ex nostra hac disputatione colligant, Ecclesiam non esse apud eos, apud quos non sunt Episcopi. Respondeo: Ecclesiæ quidem Catholicæ consuetudinem esse, ut Episcopi legitime ordinent: sed si quis à presbytero ordinatus fuerit, ordinatio illa etiam vera est, ex eiusdem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ iudicio. Nam quod in Baptismo hæreticorum iudicare solebat Ecclesia, Baptismum male ab illis dari, male ab iisdem accipi, quamdiu in hæresi perstiterint; ipsum tamen Baptismum verum esse, nec iterandum esse, quum isti ad Ecclesiam Catholicam accesserint: idem iudicandum est de ordinatione; etiamsi non legitime data fuerit, veram tamen esse, nec iterandam in Ecclesia Catholica. Itaque quum Parmenianus Donatista docuisset, Baptismum non quidem amittere, qui recedit ab Ecclesia, sed ius dandi amittere; sic Augustinus respondet: {a} Hoc multis modis frustra dicitur, quia nulla ostenditur causa, cur ille, qui ipsum Baptismum amittere non potest, ius dandi amittere possit. Utrumque enim Sacramentum est, & quadam consecratione hominis datur; illud quum baptizatur; istud, quum ordinatur: ideoque in Catholica utrumque non licet iterari. Hæc Augustinus. Quo loco multa habet in eandem sententiam. Deinde hæc verba subiicit: Sicut autem habent in Baptismo, quod per eos dari possit, sic in ordinatione ius dandi. Virumq; quidem ad perniciem suam, quamdiu charitatem non habent vnitatis. Sed tamen aliud est, prorsus non habere, aliud perniciose habere, aliud salubriter habere. Hæc ille.
units.tr: But if the Papists, those troublemakers, shout at us and gather from this discussion that the Church is not among those who have no bishops, I answer: it is indeed the custom of the Catholic Church that bishops ordain lawfully; but if anyone has been ordained by a presbyter, that ordination too is valid, by the judgment of the same Catholic Church. For just as the Church used to judge concerning the baptism of heretics, that it was wrongly given by them and wrongly received from them as long as they persisted in heresy, yet that the baptism itself is valid and not to be repeated when these people come to the Catholic Church, so the same must be judged of ordination: even if it was not given lawfully, it is nevertheless valid and is not to be repeated in the Catholic Church. Thus, when Parmenian the Donatist taught that one who withdraws from the Church does not indeed lose baptism but loses the power of giving it, Augustine replied: {a} This is said in vain in many ways, because no reason is shown why he who cannot lose baptism itself should be able to lose the power of giving it. Each is a sacrament, and is given by a certain consecration of the man: the one when he is baptized, the other when he is ordained; and therefore neither may be repeated in the Catholic Church. So Augustine. In that place he has much to the same effect. Then he adds these words: Just as they have in baptism what can be given through them, so they have in ordination the power of giving. Each, indeed, to their own destruction, as long as they lack the charity of unity. But it is one thing to have nothing at all, another to have it to one's ruin, and another to have it to one's salvation. So he.

units.la: Iohannes Episcopus Rauennæ dubitabat, an reordinandi essent, qui ita ordinati fuerant; ad eum Gregorius sic scribit: Illud autem, quod dicitis, vt is, qui ordinatus est, iterum ordinetur, valde ridiculum est. Absit autem à fraternitate vestra, sic sapere. Sicut enim baptizatus semel, iterum baptizari non debet, ita qui consecratus est semel, in eodem iterum ordine non debet consecrari.
units.tr: John, bishop of Ravenna, doubted whether those who had been ordained in such a way should be ordained again. Gregory writes to him thus: But what you say, that he who has been ordained should be ordained again, is utterly ridiculous. Far be it from your brotherhood to think so. For just as one who has been baptized once ought not to be baptized again, so one who has been consecrated once ought not to be consecrated again in the same order.

units.la: Si vero Aduersarii vlterius vrgeant, ex Augustini ergo sententia Ecclesias illas, quæ non habent ordinationem ab Episcopis, habere ordinationem, sed ad perniciem suam: negamus hanc consequentiam: quia aliud est, recedere ab Ecclesia Romana: aliud vero, recedere ab Ecclesia Catholica. Recesserunt ab ordinatione Ecclesiæ Romanæ ex necessitate; quia post publicata Tridentina decreta, non potuerunt cum Catholica communicare, nisi recessissent ab illo conciliabulo. Recesserunt igitur ex necessitate. Quum vero ad Ecclesiæ Catholicæ consuetudinem in hac re redierint, sicut in aliis redierunt, facile inuenient Episcopos Catholicos, qui ex charitate supplebunt id, quod ex necessitate defuerat.
units.tr: But if our adversaries press further, that by Augustine's opinion those Churches which do not have ordination from bishops do have ordination, but to their own destruction, we deny this consequence, because it is one thing to withdraw from the Roman Church and another to withdraw from the Catholic Church. They withdrew from the ordination of the Roman Church out of necessity, because after the Tridentine decrees were published they could not communicate with the Catholic Church unless they withdrew from that conciliabulum. They therefore withdrew out of necessity. Since they have returned in this matter to the custom of the Catholic Church, as they have returned in other matters, they will easily find Catholic bishops who, out of charity, will supply what was lacking through necessity.

units.la: Illud vero nobis ridiculum videtur, quod
units.tr: But this seems ridiculous to us, that

units.la: • Gregor. lib. 2. indiɛt. 10. Epist. 32. illi successionem nostram, maxime scilicet accusare audeant, qui nec successionem, nec vero vocationem suam in Ecclesia DEI ostendere possunt. Nam si venerabiles Episcopi & Presbyteri, quorum successionem ab Apostolis, & septuaginta discipulis Christi deuenientem agnoscimus, hoc nobis obiecissent, ferendum viderentur. At quis Iesuitas, de successione disputantes rulerit[?]? Iesuitae sunt, qui successionis impedimentum nostris acerrime obiiciunt: quos, si Tertulliani verbis interrogemus; Quid agitis in meo, non mei? Quid vobis cum Ecclesia DEI? Quid possunt respondere? Certe Iesuitae nullam omnino vocationem habent in Ecclesia: Non sunt à CHRISTO missi, non ab Apostolis instituti, & tamen audent se in Ecclesia CHRISTI operarios iactare, consessiones audire, Sacramenta administrare, imo & Pastores à CHRISTO institutos, officiis muneribusque suis extrudere, & in eorum locum seipsos introducere. Qui ad Ecclesiae aedificationem, & Ecclesiae ministerium à Christo instituti sunt, enumerantur ab Apostolo, Apostoli, Prophetae, Euangelistae, Pa-stores, doctores: quos dedit ad consummationem sanctorum, in opus ministerii, in aedificationem Corporis Christi, donec occurramus omnes in unitatem fidei, & agnitionis Filii Dei. Hos igitur Christus instituit ad Ecclesiae aedificationem, usq; ad consummationem sanctorum, adeoq; usq; ad finem mundi: quicunq; praeter illos sese in Ecclesiae ministerio intruserint, vocationem in Ecclesia nullam probare possunt. Ac proinde Iesuitae, omnesque reliqui regularium ordines, non dico successionem ab Apostolis, sed ne vocationem quidem suam demonstrare possunt.
units.tr: {Gregory, Register book 2, indiction 10, letter 32.} they dare to accuse our succession, especially those who can show neither their succession nor their calling in the Church of God. For if the venerable bishops and elders, whose succession we acknowledge as descending from the Apostles and the seventy disciples of Christ, had brought this objection against us, it would seem to be endured. But who could bear the Jesuits, disputing about succession? It is the Jesuits who most fiercely throw the lack of succession at our people. If we question them in Tertullian's words: What are you doing in what is mine, not yours? What have you to do with the Church of God? what can they answer? Certainly the Jesuits have no calling at all in the Church: they were not sent by Christ, not instituted by the Apostles, and yet they dare to boast of themselves as workers in the Church of Christ, to hear confessions, to administer the sacraments, and even to thrust out of their offices and functions the ministers instituted by Christ and to put themselves in their place. Those whom Christ instituted for the building up of the Church and its ministry are enumerated by the Apostle: apostles, prophets, evangelists, ministers, teachers, whom he gave for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ, until we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God. Christ therefore instituted these for the building up of the Church, until the perfecting of the saints, and so until the end of the world. Whoever has thrust himself into the ministry of the Church apart from these cannot prove any calling in the Church. And so the Jesuits, and all the remaining orders of regulars, cannot demonstrate not only their succession from the Apostles but not even their calling.

units.la: Itaque Episcopos, & presbyteros, quamuis in nonnullis religionis capitibus à nobis dissentiant, tamen non solum ferendos, verum propter loci, quem occupant, dignitatem, & successionem ab Apostolis, venerabiles aesti-mamus: de quibus spes est, ipsos propter eruditionem & iudicium, quo inter eos plurimi excellunt, praestigias Iesuiticas tandem aliquando perspectas atque exploratas abominatūros, veritatem quoque nobiscum amplexaturos. Maxime vero venerabilibus Episcopis, & clero Gallicano hanc mentis sanitatem exoptamus, & precibus à Deo Opt.Max. exoptamus, apud quos Concilii Tridentini decreta authoritatem obtinere nunquam potuerunt. Et profecto, qui inter eos eruditione & vitae sanctimonia praestant, facile perspiciunt, quo tendat Iesuitarum furiosus in Ecclesia impetus: nempe non ad aedificationem, sed ad fidei destructionem, ad Ecclesiae horrendam conturbationem, ad Regum perniciem, & Rerumpublicarum ruinam. Si in Galliis, Germania, Hispania, Italia, cum Ecclesiae statum videre liceret, qui ante fraterculorum exortos Ordines in istis nationibus florere solebat, Ecclesiam omnino perditam non possemus deplo-
units.tr: Accordingly, bishops and elders, although they differ from us in some heads of religion, we judge to be not only to be endured but also venerable, on account of the dignity of the place they occupy and their succession from the Apostles. Of them we hope that, because of their learning and judgment, in which very many of them excel, they will at last abhor the Jesuitical tricks, once they have been seen through and examined, and will embrace the truth along with us. Above all we wish this soundness of mind for the venerable bishops and the Gallican clergy, and we pray for it from God, Best and Greatest, among whom the decrees of the Council of Trent have never been able to obtain authority. And indeed, those among them who excel in learning and holiness of life readily perceive whither the furious assault of the Jesuits in the Church tends: namely, not to edification but to the destruction of faith, to the dreadful disturbance of the Church, to the ruin of kings and the overthrow of commonwealths. If in France, Germany, Spain and Italy it were possible to see the state of the Church which used to flourish in those nations before the orders of little brothers arose, we could not deplore the Church as utterly lost

units.la: dep nic tat om Ecc eni Re co sub rui me aut mi mu ex co cu hy cu fa du Ec cu fr W m ue fi pl d u o deplorare. Et quid est, quod Ecclesiis Britannicis hanc, qua Dei misericordia & benignitate fruimur, felicitatem praestiterit, nisi quod omnes fraterculorum Ordines radicitus ex Ecclesia nostra extirpatos videamus? Fratres enim primi induxerunt noua illa dogmata, Reges non esse Reges Clericorum, nec Clericos Regibus suis, sed Papae tantummodo esse subditos. Fratres commenta illa excogitarunt, de accidentibus sine subiecto in Sacramento altaris, & quod nulla substantia panis aut vini remaneat post consecrationem: primi obedientiam caecam intulerunt; primi multas pecuniarias in Ecclesia induxerunt, & ex ipsis peccatis populi quaestu sibi sordidum confecerunt: & humilitate antiquorum conculcata, superbiam, auaritiam, simoniam, & hypocrisin in Ecclesiam intulerunt, bella procurarunt: primi articulum illum fidei, Credo sanctam Ecclesiam Catholicam, destruxerunt; dum profanos atque impios homines sanctae Ecclesiae membra esse docuerunt, Christumq; cum Diabolo coniunxerunt. Haec, & plura a fraterculis inuenta fuisse, obseruat Iohannes Wiclefus. Sed haec olim. Iesuitae vero noua monstra quotidie addunt Patrum suorum inuentionibus, quibus Ecclesiam & Regna dissipent. Ex hoc venenato fonte doctrina illa profluit, de Regibus deponendis, interficiendis, de subditis a fide suorum Principum reuocandis. Quod si venerabiles Episcopi ae quis oculis prospicere nolint Ecclesiae, & Regno-
units.tr: ...to lament. And what is it that has granted our British Churches this happiness, which by God's mercy and goodness we enjoy, if not that we see all the orders of the friars uprooted from our Church? For the friars first introduced those new doctrines: that kings are not kings of the clergy, and clergy are not subject to their own kings, but only to the Pope. The friars devised those fictions about accidents without a subject in the sacrament of the altar, and that no substance of bread or wine remains after consecration. The friars first introduced blind obedience; they first introduced many pecuniary exactions into the Church, and from the very sins of the people they made a filthy profit for themselves. Trampling down the humility of the ancients, they brought pride, avarice, simony and hypocrisy into the Church, and they stirred up wars. They first destroyed that article of the faith, I believe the holy Catholic Church, while they taught that profane and impious men are members of the holy Church, and joined Christ with the Devil. John Wycliffe observes that these and many other things were invented by the friars. But that was long ago. The Jesuits, however, add new monsters every day to the inventions of their fathers, by which they scatter the Church and the kingdoms. From this poisoned spring flows that doctrine about deposing and killing kings, and about calling subjects back from the faith of their princes. But if the venerable bishops are unwilling to look with their eyes on the ruin of the Church and of all the kingdoms,

units.la: rum omnium ruinam, non possunt certe non videre, ad suum officium hoc pertinere, ut lesuitarum furores, quantum in se est, cohibeant, & prospiciant, ne quid Ecclesia detrimeti capiat. Haec multis ante seculis praeviderat Iohannes Wiclefus, & praedixerat eventura.
units.tr: they certainly cannot fail to see that it belongs to their office to restrain the fury of the Jesuits, as far as in them lies, and to take care that the Church suffers no harm. John Wycliffe foresaw this many centuries ago, and had foretold what would happen.

units.la: Verba eius referam: a [?] Olim Episcopi nostri dicuntur pseudofratres, tanquam Diabolos odivisse, & in tempore Domini Armachani, dicuntur ipsum in sumptibus contra hos pseudoordines defendisse, sed modo facti sunt amici, Herodes & Pilatus, qui prius intra se fuerant inimici. Duo igitur prognostico in hac parte. Primum, quum ista confoederatio non sit fundata in Lege Domini nostri Iesu Christi, quod non stabit, sed cessabit ad damnum utriusq; partis, sive alterius, cum non sit bona societas Christiani cum Belial. Secundum est, quod vel oportet nostros Episcopos, & Regni Proceres opiniones istorum pseudofratrum deserere in hac parte, vel quod cum illis sint in haeresi innoluti. Haec ille. Atque haec est illa haeresis decantata Wiclefi, quod Episcopis & presbyteris, contra fraterculorum novitates adhaereret, & quod antiquam Ecclesiae Romanae doctrinam, contra istorum figmenta propugnaret.
units.tr: I will quote his words: Formerly our bishops are called pseudo-friars, and are hated as devils; and in the time of the Lord Armachanus they are said to have defended him in his expenses against these pseudo-orders; but now they have become friends, Herod and Pilate, who before had been enemies between themselves. There are therefore two prognoses in this matter. First, since this confederation is not founded on the law of our Lord Jesus Christ, it will not stand, but will cease, to the loss of both parties, or of one of them, since there is no good fellowship of a Christian with Belial. Second, either our bishops and the nobles of the realm must abandon the opinions of these pseudo-friars in this matter, or they are entangled with them in heresy. So he. And this is that much-talked-of heresy of Wycliffe: that he adhered to the bishops and presbyters against the novelties of the friars, and that he defended the ancient doctrine of the Roman Church against their fabrications.

units.la: Reddite nobis, Venerabiles Episcopi, imo reddite Christo Ecclesiam, qualem invenerunt Ordines isti pseudofratrum, necamplius optabimus. Eiicite Iesuitas, regularesque reliquos, quorum vocatio nulla est in Ecclesia Christi: eiicite una cum istis nova dogmata, & figmenta ab istis excogitata, ab istis inuecta: quod profecto facietis sedulo, si
units.tr: Give us back, venerable bishops, nay, give back to Christ the Church, such as those orders of pseudo-friars found it, and we shall desire no more. Cast out the Jesuits and the rest of the regular clergy, whose calling is no calling in the Church of Christ; cast out with them the new doctrines and fictions devised by them and introduced by them. This you will surely do diligently, if

units.la: [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] Christo vestram operam in Ecclesia probare velitis. Hæc nisi vos præstiteritis, fieri non potest, quin eueniat, quod futurum prædixit Wiclefus, vt vos vna cum illis in eorum hæresi inuoluatis.
units.tr: [illegible passage] you wish to prove your labour in the Church to Christ. Unless you do this, it cannot but come to pass what Wycliffe foretold: that you would be entangled together with them in their heresy.

units.la: CAPVT XII. De Erroris origine.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII. On the origin of error.

units.la: HActenus disputauimus de Ecclesiæ sanctitate, amplitudine, communione cum Capite, & inter se, de ratione cognoscendi Ecclesiam certissimâ per regulam fidei, de successione & ordinatione. Nunc ad originem erroris aperiendam accedimus. Obseruandū igitur est, varios de Ecclesia errores apud Pontificios receptos esse, qui tamen omnes ad duo capita reduci posse videtur, nempe ad Caput, & membra Ecclesiæ. De illis erroribus, qui sunt de membris Ecclesiæ, superius ea diximus, ex quibus constare potest, ante annum Christi millesimum, id est, ante Satanæ solutionem, inauditum fuisse in Ecclesia, membra Ecclesiæ esse homines non sanctos. Post annū millesimum communis sententia Ecclesiæ Romanæ, Bellarmino teste, usque ad Concilium Tridentinum, imo usq; ad ipsum Bellarminū, veritatem constanter retinuit, sicut superius demonstrauimus. At fratres, ad Papæ arbitrium, & Romanæ Curiæ placita doctrinam hanc antiquam mutarunt, atq; ita mutarunt, vt alia iam significatio affingeretur huic verbo, Ecclesiæ, quam superioribus seculis intelligi solebat. Tandem enim per Ecclesiam nihil aliud intelligi voluerunt corruptores isti, quam Papam, & Cardinales Romæ. Ita ut jam Ecclesia, quæ prius ubique sparsa fuerat, Romæ tandem alligata videretur, & à cœtu fidelium, ad cœtum Cardinalium contracta. Sed hic sensus est modernus, sicut monet Marsilius Patauinus.
units.tr: Hitherto we have discussed the holiness, extent and communion of the Church with its Head and with one another, the most certain way of knowing the Church by the rule of faith, and its succession and ordination. Now we come to lay open the origin of the error. It must be observed, then, that the Papists have received various errors about the Church, which nevertheless seem all to be reducible to two heads, namely the Head and the members of the Church. Of those errors which concern the members of the Church, we have said above what can establish that, before the year of Christ 1000, that is, before the loosing of Satan, it was unheard of in the Church that the members of the Church were unholy men. After the year 1000, the common opinion of the Roman Church, by Bellarmine's witness, held the truth steadily until the Council of Trent, indeed until Bellarmine himself, as we have shown above. But these brothers, at the discretion of the Pope and at the pleasure of the Roman Curia, changed this ancient doctrine, and changed it so that another meaning was now attached to the word Church, different from what was usually understood in earlier centuries. For at last those corrupters chose to understand by the Church nothing other than the Pope and the Cardinals at Rome; so that the Church, which had previously been scattered everywhere, now seemed bound at Rome and drawn in from an assembly of the faithful to an assembly of Cardinals. But this sense is modern, as Marsilius of Padua warns.

units.la: Sic enim de hac re scribit: {a}Apud modernos maxime importat hoc nomen, Ecclesia, omnes Presbyteros, seu Episcopos, atq; Diaconos, qui ministrant, & præsunt in Metropolitana, fi[?] u principali omnium Ecclesiarum, quemadmodum hoc Ecclesia Romana urbis dudum obtinuit, cuius ministri & præsidentes sunt Papa, & Cardinales ipsius, qui jam ex usu quodam obtinuerunt dici Ecclesia. Hæc ille. Sed hæc est moderna Ecclesiæ significatio, neque Scripturis, neque Patribus probata.
units.tr: For he writes thus about this matter: {a}Among the moderns this name, Church, chiefly signifies all the presbyters, or bishops, and deacons, who minister and preside in the metropolitan or principal church of all the churches, just as the Roman Church of the city has long held this place, whose ministers and presiders are the Pope and his Cardinals, who by a certain custom have now come to be called the Church. So he. But this is the modern meaning of the Church, approved neither by the Scriptures nor by the Fathers.

units.la: Hæc mutatio significationis antiquæ occasio fuit omnium errorum, qui postea dormientibus hominibus, tanquam zizania, ab inimico homine introducta fuerunt: quæ zizania hodie pro Romano tritico ventilantur. Constat igitur, Ecclesiam mutatam esse apud Pontificios ab ea, quæ fuerat. Originem huius mutationis notamus post annum millesimum inchoatam à fraterculis, quæ tamen mutatio confirmationem suam autoritatemque nuper obtinuit. Adeoque omnia jam mutata constant, quæ Ecclesiam constituunt, Caput, membra, regula, ut & ipsa denique vis & significatio nominis mutetur: qua quidem in re infiinsignem Pontificiorum fraudem observamus. Nam ut facilius imperitis imponant Ecclesiae nomen, Ecclesiae authoritatem ubique ingeminant, nos vero apud vulgus hoc odio grauare volunt, quasi Ecclesiae Catholicae authoritas apud nos minus valeret. At quaestio non est de Ecclesiae authoritate, sed de ipsa Ecclesia, quaenam sit, ubi quaerenda, ubi invenienda? Dicimus igitur, Ecclesiam apud Pontificios omnino mutatam esse. Ecclesia Catholica una est, non mutatur. Atque hoc est, quod in istis praevaricatoribus maxime reprehendimus, quod intelligere nolunt, Ecclesiam Catholicam a fide Catholica separari non posse: Qui fidem & veritatem deserunt, Ecclesiam se retinere putant: plane frustra, & sine authoritate, sine promissione, sine ratione. De fide Catholica non sunt solliciti, de Ecclesia multum sibi applaudunt. Confingunt se esse Ecclesiam, deinde seipsos sensumque suum, imo vero universam Ecclesiam, sicut isti arbitrantur, ita Romano Pontifici subiiciunt, vel potius profitentur[?], ut is sit os, & Caput, & sponsus, & Rector, & Rex, & Monarcha universalis Ecclesiae: hoc in Ecclesia Christi longe turpissimum est, veteribus prorsus inauditum. Et quia haec est Ecclesia illa, quam proponunt nobis multiplici sophismatum fraude deformatam: hanc Ecclesiam mutatam in Capite, in membris, in Regula, in significatione, antiquis incognitam; nos merito reiicimus. Mutam enim, & sophisticam Ecclesiam, scimus non esse Christi Ecclesiam, quæ vna est in patribus, filiisque, in præcedentibus, præsentibus, & futuris. Quæ vero tam diuersa est ab antiqua, non est vna, ac proinde nec Ecclesia.
units.tr: This change of the ancient meaning was the occasion of all the errors which were afterwards introduced, while men slept, by the enemy man, like tares; and these tares are today passed off as Roman wheat. It is clear, therefore, that the Church among the Papists has been changed from what it was. We note that the origin of this change began after the year 1000 with the little friars, and yet this change has only recently gained its confirmation and authority. Thus everything that constitutes the Church is now seen to have been altered: the Head, the members, the rule, and even the very force and meaning of the name itself. In this matter we observe a remarkable fraud of the Papists. For in order to impose the name of the Church more easily on the unlearned, they everywhere repeat the authority of the Church, while they want to burden us with hatred of it before the common people, as though the authority of the Catholic Church counted for less with us. But the question is not about the authority of the Church, but about the Church itself: what it is, where it is to be sought, where it is to be found? We say therefore that the Church among the Papists has been wholly changed. The Catholic Church is one and does not change. And this is what we chiefly reprove in those prevaricators, that they are unwilling to understand that the Catholic Church cannot be separated from the Catholic faith. Those who abandon the faith and the truth think they still retain the Church: plainly in vain, and without authority, without promise, without reason. They are not anxious about the Catholic faith, but they congratulate themselves greatly about the Church. They pretend that they are the Church, and then they subject themselves, their opinion, and indeed, as these men think, the whole Church, to the Roman Pontiff, or rather they profess that he is the mouth, the Head, the bridegroom, the Ruler, the King and universal Monarch of the Church. This is in the Church of Christ by far the most shameful thing, utterly unknown to the ancients. And because this is that Church which they set before us, deformed by a manifold fraud of sophisms, this Church changed in its Head, in its members, in its rule, in its meaning, unknown to the ancients, we rightly reject. For we know that a changed and sophistical Church is not the Church of Christ, which is one in the fathers and sons, in those who went before, in those who are present, and in those to come. But a Church so different from the ancient one is not one, and therefore not a Church at all.

units.la: Post annum igitur millesimum deformari cœperat Ecclesia in membris per fraterculos, deinde deformari in significatione, adeoque mutari in aliud; quam quod prius fuerat: maxime vero deformari in Capite. Errori de Capite primus, quod sciam, Aquinas ingenium suum accommodauit, quum noua quædam de Ecclesiæ Capite inuexerit. Inde grassare cœpit hic error in Ecclesia Romana: quia de Ecclesiæ Capite antiqua traditio innouata est, & penitus immutata. Antiqui Patres vnum Christum Ecclesiæ Caput agnoscunt, idque ex Apostoli verbis: Ipsum dedit Caput super v[?]mnem Ecclesiam, quæ est corpus ipsius. Aquinas autem à Scripturis Patribusque secessit[?]. Sic enimscribit: {a}Papa est totius Ecclesiæ Caput.
units.tr: After the year 1000, therefore, the Church began to be deformed in its members through the little friars, then deformed in its meaning, and so changed into something other than what it had been before; and most of all it was deformed in its Head. As far as I know, Aquinas first accommodated his talent to the error about the Head, when he introduced certain new notions about the Head of the Church. From there this error began to spread in the Roman Church, because the ancient tradition about the Head of the Church was renewed and wholly changed. The ancient Fathers acknowledge one Christ as the Head of the Church, and this from the words of the Apostle: He gave him to be head over all the Church, which is his body. But Aquinas departed from the Scriptures and the Fathers. For he writes thus: {a}The Pope is the Head of the whole Church.

units.la: Atque alio item loco: {b}Summum Pontifex gerit plenarie vicem Christi in tota Ecclesia.
units.tr: And in another place likewise: {b}The Supreme Pontiff fully bears the place of Christ in the whole Church.

units.la: Quamuis ergo Bonifacius III. pluribus ante Aquinatem seculis, hunc titulum sibi suisq; successoribus arripuerat, vt Oicumenicus diceretur, siue vniuersalis Episcopus, qui tamen proxime Bonifacium secuti sunt tractatores, offensi, vt videtur tam superbo, & blasphemo titulo, & grauissimo Gregorii iudicio, (vt credi par est) permoti, nusquam Romano Pontifici hunc titulum concedunt. Furtim tamen, & surreptitiis arcibus patientiam Ecclesiae tentauit Rom. Pontifex, vt primo sibi titulum oicumenici, deinde Capitis Ecclesiae arriperet. Nobis mirandum videtur, esse aliquos homines in Ecclesia doctos, qui salua conscientia titulos istos vel defendere, vel Rom. Pontifici concedere possit. Neque enim, inquit Apostolus, sibiipsi quisquam sumit hunc honorem, sed qui vocatur à Deo, sicut & Aaron. At Rom. Pontifices hunc sibi honorem sumpserunt, non à Deo vocati, testis est orbis terrarum, testis historia, testis Ecclesia, testis Romanus Pontifex Gregorius Primus, hos titulos esse profanos, vanos, nomina vanitatis, vocabula peruersa, vocabula elationis, nomen scelestum, superstitiosum, superbum, appellationem nefandi nominis, profani nominis superbiam, appellationem frivoli nominis, vanitatem stulti nominis, nomen pompaticum. Haec est Gregorii censura de titulo vniuersalis Episcopi, quum iam nomen illud Capitis Ecclesiae nondum erat excogitatum, Romano Pontifici nondum delatum. Praeuidebat tamen vir sanctus, ex oicumenici titulo, alterum necessario sequi.
units.tr: Although Boniface III, many centuries before Aquinas, had seized for himself and his successors this title, that he should be called Oecumenical, or universal bishop, yet the writers who followed Boniface closely, offended, as it seems, by so proud and blasphemous a title, and (as it is fitting to believe) moved by the very grave judgment of Gregory, nowhere grant this title to the Roman Pontiff. Nevertheless the Roman Pontiff, by stealth and by underhand devices, tried the patience of the Church, so that he might first seize for himself the title of Oecumenical, and then that of Head of the Church. It seems astonishing to us that there are learned men in the Church who could, with a clear conscience, either defend these titles or concede them to the Roman Pontiff. For, says the Apostle, no one takes this honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. But the Roman Pontiffs have taken this honour to themselves, not being called by God; the world, history, the Church, and the Roman Pontiff Gregory the First bear witness to this, who declared these titles to be profane, vain, names of vanity, perverse words, words of arrogance, a wicked and superstitious name, a proud appellation, the appellation of an unspeakable name, the pride of a profane name, the appellation of a frivolous name, the vanity of a foolish name, a pompous name. This is Gregory's judgment on the title of universal bishop, at a time when that name of Head of the Church had not yet been devised and had not yet been transferred to the Roman Pontiff. Yet the holy man foresaw that the second would necessarily follow from the first, from the title of Oecumenical.

units.la: Itaque sic scribit: a Sub vno Capite omnes membra sunt Ecclesiae, sancti ante Legem, sub Lege, sancti sub gratia: & nemo se vnquam vniuersalem vocari voluit. Quibus verbis vtrumque titulum aeque damnat Gregorius. Ratio Gregorii obseruanda est: quia Episcopus, quicunque sit, membrum est Ecclesiae Catholicae; nemo autem potest esse & membrum,& Ca-put Ecclesiæ Catholicæ. Itaque Gregorius sic scribit: {a}Vniuersa sibi tentat asscribere, & omnia, quæ soli vni Capiti cohærent, videlicet Christo, per elationem pompatici sermonis, eiusdem Christi sibi studet membra subiicere. Hæc Gregorius. Quibus verbis friuolum illud effugium de Capite ministeriali penitus disperdit. Nam si quis opponat, Romanum Pontificem esse Vicarium Christi, & Caput ministeriale: Responder Gregorius, soli vni Capiti tribuendum esse hunc honorem, non ergo Vicario: esse solum vnum Caput Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, non igitur locum esse Capiti ministeriali in Ecclesia vniuersa; neminem debere membra sibi eiusdem Christi subiice[illegible, ~5 letters] Vicarium Christi, aut
units.tr: And so he writes: {a}Under the one Head all are the members of the Church, the saints before the Law, under the Law, the saints under grace; and no one has ever wished to be called universal. By these words Gregory condemns both titles equally. Gregory's reasoning is to be observed: because a bishop, whoever he may be, is a member of the Catholic Church; but no one can be both a member and the Head of the Catholic Church. Gregory therefore writes thus: {a}He tries to ascribe to himself universal things, and all that cleaves only to the one Head, namely Christ, through the pride of a pompous speech, he strives to subject the members of that same Christ to himself. So Gregory. By these words he utterly destroys that flimsy escape of a ministerial Head. For if anyone objects that the Roman Pontiff is the Vicar of Christ and a ministerial Head, Gregory answers that this honour belongs to one Head alone, and not therefore to a Vicar; that there is only one Head of the Catholic Church, and therefore there is no room for a ministerial Head in the universal Church; and that no one ought to subject the members of that same Christ to himself, the Vicar of Christ, or [illegible]

units.la: Bernar[?] natem[?] planet[?] optime[?] Christi[?] definit[?] stolo[?] Quis a[?] pus Pa[?] Pof[?] pæau[?] lastic[?] facu[?] modu[?] state[?] Scho[?] pa e[?] re : neminem igitur esse Vicarium [?] ...
