units.la: Caput ministeriale in Ecclesia vniuersa.
units.tr: The ministerial head in the universal Church.

units.la: Itaque qui Gregorium sequuti sunt ante Aquinatem Scriptores Ecclesiastici, quum ex industria de Ecclesiæ Capite disputent, vnumquę [?] Christum vnius Ecclesiæ Caput esse confirment, non est dubium, quin Romani Pontificis profanam arrogantiam irriserint, quandoquidem nusquam ei concedunt hunc honorem, quem ipse sibi tam in fano studio quæsiuerat. Christum Ecclesiæ Caput vnicum, constanter docent post Gregorii Primi, & Bonifacii Tertii tempora, Cassiodorus , Iustus Orgelitanus , Leo II. Toletan. Concilium VIII. Beda , Alcuinus , Angelomus , Theophylactus , Smaragdus , Bernar-
units.tr: Therefore the ecclesiastical writers who followed Gregory before Aquinas, when they deliberately discuss the Head of the Church and affirm that Christ alone is the Head of the one Church, undoubtedly mocked the profane arrogance of the Roman Pontiff, since they nowhere grant him that honour, which he had sought for himself with such shameless zeal. After the times of Gregory the First and Boniface the Third, Cassiodorus, Justus of Urgel, Leo II, the Eighth Council of Toledo, Bede, Alcuin, Angelomus, Theophylact, Smaragdus, Bernard [...]

units.la: cent [?] tion [?] mat [?] cem [?] esse [?] tem [?] sen [?] lio [?] cer [?] be [?] di [?] im [?] pr [?] P [?] fi [?] Bernardus{a}. Denique quicunq; ante Aquinatem de Capite Ecclesiæ disputarunt, idem plane tradunt. In eoque cum antiqua Ecclesia optime istis conuenit, Ecclesiam esse corpus Christi. Nec breuius aut lucidius se Ecclesiam definire posse existimant, quam si cum Apostolo Ecclesiam dicant esse corpus Christi. Quis autem unquam Ecclesiam dixit esse corpus Papæ?
units.tr: [...] Bernard{a}. In short, all who wrote about the Head of the Church before Aquinas teach exactly the same thing. In this they agree well with the ancient Church, that the Church is the body of Christ. Nor do they think that they can define the Church more briefly or more clearly than by saying, with the Apostle, that the Church is the body of Christ. But who has ever called the Church the body of the Pope?

units.la: Postquam Thomæ Aquinatis ingenio Papæ autoritas magis invaluisset, tandem Scholasticorum insequentium improba industria factum est, adiuvantibus Canonistis, ut nec modus, nec limites immoderatam istam potestatem coercere possent. Atque hinc est illa Scholasticorum nonnullorum sententia, Papa est Ecclesia virtualiter: quod profecto a recentioribus istis Iesuitis non minore contentione proponitur. Quum enim docent, Romanum Pontificem esse os Ecclesiæ, Pontificem etiam malum, esse Caput verum, nullam esse Ecclesiæ, aut generalis Concilii autoritatem sine Romani Pontificis consensu, Papæ sententiam, vel cum Concilio, vel sine Concilio, certissimam esse, nec posse errare, Pontificem a nullo mortalium iudicari vel puniri debere, aut posse, Episcopos omnes a Papa iurisdictionem accipere; Quid aliud agunt tam importuna contentione, quam ut sese plane prodant, quum Ecclesiæ nomen prætendunt, Papæ unius autoritatem extollere, atque hoc sibi intus canere; Papam esse Ecclesiam virtualiter. Quicquid de Ecclesia iactant, illud manet apud eos fixum,& certum, vnum Papam esse Ecclesiam illam, pro qua digladiantur. Itaque nonnulli eorum aperte hoc ipsum profitentur. Sic enim scribit Gregorius de Valentia: {a} Nomine Ecclesiæ intelligimus eius Caput, id est, Romanum Pontificem.
units.tr: After the authority of the Pope had gained greater strength through the genius of Thomas Aquinas, it came about, through the wicked diligence of the later Scholastics, with the help of the canonists, that neither measure nor limit could restrain that immoderate power. From this comes the opinion of some Scholastics that the Pope is virtually the Church; and this is put forward with no less vehemence by those recent Jesuits. For when they teach that the Roman Pontiff is the mouth of the Church, that a wicked Pontiff is nonetheless the true Head, that no authority of the Church or of a general council is valid without the consent of the Roman Pontiff, that the Pope's judgement, whether with or without a council, is most certain and cannot err, that the Pontiff ought not, or cannot, be judged or punished by any mortal, and that all bishops receive their jurisdiction from the Pope; what else are they doing with such troublesome insistence, except betraying themselves plainly, while they put forward the name of the Church in order to exalt the authority of the one Pope, and sing this to themselves in private: the Pope is virtually the Church? Whatever they boast about the Church, this remains fixed and certain for them, that the one Pope is that Church for which they fight. Accordingly some of them openly profess this very thing. For Gregory de Valentia writes thus: {a} By the name of the Church we understand its Head, that is, the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Hoc est igitur diligenter obseruandum, a nobis vero iterum atque iterum monendum; Tridentinos, quum de Ecclesia disputant, longe aliud intelligere per Ecclesiæ nomen, quam quod a Scripturis Patribusque traditum sit: proinde omnia confundunt. Nam priusquam de Ecclesiæ autoritate quicquam pronuntiant, oportuit de definitione convenire: quod quia non faciunt, nunquam ad idem disputant, sed sophismatis complent omnia: & quod est hominum indoctissimorum maximè proprium, vt confuse & caligihose[?] ea tractent, quæ distinctionibus splendere debuerant, quæ autem simpliciter, & sine fuco tradenda sunt, ea distinctionibus infensatis obruant; in eo ita accurate laborant Iesuitæ nostri, vt his ipsis artibus, quæ homines indoctos maximè produnt, isti doctissimorum virorum famam nomenque ve-mentur[?].
units.tr: This therefore must be carefully observed, and by us again and again warned: when the Tridentines discuss the Church, they understand by the name of the Church something quite different from what has been handed down by the Scriptures and the Fathers; and therefore they confuse everything. For before they pronounce anything about the authority of the Church, they ought to have agreed on a definition; because they do not do this, they never argue about the same thing, but fill everything with sophistries. And, what is most especially the mark of the most unlearned men, they treat confusedly and obscurely those things which ought to shine with distinctions, and they smother with overwrought distinctions those things which ought to be delivered plainly and without disguise. In this our Jesuits labour so carefully that by these very arts, which most betray unlearned men, they lay claim to the fame and name of most learned men.

units.la: Non putamus quenquam reperiri posse hominem doctum, & pium, qui credat vera esse, quæ scribunt Iesuitæ de Romanæ Ecclesiæ Capite, Ecclesiæ sponso, Ecclesiæ domino, & monarcha. Nam quod hanc scilicet autori-
units.tr: We do not think that any learned and pious man can be found who believes that the things the Jesuits write about the Head of the Roman Church, the spouse of the Church, the lord of the Church and its monarch, are true. For as to the fact that they are accustomed to show this authority over the whole Church from certain passages of Scripture,

units.la: tatem tatem leant bunt sum S confi noru prim fcrip fuiff prol temp per liffe bus anti non gun den nis fam duc ces & tor ris Ec gen det cup sic pri qu tatem in universam Ecclesiam ostendere soleant è Scripturis quibusdam: qui hæc scribunt, intelligunt, sese hoc movere contra sensum Scripturarum, & antiquitatis unanimem consensum. Intelligunt arte confictas Romanorum Pontificum Epistolas decretales, quæ primum autoritatem Romani Pontificis ex iis scripturis probandam susceperunt, nullam fuisse antiquitatis vocem in eam sententiam prolatam: Intelligunt, Romanos Pontifices tempore S. Augustini, quum autoritatem super alias Ecclesias affectauerant, non protulisse Scripturas, quales è confictis decretalibus hodie proferunt Iesuitæ; sed quia nihil ex antiquitate producere potuerunt, idcirco canonem Niceni Concilii confinxisse: Intelligunt, hanc Romanorum Pontificum impudentiam ab Augustino, pluribusque Africanis Conciliis convictam, reiectam, & repressam fuisse. Num quis vero animum suum inducere poterit, ut credat, Romanos Pontifices Niceni Concilii canonem à seipsis confictum proferre voluisse, si tum temporis autoritatem hanc Romani Pontificis è Scripturis probari potuisse putassent? Et quis est de Ecclesiæ iudicio, Patrumq; antiquorum diligentia tam abiecte sentiens, ut existimet tandem post mille annos, quum iam tenebræ oc-cuparent Ecclesiam; autoritatem Rom. Pontificis in Scripturis primum inuentam, quam prioribus & purioribus seculis Ecclesia antiqua, Patresque omnes ignorauerant. Non potest igitur fieri, vt hæc à Iesuitis scrio scribantur. Malam causam malo animo agunt, ambitione occæcati, quemadmodum de huiusmodi fraterculis grauiter iudicat Æneas Syluius.Cuius verba sunt hæc: {a}Sunt aliqui, siue auidi gloriæ, siue quod adulando præmia expectent, qui peregrinas quasdam sententias, & omnino nouas prædicare doctrinas cœperunt; ipsumq; summum Pontificem ex iurisdictione sacri Concilij demere non verentur: excæcauit eos ambitio. Hæc ille. De eadem etiam hominum fæce sic scribit: {b}Nec considerant miseri, quia quæ prædicant tantopere verba, aut ipsorum summorum Pontificum sunt, suas fimbrias extendentium, aut eorum, qui eis adulabantur. Hæc igitur Romani Capitis autoritas in Ecclesiam, quam non à Deo delatam, sibi sumpsit Romanus Pontisex, antiquos Ecclesiæ Patres latuit.
units.tr: authority over the whole Church, from certain passages of Scripture: those who write these things understand that they are moving against the sense of the Scriptures and the unanimous consent of antiquity. They understand that the Roman Pontiffs' decretal letters, cunningly forged, which first undertook to prove the authority of the Roman Pontiff from those Scriptures, had no voice of antiquity in favour of that opinion. They understand that the Roman Pontiffs, when in the time of St Augustine they aspired to authority over the other churches, did not put forward Scriptures of the kind that the Jesuits today bring out of the forged decretals; but since they could produce nothing from antiquity, they therefore forged the canon of the Council of Nicaea. They understand that this shamelessness of the Roman Pontiffs was refuted, rejected and repressed by Augustine and by many African councils. But could anyone bring himself to believe that the Roman Pontiffs would have wished to produce a canon of the Council of Nicaea forged by themselves, if at that time they had thought that this authority of the Roman Pontiff could be proved from the Scriptures? And who, feeling so meanly about the judgement of the Church and the diligence of the ancient Fathers, could think that after a thousand years, when darkness already held the Church, the authority of the Roman Pontiff was at last first discovered in the Scriptures, which the ancient Church and all the Fathers in earlier and purer ages had been ignorant of? It cannot therefore be that these things are written by the Jesuits in good faith. They act with a bad cause and a bad mind, blinded by ambition, as Aeneas Sylvius judges gravely of such little brothers. His words are these: {a}There are some, either greedy for glory or because they expect rewards by flattery, who have begun to preach certain foreign opinions and entirely new doctrines; and they do not hesitate to remove the Supreme Pontiff himself from the jurisdiction of the sacred Council: ambition has blinded them. So he. Of the same dregs of men he writes thus: {b}Nor do the wretched consider that the words which they preach so eagerly are either those of the supreme Pontiffs themselves, who stretch out their own fringes, or of those who flatter them. Therefore this authority of the Roman Head over the Church, which the Roman Pontiff claimed for himself and which was not conferred by God, was hidden from the ancient Fathers of the Church.

units.la: Ante Aquinatem Bernardus nimium magnifice de Romano Pontifice locutus videtur, quem vocat {c}Principem Episcoporum, hæredem Apostolorum, Patriarchatu Abraham, Primatu Abel, Ordine Melchisedech, dignitate Aaron, autoritate Mosen, iudicatu Samuelem, potestate Petrum, vnctione Christum. Hæc quidem magnifica sunt, & maiora, quam ante illum apud quenquam alium reperiuntur: quædam etiam impia, quamuis forte non impie dicta. Nam si in commodum interpretetem incidetint, videri possunt à Bernardo posita tantum ad ostendendum spiritualem primatum, non tempofalem. Nam Bernardus ( vt multi etiam alii viri boni,) noluit pertinaci studio cum Papa litigare de spirituali potestate, quia hanc potestatem Papa sibi iam tum conciliasse videbatur. Affectaverat eam antea, sed depulsus erat ab hac affectatione, ab antiquis Patribus, Episcopis, Conciliis. Sed post annum millesimum, soluto tandem Satana, potestatem hanc spiritualem, quam vocant, super Episcopos Occidentis saepius affectatam, tandem aliquando, tanquam victor evadens obtinuit: verum nullo alio jure, quam per Pon-tificios canones. Illud enim eodem loco diserte notat Bernardus, his verbis: {a}Juxta canones tuos, alii in partem sollicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem potestatis vocatus es. Recte observat Bernardus, hanc novam Romani Pontificis potestatem, habitam secundum canones ipsius, non secundum Scripturas, nec secundum decreta Ecclesiae Catholicae, non ex judicio Patrum; sed tantum, inquit, juxta canones tuos.
units.tr: Before Aquinas, Bernard seems to have spoken too magnificently of the Roman Pontiff, whom he calls {c}the Prince of Bishops, heir of the Apostles, in patriarchate Abraham, in primacy Abel, in order Melchizedek, in dignity Aaron, in authority Moses, in judgement Samuel, in power Peter, in anointing Christ. These things are indeed magnificent, and greater than are found before him in anyone else; some of them are even impious, although perhaps not impiously said. For if they fall into a favourable interpretation, they may seem to have been put forward by Bernard only to show a spiritual primacy, not a temporal one. For Bernard (like many other good men) was unwilling, with stubborn zeal, to contend with the Pope about spiritual power, because the Pope already seemed to have won this power to himself at that time. He had aspired to it earlier, but he had been driven back from this aspiration by the ancient Fathers, bishops and councils. But after the year one thousand, when Satan was at last loosed, this spiritual power, as they call it, which had been often aspired to over the bishops of the West, at last, like a victor, he obtained, but by no other right than through the Pontifical canons. For Bernard clearly notes this in the same place, in these words: {a}According to your canons, others were called to a share of the care, but you were called to the fullness of power. Bernard rightly observes that this new power of the Roman Pontiff was held according to his own canons, not according to the Scriptures, nor according to the decrees of the Catholic Church, nor by the judgement of the Fathers; but only, he says, according to your canons.

units.la: Incidit Bernardus, sicut supra admonui, in fatalia illa tempora, post annum millesimum, quum jam Papa potestatem illam diu quaesi-tam, in Episcopos obtinuerat. Itaque Bernardus potestatem hanc spiritualem, quam a tam multis concessam, viderat, ipse quoque toleravit: quid enim facere potuit? Sed tamen de Capite & membris Ecclesiae sanam doctrinam retinuit. Nunquam Papam vocat Ecclesiae universalis Caput, nec reprobos Ecclesiae membra.
units.tr: Bernard fell, as I warned above, into those fatal times after the year one thousand, when the Pope had already obtained over the bishops that power which he had long sought. So Bernard too tolerated this spiritual power, which he had seen conceded by so many: for what could he do? Yet he still kept sound doctrine concerning the Head and the members of the Church. He never calls the Pope the Head of the universal Church, nor calls the reprobate the members of the Church.

units.la: Quæ igitur è Bernardo obseruamus, osten-dunt nobis, quibus gradibus ascenderit Papa ad hanc sublimitatem, & per consequens, quibus gradibus in præceps deiecta sit Ecclesia per Papæ fastum, ad hanc miseriam. Primus gradus erat potestas super Episcopos, quam Cypriani & Augustini seculo affectatam, non potuit obtinere; Bernardi ætate obtinuerat. Secundus gradus est, vt haberetur Caput Ecclesiæ vniuersæ; quæ potestas Thomæ Aquinatis ingenio quæsita atque aucta videbatur. Ex istis Papa ascendere, Ecclesia vero ruere cœpit.
units.tr: What we note from Bernard therefore shows us by what steps the Pope climbed to this height, and consequently by what steps the Church was cast headlong through the Pope's pride into this misery. The first step was power over bishops, which he had aimed at in the age of Cyprian and Augustine but could not obtain; in Bernard's age he had obtained it. The second step was to be held the Head of the whole Church; this power seemed to have been sought out and enlarged by the ingenuity of Thomas Aquinas. By these steps the Pope rose, and the Church began to fall.

units.la: Si Thomæ Aquinatis doctrinam de Ecclesiæ Capite, cum Bonifacii III. facinore contulerimus, artes quædam Ecclesiæ Romanæ in lucem prodire videbuntur, quæ sunt nobis observandæ. Nam doctrinæ immutatio in Ecclesiam Romanam sero inuecta videtur, disciplin-æ vero corruptelæ longius præcessisse. Postquam enim de facto Ecclesia Romana, Caput omnium Ecclesiarum, & Episcopus Romanus vniuersalis a Phoca declaratus est, discipli-na Ecclesiæ Romanæ statim mutata, ab ea, quam Gregorius magna integritatis laude retinuerat, deflexit, & collapsa penitus corruit. At vero doctrina de Ecclesiæ Capite non statim cum disciplinæ depravatione, sed longo post tempore corrumpi cœperat. Sicut e-nim quæ virgo quondam insigni pudicitiæ laude floruerat, non statim à virginitatis amore in impudentiam prorumpere solet, sed paulatim ad mala assuescere, deinde præcipi-tari per flagitia: sic Rom. Ecclesia quondam virgo moriturae virginitatis signa quaedam in disciplina immutata dederat, postea vero præcipiti furore adulterari coepit. Itaq; postquam Anno Christi 606. à Bonifacio III. subuersa est Ecclesiae Rom. disciplina, tandem aliquando post aliquot secula reperti sunt, qui hoc Pontificis factum (quod Gregorius vocat profanum, superbum, impium, flagitiosum) tanquam legitimum defenderent. Ita doctrina haec noua de Capite Ecclesiae, ad facti defensionem excogitata, ab Aquinatis quidem ingenio, sed à Rom. Pontificum mandato, atque præscripto prodiisse videtur. Et certe frequenter vsurata est haec ars, & celebrata. Nam & decimae prius de facto ab Ecclesiis sorreptae sunt, deinde factum hoc à Theologorum ingeniis velut ex Pontificum præscripto defensicatum est. Itaque nihil nouum faciunt Iesuitae, quum sententias nouas, insolentes, inauditas, ex Pontificum præscripto Ecclesiae obtrudunt.
units.tr: If we compare the doctrine of Thomas Aquinas concerning the Head of the Church with the crime of Boniface III, certain arts of the Roman Church will appear, which we ought to observe. For the change of doctrine seems to have been introduced into the Roman Church late, whereas the corruption of discipline had gone on much earlier. For once the Roman Church, the Head of all churches, and the Roman bishop as universal, had been declared in fact by Phocas, the discipline of the Roman Church was at once changed; it departed from that which Gregory had kept with great praise for its integrity, and it collapsed utterly and fell. But the doctrine concerning the Head of the Church did not begin to be corrupted at once with the corruption of discipline, but only after a long time. For just as a virgin who once flourished with a notable reputation for chastity does not usually break out at once from love of virginity into shamelessness, but gradually grows accustomed to evil and then plunges headlong into disgraceful acts: so the Roman Church, once a virgin, gave certain signs of her dying virginity in the change of discipline, but afterwards began to be defiled with headlong frenzy. Therefore, after the discipline of the Roman Church was overthrown by Boniface III in the year of Christ 606, at length, some centuries later, men were found who defended this act of the Pontiff (which Gregory calls profane, proud, impious and shameful) as lawful. Thus this new doctrine concerning the Head of the Church, devised to defend the deed, seems to have come forth from the ingenuity of Aquinas, but at the command and prescription of the Roman Pontiffs. And certainly this art has been frequently practised and celebrated. For tithes too were first seized from the churches in fact, and then this deed was defended by the wits of theologians as if by the prescription of the Pontiffs. So the Jesuits do nothing new when they thrust new, unusual and unheard-of opinions upon the Church by the prescription of the Pontiffs.

units.la: Quanquam autem videatur Aquinas ea ex præscripto docuisse, sicut alios etiam fecisse comperimus: ne tamen omnia Pontificum libidini reliquisse videretur, limites quosdam huic potestati adhibuit. {a}Potestas, inquit, Præ-latis spiritualis, qui non est dominus, sed dispensator, in aedificationem data est, & non in destructionem. Aquinas ergo Papam Caput esse docuit, non dominans, sed dispensans, & ministrans. Verum isti limites ad Papæ dominatum cohibendum inutiles fuerunt. Ita limitata quo-dammodo erat Aquinatis sententia. Iesuitae vero huic potestati, nec modum, nec metas re-rum, nec tempora ponunt.
units.tr: Although Aquinas seems to have taught these things by prescription, as we find that others also did, yet, lest he should seem to have left everything to the Pontiffs' lust, he set certain limits to this power. The spiritual power, he says, given to prelates, who are not lords but dispensers, has been given for building up and not for destruction. Aquinas therefore taught that the Pope is Head, not as lord but as dispenser and minister. But these limits were useless for restraining the Pope's dominion. Thus the opinion of Aquinas was in some sense limited. The Jesuits, however, place no measure, no bounds of things, and no times upon this power.

units.la: Sequitur, ad demonstrandam Ecclesiae Pontificiae antiquitatem, ut ostendamus, recentia ista, & nuperrime nata Iesuitarum figmenta: Papam esse supra Ecclesiam; nullam esse Ecclesiae authoritatem sine Papae consensu: Papam er-rare non posse: Papam a nemine iudicandum: Epi-scopos omnes a Papa iurisdictionem accipere. Et quia Ecclesia Pontificia hodierna, in istis figmentis universa consistit, Ecclesia haec Pontificia, ex istis dogmatibus publice receptis, antiquitatem suam, atque originem demonstrabit. Fuerunt haec figmenta primo inter privatas opiniones iactata; privatas opiniones dico, non antiquorum Patrum, sed eorum, quos Iohannes Gerson, Æneas Syluius, & alii viri docti, vocare solent Pontificum adulatores. Nam fraterculi quidam, & Canonistae, cōtra Ecclesiam Romanam, hanc Pontificis potestatem mendaciis & adulationibus introductam, per ambitionem & impudentiam extulerunt. Ita ut quae privatae nuper fraterculorum & Canonistarum opiniones fuerunt, tandem Ecclesiae dogmata publice recepta habebantur, sed non ante Concilii Tridentini tempora.
units.tr: It follows, to demonstrate the antiquity of the Papist Church, that we should show these recent and newly born figments of the Jesuits: that the Pope is above the Church; that there is no authority of the Church without the consent of the Pope; that the Pope cannot err; that the Pope is to be judged by no one; that all bishops receive their jurisdiction from the Pope. And since the present Papist Church consists entirely of these figments, this Papist Church will demonstrate its antiquity and origin from these dogmas publicly received. These figments were first bandied about as private opinions; I say private opinions, not of the ancient Fathers, but of those whom John Gerson, Aeneas Sylvius and other learned men are accustomed to call flatterers of the Pontiffs. For certain little friars and Canonists, against the Roman Church, put forward through ambition and impudence this power of the Pontiff, introduced by lies and flatteries. So that what were recently private opinions of friars and Canonists were at length held to be public dogmas of the Church, but not before the times of the Council of Trent.

units.la: Atque ut facilius Ecclesiae Pontificiae mutatio intelligatur, hoc loco observabimus distinctionem illam inter Ecclesiam & Curiam Roma-
units.tr: And so that the change of the Papist Church may be more easily understood, at this point we shall observe that distinction between the Church and the Roman Curia, of which we have often spoken.

units.la: Roma fia co prosit diens dum l- mine vt nec Cath- Fides [?]sto in bet T- manif- Eccle- mus i- mus Perso- re ar- quale [?]stione di; v[?] çam tem lo[?] cipit muta- tem mel- rint incu- ritat & n den Romanam, de qua sæpius monuimus. Ecclesia consistit ex personis fidem Catholicam profitentibus. Fides Catholica à Christo prodiens, illuminat Ecclesiam, sicut hunc mundum lumen Solis. Nec enim mundus sine lumine agere, nec lumen sine Sole esse potest: ut nec Ecclesia sine fide Catholica, nec fides Catholica sine suo Sole Christo esse potest. Fides igitur Catholica transmissa est à Christo in Ecclesiam per comites ipsius, sicut habet Tertullianus. Mutatio ergo fidei probat manifestam mutationem Ecclesiæ. Fidem in Ecclesia Pontificia mutatam, supra probavi-mus in regula fidei mutata. Hoc loco quæri-mus de personis, hanc fidem profitentibus. Personæ sunt homines, qui vel ex suo munere atque officio tradunt fidem Catholicam, quales sunt Episcopi & Pastores, qui successionem habent ab Apostolis, & ius prædican-di; vel qui suscipiunt doctrinam Catholicam, sicut populus credentium. Mutatio autem fidei non est multum metuenda à populo, quia populus non tradit, sed tantum suscipit fidem. Verum à peruersis doctoribus mutatio omnis metuenda est. Quoniam autem populus pertinacius inhæret iis, quæ semel penitus susceperit, sive vera, sive falsa fuerint: idcirco pastoribus & doctoribus maior incumbit cura, ut summa cum fide ac synce-ritate non suas opiniones, sed Christi fidem & mandata tradant. Fides ergo Christi tradenda est, non hominum placita. Neque vero tradenda est passim ab omnibus sine discrimine: Deus enim non est author confusionis, sed ordinis; sed ab iis tradenda, qui legitimam habent vocationem ad munus prædicandi, & successionem ab Apostolis. Ecclesia igitur mutata probabitur, si vel fides Catholica à Christo excepta[?] non tradatur, vel si tradatur ab iis, qui non habent ius prædicandi.
units.tr: …Roman [Church], of which we have often spoken. The Church consists of persons professing the Catholic faith. The Catholic faith, coming forth from Christ, illuminates the Church, as the sun's light illuminates this world. For the world cannot act without light, nor can light exist without the sun: so the Church cannot exist without the Catholic faith, nor the Catholic faith without its sun, Christ. The Catholic faith was therefore handed on from Christ to the Church through his companions, as Tertullian says. A change of faith therefore proves a manifest change of the Church. We have proved above that the faith has been changed in the Papist Church, in the changed rule of faith. Here we shall ask about the persons who profess this faith. Persons are men who either by their office and function hand on the Catholic faith, such as bishops and ministers, who have succession from the Apostles and the right of preaching; or who receive the Catholic doctrine, such as the people of believers. A change of faith is not much to be feared from the people, because the people do not hand on the faith but only receive it. But from perverse teachers every change is to be feared. And since the people cling more stubbornly to those things which they have once wholly received, whether true or false, therefore a greater care lies upon the ministers and teachers, that with the greatest faithfulness and sincerity they hand on not their own opinions but the faith and commands of Christ. Therefore the faith of Christ must be handed on, not the opinions of men. Nor indeed is it to be handed on everywhere by everyone without distinction: for God is not the author of confusion but of order; it is to be handed on by those who have a lawful calling to the office of preaching and succession from the Apostles. The Church will therefore be shown to have changed if either the Catholic faith received from Christ is not handed on, or if it is handed on by those who do not have the right of preaching.

units.la: Quod si fides huiusmodi proponatur, quæ neque à Christo transmissa est, neque tradita[?] ab iis, qui ius habent prædicandi, sicut sunt illi, qui ad prædicandi munus sese in Ecclesia obtrudunt, quum legitimam vocationem non habeant, nec successionem ab Apostolis: num quis existimare poterit, talem Ecclesiam esse Ecclesiam Christi, in qua huiusmodi confusio regnat?
units.tr: But if a faith of such a kind is put forward, which has been handed down neither from Christ nor by those who have the right of preaching, such as those who thrust themselves forward in the Church to the office of preaching, though they have no lawful calling nor succession from the Apostles: can anyone think that such a Church, in which this kind of confusion reigns, is the Church of Christ?

units.la: Talis autem est Ecclesia hodierna Pontificia, in qua nec fides Catholica traditur, nec qui tradunt, ius habent prædicandi, aut successionem ab Apostolis. Nam qui fidem hanc, quam nunc Pontificiam dicimus, primo prædicarunt, fraterculi erant, qui non fidem Catholicam, sed sua commenta tradiderunt, quique in Ecclesia nullam habent legitimam vocationem, non ius prædicandi, non successionem ab Apostolis.
units.tr: Yet such is the present Papist Church, in which the Catholic faith is not handed on, nor do those who hand it on have the right of preaching or succession from the Apostles. For those who first preached this faith, which we now call Papist, were little friars, who handed on not the Catholic faith but their own inventions, and who have in the Church no lawful calling, no right of preaching, and no succession from the Apostles.

units.la: Qui Ecclesiæ formam accuratius contemplantur, ab Anno Christi millesimo ducentesimo, videbunt duas veluti facies huius Occidentalis Ecclesiæ; Vnam antiquæ Ecclefiæ perdurantis in successione Apostolorum; Alteram, nouæ exorientis, in fraterculorum & Canonistarum nouis institutionibus, qui nullam habent vocationem, nec ius prædi- candi, nec successionem, sed lubito viden- tur post tempus solutionis Satanæ è terra pro- gnati, vel è puteo abyssi exorti, sine successio- ne ab Apostolis, sine authoritate ab Ecclesia, solius Romani Pontificis arbitrio instituti & confirmati.
units.tr: Those who look more carefully at the form of the Church will see, from the year of Christ 1200 onward, two faces, as it were, of this Western Church. One is that of the ancient Church, persisting in the succession of the Apostles. The other is that of a new Church arising from the new institutions of the friars and the canonists, who have no calling and no right to preach, and no succession. They seem to have sprung up at will, as if released after the time when Satan was loosed from the earth or had come up out of the pit of the abyss, without succession from the Apostles and without authority from the Church, instituted and confirmed by the sole decision of the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Hæc autem fides, quamvis in Ecclesiæ gre- mio exoriens, non Ecclesia, sed, sicut doctis- simus vir Iohannes Feildius noster, S. Theo- logiæ Doctor, quem honoris & dignitatis causa nomino, obseruauit; Romanæ Ec- clesiæ factio tantummodo habenda est, si- ne Romana Curia. Interea Ecclesia Ro- mana vixit, durauitque, donec paulatim ab hac factione, siue Romana Curia supe- rata, ac tandem velut absorpta [?] videretur.
units.tr: This faith, although it arose within the bosom of the Church, is not the Church. As our most learned man, John Feild, Doctor of Sacred Theology, whom I name out of respect for his honour and dignity, has observed, it is to be regarded only as a faction of the Roman Church, namely the Roman Curia. Meanwhile the Roman Church lived on and endured, until it was gradually overcome by this faction, or the Roman Curia, and at last seemed as if it had been absorbed.

units.la: Itaque plurimos videmus viros doctos, pios- que, nonnunquam etiam Principes reli- giosos, quoties se à Romani Pontificis ty- rannide oppressos sentiebant, vel metue- bant, provocasse à Romano Pontifice, & Romana hac Curia, ad Romanam Eccle- siam.
units.tr: Thus we see very many learned and pious men, and sometimes even religious princes, whenever they felt or feared that they were oppressed by the tyranny of the Roman Pontiff, appealing from the Roman Pontiff and this Roman Curia to the Roman Church.

units.la: Legimus in scriptis Guilielmi Occham, Michaelem Cezenam, quem Iohannes Pa- pa XXII[?]. Anno Christi millesimo trecente- simo octauo deposuit, appellasse ab iniusta apæ tyrannide, & à Romana Curia, ad Ecclesiam Romanam : quo loco de Romana Curia grauissime conqueritur Cezenas. Verba Appellationis hæc sunt : a Habito prius magno & maturo consilio ab ipso Domi-no Iohanne, & dicta eius assertione, & arrestatione infra tempus legitimum, meo nomine, & fratrum, mihi adhærentium, & adhærere volentium, iam dicti Ordinis, secundum quod tradunt canonica sanctiones, ad sanctam Romanam Ecclesiam Catholicam & Apostolicam appello. Hæc ille. Testatur idem Cezena, hæc se egisse consensu & approbatione Magistrorum & Baccalaureorum in sacra pagina de Parisiis, & de Anglia. Sensum igitur, & iudicium Ecclesiæ huius seculi observemus fuisse huiusmodi, ut iudicarent, Papam non esse Caput Ecclesiæ, non fuisse super Ecclesiam : Ecclesiam Catholicam potuisse consistere sine regimine Papæ Romani. Nam qui à Romano Pontifice ad Ecclesiam Catholicam appellant, Ecclesiam probant sine Romano Pontifice consistere potuisse; Papam cum sua Curia reiiciunt, ut Ecclesiæ Romanæ Catholicæ iudicio ab iniuria Pontificis vindicarentur. Quid nos amplius dicimus, aut docemus? Testatur Cezenas, hanc Appellationem à Romano Pontifice, fuisse secundum canonicas sanctiones. Canones igitur Ecclesiæ illo sæculo huiusmodi Appellationem probabant. Sed Romanus Pontifex per tyrannidem antiquis & æquissimis Ecclesiæ canonibus velut antiquatis, suas decretales Epistolas pro canonibus, quanquam resistentibus Episcopis, vt testis est Ni-colaus Papa,distin.19.cap.si Romanorum.Ecclesiæ obtrusit.
units.tr: We read in the writings of William Occam and of Michael of Cesena, whom Pope John XXII deposed in the year of Christ 1328, that he appealed from the unjust tyranny of that pope, and from the Roman Curia, to the Roman Church. In this passage Cesena complains most gravely of the Roman Curia. The words of the appeal are these: After a great and mature deliberation had beforehand with the Lord John himself, and after his assertion and detention within the lawful time, I appeal in my own name and in the name of the brothers who adhere to me and wish to adhere to me, of the aforesaid Order, according as the canonical sanctions teach, to the holy Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church. So he. The same Cesena testifies that he did these things with the consent and approval of the masters and bachelors in sacred theology at Paris and in England. Let us observe, therefore, that the sense and judgment of the Church of that age was of this kind: they judged that the Pope was not the Head of the Church and was not above the Church, and that the Catholic Church could subsist without the government of the Roman Pope. For those who appeal from the Roman Pontiff to the Catholic Church prove that the Church could subsist without the Roman Pontiff; they reject the Pope with his Curia, so that by the judgment of the Roman Catholic Church they might be protected from the wrong done by the Pontiff. What more do we say or teach? Cesena testifies that this appeal from the Roman Pontiff was in accordance with the canonical sanctions. The canons of the Church of that age therefore approved such an appeal. But the Roman Pontiff, by tyranny, as if the most ancient and most equitable canons of the Church had been set aside as obsolete, forced his decretal letters upon the Church in place of canons, though the bishops resisted, as Pope Nicholas testifies, distinction 19, chapter si Romanorum.

units.la: Natrateriam[?] Crantzius, Iohannem Seme-cam,autorem glossæ ordinariæ, in decretum Gratiani iniuste excommunicatum à Clemente Papa IV. & ab officio ac munere deiectum,appellasse à Papa ad Concilium. Eodemque modo Ludouicus Bauarus Imperator iniuste excommunicatus à Iohanne XXII. ab eius iniusta sententia appellauit ad generale Concilium, & ad sanctam Catholicam Ecclesiam ; sicut narrat {a}Nau-clerus. Philippus etiam Rex Franciæ, ab in-iuria Bonifacii VIII. sicut idem {b}author haber,appellauit ad Concilium. Ita rem vi-tatam videmus, vt oppressi à Papa, appellarent à sententia Papæ ad Concilium, & Ecclesiam Romanam. Quod certe fieri non potest, nisi Ecclesia à Romano Pont.fice separata, authoritatem intelligatur habere in ipsum Romanum Pontificem. Ex qua quidem consuetudine Ecclesiæ constat, aliam apud maiores nostros habitam fuisse Romanam Curiam, cum suo Capite, Romano Pontifice, quæ sine hoc Capite non esse, non consistere potuit : aliam vero Romanam Ecclesiam, quæ authoritatem in Romanum Pontificem exercere consueuerat,& sine Romano Pontifice consistere potuit.
units.tr: Crantzius also relates that John Semeca, author of the ordinary Gloss on Gratian's Decretum, was unjustly excommunicated by Pope Clement IV and deposed from office and function, and appealed from the Pope to a Council. In the same way Emperor Louis of Bavaria, unjustly excommunicated by John XXII, appealed from that unjust sentence to a general Council and to the holy Catholic Church, as Nauclerus narrates. King Philip of France also, from the injury of Boniface VIII, as the same author records, appealed to a Council. So we see it was such a common practice for the oppressed to appeal from the Pope's sentence to a Council and to the Roman Church. This certainly could not happen unless the Church, as distinct from the Roman Pontiff, were understood to have authority over the Roman Pontiff himself. From this custom of the Church it is clear that among our ancestors there was one Roman Curia, with its head, the Roman Pontiff, which could not exist or subsist without this head; but there was another, the Roman Church, which was accustomed to exercise authority over the Roman Pontiff and could subsist without the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: Quærimus ab Aduersariis ; vbinam gentium iam sit Romana hæc Ecclesia, quæ esse
units.tr: We ask our adversaries: where in the world is this Roman Church now, which is to be…
