Haec ergo pulcherrime coniungit Apostolus, quem proposuit Deus propitiationem per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad declarandam iustitiam suam per remissionem praecedentium peccatorum, & iustificati gratis per gratiam ipsius, per redemptionem, quae est in Christo Iesu. Iterumque, in quo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem ipsius, remissionem peccatorum secundum divitias gratiae ipsius. Haec passim apud Apostolum fides ergo nostra, remissionem peccatorum à Deo reconciliato accipit, reconciliatur autem Deus non propter nostrum opus, aut meritum, sed propter meritum Christi. Hinc etiam alteram illam, velut partem iustificationis nostrae, consurgit, nempe imputatio iustitiae Christi. Probat enim Apostolus ex Davide, cui beatitudinem hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam absque operibus. Haec autem iustitia, quam Deus imputat credentibus, est iustitia Christi, itaque Apostolus docet Christum factum nobis à Deo iustitiam, sicut & sapientiam, & sanctificationem, & redemptionem, sic enim scribit: ne glo-riatur ulla caro coram eo, sed & vos estis in Christo Iesu, qui factus est nobis sapientia à Deo, & iustitia & sanctificatio, & redemptio. Ergo ipse sapientia nostra est stultitia, iustitia nostra iniquitas, sanctificatio nostra impuritas, qui credit, sapit per sapientiam filii imputatam, iustificatur per iustitiam filii imputatam, sanctisanctificatur per sanctificationem Christi impu-tatam, sic enim veritas loquitur de credentibus[?], in se: Et pro eis ego sanctifico meipsum, vt sint & ipsi sanctificati in veritate.
units.tr: ...faith [?] ...[?] ...the Apostle [?] ...by faith [?] ...redemption [?] ...the remission of sins [?] ...our [?] ...not [?] ...on account of [?] ...that [?] ...the Apostle [?] ...forgiveness [?] ...Jesus [?] ...the saints [?] ...justified [?] ...the first [?] ...denies, but he who believes that he is justified through the blood of Christ sets forth the true merit by which God is reconciled, on which faith rests. The Apostle therefore joins these things most beautifully, whom God set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness through the remission of the sins that went before, and that we are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. And again, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of his grace. Throughout the Apostle, our faith receives the forgiveness of sins from God, who is reconciled; but God is reconciled not on account of our work or merit, but on account of the merit of Christ. Hence there also arises that other part, as it were, of our justification, namely the imputation of Christ's righteousness. For the Apostle proves it from David, to whom he ascribes the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works. This righteousness, which God imputes to believers, is the righteousness of Christ; so the Apostle teaches that Christ was made by God our righteousness, as also our wisdom, sanctification and redemption. For thus he writes: "that no flesh should glory before him; but you are in Christ Jesus, who was made to us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." Therefore our own wisdom is folly, our righteousness iniquity, our sanctification impurity; he who believes is wise through the imputed wisdom of the Son, is justified through the imputed righteousness of the Son, is sanctified through the imputed sanctification of Christ. For so the truth speaks of believers, concerning himself: "And for their sake I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth."

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: De obedientia Christi actiua.
units.tr: On the active obedience of Christ.

units.la: SEd quia nouam litem, atque inauditam antea in Ecclesia suscitarunt nonnulli, de obedientia Christi actiua, quam negant imputatam nobis esse, aut ad iustificationem nostram esse necessariam: hanc nouitatem hoc loco succincte examinabimus, vt facilius deinceps progrediamur. Quod igitur de obedientia Christi actiua, & passiua comminiscuntur, vt a iustificatione excludant obedientiam actiuam, passiuam autem, quam vocant, tantummodo retineant: vt scilicet cornicum oculos effigere, & acutius ipsi perspicere videantur, quam hactenus Ecclesia Christi perspexerit: mirandum nobis videtur, de rebus sacris aliquos ea proferre audere, quae ante ipsos nemo protulit: Quae scriptura? quis antiquorum patrum e scripturis hæc docuit? Certe Apostolus docet, non solum redemptionem Christi, id est, passiuam obedientiam factam esse nostram: verum etiam sapientiam Christi, & iustitiam Christi, & sanctificationem Christi, hoc est, obedientiam actiuam, etiam nostram factam esse a Deo, & pluribus verbis vrget Apostolus ad hanc obedientiae imputationem demon-strandam. strandam. Deinde quum Apostolus suam iu-stitiam propriam reiiciat, vt iustitia Dei iusti-ficetur: non habens inquit iustitiam meam, quæ ex lege est, sed iustitiam, quæ ex Deo est: Et; iustitia Dei per fidem in omnes credentes: quærimus quæ-nam sit hæc iustitia Dei nobis imputata? num dicent iustitiam esse Christi tantum passiuam? ergo Christus iustus, dicetur tantummodo, quia mortuus est, non autem quia iuste vixit. Num ferendus videbitur, qui ita docuerit? Iustitia igitur Dei donata nobis, est, Iustitia Christi facta nostra, vel Christus à Deo factus nobis est iustitia. Quid est quod hic hærent in morte Christi? nam mors Christi redemptio nostra dicitur. Iustitia nostra non dicitur. Necesse igitur est vt præter redemptionem no-stram per mortem Christi, aliud etiam proferant in Christo, quod nobis factum sit à Deo iustitia, & sanctificatio. Et quid proferre possunt, nisi obedientiam Christi, quam isti vocant actiuam?
units.tr: But since some men have raised a new and hitherto unheard-of dispute in the Church, over the active obedience of Christ, which they deny is imputed to us or necessary for our justification, I will here examine this novelty briefly, so that we may proceed more easily afterwards. What they invent about the active and passive obedience of Christ, so that they exclude active obedience from justification and keep only what they call passive obedience, as if they could pick out crows' eyes and see more sharply than the Church of Christ has seen until now, seems to us strange: that some should dare to put forward on sacred matters things that no one before them has put forward. What Scripture says this? Which of the ancient Fathers taught this from the Scriptures? Certainly the Apostle teaches that not only the redemption of Christ, that is his passive obedience, but also the wisdom, righteousness and sanctification of Christ, that is his active obedience, have been made ours by God, and the Apostle presses this point in many words, to show that this obedience is imputed. Then, since the Apostle rejects his own righteousness so that he may be justified by the righteousness of God, saying: not having my own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is of God; and: the righteousness of God through faith in all who believe; we ask what this righteousness of God is that is imputed to us. Will they say that the righteousness of Christ is only passive? Then Christ would be called righteous only because he died, and not because he lived righteously. Would such a teacher seem bearable? So the righteousness of God given to us is the righteousness of Christ made ours, or Christ was made righteousness to us by God. Why do they cling to the death of Christ? For the death of Christ is called our redemption, but it is not called our righteousness. It is necessary, then, that besides our redemption through the death of Christ, they put forward something else in Christ that has been made by God our righteousness and sanctification. And what can they put forward except the obedience of Christ, which they call active?

units.la: Porro Iohannes sic docet: de plenitudine eius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia. Nobis igitur communicabilis est Christi gratia. Sed quæ gratia? certe gratia vocationis nostræ ex ipsius plenitudine nobis prouenit. Et vt diuitias gratiæ suæ, & velut reconditos thesauros Ecclesiæ suæ aperiat, qui est bonorum omnium munificus largitor, pro gratia vocationis conferet etiam gratiam iustificationis, id est, gratiam pro gratia. Pro gratia iustificationis accipimus etiam ex eius plenitudine gratiam tiam sanctificationis, id est, gratiam pro gra-tia. Quod si ex Christi plenitudine accipimus vocationem, iustificationem, sanctificationem: hum quis est, qui hæc omnia ad passivam obedientiam referet? iustificatio, & sanctificatio ex cius plenitudine, quid est nisi idipsum, ꝗ docuit Apostolus, Christum à Deo factū nobis iustitiam, & sanctificationem. Ita iustitia, & sanctificatio imputantur nobis, non tantū obedientia passiua. Deinde qui iustificationem in remissione peccatorum ita statuunt, ut iustitiam Christi imputatam negent, & sponsam Christi nudam relinquunt sine ornamentis, & sponsalibus gemmis. Nam peccatorum remissio turpitudinem quidem aufert, sed non pulchritudinem illam, miroretq; præstat nobis qui diuinum fauorem deducat nobis, & conciliat. Propter peccata mea dimissa, non iam habet Deus in me quod iram eius, & odiū prouocet, sed nec habet inde, quod diligat. Et quid mihi proderit peccatorum meorum remissio, nisi & Dei fauorem ac dilectionem obtineam? vt ergo in sanguine Christi, atque in morte eius peccatorum remissionem habemus, sic in iustitia Christi, & sanctificatione, sponsa Christi sua habet ornamenta & monilia quibus & fauor Dei, & amor sponsi cóci-liatur. De quibus sponsalibus ornamentis legimus apud Hoseam Prophetā: Et sponsabo te mihi in sempiternū, & sponsabo te mihi in iustitia, & in iudicio, & in misericordia, & in miserationibus, & sponsabo te mihi in fide, & scies quia ego Dominus. Non tiam Not nep & al sino sunt tion retn dian ita p Ecc doc Chr nos esse por fatu bile sun cate retn sed opt De det gia leg ob tis ob iul vt Non igitur omnis iustificatio sponsæ in remissione peccatorum ponitur, habet n. & alia ornamēta, & alba vestimēta, & datū est ei vt cooperiat se byssino splendenti,& cādido. Byssinū n. iustificationes sunt sanctorū. Quis hæc ornamenta, & iustificationes sanctorū ad passiuā obedientiā tantūmodo retulerit? Apostolus etiā sic docet: sicut per inobedientiā vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per obedientiā vnius, multi constituētur iusti. Certe Ecclesiā Christi magno bono fraudare conātur, qui docent Adæ inobedientiā actiuā nobis imputari, Christi obedientiā nō imputari. Iā vero obedientia nostra, nisi aliquo modo legi satisfaciat, nō potest esse Deo accepta. Obedientia nostra in nobis non potuit, sed obedientia nostra in Christo poterit satisfacere. Itaq; Apostolus sic docet. Quod impossi-bile erat legi, in quo infirmabatur per carnē Deus filium suum mittens in similitudinem carnis peccati, & de peccato damnauit peccatum in carne, vt iustitia legis impleretur in nobis, qui non secundum carnem ambulamus, sed secundum spiritum. Apostolus, qui testatur ex operibus legis nullam carnem iustificari coram Deo, ac proinde iustitiam Dei super omnes credentes manifestatam esse: hic tamen iustitiā legis in nobis implere docet. Quomodo a. iustitia legis impletur in nobis, nisi quia actiua Christi obedientia nostra est? aut vt doctissimi interpretis verbis vtar, qā dū nobis accepta fertur Christi obedientia, legi satisfactū est, vt ꝑ iustis censeamur [?].
units.tr: Further, John teaches thus: of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace. Therefore the grace of Christ can be communicated to us. But what grace? Surely the grace of our calling comes to us from his fullness. And so that he may open the riches of his grace and the hidden treasures of his Church, he who is the generous giver of all good things will bestow, in place of the grace of calling, also the grace of justification, that is, grace for grace. In place of the grace of justification we also receive from his fullness the grace of sanctification, that is, grace for grace. If we receive calling, justification and sanctification from the fullness of Christ, who is there who would refer all of these to his passive obedience? Justification and sanctification from his fullness are nothing other than what the Apostle taught, that Christ was made by God our righteousness and sanctification. So righteousness and sanctification are imputed to us, not passive obedience alone. Next, those who so define justification as consisting in the remission of sins, that they deny the imputed righteousness of Christ, leave the bride of Christ naked, without ornaments and betrothal jewels. For the remission of sins takes away the ugliness, but not that beauty, and it does not bring us the favour of God or make us acceptable to him. Because my sins are forgiven, God no longer has in me something that provokes his wrath and hatred, but he does not therefore have anything in me that he loves. And what good will the remission of my sins do me, unless I also obtain the favour and love of God? Just as we have the remission of sins in the blood and death of Christ, so in the righteousness and sanctification of Christ the bride of Christ has her own ornaments and necklaces, by which the favour of God and the love of the bridegroom are won. We read of these betrothal ornaments in the prophet Hosea: And I will betroth thee unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness, and in mercies; I will even betroth thee unto me in faithfulness, and thou shalt know that I am the Lord. Therefore not every justification of the bride is placed in the remission of sins; she also has other ornaments, and white garments, and it has been given to her that she should clothe herself in fine linen, bright and clean. For the fine linen is the righteousnesses of the saints. Who has referred these ornaments and the righteousnesses of the saints to passive obedience alone? The Apostle also teaches thus: as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. Surely those who teach that the disobedience of Adam is imputed to us in its active form, but the obedience of Christ is not imputed, try to defraud the Church of Christ of a great good. Indeed our own obedience, unless it satisfies the law in some way, cannot be acceptable to God. Our obedience could not satisfy in us, but the obedience of Christ in us can satisfy. And so the Apostle teaches thus: What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh but after the Spirit. The Apostle who testifies that no flesh is justified before God by the works of the law, and that therefore the righteousness of God has been manifested upon all who believe, nevertheless here teaches that the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in us. But how is the righteousness of the law fulfilled in us, unless because the active obedience of Christ is ours? Or, to use the words of a most learned interpreter, because the obedience of Christ is reckoned to us, the law is satisfied, so that we are counted righteous.

units.la: Sed dicunt isti, qui hanc nouitatem inducunt; iustificationem legis à nobis impleri: hoc est, vt iustificemur præditi ea iustitia, quam lex à nobis postulat,lex n. à nobis postulat aut per- sectâ obedietiâ,aut pœnâ nos a. perfectâ obe- dientiâ non præstitimus, at pœnam luimus in Christo;is n. ꝓ nobis luit,ergo legi satisfeci- mus in Christo : hæc dicunt illi, qui exclude- re volunt iustitiam & sanctificationem Christi ab ecclesia; nec intelligunt quam dissoluras scopas adferant. Si quis intelligat sensum su- perioris sententiæ is hic erit. Præditi ea iusti- tia q̄ lex postulat, tantummodo luuat pœnam illam quam minatur lex. At, ô bone vir, hoc non est præditum esse iustitia quam postulat lex, vt pœnam tantummodo luas. Nam iusti- tia, est legis obedientia, non pœna legis. Pœ- na iniustis ponitur, nō autem iustis. Pœna igi- tur est iniustitiæ argumentum non autem iu- stitiæ. Apostolus docet nos legis iustitiam im- plere: tu exponis ea verba, nos præditos esse legis iustitia. Iustidam implere, & iusticia præ- ditum esse, non significat iniustum esse, aut reputari: at pœnam legis luere, significat in- iustum reputari: hæc non cohærent.
units.tr: But those who introduce this novelty say that the righteousness of the law is fulfilled by us: that is, that we are justified by being endowed with that righteousness which the law demands of us. For the law demands of us either perfect obedience or punishment. We have not rendered perfect obedience, but we have paid the punishment in Christ; for he paid it on our behalf. Therefore we have satisfied the law in Christ. This is what they say who wish to exclude the righteousness and sanctification of Christ from the Church, and they do not see what a dissolving broom they bring. If anyone understands the sense of the above statement, it is this: to be endowed with that righteousness which the law demands merely means to pay off the penalty which the law threatens. But, my good sir, this is not being endowed with the righteousness the law demands, so that you only pay the penalty. For righteousness is obedience to the law, not the penalty of the law. A penalty is laid on the unrighteous, not on the righteous. The penalty, then, is a mark of unrighteousness, not of righteousness. The Apostle teaches that we fulfil the righteousness of the law; you interpret those words to mean that we are endowed with the righteousness of the law. To fulfil righteousness and to be endowed with righteousness does not mean to be or to be reckoned unrighteous; but to pay the penalty of the law does mean to be reckoned unrighteous. These things do not cohere.

Nam sicut Christus ꝓ nobis pœnā luit, sic ꝓ nobis etiam obedientiā perfectam præ- stitit. Nos inquis, obedientiam perfectam, q̄ lex postulat, non præstitimus, at pœnam lui- mus in Christo, quia ille ꝓ nobis luit. Quæro à te, quicunque es, qui hæc doces (nomini n. parco, ne in hominis contumeliâ, non in veritatis necessariû testimonium hæc dicta videantur) quæro igitur ex te utrû existimes, Christû perfectâ obedientiam actiuâ præstitisse? Responde aliquid certû. Quis Christianus negare potest, Christum perfectam obedientiâ præstitisse? præstitit ergo. Quæro deinde, cui bono, in quê finê, p quib' [?]stiterit? p seipso, an p Ecclesia sua? Nû dices Christû [?]stitisse quidê, at non nobis [?]stitisse? Ecclesia Christi non ferét istas voces, si dicas, Christi obedientiâ frustra fuisse. Certû est, Christum perfectam obedientiam præstitisse: æque certum est, Ecclesiam non præstitisse; Ecclesia igitur tanto ornamento prorsus spoliata esse, nisi è plenitudine Christi sumat, idq; ex se habere non potuit. Quia igitur non erat necesse, ut Christus obediret pro se, sequitur ut dicamus, p nobis eû hoc præstitisse. Pro nobis, credentibus in ipsum, p quibus à Deo factus est iustitia, p quibus & sanctificauit seipsû, ut nos sanctificari simus in veritate. Vide quãto bono Ecclesiâ spolianeris, si negas pfectam [?] Christi obedientiâ nostrâ esse? At si nostrâ esse concedas: quomodo nostra esse potest, nisi q a nobis credentibus impurata est. E. ut sapientia Dei facta est nostra, q a nobis est impurata, iustitia Dei nostra facta, q a nobis imputata, sanctificatio Dei nostri nostra facta, q a nobis imputata; sic obedientia Dei nostri nostra facta est, quia nobis imputata.
units.tr: Further, that Christ paid the penalty on our behalf, who can deny except one who denies Christ? We therefore do not deny the power of the death of Christ; but why do you deny that power of the righteousness of Christ? For just as Christ paid the penalty on our behalf, so he also rendered perfect obedience on our behalf. You say that we have not rendered the perfect obedience that the law demands, but that we have paid the penalty in Christ, because he paid it for us. I reply: he also rendered perfect obedience on our behalf. Why do you observe the penalty and not observe the obedience? I ask you, whoever you are who teach these things (I spare your name, lest these words seem to be aimed at the insult of a man rather than at the necessary testimony of the truth), I ask you then whether you think that Christ rendered perfect active obedience. Give a definite answer. What Christian can deny that Christ rendered perfect obedience? So he did render it. I ask next, for whose benefit, and to what end, and for whom did he render it? For himself, or for his Church? Will you say that Christ rendered it indeed, but not for us? The Church of Christ will not bear those words, if you say that the obedience of Christ was in vain. It is certain that Christ rendered perfect obedience; it is equally certain that the Church did not render it. The Church, then, would be utterly stripped of such an ornament, unless she receives it from the fullness of Christ, and she could not have it from herself. Since, therefore, it was not necessary for Christ to obey for himself, it follows that we must say he did this for us: for us who believe in him, for whom he was made righteousness by God, and for whom he also sanctified himself, that we too might be sanctified in truth. See how great a good you deprive the Church of, if you deny that the perfect obedience of Christ is ours! But if you concede that it is ours, how can it be ours unless it has been imputed to us who believe? Therefore, just as the wisdom of God has become ours because it has been imputed to us, and the righteousness of God has become ours because it has been imputed to us, and the sanctification of our God has become ours because it has been imputed to us; so the obedience of our God has become ours, because it has been imputed to us.

units.la: Postremo, patres è scripturis cōstanter tradiderunt, sicut deinceps demonstrabimus, Christum nos sua, non nostra iustitia, iustos fecisse: &, assignatam esse homini iustitiā alie-nam, qui caruit sua. Hæc a. quomodo vera esse possunt, nisi vt dicamus, obedientia Christi, iustitiam, & sanctificationē, esse nostra, & no-bis credentibus imputatam. Sufficiant hæc ad hanc nouitatem coercendam, quæ nuper sine autoritate, sine ratione excogitata est, q̄ sacræ scripturæ, q̄ patres è scripturis vbiq; conuellunt, q̄ Ecclesia magno consensu vsq; ad Mart. Lutheri tempora ignorā habuit. Nec quisquā acrius, aut illustri[?] in hac re veritā é ppugnat[?], quam Lutherus ipse, & magni illi è Germania viri, qui in Euangelio ppagando[?] Luthero successerunt. Vt mirum videatur, Germano cuiquam hanc nouitatem placere poruisse[?]. Hæc de obedientia Christi imputata. Nunc ad institutam controuersiam redeamus.
units.tr: Lastly, the Fathers have consistently taught from the Scriptures, as I shall demonstrate in what follows, that Christ made us righteous by his own righteousness, not ours, and that an alien righteousness is assigned to a man who lacks his own. How can these things be true, unless we say that the obedience of Christ, his righteousness and sanctification, is ours and is imputed to us when we believe? Let these things suffice to check this novelty, which has been devised recently, without authority and without reason, a novelty that the Holy Scriptures and the Fathers, drawing on the Scriptures, overturn everywhere, and which the Church held in ignorance with great agreement until the times of Martin Luther. Nor does anyone defend this truth more keenly or more brilliantly than Luther himself and those great men of Germany who succeeded Luther in spreading the Gospel. It seems strange that this novelty could please any German at all. So much on the imputed obedience of Christ. Now let us return to the controversy we have undertaken.

units.la: Veritas de sola fide iustificante probatur testimoniis Græcorum.
units.tr: The truth that faith alone justifies is proved by the testimony of the Greeks.

units.la: HAnc de fide iustificante doctrinā ex sacris lit. excepta, vnanimi cōsensu purā conseruarunt[?] & tradidē[?], vt patres, Græci sic docuerunt.
units.tr: The Fathers of the Greeks taught this doctrine of justifying faith, received from the sacred letters, and they preserved and handed it down with one common agreement, as follows.
