Athanasius ait: {c}Ostendis Apostolum legas execrabiles reddi homines, & maledictionis subesse, fide vero benedictis accumulari. Nunc plane demonstrat fidem ipsam etiam solam, iustificandis in se habere virtutem. Basilius sic docet; & Apostolus docet, qui gloriatur, in domino gloriari, nam ea demum perfecta & omnimoda gloriatio est in Deo, quando nec propter sua quis iustitiam extollitur, sed agnoscit se quidem vera destitui iustitia, verum solam in Christum fide iustificari esse. Gregorius Nazianzenus requiri docet ad iustificationem e tantummodo credere. Epiphanius sic habet: {f}Ex fide est iustitia cur[?]a opera legis.
units.tr: ha[?] forgiven you." And again the same: "Nor is any good work of his described in the Gospel, but Jesus says, for this faith alone," etc. Eusebius, among the errors of the Hebionites, also records this: that the worship of the law must be kept, as if faith in Christ alone were not enough. Athanasius says: "You see that the Apostle shows men are made accursed by the law and lie under the curse, but are loaded with blessings by faith." Now he plainly shows that faith itself, even alone, has the power to justify. Basil teaches thus: "And the Apostle teaches that he who boasts should boast in the Lord; for that is a perfect and complete boasting in God when no one exalts himself for his own righteousness, but recognises that he is indeed lacking true righteousness, and that he is justified by faith in Christ alone." Gregory Nazianzen teaches that to be justified one needs only to believe. Epiphanius has this: Righteousness is by faith, apart from the works of the law.

units.la: Chrysostomus sic docuit: {g}fides per seipsam plena est bonis operibus. Ante opera fides primo induscenda est. Idemq;: Sicredis, cur fides alia infers, quasi fides non sufficiat iustificare sola? Atq; alibi {h}ex sola fide nos salvamur, atq; iterum {i}sola fide apu[?] est.
units.tr: Chrysostom taught thus: Faith in itself is full of good works. Faith must be introduced first, before the works. And again: "Why do you believe, and then add other things, as if faith were not enough to justify by itself alone?" And elsewhere: "We are saved by faith alone," and again: "It is by faith alone that he is."

units.la: Theodoret{*} in hanc sententiam sic habet. {k}Nō nostra spē credimus, sed votis accessimus, & quia accessimus, nō exegit vitæ puritate, & innocentia, sed sola fide suscepta, condonavit peccata. Ideoq; in illa verba: iustificati gratis per gratiam ipsius, sic ait: {l}sola n. fide allata peccatorum remissione accepimus, quoniā velut redemptionis quodda pretiū dominus corpus suū obtulit. {m}Fides dedit vobis peccatorum remissionē, vos ab omni reprehensione alienos, iustosq; lauacri regenerationem effecit. {a}Bonorum operum implementum eos quidem qui operantur coronat, sed Dei benignitatem, & humanitatem non ostendit.
units.tr: Theodoret, on this sentence, has this: "We do not believe with our own hope, but we have drawn near with our prayers; and because we have drawn near, he did not demand purity and innocence of life, but, received by faith alone, he pardoned our sins." And on those words, justified freely by his grace, he says: "For we received the remission of sins by faith alone, since the Lord offered his body as a kind of price of redemption." "Faith gave you the remission of sins, and made you free from all reproach, and just, through the regeneration of the laver. The fulfilment of good works crowns those who work, but it does not show the goodness and kindness of God."

units.la: Fides autem facit verumq; manifestum, {b}Iustitia ex fide est donum Dei vniuersorum. De iustitia vero Christi imputata sic docet: {c}Diuina misericordia cum omnes homines essent sub maledicto, & peccati laqueis essent implicati, per vnum iustitiam dedit omnibus salutē. & mox Ostedit Apostolus vnius iustitiā fuisse communis peccati salutare medicamentū. Deinde sic etiam docet: {d}Iustitia Dei non revelatur omnibus, sed iis qui habent oculos fidei. Illum sola fide comprehendi, vox Ecclesiae quaerentis & inuenientis Christum.
units.tr: But faith makes this plain: righteousness through faith is the gift of God to all. Concerning the imputed righteousness of Christ he teaches thus: When the divine mercy saw that all men were under the curse and entangled in the snares of sin, it gave salvation to all through the righteousness of one. And soon after: the Apostle shows that the righteousness of the one was the saving remedy for common sin. Then he also teaches thus: The righteousness of God is not revealed to all, but to those who have the eyes of faith. That he is grasped by faith alone is the voice of the Church seeking and finding Christ.

units.la: Oicumenius: {e}Gratis, hoc est, absq; tuis rectis operibus salutaris ac rursum ita, vt nihil conferas aliud, praeter fidem. Theophylactus: {f}Demonstrato quod lex maledictos faciat, fides vero benedicat. Ostendit iam nunc, & quod sola fides iustificat. Et paulo post: Lex enim non solum fidem postulat, verumetiam opera. Pulchre autem dixit apud Deum. Apud homines enim iusti fortasse videri queant lege decreti, vt Pharisaei, iustificantes seipsos coram hominibus.
units.tr: Oecumenius: "Freely," that is, without your own righteous works; and again, so that you contribute nothing else besides faith. Theophylact: Having shown that the law makes men accursed, but faith blesses them, he now shows also that faith alone justifies. And a little later: For the law demands not only faith but also works. But he rightly said "before God," for before men some may seem just by the law, like the Pharisees, who justify themselves before men.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Continet testimonia Latinorum Patrum.
units.tr: Containing the testimonies of the Latin Fathers.

units.la: HActenus Graecos audiuimus. Sequuntur Latini. Irenaeus sic docet: {a}Omnes oportet credere, sicut Abraham credidit & imputatum est ei ad iustitiam. Et subiunxit Irenaeus: fides quae est ad Deum iustificat hominem. Cyprianus idem habet: {b}Si Abraham Deo credidit, & deputatum est ei ad ei ad justitiam, utique quisquis Deo credit, & fide vivet justus inuenitur, & jam pridem in Abraham fideli benedictus, & justificatus ostenditur, sicut bea-tus Apostolus Paulus probat. {a}Fide autem stare justitiam, & illic esse vitam, praedictum est apud Abacuc: justus ex fide vivet. {b}Fidem in totum prodesse, & tantum nos posse quantum credimus. In qua sententiam sic habuit etiam alibi. {c}Quantum illuc fidei capacis afferimus, tantum gratiae haurimus. Haec Cyprian. Arnobius sic docuit: {d}Nemo sine operibus, siue precibus commendatus, aut sacrificiis salvus fit, sed solo auxilio Christi. Hilarius etiam sic ait: {e}Monet scribas remissum ab homine peccatum, hominem enim tantum in Jesu inrebantur[?]: & remissum ab eo, quod lex laxare non poterat: sola enim fides justificat. Idemque in parabolam duorum filiorum sic docet: {f}Junior scilicet obediens professioni, licet non efficiens in tempore, quia sola fides justificat.
units.tr: Thus far we have heard the Greeks. Now come the Latins. Irenaeus teaches thus: All must believe, just as Abraham believed and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. And Irenaeus added: faith which is toward God justifies man. Cyprian has the same: If Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, then whoever believes God and lives by faith is found righteous, and is shown to have been blessed and justified long ago in the faithful Abraham, as the blessed Apostle Paul proves. Moreover, that righteousness stands by faith, and life is there, was foretold in Habakkuk: the just shall live by faith. Faith avails entirely, and we can do as much as we believe. In agreement with this he also said elsewhere: As much as we bring of receptive faith, so much grace we draw in. Thus Cyprian. Arnobius taught thus: No one is saved without works, or prayers, or sacrifices, but by the help of Christ alone. Hilary too says: He warns the scribes that sin is forgiven by a man, for they were saying that only God can forgive sins; and that was forgiven by him which the law could not loosen, for faith alone justifies. And in his exposition of the parable of the two sons he teaches thus: The younger, plainly obedient in profession, though not in deed at the time, is justified because faith alone justifies.

units.la: Ambrosius autem eandem retinuit doctrinam, sic enim scribit: {g}Beati quorum remissæ sunt iniquitates &c. manifeste beatisunt[?] quibus sine labore vel opere aliquo remittuntur iniquitates & peccata tegantur, nulla ab his requisita paenitentia opera, nisi tantum, ut credant. {h}Hoc consequi-mur quod credimus, credentes enim Christum esse Dei filium, a Deo adoptamur in filios, nihil ultra potuit donare credentibus, quam ut filii Dei dicantur, perfidia abdicatus[?]. & mox: Pro infinita enim magni-ficentia sua Deus hoc donamit[?] diligentibus se, quod sua dignum est maiestate, non quod homines merentur, quia in dono plus dantis, quam accipientis conconsideratur sublimitas. {a}Fides data est quae iusti-ficat confugientes ad se, ut remittat eis quos lex te-net reos, ut agentes sub fide, liberi sint à peccato &c de Dauidis peccato scribens, ficait: {b}Arbitra-mur secundum Apostolum, iustificari hominem per fidem sine operibus legis, iustificetur ergo ex fi-de Dauid, qui per legem peccatum agnouit, sed peccati veniam ex fide credidit. {c}Iustitia Dei di-cta est, quae videtur esse misericordia, quia de pro-missione originem habet. & mox. Iustificati gra-tu[?], quia nihil operantes, neque vicem reddentes, sola fide iustificati sunt dono Dei.
units.tr: Ambrose too kept the same doctrine, for he writes thus: Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, etc. Plainly they are blessed to whom iniquities are forgiven without any labour or work, and sins are covered, no repentance or works being required of them, but only that they believe. We obtain what we believe; for by believing that Christ is the Son of God, we are adopted by God as sons. He could give believers nothing beyond being called sons of God, having renounced unbelief. And soon after: For in the infinite magnificence of his greatness, God gives to those who love him what is worthy of his majesty, not what men deserve, because the loftiness is weighed more in the gift of the giver than in the reception of the recipient. Faith is given which justifies those who flee to him, so that he may remit to them those whom the law holds guilty, so that those acting under faith may be free from sin. Writing about David's sin he says: We judge, according to the Apostle, that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law; David therefore was justified by faith, who recognised his sin through the law, but believed in forgiveness of sin through faith. The righteousness of God is said to be that which seems to be mercy, because it has its origin in the promise. And soon after: Justified freely, because they were doing nothing and rendering no recompense, they were justified by faith alone, by the gift of God.

units.la: De iustitia Christi imputata sic docet Ambrosius: {d}Iustitiam hanc dicit Apostolus, quae apud Deum imputatur iustitia, id est, fidei, quia & lex habuit iustitiam, sed ad præsens, non quae iustificaret apud Deum, remittere enim peccata non potuit, ut de peccatoribus faceret iustos, & mox: Manifestatiu[?] peccatis suis conclusi sunt, ut se excusare non possent, sed quaerent misericordiam, ut veniens, qui promiserat Abraha, fidem solam ab ab iis posceret, quam habuit Abraham, ut malorum suorum veniam, & iustificationem merentur. Et in eandem sententiam alibi sic habet: {e}Ideo nemo glorietur in operibus, quia nemo facit in suis iustificatur, sed qui iustus est, donatum habet, quia per lavacrum iustificatus est, fides ergo est, quae liberat per sanguinem Christi, quia beatus ille, cui peccatum remittitur, & venia datur. Hieronymus idem docet: {f}Ignorantes quod Deus ex sola fide iustificat, & iustos se ex operibus legis quam non custodierunt, esse putantes, noluerunt se remis-sioni subiicere peccatorum. Idemque: non ex operibus legis, sed sola fide, sicut gentes, vitam in Christo inuenisse te nosti.
units.tr: Ambrose teaches thus about the imputed righteousness of Christ: The Apostle calls this righteousness which is imputed before God, that is, of faith, because the law also had righteousness, but for the present time, not such as would justify before God; for it could not remit sins, so as to make sinners righteous. And soon after: They were shut up, made manifest by their sins, so that they could not excuse themselves, but sought mercy, so that he who had promised Abraham, coming, might ask from them faith alone, which Abraham had, so that they might merit forgiveness of their evils and justification. And in the same sense he says elsewhere: Therefore let no one glory in works, for no one is justified by what he does; but he who is just has it given to him, because he is justified through the washing; it is faith, therefore, which frees through the blood of Christ, for blessed is he to whom sin is forgiven and pardon given. Jerome teaches the same: Ignorant that God justifies from faith alone, and thinking themselves righteous by the works of the law which they did not keep, they were unwilling to submit themselves to the remission of sins. And again: Not by the works of the law, but by faith alone, as the Gentiles did, you know that you found life in Christ.

units.la: Augustinus autem diligentius, atque accuratius haec tractat, sic enim scribit. {a}Quum dicat Apostolus, gratis iustificari hominem sine operibus legis per fidem, non hoc agit, ut percepta & professa fide opera iustitiae contemnantur: sed ut sciat se quisque per fidem posse iustificari, etiam si legis opera non praecesserunt: sequuntur enim iustificatum, non praecedunt iustificandum. {b}Colligimus non iustificari hominem praeceptis bonae vitae, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi, hoc est, non lege operum sed lege fidei, non littera sed spiritu, non factorum merito, sed gratuita gratia, quo libro cap. 14. docet Augustinus, opera illa reiecta a iustificatione non solum esse ceremonias, sed & decalogi praecepta, idque fusius. {c}Haec est (inquit idem) ex qua iustus vivit, haec est fides, qua creditur in eum, qui iustificat impium, haec est fides, per quam excluditur gloriatio sive ut abscedat quae in nobis inflamur, sive ut emineat quae in domino gloriamur, haec est fides quae impetratur largitas spiritus, de quo dicitur, nos enim spiritu ex fide spem iustitiae expectamus, haec est fides, quae salvi fiunt, quibus dicitur, gratia salvi facti estis per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, postremo haec est fides, quae per dilectionem operatur, non per timorem, non formidando poenam, sed amando iustitiam. {d}Si non gratia mortuus [?] est Christus in illo solo iustificatur impius, cui credenti in eum, qui iustificat impium, deputatur fides ad iustitiam.
units.tr: Augustine, however, treats these matters more diligently and accurately, for he writes thus. Since the Apostle says that a man is justified freely, without the works of the law, through faith, he does not mean that works of righteousness are to be despised once faith is received and professed, but that each one may know that he can be justified through faith even if the works of the law have not gone before; for works follow the justified, they do not precede the one to be justified. We conclude that a man is not justified by the precepts of a good life, except through faith in Jesus Christ; that is, not by the law of works but by the law of faith, not by the letter but by the Spirit, not by the merit of deeds but by free grace. In book 14, chapter 14, Augustine teaches that those works rejected from justification are not only the ceremonies but also the precepts of the decalogue, and he does this at greater length. This (he says again) is the faith by which the just live; this is the faith by which we believe in him who justifies the ungodly; this is the faith through which boasting is excluded, whether that which we are puffed up with in ourselves may depart, or that which we glory in the Lord may stand out; this is the faith which obtains the abundance of the Spirit, of whom it is said, For we through the Spirit by faith await the hope of righteousness; this is the faith by which those are saved to whom it is said, By grace you are saved through faith, and this not of yourselves; lastly, this is the faith which works through love, not through fear, not dreading punishment, but loving righteousness. If Christ had not died in grace, the ungodly is justified by him alone in whom, believing in him who justifies the ungodly, faith is reckoned for righteousness.

units.la: De iustitia vero imputata, & nobis donata, sic disputat Augustinus. {a}Iustitiæ Dei manifestata est, hanc ignorantes qui suam voluntatem constituere, & huic noluerunt esse subiecti, iustitia, inquit, Dei manifestata est, non dixit iustitia hominis, vel iustitia propria voluntatis, sed iustitia Dei, non qua Deus iustus est, sed qua induit hominem, quum iustificat impium. {b}{b}Hæc est iustitia Dei, quæ in testamento vete-ri velata, in novo revelatur, quæ ideo iustitia Dei di-citur, quod impartiendo eam, iustos facit. quo libro,cap.18. vocat indumentum iustitiæ fidei, quæ induti non nudi inveniamur. & : Hæc est illa iustiti-
units.tr: Concerning imputed righteousness, which is given to us, Augustine argues thus. The righteousness of God has been made manifest; those who, ignoring it, wished to establish their own will and were unwilling to be subject to it, do not have it. He says, the righteousness of God has been made manifest; he did not say the righteousness of man, or the righteousness of one's own will, but the righteousness of God: not that by which God is righteous, but that with which he clothes man when he justifies the ungodly. This is the righteousness of God, which in the Old Testament was veiled, and is revealed in the New; it is called the righteousness of God because by imparting it he makes men righteous. In book 18, chapter 18 of the same work, he calls it the garment of the righteousness of faith, in which we are found clothed, not naked. And: This is that righteousness of faith

units.la: tia per nos su[?] vera ni[?] gustin[?] sense [?] sputat[?] quide[?] tistæ: tinct[?] adiut[?] pecca[?] posit[?] Eccle[?] nus [?] tia fidei , non qua ipse iustus est , sed quia nos ab ea iusti facti, nemo ergo Christianorum aberret ab hac fide, quae sola Christiana est.
units.tr: of faith, not that by which he himself is righteous, but because we have been made righteous by it. Therefore let no one of the Christians stray from this faith, which alone is Christian.

units.la: Quod si illud quenquam forte moueat, quod Augustinus sæpius de hac iustitia disputans, vocat eam iustitiam Dei, non qua Deus iustus est, sed qua nos iustos facit, vt inde colligat, Christi iustitiam non esse nobis imputatam, opinione Augustini ; quia videri potest Augustinum negare, iustitiam Christi nostram esse, quum negat iustitiam Dei, qua Deus iustus est, nostram esse : Respondeo, ex Augustini verbis manifestis Augustini sensum deduco , certum est ex Augustini sententia gratiam iustificationis in imputatione iustitiae CHRISTI, oblatam nobis , & donatam quam salubérrimam doctrinam tradit Augustinus his verbis. {c}Gratia per dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, in qua nos sita, non nostra, iustitia iustos facit, ut ea sit vera nostra iustitia, quae nobis ab illo est. Hæc Au-gustini verba sine dubio ostendunt, quid senserit de iustitia Christi nobis imputata, di-sputat eo loco contra Pelagium, qui verbis quidem gratiam concessit, sicut hodie Sco-tistæ: sed vim, virtutemque eius penitus ex-tinctam voluit; docebat enim, gratiam esse adiutorium Dei, quo adiuuamur, ad non peccandum, in natura, & libero arbitrio positam. Ad hunc pestilentem errorem ab Ecclesia profligandum, confugit Augusti-nus ad fontem gratiæ, in imputationis doc-trina aperiendum, nam propter Christum non imputatur nobis peccata nostra, & Christi iustitia imputatur, hæc una imputationis doctrina Pelagianos, & Scotistas Tridentinos ex Ecclesia profligabit.
units.tr: But if this should perhaps move anyone, that Augustine, discussing this righteousness often, calls it the righteousness of God, not that by which God is righteous, but that by which he makes us righteous, so that from this one may infer that, in Augustine's opinion, the righteousness of Christ is not imputed to us, because it may seem that Augustine denies that the righteousness of Christ is ours, since he denies that the righteousness of God by which God is righteous is ours: I reply that from Augustine's plain words I deduce Augustine's meaning. It is certain that, in Augustine's view, the grace of justification is offered and given to us in the imputation of the righteousness of Christ, which Augustine sets out in these words, a most wholesome doctrine: Grace, through our Lord Jesus Christ, in which we are set, not our own righteousness, makes us righteous, so that that is our true righteousness which comes to us from him. These words of Augustine undoubtedly show what he thought about the righteousness of Christ imputed to us. He argues in that place against Pelagius, who indeed conceded grace in words, as the Scotists do today, but wished its force and power entirely extinguished; for he taught that grace is God's help, by which we are assisted not to sin, placed in nature and free will. To overthrow this pestilent error, which the Church had to be rid of, Augustine had recourse to the fountain of grace, opening up the doctrine of imputation; for on account of Christ our sins are not imputed to us, and the righteousness of Christ is imputed. This one doctrine of imputation will drive the Pelagians and the Tridentine Scotists out of the Church.

units.la: Quum igitur Augustinus doceat, nos iustos esse iustitia Dei, non qua ipse iustus est, refutare voluit opinionem illam, quæ tum forte apud aliquos hæreticos locum habue-rat nuper vero ab Osiandro ex inferis excita-ta est, de essentiali iustitia Dei, insani homi-nes hæc verba rapiebant, ad iustitiam, quæ Deus ipse iustus est, hoc opinionis monstrum est ab Augustino reiectum, quia iustitia illa, quæ imputatur credentibus, non est iusti-tia essentialis Dei, qua Deus ipse iustus est, sed est iustitia, quam IESVS CHRISTVS dominus noster præstitit, dum perfectam legis obedientiam impleuit, dicitur autem iu-stitia Dei, quamuis Christus homo præstiterit hanc iustitiam, sicut sanguis Christi dicitur sanguis Dei, quamuis Christus homo effu-derit illum sanguinem, propter unionem per-sonalem.
units.tr: Since Augustine teaches that we are righteous by the righteousness of God, not by the righteousness by which God himself is righteous, he wished to refute that opinion, which had perhaps held some place among certain heretics and was recently revived from the dead by Osiander, concerning the essential righteousness of God. Foolish men seized on these words and applied them to the righteousness by which God himself is righteous. Augustine rejected this monstrous opinion, because the righteousness that is imputed to believers is not the essential righteousness of God, by which God himself is righteous, but the righteousness that our Lord Jesus Christ rendered when he fulfilled the perfect obedience of the law. It is called the righteousness of God even though Christ, as man, rendered this righteousness, just as the blood of Christ is called the blood of God even though Christ, as man, shed that blood, on account of the personal union.

units.la: Gratianus etiam quædam ex Augustino, pro sola fide, collegit quæ sunt huiusmodi. {a}Quod si charitas à fide Christianorum seiungi nequit, cui scilicet soli venia promittitur, quomodo qui charitatem non habuerit, fidem Christianorum habuit, id est, in Christum credidit? Et mox: Hoc est enim manducare panem vinum [?], quàd credere in Christum, id est, amando tendere in ipsum, cum ergo reprobus in eum non credit, quem non manducauit, & ita fidem Christianorum, qua sola peccata relaxantur, non habuit, quomodo si vivit dominus cui omne iudicium dedit pater, iudicium perpetuæ damnationis effugiet?
units.tr: Gratian also gathered from Augustine some passages of this kind in support of faith alone: If charity cannot be separated from the faith of Christians, to whom alone forgiveness is promised, how is it that he who has not charity has the faith of Christians, that is, has believed in Christ? And soon after: For this is to eat the living bread, to believe in Christ, that is, by loving to strive toward him. Therefore, when the reprobate does not believe in him, he has not eaten him, and so he has not had the faith of Christians, by which alone sins are forgiven. How then, if the Lord lives, to whom the Father has given all judgment, will he escape the judgment of everlasting damnation?

units.la: Prosper eandem post Augustinum doctrinam retinuit, sic enim ille: {b}Iustificati sumus gratis, quia nihil operantes, neque vicem reddentes, sola fide iustificati sunt dono Dei: Idemque: {c}Fides qua iustificatur impius, nisi ex Dei munere non habetur, eaque nullis præcedentibus meritis tribuitur, sed ad hoc donatur, ut principium possit esse meritorum: ut quum ipsa data fuerit, non petita ipsius iam petitionibus bona cetera consequantur. {d}Vi-lesceret enim redemptio sanguinis Christi, nec misericordia Dei humanorum operum prærogativa succumberet, si iustificatio quæ fit per gratiam, meritis præcedentibus deberetur, ut nō manum largienru[?], sed merces esset operantu[?]. Hæc Prosper. Leo I. sic habet. {a}Sola fides catholica viuificat, & sanctificat. Primasius autem sic: {b}Impium per solam fidem iustificat Deus, non opera. Idemque: {c}Non ex operibus, sed sola fide per gratiam habere te nosti. Iterumque: {d}nobis sola fides sufficit ad iustitiam. Sedulius, {e}Conuersum impium per solam fidem iustificat Deus, non per bona opera, quia non habuit prius, alioqui per impietatu[?] opera fuerat puniendus, hoc dicit, quia sine operibus legis credenti impio in Christum reputatur fides eius in iustitiam. Et mox: Quomodo Abraham credens ex Gentibus per solam fidem iustificatus est, ita cæteri, fidem eius imitantes saluantur. Cassiodorus: {f}Constat pro nihilo peccatores saluos fieri, quando certum est, conuersionem gratuita largitate largiri. Fulgentius, {g}In sanctu[?] coronat Deus iustitiam, quam eis ipse gratis tribuit, gratis seruauit, gratis perfecit, iniquos autem condemnabit pro impietate & iniustitia, quam in eis ipse non facit, in illis enim opera sua iustificat, in ipsis opera non sua condemnat. Iterumque. {h}Posset Apostolus quos dixit vasa misericordiæ, vasa iustitiæ cupare, sed si vasa iustitiæ vocarentur, forsan ex seipsis iustitiam habere putarentur.
units.tr: Prosper, after Augustine, retained the same doctrine, for he says: We have been justified freely, because we work nothing and render nothing in return; we are justified by faith alone, by the gift of God. And again: The faith by which the impious man is justified is not had except by the gift of God, and it is bestowed on no preceding merits, but is granted so that it may be the beginning of merits, so that when it has been given, the other goods may follow, not by our asking, but by its own petitions. For the redemption of Christ's blood would be cheapened, and the mercy of God would yield to the priority of human works, if justification, which comes through grace, were owed to preceding merits, so that it would be not a free hand giving but a wage for those who work. So Prosper. Leo I says: Only the catholic faith quickens and sanctifies. Primasius writes: God justifies the impious man through faith alone, not through works. Again: You know that you have it not from works, but by grace through faith alone. And again: Faith alone is sufficient for us for righteousness. Sedulius: God justifies the converted impious man through faith alone, not through good works, because he did not have them beforehand; otherwise he would have been punished for the impious works. This means that, without the works of the law, the faith of the impious man who believes in Christ is reckoned to him for righteousness. And soon after: Just as Abraham, believing, was justified through faith alone from among the Gentiles, so the rest who imitate his faith are saved. Cassiodorus: It is agreed that sinners are saved for nothing, since it is certain that conversion is bestowed by gratuitous bounty. Fulgentius: God crowns in the saints the righteousness that he himself freely bestowed on them, freely preserved, and freely perfected, but he will condemn the wicked for their impiety and unrighteousness, which he himself does not work in them. For in the saints he justifies his own works; in the wicked he condemns works that are not his own. And again: The Apostle, who called them vessels of mercy, could have called them vessels of righteousness, but if they were called vessels of righteousness, perhaps they would have been thought to have righteousness from themselves.

units.la: Gregorius Magnus hanc doctrinam summa fide retinuit, & tradidit: sic n[?]. docet: {i}Non de meis meritis confidens, vt me saluum facias supplico, sed de sola misericordia tua presumes[?] impetrare, & non de meritis spero. {k}Misericordia est qua sine vllis precedentibus meritis, pœnitentibus, veniam tribuit. {l}Iustitia Dei, fides est, sicut scriptum est: credidit Abraham Deo, & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam, &c. quia iusti ex fide viuunt, {m}Ipsa iustitia nostra ad examen diuina iustitia deducta iniustitia est, & sordet in districtione Iudicis quod in aestimatione fulget operantis. {a}non charitas fidem, sed fides charitatem praecedit, nemo enim potest amare quod non crediderit.
units.tr: Gregory the Great held and taught this doctrine with the greatest faith; he teaches thus: Not trusting in my merits, I beg that you save me, but I presume to obtain it from your mercy alone, and I hope not from merits. Mercy is that by which, without any preceding merits, he grants pardon to the penitent. The righteousness of God is faith, as it is written: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, etc., because the righteous live by faith. Our own righteousness, when brought to the judgment of divine righteousness, is unrighteousness, and what shines in the estimation of the one who works is foul in the strictness of the Judge. Charity does not precede faith, but faith precedes charity, for no one can love what he has not believed.

units.la: De iustitia Christi credentibus imputata, egregie Gregorius: sic enim scribit: {b}Iustitia nostra dicitur, non quae ex nostro nostra est, sed quae divina largitate fit nostra. {c}Iustitia vestimento comparatur, cum per Propheram [?] dicitur, Sacerdotes tui induantur iustitia. {d}Omnes superna patria electi, sancti quidem, & iusti sunt, sed participatione sapientia, non comparatione. Lumen sapientia, lumen, & serui sapientia vocari solent, sed illa lumen illuminans, isti lumen illuminatum, sicut scriptum est, erat lux vera, quae illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum: isti autem tantummodo dicitur, vos estis lux mundi. Iustitia quidem, sapientia, iustitia, & serui sapientia nuncupantur, sed illa iustitia iustificans, isti iustitia iustificata, de Deo quippe, qui est sapientia, dicitur; ut sit ipse iustus & iustificans: isti vero dicunt, ut nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso, aliter ergo venerandum est lumen illuminans aliter lumen illuminatum: aliter iustitia iustificans, aliter iustitia iustificata. Sic Gregorius. Beda etiam idem docuit: {e}Iustruit [?] David, ut nemo vel libertatem arbitrii, vel merita sua sufficere sibi ad beatitudinem credat, sed sola gratia Dei se salvari posse intelligat. Iterumque: {f}Per iustitiam factorum nemo iustificabitur, sed per solam iustitiam fidei. Alkuinus: {g}Fides catholica humanum genus sola sanctificat. {h}Constat neminem ad veram pervenire posse beatitudinem, nisi Deo placeat, & Deo neminem placere posse, nisi per fidem. Strabus An-glosaxo, autor glossæ ordinariæ, in illa verba; arbitramur hominem iustificari per fidem sine operibus, sic scribit: {a}Non quin credens post per dilectionem debeat operari, ut Abraham filium suum immolare voluit, sequuntur enim opera iustificatum, non precedunt iustificandum: sed sola fide sine operibus precedentibus homo fit iustus. Idem etiam in Epistolam Iacobi scribens, demonstrat quomodo sint inter se concilianda Pauli, & Iacobi verba. {b}Abraham per fidem sine operib. iustificatus dicitur, de operibus quæ precedebant intelligitur, quia per opera quæ fecit, iustus non fuit, sed sola fide. Rabanus Maurus. d per solam Christi gratiam ab omni scandalo liberantur electi.
units.tr: Concerning the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, Gregory writes admirably; for he writes thus: Our righteousness is said to be not that which is ours from ourselves, but that which by divine bounty becomes ours. Righteousness is compared to a garment, when it is said through the Prophet, Let your priests be clothed with righteousness. All the elect in the heavenly fatherland are holy and righteous, but by participation in wisdom, not by comparison. The light of wisdom and the servants of wisdom are usually called light, but the former is the light that illumines, the latter the light that is illumined, as it is written: That was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world; but of the others it is said only: You are the light of the world. Righteousness, wisdom, and the servants of wisdom are indeed called righteousness, but the former is justifying righteousness, the latter righteousness that is justified. For it is said of God, who is wisdom, that he may be himself just and justifying; but of them it is said that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Therefore the illuminating light is to be revered otherwise than the illuminated light; justifying righteousness otherwise than justified righteousness. So Gregory. Bede also taught the same: David instructs that no one should believe that free will or his own merits are sufficient for him for blessedness, but should understand that he can be saved by the grace of God alone. Again: No one will be justified by the righteousness of works, but by the righteousness of faith alone. Alcuin: The catholic faith alone sanctifies the human race. It is agreed that no one can attain to true blessedness unless he pleases God, and that no one can please God except through faith. Strabo the Anglo-Saxon, author of the Glossa Ordinaria, on the words we consider that a man is justified by faith without works, writes thus: Not that the believer must afterwards work through love, as Abraham wished to sacrifice his son; for works follow the one who has been justified; they do not precede the one who is to be justified. But a man becomes righteous by faith alone, without preceding works. The same, writing also on the Epistle of James, shows how the words of Paul and James are to be reconciled: Abraham is said to be justified by faith without works, is understood of the works that preceded, because he was not righteous through the works he did, but by faith alone. Rabanus Maurus: The elect are delivered from every stumbling block by the grace of Christ alone.

units.la: CAPUT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Sequuntur testimonia eorum, quos Pontificii suos vocant, ut una unius[?] Ecclesiæ vox ubique agnoscatur.
units.tr: Here follow the testimonies of those whom the Papists call their own, so that the one voice of the one Church may be recognised everywhere.

units.la: Emigius Epilcopus Antisiodorens. {c}Vi-ta æterna non est de merito, sed ex voluntate eius, id est, sola misericordia. Idemque {d}Revera isti soli beati, isti soli salvi sunt, qui per gratiam iustificantur, & non ex meritis. Smaragdus. {e}Necesse est sola fide Christi salvari credentes. Idemque. {f}Secundum quod proposuit, non ex operibus legis, nec legalibus sacrificiis, sed sola fide, & sanguinis fui effusione saluare nos praescierat, multo magis glorificauit operantes. Gislebertus: {a}Credendum est, quia sola fide saluari sumus, siue propria, qui credere potuere, siue aliena, qui credere non potuere. Atque iterum. {b}Manifestum est, Abraham patrem nostrum prius placuisse per fidem, quam per circumcisionem: dum videmus infinitum nu- merum periisse circumcisum, & alios absque hoc si- gno etiam ante aduentum Christi, sola fide gra- tiam Christi promeruisse. Anselmus. {c}In gratia Dei, quae data est in Christo Iesu, non Petro, vel Paulo, gratia enim data est in Christo, quia hoc constitutum est a Deo, ut qui credit in Christo saluus fit sine opere, sola fide, & gratis accipiat remissionem peccatorum. Atque iterum, {d}Iustificatio quae ex fide est, pacem cum Deo facit, quia inimicas praesumptiones humanorum meritorum expellit, & animam Deo humiliter sub- iicit, dum de sola gratia saluari cognoscit. &c mox: {e}Ab Ada viro sola Christi gratia liberat, quo non secundum merita hominum, sed gratis da- tur, quoniam Deus misericors est. Ansbertus {f} In illo autem ei damus gloriam, quo nullis prace- dentibus meritis bonorum operum, sed sola nos eius misericordia ad tantam dignitatem peruenisse fa- teamur.
units.tr: Emigius, Bishop of Auxerre: Eternal life is not from merit, but from his will, that is, from mercy alone. And again: Truly those alone are blessed, those alone are saved, who are justified by grace and not from merits. Smaragdus: Believers must necessarily be saved by faith in Christ alone. And again: According to what he had purposed, he had foreknown that he would save us not by works of the law, nor by legal sacrifices, but by faith alone and by the shedding of his blood; much more did he glorify those who work. Gislebertus: We must believe that we are saved by faith alone, whether our own faith, if they were able to believe, or another's, if they were not able to believe. And again: It is clear that Abraham, our father, was pleasing to God through faith before circumcision, since we see that an countless number who were circumcised perished, and others without this sign, even before the coming of Christ, obtained the grace of Christ by faith alone. Anselm: In the grace of God which is given in Christ Jesus, not to Peter or to Paul, for grace is given in Christ, since it has been established by God that whoever believes in Christ is saved without works, by faith alone, and receives the forgiveness of sins freely. And again: Justification which is by faith makes peace with God, because it drives out the hostile presumptions of human merits and humbly subjects the soul to God, while it acknowledges that it is saved by grace alone. And soon after: From Adam the man, grace alone delivers us, which is given not according to the merits of men but freely, since God is merciful. Ansbert: But we give glory to him in that we confess that we have come to such dignity not by any preceding merits of good works, but by his mercy alone.

units.la: Bernardus hanc doctrinam magna fide à patribus excepiam Ecclesiae tradidit. Postquam enim Augustini, atque Ambrosii sententiam de iustificatione exposuisset, sic ait: {g}Ab his duobus columnis credere mihi difficile a-[illegible, ~7 letters]. Cum his, inquam, me aut errare, aut sapere fateor, fateo[?] uari[?] in ext[?] sola[?] obtin[?] sic sol[?] fufio[?] dubio[?] artic[?] dus [?] prim[?] fidem [?] ftri su[?] Sed [?] vt p[?] magi[?] subni[?] tiam
units.tr: Bernard handed down this doctrine to the Church, having received it from the Fathers with great faith. For after he had set out the opinion of Augustine and Ambrose concerning justification, he says thus: It is difficult for me to believe from these two pillars [...]. With these men, I say, I confess that I either err or am wise [...].

units.la: D[?] Quid [?] tiam [?] boli [?] caru[?] cum [?] tuit [?] tus de[?] num[?] cond[?] ftum [?] tior [?] habe[?] falu[?] fateor, credens, & ipse, sola fide hominem posse salvari. {a}Quomodo is qui alieno debito se teneri forte in extremis positum recolit, si defit unde persoluat, sola nihilominus poenitentia, & cordis contritione obtinere veniam creditur; nec iam pro eo damnetur: sic sola fides, & mentis ad Deum conuersio, sine effusione sanguinis, sine perfusione aquae, salutem sine dubio operatur volenti, sed non valenti prohibente articulo baptizari. De fidei certitudine Bernardus sic docet. {b}Petrus Abailardus haereticus in primo limine theologiae suae, vel potius stultiloquio, fidem definit aestimationem, stulti ergo martyres nostri sustinentes tam acerba propter incerta. & mox. Sed absit ut putemus in fide vel ipsa nostra aliquid ut in putat[?], dubia aestimatione pendulum, & non magis totum, quod in eo est, certa ac solida veritatis subnixum. haec, & plura habet in hanc sententiam Bernardus.
units.tr: I confess, believing myself too, that by faith alone a man can be saved. Just as one who, lying at the point of death, recalls that he is bound by another's debt, and has nothing from which to pay it, is nevertheless believed to obtain pardon by repentance and contrition of heart alone, and is not then condemned for it: so faith alone, and the turning of the mind to God, without the shedding of blood and without the washing of water, undoubtedly works salvation for one who is willing but unable to be baptised because of the article (of death) preventing it. Concerning the certainty of faith, Bernard teaches thus: Peter Abelard, the heretic, in the first threshold of his theology, or rather in his foolish talk, defines faith as an estimation; therefore our martyrs, who endured such bitter things, were fools because of uncertain things. And soon after: But far be it from us to think that our faith itself hangs on some uncertain estimation, and is not rather wholly, as it is, supported by the certain and solid truth. Bernard has these and more to this effect.

units.la: De iustitia Christi imputata sic docet. {c} Quid ex se agere poterat, ut semel amissam iustitiam recuperaret homo servus peccati, vinctus diaboli? assignata est ei proinde aliena iustitia, quae caruit sua. Et mox. Cur non aliunde iustitia, cum aliunde reatus? alium qui peccatorem constituit, alius qui iustificat a peccato, nec versor sic erutus de depotestate tenebrarum, repelli a patre Lumi-num, iustificatus gratis in sanguine filii eius, non condemnabit iustum, qui misertus est peccatori, iustum me dixerim; sed illa iustitia[?] & sane mihi tutior donata, quam innata. nam ista quidem gloriam habet, sed non apud Deum, illa autem quam sit fulmen efficax, materiam non habet gloriandi. nisi in Domino. {a}Est & iudicium; vt qui contemnunt Dei misericordiam & iustitiam, & suam volunt constituere ( quae profecto non iustificat sed accusat ) eidem sua iustitia relinquantur opprimendi magis, quam iustificandi. {b}Christus factus est a Deo nobis sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, redemptio, sapientia in praedicatione, iustitia in absolutio-ne peccatorum, sanctificatio in conversatione quam habuit cum peccatoribus, redemptio in passione, quam sustinuit pro peccatoribus. {c}At vero iusti-tia tua tanta ubique fragrantia spargitur, vt non solum iustus, sed etiam ipsa dicatur iustitia, & iu-stitia iustificans, quamobrem quisquis pro pecca-tis compunctus elurit[?] ac sitit iustitiam, credat in te, qui iustificas impium, & solam iustificatus per fidem, pacem habebit apud Deum. {d}Ego utique misericordias domini in caeterum cantabo, numquid iustitias meas? domine memorabo iustitiae tuae solius, ipsa est enim & mea, nempe factus es mihi tu iustitia a Deo, numquid mihi verendum ne non vna ambobus sufficiat? {e}Beatus vir, cui non imputabit Dominus peccatum, ait sanctus, non dixit, qui non fecit peccatum, non est enim hic aliquis, nisi vnus, & hic est filius Dei, qui peccatum non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore eius, omne ergo, quod ipse mihi non imputare decreverit, sic est quasi non fuerit. Hactenus Bernardus, de sola fide, de certitudine fidei, de peccatis non imputatis, de iustitia Christi imputata antiquae Ecclesiae integritatem retinet, a qua longe ab-sunt Tridentini.
units.tr: Concerning the imputed righteousness of Christ he teaches thus: What could man, a slave of sin and bound by the devil, do of himself so as to recover the righteousness once lost? Therefore another's righteousness was assigned to him, since his own was lacking. And soon after: Why should righteousness not come from elsewhere, since guilt came from elsewhere? One who made the sinner, another who justifies from sin; nor, being thus snatched from the power of darkness, shall I be rejected by the Father of lights, justified freely in the blood of his Son. He will not condemn the righteous one, who has had mercy on the sinner. I would call myself righteous, but that righteousness is more secure for me when given than when innate. For the latter has glory, but not before God; the former, however, which is a powerful thunderbolt, has no matter for boasting except in the Lord. There is also judgment: that those who despise God's mercy and righteousness, and want to set up their own righteousness (which surely does not justify but accuses), be left to their own righteousness to be oppressed rather than justified. Christ was made by God our wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, redemption: wisdom in preaching, righteousness in the forgiveness of sins, sanctification in the dealings he had with sinners, redemption in the passion which he endured for sinners. But your righteousness is spread everywhere with such fragrance that you are called not only righteous but righteousness itself, and justifying righteousness; wherefore whoever, pricked for his sins, hungers and thirsts after righteousness, let him believe in you, who justify the ungodly, and being justified by faith alone he will have peace with God. I will indeed sing of the mercies of the Lord forever; shall I sing of my righteousness? Lord, I will remember your righteousness alone, for it is also mine; indeed you have been made to me righteousness from God. Am I to fear that one is not enough for both of us? Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin, says the holy man; he did not say, who has not committed sin. For there is no one here except one, and he is the Son of God, who committed no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth. Therefore whatever he has decided not to impute to me is as if it had not happened. Thus far Bernard, on faith alone, on the certainty of faith, on sins not imputed, on the imputed righteousness of Christ. The integrity of the ancient Church is kept, from which the men of Trent are far removed.

units.la: Rupertus {f}Sola fides Iesu Christi iustificare potest dit, q bile es rum. pertin bus, c ne do ftod ingen fe sal Vict tur, perib tia fi falut sicut iusti oper bona P dere dere ire, vari ipsa Aqu tes do f g I non Ni men potest, atque iterum: {a}Iustitia haec in fidem ten· dit, quia non propter opera, sed propter fidem possibile est quandoque coram illo iustificari. atque iterum. {b}Sperare in nomine domini est deponere pertinaciam, qua se iustificari arbitrantur ex operibus, & omnem iustificationem credere in solo nomine domini, in fide Iesu Christi. Honorius Augustodun. {c}Hi qui se miseros, & a iustitia nudos ingemiscunt, pauperes domini sunt, quia se non possunt salvari, nisi sola Dei gratia norunt. Hugo de S. Victore: {d}Lex scripta, lex factorum appellatur, quia homines legis totam iustitiam suam in operibus legis constituebant, lex autem fidei vel gratia sic dicitur, quia homines gratia totam summam salutis suae, in sola gratia constituunt: scientes quod sicut nemo salvabitur ex iustitia operum, sic nemo iustificabitur ex operibus iustitiae, non enim ex bonis operibus iustitia, sed ex iustitia, hoc est, iustificatione, bona opera.
units.tr: Rupert: Faith in Jesus Christ alone is able to justify [...] Again: This righteousness tends toward faith, because it is possible to be justified before him sometimes not on account of works, but on account of faith. And again: To hope in the name of the Lord is to lay aside the obstinacy by which men think they are justified by works, and to believe all justification in the name of the Lord alone, in faith in Jesus Christ. Honorius of Autun: Those who groan that they are wretched and naked of righteousness are the poor of the Lord, because they cannot be saved unless they know it by the grace of God alone. Hugh of St. Victor: The written law is called the law of works, because men set all their righteousness in the works of the law; but the law of faith or of grace is so called, because men place the whole sum of their salvation in grace alone, knowing that as no one will be saved by the righteousness of works, so no one will be justified by the works of righteousness; for good works come not from righteousness, but righteousness, that is, justification, comes before good works.

units.la: Petrus Lumbardus {e}Credere Deum, est credere quod ipse sit Deus, quod etiam mali faciunt, credere in Deum, est credendo amare, credendo in eum ire, credendo ei adhaerere, & eius membris incorporari, per hanc fidem iustificatur impius, ut deinde ipsa fides incipiat per dilectionem operari. Thomas Aquinas: {f}Ostendit Apostolus hic Iudaeos, & Gentes esse aequales, quantum ad statum gratiae, ostendendo sola fide Christi fieri iustificationem. Iterumque {g}Data est lex, ut cognosceretur peccatum, Rom. 7. non est ergo in eu[?] iustificationis ipsius, sed in sola fide. Nicolaus Gorham {h}Sufficit ad iustificationem, quod aliquis credat, nec exigitur, quod operetur ad {a}ad hoc. atque iterum. Si solum[?] credit in Christum, licet non operetur, reputatur ideo eius fides sola ad iustitiam sufficientem. Eandem doctrinam alii deinceps retinuerunt usque ad tempora Concilii Tridentini: Qui igitur Mart. Lutherum huius doctrinae autorem ferunt, sicut plurimi inter Pontificios effatiunt, insignis mendacii arguuntur, quum ab Ecclesiae exordio, non interruptam Ecclesiae vocem audiunt, in hanc sententiam, usque ad Lutheri tempora, ac deinceps etiam, erat enim haec doctrina, de sola fide iustificāte, recepta communi consensu in Ecclesia Romana, ante Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: Peter Lombard: To believe God is to believe that he is God, which even evil men do; to believe in God is to love by believing, to go to him by believing, to cling to him by believing, and to be incorporated into his members; through this faith the ungodly is justified, so that afterwards that faith may begin to work through love. Thomas Aquinas: The Apostle here shows that Jews and Gentiles are equal as to the state of grace, showing that justification comes about by faith in Christ alone. And again: The law was given that sin might be known, Rom. 7. there is therefore no part of justification itself in it, but in faith alone. Nicolas Gorham: It is enough for justification that someone believes, nor is it required that he works for this. And again: If he believes in Christ only, even though he does not work, his faith alone is therefore reckoned sufficient for righteousness. Other men afterwards held the same doctrine down to the time of the Council of Trent. Therefore those who name Martin Luther as the author of this doctrine, as very many among the Papists assert, are convicted of notorious falsehood, since from the beginning of the Church they hear the unbroken voice of the Church in this opinion, down to the times of Luther and afterwards; for this doctrine, of justification by faith alone, was received by common consent in the Roman Church before the Council of Trent.

units.la: Scripsit librum de iustificatione, Gaspar Contarenus Cardinalis vir doctus, & pius, postquam iam Lutherus, aliique suam sententiam de hac re declarassent. Quo libro testatur, Protestantes & Catholicos in hac re convenire. Recte Contarenus, qui, quum ex industria Protestantium doctrinam examinasset, nihil in ea invenire se profitetur, quod a Catholicorum sententia dissentiret. At in sententia de iustificatione non convenit Protestantibus cum Concilio Tridentino, non igitur erat illud Concilium conventus Catholicorum. Et quia Catholicorum sententiam de iustificatione Contarenus eo libro explicandam susceperat, non erit alienum, si verba eius etiam suius[?] de hac re observemus, ut constare possit, quinam sint, qui cum Ecclesia Catholica consentiant, quinam etiam sint Tridentini isti, qui cōtra Ecclesiæ Catholicæ doctrinam, ipsorum Cardinalium iudicio figmetum suū posuerūt. Scripsit hæc Cōtarenus Anno dom. 1541. quadriennio fere ante primam sessionē eius Concilii, à Paulo 3. inchoatam. Ita, ut in hac quæstione, quæ est grauissima, Cardinalis eo consilio laborasse videatur, ut lucem Tridentinis præferret, admoneretque de vera, & antiqua iustificationis tractatione, quam animadverterat ipse in Ecclesia, ad eum usque diem fuisse conservatam, utcunque aliter fraterculi quidam Scotistæ docuerant. Hanc vero Catholicorum sententiam sic exponit Cardinalis.
units.tr: Gaspar Contarenus, a learned and pious cardinal, wrote a book on justification after Luther and others had already declared their opinion on this matter. In that book he testifies that Protestants and Catholics agree on this point. Contarenus is right: having examined the Protestants' doctrine with care, he professes that he finds nothing in it that differs from the opinion of the Catholics. But on justification the Protestants do not agree with the Council of Trent, so that Council was not an assembly of Catholics. And since Contarenus had undertaken in that book to set out the Catholic opinion on justification, it will not be out of place to observe his own words on the matter, so that it may be clear who agree with the Catholic Church, and who those Tridentines are who, against the doctrine of the Catholic Church, set up their fabrication by the judgement of the cardinals themselves. Contarenus wrote these things in the year of the Lord 1541, about four years before the first session of that Council, which Paul III had begun. So in this question, which is most weighty, the cardinal seems to have laboured with the aim of setting a light before the Tridentines, and of admonishing them about the true and ancient treatment of justification, which he had observed to have been preserved in the Church up to that day, however differently some little Franciscan friars of the Scotist school had taught. Now the cardinal sets out this Catholic opinion as follows.

units.la: {a} Attingimus, inquit, ad duplicem iustitiam, alteram nobis inhærentem, quam incipimus esse iusti, & efficimur consortes diuinæ naturæ, & habemus charitatem diffusam in cordibus nostris: alteram vero non inhærentem, sed nobis donatam cum Christo, iustitiam, inquam, Christi, & omne eius meritum, quod autem Deus donaverit nobis Christum, & omnia cum eo, est textus Apostoli, ad Rom. His rectè[?] nullum posse contradicere. Restat inquirere, utra debeamus niti, & existimari nos iustificari coram Deo. Ego profecto existimo pium, & Christiane dici, quod debeamus niti, nisi, niti, inquam, tanquam stabili, quæ certa nos sustentat, iustitia Christi nobis donata, non autem sanctitate, & gratia nobis inhærente. Hæc ille. sed pergat Cardinalis.
units.tr: {a} We come, he says, to a twofold righteousness: one inherent in us, by which we begin to be righteous and are made partakers of the divine nature, and have the charity poured into our hearts; the other not inherent but given to us together with Christ, the righteousness, I say, of Christ, and all his merit. That God has given us Christ, and all things with him, is the text of the Apostle in Rom. No one can reasonably contradict this. It remains to inquire on which of the two we ought to rest, and be reckoned justified before God. For my part I think it pious and Christian to say that we ought to rest, I say rest, as on something stable which sustains us with certainty, on the righteousness of Christ given to us, and not on the holiness and grace inherent in us. Thus he. But let the cardinal go on.

units.la: {b}Hac sola, inquit, certa, stabili nobis niten-dum est, & ob eam solam credere nos iustificari coram coram Deo, id est, iustos haberi. Hic est pretiosus ille Christianorum thesaurus, quem qui invenit, vendit omnia quae habet, ut emat illum. Et post: Inde est, quod experimento videmus viros sanctos, qui quanto magis in sanctitate proficiunt, tanto minus sibi placent, ac propterea tanto magis intelligunt se indigere Christo, & iustitia Christi sibi donata, ideoque se relinquunt, & soli Christo incumbunt, hoc non ob eam accidit causam, quod facti sanctiores minus videant, quam prius, neque quoniam facti sunt animo demissiori & viliori, imo quanto magis in sanctitate proficiunt, tanto maiori sunt animo, tanto sunt perspicaciores. Quamobrem facti perspicaciores magis intuentur sanctitatis & iustitiae inhaerentis tenuitatem, cum quia perspiciunt multas maculas, quae eorum oculos, factos perspicaciores magis offendunt: ac propterea agnoscunt, non sibi nitendum esse sanctitate, charitate, & gratia sibi inhaerente, sed confugiendum sibi esse ad Christum, & gloriam Christi ipsis donatam, qua nituntur, & incumbunt. Haec ille, & plura etiam in hanc sententiam.
units.tr: {b} On this alone, he says, we must rest as on something certain and stable, and because of it alone believe that we are justified before God, that is, held to be righteous. This is that precious treasure of the Christians, which whoever finds, sells all that he has in order to buy it. And afterwards: Hence it is that by experience we see holy men who, the more they advance in holiness, the less they please themselves, and therefore the more they understand that they need Christ and the righteousness of Christ given to them; and so they leave themselves and lean on Christ alone. This does not happen because, having become holier, they see less than before, nor because they have become humbler and of lesser spirit; rather, the more they advance in holiness, the greater their spirit and the keener their sight. Wherefore, having become keener-sighted, they gaze the more upon the slightness of inherent holiness and righteousness, both because they perceive many stains which, now that their sight is sharper, offend their eyes the more; and therefore they acknowledge that they must not rest on the holiness, charity and grace inherent in them, but must flee to Christ and to the glory of Christ given to them, on which they lean and rest. Thus he, and more also to this effect.

units.la: Probat etiam Cotarenus hanc esse doctrinam Thomae Aquinatis, deinde ad Scotistarum obiectiones respondet. Nam Scotistae erant, qui hanc lucem absconderunt. Denique quum ad omnes obiectiones respondisset, locosque e scripturis adductos explicasset, sic tandem infert. {a}Mihi videntur hi loci adducti esse adeo perspicui, quod nullam dubitationem facere possint in sententia hac, in qua
units.tr: Cotarenus also proves that this is the doctrine of Thomas Aquinas, and then answers the objections of the Scotists. For it was the Scotists who hid this light. Finally, having answered all the objections and explained the passages of Scripture adduced, he concludes thus: These passages seem to me so clear that they can raise no doubt about this opinion, in which

units.la: qua C non fa Haec Con telli sueri um T alia, pore tis ef Cat nali nob nos clef Co teft nui Co ger Pri in cu lu Be ne ci tu R e u n qua Catholici, & Protestantes conuenerunt. Et quod non satis recte intelligantur ab iis, qui eis nituntur.
units.tr: in which Catholics and Protestants have agreed. And these passages are not sufficiently rightly understood by those who rely on them.

units.la: Hæc Cardinalis Contarenus, paulo ante Concilium Tridentinum inchoatum. Ita intelligimus ex confessione huius viri, quænam fuerit Catholicorum sententia ante Concilium Tridentinum, de iustificatione: quod si alia, & plane contraria sententia ex eo tempore inualuerit, viderint nouatores, nobis satis est Originem huius mutationis indicasse. Catholicorum sententiam sic explicat Cardinalis: Hac sola iustitia Christi, certa stabili nobis nitendum est, & ob eam solam credere nos iustificari coram Deo. At contra hanc Ecclesiæ doctrinam, catholicam habitam ante Concilium Tridentinum, perpetuis Ecclesiæ testimoniis: Concilium illud anathema denuntiat, Session. 6. Can. 11. Vicerunt in illo Concilio Scotistæ. Concilium enim illud,nec generale erat, contra quod multi Reges, & Principes protestati sunt. Quidam etiam in ipso Concilio, in medio Patrum, non publicum Concilium, sed priuatum conuenticulum habendum esse censuerunt. Sicut Abbas Bellofanus Galliæ Regis legatus Regis sui nomine denuntiarat. Nec liberum erat Concilium illud, in quo nemo suffragium ferre potuit, qui non prius iuramento obligatus esset Rom. Pontifici. Nec legitimum Concilium esse potuit, quia non legitima autoritate conuocatum fuerat. Pontificii enim vnius Romani Pontificis autoritatem sufficere prædicant. ad generalia Concilia cöuocanda, qua tamen autoritate generalia Concilia nunquam fuerunt conuocata, nec erunt in posterum. Mitto fraudem, artes, stratagemata in eodem Concilio dolo malo peracta: quod quum quosdā sensissent paulo liberiores in dicendo, iuuentā ratio fuit, vt iis reuocatis, atq; summotis, alii summitterentur nequiores: quod maximus Episcoporum numerus esset ex Italia: ꝗ ad extremum eum tum [?], decem & tres Cardinales subito crearentur, Itali omnes, qui ad Concilium missi, suffragiorum numero, atq; auxilio, rem Tridentinam, alioqui ruituram, restituerunt: Quod deniq; veneficiis grassarentur. Nam qui virtute, & sanctitate cæteris præstare videbantur, è medio sublati sunt, inter quos erat Cardinalis Contarenus, qui veneno extinctus est, ne insignis eruditio, & pietas huius viri Scotisticum illud Conciliabulum conturbasse videretur.
units.tr: This is Cardinal Contarenus, who died shortly before the Council of Trent began. From the confession of this man we understand what the opinion of the Catholics was before the Council of Trent concerning justification. If a different and plainly contrary opinion has prevailed since that time, let the innovators see to it; for us it is enough to have pointed out the origin of this change. The Cardinal explains the Catholic opinion thus: "We must rest on this sole righteousness of Christ, certain and steadfast, and on it alone believe that we are justified before God." But against this doctrine of the Church, held as Catholic before the Council of Trent and attested by the perpetual testimonies of the Church, that Council pronounces an anathema (Session 6, Canon 11). The Scotists prevailed in that Council. For that Council was not general, and many kings and princes protested against it. Some, even within the Council itself, in the midst of the Fathers, judged that what was held was not a public council but a private conventicle; as Abbot Bellofanus, legate of the King of France, declared in his king's name. Nor was that Council free, since no one could give a vote who was not first bound by oath to the Roman Pontiff. Nor could it be a lawful council, since it had not been convoked by lawful authority. For the Papists maintain that the authority of the one Roman Pontiff is sufficient for convoking general councils; yet by that authority general councils were never convoked, nor will they be in the future. I say nothing of the fraud, the tricks and the stratagems carried out in that same Council by evil design: how, when some had spoken somewhat too freely, the plan was to recall and remove them and send in others more worthless in their place; how the greatest number of bishops came from Italy; and how, at the end, thirteen Cardinals were suddenly created, all Italians, who were sent to the Council and by their number of votes and their help restored the Tridentine business, which would otherwise have collapsed. Finally, that they resorted to poisonings: for those who seemed to excel the rest in virtue and holiness were removed from the midst, among them Cardinal Contarenus, who was killed by poison, lest his distinguished learning and piety should seem to have disturbed that Scotist conventicle.

units.la: CAPUT VII
units.tr: CAPUT VII

units.la: Obiectiones, & aduersariorum responsiones ad patrum testimonia, diluuntur.
units.tr: Objections, and the opponents' answers to the testimonies of the Fathers, are refuted.

units.la: Hactenus vnam Ecclesiæ vocem per diuersa secula in scripturibus in patribus, ac recentioribus scriptoribus sonantem audiuimus, & in Ecclesia conseruatam, usque ad Concilium Tridentinum. Hæc est illa Ecclesia vera, visibilis, in qua per successiones, vera fides semper eadem tradita est. Pontificia siue Iesuitica ista Ecclesia, quæ hodie fidè hanc oppuguat, nup nata, nouam fidē exhibet. Est ergo pontificia ista ecclesia (quam Romanam Ecclesiam non dicimus, sed Romanam curiam) prorsus alia ab antiqua fide. Alia autem, & posterior fides, quid est, nisi error? Iam priusquam erroris huius originem aperiamus, videam[?], qd ad haec Cardinalis Bellarminus respondeat. Ex tanta nube testiū, paucissimos ꝑfert Bellarminus quibus sic respondet. Opera à patribus reiecta à iustificatione, vel esse opera externa, ita eludit testimonium Origenis: vel opera legis, sicut respondet Hilario: vel opera naturæ viribus facta sine fide, atq; ita eneruat Basilii: vel opa ceremonialia, atq; hac arte Ambrosii testimonium suspendit. Saepius illud velut unicum refugium inculcat; opera hæc esse naturæ viribus facta sine gratia. Ergo ad solam fidem toties à patribus repetitam, ad doctrinam de imputatione iustitiæ Christi, tanta fide à patribus conseruata, plane nihil habet q dicat. Vbi sunt ergo, qui solam fidem ante Lutherū inaudita clamitant? Hæc sunt effugia hominum ad lucem caligantium. De opere interno, & externo, q cōminiscitur, vt à patribus reiecta esse doceat opera externa, nō a. interna: nec omnino falsum est, nec causam hanc pontificiam omnino iuuat. Nam si concedamus, omnia opera interna nō esse reiecta à iustificando, qd ex eo colliget pontificii nā & fides ipsa, est op'internū. Ioh. 6. 28. Quid faciemus, vt operemur opera Dei? Respondet Iesus; hoc est opus Dei, vt credatis in illū, quē misit il-le. De operib' ceremonialib' q nugat, ex eadē[?] The final word of the column is partly illegible; the catchword below reads est officina Sophistica. Neque enim opus erat patribus ad populum Christianum loquentibus, tam enixe ceremonialia reiicere, unde periculum nullum metuebatur. Quod ipsum quoties monere voluerunt, non operum, sed ceremoniarum aut sacrificiorum[?] appellatione utuntur. Postremo diserta patrum verba euincunt, eos non de ceremonialibus, sed de moralibus scripsisse. Nam opera illa excludunt à iustificatione, quæ sequuntur iustificatum. Hæc autem non sunt ceremonialia, sed moralia. Quod addit de operibus legis, & de operibus sine fide, vel factis naturæ viribus sine gratia, ex eadem prodit vanitate.
units.tr: Hitherto we have heard one voice of the Church sounding through the different ages in the Scriptures, in the Fathers and in more recent writers, and preserved in the Church down to the Council of Trent. This is that true, visible Church, in which the true faith has always been handed down unchanged through successions. The Papist, or Jesuit, church which today assails this faith is newly born and presents a new faith. This Papist church (which we call not the Roman Church but the Roman court) is therefore utterly different from the ancient faith. But a different and later faith is nothing other than error. Before we uncover the origin of this error, let us see how Cardinal Bellarmine replies to these points. Out of so great a cloud of witnesses, Bellarmine brings forward very few, and to these he responds thus. Works which the Fathers rejected from justification are either external works, so he evades the testimony of Origen; or works of the law, as he answers Hilary; or works done by the powers of nature without faith, and so he weakens the testimony of Basil; or ceremonial works, and by this device he sets aside the testimony of Ambrose. He often hammers in that one refuge as if it were the only one: these works are done by the powers of nature without grace. So he has absolutely nothing to say against faith alone, so often repeated by the Fathers, nor against the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which the Fathers preserved with such faith. Where, then, are those who cry out that faith alone was unheard of before Luther? These are the evasions of men who grope in the dark. As for the distinction between internal and external works, which he devises so as to teach that the Fathers rejected external works and not internal ones: this is neither wholly false nor does it help the Papist cause at all. For if we grant that not all internal works are excluded from justifying, the Papists will infer from this that faith itself, being an internal work, [is part of justification]. John 6:28: "What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?" Jesus answers: "This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent." As for what he trifles about concerning ceremonial works, it comes from the same [...] and is a sophistical workshop. For the Fathers, speaking to the Christian people, had no need to reject ceremonial works so earnestly, since no danger from them was feared. When they wished to warn against this very thing, they used the name not of works but of ceremonies or sacrifices. Lastly, the explicit words of the Fathers prove that they wrote not about ceremonial but about moral works. For the works they exclude from justification are those which follow the justified man, and these are not ceremonial but moral. What he adds about works of the law, and about works without faith, or done by the powers of nature without grace, springs from the same vanity.

units.la: Ut igitur omnes istas offucias paucis retegamus: hoc esto nobis demonstrandū, opera ipsa legis facta per gratiam exclusa esse à iustificatione. Hoc si è scripturis, patribusq; confirmemus, os Pharisæis obturabitur. Quandoquidem fidei iustificationem ita diserte exponat Apostolus, ut opera legis excludat, interrogabimus beatum Apostolum, ut exponat ipse mentè suâ, & dicat, quænâ opera intelligat? Respondet Apostolus Ephes. 2. 9.10. quo loco, quum fide, ut solet, astruat, reiectis operibus; non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur: statim hæc verba subiungit: Nam ipsius opus sumus conditi in Christo Iesu ad opera bona, quæ præparauit Deus, ut in illis ambulemus. Quærimus quænâ sint opera illa, de quibus hic loquitur Apostolus? Ipso facto[?] opera, quæ Deus præparauit, ut in illis ambulemus. Apostolus igitur excludens opeus erat venti- unde ipsum m, sed latio. verba ed de exclu- ifica. a, sed & de us fira[?] à iustificatione, deinde optimus ipse sui interpres exponit, opera illa esse ad quæ à Deo conditi sumus, ut in illis ambulemus: profecto infallibiliter probat, opera per gratiâ facta reiici à iustificatione: opera a. esse ad quæ, non ex quibus, aut per quæ iustificamur: ac proinde non esse formam iustificationis, qua ut loquuntur sophistæ Tridentini, formaliter iustificamur, sed finem esse, ad quem, & effectum iustificationis.
units.tr: To expose all these tricks briefly, let this be what we must demonstrate: that the works of the law themselves, when done through grace, are excluded from justification. If we confirm this from Scripture and the Fathers, the mouths of the Pharisees will be stopped. Since the Apostle explains justification by faith so plainly that he excludes the works of the law, let us ask the blessed Apostle to explain his own mind and say what works he means. The Apostle answers in Ephesians 2:9-10. There, while as usual he asserts faith and sets works aside, "not of works, lest anyone should boast," he immediately adds these words: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that we should walk in them." We ask: what are those works of which the Apostle speaks here? Clearly they are the works which God prepared, that we should walk in them. The Apostle, therefore, excludes works from justification, and then his best interpreter, himself, explains that those works are the ones for which we were created by God, that we should walk in them. He thus infallibly proves that works done through grace are rejected from justification: they are works for which we are created, not works from which or through which we are justified. Consequently they are not the form of justification, by which, as the Tridentine sophists say, we are formally justified, but the end toward which justification is directed and its effect.

units.la: Apostolus etiam docet: Ex operibus legis non iustificabitur omnis caro coram illo, p legē n. agnitio peccati. Quū ostēdisset iustificationē ex lege non esse: exponit q̃ legē intelligat, nēpe morale: quia lex illa, q̃ deducit homines in agnitione peccatorū suorū, moralis est. Certū n. est, nulla al[?] á esse legē quæ, quū nó posset iustificare, homines ppter[?] infirmitate carnis nostrę, potest tamē ostédere nobis peccata nostra, & omnes homines conuincere peccati, reosq; coram Deo cōstituere, q̃ legē morale. Lex igitur moralis est, q̃ à iustificatione nostri excluditur. Idemq; demōstratur ex natura iustificationis, atq; imputationis. Quia peccatū nō imputatur credētib' in Christū. Hinc beatitudinē nostrā exponit Apostolus: Quēadmodū etiā Dauid definit beatitudinē hominis, cui Deus imputat iustitiam absq; operibus. Beati quorū remissæ sunt iniquitates, & quorū tecta sunt peccata, beatus vir cui nó imputauit Dominus peccatū. Peccatū tollitur imputatione, iustitia a. donatur imputatione. Hæc est virtus supra virtutem legis moralis, quæ nec peccátorum remissione, nec imputatione nouit. Ex hac iustitiæ imputatæ cognitione, tanq; ex regula, intelligimus multos scripturæ locos, qui de iustitia operû loquuntur. Domin' semel in beatitudinis seu iustificationis consortium recepit, ita ut peccata illis sua non imputet, iustitiam a. filii sui imputet:illi non modo sibi propitium habent Deum, sed & operibus suis, quorum maculæ & næui Christi puritate obteguntur, hinc est, qꝑ opera hominis iustificati iusta reputantur, & iustificatus iu-stus.
units.tr: The Apostle also teaches: "By the works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him, for through the law comes the knowledge of sin" (Rom. 3:20). Having shown that justification is not from the law, he explains which law he means, namely the moral law, for that law which leads men to a knowledge of their sins is moral. For it is certain that there is no other law which, although it cannot justify men because of the weakness of our flesh, can nevertheless show us our sins, convict all men of sin, and render them guilty before God, other than the moral law. The moral law, therefore, is what is excluded from our justification. The same is shown from the nature of justification and of imputation, because sin is not imputed to those who believe in Christ. Hence the Apostle describes our blessedness, just as David also defines the blessedness of the man to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not impute sin" (Ps. 32:1-2; Rom. 4:6-8). Sin is taken away by imputation, and righteousness is bestowed by imputation. This is a power above the power of the moral law, which knows neither the remission of sins nor imputation. By this knowledge of imputed righteousness, as by a rule, we understand many passages of Scripture which speak of the righteousness of works. When the Lord has once received someone into the fellowship of blessedness and justification, so that he does not impute his sins but imputes the righteousness of his Son, that man has God not only propitious to him, but also his works, whose spots and blemishes are covered by the purity of Christ. Hence it is that the works of the justified man are reckoned righteous, and the justified man is reckoned righteous.

units.la: Hæc igitur opera gratiæ, ad quæ faciendâ creati sumus in Christo Iesu, ex noua creatione, hoc est, ex iustificatione, sunt eadem opera legis. Lex iubet, sed vires non ministrat, gratia.
units.tr: These works of grace, then, for which we were created in Christ Jesus through the new creation, that is, through justification, are the same works as those of the law. The law commands, but does not supply strength; grace does.

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] gustinus mus à opera obiicia p fide, [?] lex. Re excuti explic opera lex pe ta anit obedi minas tia, q r remo sint o dat vt faciamus, quæ lex iubet. At lex persectam obedientiā postulat; obedientia nostra imperfecta est. Christus igitur interponit obedientiam suam perfectā; quæ quia nostra est, imperfectum illud nostrū in ratione nō venit coram Deo: quia propter Christū, nec imperfectio operū nostrorū, nec peccata nobis imputantur. Itaq; nos etiam legem implere dicimur, quum sincerum obedientiæ amorem præstamus. In hanc sententiā illud à patribus sæpius iactatur; q lex imperat, fides impetrat; Augusti. ergo : {a}per legem agnitio peccati, per fidem impetra-tio gratia contra peccatū, per gratiam sanatio anima à vitio peccati, per animæ sanitatem libertas ar-bitrii, per liberū arbitriū iustitia dilectio, per iustitiæ dilectio-
units.tr: Augustine, in the place where he objects to works through faith... the law. Hence the works of the law are excluded, and the law commands that we do what it orders. But the law demands perfect obedience, and our obedience is imperfect. Christ therefore interposes his perfect obedience. Because this obedience is ours, our imperfect obedience does not come into account before God, since for Christ's sake neither the imperfection of our works nor our sins are imputed to us. So we too are said to fulfil the law when we render a sincere love of obedience. To this effect the Fathers often repeat the saying: the law commands, faith obtains. Augustine says: through the law comes the knowledge of sin, through faith the obtaining of grace against sin, through grace the healing of the soul from the vice of sin, through the health of the soul the freedom of the will, through the free will righteousness, through the love of righteousness
