units.tr: ...the same justification... the obedience of God... the Apostle... works... the law... [remainder of the line illegible in the scan]

units.la: dilectionem legis operatio. Quibus verbis Augustinus à transgressione nostra, qua excidimus à lege, circumducit nos quasi in circulo ad opera gratiæ, quæ sunt opera legis. Quod si quis obiiciat, opera legis à scholasticis intelligi, non quæ p fide, & dilectione fiunt, sed q-p[?] minas extorquet lex. Respondeo, scholasticorum speculationes hic non excutio, q nec opera gratiæ nec opera legis recte explicarunt. Nam opera p minas extorta quomodo opera legis dici possint non video; quandoquidem lex perfecta obedientiam postulat ex toto corde, tota anima, & tota mente. Minatur quidem lex non obedientibus poenas, sed obedientia extorta per minas non est legis obedientia. Deinde patrum sententia, q nos exquirimus, ab huiusmodi arguties longe remota est. Patres n. ita opera intelligunt, ut eadem sint opera, & à lege imperata, & à gratia impetrata, eadeq; à iustificatione omnino exclusa. Lex ex iustitia requirit hæc opera, fides a. ea præstat ex obedientia. Iustificatus n. quum semel misericordiam Dei in se agnouerit, ingratissimum se, atq; miserrimum omnium hominum iudicat, nisi p tanta infinita misericordia in bonis operibus, obedientiæ, & gratitudinis testimoniis exhibeat. Charitas n. Christi urget nos, æstimates hoc quoniam si vnus ꝓ omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui fuerunt. Et ꝓ omnibus mortuus est Christus, ut qui viuunt, iam non sibi viuant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit, sicut docet Apostolus. Hæc est illa charitas, urges & constringes nos, qui iustificatos homines non patitur esse otiosos, sed ut semper bonis operibus studeant, mouet, imo commouet, coërcet, excitat. Itaq; fides illa Iesuitica execranda sæpe in Eccl. Christi habita est, qua docet: fidem veram posse reipsa à dilectione cæterisque virtutibus separari.
units.tr: dilectionem legis operatio. By these words Augustine leads us round, as in a circle, from our transgression, by which we fell away from the law, to the works of grace, which are the works of the law. If someone objects that the Schoolmen understand by "works of the law" not those done through faith and love, but those extorted by the threats of the law, I answer that I do not here examine the speculations of the Schoolmen, who explained neither the works of grace nor the works of the law correctly. For I do not see how works extorted by threats can be called works of the law, since the perfect law demands obedience from the whole heart, the whole soul and the whole mind. The law indeed threatens punishment to the disobedient, but obedience extorted by threats is not obedience to the law. Further, the opinion of the Fathers, which we are seeking, is far removed from such subtleties. For the Fathers understand works in such a way that the same works are both commanded by the law and obtained through grace, and are wholly excluded from justification. The law requires these works from justice; faith, however, performs them from obedience. For the justified man, once he has recognised God's mercy towards himself, judges himself the most ungrateful and wretched of all men unless, out of such infinite mercy, he shows forth good works as evidence of obedience and gratitude. For "the love of Christ constrains us, judging this, that if one died for all, then all have died; and Christ died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who died and rose again for them," as the Apostle teaches. This is that love which urges and constrains us: it does not allow justified men to be idle, but moves, indeed stirs, restrains and rouses them to strive always for good works. Therefore that accursed Jesuit faith, so often condemned in the Church of Christ, which teaches that true faith can really be separated from love and the other virtues, has been rightly rejected.

units.la: Nam si per fidem veram intelligant fidem iustificantem, certum est, non posse fidem & charitatem cõiunctā semel, separari. Sin fidei professionem intelligãt, dicimus, hanc fidem separari posse à charitate, atq; à iustificatione. Nec esse, q nos quærimus fidem iustificantē. Ioh.12.dicitur:multi ex principibus crediderunt in eum, sed non confitebantur, dilexerunt enim magis gloriam hominũ, quam gloriam Dei. {a}Ex quibus verbis concludit Bellarminus, atque ex similibus locis: fidem fuisse absque charitate.
units.tr: For if by true faith they mean justifying faith, it is certain that faith and charity, once joined, cannot be separated. But if they mean a profession of faith, we say that this faith can be separated from charity and from justification, and that this is not the justifying faith that we are seeking. In John 12 it is said: "Many of the rulers believed in him, but did not confess it, for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God." From these words Bellarmine concludes, and from similar passages, that there was faith without charity.

units.la: Respondeo: hic scripturæ locus, aliiq; similes: sunt de fidei externa professione, non a. de fide iustificante. Fides a. hæc iustificans Iesuitis est penitus ignota, qui externam fidei professionem, & sacramentorum communionem, quæ sensu ipso percipitur, sufficere sibi arbitrantur. Fides ergo non potest esse sola, si effectus, & fructus iustificationis consideretur, qua charitas Christi cogit nos: qa finis præcepti est charitas, de corde puro, & conscientia bona, & fide non ficta: quia conditi sumus in Christo Iesu ad bona opera: quia fides per charitatem operatur. Quibus verbis describit Apostolus fructū[?] fidei iustificatis, q non est ficta, q si fidei iustificatis natura consideretur in suis principiis fides sola iustificat sine charitate, & bonis operibus: quia fides præcedit charitate, & bona opera. Nā qa credimus, ideo operamur; nō a. ideo credimus qa operamur: quia charitas & opera icsequuntur iustificatum, non præcedunt iu-stificandum: quia gloriatio exclusa est.
units.tr: I answer: this passage of Scripture, and others like it, concern the external profession of faith, not justifying faith. But this justifying faith is wholly unknown to the Jesuits, who think that an external profession of faith and communion in the sacraments, which is perceived by the senses themselves, is sufficient for them. Faith therefore cannot be alone if the effect and fruit of justification is considered, which the love of Christ compels us to, because the end of the command is charity, "from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned"; because we are created in Christ Jesus for good works; because "faith works through love." In these words the Apostle describes the fruit of the faith of the justified, which is not feigned. But if the nature of justifying faith is considered in its principles, faith alone justifies without charity and good works, because faith precedes charity and good works. For we do not believe because we work, but we work because we believe; charity and works follow the justified man, they do not precede the man being justified, since boasting is excluded.

units.la: Opera igitur, quæ excluduntur à iustifica-tione, non sunt tantum opera naturæ viribus facta, quæ præcedunt iustificationem, verum opera per gratiam facta, opera quæ sequun-tur iustificatum. Augustino: opera omnia no-stra, quia nullum opus nostrum gloriationem excludit. Basilio: opera omnia præter vnam fidem, quia ipsa per se plena est bonis operi-bus. Chrysostomo: opera omnia apud Deum, non autem apud homines. Theophylacto: o-pera, quia opera imputationem iustitiæ non admittunt. Irenæo: opera quæ merito[?] ostentant, quia fides meritum nullum quærit. Cy-priano: opera quæ aliquid[?] Christi admittunt quidem, sed non solum. Arnobio: opera, quæ iustificationem nō sinunt esse gratia[?]. Ambro-sio: opera quibus qui se iustos esse putant, sit vt nolint se subiicere remissioni peccatorum. Hieronymo: opera, quæ in iustificatione im-pii nulla esse potuerunt, præter impietatis o-pera. Sedulio: opera, quæ impedirent, ne iu-stificati dicerentur vasa misericordiæ. Fulgen-tio: opera omnia nostra, quia ipsa iustitia no-stra, quæ est ex operibus, iniustitia est, & sor-det. Gregorio: opera, in quibus est iustitia factorum. Venerabili Bedæ: opera ipsa, quæ debemus post iustificationem operari. Glos-sa ordinariæ[?]: opera, quæ Christi gratiam non permittunt solam. Rabano: opera nostra omnia, quia opera nostra inimicas[?] præsumptiones non possunt expellere, & animam DEO humiliter subiicere, Anselmo: opera nostra, quia aliena iustitia iustificati sumus, non propria nostra Bernardo: opera, quæ non permittunt homines sperare in solo nomine Domini, & deponere pertinaciam, qua se operibus iustificatos arbitrantur, Ruperto: opera, quæ iustificatus debet deinceps per dilectionem operari Lumbardo: opera, quia in eis nulla est iustificationis spes, Aquinati.
units.tr: Therefore the works which are excluded from justification are not merely works done by the strength of nature, which precede justification, but also works done through grace, the works which follow the justified man. Augustine: "all our works, because no work of ours excludes boasting." Basil: "all works apart from faith alone, because faith in itself is full of good works." Chrysostom: "all works, before God, but not before men." Theophylact: "works, because works do not admit the imputation of righteousness." Irenaeus: "works which display merit, because faith seeks no merit." Cyprian: "works which admit something of Christ indeed, but not alone." Arnobius: "works, which do not allow justification to be grace." Ambrose: "works by which those who think themselves righteous are so disposed that they are unwilling to submit to the forgiveness of sins." Jerome: "works, which in the justification of the ungodly could be nothing but works of impiety." Sedulius: "works, which would prevent the justified from being called vessels of mercy." Fulgentius: "all our works, because our own righteousness, which is from works, is unrighteousness and filth." Gregory: "works, in which there is the righteousness of deeds." Venerable Bede: "the very works which we ought to perform after justification." The ordinary gloss: "works, which do not permit grace of Christ to stand alone." Rabanus: "all our works, because our works cannot expel hostile presumptions and humbly subject the soul to God." Anselm: "our works, because we are justified by another's righteousness, not our own." Bernard: "works, which do not permit men to hope in the name of the Lord alone, and to put aside the obstinacy by which they think themselves justified by works." Rupert: "works, which the justified ought henceforth to perform through love." Lombard: "works, because in them there is no hope of justification." Aquinas...

units.la: Quæ profecto omnia facile euincunt, patres cum Apostolo opera ipsa per gratiam facta reiecisse iustificando. Patres igitur solam fidem prædicant, quam etiam nonnunquam solam misericordiam appellant, & solam gratiam, & solum verbum, & solum DEI nomen, & solam Christi auxiliam, non quod fides sit aut misericordia, aut gratia, aut verbum, aut auxilium Christi: sed quod ex istis & per hæc sit fides. Atque istis omnibus opera excluduntur, vt stabiliatur suus[?] ille DEI tantum, qui Tridentino percutitur anathemate.
units.tr: All these things indeed easily prove that the Fathers, with the Apostle, rejected works done through grace themselves in justifying. The Fathers therefore preach faith alone, which they sometimes also call mercy alone, and grace alone, and the Word alone, and the name of God alone, and the help of Christ alone; not because faith is mercy, or grace, or the Word, or the help of Christ, but because faith comes from these and through them. And by all these works are excluded, so that that "God alone" which is struck with the anathema of Trent may be established.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: De erroris origine.
units.tr: On the origin of the error.

units.la: IAm de origine erroris huius dicamus. Solus fidei iustificationem ex Romana Ecclesia nemo disertis verbis negavit, antequam Martin. Lutherus eandem e scripturis docuifhom doct fuiff plur rum tur. re po verf ad L à Patine rore nat S ins nirh ecu ror infe iafi & s que ma arg exp fortia fid inf dec inf set. Itaque quum inepti atque impudentes homines ex ignorantia nobis obiicere soleant, doctrinam de sola fide iustificante nunquam fuisse ante Lutherum audiam[?] (sic enim complures Pontificii effutire[?] solent) quis non istorum vel ignorantiam, vel impudentiam miretur. Nos enim plane contrarium confirmare possumus, & omnibus antiquos scriptores veritatibus[?] conflat, hanc doctrinam usque ad Lutheri, & Tridentini Concilii tempora à Patribus, à recentioribus Theologis continenter praedicatam, contrarium autem errorem tum primum ex contradicendi studio natum.
units.tr: Now let us speak of the origin of this error. Before Martin Luther taught justification by faith alone from the Scriptures, no one in the Roman Church expressly denied it. [The rest of this paragraph is illegible in the scan.] So when foolish and shameless men, out of ignorance, object to us that the doctrine of justification by faith alone was never heard of before Luther (as many Papists are wont to babble), who would not marvel at either their ignorance or their shamelessness? For we can plainly prove the opposite, and it is evident from all the ancient writers that this doctrine was continuously preached by the Fathers and by more recent theologians right up to the times of Luther and the Council of Trent, while the contrary error arose only then, from a zeal for contradiction.

units.la: Sparsa sunt apud Scholasticos erroris huius semina, sed quae in zizaniorum[?] pernitiosam segetem[?] multo pestilentius in recentioribus seculis exercuerant. Occasio erroris erat à distinctione fidei in formatam[?], & informem, de qua ut[?] quaerere solent Scholastici theologi 3. sententiar.[?] distinctione 21. & 22. & Aquinas 2. 2. quaestione 4. artic. 3. quoloco quaerit Aquinas, an charitas sit forma fidei, & respondet affirmando. Quod si argutias Scholarum sectari placuerit, multo expeditius, probare possemus, fidem esse formam charitatis. Verum ex eo pronuntiari coepit in Scholis charitatem esse formam .fidei. Ex quo inferunt alii, formam fidem iustificare. Iesuitae tandem concludunt, fidem solam non iustificare, quia non fides informat, sed formata iustificat. Sed illi non videntur sensum Theologorum [?]suorum accipere, non enim sunt haec contradicentia Theologis, fides formata iustificat, & sola fides iustificat, quandoquidem sunt inter eos, qui utrumque tenent. Quod autem dicitur à Theologis, fidem illam iustificare quae formata est, si probe intelligatur, non reiicimus, & recte informem reiciunt illi, quanquam de fidei forma crassius loquuntur Scholae. Aquinas ipse, non tam male, quam confuso, & crasso more, id est, non suo more agit, verum formam intelligit Aquinas non internam illam, quae naturam constituit, sic enim ipse sese explicat. {a} Charitas, inquit, est forma fidei, in quantum per charitatem actus fidei perficitur.
units.tr: The seeds of this error were scattered among the Schoolmen, but in more recent centuries they grew into a far more pestilent crop of tares. The occasion of the error was the distinction between formed and unformed faith, about which the scholastic theologians are accustomed to ask in the Sentences, distinctions 21 and 22, and Aquinas in 2.2, question 4, article 3, where Aquinas asks whether charity is the form of faith and answers in the affirmative. If we wished to pursue the subtleties of the schools, we could prove much more easily that faith is the form of charity. But from this it began to be said in the schools that charity is the form of faith, and from this some infer that the formed faith justifies. The Jesuits finally conclude that faith alone does not justify, because it is not faith that informs, but the formed faith that justifies. Yet they do not seem to grasp the sense of their own theologians. For these statements do not contradict the theologians: "formed faith justifies" and "faith alone justifies" are not opposed, since there are those who hold both. As for what the theologians say, that it is the formed faith that justifies, we do not reject it if it is properly understood, and rightly do they reject the unformed; although the schools speak of the form of faith rather crudely. Aquinas himself, not so badly as in a confused and crude manner, that is, not in his usual way, understands by form not that inner form which constitutes the nature. For he explains himself thus: Charity, he says, is the form of faith, insofar as the act of faith is perfected through charity.

units.la: Deinde concedit Aquinas, proprie loquendo, charitatem non esse formam, sed finem fidei; verum contendit ille, in voluntariis finem esse pro forma statuendum, sic enim ait: {b} Actus voluntarii, species recipiunt à fine; qui est voluntatis obiectum. Id autem à quo aliquid speciem sortitur, se habet ad modum formae in rebus naturalibus, & ideo cuiuslibet actus voluntarii forma quodammodo est finis, ad quem ordinatur. Haec Thomas, valde quidem confuse, atque improprie. Nam Thomae ipsius concessione, finis in voluntariis habet rationem obiecti. Sed quis unquam dixit, charitatem esse fidei obiectum? hoc nec Iesuitae dixerint. quod si obiecti rationem non habet, certe nec finis rationem habere potest, si finis intelligatur habere rationem obiecti. Chari-
units.tr: Next, Aquinas concedes that, properly speaking, charity is not the form of faith but its end; yet he contends that in voluntary acts the end is to be reckoned as the form, for he says: "Acts of the will receive their species from the end, which is the object of the will. Now that from which a thing receives its species stands in the manner of a form in natural things; and therefore the form of any voluntary act is in a certain way the end to which it is ordered." Thus Thomas, very confusedly and improperly indeed. For by Thomas's own admission, the end in voluntary acts has the character of an object. But who ever said that charity is the object of faith? Not even the Jesuits would say so. And if charity does not have the character of an object, it certainly cannot have the character of an end, if the end is understood to have the character of an object. Chari-

units.la: Verissimum est, quod Augustinus habet contra Iulianum Pelagianum, qui virtutes infidelium inficiabat[?]: virtutes non officiis, sed finibus à vitiis discernendas esse. Finis autem ille, qui virtutem efformat, & secernit à vitiis, obiecti rationem habere potest, quae movet & excitat: hac ratione fides potest esse finis charitatis, quia fides movet & excitat charitatē, charitas autem non sic se habet ad fidem, non enim ideo credimus, quia bene operamur, sed ideo bene operamur, quia credimus. Fides ergo est quodammodo finis charitatis, ut & caeterarum aliarum virtutum, non enim sunt virtutes, quae non referuntur quodammodo ad fidem. Itaq; vera virtus est tantummodo in fidelibus, quamquam enim alii in officiis ipsis versentur, quia tamen ad verum finem non attingunt, non habent virtutes veras. Atque hoc est, quod Augustinus affirmat contra Iulianum, qui virtutes infidelium inficiabat[?], virtutem non officiis, sed finibus distingui à vitio. Itaque sententia Aquinatis de forma fidei non est sua, quia fides charitatem distinguit, efformat, regulat: charitas autem fidem non efformat, sed tantum ostendit, quamquam effectum finem suam causam[?].
units.tr: It is most true, as Augustine says against Julian the Pelagian, who denied the virtues of unbelievers, that virtues are to be distinguished from vices by their ends, not by their outward works. That end which shapes a virtue and separates it from vices can have the character of an object that moves and stirs the will. In this way faith can be the end of charity, because faith moves and stirs charity; but charity does not stand in the same relation to faith. For we do not believe because we act well, but we act well because we believe. Faith is therefore in a way the end of charity, and of the other virtues as well, for there are no virtues that are not somehow referred to faith. Hence true virtue is found only in believers. Although others engage in the very works of duty, because they do not reach the true end, they do not have true virtues. This is what Augustine affirms against Julian, who denied the virtues of unbelievers, namely that virtue is distinguished from vice not by works but by ends. Therefore the opinion of Aquinas about the form of faith is not his own, since faith distinguishes, shapes and regulates charity, whereas charity does not shape faith but only indicates it, although it is the effect and shows its end as its cause.

units.la: Deinde sententia Aquinatis nihil adiuuat Iesuitas. Illi enim colligunt, ab operum inhaerentia iustificari homines iustificari[?], quia charitas, ut supponunt illi, est forma fidei. At Thomas mas, qui charitatem docuit esse formam fidei, diserte tamen affirmat, in operibus nullam esse spem iustificationis, sed in sola fide. Solius igitur fidei iustificationem tradit Aquinas, quam isti [?]negant. Praeterea Aquinas charitatem formam fidei docet esse, quae fidem perficitur per charitatem: hoc est, sicut se exponit Aquinas, fides informis expectatur, & ostenditur per charitatem. Haec enim sunt Aquinatis verba: {e}Iacobus loquitur de operibus sequentibus fidem, [?]quae docetur iustificare, non secundum quod iustificare dicitur ipsum, sed secundum quod dicitur iustificatio manifestatio, vel ostensio, vel confirmatio: ea enim fieri dicitur, quando perficitur & ostenditur. Haec ille. Plurimum igitur a sententia Aquinatis dissentiunt [?]lectores. Nam quum sententiam nostram oppugnant lectores, quae profecto in hoc negotio eadem est omnino cum sententia Aquinatis: nonne in nostra sententia oppugnanda Aquinas manifesto oppugnat? Ex Aquinatis igitur sententia non bene intelligunt de forma fidei, falso, & inepte colligunt lectores contra mentem Aquinatis, fidem solam non iustificare.
units.tr: Further, Aquinas's opinion does nothing to help the Jesuits. For they infer that men are justified by the inherence of works, because charity, as they assume, is the form of faith. But Thomas, who taught that charity is the form of faith, nevertheless plainly affirms that in works there is no hope of justification, but only in faith alone. Aquinas therefore teaches the justification of faith alone, which these men deny. Moreover, Aquinas teaches that charity is the form of faith, which is perfected through charity. That is, as Aquinas himself explains, unformed faith is looked for and shown through charity. For these are Aquinas's words: James speaks of the works following faith, which are said to justify, not insofar as they themselves justify, but insofar as justification is called a manifestation, or showing, or confirmation; for that is said to be done when it is perfected and shown. So he. The lecturers therefore differ greatly from Aquinas's opinion. For when the lecturers attack our opinion, which in this matter is altogether the same as Aquinas's, does not Aquinas plainly attack it too? From Aquinas's opinion, then, they do not rightly understand the form of faith; they falsely and foolishly infer, against Aquinas's mind, that faith alone does not justify.

units.la: — Non erit inutile aut alienum, [illegible, ~10 letters] zizaniorum inter fruges exerescentium [illegible, ~12 letters], quam succincte fieri potest, aperire, & ostendere. Aquinas primus illud introduxisse videtur, fidei formam esse charitatem, cuius sententiae vestigia quaedam ex Lombardo hauserat, reliqua addidit. Non quidem pessime sentiens (si mentem eius commode accipiamus) neque praesentia quam ex

Aquinas seems to have been the first to introduce the view that charity is the form of faith. He had drawn some traces of this opinion from Lombard, and added the rest. He did not think very badly (if we take his meaning fairly), nor was he [illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~25 letters] ex eis re tragœdiæ erant deinceps excitandæ. Postea Iob. Scotus doctrinâ meriti ex congruo multum amplificauit. Quæ doctrina quamuis ad aliam quæstionem proprie pertineat, ita tamen cū hac quæstione arctè cohæret, vt meriti doctrina semel suscepta iustificationis doctrinā penitus oppressèrit: sic ergo est meriti doctrina primam introduxit. Aquinas fundamenta iecit meriti, tam de congruo, quam de condigno: sicut scribit: si [illegible, ~8 letters] opus ma- ritorum, secundum quod procedit ex libero arbitrio, [illegible, ~10 letters] sicut potest esse condignum, propter maximam in-[?] qualitatem, seu si ad congruum, propter quandam æqualitatem. Videtur enim congruum, vt homini opera-[?] tanti secundum suam virtutem, tunc recompensetur secundum conditionem gratiæ suæ. Iustitia autem inæqualitatis de operum meritorum, secundum quod procedit ex gratia spiritus S. sic ad mercedem vitæ æternæ condigna. Hæc Thomas. Scotus autem, quod attinet ad meritum de condigno, dissentit à Thoma; sed doctrinam meriti de congruo, vel ad infantem usque extulit.
units.tr: [illegible] from these the tragedies were to be stirred up afterwards. Afterwards John Duns Scotus greatly enlarged the doctrine of merit de congruo. Although this doctrine properly belongs to another question, it so closely coheres with the present question that once the doctrine of merit was received, it utterly crushed the doctrine of justification. Thus Aquinas first introduced the doctrine of merit: he laid the foundations of merit, both de congruo and de condigno, as he writes: if [illegible] the work of men, insofar as it proceeds from free will, [illegible] can be condign, on account of its great inequality; or if congruous, on account of a certain equality. For it seems fitting that when a man works [illegible], he be recompensed according to his own virtue and then according to the condition of his grace. But the justice of the inequality of meritorious works, insofar as they proceed from the grace of the Holy Spirit, is thus worthy of the reward of eternal life. So Thomas. Scotus, however, as far as merit de condigno is concerned, dissents from Thomas; but the doctrine of merit de congruo he extolled even to the point of infants.

units.la: Scoti placita de hac re sunt hæc: b Peccatum patet se naturaliter, nam communi influentia [?] Dei. & mox: Pa-[?] rat motum peccatum sic consideratum deserere, & ille motus potest reuirescere, & merendi gratia. Ex posteà: Ille motus dicitur attritio, & ad dispositio fuit meritum ex congruo ad remissionem peccati mortalis. Ex paulo post: Quod si attritio sit perfecta contritio in re-[?] motu, videtur omnino dispositio sufficiens [illegible, ~6 letters]. ad iusticiam[?] in termino illius attritionis acquirendam & deinceps: Si manet idem motus contra peccatum in esse naturae, & moris, qui primi fuit attritionis, in illo instanti fit contritio. Idemq; fere docet lib. 2. dist. 28. Quem sequuntur recentiores Scholastici plerique, traduntque actum illum, quo homo vltimum quod potest, facit, vt illi gratia communicetur, esse, secundum Scotum, ex puris naturalibus, & meritorium ex congruo.
units.tr: The opinions of Scotus on this matter are these: b Sin is naturally open to itself, for by the common [?] influence of God. And soon after: the motion of the mind may abandon sin when it is considered in this way, and that motion can revive, and so the grace of merit. Later: that motion is called attrition, and it was a merit of congruity, a disposition towards the forgiveness of mortal sin. A little later: if attrition is perfect contrition in the motion of the will, then it seems wholly sufficient [illegible, ~6 letters]. for acquiring justice at the end of that attrition, and thereafter: if the same motion against sin remains in the being and manner of nature, which was that of the first attrition, then at that instant contrition occurs. He teaches almost the same thing in Book 2, distinction 28. Most of the more recent Schoolmen follow him, and they hold that the act by which a man does what he can at the last, so that grace is imparted to him, is, according to Scotus, from purely natural powers, and is meritorious by congruity.

units.la: Hæc est sententia Concilii Tridentini, sicut ex superioribus canonibus constare potest, & ex Bellarmini verbis, huiusmodi Concilii mentem aperientibus:{a} potest homo nondum reconciliatus per opera poenitentiae imparari, & mereri ex congruo gratiam iustificationis. Hæc ille. Sequuntur ergo Tridentini Scoti placita, quamquam reclamantibus viris doctis, summis, quia hæc sententia plane nihil differt ab errore Pelagianorum, quod multi viri docti ex Rom. Ecclesia testantur, maxime vero Franciscus Victoria, cuius verba subiungam.{b} Homines alioquin acres & docti, hic in hac disputatione peccant, & errant, ex eo quod non bene sentiunt de contritione: primo, quod contritio est ita sufficiens ad remissionem peccatorum, vt quasi ex sufficienti dispositione remissio, & gratia posita contritione, videantur promereri, vt merito ponant congruam ad primam gratiam, contra Apostolum Paulum, non considerantes, quod quacunque dispositione posita in peccatore, est omnino retributio gratiae in collationem gratiae, & tam gratis remittuntur peccata, sicut data fuit gratia illa in primo flatu, sine magis, nec oportet imaginari aliud meritum, nisi per eam misericordiam diuinam. Nec plus contriti-tio est meritum ad gratiam, vel remissionem pec-catorum, quae bona opera sunt meritum ad prede-stinationem. Haec enim erat bona pars erroris Pelagia-norum, si ego quem mirillige. Haec Victoria di-serte, & libere disputare contra Scotistarum errores, in concilio Tridentino iam tandem receptum.
units.tr: This is the view of the Council of Trent, as can be gathered from its earlier canons and from the words of Bellarmine, who explains the mind of this Council: a man not yet reconciled may by the works of repentance prepare himself, and merit by congruity the grace of justification. So far he. Therefore the Tridentine doctrine follows the opinions of Scotus, although learned and eminent men object, because this view differs in no way from the error of the Pelagians; many learned men of the Roman Church bear witness to this, above all Francisco de Victoria, whose words I shall add.{b} Otherwise keen and learned men here in this disputation sin and err, because they do not think rightly about contrition. First, they hold that contrition is so sufficient for the remission of sins that, as if from a sufficient disposition, forgiveness and grace are seen to be earned once contrition is posited, so that they put it as a congruous merit towards the first grace, against the Apostle Paul, not considering that whatever disposition is posited in the sinner, it is entirely a repayment of grace for the bestowing of grace, and sins are forgiven as freely as that grace was given in the first breath, without any more, nor ought we to imagine any other merit, except through that divine mercy. Nor is contrition more a merit towards grace or the remission of sins than good works are a merit towards predestination. For this was the main part of the error of the Pelagians, whom I... illegible. Here Victoria clearly and freely disputes against the errors of the Scotists, and this doctrine has now at last been received at the Council of Trent.

units.la: Alterum est Scholasticorum commen-tum, quod priorem doctrinam de iustificatione è scripturis exceperat, atque è patribus tradita, mirabilem attulit confusionem. Nam Petrus Lumbardus quaerit, {a}gratia sit virtus [?] iam conclusionem in summam veritatis per-niciem. Theologi subsequentes arripuere. Il-taque sic habet Scotus: {b}Gratia formaliter est virtus, quae est charitas. Et paulo post: Illud, prop-ter quod Deus acceptat hominem, et signum beatitudinis dignitatem quae est in correspondentia meriti ad præmium, illud dicitur gratia, & ita aliquam im-perfectionem caritatis illud quod est gratia. Haec Scotus. Hoc est venenum Babylonicum quod Tridentinum propinavit Scotus.
units.tr: The other is the invention of the Schoolmen, which, after taking the earlier doctrine of justification from the Scriptures and handing it down from the Fathers, brought in a wonderful confusion. For Peter Lombard asks whether grace is a virtue [?], and brought the conclusion into the sum of the ruin of truth. Later theologians seized upon it. Scotus therefore states it thus: {a}Grace formally is a virtue, which is charity. And a little after: That on account of which God accepts a man, and the sign of blessedness, the worth which lies in the correspondence of merit to reward, that is called grace, and so something of the imperfection of charity is what is grace. So Scotus. This is the Babylonian poison which Scotus poured out for the Tridentine Council.

units.la: Libet hic antiqui serpentis versutiam con-templari. Pelagius in lucem primo prorupit, qui gratiam Dei negavit, liberum arbitrium ex-tollebat. Pelagius lamulento Ecclesiae iudicio damnatus est. Reuixit tamen Pelagius in Sco-tistis, qui ad Pelagianissimum illum, de merito congrui, aliam etiam fraudem excogitarunt, vt sub gratiae explicatione, ac definitione, gra-tia Dei penitus everterent. Hoc agunt Scoti-stae.
units.tr: It is worth here contemplating the cunning of the ancient serpent. Pelagius first burst forth into the light; he denied the grace of God and exalted free choice. Pelagius was condemned by the judgment of the Church. Yet Pelagius revived in the Scotists, who, to match that most Pelagian doctrine of merit of congruity, devised another fraud, so that under the explanation and definition of grace they might utterly overturn the grace of God. This is what the Scotists are doing.

units.la: {a} lib. 2. dist. 27.
units.tr: Book 2, distinction 27.

units.la: {b} lib. 2 dist. 27. quaest. 1. stæ, atq; exinde Tridentini. Nam quum nul-lam aliam gratiæ cognitionem tradant, quæ vt sit virtus nostra, & qualitas nobis inhærens, quid aliud egit serpens ille, qui hanc (eam exhibuit, quam vt gratiæ diuinæ cognitionem vniuersam extinguerer. Gratia præcisè non est qualitas nobis inhærens, sed est diuini fa-[?]ui Christo propositi [?] executio, hoc est, sicut Vic-toria è patribus scripturisq; habet, puta misericordia [?] diuina, vel favor ille Dei, cui condi-lium Tridentinum malè dixit. Nam quæ est iustificationis, eadem est vocationis nostræ, & prædestinationis gratia. Si quis autem gratiam vocationis aut prædestinationis dicat esse non favorem Dei tantum, sed formaliter virtutem nostram, quæ est Chamas, non ille de sacris literis, sed de mystico illo Babylonis poculo haurit.
units.tr: Book 2, distinction 27, question 1. The Scotists do this, and thence the Tridentines. For since they hand down no other knowledge of grace, one which is our virtue and a quality inhering in us, what else has that serpent done, who has presented this one, in order to extinguish the whole knowledge of divine grace? Grace is not strictly a quality inhering in us, but is the execution of the divine favour purposed in Christ, that is, as Victoria has from the Fathers and the Scriptures, namely the divine mercy, or that favour of God, which the Tridentine Council wrongly called... For the grace of justification is the same as the grace of our calling and of predestination. But if anyone says that the grace of calling or of predestination is not only the favour of God, but formally our virtue, which is charity, he draws this not from the holy letters but from that mystical cup of Babylon.

units.la: Necessarium videtur hoc loco admonere, de profunditoribus Satanæ in canone illo Concilii Tridentini, quem initio huius disputationis propositi, quo canone anathemata dicunt iis, qui homines iustificari docent, vel sola imputatione iustitiæ Christi, vel sola peccatorum remissione, exclusa gratia, & charitate quæ diffunditur in cordibus eorum per Spiritum sanctum qui illis inhæret: aut etiam gratiam qua iustificamur, esse tantum favorem Dei. Hactenus canon Tridentinus.
units.tr: It seems necessary here to warn about the deep things of Satan in that canon of the Council of Trent, which I set out at the beginning of this disputation, by which canon they pronounce anathema on those who teach that men are justified either by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ alone, or by the remission of sins alone, excluding grace and charity which is poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit who dwells in them; or who say that the grace by which we are justified is merely the favour of God. So far the Tridentine canon.

units.la: Quis non miretur insulsitatem decreti huius? ex uno discite omnia. Nam quomodo nō-[?]
units.tr: Who would not marvel at the foolishness of this decree? From one thing learn all. For how...

units.la: [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~45 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~40 letters] [illegible, ~35 letters] potest homo iustificari sola imputatione iu-stitiae Christi, vel sola peccatorum remissione, exclusa gratia? Num qui gratiam solam praedicat, & gratiam excludere possit? Nos qui iustificationem fieri imputatione iustitiae Christi docemus, cum Apostolo, cum Patribus, gratiam solam praedicamus. Hæc enim est gratia illa, quam verum semper agnouit Ecclesia Christi, ut credentibus in Christum peccata non imputentur, iustitia vero Christi imputetur. Concilium Tridentinum dixit, eos excludere gratiam, qui iustificationem affirmant esse in imputatione, hoc est, in sola gratia. Hoc quidem ante patres vertigine raptos impulit hanc nostram & demum eos [?] Sed profecto in hos scopulos abiicit necesse erat eos, qui gratiam Dei, non tantum tanquam, & misericordiam esse volunt, sed virtutem nostram.
units.tr: [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] can a man be justified by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ alone, or by the remission of sins alone, excluding grace? Or can he who preaches grace alone exclude grace? We who teach that justification takes place by the imputation of Christ's righteousness, with the Apostle, with the Fathers, preach grace alone. For this is that grace which the Church of Christ has always acknowledged as true, that sins are not imputed to those who believe in Christ, and that the righteousness of Christ is imputed. The Council of Trent said that those who affirm justification to lie in imputation exclude grace, that is, grace alone. Indeed, this drove our men, carried off by the giddiness of the Fathers, to... But surely those who wish the grace of God to be not merely favour and mercy, but our virtue, must necessarily be cast onto these rocks.

units.la: Itaq; in ista verborum confusione pergunt. Tridentini Patres, in eodem canone, & fumum abyssi eiaculantur. Gratia [illegible, ~8 letters] inquinant, & [illegible, ~10 letters] fundunt [?]. Quemadmodum gratiam negant esse fumum Dei nostrum [?], ita eodem fumo charitatem Dei oculis & conspectu sequentium absconduntur. Nam Apostolus affirmat charitatem Dei effusam esse in cordibus no-stris per Spiritum S. qui datus est nobis. Tridentini veteratores expunxerunt vocem illam (Dei) ut ex industria sensum Dei obscurent. Et quod Apostolus de charitate Dei dixit,
units.tr: So they persist in this confusion of words. The Tridentine Fathers, in the same canon, also belch out the smoke of the abyss. Grace [illegible] they defile, and [illegible] they pour out. Just as they deny that grace is the favour of our God, so by the same smoke they hide the charity of God from the eyes and sight of those who follow them. For the Apostle affirms that the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. The Tridentine sophists have struck out that word "of God," so that they may deliberately obscure the sense of God. And what the Apostle said of the charity of God,

units.la: [no footnote printed on this page] dixit, qua nos Deus prosequitur: id illi im-mani sacrilegio immutando, & omittendo, Apostoli verba ad charitatem nostram rapi-unt, sicut est virtus Theologica. Apostolus de charitate Dei disputat eo loco.
units.tr: [no footnote printed on this page] said, with which God pursues us: this they change and omit with monstrous sacrilege, and snatch the Apostle's words over to our charity, as if it were a theological virtue. The Apostle is disputing about the charity of God in that passage.

units.la: Postquam enim charitatem Dei in cor-dibus nostris effusam esse docuisset, charita-tem illam verbo proximè sequentibus sic explicat: Christus enim quum adhuc viribus essemus, sue tempore pro impiis mortuus est. Et ita-rum: Commendat suam ergo nobis charitatem Deus, in quod quum adhuc peccatores, Christus pro no-bis mortuus est. Num quis affirmabit, Apostolum hic agere de charitate nostra, qua nos di-ligimus Deum? affirmant Tridentini, & contra Apostolum insurgunt. Commendat suam erga nos charitatem Deus, inquit Apostolus. At isti dicunt se commendare suam erga Deum charitatem. Quod ergo Johannes docet. In hoc est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse Deus dilexit nos, & misit filium suum propitiationem pro peccatis nostris: id Tridentini patres, scilicet catholici, non verebuntur immutare hoc modo: imo in hoc est charitas, non quod Deus dilexerit nos, sed quod nos dilexerimus Deum. Quam absurditatem, & obganniendi [?] insulsitatem vitare non possent, qui gratiam Dei in virtutem nostram, & charitatem divinam, in charitatem nostram convertunt. Charitas autem illa Dei, de qua tam diserte loquuntur Paulus, & Johannes Apostoli; quid est nisi pura misericordia, & fauor ille Dei tantum, quem de Ecclesia sublatum, & anathemate extinctum esse voluit Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: For after he had taught that the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts, he explains that charity in the words immediately following: For Christ, when we were still weak, died in due time for the ungodly. And again: God therefore commends his charity towards us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Will anyone affirm that the Apostle here is speaking of our charity, by which we love God? The Tridentines affirm it, and rise up against the Apostle. God commends his charity towards us, says the Apostle. But these men say that they commend their charity towards God. What John therefore teaches: Herein is charity, not that we loved God, but that God himself loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins: this the Tridentine fathers, that is the Catholics, will not hesitate to change in this way: indeed, herein is charity, not that God loved us, but that we loved God. Those who turn the grace of God into our virtue, and the divine charity into our charity, could not avoid this absurdity and dull foolishness of snarling. But that charity of God, of which Paul and the Apostle John speak so plainly, what is it but pure mercy and that favour of God alone, which the Council of Trent wished to be taken from the Church and extinguished by anathema?

units.la: Aquinas igitur, & Scotus Ecclesiam ingrediuntur tanquam duo fulmina belli Pontificii, tremendi ac robusti duces cum vastatoribus exercitibus. Et quanquam magnam Thomas cum suis Thomistis cladem dederat, in multis tamen ab illo intacta atque mutilata, imo & ab eodem propugnata antiqua doctrina perstiterat, genuina patrum traditio in multis valuit. Quicquid vero à superioribus Thomistarum iniuriis intactum integrumque remansit: id omnie Scotus cum hominedo Locustarum, Scotistarum inquam agmine subsecutus expoliauit, atque in captiuitatem Babylonicam abduxit. Istorum enim fumo [illegible, ~9 letters], inquit Iohannes: ut Scoti nomen in ipso Locustarum exitu quodammodo prodigium esse videatur. Quoties vero à Thoma primores fontes sectante, dissident Scotistae, Tridentini patres [illegible, ~8 letters] ex industria relicto Aquinate, ut plurimum Scoti sequuntur placita, interdum etiam deteriora secuti, Scotorum ipsum improbitate & corruptela superant. Obseruandum est interim, opiniones istas siue Thomistarum, siue Scotistarum, fuisse tantum inter priuatas opiniones fraterculorum habitas, non autem inter Ecclesiae Romanae decreta. creta, antequam in Concilio Tridentino pro decretis sancirentur.
units.tr: Aquinas and Scotus therefore enter the Church like two thunderbolts of Papist war, fearsome and mighty commanders leading their devastating armies. Although Thomas, with his Thomists, had dealt a great blow, the ancient doctrine remained standing, untouched and unmaimed in many places, indeed defended by Thomas himself, and the genuine tradition of the Fathers prevailed in many matters. Yet whatever remained intact and whole after the earlier injuries of the Thomists, Scotus, followed by the locust-like host of his Scotists, has stripped bare and led off into Babylonian captivity. For John says that from their smoke came locusts, so that the name of Scotus seems in a sense to be a portent in the very going out of those locusts. Whenever the Scotists dissent from Thomas, who follows the earlier sources, the Fathers of Trent, having deliberately left Aquinas aside, mostly follow the opinions of Scotus, and sometimes even follow worse opinions, surpassing Scotus himself in wickedness and corruption. Meanwhile it must be observed that these opinions, whether of the Thomists or of the Scotists, were held only among the private opinions of the friars, and not among the decrees of the Roman Church, until they were sanctioned as decrees at the Council of Trent.

units.la: Reliquum est, ut dissensiones inter Theologos, & Iesuitas in hac re observemus. Ut facilius constare possit, quantum a patrum sententia Theologorum [?] dissenserit, quantum etiam a Theologis discrepent Iesuitae. Nam de fide formata, & informi, mirificae sese produnt inter Scholasticos & Iesuitas, vel contradictiones, vel absurditates. Fidem enim informem Theologi eam intelligunt, quae sine charitate. At Iesuitae pro fide catholica declamantes, nullam nobis aliam fidem relinquunt, quam informem. De informi fide Lombardus sic scribit: {a} Fides quam daemones & iusti [?] Christiani habent, qualis mera est, sed informis, quae sine charitate est. Haec ille. At Cardinalis Bellarminus novam, & admirabilem traditionem a Tridentino concilio inue-niam promulgat his verbis: {b} Fides impiorum & daemonum est vera, & nulla fides ex parte obiecti. Deinde probat etiam hanc fidem esse catholicam, & iustificantem. Quod autem huius nequitiae patronum adducit Augustinum, facit ut solet frustra, & falso. Quod igitur Scholasticis est fides informata, hoc Iesuitis est fides catholica. Iure quidem; nam se catholicos Iesuitae, Ecclesiam suam catholicam, fidem suam catholicam, nullo modo probare se posse confidunt, nisi quomodo ( horrenda [illegible, ~6 letters] in Ecclesiam Dei blasphemia) fidem dæ-monum, & improborum catholicam statu-ant. Hoc Bellarmino, cæterisque Iesuitis fa-miliare est, ut quum catholicam fidem de-scribant, aliam nobis nullam ostendant, quam informem illam dæmonum, & repro-borum.
units.tr: It remains for us to observe the disagreements between the theologians and the Jesuits on this matter, so that it may more easily be seen how far the Theologians have departed from the opinion of the Fathers, and how far the Jesuits differ even from the Theologians. For concerning formed and unformed faith, the Scholastics and the Jesuits display remarkable contradictions and absurdities. The Theologians understand unformed faith as that which is without charity. But the Jesuits, declaiming for the Catholic faith, leave us no other faith than the unformed. On unformed faith Lombard writes thus: The faith which devils and just [?] Christians have is mere, but unformed, which is without charity. So he. But Cardinal Bellarmine proclaims a new and wonderful tradition, found in the Council of Trent, in these words: The faith of the wicked and of devils is true, and there is no faith on the side of the object. Then he also proves that this faith is Catholic and justifying. As for his citing Augustine as the patron of this wickedness, he does, as usual, in vain and falsely. So what is formed faith to the Scholastics is Catholic faith to the Jesuits. Rightly so; for the Jesuits trust that they cannot prove themselves Catholic, their Church Catholic, or their faith Catholic, in any way other than by asserting the faith of devils and of the wicked to be Catholic, a horrible blasphemy against the Church of God. It is characteristic of Bellarmine and the other Jesuits that, when they describe the Catholic faith, they show us no other than that unformed faith of devils and reprobates.

units.la: Istorum de fide apud Pontificios inde orti sufficere videntur, ut quod nullam ad-hibeant distinctionem fidei. Hæc res ma-gnam, ut solet confusionem parit. Necessa-ria igitur videtur fidei distinctio. Fides autem in scripturis variè sumitur: vel est enim fi-des historica, quæ ista dicitur, quia fidem habere possumus rei, nihil interim commo-di aut utilitatis expectamus ex ea re, quam credimus. De hac fide Iacobus loquitur, ubi ait, dæmones credere, & contremisce-re: vel fides est professio fidei, adeoque i-pla religio. Sic dicitur obedientia fidei Romanorum primo, quo loco fides pro fidei pro-sessione, atque universa religione ponitur. Fides autem, sicut notat fidei professio-nem, potest esse vel vera, vel temporaria, qualis describitur Matth. decim. tertio, vi-gesimo primo, vel dubia, & subdola, qualis describitur Iohan. secundo 24. ubi Dominus credentibus in se non credit: & Iohannis duodecimo 44. ubi qui in eum credebant ho-minum gloriam anteposuerant gloriæ Dei. De fide miraculosa non est necesse ut di-cam. Hæc quæ breviter dicta sunt, ofte[?]nostendere possunt occasionem eorum erro- rum qui apud Pontificios invaluerunt. Nam nihil altius de fide sentiunt, quam ut fidem describant quae est vel historica, vel quae est fidei, & religionis externa professio. At praeter istas fidei acceptiones alia est etiam in Sacris scripturis, fides iustificans, quae certa fiducia recumbit in promissionem Dei, & remissionem peccatorum promissam sine haesitatione recipit. Ignorantia distinctionis huius ex manifestis scripturis exceptae, Pontificios in errorum Labyrinthos deducit, ita, ut tanquam caeci ambulent, & andabatarum more in tenebris dimicent. Sic enim de fide, de obiecto fidei, de gratia, de iustificatione disputant, ita confuse, & tenebricose, ut mirum non sit si veritas istos fugiat, qui lucem ex industria fugere videntur, & de illis rebus disputare audent, quas non intelligunt. Nam fidem, gratiam, iustificationem quomodo possunt, aut qui non habent intelligere, aut qui non intelligunt docere?
units.tr: From these things among the Papists concerning faith, it seems sufficient to explain how it arises that they make no distinction of faith. This matter, as usual, produces great confusion. A distinction of faith therefore seems necessary. Now faith is taken in various senses in the Scriptures: either it is historical faith, so called because we can have faith in a thing while expecting no advantage or benefit from the thing we believe. James speaks of this faith when he says that devils believe and tremble. Or faith is the profession of faith, and so is religion itself. Thus the obedience of faith is spoken of in Romans 1, where faith is put for the profession of faith and the whole religion. Faith, however, as it denotes the profession of faith, may be either true or temporary, as described in Matthew 13.21, or doubtful and deceitful, as described in John 2.24, where the Lord does not trust those who believed in him, and in John 12.44, where those who believed in him preferred the glory of men to the glory of God. I need not speak of miraculous faith. These things, briefly said, can show the occasion of those errors which have prevailed among the Papists. For they think of faith no more deeply than to describe it as either historical, or as the external profession of faith and religion. But besides these senses of faith, there is also in the Holy Scriptures another, justifying faith, which rests with firm trust on the promise of God, and receives without hesitation the forgiveness of sins that is promised. Ignorance of this distinction, drawn from plain Scripture, leads the Papists into the labyrinths of error, so that they walk like the blind and fight in darkness like gladiators. For they dispute about faith, the object of faith, grace and justification in such a confused and murky way that it is no wonder that truth flees from those who seem deliberately to flee the light, and dare to discuss those things which they do not understand. For how can those who do not have understanding, or those who do not understand, teach faith, grace and justification?

units.la: Quum igitur dicat Bellarminus, improborum, & daemonum fidem, veram, rectam, catholicam esse ex parte obiecti: non est silentio praetereundum, quod de obiecto fidei iustificantis tradit. {a} Obiectum fidei iustificans, inquit, non est speciale misericordia, sed omnia quae revelantur Dei in scriptura. Haec ille. Si de fide loqueretur, sicut est professio fidei, recte dixisse videretur, sed distinctiones[?].
units.tr: Since Bellarmine says that the faith of the wicked and of devils is true, right and Catholic on the side of the object, it must not be passed over in silence what he teaches about the object of justifying faith. The object of justifying faith, he says, is not a special mercy, but all things that are revealed by God in Scripture. So he. If he were speaking of faith as the profession of faith, he might seem to have spoken rightly, but [distinctions?]

units.la: ologi de fid sunt quod quisque credat firmiter termin dine, cessit Quic net[?], quæ lucem rebus afferre possunt, ex-horrent Iesuitæ. Bellarminus hæc de fide Iustificante intelligi vult. Sic enim idem repetit: {a}Obiectum fidei iustificantis, quod hæretici restringunt ad solam promissionem misericordiæ specialis, catholici tam late patere volunt, quam late patet verbum Dei. Quam potius certam promissionem misericordiæ specialis, non tam ad fidem, quam ad præsumptionem pertinere contendunt. Hæc ille. Loquitur semper de fide iustificante. Superius ex Lumbardo ostendimus, fidem quam Bellarminus iustificantem vocat, eandemque & dæmonum fidem esse affirmat esse fidem informem. Ita fides informis Bellarmino iustificans est. Iam vero ostendemus à Scoto, hanc fidem quam Iesuitæ iustificantem vocant, nihil esse aliud quam fidem ex puris naturalibus acquisitam.
units.tr: [Garbled in the scan; rendered as far as the sense allows:] Theologians hold that faith is that by which each person firmly believes... The Jesuits shrink from those things which can bring light to the matter. Bellarmine wants these things to be understood of justifying faith. For he repeats the same thing: The object of justifying faith, which heretics restrict to the promise of special mercy alone, Catholics wish to extend as widely as the Word of God extends. Rather, they contend that the certain promise of special mercy belongs not so much to faith as to presumption. So he. He always speaks of justifying faith. Above, from Lombard, we have shown that the faith which Bellarmine calls justifying, and which he affirms to be also the faith of devils, is unformed faith. Thus unformed faith is justifying for Bellarmine. Now we shall show from Scotus that this faith, which the Jesuits call justifying, is nothing other than faith acquired from purely natural powers.

units.la: Quum de obiecto fidei disputant Theologi, distinctionem illam tractare solent, de fide acquisita, & infusa. De quare hæc sunt Iohannis Scoti placita. {b}Certum est quod in nobis est fides revelatorum[?] credibilium[?] ac-quisita. Plura ex eodem adiiciam. {c}Præter credulitatem articulorum revelatorum, ut hanc firmiter credat omnibus articulis revelatis, & determinetur ad alteram partem sua opposita formidine, non operatur propter fidem infusam; hæc necessitas enim potest ex hac nasci. Hæc Scotus. Quicquid ergo de fide iustificante docet Bellarminus, illud Scotus fatetur verum ef-se, de fide acquisita. Quia fides acquisita ap-prehendit credibile reuelatum in scriptura. Sed plura (si placet) proferre Scotus, vt fi-des hæc Tridentina certius teneatur.
units.tr: When the Theologians dispute about the object of faith, they are accustomed to treat the distinction between acquired and infused faith. Concerning this, these are the opinions of John Scotus: It is certain that in us there is acquired faith of the revealed [?] credible [?] things. I shall add more from the same author: Apart from the believing of the revealed articles, so that a person firmly believes all the revealed articles and is determined to one side against the opposite fear, he does not act by infused faith; for this necessity can arise from that. So Scotus. Whatever Bellarmine teaches about justifying faith, therefore, Scotus admits to be true of acquired faith. For acquired faith apprehends the credible thing revealed in Scripture. But let Scotus, if you please, set forth more, so that this Tridentine faith may be held more surely.

units.la: {a}Fide, inquit, acquisita ex parte motus[?], aliter potest homo assentiri omnibus reuelatis a Deo. Et mox: Hæc igitur tenendum est tanquam certum, quod reuelatorum in scriptura est, sola acquisita fides, generata ex auditu & ex affectu nostro[?], quæ ex formata adhæret[?]. Hæc ille.
units.tr: By acquired faith, he says, on the side of motion, a man can assent to all things revealed by God in a different way. And soon after: Therefore this must be held as certain, that for the things revealed in Scripture there is only acquired faith, generated from hearing and from our affection, which adheres to the formed faith. So he.

units.la: Denique differentiam fidei acquisitæ, & infusæ ostendit non esse ex parte habituum, sed ex parte obiectorum (sic recte Scoti sententiam retulit Vellosillus[?] in aduersariis suis. Sic enim obseruauit ille.
units.tr: Finally, he shows that the difference between acquired and infused faith lies not on the side of the habits but on the side of the objects (Vellosillus rightly reported Scotus's opinion in this way in his adversaries; for he observed thus). Although Scotus does not have this in the passage that he noted, [if there is no difference on the side of the objects between justifying and acquired faith, as Scotus contends, and Bellarmine from Scotus, it will certainly follow that justifying faith is acquired, not infused...]

units.la: Quanquam hoc non habeat Scotus in eo quem is annotauit loco) quod si ex parte obiectorum nulla sit differentia inter fidem iustificantem, & acquisitam (sicut contendit Scotus, & e Scoto Bellarminus) sequetur profecto fidem iustificantem esse acquisitam, non infusam.
units.tr: Although Scotus does not hold this in the passage he annotates, yet if there is no difference in respect of objects between justifying faith and acquired faith (as Scotus contends, and Bellarmine after Scotus), it will surely follow that justifying faith is acquired, not infused.

units.la: Quanquam igitur cum primariis Theologis non consentiant recentiores, optime tamen leniter cum Scotistis conuenit. Magister fidem formatam requiri docet, quia informis, quæ est sine charitate, est dæmonum, & improborum. At Bellarminus hanc informem fidem sine charitate, quæ est dæmonum, & improborum, docet esse catholicam, & iustificantem. Formata fides ergo non
units.tr: Although the more recent writers do not agree with the chief theologians, they nonetheless agree quite well with the Scotists. The Master teaches that formed faith is required, because unformed faith, which is without charity, belongs to demons and the wicked. But Bellarmine teaches that this unformed faith without charity, which belongs to demons and the wicked, is Catholic and justifying. Formed faith, therefore,
