units.la: non requiritur, quandoquidem apud Sco-tistas & Iesuitas, nullus est fidei formatæ v-sus. Magister charitatem requiri docet in fi-de formata ; qua homo diligat Deum super omnia, & proximum sicut seipsum. Ad hoc veteres Theologi idem infusam necessari-am esse docuerunt. At Iohannes Duns no-ster diserte affirmat : a posse hominem ex viribus naturalibus diligere Deum super omnia, & proximum sicut seipsum. Haec Scotus. Vel ergo Charitas est ex viribus naturalibus, vel non est necessaria, quandoquidem id agere possunt Scotistæ ex viribus naturalibus, quod charitas ipsa [?]. Maxima pars Scholasticorum recentium hanc sententiam sequitur, & in Pelagianorum cathedram transit [?]. Hæc placita Scotistæ sua, & Iesuitæ, qui nunc a Romano Pontifice ad aciem profligatam, ac plane deplorata restituendam Scotistis successoribus nolitce summittuntur [?]. Scotus enim fidei acquisitæ obiectum contendit esse credibile revelatum in scripturis, hoc est, quaecunque Deus revelavit in scripturis, ut loquitur Bellarminus. Hoc autem affirmat idem Bellarminus esse obiectum fidei iustificantis. Fides ergo iustificans, ac acquisita non differunt ex parte obiecti. Atque hæc est fides horribilis Bellarmini, eadem iustificans, catholica, recta; eadem-que informis improborum, eademque dæmoniorum.
units.tr: is not required, since among the Scotists and the Jesuits there is no use of formed faith. The Master teaches that charity is required in formed faith, by which a man loves God above all things and his neighbour as himself. To this the older theologians likewise taught that infused charity is necessary. But our John Duns plainly affirms that a man can, from natural powers, love God above all things and his neighbour as himself. So Scotus. Either, then, charity comes from natural powers, or it is not necessary, since the Scotists can do from natural powers whatever charity itself does. The greater part of the recent Scholastics follows this opinion and passes into the chair of the Pelagians. These are the opinions of the Scotists and of the Jesuits, who are now being put forward by the Roman Pontiff to restore to the Scotist successors a battle line that has been routed and utterly despaired of. For Scotus contends that the object of acquired faith is the credible revealed in the Scriptures, that is, whatever God has revealed in the Scriptures, as Bellarmine puts it. Bellarmine himself affirms that this is the object of justifying faith. Justifying faith and acquired faith therefore do not differ in respect of object. And this is Bellarmine's horrible faith: the same faith justifying, Catholic, and right; the same faith unformed and belonging to the wicked, and the same belonging to demons.

units.la: Cum famosas istas speculationes de obiecto fidei ex puteo abyssi in Ecclesiam intulerint Scotistæ, à Scotistis exceperunt Iesuitæ: necessarium videtur de obiecto fidei iustificantis succincte dicere, ut inter varias hominum commenta aliquid certum è verbo Dei teneamus. Qui obiectum fidei iustificantis ponunt omnia in scripturis revelata, in eo errant quod non distinguunt inter externam fidei professionem, & fidem iustificantem. Scotus, cum de obiecto fidei agit, fidem intelligit, ut continet fidei professionem. Hæc à Iesuitis ad fidem iustificantem rapiuntur. Nos, missis contentionibus, aliisque fidei acceptionibus, de obiecto fidei iustificantis hoc loco quæremus.
units.tr: Since the Scotists introduced those famous speculations about the object of faith out of the pit of the abyss into the Church, and the Jesuits have received them from the Scotists, it seems necessary to say briefly what the object of justifying faith is, so that amid the various inventions of men we may hold to something certain from the Word of God. Those who place the object of justifying faith in all things revealed in Scripture err in that they do not distinguish between the outward profession of faith and justifying faith. When Scotus treats of the object of faith, he understands faith as it includes the profession of faith. This is what the Jesuits snatch up and apply to justifying faith. We, setting aside these disputes and the other senses of "faith", will here inquire into the object of justifying faith.

units.la: De obiecto fidei iustificantis agit Apo-stolus 4. c. ad Rom. Propterea, inquit, ex fide est, ut sit per gratiam, quo firma sit promissio universæ semini. Quatuor inter se divino vinculo concatenata aperit Apostolus hoc loco: gratiam, fidem, promissionem, & promissionis firmitudinem, vel certitudinem salutis. Propterea ex fide, ut sit per gratiam. Ergo fides est per gratiam excitatur à gratia. In quem finem excitatur fides à gratia? ut firma sit promissio. Fides ergo à gratia excitatur, ut in promissionem firmiter recumbat. Promissio igitur est obiectum fidei iustificantis proprium. Quia fides à gratia excitatur, ut apprehendat obiectum suum, apprehendit ante promissionem? Quan-tum ram I quant I. go fid inde Bella fram per g firm ti & unt clam nem grat igitu ex n tur. his quan de. ma gicu cor hoc inde cian cess his. rit ræ. firm ram lucem afferunt pauca Apostoli verba? quantam confusionem Scotistis & Iesuitis?
units.tr: The Apostle treats of the object of justifying faith in Romans chapter 4. "Therefore," he says, "it is of faith, that it might be by grace, so that the promise might be firm to all the seed." In this place the Apostle sets out four things joined together by a divine bond: grace, faith, the promise, and the firmness, or certainty, of salvation through the promise. "Therefore of faith, that it might be by grace." Faith, therefore, is by grace; it is stirred up by grace. To what end is faith stirred up by grace? That the promise may be firm. Faith is therefore stirred up by grace so that it may rest firmly upon the promise. The promise, then, is the proper object of justifying faith. Because faith is stirred up by grace in order to lay hold of its object, [does it] lay hold of the promise beforehand? How much light do these few words of the Apostle bring! How great a confusion for the Scotists and the Jesuits!

units.la: 1. Propterea ex fide, ut sit per gratiam. Ergo fidei est per gratiam, & ex gratia, ac proinde falsum est, atque impium quod docuit Bellarminus. {a}Fidem & conversionem nostram esse in potestate liberi arbitrii. 2. Est per gratiam, ut firma sit promissio: ergo est firma promissionis certitudo omni credenti, & falsum est atque impium, quod garriunt Iesuitae. {b}Firmam promissionem hanc fidu-ciam[?] non ad fidem, sed ad praesumptionem pertinere. 3. Propterea ex fide ut sit per gratiam, quae firma sit promissio. Firmitudo igitur promissionis, ex fide nostra, non ex meritis nostris, sed ex sola fide nascitur. Contra Bellarmini errorem quem his verbis ponit: {c}Fiducia sanctorum quam de Deo concipiunt, non ex sola fide, sed ex bonis meritis nascitur. 4. Ut firma sit promissio universo semini, Firmitudo igitur promissionis, & fiducia certa misericordiae est gratia concessa omni semini, hoc est, omnibus vere credentibus: ergo falsum est atque impium, hanc fiduciam non omnibus vere credentibus concessam esse, sed tantum Prophetis, Apostolis, & paucis aliis per extraordinariam Spiritus S. revelationem. Quod docent Iesuitae. 5. Propterea ex fide, ut sit per gratiam, ut firma sit promissio: Fides igitur per gratiam, recumbit in promissionem, & proinde pro-missio est proprium obiectum fidei iustifi-cantis.
units.tr: (1) "Therefore of faith, that it might be by grace." Therefore faith is by grace and from grace, and so what Bellarmine taught is false and impious: that {a} our faith and conversion are in the power of free choice. (2) "It is by grace, that the promise may be firm." Therefore the certainty of the firm promise belongs to every believer, and what the Jesuits babble is false and impious: that {b} this firm confidence in the promise belongs not to faith but to presumption. (3) "Therefore of faith, that it might be by grace, that the promise might be firm." The firmness of the promise is born of our faith, not of our merits, but from faith alone. This stands against Bellarmine's error, which he states in these words: {c} the confidence the saints conceive concerning God arises not from faith alone but from good merits. (4) "That the promise might be firm to all the seed." Firmness of the promise and the certain confidence in mercy is the grace given to all the seed, that is, to all who truly believe. Therefore it is false and impious to say that this confidence is granted not to all who truly believe, but only to the Prophets, the Apostles, and a few others through an extraordinary revelation of the Holy Spirit, which is what the Jesuits teach. (5) "Therefore of faith, that it might be by grace, that the promise might be firm." Faith, therefore, by grace rests upon the promise, and so the promise is the proper object of justifying faith.

units.la: Idem constat ex fidei definitione. Fides, inquit Apostolus, est sperandarum substantia rerum, & argumentum non apparentium[?]. Quae enim in promissione gratiae continentur, sperantur, & non apparent. Quum ergo fidem definiat Apostolus per ea, quae sperantur, & non apparent, quia haec misericordiae promissionem declarant, idem prorsus est, ac si diceret, fidem esse substantiam, & argumentum promissionis Dei. Quia fides iustificans recumbit in promissionem, hoc est in ea quae sperantur, & non apparent, tanquam in verum & proprium obiectum.
units.tr: The same is clear from the definition of faith. "Faith," says the Apostle, is the substance of things hoped for, and the evidence of things not seen. For the things contained in the promise of grace are hoped for and are not seen. Since the Apostle defines faith by those things which are hoped for and not seen, because these declare the promise of mercy, it is altogether the same as if he said that faith is the substance and the evidence of God's promise. Justifying faith rests upon the promise, that is, upon those things which are hoped for and not seen, as upon its true and proper object.

units.la: [?]Deinde Apostolus sic docet: adversus promissionem Dei non disceptauit infidelitate, [illegible, ~6 letters] fide, dans gloriam Deo. Quibus verbis docet Apostolus, quid intersit inter fidem & infidelitatem. Fidem enim fiduciam promissionis describit. Qui ergo fiduciam promissionis à fide iustificante excludunt, (quod faciunt Lutherani, maxime vero Cardinalis Bellarminus) quid reliquum faciunt, nisi illud, quod Apostolus hoc loco vocat ἀπιστίαν[?], haec autem de promissione, seu infidelitatem. Apostolus etiam eodem loco ait: Abraham roboratus est fide, dans gloriam Deo, certo persuasus, quod ubi quid promisit, possit etiam praestare. Ideo impu-
units.tr: Next the Apostle teaches thus: "He did not waver in unbelief at the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God." By these words the Apostle teaches what the difference is between faith and unbelief. For he describes faith as trust in the promise. Those, therefore, who exclude trust in the promise from justifying faith (as the Lutherans do, and especially Cardinal Bellarmine) what do they leave, except that which the Apostle here calls unbelief [ἀπιστίαν], and this concerns the promise? The Apostle also says in the same place: "Abraham was strengthened by faith, giving glory to God, being fully persuaded that what he had promised, he was also able to perform." Therefore impu-

units.la: Imputatum est illi in iustitiam. Non au-rem scriptum est, propter ipsum tantum, im-putarum fuisse illi, sed etiam propter nos, qui-bus imputabitur: quo loco Apostolus agit de fide quae iustificatus est Abraham. Unde iste Thesis certo firmantur. Prima: Fides iustifi-cans est fides imputata in iustitiam. Secunda: Fi-des insufficiens est fides, quae fidelis certo persuasa est de promissione Dei. Tertia: Fides [?] Abraham, et eadem est, quoad benedictionem et remissionem imputationis. Haec omnia in disseris Apostoli verbis inhae-rent.
units.tr: "It was imputed to him for righteousness." Yet it was not written that it was imputed to him for his sake alone, but also for ours, to whom it will be imputed. In this passage the Apostle treats of the faith by which Abraham was justified. From this these theses are firmly established. First: Justifying faith is faith imputed for righteousness. Second: Faith is sufficient if the believer is certainly persuaded of God's promise. Third: Faith [illegible] of Abraham, and it is the same as regards the blessing and the remission of imputation. All these things inhere in the words of the Apostle's argument.

units.la: Sic ergo contra Iesuitarum [illegible, ~8 letters] confirmat nos Apostolus. Fides est, qua promissio firma est, et hanc promissionis est fides promissionis. Firmitudo haec promissionis est [?] fiducia haec est sine haesitantia. Apostolus haesitantiam ex cludicine adversum promissionem Dei discepsimus infidelitate, ut roboratus fide, dantes gloriam Deo. Remota ergo hac schola Iesuitarum tentationes, qui pugnant pro haesitantia, docentes omnes homines in fide debere promissionem non esse ac-ceptam fiducia excipiendam, fiduciam promissionis esse praesumptionem. Ita tamen haesitantiam igitur, et [illegible, ~6 letters] inducunt, fidem penitus tollunt. Tamen si quis fidem definiens fiduciam finitem, et haesitantiam, sicut sensus, nam fanus videbitur? At hoc docent Iesuitae. Eo mo Ecclesiam Christi immidis clamoribus exagitant, ut hanc fidem inferre possint. Apostolus Christi insanos illorum clamores compescat. Sic enim proponit Apostolus: Fides quæ in promissione Dei hæsitat, est ἀπιστία[?]: hoc est manifestis Apostoli verbis certo constat. At assumunt Iesuitæ, fides catholica hæsitat in promissione Dei. Non enim est fides, inquiunt, sed præsumptio, si quis apprehendat certam, & firmam prædemissionem[?] misericordiæ. Concludimus nos fidem, quam isti vocant catholicam, esse omnino dubiam[?]. Eodemque modo probamus fidem istorum non dare gloriam Deo: quia quæ hæsitat in promissione non dat gloriam Deo, ex eodem Apostolo. Atque hæc est fides Iesuitarum catholica, scilicet, & quæ[?] Deo gloriam dare non potest. Nunquam salutem illis spondere possit, qui fidem catholicam ita mutarunt, ut eius loco horrendam confusionem de an-imæ[?] intulerint? Non dubito quin inter Pontifices plurimi sint, qui ab hac Tridentinæ fidei traditione penitus abhorreant. Illud tamen non dubitanter affirmaverim, neminem ex verbo Dei salutem istorum probare posse, qui hanc sequuntur traditionem: sicut faciunt Iesuitæ omnes.
units.tr: So the Apostle confirms us against the Jesuits' [illegible] in this way. Faith is that by which a promise is made firm, and this is the faith of the promise. This firmness of the promise is a trust that is without hesitation. The Apostle, in James 1, condemns hesitation against the promise of God as unbelief, so that being strengthened in faith they give glory to God. Let this school of the Jesuits, then, be set aside: those who fight for hesitation, teaching that all men ought in faith not to receive a promise with trust, and that trust in the promise is presumption. In this way they bring in hesitation and [illegible], and utterly abolish faith. Yet if anyone defines faith as a limited trust, and hesitation as a sense, will he not seem mad? But this is what the Jesuits teach. In this way they harass the Church of Christ with shouting, so that they may bring in this faith. Let the Apostle restrain their mad clamours against Christ. For the Apostle thus sets it forth: faith that wavers in the promise of God is [unbelief, ἀπιστία]. This is certain from the Apostle's own words. But the Jesuits assume that Catholic faith wavers in the promise of God. For they say it is not faith, but presumption, if anyone lays hold of the certain and firm promise of mercy. We conclude that the faith which they call Catholic is altogether doubtful. And in the same way we prove that their faith does not give glory to God, because whatever wavers in the promise does not give glory to God, according to the same Apostle. And this is the Catholic faith of the Jesuits, which cannot give glory to God. Can it ever promise salvation to those who have so changed the Catholic faith that in its place they have introduced a dreadful confusion of the soul? I do not doubt that among the Pontiffs there are very many who utterly abhor this tradition of the Tridentine faith. Yet this I would affirm without hesitation: no one can prove from the Word of God the salvation of those who follow this tradition, as all the Jesuits do.

units.la: Hæc est fides illa, quam contra scripturas, contra antiquos patres, imo contra Ecclesiam Romanam à Scotistis hodie[?] Concilium Tridentinum. Nam ante tempora huius Concilii vixit, viguitque etiam in Romana Ecclesia fides catholica. Videntur[?] illi quam spem salutis habere possint, qui abuti-[?]
units.tr: This is that faith which the Council of Trent has today set up against the Scriptures, against the ancient Fathers, and indeed against the Roman Church itself, as the Scotists do. For before the time of this Council the Catholic faith lived and flourished even in the Roman Church. How can those have any hope of salvation who abuse [...]

units.la: antiq Nos c ma fi [pirit hem instic quem nom non dede cred bus nam qui prom in pr ad p hanc tur, nere mine virtu Con man impi bant func horr mini cart tiis antiquam fidem Catholicam immutarunt. Nos quum promissioni DEI adhæremus firma fide, DEVM habemus authorem, cuius spiritu credentes ducuntur: Apostolum habemus Doctorem, cuius doctrina Ecclesia instituitur: Abrahamum habemus patrem, quem sequimur, cuius fides ab Apostolo eo nomine laudatur, quod in promissione DEI non hæsitaverit [illegible, ~6 letters] sed roboratus fide dederit gloriam DEO.
units.tr: [...] they have changed the ancient Catholic faith. But we, since we cleave to the promise of God with a firm faith, have God as our author, by whose Spirit believers are led. We have the Apostle as our teacher, by whose doctrine the Church is instructed. We have Abraham as our father, whom we follow, and whose faith the Apostle praises on this account, that he did not waver in the promise of God, but being strengthened in faith gave glory to God.

units.la: Exemplum patrum credentium ab Apostolo credentibus omnibus propositur. Dicant ergo Iesuitæ, quem patrem, quem authorem sequantur ipsi, qui [illegible, ~8 letters] hæsitantiam, & infidelitatem in promissione [?] inculcant? & firmam in promissione fiduciam, non ad fidem, sed ad præsumptionem pertinere docent. In hanc cæcitatem iusto DEI iudicio abripiuntur, qui veritatem cum flagitiosa vita se retinere posse sperant.
units.tr: The Apostle sets the example of the believing Fathers before all believers. Let the Jesuits therefore say whom they themselves follow as father and author, they who inculcate hesitation and unbelief in the promise, and teach that firm trust in the promise belongs not to faith but to presumption. Those who hope they can keep the truth together with a disgraceful life are carried off into this blindness by the just judgment of God.

units.la: Contendunt Iesuitæ, homines impuros, in quibus nulla est interna virtus, esse veræ sanctæ Ecclesiæ membra. Contendit Cardinalis Bellarminus, Romanorum Pontificum scelera, & flagitia non impedire, quin iidem Pontifices sint lapis probatus, angularis, pretiosus, in fundamento fundatum ab Esaia propheta prædictus, quem horrendum hæc in CHRISTVM blasphemiam continent; sed ita oportuit eos excæcari, qui veritatem cum scelerib[?]us, & flagitiis coniungere volunt. CVRISTVS dor[?]minus minus Ecclesiam suam longe aliter instituit. Si quis, inquit, voluerit voluntatem eius facere, cognoscet de doctrina, utrum a DEO sit, an ego a meipso loquar. Qui a semetipso loquitur, gloriam propriam quaeris: qui autem quaerit gloriam eius, qui misit eum, hic verax est, & iniustitia in illo non est. Iesuitae igitur, qui ut impurus viuunt, sanctitatem in Ecclesiae membris non esse necessariam arbitrantur, qui voluntatem Papae facere volunt, qui ex semetipsis loquuntur; versantur Dei quomodo reiici possunt? recte, & laudè sanctus Aug. filius. {a}In ignorantia [?] versantur, [illegible, ~6 letters] alterutrum [?]. Errant autem quicunque pariter versantur [?] in re sese cognoscere, quam ... sequuntur [illegible, ~8 letters]. Hæc ille.
units.tr: The Jesuits contend that impure men, in whom there is no inward virtue, are true members of the holy Church. Cardinal Bellarmine contends that the crimes and disgraceful deeds of the Roman Pontiffs do not prevent those same Pontiffs from being the tested, precious corner stone, founded upon the foundation foretold by the prophet Isaiah; these claims contain a dreadful blasphemy against Christ. But those who wish to join the truth with crimes and disgraceful deeds had to be blinded in this way. The Lord Christ established his Church far differently. If anyone, he says, wishes to do his will, he will know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself. He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory; but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him, the same is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him. The Jesuits, therefore, who live as impure men and think that holiness is not necessary in the members of the Church, who want to do the will of the Pope, who speak from themselves, how can they be reckoned as dwelling in God? Rightly and praiseworthily says the holy son of Augustine: they dwell in ignorance, [...] one with another. Those who dwell together in this way err, as they do not know themselves in the matter, which [...] they follow. So far he.

units.la: Hæc nobis necessaria videbantur admonuisse, ut constare possit, ex quo fonte Iesuitae hodie solum fide iustificationem impugnent: ex doctrina Scoti, antiquis ignota. Illi quidem sophismata sua quid aliud agunt, quam ut fidem iustificantem è fidelium oculis abscondant, & convertant in fidem historicam, in acquisitam, in informem, denique in daemonum fidem, nihil est enim in fide Scriptarum [?], & Iesuitarum [?], quod non sit etiam in fide daemonum.
units.tr: We thought it necessary to remind of these things, so that it may be clear from what source the Jesuits today attack justification by faith alone: from the teaching of Scotus, unknown to the ancients. Indeed, what else do their sophistries accomplish than to hide the justifying faith from the eyes of the faithful, and to turn it into historical faith, acquired faith, unformed faith, and finally into the faith of demons? For there is nothing in the faith of the Scotists and the Jesuits that is not also in the faith of demons.

units.la: Quanto ratior est fides nostra, quae verbo Dei innititur, testimonium habens à lege, & Prophetis, ab Apostolis, ab vniuersa Ecclesia, ab ipsis denique aduersariis. Ut igitur inuiiustitiæ veritatis vis appareat, à coacto illo, & vi veritatis extorto Bellarmini testimonio, quod superius posuimus, tandem concluda-mus, & Propter meritorum proprie iustitiæ, & priuatim nostræ gloriæ, certissimum est fidu-ciam in sola DEI misericordia, & benignitate posse. Hæc ille. Quod quidem est, ac si diceret: quanquam ego ad scribendum a Ro-mano Pontifice coactus hæc contra solam fidei iustificationem, & solam misericordiam fiduciam scripserim: proferor tamen hanc doctrinam, quam oppugnasti, certissimam esse. Et quia nulla sententia de fide tutissima esse potest, nisi quia est verissima, eandem proferri cogor verissimam esse: ex proinde contrariam sententiam, quam de operum meritis ex congruo hominum nondum renatorum confirmare volui, esse falsis-simam.
units.tr: How much more reasonable is our faith, which rests on the Word of God, having testimony from the Law and the Prophets, from the Apostles, from the whole Church, and finally from the adversaries themselves. So that the power of the truth may appear from the forced testimony of Bellarmine, which was wrung from him by the force of the truth and which we set out above, let us at last conclude: "On account of the merits of one's own righteousness and one's own private glory, it is most certain that trust can rest in the mercy and kindness of God alone." So far he. This is as if he said: although I was compelled by the Roman Pontiff to write these things against justification by faith alone and trust in mercy alone, I nevertheless declare this doctrine, which you have attacked, to be most certain. And since no opinion about faith can be most safe unless it is most true, I am compelled to declare it most true; and therefore the contrary opinion, which I wished to confirm concerning the merits of works from the congruous merit of men not yet reborn, is most false.

units.la: QVARTAE CON-troversiae PARS PRIMA: Contra Pontifices, DE GRATIA INHÆ-RENTE
units.tr: FOURTH CONTROVERSY, PART ONE: Against the Papists, ON INHERENT GRACE

units.la: THESES PONTIFICIÆ.
units.tr: THE PAPAL THESES.

units.la: Si quis dixerit homines iustificari sola impu-tatione iustitiae Christi, vel sola peccatorum remissio-ne, exclusa gratia, & charitate, quae in cordibus eo-rum per Spiritum S. diffunditur, atque illis inhaeret: aut etiam gratiam [?], qua iustificamur, esse tantummodo fauorem Dei, anathema sit. Concil. Trid. sess. 6. can. 11.
units.tr: If anyone shall say that men are justified by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ alone, or by the remission of sins alone, excluding grace and charity, which is poured out in their hearts by the Holy Spirit and inheres in them; or that the grace by which we are justified is only the favour of God, let him be anathema. Council of Trent, sess. 6, can. 11 [?].

units.la: Est gratia (quemadmodum Tridentina Synodus ab omnibus credendum proposita [?], anathematis decreuit) non solum per quam peccatorum fit remissio, sed diuina qualitas in anima inhaerens, ac veluti splendor quidam, & lux, quae animarum nostrarum maculas omnes delet, ipsasque animas pulchriores, & splendidiores reddit. Catechismus Concil. Trid. tractat. de sacram. baptismi.
units.tr: Grace is (as the Synod of Trent, proposed to be believed by all, has decreed under anathema) not only that through which sins are remitted, but a divine quality inhering in the soul, and as it were a certain splendour and light, which wipes away all the stains of our souls and makes the souls themselves more beautiful and more resplendent. Catechism of the Council of Trent, treatise on the sacrament of baptism.

units.la: Theologorum communis sententia est, gratiam esse habitum supernaturalem, à Deo nobis infusum, quo anima exornatur, & perficitur, adeoque ipsa Deoque grata & accepta reddit. Bellarm. lib. 1. de grat. & lib. ii. arb. cap. 4. [?]
units.tr: The common opinion of the theologians is that grace is a supernatural habit, infused into us by God, by which the soul is adorned and perfected, and so is made pleasing and acceptable both to itself and to God. Bellarmine, lib. 1, de grat. and lib. 2, arb., cap. 4.

units.la: Certe si gratia iustificans à virtutum Theologica-rum habitibus distinguenda sit, ergo Concilium Triden-
units.tr: Certainly, if justifying grace is to be distinguished from the habits of the theological virtues, then the Council of Trent could be rebuked;

units.la: tinum reprehendi posset: gratia ergo iustificans non distinguitur ab habitu charitatis. Bell.ibid.c.6.
units.tr: therefore justifying grace is not distinguished from the habit of charity. Bellarmine, ibid., c. 6.

units.la: Potest homo vendum[?] reconciliatus per opera pae-nitentia impetrare, & mereri ex congruo gratiam iustificationis. Bellar.de iustific. lib.5. c.22.
units.tr: A man who has been reconciled can, by works of repentance, truly obtain and merit de congruo the grace of justification. Bellarmine, de iustificatione, lib. 5, c. 22.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: Status quaestionis explicatur.
units.tr: The state of the question is explained.

units.la: IN quæstione de gratia Dei, Pontificii veri-tatem, per [?]ohærentiam suam conturbant, contra quam nobis hoc loco certandum est.
units.tr: IN the question concerning the grace of God, the Papists disturb the truth by their inconsistency, and it is against this that we must contend here.

units.la: Quæstio hæc de gratia iustificationis, vt gra-uissima est, ita cognitione nostra dignissima: vnde maximam tractatio hæc secum adferet utilitatem, & fructum. Ex ea enim constabit ipsos fontes religionis apud Pontificios vene-no[?] infectos esse, atque ex hoc perniciosissimo fonte corrupto, alios errores facile profluxisse.
units.tr: This question, concerning the grace of justification, is as weighty as it is worthy of our knowledge. The treatment of it will therefore bring the greatest usefulness and fruit. For it will become plain that the very sources of religion among the Papists are infected with poison, and that from this most pernicious corrupted source other errors have easily flowed.

units.la: Pelagiani veteres, & quicunque errores de gratia, vel excogitarunt, vel ab aliis inuentos suscipiunt, in eo maxime peccarunt, quod reiectis scripturis, aliam huius verbi acceptionem amplectuntur, quam sacræ literæ prodidere. Nam Pelagius gratiam quidem prædicabat, sed intelligebat liberum arbitrium, & gratiam illam, quam hominem accepisse putabat, in creatione. Eodemque modo Tridentini gratiam Dei prædicant, sed gratiam ab ipsis confictam, quam e scriptura ostendere non possunt. Nam Tridentini sententiam suam ita exponunt, vt gratiam distinguant in eam, quæ gratis data est, & quæ gratum facientem, gragratum facit, gratis datam docent esse donum supernaturale, absque vllo debito collatum, præcipue ad aliorum salutem: de hac gratia nō est quæstio inter nos. Gratiam autem gratum facientem dicunt esse, vel permanentem, siue habitualem, vel auxilii speciales: gratiam illam permanentem, habitum esse, vel qualitatem, per modum habitus nobis inhærentem, quæ quidem qualitate nos Deo gratos esse, atque iustificatos [?] cōstituunt [?]: hanc autem habitualem qualitatem nihil aliud esse quam charitatem. Sic ille gratiam explicant.
units.tr: The ancient Pelagians, and all who have either devised errors about grace or taken up those invented by others, sinned chiefly in this: they rejected the Scriptures and embraced a meaning of this word different from the one the holy letters hand down. For Pelagius did indeed preach grace, but he understood free will by it, and that grace which he thought man had received in creation. In the same way the Tridentines preach the grace of God, but a grace invented by themselves, which they cannot show from Scripture. For the Tridentines explain their view by distinguishing grace into that which is given freely (gratis data) and that which makes one acceptable (gratum faciens). They teach that the grace given freely is a supernatural gift, bestowed without any debt, chiefly for the salvation of others; concerning this grace there is no dispute between us. But they say that the grace which makes one acceptable is either permanent, or habitual, or grace of special help. They say that the permanent grace is a habit, or quality, inhering in us by way of a habit, and that by this quality we are made pleasing to God and justified; and they say that this habitual quality is nothing other than charity. Thus they explain grace.

units.la: Nos de gratia Dei, verbum Dei consulendum iudicamus, quia nisi scripturarum locum sequamur ducem, ab errore liberari non possumus: distinctionem superiorem gratiæ in gratis datam, & gratum facientem, non repudiamus, quia in scriptura continetur, nō quo Apostolo χαρισματα vocentur, gratiæ à Scholasticis gratis datæ appellantur. Sed nos hic gratiam illam quærimus, quæ saluamur, nō iam de aliis gratiæ acceptionibus solliciti, in hac potissimum insistimus. Gratia apud Latinos scriptores, vt & χαρις apud Græcos, decorem significat, & venustatem. At in vsu linguæ Hebraicæ hanc vocabuli vim non reperies, sed vsitata locutio est apud Hebræos, inuenit gratiam in oculis eius. De Deo dicitur, quod inuenerit gratiam in oculis Domini, in Heb est מָצָא־חֵן [?], i.e. inuenit misericordiam. Hinc illæ vsitatissimæ locutiones in sacris litteris, si inueni gratiam in oculis tuis; Hebraicè est, si inueni misericordiam. Igno-[?]
units.tr: As for us, we judge that concerning the grace of God the Word of God must be consulted, because unless we follow the testimony of the Scriptures as our guide, we cannot be freed from error. We do not reject the above distinction of grace into grace given freely and grace making one acceptable, because it is contained in Scripture; not in the sense that those things which the Apostle calls [χαρισματα] charismata [χαρισματα] are called by the Schoolmen "graces given freely." But here we seek that grace by which we are saved, and not concerned now with the other meanings of grace, we dwell chiefly on this one. In Latin writers grace signifies comeliness and charm, as also [χαρις] charis [χαρις] does among the Greeks. But in the use of the Hebrew language you will not find this force of the word; rather it is a common expression among the Hebrews, "he found grace in his eyes." Concerning God it is said that he found grace in the eyes of the Lord; in Hebrew it is [מָצָא־חֵן], that is, he found mercy. Hence those most common expressions in the holy letters, "if I have found grace in your eyes"; in Hebrew it is "if I have found mercy."

units.tr: [illegible]

units.la: Ignorantiæ idiomatû fefellit incautos ho- mines in vsu huius verbi. Nam si quis reliquis[?] fontibus Hebraicis, in vsu Latinæ, aut Græcæ linguæ vim huius verbi quærat, longè erit à veritate. Græcè igitur explicatio è sacris lite- ris petenda est. Quod ad verbi vim attinet, i- dem prorsus est gratia; quod Hebraeis mise- ricordia. Apostoli igitur in Novo Testamen- to gratiæ vocabulo vsurtur, vt patefaciant misericordiam Dei, & supereminentem [illegible, ~6 letters] [illegible, ~12 letters] charitatem, quæ in Christo Iesu manife- stata est, in liberandis hominibus à captivitate diaboli, [illegible, ~10 letters] à qua les[?] liberati sunt peccatorum suorum. [illegible, ~20 letters] proinde sapissime opponitur superemineti hæc Dei charitas, ergo et superibus nobis, & salutis nostræ, nobis salvatus; vt in Ec- clesia credentium certo constare possit, hanc liberationem excellentem, non à lege, sed à Christo, non omnino à sepiis, sed à Dei favore & misericordia habere. Atque hæc ab illa supereminente Dei charitate, et favor, quæ sapientiæ novi testamenti ascri- bitur, gratia & supereminens magnitudo virtutis [illegible, ~8 letters] qua suam, qui suscitavit eum[?] [illegible, ~8 letters] potentia virtutis eius, vt possent comprehendere cum omnibus sanctis, et scire supereminentem charitatem Christi. In Scriptura sanctis charitatem CHRISTI. In Scriptura appellat gratiam, supereminentem magni- tudinem virtutis eius in nos & supereminen- tem charitatem: constat autem in coniunctio- ne CHRISTI.
units.tr: Ignorance of the idioms has misled unwary men in the use of this word. For if anyone seeks the force of this word from other Hebrew sources, or from the usage of Latin or Greek, he will be far from the truth. The explanation must therefore be sought in Greek from the holy letters. As far as the force of the word goes, grace is altogether the same as what mercy is to the Hebrews. The Apostles, therefore, in the New Testament use the word grace so as to make known the mercy of God and his surpassing [illegible] [illegible] charity, which has been manifested in Christ Jesus in delivering men from the captivity of the devil [illegible], by which they have been freed from their sins. [illegible] Therefore this surpassing charity of God is very often opposed to our works, and to our salvation, so that in the congregation of believers it may be certain that this excellent deliverance is had not from the law, but from Christ, and not at all from our works, but from the favour and mercy of God. And so this favour and grace, which is ascribed to the wisdom of the New Testament, flows from that surpassing charity of God, and [the surpassing greatness of his power] [illegible], according to that working of the strength of his power, which he exerted in raising him up, that they might be able to comprehend with all the saints and to know the surpassing charity of Christ. In Scripture he calls it grace, the surpassing greatness of his power toward us, and the surpassing charity; and this is established in union with Christ.

units.la: Hæc est gratia Dei, cuius sana doctrina[?] in Ecclesia conseruata fuit, & per successiones tradita, & celebrata, donec Scholastici Theologi suis horrendis figmentis commu-tarunt eam. Tunc enim inimicus humani ge-neris, dormientibus hominibus venit, & in-seminauit zizania in medio tritici, & ab-iit. Hæc zizania postquam radices alvoris[?] in fraterculorum opinionibus egerunt, maxi-me apparuerunt in Concilio Tridentino. Dominus autem messis suo tempore manda-bit messoribus suis, vt ea in fasciculos colli-g[illegible, ~4 letters] ad comburendum.
units.tr: This is the grace of God, whose sound doctrine was preserved in the Church, handed down through successive generations, and celebrated, until the Scholastic theologians changed it by their dreadful fictions. For then the enemy of the human race came while men were sleeping, and sowed tares in the midst of the wheat, and went away. After these tares had put down roots in the opinions of the brethren, they became most evident at the Council of Trent. But the Lord of the harvest will in his own time command his reapers to gather them into bundles for burning.

units.la: Nec potuerunt Tri-dentini manifestum a CHRISTO ad Pela-gium tranire, quam vt hanc saluberrimam doctrinam corrumperent. Relicto enim Chri-sto & Euangelio, vt meriti fundamentum sta-bilire possint, confingunt gratiam, qua salui-mur, & iusti ficamur, esse qualitatem animæ in-hærentem, animæ nitorem, habitum inhæ-rentem, habitum ipsum dicunt, per præpara-tiones, & dispositiones nostras acquiri posse, sicut externa philosophia docet per multas dispositiones habitus tandem acquiri. Iohan. Scoto, quem sequuntur Tridentini [illegible, ~4 letters], docet istas dispositiones & præparationes pec-catore posse ex puris naturalibus in præstare[?], vt illi gratia ex merito congrui[?] communicetur. Quanquam sunt quidam inter pontificios theologos, quos tandem pudere cœpit huius tam crassi Pelagianismi. Et[?] speramus, re bene explorata, plures etiam futuros, qui in hac re Tri-
units.tr: Nor could the Tridentines pass openly from Christ to Pelagius, except by corrupting this most wholesome doctrine. For, leaving Christ and the Gospel, in order to establish a foundation of merit, they invent that the grace by which we are saved and justified is a quality inhering in the soul, a lustre of the soul, an inherent habit; they say that the habit itself can be acquired through our preparations and dispositions, just as external philosophy teaches that a habit is at last acquired through many dispositions. John Scotus, whom the Tridentines follow [illegible], teaches that the sinner can by these dispositions and preparations, from purely natural powers, bring it about that grace is communicated to him from congruous merit. Yet there are some among the Papist theologians whom shame at this so gross Pelagianism has begun to seize. And we hope that, once the matter is well examined, there will be more who in this matter [illegible].

units.la: Triden[?] nò esse clesiam[?] gratia[?] nè fau[?] charit[?] Christ[?] lica; a[?] ritas[?] ex Tr[?] Conc[?]
units.tr: [Largely illegible.] ... the Church ... grace ... charity ... Christ ... catholic ... truth ... from the Council of Trent ...

units.la: P&[?] fa[?] nem[?] dem[?] inqu[?] ria, f[?] in ea[?] pro in[?] cum[?] men[?] debi[?] non[?] cred[?] imp[?] strat[?] & g[?] ces[?] Tridentina principia deferenda sibi necessa-rio esse, indicabunt. Quæstio igitur inter Ecclesiam Catholicam, & Pontificios est; vtrum gratia Dei qua iustificamur, sit misericordia, sine fauor Dei tantum, & supereminens illa Dei charitas, qua nos peccatores dilexit Deus in Christo, sicut semper docuit Ecclesia Catholica; an verò habitus, inhærens nobis, vel charitas nostra, & nitor, & splendor animæ, sicut ex Theologorum nouis commentis docet Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: ... must be abandoned by them, and that the principles of Trent are necessary to be abandoned. The question, therefore, between the Catholic Church and the Papists is this: whether the grace of God by which we are justified is only the mercy and favour of God, and that surpassing charity of God by which God loved us sinners in Christ, as the Catholic Church has always taught; or whether it is rather a habit inhering in us, or our charity, and a lustre and splendour of the soul, as the Council of Trent teaches from the new inventions of the theologians.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: E Scripturis probatur gratia Dei.
units.tr: That the grace of God is proved from Scripture.

units.la: PRimo, vt instituti nostri ratio postulat, ex sacra scriptura gratiam, & gratiæ cognitionem quæremus. Deinde ad hunc lydium[?] lapi-dem reliqua examinabuntur. Ei qui operatur, inquit Apostolus, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito: ei vero qui non operatur, sed credit in eum, qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides sua pro iustitia. quo loco Apostolus docet, meritum cum fide, & gratia, consistere non posse. nam merces quæ ex merito debetur, quid est nisi debitum? at merces illa ex debito, vel merito, non est ex gratia. quia ei qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui iustificat impium, fides sua imputatur pro iustitia, atque ita gratia demō-stratur. Itaque in iustificatione impii, fides & gratia Dei sola commendatur nobis. Simer[?]-ces, & debitum, & meritum hoc de congruo, cum gratia consistere non potest, quomodo poterit hæc gratia esse habitus inhærens? quia habitus, ex operationibus consurgit, gratia operationes excludit: quia ei qui non operatur, merces imputatur ex gratia. Nec sufficiet distinctio habitus, in infusum, & acquisitum; nam quamvis Tridentini infusum hunc habitum agnoscant, pertinaciter tamen hanc conclusionem retinent, hunc habitum ex multis præparationibus, & dispositionibus habere. Atque ita hunc habitum explicat Scotus, quique eum sequuntur, vt nihil plane differat ab habitu acquisito. Et ratio manifesta concinit: nam si habitus hic per dispositiones, & præparationes nostras habeatur, quomodo differt ab habitu acquisito? at omnes Tridentini in eo consentiunt, quod per dispositiones & præparationes nostras acquiri possit. Frustra igitur nomen infusi habitus retinetur, quo Pelagianismus concedit[?], incautis non appareat. Impius iustificatur ex gratia, non operans, sed tantum credens in eum, qui iustificat impium: nō ergo ex habitu inhærente. Quando impius iustificatur, & ex impio fit pius per gratiam; ostendunt nobis Tridentini, quis habitus aut nitor inhæreat impio, quem si nemo mortalium ostendere potest, quid est quod non cedant virtuti, nam in iustificatione impii omne debitum, ac proinde omne meritum, omnes præparationes nostras, omne nobis inhærens excludit Apostolus, vt gratiam solam stabiliat.
units.tr: First, as the plan of our undertaking requires, we will seek grace, and the knowledge of grace, from holy Scripture. Afterwards the remaining matters will be tested by this touchstone. To him who works, says the Apostle, the wage is not reckoned as grace, but as debt; but to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. In this passage the Apostle teaches that merit cannot stand together with faith and grace. For what is a wage that is owed for merit, if not a debt? But a wage owed as a debt, or as merit, is not of grace. Grace is shown by the fact that to him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. So in the justification of the ungodly, faith and the grace of God alone are commended to us. Wage, debt, and merit of this kind, which they call merit of congruity, cannot stand together with grace. How then can this grace be an inherent habit? For a habit arises from works, while grace excludes works, since to him who does not work the wage is reckoned as grace. Nor will the distinction between infused and acquired habit suffice. For although the Tridentines acknowledge this habit as infused, they stubbornly maintain the conclusion that it is had through many preparations and dispositions. And so Scotus explains this habit, and those who follow him, so that it differs in no way from an acquired habit. The plain reasoning agrees: for if this habit is had through our dispositions and preparations, how does it differ from an acquired habit? But all the Tridentines agree in this, that it can be acquired through our dispositions and preparations. The name of an infused habit is therefore retained in vain, and by it Pelagianism is granted to the unwary without their noticing. The ungodly is justified by grace, not by working but only by believing in him who justifies the ungodly; therefore not by an inherent habit. When the ungodly is justified, and from ungodly becomes godly through grace, the Tridentines should show us what habit or lustre inheres in the ungodly person. If no mortal can show this, why do they not yield to the power of Scripture? For in the justification of the ungodly the Apostle excludes every debt, and therefore every merit, all our preparations, and everything inherent in us, in order to establish grace alone.

units.la: Deinde sic etiam docet Apostolus: Propterea ex fide, ut sit per gratiam, ut firma sit promissio universo semini. Habitus ille inhaerens, intelligitur esse in caritate nostra, atque in operibus. At Apostolus dicit: Propterea ex fide, ut sit per gratiam. Ergo in iustificatione impii fides & gratia statuitur, sine operibus, & inhaerente qualitate nostra. In iustificatis caritas sese[?] prodit, & bona opera fiunt, tanquam fructus huius gratiae. Neque operationes sunt sine gratia: sed nos gratiam quaerimus, qua iustificatur impius coram Deo, quam in[?] virtute nobis inhaerente esse negat Apostolus. Ac proinde electio Dei gratuita, quae ex solo Dei beneplacito consistit, dicitur electio gratiae, Rom. 11. 5. Reliquiae, inquit, salua est secundum electionem gratiae. Ergo Deus per gratiam elegit homines ad fidem, & salutem. Quod si gratia haec sit habitus nobis inhaerens, iam electio, & praedestinatio erit secundum qualitates nostras inhaerentes. Itaque anathema Tridentinum sic ex[?] Apostolo refutamus; gratia est secundum quam Deus eligit, & praedestinat homines ad fidem, & salutem, est igitur misericordia, & favor Dei tantummodo.
units.tr: Again, the Apostle teaches thus: "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace, so that the promise might be firm to all the seed." That inherent habit is understood to lie in our charity and in our works. But the Apostle says: "Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace." Therefore in the justification of the ungodly, faith and grace are set up, without works and without any inherent quality of ours. In the justified, charity shows itself, and good works are done as the fruit of this grace. Nor are the works without grace; but we are seeking the grace by which the ungodly is justified before God, which the Apostle denies is in any virtue inherent in us. Accordingly the free election of God, which rests on the sole good pleasure of God, is called the election of grace, Rom. 11:5: "There is a remnant saved according to the election of grace." Therefore God chose men by grace to faith and salvation. But if this grace were an habit inherent in us, then election and predestination would be according to our inherent qualities. Thus we refute the Tridentine anathema by the Apostle's own words: grace is that according to which God chooses and predestines men to faith and salvation; it is therefore the mercy and favour of God alone.

units.la: Apostolus etiam sic disputat: Quod si per gratiam, non iam ex operibus, alioquin gratia iam non est gratia: si ex operibus, iam non ex gratia, alioquin opus iam non est opus. Haec Apostolus. Quid ergo respondebunt Iesuitae, si ratione sic colligat: Quod si per gratiam, iam non ex habitibus inhaerentibus, aut ex aliquo animæ nitore habituali ; alioqui gratia iam non est gratia. nam disputat de gratia elec-tionis, quæ, sicut excludit opus nostrum, sic omne nobis inhærens. Atque vt intelligamus, gratiam Dei esse quiddam extra nos, non in nostris habitibus aut virtutibus situm, Apostolus gratiam Dei in propósito Dei recon-ditam, atque inde nobis proficientem ostendit, itaque propositum vocat propositum gra-tiæ Rom. 4. 5. sicut & electio dicitur electio gratiæ Rom. 11. 5. & prædestinatio dicitur præparatio gratiæ. quia prædestinatio est se-cundum propositum; ex prædestinatione autem est vocatio, ex vocatione iustificatio, ex iustificatione glorificatio. Hanc Augustinus observat, plenitudinem Christi in Ecclesiam defluentem, quia ex plenitudine eius omnes accepimus, & gratiam pro gratia quid est, gratiam pro gratia? gratia prædestinationis, & gratia vocationis, est gratia ex misericordia Dei tantummodo: pro qua, & vt qua est fi-des. pro fide iustificatio, hoc est gratia pro gratia. pro iustificatione sanctificatio, & tan-dem glorificatio, id est, gratia pro gratia. nam vitam æternam gratiam esse, & gratuitum Dei donum docet Apostolus Rom. 6. 23. Stipendium, inquit, peccati est mors: at vitæ æ-terna est χάρισμα θεοῦ [?], id est, donum Dei gratuitum. Hæc autem gratia, quæ datur secun-dum propositum, & electionem, quæ datur per prædestinationem, per vocationem, per [illegible, ~7 letters], per iustificationem : num quis sanos existiexistimabit esse qualitatem nobis inhæren-tem? num eligimur per qualitatem nobis in-hærentem: num prædestinamur per qualita-tem inhærentem? num vocamur per qualita-tem nobis in hærenem?
units.tr: The Apostle also argues thus: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. If it is of works, it is no longer of grace; otherwise work is no longer work." So the Apostle. What then will the Jesuits answer if he reasons in this way: "But if it is by grace, it is no longer of inherent habits or of any habitual lustre of the soul; otherwise grace is no longer grace"? For he is disputing about the grace of election, which excludes not only our works but everything inherent in us. And so that we may understand that the grace of God is something outside us, not placed in our habits or virtues, the Apostle shows that the grace of God is hidden in the purpose of God and from there comes to us. Accordingly he calls it "the purpose of grace" (Rom. 4:5), just as election is called "the election of grace" (Rom. 11:5), and predestination is called "the preparation of grace", because predestination is according to purpose; from predestination comes calling, from calling justification, and from justification glorification. Augustine observes this, that the fullness of Christ flows into the Church: "because of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace" [John 1:16]. What is "grace for grace"? The grace of predestination and the grace of calling is grace from the mercy of God alone; in return for it, and as it is, comes faith; for faith comes justification, that is, grace for grace. For justification comes sanctification, and at last glorification, that is, grace for grace. For the Apostle teaches that eternal life is grace and the free gift of God, Rom. 6:23: "The wages of sin is death; but eternal life is the gift of God [χάρισμα θεοῦ], that is, the free gift of God." Now this grace, which is given according to purpose and election, which is given through predestination, through calling, through [illegible] and through justification: will anyone sensible think that it is a quality inherent in us? Are we chosen through a quality inherent in us? Are we predestined through an inherent quality? Are we called through a quality inherent in us?

units.la: Eadem verò veritas constat ex iis scriptu-ris locis, quæ charitatem Dei nobis com-mendant. Nam sicut docet Apostolus: Charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Christus enim, quum adhuc infirmi essemus, secundum tempus pro impiis mortuus est, &c. Commendat autem suam charitatem erga nos Deus, quod quum adhuc peccatores essemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est. Ex qui-bus verbis genuina gratiæ explicatio petenda est: ut gratiam intelligamus in charitate Dei constitutam, non in charitate nostra. Hic sese Tridentini expediunt, qui docent gratiam, qua iustificamur, non esse tantum fauorem Dei, sed virtutem nobis inhærentem seu charitatem nostram. Apostolus aitcharitatem Dei effusam esse in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Prius docuerat, iustificatos nos ex fide pacem habere erga Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem etiam habemus aditum in hanc gratiam, in qua stamus. Tridentini, qui ex habitibus inhærem-tibus iustificari se credunt, hanc pacem apud Deum penitus ignorant. Itaque Cardin. Bel-larminus multas paginas consumit, ut pro-ber incertitudinem gratiæ & iustitiæ nec emi-[illegible, ~7 letters] ramur, si Tridentini pacem hanc apud Deum invenire non possint. Ubi enim est incertitudo gratiæ & iustitiæ, pax erga Deum esse non potest. At quum iustificati habeamus pacem erga Deum, & aditum ad hanc gratiam in qua stamus; quod docet Apostolus: operibus autem suis, & inhærenti qualitate, & habituali suo nitore iustificati, incerti semper sint de gratia,& pace erga Deum, quod fatentur Tridentini: num quod aliud evidentius, aut illustrius argumentū produci potest, quam hoc, quo veritas, & sapientia, & filiis suis, atque etiam ab inimicis suis iustificatur. Gratia divina certa est, quæ pacem apud Deum præstat, gratia Tridentina incerta est, nec pacem erga Deum præstare potest: non est ergo hæc Dei gratia. Quod iustificamur, quod pacem habeamus, quod gloriemur sub spe gloriæ, quod gloriemur in afflictionibus, eorum[?] hoc est ex gratia. Deinde progreditur Apostolus: si quis enim quærat, unde sit hæc tanta gratia? Respondet Apostolus, ex charitate Dei. Nam charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. Non est ergo ex nobis, sed a Deo, non ex inhærenti qualitate nostra, sed ex effusa charitate Dei.
units.tr: Moreover, the same truth is established by those passages of Scripture which commend the love of God to us. For, as the Apostle teaches: "The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. For Christ, while we were still weak, died for the ungodly in due time," etc. But God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners Christ died for us. From these words the genuine explanation of grace is to be sought: that we understand grace to lie in the love of God, not in our own love. Here the Tridentines extricate themselves, since they teach that the grace by which we are justified is not merely the favour of God, but a virtue inherent in us, or our own charity. The Apostle says that the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Earlier he had taught that we, justified by faith, have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we also have access into this grace in which we stand. The Tridentines, who believe they are justified by inherent habits, know nothing at all of this peace with God. So Cardinal Bellarmine spends many pages trying to prove the uncertainty of grace and righteousness, and that we cannot be assured of them, if the Tridentines cannot find this peace with God. For where there is uncertainty of grace and righteousness, there cannot be peace with God. But since we who are justified have peace with God and access to this grace in which we stand, as the Apostle teaches, while those who are justified by their works, their inherent quality and their habitual lustre are always uncertain about grace and peace with God, as the Tridentines confess: what more evident or illustrious argument can be brought forward than this, by which truth and wisdom, and their sons, and even their enemies, are justified? Divine grace is certain, and it gives peace with God; Tridentine grace is uncertain and cannot give peace with God; therefore this is not the grace of God. That we are justified, that we have peace, that we rejoice in hope of glory, that we rejoice in afflictions, all this is of grace. Then the Apostle goes on: if anyone asks, whence comes so great a grace? The Apostle answers: from the love of God. For the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. It is therefore not from us but from God; not from an inherent quality of ours, but from the love of God poured out.

units.la: Ac[?] dicunt Tridentini, charitatem illam Dei, quam docet Apostolus effusam esse in cordibus nostris, esse gratiam, & charitatem nobis inhærentem, quæ nos diligimus Deum. Sic docet Concilium Trident. sub pœna anathemathemaris, sess. 6. Apostoli igitur verba sunt accuratius executienda. Charitas Dei effusa est, Vtitur[?] Apostolus effundendi verbis[?], ut exprimatur benignitas donantis, non virtus recipientis hanc gratiam. Ac proinde non pro expectatione, aut meritis nostris, tanquam merces reddimus, sed provoluntate[?], & ad mensuram donantis effundi-tur. Charitas ergo haec Dei est, non nostra inhaerens: non enim mihi Deus commendat charitatem meam, sed commendat Deus nobis, inquit Apostolus, charitatem suam.
units.tr: And the Tridentines say that this love of God, which the Apostle teaches is poured out in our hearts, is grace and a love inherent in us, by which we love God. So the Council of Trent teaches under anathema, session 6. The words of the Apostle must therefore be examined more carefully. The Apostle uses the verb "poured out" to express the kindness of the giver, not the power of the one who receives this grace. Accordingly, we do not pay it back as a wage, in return for our expectations or merits, but it is poured out freely and in the measure of the giver. This love is therefore God's, not our own inherent love. For, as the Apostle says, God does not commend my love to me, but God commends his own love to us.

units.la: Charitas ergo haec Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris. Quare in cordibus nostris? Dicitur in Psalmis: effusa est gratia in labiis tuis. Quae verba de Christo prolata sunt, sed quae de Capite in scripturis dicuntur, ad membra relata intelliguntur, quatenus à Capite in membris communicatio gratiae. Est itaque gratia effusa in labiis nostris, & gratia effusa in cordibus nostris. In cordibus nostris ad credendum, in labiis nostris ad confessi-dum: Corde enim creditur ad iustitiam, ore autem confessio fit ad salutem. Gratia primum est in cordibus eius, deinde in labiis. A corde fluit ad labia, atque ad omnes corporis animaeque potentias. Totus enim homo, & omnia quae sunt in homine suaviter Deo subiiciuntur simulac haec gratia locum sedemque suam acceperit in corde hominis effusa. Hinc est quod sapiens ait: cor sapientis erudidiet os eius, & labiis eius addet gratiam. Itaque gratia est in ore, & in labiis, sed quæ procedit à corde; in corde à Deo est. Hæc est virtus illa, quæ mutat cor nostrum, id est, cor durum. Nam quod nostrum est cor, durum est. Sed hæc virtus Dei cor nostrum durum mutat, & potentia sua emollit; antequam Deus hanc gratiam effundat, cor nostrum durum est. Sed gratia effusa in cordibus nostris, ex duris carnea, & iam mollita reddit. Itaque cor mollitum iam nostrum etiam est. Sed virtus illa, qua mollitur cor, nostra non est, habitus noster inhærens non est. De hac virtute contendimus cum Triden-tinis.
units.tr: This love of God, then, is poured out in our hearts. Why in our hearts? It is said in the Psalms: Grace is poured out on your lips. These words were spoken of Christ, but what is said of the Head in the Scriptures is understood as applying to the members, insofar as grace is communicated from the Head to the members. Grace is therefore poured out on our lips, and grace is poured out in our hearts: in our hearts for believing, on our lips for confessing. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation (Rom. 10:10). Grace is first in the heart, then on the lips. It flows from the heart to the lips and to all the powers of body and soul. For the whole man, and everything in man, is gently made subject to God as soon as this grace, poured out, has received its place and seat in the heart. Hence the wise man says: The heart of the wise teaches his mouth, and adds grace to his lips (Prov. 16:23). Grace is thus in the mouth and on the lips, but it proceeds from the heart; in the heart it is from God. This is the power that changes our heart, that is, a hard heart. For our heart by nature is hard. But this power of God changes our hard heart and softens it by his might; before God pours out this grace, our heart is hard. Yet grace, poured out in our hearts, makes the hard heart of stone into one of flesh, now softened. So the heart, now softened, is also ours. But that power by which the heart is softened is not ours; it is not an inherent habit of ours. It is over this power that we contend with the Tridentines.

units.la: Hæc autem virtus optimè describitur hoc loco ab Apostolo. Docet enim unde sit? quænam sit? vbi sit? per quam denique potentiâ[?], aut operationem sit, atque operetur in nobis? Si quæras unde sit? est à Deo, quia charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris. Si quæras, quænam sit? sic illam explicat Apostolus: commendat Deus suam charitatem erga nos, quod quum adhuc peccatores essemus Christus pro nobis mortuus est. gratia ergo illa, quam Deus nobis commendat, est virtus Christi crucifixi & pro nobis peccatoribus mortui. Si quæras vbi sit? est in cordibus nostris, in quibus Dei charitas effusa est. Si quæras per quam potentiam, aut operationem sit, atque operetur in nobis, respondeo est in illis verbis, per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est no-bis. Ita- quæ ec est est, du- du- inte- no- ordi- llita et- no- non len- hoc uz- tiā, no- ba- ux- lus: os, ori- lla, tus ous no- ax- fit, llis io- is. bis. Hic ergo est charitas Dei, virtus Christi, operatio Spiritus Sancti. nihil hic meum inve-nio, nisi cor, in quod effusa est hæc gratia. Sed nec cor meum recipere potest hanc gratiam, nisi à Deo mutatum, imo verò, & nova crea-tione denuo creatum. ac proinde ad illum cla-mare non cessabo, cum Propheta: cor mundum crea in me Deus, & Spiritum rectum innova in vis-scribus meis. Jam ergo ubi est nitor ille, & splendor, scilicet, animæ inhærens, & Deo nos gratos & justos reddens? gratia hæc est virtus Christi pro nobis peccatoribus mortui, quæ cum merito de congruo stare non potest. quia peccator nondum reconciliatus Deo, nihil habet intra se, quo Deum placare possit, do-nec hæc charitas Dei cor eius tangat. Fons i-gitur gratiæ extra est, à Deo. Sedes in qua effu-ditur intus est cor nostrum, jam novum, jam denuo creatum; vis operans, quæ tantum bo-num in cordibus nostris operatur, est opera-tio Spiritus Sancti. Ergo nec virtus nostra est, nec qualitas nostra, non opus nostrum, non operatio nostra. nihil nostrum dicere possu-mus, nisi cor, cor durum ex natura: cor de no- no creatum, ex gratia. Non quæro hoc loco de voluntatis libero arbitrio. Scio me libere vo-luisse quodcunque volui, sive quum volun-tas hæc duro cordi serviebar, sive quum de novo creato cordi inseruit. Voluntas liberè voluit quicquid voluit. Hoc unum mihi cer-tum est, liberatum me ex miseria mea, ac ju-stificatum per gratiam. Hanc autem gratiam
units.tr: The Apostle describes this power very well in this passage. For he teaches whence it is, what it is, where it is, and finally by what power or operation it is and works in us. If you ask whence it is, it is from God, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts. If you ask what it is, the Apostle explains it thus: God commends his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. That grace, then, which God commends to us, is the power of Christ crucified and dead for us sinners. If you ask where it is, it is in our hearts, in which the love of God is poured out. If you ask by what power or operation it is and works in us, I answer: it is in those words, through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. Here, then, is the love of God, the power of Christ, the operation of the Holy Spirit. I find nothing of mine here, except the heart into which this grace is poured. Yet my heart cannot receive this grace unless it has been changed by God, indeed created anew by a new creation. Accordingly I will not cease to cry out to him with the Prophet: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me (Ps. 51:10). Where, then, is that brightness and splendour, namely a quality inhering in the soul, which makes us pleasing and righteous to God? This grace is the power of Christ, dead for us sinners, which cannot stand together with merit of congruity, because a sinner not yet reconciled to God has nothing within himself by which he can placate God, until this love of God touches his heart. The fountain of grace is therefore outside us, in God. The seat into which it is poured is within our heart, now new, now created anew. The working power which works so great a good in our hearts is the operation of the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is neither our power nor our quality, neither our work nor our operation. We can call nothing ours except the heart: the heart, hard by nature, created anew by grace. I do not inquire here about free will of the will. I know that I have freely willed whatever I willed, whether when this will was a slave to a hard heart or when it was joined to the newly created heart. The will freely willed whatever it willed. This one thing is certain to me: that I have been set free from my misery and justified by grace. But this grace

units.la: non esse virtutem mihi inhærentem, sed virtutem Christi pro me peccatore mortuo. Et certo persuasus sum, omnes Tridentinos diabolos hanc mihi fidem eripere non posse. Hæc monui ex occasione huius loci à Tridentinis improbe in alienum sensum detorti.
units.tr: is not an inherent virtue in me, but the virtue of Christ, dead for me the sinner. I am firmly persuaded that all the Tridentine devils cannot snatch this faith from me. I have made these remarks on the occasion of this passage, which the Tridentines have shamelessly twisted into a foreign sense.

units.la: Tridentini ergo, qui charitatem hanc Dei, in charitatem nostram converterunt contra diserta Apostoli verba, tanquam cæci in suam perniciem ruunt. Christus enim mortuus est pro nobis peccatoribus, infirmis, impiis, inimicis suis. Vbi tunc erat nitor ille animæ inhærens, quum nos peccatores fuimus, infirmi, nullas vires habentes, impii, inimici? Vbi nam gentium tunc erat gratia ista Tridentina, inhærens ista virtus? Certe ipsorum confessione nondum erat. At gratia Dei tunc erat illustris, & per nostram etiam miseriam illustrior: per gratiam enim liberati sumus ab hac miseria. Num quis tam vecors repertus est, aut forte in posterum reperietur, qui dicet nos liberatos esse ex miseria nostra, ex peccatorum seruitute, & iugo Diaboli per aliquam nobis inhærentem qualitatem, aut nitorem internum? furiosos esse constabit qui ita docuerint. Expediant ergo se Tridentini: & dicant, quomodo gratia qua iustificamur, qua liberamur à miseria, fit virtus nobis inhærens, vt non etiam virtute nostra liberemur à peccatis & miseria. Vel si hæc expedire non possint, cedant manifestæ veritati, & contra ana[?] anathe[?] liberat[?] à char[?] tatem [illegible, ~8 letters] quum mortu[?] Ha[?] test ep[?] ritare [illegible, ~6 letters] mus? a[?] gladius [illegible, ~8 letters] magne [?] infirm[?] tudo [?] sarsep[?] Domi[?] ni spe[?] charit[?] est m[?] conse[?] est [?] solea[?] nulla[?] hære[?] uare [?] tinan[?] ficata [?] serua[?] anxi[?] Hæc [?] tere [?] test. anathema Tridentinum dicant, gratiam qua liberamur à peccatis nostris, & miseria, esse à charitate Dei tantum modo. Quia charitatem suam Deus commendat nobis, quod quum essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus est.
units.tr: The Tridentines, then, who have turned this love of God into our love, against the plain words of the Apostle, rush headlong like blind men to their own destruction. For Christ died for us sinners, weak, ungodly, his enemies. Where, then, was that brightness of an inherent soul, when we were sinners, weak, having no strength, ungodly, enemies? Where, indeed, was that Tridentine grace of the nations then, that inherent virtue? Certainly, by their own confession, it did not yet exist. But the grace of God was then conspicuous, and more conspicuous through our very misery: for we have been freed from this misery by grace. Has anyone been found so mad, or will anyone be found in future, who will say that we have been freed from our misery, from the slavery of sin and the yoke of the Devil, through some quality inhering in us or some inner brightness? It will be plain that those who have taught this are mad. Let the Tridentines then extricate themselves, and say how the grace by which we are justified and freed from misery becomes a virtue inhering in us, so that we are not also freed from sins and misery by our own virtue. Or if they cannot explain this, let them yield to the manifest truth, and, against the Tridentine anathema, say that the grace by which we are freed from our sins and misery is only from the love of God, because God commends his love to us, in that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.

units.la: Hinc est illa charitas Christi, à qua nihil po-test separare credentes. Quis nos separabit à charitate Christi? an tribulatio? an angustia? an fames? an nuditas, an periculum? an persecutio? an gladius? certum sum, quod neque mors, neque vita, neque Angeli, neque Principatus, neque virtutes, neque instantia, neque futura, neque fortitudo, neque altitudo, neque profundum, neque creatura alia, poterit nos separare à charitate Dei, quae est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Ex hoc loco recolant Tridentini spem suam, & gratiam quam sectantur in charitate sua, ut putant ipsi, sitam, quae ita est mutabilis, incertan[?]que, ut ipsorum confessione nihil illa incertius esse possit. Hinc est, quod de incertitudine salutis disputare solent, quia relicta charitate Dei, à qua nulla creatura credentes separare potest, inhærent in figmento suo, quod ipsos adiuvare[?] non potest. Miseram gratiam Tridentinam ab haminibus otiosis inviliter[?] confictam[?], & fabricatam, quæ cultores suos non servare, nec sanare possit, sed incertos, dubios, anxios conscientiæ stimulis vexatos dimittit. Hæc est illa gratia, quæ nec salutem promittere, nec pacem conscientiis præstare potest.
units.tr: Hence comes that love of Christ, from which nothing can separate believers. "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? or anguish? or famine? or nakedness, or peril? or persecution? or the sword? I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor might, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." From this passage let the Tridentines consider their hope, and the grace they pursue in their own love, which they think is located there, a grace so changeable and uncertain that, by their own admission, nothing can be more uncertain than it. Hence they are accustomed to dispute about uncertainty of salvation, because, having abandoned the love of God, from which no creature can separate believers, they cling to their own fiction, which cannot help them. They have devised a wretched Tridentine grace, foolishly contrived and fabricated by idle men, which can neither preserve nor heal its worshippers, but leaves them uncertain, doubting, and anxious, vexed by the goads of conscience. This is that grace which can neither promise salvation nor give peace to consciences.

units.la: CAPUT III
units.tr: CAPUT III

units.la: Bellarmini responsio diluitur, & gratia confirmatur.
units.tr: Bellarmine's answer is refuted, and grace is confirmed.

units.la: Bellarminus, ne nihil dixisse videatur, responsionem excogitat ipso nihilo leviorem. Nam sic ait: {a}Deus duobus modis nos diligit, uno modo, vt simus iusti, alio modo, quia sumus iusti, & sancti. Haec ille: sed nihil ad propositum. Non enim negamus, Deum sanctos suos diligere; quia quos semel dilexit, semper diligit. Quum dilexit suos, qui erant in mundo, usq; ad finem dilexit eos. Sed omnia controversia est, de priore modo, quo Deus nos diligit, vt iusti, & sanctifimus [?]. Nam haec est illa gratia iustificationis, quae quia prior est charitate nostra, & causa charitatis nostrae, certe haec est gratia, quam nos prior dilexit Deus, non potest esse virtus nostra.
units.tr: Bellarmine, so as not to seem to have said nothing, devises a reply that is no lighter than nothing. He says: {a}God loves us in two ways: in one way, that we may be righteous; in another way, because we are righteous and holy. So he says, but this has nothing to do with the question. For we do not deny that God loves his saints, since whom he has once loved, he always loves. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. The whole controversy concerns the first way in which God loves us, namely as righteous and most holy. For this is the grace of justification, which, since it comes before our love and is the cause of our love, is certainly the grace by which God loved us first. It cannot be our own virtue.

units.la: Sed attendite artificium Sophistae. {b}Charitas quae in nobis est, inquit, quum effectum, & obiectum est benevolentiae Dei, vt effectum, est illa posterior, vt obiectum est prior. Nescio quid noui monstri semper parturiant Ieluitae. Vt probet, charitatem nostram esse aliquo modo priore charitate Dei, fingit horrendum figmentum: charitatem nostrum esse obiectum charitatis diuinae; atq; vt est obiectum, ita esse priorem. Atque ita Sophisticae Bellarmini plane enervat Theologiam Iohannis Apostoli. Nam si charitas nostra est obiectum charitatis Dei, ac proin-
units.tr: But notice the sophist's trick. The love that is in us, he says, is both the effect and the object of God's benevolence. As effect it is later; as object it is earlier. I do not know what new monsters the Jesuits are always giving birth to. To prove that our love is in some way prior to God's love, he invents a horrible fiction: that our love is the object of divine love, and that as object it is prior. So Bellarmine's sophistry plainly undermines the theology of the apostle John. For if our love is the object of God's love, and therefore prior, then John has misled us when he teaches that love consists not in our having loved God, but in his having loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Therefore the object of divine love was not our love but our misery. And lest anyone should boast of a love of ours that went before, John also teaches that our love has an antecedent cause: We love him, he says, because he first loved us. Who would think that such audacity of the Sophists should be tolerated against such plain words of Scripture?

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] proin- docet [?] rimus [?] filius [?] Ergo nostra praeut [?] idem tem [?] eum [?] eam [?] phil [?] [illegible, ~20 letters] rump [?] lx [?] nostr [?] mon [?] quid [?] liqui [?] arqu [?] cat [?] obst [?] tum [?] ne d [?] erro [?] lium [?] cuer [?] iam [?] que [?] Pro [?] fa E [?] &tan [?] proinde prior; fefellit nos Iohannes, quum docet; in hoc esse charitatem, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & miserit filium suum, vt esset propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Ergo obiectum charitatis diuinæ, non erat nostra charitas, sed nostra miseria. Et ne quis præuisam charitatem nostram iactare possit, idem Iohannes docet, esse causam antecedentem charitatis nostræ. Nos, inquis, diligimus eum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos. Quis in tam perspicuis Scripturæ verbis, tantam Sophistarum audaciam ferendam putet?
units.tr: Next, these claims break out into open Pelagianism. For the object, as the Scholastics put it, is the moving cause, not the thing moved. If, then, our love is the object of God's love, it is not moved by God's love but moves it. And what is this but what Pelagius taught: that there is something in us which could move God and stir him to love us? If someone says that Bellarmine has blocked the way to this error, since at the beginning he said that grace which makes us pleasing is a supernatural gift bestowed without debt, we answer that this error is not avoided in this way, but that it is leaping from one Pelagianism into another. For those who taught that men are predestined on account of foreseen faith stuck in the mire of Pelagianism, and on that account were condemned by Augustine, Prosper, Leo, Celestine, and indeed the whole Church. And those who today boast of foreseen faith are caught in the same game, although they acknowledge faith to be a supernatural gift of God. What difference does it make whether you introduce the opinion of foreseen faith or of foreseen love? Except that they seem to be sinning less, since they hold that God's love was stirred up by faith foreseen rather than by love foreseen.

units.la: Deinde in apertum Pelagianismum ista erumpunt. Nam obiectum, vt loquuntur Scholastici, est mouens, non motum. Si ergo charitas nostra sit obiectum charitatis diuinæ, non mouetur à charitate Dei, sed mouet illam. Et quid est hoc, nisi quod docuit Pelagius, esse aliquid in nobis, quod Deum mouere potuit, atque excitare, vt nos diligeret. Si quis dicat Bellarminum aduersus hunc errorem viam obstruxisse, quum initio dixerit, gratiam gratum facientem esse donum supernaturale sine debito collatum: respondemus, neque sic errorem hunc vitari; sed hoc esse ex uno in alium Pelagianismum transilire. Nam qui docuerunt, homines prædestinari propter præuisam fidem: in Pelagianismi luto hæserunt, atque eo nomine damnati sunt ab Augustino, & Prospero, Leone, Cælestino, adeoque vniuersa Ecclesia. Et qui hodie fidem præuisam iactant, in eodem ludo hærent, quamuis fidem donum Dei supernaturale agnoscant. Quid vero refert, fidei ne prævisæ, an charitatis prævisæ opinionem induxeris? nisi quod molimus videantur peccare, quia fide, quam quia charitate prævisa Dei [?]amorem excitatum statuunt.
units.tr: Further, Bellarmine speaks self-contradictory things and joins impossibilities together. For while he teaches that our love is a supernatural gift of God, given without debt, he then affirms that our love is the object of divine love. Who can reconcile these contradictions? If it is a gift, it is already given by God. But all the gifts of God proceed from God's goodwill. Therefore God loved first those to whom he gave this gift. But if you say "object," meaning that it is in some way before God's love, then God's love did not give us our love, because on this fiction our love existed before it was given to us by God. And so it would have to be said that our love, as object of divine love, moved God to give us our love. Who can either say or understand this absurdity? Yet according to Bellarmine's opinion it had to be said. This is the hiding-place of darkness into which the Tridentine wisdom, raging like a madman, leads insane men. But the way of truth is plain and clear, pointed out by the apostle John: that grace of God is founded in mercy, not in our love, but in God's love, by which he loved us first.
