units.la: Porro Bellarminus contradicentia loquitur, & impossibilia inter se coniungit. Nam quum doceat, charitatem nostram esse donū Dei supernaturale, sine debito: deinde idem affirmet, charitatem nostram esse obiectum diuinæ charitatis; quis hoc pugnantia componet? si donum est supernaturale, iam Deus donauit. At omnia Dei dona, ex benevolentia Dei proueniunt. Itaque Deus prius dilexit eos, quibus hoc donum dedit. At si obiectum dicas, id est, quocunq; modo ante charitatem Dei; iam charitas Dei non donauit nobis charitatem nostram. Quia ex hoc figmento charitas nostra erat antequam à Deo donata nobis esset. Atq; ita dicendum foret; charitas nostra obiectum charitatis diuinæ monuit Deum, ut donaret nobis charitatem nostram. Quis hanc absurditatem aut dicere, aut intelligere potest? At necessario sic dicendum erat ex Bellarmini sententia. Hoc est latibulum tenebrarum in quo insanos homines Tridentina insaniens sapientia inducit. Sed via veritatis perspicua est, & illustris, à Iohanne Apostolo præmonstrata; gratiam Dei, in misericordia factam esse, non in charitate nostra, sed in charitate Dei, qua nos prior dilexit. De [illegible, ~2 letters] minus bienter Christ paret [?] tiam [?] tionis [?] ftinau scripti vel pr tio inf prion stratu peribu illustr modo cordi tibus Q rudie fides iustifi nobis quam ptum post ribus nihil vele dem cati regu 3.
units.tr: Concerning the grace of God, our opponents so argue that men, carried away with admiration of themselves and puffed up, seek grace within themselves. Meanwhile Christ, as if shut out, nowhere appears. We, however, taught by the divine writings, seek the grace of God in Christ. The grace of predestination is in Christ, in whom he predestined us. Scripture places this grace in the mercy of God. In making this known, either the purpose of grace is opened up, or the imputation of Christ's righteousness is taught, or the price of our redemption is shown in the blood of Christ, or justification by faith alone, apart from works, is established. By these ways the grace of God is made clear in the Scriptures. But in whatever way it is revealed, grace is always placed in God's mercy and acceptance, not in our habits.

units.la: De gratia Dei ita disputant aduersarii, vt homines in admirationem sui rapti, atque superbientes, gratiam intra se quaerant. Interim Christus, veluti foras[?] exclusus, nusquam apparet. Nos autem à diuinis literis instituti, gratiam Dei in Christo quaerimus. Praedestinationis gratia in Christo est, in quo nos praedestinauit. Hanc gratiam in Dei misericordia scripturae constituunt, in qua re manifestanda, vel propositum gratiae aperitur, vel imputatio iustitiae Christi docetur, vel pretium redemptionis nostrae in sanguine Christi demonstrat, vel solius fidei iustificatio, exclusis operibus, statuitur. Per istos modos gratia Dei illustratur in scripturis. Quocunque autem modo patefiat, gratia semper in Dei misericordia, & acceptatione ponitur, non in habitibus nostris.
units.tr: In this matter there are four things ordered to us: justification, grace, the blood of Christ, and faith. Scripture orders these four in this way: the blood of Christ merits justification, grace bestows it on us, and faith lays hold of it. Nor does Scripture allow anything of ours to be admitted in this business besides these. For our love follows justification together with holy works. But in order that the ungodly may be justified before God, there is nothing that can either merit or receive this grace, except the blood of Christ and our faith. Further, the apostle sets the kingdom of grace against the kingdom of sin and death. Does the apostle describe this kingdom as a virtue of ours, or as some habit inhering in us? Where sin abounded, grace abounded much more, so that as sin reigned unto death, so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life. What is that grace which abounded when our sins had increased? The wretched Papists either cannot or will not understand this grace. This grace, which abounded above all our sins, which destroyed the kingdom of sin, which reigns through righteousness unto eternal life, is not anything of ours: it is not a virtue, not a habit, but the mercy and free acceptance of God, and the favour of God alone, who imputed the righteousness of Christ to us who believe. For this reason the apostle calls it the righteousness of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe.

units.la: Quatuor sunt ordinata ad nos in hac re-rudiendos[?]. Iustificatio, gratia, sanguis Christi, fides. Quatuor haec ita in scripturis ordinantur[?]: iustificationem Christi sanguis meruit, gratia nobis donat, fides apprehendit. Nec quicquam praeterea nostrum in hoc negotio scriptura admitti patitur. Nam Charitas nostra post iustificationem accedit cum sanctis operibus. Sed vt impius iustificetur coram Deo, nihil est quod hanc gratiam vel mereri possit, vel excipere; praeter sanguinem Christi, & fidem nostram. Deinde Apostolus regno peccati, & mortis, regnum gratiae opponit. Num regnum describit Apostolus virtutis nostrae[?] aut[?] habitus alicuius inhærentis nobis? Vbi au-tem est peccatum superabundauit gratia, vt quem-admodum regnauerat peccatum in mortem, ita, in-quit, gratia regnaret per iustitiam in vitam æternam. Quænam est illa gratia, quæ superabundauit, quum aucta essent peccata nostra? miseri Pó-tificii hanc gratiam, vel non possunt, vel no-lunt intelligere. Gratia hæc, quæ super omnia peccata nostra abundauit, quæ regnum pec-cati destruxit, quæ regnat per iustitiam in vi-tam æternam, nihil nostrum est, non virtus, non habitus opster[?], sed misericordia, & gra-tuita acceptatio Dei, & fauor Dei tantummo-do, qui iustitiam Christi nobis credentibus imputauit, quam propterea vocat Apostolus iustitiam Dei, per fidem Iesu Christi, in omnes, & super omnes credentes.
units.tr: There are four things set before us in this matter: justification, grace, the blood of Christ, and faith. Scripture arranges these four in this way: the blood of Christ merits justification, grace bestows it upon us, and faith lays hold of it. Scripture allows nothing of ours to be admitted into this business besides these. For our charity comes after justification, along with good works. But for the ungodly to be justified before God, there is nothing that can either merit this grace or receive it, apart from the blood of Christ and our faith. Next, the Apostle sets the kingdom of grace over against the kingdom of sin and death. Does the Apostle describe this kingdom as a power of ours, or as some habit inhering in us? "Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound; that as sin reigned unto death, even so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life." What is that grace which abounded when our sins had increased? The wretched Papists either cannot or will not understand this grace. This grace, which abounded above all our sins, which destroyed the kingdom of sin, and which reigns through righteousness unto eternal life, is nothing of ours: it is not a virtue, not a habit, but only the mercy and free acceptance of God, and the favour of God, who imputed the righteousness of Christ to us who believe. For this reason the Apostle calls it the righteousness of God, "through faith in Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all who believe."

units.la: Hæc igitur gratiæ explicatio ad salutem nostram conficiendam tanto sacrarum libe-rarum consensu statuitur; tot, ac tanta ferè se-cum salutis mysteria, de Christi pretioso illo sanguine, de prædestinatione, de vocatione, de fide, de iustificatione (quæ omnia è gratiæ Thesauro prodeunt, in eoque recondita ser-uantur) vt qui hunc lapidem loco suo moue-re ausus fuerit, vniuersam salutis nostræ stru-cturam concutere, atque occultis cuniculis subuertere deprehenditur. Itaque hæc virtus & potentia Dei in scripturis suis loquentis, tanta luce, & splendore, ipsorum etiam non-nunquam Pontificiorum oculos perstringet, vt vel inuitos in admirationem trahat, & ab errore etiam aliquando liberet; Quemadmo-dum Albertum Pigghium perstrinxerat, qui æternum Pontificium excussit. Sic enim do-cet: a Gratia acceptionem variam, non è Scholis, sed ex diuinis scripturis peramus, quandoquidem in illis fere imaginantur gratiam Dei, qualitatem alt-quam increatam animæ nostræ à Deo, vel eandem cum charitate habitam, vel distinctam ab eadem. Quæ commentitia uniuersa existimo, nec ex scripturis vllam authoritatem habere. Hæc ille. Dicunt Pō-tificii Pigghiam, alioqui Catholicum docto-rem, seductum ex lectione librorum Caluini. At Pigghiusipse testatur, se sententiam suam è le-ctione scripturarum hausisse. ô [?] Caluinum, vel aduersariorum testimonio beatum, cuius scripta tantum cum sacris scripturis consensum retinent, vt quod Pontificius Doctor celeberrimus fatetur se ex Sacræ scripturæ le-ctione habuisse, id alii Pontificii, lectioni li-brorum Caluini tribuant. Profecto nisi Scho-liasticorum sententia cum manifestis scriptu-ris pugnasset, nunquam illam deseruisset P g-ghius [?]. Sacrarum ergo scripturarum virtute ab errore Scholasticorum retra-ctus est Pigghius, quæ & Cardinalem Bellarminum retrahere possent, si eas sincerè, animo veritatis studiolo legere, & tractare voluissent.
units.tr: This explanation of grace is therefore established for the completing of our salvation by such great agreement of the sacred books; with it there go so many and such great mysteries of salvation: concerning the precious blood of Christ, concerning predestination, calling, faith and justification (all of which come forth from the treasury of grace and are kept stored up within it). So that whoever has dared to move this stone from its place is found to shake the whole structure of our salvation and to overturn it by hidden mines. Thus this power and might of God speaking in his Scriptures, with such light and splendour, will strike even the eyes of some Papists at times, so that it either draws them, though unwilling, into admiration, or even sometimes frees them from error; just as it struck Albert Pighius, who shook off the Papal yoke. For he teaches thus: "Let us seek the various acceptations of grace not from the schools but from the divine Scriptures, since in the schools they commonly imagine the grace of God to be some uncreated quality in our soul from God, either the same as charity or distinct from it. I judge all these fictions to have no authority from the Scriptures." Thus he. The Papists say that Pighius, otherwise a Catholic teacher, was led astray by reading the books of Calvin. But Pighius himself testifies that he drew his opinion from reading the Scriptures. O Calvin, blessed even by the testimony of his adversaries, whose writings retain such agreement with the holy Scriptures that what the most celebrated Papist teacher confesses he had from reading the holy Scripture, other Papists attribute to the reading of Calvin's books. Certainly, unless the opinion of the Schoolmen had clashed with the plain Scriptures, Pighius would never have abandoned it. Pighius was therefore drawn back from the error of the Schoolmen by the power of the holy Scriptures; and these could draw back Cardinal Bellarmine too, if he had been willing to read and handle them sincerely, with a mind eager for the truth.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: De Opere operato.
units.tr: On the Work Wrought (Opere operato).

units.la: QVI semel à gratiæ cognitione excid-rūt, præcipites ruunt, nec vbi sistere possint, inucinueniunt. Atque hinc est, quod Pontificii gra-tiam sacramentis & aliis institutionibus alli-gatam somniant, ita, vt nec fide, nec bono aliquo motu opus sit, quandoquidem ex ipso, vt loquuntur, opere operato, gratiam con-sequi possint. Haec est gratia Pontificia. Et ne quis nos iniuriam istis bonis viris fecisse existimet, hoc loco Pontificiorum sententiam de opere operato, quanta possumus breuitate aperiemus. Haec enim sententia, & Pontificiorum prodit superstitiosam vanitatem, & gratiam Dei vehementer ob-scurat.
units.tr: Those who have once fallen away from the knowledge of grace tumble headlong and, finding nowhere to stop, come to no firm footing. Hence it is that the Papists dream of a grace bound to the sacraments and other institutions, so that, as they say, they can obtain grace from the work wrought (ex opere operato) without any faith or any good motion of the heart being needed. This is the Papist grace. And lest anyone think we have wronged these good men, I shall set out the Papists' teaching on the work wrought, as briefly as I can, in this place. For this doctrine both betrays the superstitious vanity of the Papists and greatly obscures the grace of God.

units.la: Mart. Chemnicius è Scholasticis ostendit, opinionem operis operati esse, vt sacramenta dicantur conferre gratiam ex opere operato, etiamsi in suscipiente non sit bonus interior motus; modo non ponatur obex. Hanc peregrinam, & inconditam sententiam Scholasticorum fuisse docet ex Gabriele, qui omnium sententiariorum disputationes & opiniones in vnum collegit: ex Petro Palude, Marsilio, Alberto, Mensingero.
units.tr: Martin Chemnitz, drawing on the Scholastics, shows that the opinion of the work wrought is this: that the sacraments are said to confer grace ex opere operato, even if there is no good inward motion in the recipient, provided that no obstacle is placed in the way. He teaches that this strange and crude view of the Scholastics was taken from Gabriel, who gathered together the disputations and opinions of all the sentence-commentators, and from Peter Paludanus, Marsilius, Albert and Mensinger.

units.la: Exclamat Bellarminus, falsam esse hanc expositionem operis operati, Scholasticis iniuriam fieri, miserum Chemnicium Scholasticos non potuisse intelligere. Haec Bellarminus magno strepitu agit, neque tamen recedit ipse ab hac sententia. O miseram conditionem eorum, qui veritatem oppugnant. Pudet erroris, quem tamen mordicus retinent, nec abiiciunt hypocritae sen-tentiam,
units.tr: Bellarmine cries out that this explanation of the work wrought is false, that injustice is done to the Scholastics, and that wretched Chemnitz was unable to understand the Scholastics. Bellarmine carries on this with great noise, and yet he himself does not withdraw from this opinion. O the wretched condition of those who oppose the truth! They are ashamed of the error, which nevertheless they hold on to stubbornly, and the hypocrites do not cast off the opinion.

units.la: CAPVT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: tentiam, quam damnandam iu[?]
units.tr: ...opinion, which ought to be condemned...

units.la: Gabrielem citat Chemnicius tem. & Praeter exhibitionem signi f[?] non requiritur bonus motus interior m[?] Respondet Bellarminus, corrupte brielem, nam mox subiungit, qu[?] congruo, vel condigno merearur[?] non igitur Gabriel excludit mor[?] num, disponentem ad gratiam, [?] torium gratiæ. Hæc Bellarminus. demus: ipsum hunc motum dispon[?] Biele, & Scholastici, ac proinde ex [?] rum sententia, esse motum merito[?] riæ. Itaque sine causa reprehenditu[?] nicius, & vanæ est responsio Bellarm[?] quum motus internus, disponen[?] tiam sit meritorius, idem dicit B[?] nus, ac si respondisset, Bielem no[?] dere motum meritorium, sed mot[?] ritorium.
units.tr: Chemnitius cites Gabriel: Apart from the exhibition of the sign, no good internal motion is required. Bellarmine replies that Chemnitius has corrupted Gabriel, for Gabriel immediately adds, "who merits by congruent or condign merit." So Gabriel does not exclude every internal good motion disposing to grace, but only a meritorious one. Let us grant this: that the disposing motion itself is, according to Biel and the Scholastics, and therefore according to their opinion, meritorious of grace. Then Chemnitius is criticised without cause, and Bellarmine's answer is empty. For when the internal disposing motion is meritorious, it is the same as if he had replied that Biel excludes not a meritorious motion but a non-meritorious one.

units.la: Iam vero, motum hunc disponen[?] gratiam, esse meritorium gratiæ de c[?] proximis verbis fatetur Bellarminus; subiungit. {b}Nam et si illa dispositio pore[?] ritoria de congruo, vel etiam augmentu[?] de condigno, si sit actus ex charitate procede[?] fia est gratia, quæ datur ob dispositionem alia, q[?] ex vi sacramenti. Hæc ille. Sequamur p[?] ipsum per tenebras istas, tanquam Caru[?] fumu atq; flammas eiaculan[?] e, vt in[?] latere posset. Quæstio est, an in opere [?] bonus intern° motus aliquis à Gabriel[?] udicant. sic docen-oris exhibiti, suscipiente. citari Ga-lo motu de r gratiam: um inter-sed meri-Respon-entem. ex Pontificio-rium gra-ur Chem-nini Nam s ad gra-Bellarmi-in exclu-um me-arem ad ongruo, {b}sicenim st effeme-m gratia stamea- quedatur aulisper Italium, ebris operato statua-tur; tur; non bonus motus internus disponens ad gratiam, sed meritorius gratiæ excluditur, inquit, Bellarminus. At motus ille disponens, est etiam meritorius, inquit idé Bellarminus; Lutherani tardiores, non possunt istas tam profundas absurditates intelligere, nec tam pugnantia inter se componere. Sed videamus Romanum ingenium; quamuis ista dispositio potest esse meritoria de congruo, & condi-gno, tamen alia est gratia, quæ datur per motum disponentem meritorium, alia quæ datur ex vi sacramenti. At vera Christi gratia una est atque eadem, non alia, atque alia. Non enim aliam gratiam docet Ecclesia dari extra sacramenta, aliam in sacramentis, sed una est Dei gratia, non alia; ab eodem Christo, sive cum sacramentis, sive sine sacramentis donata, qui non est alius atque alius, sed unus idemque in omnibus suis. Sed commenticia Antichristi gratia, est alia atque alia. Verumtamen hoc illi concedamus, quod nisi concesserimus, probare non poterit, aliam esse gratiam huius dispositionis, aliam sacramenti. Quid hoc ad Chemnicium, qui hoc loco non de dispositionibus, sed de sacramentis loquitur. Probat Chemnicius, in sacramentorum receptione, ex Pontificiorum sententia, opus operatum satis esse, sine bono motu interno. Respondet Bellarminus gratiam illam, quæ est ex merito de congruo non sine bono motu esse, sed gratiam, ex vi sacramenti conferri quidem sine bono motu mentis interno. Et quid aliud erat,
units.tr: Now, that this motion which disposes a man to grace is itself meritorious of grace, Bellarmine admits in the words just quoted, and he adds: For although that disposition may be meritorious de congruo, or even increase grace de condigno, if it is an act proceeding from charity, there is a grace which is given on account of the disposition, and another which is given by the force of the sacrament. Thus he. Let us follow him through those shadows, as though through smoke and flashes of flame, so that the question may be seen clearly: whether in the work done (opus operatum) some good internal motion is required by Gabriel. Here the author's garbled text (Chemnitz, Lutherans, Bellarmine) is hard to recover word for word, but the sense is this: Bellarmine says that the good internal motion which disposes to grace is excluded, while the same motion is still meritorious. Yet the Lutherans, who are slower, cannot grasp such profound absurdities or reconcile such contradictory statements. Let us look at the Roman way of thinking. Although that disposition may be meritorious de congruo and de condigno, yet one grace is given through the meritorious disposing motion and another grace is given by the force of the sacrament. But the true grace of Christ is one and the same, not one thing and then another. For the Church does not teach that one grace is given outside the sacraments and another within them; there is one grace of God, not another, bestowed by the same Christ, whether with the sacraments or without them. He is not one Christ and then another, but one and the same in all his members. The grace of Antichrist, however, is one thing and then another. Nevertheless, let us concede this to them, since without conceding it they could not prove that the grace of this disposition is one thing and the grace of the sacrament another. But what does this have to do with Chemnitz, who in this place is speaking not of dispositions but of sacraments? Chemnitz proves that, according to the opinion of the Papists, in the reception of the sacraments the work done is enough without a good internal motion. Bellarmine replies that the grace which is de congruo merited is not without a good motion, but that grace is conferred by the force of the sacrament, indeed without a good internal motion of mind. And what else was Chemnitz contending, than what the Schoolmen teach?

units.la: erat; liastic licet fund omn ditor tur. bon mot tium mot nun çilia mot sitio çilia reft a p mit inft riu Qu mo iu ce ca op re d d [?] erat, quod Chemnicius contendit, à Scho-lasticis doceri ? Deinde (nisi forte miseri scilicet Lutherani non possint intelligere profunditatis Sarpianæ [?] in Iesuitis sese efferentis) omnis bonus motus in opere operato excluditur, quia omnis meritorius motus excluditur. Nam nullus est apud Pontificios motus bonus qui non sit meritorius ; quum etiam motum aliquem non bonum faciant meritorium. Quod ex Bellarmino sic probamus. Homo nondum reconciliatus nondum habet bonum motum mentis: at homo nondum reconciliatus mereri posset: sequitur ergo aliquem motum non bonum esse meritorium [?]. Propositio vera est ex Apostolo: quia nondum reconciliatus, hoc est impius nihil boni cogitare potest. Assumptio est Bellarmini, sic enim docet: {a}potest homo nondum reconciliatus per opera pœ-nitentia impetrare, & mereri ex congruo gratiam iustificationis. Iam, si motus non bonus meritorius sit, omnis bonus motus meritorius erit. Qui ergo docent, in opere operato nullum motum meritorium requiri, docent certe nullum bonum motum requiri.
units.tr: Furthermore (unless perhaps the wretched Lutherans cannot understand the profundity of Sarpi's, which the Jesuits put forward), every good motion is excluded in the work done, because every meritorious motion is excluded. For among the Papists there is no good motion which is not meritorious, since they make even some motion which is not good meritorious. We prove this from Bellarmine as follows. A man not yet reconciled does not yet have a good motion of mind; but a man not yet reconciled can merit; it follows, therefore, that some motion which is not good is meritorious. The proposition is true by the Apostle's word: because one who is not yet reconciled, that is, impious, can think nothing good. The assumption is Bellarmine's, for thus he teaches: a man not yet reconciled can, by works of repentance, obtain and merit de congruo the grace of justification. Now, if a motion which is not good is meritorious, every good motion will be meritorious. Those, therefore, who teach that no meritorious motion is required in the work done certainly teach that no good motion is required.

units.la: Quod si hæc sententia Pontificiis non placeat, quare non diserte sese exprimunt ? dicant anathema omnibus docentibus, in opere operato, ad gratiam consequendam, non requiri bonum motum mentis. Hoc enim dicunt, imo contrarium habet Concilium Tridentinum.
units.tr: But if this opinion does not please the Papists, why do they not express themselves plainly? Let them pronounce an anathema on all who teach that, for obtaining grace in the work done, a good motion of mind is not required. For this is what they say, or rather the Council of Trent holds the contrary.

units.la: Est igitur hæc communis sententia Scho-lastilasticorum[?]; sacramenta ex opere operato cō-ferre gratiam, ita vt non requiratur bonus motus mentis meritorius. Sic docuit Scotus nostèr. {a} Sacramentum ex virtute operis operati confert gratiam, ita quod non requiritur bonus motus interior, qui meretur gratiam, sed sufficit, quod suscipiens non ponat obicem. Iam qui omnem mo-tum internum meritorium excludunt, certe fidem excludunt, quia fides est motus meritorius si quis alius sit. Itaq; nos nullam istis iniuriam facimus, quum dicimus, ex eorum sententia in opere operato fidem non requiri. Et nelogius[?] quaeramus, Bellarminus ipse fatetur, gratiam iustificationis per sacramenta ita dari, vt non excitetur actualis fides, aut dilectio. Sic enim ille: {b} Sacramenta iustificant, at certe non iustificant, nisi concurrendo per modum instrumenti, ad infusionem iustitiae habitu-lis. Nam si iustificare deberent excitando actualem fidem & dilectionem, frustra adhiberetur baptismus infantibus & frustra baptizarentur, vel reconciliarentur, si qui vi morbi vsum rationis & sensum amisissent. Haec ille. Respondemus hanc rationem falso inniti fun-damento. Falsum est, sacramenta per modum instrumenti infundere iustitiam habitua-lem.
units.tr: This, therefore, is the common opinion of the Scholastics: that sacraments confer grace by the work done, so that a meritorious good motion of mind is not required. Thus taught our Scotus: A sacrament, by the virtue of the work done, confers grace, so that a good inner motion which merits grace is not required, but it suffices that the recipient does not place an obstacle. Now those who exclude every meritorious internal motion certainly exclude faith, since faith is a meritorious motion if any motion is. Therefore we do them no injustice when we say that, on their opinion, faith is not required in the work done. And, lest we look further, Bellarmine himself admits that the grace of justification is given through the sacraments in such a way that actual faith or love is not stirred up. For thus he writes: Sacraments justify, but certainly they do not justify unless they concur by way of instrument to the infusion of habitual righteousness. For if they were to justify by stirring up actual faith and love, baptism would be administered to infants in vain, and they would be baptized or reconciled in vain, if those who by force of disease had lost the use of reason and sense. Thus he. We answer that this argument rests on a false foundation. It is false that sacraments infuse habitual righteousness by way of an instrument.

units.la: Primo, non habent sacramenta modum instrumenti infusorii, sed modum signaculi. Deinde non infundunt gratiam, quae prius non inerat, sed obsignant eam, quae suscepta fuerat in credentibus. Postremo non infundunt habitum illum, quia talis habitus non est. Nulla est enim gratia iustificationis, quam non apprehendit fides. Apostolus docet, sacramenta esse signacula fidei. Rom.4.11. nec valet di-stinctio illa Pontificiorum, qua distinguunt inter sacramenta legis, & Euangelii. Nam utcunque hæc distingui possint: certum est tamen, in ea re convenire, ad quam rem confirmandam, Apostolus verba illa adducit, ut & imputationis, & sacramentorum doctrinam confirmet. Loquitur enim de A-brahamo, non sub lege, sed in præputio, in eumq; finem hæc affert Apostolus, ut Abrahamus intelligatur pater omnium credentium in præputio. Sic enim dicit Apostolus: Abrahamo fides imputata est pro iustitia, & signum accepit circumcisionis signaculum iustitiæ fidei, quæ fuerat in præputio, ut esset pater omnium credēn-tium in præputio, ut imputaretur etiam ipsis iustitia. Ex quibus Apostoli verbis constat, sacramenta in præputio esse signacula fidei. Constat etiam, Abrahamum hoc loco omnibus in Ecclesia credentibus exemplar proponi: quia dicitur pater credentium in præputio, quia in præputio accepit sacramentum, signaculum iustitiæ fidei. Itaque sic disputamus. Omnes credentes eodem modo iustificantur, quo Abraham iustificatus fuit. Hæc propositio certissima est, quia Abraham hoc respectu dicitur pater omnium credentium in præputio. At Abraham non fuit iustificatus per sacramenta, concurrendo per modum instrumenti, ad infusionem iustitiæ habitualis: sed p imputationem justitiæ. Omnes ergo credentes eodem modo justificantur. Et est hæc ipsa conclusio Apostoli: ut imputetur, inquit, etiam ipsis justitia. Videmus quanta sit repugnantia inter doctrinam Tridentinam, & Doctrinâ Apostolicam, de virtute sacramentorum. Nos virtutem & usum sacramentorum ex manifestis scripturis ostendimus. At num possunt Tridentini è scripturis ostendere figmêta[?] sua, de instrumenti modo de infusionibus suis, de habituali justitia infusa ira[?], ut non sit fide apprehensa? Hæc è Scoto, Gabriele, reliquisve eiusdem fermenti facile sumere possunt, è scripturis non possunt. Sanctus Petrus etiam de Baptismo idem habet, quod Paulus de circumcisione docuerat; docet enim, baptismum non esse in infusionibus, aut infusionibus, aut habitibus sine fide; quod somniant isti: sed esse bonæ conscientiæ stipulationem apud Deum. Hæc stipulatio apud Deum sine fide esse non posset: nec ergo Baptismus. Sic igitur sacramentorum genuinum usum è Sacris literis colligimus, qui ex Scholasticis frustra quæ-ritur.
units.tr: First, the sacraments do not have the mode of an infusing instrument, but the mode of a seal. Second, they do not infuse a grace which was not previously present, but they seal that grace which had been received by believers. Last, they do not infuse that habit, because no such habit exists. For there is no grace of justification which faith does not apprehend. The Apostle teaches that sacraments are seals of faith (Rom. 4.11). Nor does that distinction of the Papists avail, by which they separate the sacraments of the law from those of the Gospel. For however these may be distinguished, it is certain that they agree in the matter which the Apostle adduces those words to confirm, namely the doctrine of imputation and of the sacraments alike. For he speaks of Abraham, not under the law but in uncircumcision, and the Apostle brings this forward for the purpose of showing that Abraham is to be understood as the father of all believers in uncircumcision. For thus the Apostle says: Faith was imputed to Abraham for righteousness, and he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had in uncircumcision, so that he might be father of all believers in uncircumcision, that righteousness might be imputed to them also. From these words of the Apostle it is clear that sacraments in uncircumcision are seals of faith. It is also clear that Abraham is set forth in this place as an example to all believers in the Church, since he is called the father of believers in uncircumcision, because in uncircumcision he received the sacrament, the seal of the righteousness of faith. So we argue thus. All believers are justified in the same way that Abraham was justified. This proposition is most certain, because Abraham in this respect is called the father of all believers in uncircumcision. But Abraham was not justified through sacraments concurring by way of instrument to the infusion of habitual righteousness, but through the imputation of righteousness. Therefore all believers are justified in the same way. And this is the very conclusion of the Apostle: that righteousness, he says, may be imputed to them also. We see how great the contradiction is between the Tridentine doctrine and the apostolic doctrine concerning the power of the sacraments. We show the power and use of the sacraments from plain Scripture. But can the Tridentines show from Scripture their fictions: the mode of an instrument, their infusions, and habitual righteousness infused which is not apprehended by faith? These things they may easily take from Scotus, Gabriel and the others of that leaven, but not from Scripture. Saint Peter also says about baptism what Paul had taught about circumcision. For he teaches that baptism is not a matter of infusions, or of habits without faith, as those men dream, but is the pledge of a good conscience before God. Such a pledge before God could not exist without faith, and therefore neither could baptism. Thus we gather the genuine use of the sacraments from the Sacred Letters, which is vainly sought from the Scholastics.

units.la: Neque tamen frustra Baptismus datur infantibus; quia fides, & stimulatio apud Deum necessario, secundum scripturas, requiritur in Baptismo: nam infantes baptizantur in fide parentum. Quia promissio datur fidelibus & ipsorum liberis. Act. 2. 38. & Gen. 17. sicut & circumcidebantur infantes. Quod si sacramenta conferrent gratiam justificationis si-ne fi-
units.tr: Nevertheless, baptism is not given to infants in vain, because faith and the stipulation before God are necessarily required in baptism according to the Scriptures: infants are baptized in the faith of their parents. The promise is given to believers and to their children: Acts 2:38, and Gen. 17, where infants were circumcised as well.

units.la: ne fid nus: c ficatio stifica natist ter p sanct tiam ption quot, indui modo stinu perce Bifi mali ergo re o iust cat. F obs Aq can quia Chr col Au ad no igi in ne fide ex opere operato, ut habet Bellarmi-nus: omnes baptizati haberent gratiam iusti-ficationis, & sanctificarentur: nam gratia iu-stificat, & sanctificat. Augustinus contra Do-natistas disputans, distinctionem adhibet in-ter perceptionem sacramentorum, & gratiam sanctificationis; qua infallibiliter probat, gra-tiam non necessario conferri per ipsam perce-ptionē sacramenti ex opere operato. {a}Quot-quot, inquit, in Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis: at auari[?], multi, ebriosi baptizantur: quo-modo ergo Christum induunt? Respondet Augustinus: Induunt homines Christum aliquando vsq; ad perceptionē sacramenti, aliquando vsq; ad vitæ sanctificationem. Primum commune esse potest bonis & malis: alterum proprium piorum. Hæc ille. Huius ergo iudicio ipsa perceptio sacramenti ex opere operato non sanctificat, non confert gratiā iustificationis: quia gratia hæc semper sanctifi-cat.
units.tr: If sacraments conferred the grace of justification without faith, ex opere operato, as Bellarmine holds, then all who were baptized would have the grace of justification and be sanctified, for grace both justifies and sanctifies. Augustine, disputing against the Donatists, draws a distinction between the reception of the sacraments and the grace of sanctification, and by this he infallibly proves that grace is not necessarily conferred through the mere reception of the sacrament ex opere operato. "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ," but many avaricious and drunken people are baptized: how then do they put on Christ? Augustine answers: Men put on Christ sometimes as far as the reception of the sacrament, sometimes as far as the sanctification of life. The first can be common to good and bad; the second belongs to the pious alone. So he. By his judgment, therefore, the mere reception of the sacrament ex opere operato does not sanctify and does not confer the grace of justification, because this grace always sanctifies.

units.la: Hæc responsio Augustini eo est accuratius obseruanda, quia ex eodem scripturæ loco, Aquinas sic concludit: {b}Sacramenta noua legis causant gratiam per modum instrumenti, nempe quia Apostolus dicit, quotquot baptizati estis in Christo, Christum induistis. Aquinas non recte colligit: nam duplex est responsio: Prior est Augustini, in illa distinctione superius a nobis adducta. Quia affirmat Augustinus, malos qui non sanctificantur, sacramenta percipere; ipsa igitur perceptio non causat gratiam per modum instrumenti, sicut docet Aquinas. Altera responsio est, vt intelligamus Apostolum loqui de filiis Dei qui vere credunt. Hanc autem fuisse Apostoli mentem, constat ex integra comprehensione totius sententiae, nam integra sententia est haec: Omnes enim filii Dei estis, per fidem in Christo Iesu; nam quicunque Christo baptizati estis, Christum induistis. Apostolus hic loquitur de filiis Dei, vere iustificatis & sanctificatis, atque de eorum fide. Fraudulenter ergo faciunt, qui fidem à sacramentis amotam cogitant, vt ipsa sacramenta per se sine fide de gratiam conferre intelligantur. Constat igitur, sententiam Pontificiorum de opere operato esse huiusmodi, vt dicant, sacramenta conferre gratiam, vel causare, sicut aiunt isti, per modum instrumenti, ex opere operato, sine fide. Scholastici docent, nullum motum meritorium requiri: fatetur Bellarminus, fidem actualem non requiri, hoc est, fidem illam, quae iustitiam imputatam apprehendat, non hic esse necessariam. Ea fidem quam includit Apostolus, excludunt isti. Iure igitur dicimus, hanc esse istorum sententiam, in opere operato non requiri fidem, quae promissionem apprehendat.
units.tr: We must observe Augustine's answer all the more carefully because Aquinas draws his conclusion from the same passage of Scripture: The sacraments of the new law cause grace by way of an instrument, namely because the Apostle says, "As many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Aquinas does not draw the conclusion correctly, for there are two answers. The first is Augustine's, in the distinction we have cited above: he affirms that wicked people who are not sanctified receive the sacraments, so the mere reception does not cause grace by way of an instrument, as Aquinas teaches. The second answer is that we should understand the Apostle to be speaking of the sons of God who truly believe. That this was the Apostle's meaning is clear from the whole context, for the full sentence reads: For you are all sons of God, through faith in Christ Jesus; for as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. The Apostle here speaks of the sons of God, truly justified and sanctified, and of their faith. Those who think of faith as removed from the sacraments, so that the sacraments are understood to confer grace by themselves without faith, act deceitfully. It is therefore clear that the Papists' doctrine of ex opere operato is this: that the sacraments confer grace, or cause it, as they say, by way of an instrument, ex opere operato, without faith. The Schoolmen teach that no meritorious motion is required; Bellarmine admits that actual faith is not required, that is, that faith which apprehends the imputed righteousness is not necessary here. The faith the Apostle includes these men exclude. Rightly, then, we say that it is their doctrine that faith which apprehends the promise is not required in the ex opere operato.

units.la: Ex istis interpretibus nos sensum Concilii Tridentini investigamus, vbi sic docet: I. Si quis dixerit, per ipsa nova legis sacramenta ex opere operato non conferri gratiam, sed solam fidem divinae promissionis, ad gratiam consequendam sufficere, anathema sit. Insidiosè ista ponuntur à Tridentinis, quasi nova sententia sola fides ita prae-dica[?] dicarent mentor opponi promiss[?] mentis theû[?] cili[?] fo[?] docet quiri. recte[?] prehen[?] mais[?] &u[?] cl[?] opini[?] cis ex[?] nec a[?] dæ fi[?] pli p[?] vel r[?] mu[?] Sch[?] nit vny[?] nu[?] per Po[?] rit[?] m[?] o[?] r[?] q[?] dicaretur, ut usum reiceremus verbi, & sacra-mentorum. Sed quum Tridentini hæc duo opponunt, opus operatum, & fidem, quæ in promissione excipit gratiam, siue in sacra-mentis, siue extra sacramenta; ex hac anti-thesi satis constat, fidem exclusam. Quæ Con-cilii sententia illustratur à Bellarmino, quum docet fidem, quam vocat actualem, non re-quiri. Ita, si Bellarminus Concilii sententiam recte exponit, fides actualis, hoc est, fides ap-prehendens promissionem, excluditur. O-mnis igitur fides excluditur in adultis, qui a-du credunt, vel credere debent. Hæc est illa opinio noua, quam Tridentini & Scholasti-cis exceperunt, quam nec retinere possunt, nec abiicere volunt. Pudet eos huius absur-dæ fidei, & tamen mordicus retinent: vel i-psi penitus deponant, & anathemate feriant, vel ne nobis succenseant, quod ipsis tribui-mus hanc nomitatem quam dimittere nolunt. Scholasticorum omnium sententiam propo-nit Bellarminus (à qua Tridentini ne latum unguem discedere statuunt) in opere operato nullum motum meritorium requiri. Nonne penitus excludunt fidem? nam vel ipsorum Pontificiorum sententia, fides est motus me-ritorius. Concludimus itaque, hanc esse ge-nuinam Pontificiorum sententiam, in opere operato non requiri fidem.
units.tr: From these interpreters we investigate the sense of the Council of Trent, which teaches thus: I. If anyone shall say that grace is not conferred through the new sacraments of the law ex opere operato, but that faith in the divine promise alone suffices to obtain grace, let him be anathema. The Tridentines set this forth insidiously, as though it were a new opinion that faith alone were opposed to the operation of the sacraments, as if we wished to reject the use of the Word and of the sacraments. But since the Tridentines set these two things against each other, the ex opere operato and faith which receives grace in the promise, whether in the sacraments or outside them, this antithesis makes it sufficiently plain that faith is excluded. This sense of the Council is illustrated by Bellarmine when he teaches that the faith he calls actual is not required. So, if Bellarmine rightly expounds the Council's meaning, actual faith, that is, faith apprehending the promise, is excluded. All faith is therefore excluded in adults who believe, or ought to believe. This is that new opinion which the Tridentines and the Schoolmen have adopted and which they can neither keep nor abandon. They are ashamed of this absurd faith, yet they cling to it stubbornly; either let them abandon it entirely and strike it with anathema, or let them not be angry with us for attributing to them this novelty which they refuse to give up. Bellarmine sets forth the opinion of all the Schoolmen, from which the Tridentines decide not to depart a hair's breadth: that no meritorious motion is required in the ex opere operato. Do they not entirely exclude faith? For even according to the Papists' own view, faith is a meritorious motion. We conclude, therefore, that this is the genuine doctrine of the Papists: that faith is not required in the ex opere operato.

units.la: Opinio ista, quæ docet sacramenta confer-re gratiam ex vi operis operati sine bono mo-tu meritorio, nō ponenti obicem, circa Ioan-[?] nis Scoti sæculum enata videtur. Aquinas ad hanc structurâ lapides quosdam attulisse videtur, quum docuerit: Sacramenta nova legis gratiam causare per modum instrumenti, hæc occasionem Sophistis insequentibus dederunt philosophandi suo more. Verum Aquinas nihil habet de opere operato, aut de obice[?]. Hæc addita videntur à posterioribus. Atque ita fides Tridentina tanquam ramosa tunica, ex multis & variis panniculis consarcinata randem congesta coaluit. Ante hæc tempora inaudita erat hæc opinio in Ecclesia Romana. Hæc de opere operato.
units.tr: This opinion, which teaches that the sacraments confer grace by the force of the work worked, without any good meritorious motion and without placing an obstacle, seems to have arisen around the time of John Duns Scotus. Aquinas seems to have supplied some of the stones for this structure when he taught that the sacraments of the new law cause grace by way of an instrument; this gave the Sophists who followed the occasion to philosophize in their own way. Yet Aquinas says nothing of the ex opere operato or of an obstacle. These additions seem to have been made by later writers. And so the Tridentine faith, like a many-branched tunic, patched together from many and various scraps, at last came together and took shape. Before these times this opinion was unheard of in the Roman Church. So much on the ex opere operato.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Obiectiones Bellarmini examinantur & diluuntur.
units.tr: Bellarmine's objections are examined and refuted.

units.la: CArdinalis Bellarminus quum videat, se gratiam istam inhærentem probare non posse, nisi prius iustitiam Christi credentibus imputatam reiiciat, immane facinus aggreditur. Probaturus enim, hanc iustitiam inhærentem, imputationem iustitiæ Christi convellere tentat. At facilius Solem de cælo detrahet, quam Christum iustitiæ Solem de sua Ecclesia. Et in eo Iesuitarum improbitas insolentius in Ecclesia Dei se efferre videtur, quod non verentur ea monere, quæ ante ipsos nemo monere ausus fuit. Nam viri docti & graves in Ecclesia Romana, hæc inter se convenire posse docuerunt, imputationem scilicet[?] iustitiæ Christi, & iustitiam inhærentem, Nam illi iustitiam nobis inhærentem, sancti-tatem appellarunt. Sic Cardinalis Contare-nus, cuius sententiam iam commemoraui; sic multi alii. Nam in iustificatione impii in-telligunt, docentque, nos iustificatos non no-stra, sed aliena iustitia nobis imputata, nem-pe Christi. At vero quum iustificati in ope-ribus sanctitatis proficiunt, vt qui iustifica-tur, iustificetur adhuc; hanc iustitiam, siue iustificationis nostræ declarationem, atque ostensionem vocare solebant iustitiam inhæ-rentem. Contra quam sententiam nos nihil habemus quod opponamus. Hæc antiquo-rum patrum, atque Ecclesiæ Romanæ sen-tentia tamdiu in Ecclesia valuit, donec Iesui-tæ ex fraterculorum consarcinatis figmentis, aliam excogitarunt. Illud autem hoc loco ob-seruamus, doctrinam impurationis iustitiæ Christi primùm à Iesuitis reiectam fuisse. Sche-lastici enim impurationem Christi, sicut nec confirmant, ita aeque nominatim reiiciunt. Iesuitæ autem, quum videant se nō posse Scho-lasticorum commentum de merito congrui, de opere operato, de infusione habitualis gra-tiæ recipere, nisi imputationem iustitiæ Chri-sti reiiciant: maluerunt Christum cum sua iu-stitia repudiare, quam figmenta hæc non am-plecti. Audiamus iam, quibus argumentis iu-stitiam Christi imputatam reiiciat Bellarmi-nus, vt iustitiam inhærentem statuat.
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine, seeing that he cannot prove this inherent grace unless he first rejects the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, undertakes a monstrous crime. For in trying to prove inherent righteousness, he attempts to overthrow the imputation of Christ's righteousness. But it would be easier to pull the sun from the sky than to remove Christ, the Sun of righteousness, from his Church. In this the impudence of the Jesuits seems to show itself more insolently in the Church of God, since they do not hesitate to advise what no one before them dared to advise. For learned and serious men in the Roman Church have taught that these two can agree: the imputation of Christ's righteousness and inherent righteousness. They called the righteousness inherent in us "sanctity." So did Cardinal Contarini, whose opinion I have already mentioned, and so did many others. For they understand, and teach, that in the justification of the ungodly we are justified not by our own righteousness but by another's, imputed to us, namely Christ's. But when the justified make progress in works of holiness, since he who is justified is still being justified, they were accustomed to call this righteousness, or the declaration and manifestation of our justification, inherent righteousness. We have nothing to oppose to this opinion. This opinion of the ancient Fathers and of the Roman Church held sway in the Church for so long, until the Jesuits, from the patched-together fictions of their little brothers, devised another. We observe at this point, however, that the doctrine of the imputation of Christ's righteousness was first rejected by the Jesuits. For the Schoolmen, just as they do not confirm it, so likewise do not expressly reject it. The Jesuits, however, since they see that they cannot accept the Schoolmen's invention of merit of congruity, of the work wrought, and of the infusion of habitual grace unless they reject the imputation of Christ's righteousness, preferred to repudiate Christ with his righteousness rather than not embrace these figments. Let us now hear by what arguments Bellarmine rejects the imputed righteousness of Christ, in order to establish inherent righteousness.

units.la: Primo ex eo loco pugnat: Per obedientiam
units.tr: First he contends from that passage: By the obedience

units.la: vnius hominis, iusti constituuntur multi, a Non, inquit, per obedientiam vnius Christi iustos multos constitui existimamus, in eo sensu, vt merito obedientiae Christi reconcilietur nobis Deus, & ab eo iustitia donemur, quae sit qualitas animae nostrae infusa, & inhaerem. Haec illae. Egregia probatio Cardinalis: non existimamus. Doctissimus Cardinalis in maximo religionis articulo videtur balbutire, & sine sensu loqui. Merito, inquit, obedientiae Christi reconciliatur nobis Deus, & ab eo iustitia donamur, quae est nobis inhaerens. Huius sententiae pars posterior pugnat cum priore. Nam si merito obedientia Christi Deus nobis reconcilietur, ita vt a Deo iustitia donemur: quaerimus a Domino Cardinali, quaenam sit illa iustitia donata a Deo, partā autem merito obedientiae Christi? Respondet, esse nobis inhaerentem. At Dom. Cardinalis non cogitat se impossibilia contingere: nam iustitia, quae ex merito obedientiae Christi nascitur, est extra nos: quia Christus a Deo nobis facta est iustitia. Atq; hinc Apostolus hominis credentis beatitudinem definit in iustitia imputata, Christus factus a Deo nobis iustitia, iustitia nobis donata, iustitia nobis imputata: alienam iustitiam demonstrant non inhaerentem.
units.tr: of one man many are made righteous. "No," he says, "we do not hold that many are made righteous by the obedience of Christ alone, in the sense that God is reconciled to us by the merit of Christ's obedience and that righteousness, which is an infused quality of our soul and inherent in us, is given to us by him." So he says. An excellent proof from the Cardinal: "we do not hold." The most learned Cardinal seems to stammer in the greatest article of religion and to speak without sense. "By the merit of Christ's obedience," he says, "God is reconciled to us, and by him we are given righteousness, which is inherent in us." The latter part of this statement fights with the former. For if God is reconciled to us by the merit of Christ's obedience, so that we are given righteousness by God, we ask the Lord Cardinal what that righteousness is which is given by God but obtained by the merit of Christ's obedience. He answers that it is inherent in us. But the Lord Cardinal does not consider that he is asserting impossibilities. For the righteousness that arises from the merit of Christ's obedience is outside us, because Christ has been made righteousness to us by God. And hence the Apostle defines the blessedness of the believing man in imputed righteousness: Christ made by God righteousness to us, righteousness given to us, righteousness imputed to us. These show a foreign righteousness, not an inherent one.

units.la: Deinde videte quomodo Dom. Cardinalis sese implicet atq; illaqueet. Merito, inquit, Christi Deus nobis reconciliatur, & a Deo iustitia donamur quae est nobis inhaerens. Vnde est iustitia inhaerens? ex merito nostro: hic est communis consensus omnium Tridentinorum. Vnde vnd impp Car eo n tia i tia c cipi Bell recor iusti bisc dict cert mer test haec don tiar con haec domu iust qui rec stub acc no C care ra Unde est iustitia nobis à Deo donata, iustitia imputata, ex merito obedientiae Christi, inquit Cardinalis. Hic Cardinalis quo plus luctatur, eo magis suo nodo constringitur. Nam iustitia inhaerentem esse ex merito nostro, sententia est omnium eorum, qui meritu congrui recipiunt, ac proinde omnium Iesuitarum. Itaque Bellarminus sic docet: {a} Posse hominem nondum reconciliatum impetrare & mereri de congruo gratiam iustificationis. At si gratia iustificationis sit nobis ex merito congrui, ubi iam est meritum obedientiae Christi, & iustitia à Deo nobis donata? certè meritum Christi plane extinguitur per meritum hoc Iesuiticum ex congruo: nec potest Dom. Cardinalis ita plumbeus esse, quin haec videat [illegible, ~9 letters] esse, iustitia nobis à Deo donata, ex merito obedientiae Christi, & iustitia nobis inhaerens, quam homo nondum reconciliatus mereri potest ex congruo. Et tamen haec inter se pugnantia unius sententiae periodo sine sensu comprehendere voluit doctissimus Cardinalis. Quando impius iustificatur, iustitiam imputatam, à Deo donatam habet, quia propria destituitur. At quando homo non reconciliatus meretur ex congruo gratiam iustificationis, ex se gratiam sumit, non donatam accipit. Impius autem intelligitur quicunque non est reconciliatus Deo nisi ex Domini Cardinalis sententia quando impius iustificatur, intelligendum est, impium iustificare seipsum. Haec est Pelagianorum pestifera doctrina, à Tridentinis suscepta, quae gratiam Christi euacuat. Videmus ex hoc, in qua-le barathrum præcipites ruant, qui doctri-nam imputationis impugnant.
units.tr: Next, see how the Lord Cardinal entangles and ensnares himself. "By the merit of Christ," he says, "God is reconciled to us, and by God we are given righteousness, which is inherent in us." Whence comes inherent righteousness? From our own merit: this is the common consensus of all the Tridentines. Whence comes righteousness given to us by God, imputed righteousness, from the merit of Christ's obedience, says the Cardinal. Here the Cardinal, the more he struggles, the more he is bound by his own knot. For that inherent righteousness comes from our merit is the opinion of all who accept merit of congruity, and therefore of all the Jesuits. Thus Bellarmine teaches: that a man not yet reconciled can obtain and merit by congruity the grace of justification. But if the grace of justification is ours by merit of congruity, where now is the merit of Christ's obedience, and the righteousness given to us by God? Surely the merit of Christ is plainly extinguished by this Jesuitical merit of congruity. Nor can the Lord Cardinal be so leaden that he does not see that these are: righteousness given to us by God from the merit of Christ's obedience, and inherent righteousness, which a man not yet reconciled can merit by congruity. And yet the most learned Cardinal wished to comprehend these mutually contradictory things in one sentence, without sense. When the ungodly is justified, he has imputed righteousness, given by God, because he is destitute of his own. But when a man not reconciled merits by congruity the grace of justification, he takes grace from himself; he does not receive it as a gift. Now whoever is not reconciled to God is, on the Lord Cardinal's view, the ungodly. So when the ungodly is justified, it must be understood that the ungodly justifies himself. This is the pestilent doctrine of the Pelagians, taken up by the Tridentines, which empties the grace of Christ. From this we see into what abyss those fall headlong who attack the doctrine of imputation.

units.la: Pergit tamen Cardinalis, & hoc suum fo-mnium probare vult ex antithesi verborum Apostoli. dixerat enim Apostolus, quemadmo-dum per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi: & continuò adiecit; ita per obedientiam vnius hominis iusti constituuntur multi. Conflat autem, inquit Cardinalis, non non constitui peccatores per imputationem iustitiæ, quæ fuit in Adamo, sed per iniustitiam nobis inhærentem per modum habitus, igitur iusti etiam constituimur, si quid Apostoli antithesis valet, non per imputationem iustitiæ, quæ est à Christo, sed per iustitiam nobis inhærentem per modum habitus.
units.tr: Yet the Cardinal goes on, and wants to prove his dream from the antithesis in the Apostle's words. For the Apostle had said: as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, and immediately added: so by the obedience of one man many are made righteous. "It is clear," says the Cardinal, "that we are not made sinners by the imputation of the righteousness which was in Adam, but by unrighteousness inherent in us by way of habit. Therefore we too are made righteous, if the Apostle's antithesis holds, not by the imputation of righteousness which is from Christ, but by righteousness inherent in us by way of habit."

units.la: Respondeo: vtrumque constat, & imputati nobis peccatum Adæ, & iniustitiam nobis inesse inhærentem. negat Cardinalis imputationem peccati, vt facilius imputatione iustitiæ negare possit. At manifestis scripturæ testimoniis conuincitur. Deus minatur se visitaturum iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam, & quartam generationem. Quod fieri non potest, nisi impiis, & impœnitentibus filiis, imputando peccata parentum. Quod si Cardinalis hæreat in peccato Adæ, quasi non imputato: consulat Apostolum eo ipso, quem citat loco Cardinalis. Nam eodem capite A-postolus hæc habet verba: Peccatum autem non imputabatur quum lex non esset. Sed regnauit mors ab Adam vsque ad Mosen, etiam in eos, qui non peccapeccaverunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adæ. Quibus verbis intelligere potest Cardinalis, legem hoc facere, ut peccatum imputetur. Est igitur peccati imputatio, sicut & iustitiæ, potest etiam intelligere, mortem ab Adamo usque ad Mosem regnantem, probare, peccatum Adæ imputari paruulis, iis scilicet, qui nõ peccaverunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adæ, nam Adæ peccatum actuale fuerat, paruulorum autem ex Adamo nascentium peccatum est originale. Qui quamuis non peccent ad similitudinem peccati Adæ, tamen peccatum Adæ imputatum habent, ac proinde peccatores constituuntur ex imputatione.
units.tr: I answer: both are clear, both that Adam's sin is imputed to us and that unrighteousness inheres in us. The Cardinal denies the imputation of sin, so that he may more easily deny the imputation of righteousness. But he is refuted by the manifest testimonies of Scripture. God threatens that he will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation. This cannot happen unless the sins of the parents are imputed to impious and impenitent children. But if the Cardinal sticks at Adam's sin as though it were not imputed, let him consult the Apostle in the very passage the Cardinal cites. For in the same chapter the Apostle has these words: "Sin is not imputed when there is no law. But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam." By these words the Cardinal can understand that the law causes sin to be imputed. There is, then, an imputation of sin, just as there is of righteousness. He can also understand, from death reigning from Adam to Moses, that Adam's sin is imputed even to infants, namely to those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression. For Adam's sin was actual, but the sin of infants born of Adam is original. Although they do not sin in the likeness of Adam's sin, nevertheless they have Adam's sin imputed to them, and therefore they are constituted sinners by imputation.

units.la: Constat, inquit Cardinalis, nos non constitui peccatores per imputationem iniustitiæ quæ fuit in Adamo, quo modo hoc constat? aut quibus? qui hæc dicit, quomodo peccatum originale tueri potest? vel originale peccatum est prorsus negandum cum Pelagio, vel per iniustitiæ imputationem, quæ fuit in Adamo, peccatores constituimur, quia originale peccatum est peccatum imputatum, non negamus peccatum hoc inhærere, atque etiam inhabitare, sed quod addit Cardinalis, peccatores nos constitui, per iniustitiam inhærentem per modum habitus, uniuersaliter verum esse non potest, quia peccatores constituimur per peccatum originale, quod non est inhærens per modum habitus.
units.tr: "It is clear," says the Cardinal, "that we are not made sinners by the imputation of the unrighteousness which was in Adam." How is this clear? And on whose authority? He who says this, how can he defend original sin? Either original sin must be wholly denied, with Pelagius, or we are made sinners by the imputation of the unrighteousness which was in Adam, because original sin is imputed sin. We do not deny that this sin inheres, and indeed dwells in us. But what the Cardinal adds, that we are made sinners through unrighteousness inherent by way of habit, cannot be true universally, because we are made sinners through original sin, which is not inherent by way of habit.

units.la: Deinde probare contendit Cardinalis, gratiam esse habitum nobis inhærentem, ex illis verbis: Aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ saliëntis in vitam æternam. fons hic, inquit dom. Cardinalis, Spiritus sanctus est per gratiam inhabitans, porrò dubitari non potest quin per fontem intelligatur aliquid permanens & fixum, ac per hoc significatur gratia inhærens animæ, per modum habitus inhærentis. unde fluant riui bonorum operum qui saliant in vitam æternam, aqua enim tam alte ascendit, quam est altus locus, unde descendit. &c. quoniam fons iste de cœlo descendit, ideo aquæ eius ad cœlum vsq; perueniunt. Hæc Bellarminus.
units.tr: Next the Cardinal tries to prove that grace is a habit inhering in us, from those words: The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. This fountain, says the lord Cardinal, is the Holy Spirit dwelling in us through grace. Surely it cannot be doubted that by the fountain is meant something permanent and fixed, and by this is signified grace inhering in the soul, in the manner of an inhering habit. From it flow the streams of good works which spring up into eternal life; for water rises as high as the place from which it descends, etc. Since this fountain comes down from heaven, its waters therefore reach up to heaven. So Bellarmine.

units.la: Hæc atq; huiusmodi sunt argumenta Bellarmini, quibus ludificando, nugando lectorem circumagit, mihi vero bonæ horæ non sunt tam inutiliter locandæ, vt in istis refutandis morer, quæ nec dialecticæ, nec quidem sophisticæ speciem aliquam præferunt.
units.tr: These and similar are Bellarmine's arguments, by which he trifles with and wearies the reader with jests. But I must not spend good hours so uselessly as to linger over refuting them, since they show no appearance of either dialectic or even sophistry.

units.la: Istis prorsus similia sunt ea, quæ de hoc iustitiæ inhærentis figmento Aquinas disputabat. Nam postquam argumenta quædam pro more obiecerat, quum tandem contra obiectiones illas sententiam suam statuere cœpit, mirifico prorsus fundamento innititur, sicna [?] refert. Sed contra est quod super illud Psalm. 103. ut exhiberet faciem in oleo, dicit glossa, quod gratia est nitor animæ sanctum concilians amorem: sed nitor animæ est quædam qualitas, sicut & pulchritudo corporis: ergo gratia est quædam qualitas. Hæc Thomas. Ita isti in grauissimis fidei controuersiis ludunt & istorum ludos excipiunt Iesuitæ: Hoc argumento nunquam efficiet Aquinas quod propositum, nisi prius glossæ ordinahæc[?] autoritas sacrosancta statuatur in Ecclesia, unde ruto & firmiter possimus controuersias fidei definire. Sed nec glossæ sententiam recte retulit Aquinas, nam integra glossæ verba sunt hæc: Gratia ergo, & auxilium quidam, qui est ad hominem conciliandum sanctum amorem, vleumdicitur[?] hæcille, ita Glossatoris verba peruertit Aquinas. Sed & glossator ipse Augustini sententiam, quæ eo loco referre voluit, non corrumpendi, sed abbreviandi studio, ab autoris mente detorsit. Augustini enim verba sunt: Quid est exhilaratio faciei in oleo? Gratia Dei, auxilium quidam in manifestatione, sicut dixit Apostolus, unicuique datur spiritus ad manifestationem. Hæc Augustinus.
units.tr: Quite similar to these are the things Aquinas argued about this figment of inhering righteousness. For after he had put forward certain arguments as usual, when at last he began to establish his own opinion against those objections, he relies on a quite wonderful foundation, as he reports: But on the contrary, on that verse of Psalm 103, "that he might make the face shine with oil," the gloss says that grace is the brightness of the soul winning holy love. But the brightness of the soul is a certain quality, just as the beauty of the body is; therefore grace is a certain quality. So Thomas. Thus these men play games in the gravest controversies of faith, and the Jesuits take up their games. Aquinas will never achieve his purpose by this argument unless first the sacrosanct authority of this gloss is established in the Church, by which we could firmly and securely settle controversies of faith. But neither did Aquinas report the sense of the gloss correctly, for the whole words of the gloss are these: Grace therefore, and a certain help, which is for winning holy love in man, is called [...] so Aquinas perverts the words of the Glossator. But the glossator himself, with the aim not of corrupting but of abbreviating, turned away from the author's mind the opinion of Augustine, which he wished to cite in that place. For Augustine's words are: What is the brightening of the face in oil? The grace of God, a certain help in manifestation, as the Apostle said: to each is given the spirit for manifestation. So Augustine.

units.la: Excuius rei observatione cordatus lector facile iudicare poterit, quibus modis, gradibus & incrementis zizania in agro dominico accreuerint, nam hic inimici hominis improbitatem certo deprehendere licet, & quasi furem, aut latronem in flagranti crimine tenere. Apostolus in agro dominico bonum semen seminauit, unicuique, inquit, datur manifestatio spiritus ad utilitatem, loquitur Apostolus de donis spiritus, quæ dantur ad ædificationem aliorum, nam discrimina sunt inquit donorum, sed idem spiritus. Certum est Apostolum hic disputare, non de gratia iustificante, quæ dicitur à Theologis gratia gratum faciens: sed de donis Spiritus Sancti, & de gratia quæ dicitur à Scholasticis, gratis data. Augustinus verba retulit Apostoli, ita ut sensum etiam retineret. Loquitur enim de manifestatione spiritus, quę est in gratia gratis data, verbum unum addidit, gratiam enim hanc vocat nitorem, alludens ad oleum pertropologiam. Deinde de gratia, quæ est hominum ad homines, disputat Augustinus,gratia inquit quædam quæ est homi-num ad homines perspicua, ad conciliandum sanctum amorem, oleum dicitur in nitore di-uino, hic sese explicat Augustinus, ne quis hęc rapere possit ad gratiam, quæ est inter Deum & homines. Ab hoc unico verbo addito, vide-te quantam segetem [sparserit?] inimicus homo glossa ordinaria imperfecte hæc refert: nitor, inquit, quæ est ad hominis conciliandum sanctum amorem, hic vides quædam detracta, quædam addita, & sensum inversum, atque immuta-tum. Aquinas deinde hinc gratiæ definitio. ē[?] elicit, ut sit nitor animæ, sanctum concilians amorem. Theologi subsequentes hęc sine ex-aminatione suscipiunt, & referunt ad gratiam gratum facientem, addunt etiam & ipsi, esse hunc nitorem habitualem qualitatem inhæ-rentem, non re distinctam à charitate. Tan-dem Concilium Tridentinum omnes istas depravationes, immutationes, additiones collegit, & articulum Tridentinum composuit, de infuso hoc habitu, & collato in sacramen-tis ex opere operato, atque ita quod initio de gratia gratis data traditum est in scripturis, & susceptum à patribus, Theologorum & Iesuitarum improba industria, adiuvante inimico homine, conversum, & commutatum est in gratiam gratum facientem, Et sic nitor hic excogitatus, & habitualis qualitas seminata, & aucta, in segetem tandem erupit, & crescit in Ecclesia, donec domini mandato eradicabitur, obseruamus praeterea ex Aquinate, hanc opinionem enatam ex hominum ingeniis sine scripturae testimonio. Nam si potuisset haec sententia, vel scripturae, vel patrum testimonio confirmari, non dubium est, quin ea adducturus fuerit Aquinas, nec in Glossatoris verbis haesurus, itaque scripturae, & antiquitatis testimonio destitutus, quum antiquiora, & meliora invenire non potuisset, unius Glossae testimonio fretus haec docuit.
units.tr: By observing this matter, a discerning reader will easily be able to judge by what means, degrees and increases the tares have grown up in the Lord's field. For here one can plainly detect the wickedness of the enemy of man, and hold him as a thief or robber caught in the act. The Apostle sowed good seed in the Lord's field: to each, he says, is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good. The Apostle speaks of the gifts of the Spirit, which are given for the edification of others, for, he says, there are varieties of gifts but the same Spirit. It is certain that the Apostle is here arguing not about justifying grace, which theologians call grace making one pleasing, but about the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and about the grace which the Scholastics call freely given. Augustine reported the Apostle's words in such a way as to keep the sense too. For he speaks of the manifestation of the Spirit, which is in grace freely given; he added one word, for he calls this grace a brightness, alluding to oil as a trope. Then Augustine discusses the grace which is from men to men: grace, he says, which is manifest from man to men, for winning holy love, is called oil in the divine brightness. Here Augustine explains himself, lest anyone should seize these words for the grace which is between God and men. From this single added word, see how great a crop the enemy of man has sown, for the Glossa ordinaria reports these things imperfectly: brightness, it says, which is for winning man to holy love. Here you see some things omitted, some added, and the sense inverted and changed. Aquinas then draws from this the definition of grace, that it is a brightness of the soul winning holy love. Subsequent theologians receive these things without examination and refer them to grace making one pleasing, and they add themselves that this brightness is a habitual quality inhering, not really distinct from charity. Finally the Council of Trent gathered all these depravations, changes and additions, and composed the Tridentine article on this infused habit, conferred in the sacraments through the work done. And so what at the beginning was handed down in Scripture about grace freely given, and received by the Fathers, was, by the wicked diligence of Theologians and Jesuits, with the enemy of man assisting, converted and changed into grace making one pleasing. Thus this invented brightness, this habitual quality, sown and increased, at last broke out into a crop and grows in the Church, until by the Lord's command it is uprooted. We observe further from Aquinas that this opinion sprang from men's wits without the testimony of Scripture. For if this view could have been confirmed by the testimony either of Scripture or of the Fathers, there is no doubt Aquinas would have brought it forward, nor would he have stuck to the Glossator's words. So, destitute of the testimony of Scripture and of antiquity, and since he could not find older and better things, he taught these things relying on the testimony of one Gloss alone.

units.la: CAPUT VI. Testimonia Graecorum patrum referuntur.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI. The testimonies of the Greek Fathers are cited.

units.la: Hanc quaestionem de gratia, veteres ante Augustinum parcius tractarunt, quia ante Pelagium nemo illam veritatis partem in dubiam revocaverat. Nos tamen de hac re veterum traditionem adferemus, si prius lectorem admonuerimus, de supina Pontificiorum vanitate. Bellarminus enim affirmat, hanc sententiam quae gratiam habitum inhaerentem esse defendit, esse totius Ecclesiae sententiam, ad quam rem confirmandam duo recentia concilia profert, Viennense, de quo infra, & Tridentinum. At nos totius Ecclesiae sententiam, non ex recentibus testimoniis, sed ex totius antiquitatis consensu exquiramus.
units.tr: The earlier writers before Augustine treated this question of grace more sparingly, because before Pelagius no one had called that part of the truth into doubt. Yet we shall bring forward the tradition of the ancients on this matter, if first we warn the reader about the sheer vanity of the Papists. For Bellarmine affirms that this opinion, which holds grace to be an inherent habit, is the opinion of the whole Church, and to confirm this he produces two recent councils, Vienne, which I shall discuss below, and Trent. But we seek the opinion of the whole Church not from recent testimonies but from the consensus of all antiquity.

units.la: {a}Oportet me-tem habere sanam, & quæ nulla retardatur pœnitentia à boni venatione, ad quod quidem maxime diuina opus habemus gratia, rectaq; doctrina castaq; & munda animi affectione, & patris ad ipsum attractione. Hinc diuinam gratiam per patris attractionem explicat, positam ergo fatetur, non in virtute nostra, sed in sauore attrahentis. {b}Origenes: Gratia nobis per fidem primo comitgitur, sicut & Apostolus ducit, gratia salui factiestis[?] per fidem. & mox post gratiam credulitatis emendatio fit morum & vita conuersio, hæc ille. Multa sunt, quę paucis verbis exposuit Origines 1. gratia est per fidē: ergo nō per habitum indistinctum à charitate, quia fides re distinguitur à charitate 1. gratia est p fidē ergo sacramenta nō conferunt hanc gratiam ex opere operato, quia in opere operato Pontificii non requiruntur fide 1. gratia primo per fidem inest: ergo non per habitus, quia inest nobis ante omnes habitus 4. post gratiam fit vitę conuersio. Ergo habitus, & qualitates quæ in conuersione vitę consistunt, sunt effectus gratiæ, atq; ex gratia. Ex quibus omnibus constat gratiam quam nobis nuper excogitarunt pontificii, fuisse Origeni penitus ignotam.
units.tr: One must have a sound mind, and one not held back by any delay of repentance from the hunting of the good, for which we chiefly need divine grace, and right doctrine, and a chaste and pure disposition of soul, and the drawing of the Father towards him. Hence he explains divine grace through the drawing of the Father; he therefore confesses that it is placed not in our virtue but in the favour of the one who draws. Origen: Grace first accompanies us through faith, as the Apostle also teaches, "you have been saved by grace through faith"; and soon after the grace of belief, the amendment of morals and the conversion of life follow. These are his words. Origen set out many things in a few words: (1) grace is through faith, therefore not through a habit undistinguished from charity, since faith is really distinct from charity; (2) grace is through faith, therefore the sacraments do not confer this grace ex opere operato, since for the Papists faith is not required in the work done; (3) grace is present first through faith, therefore not through habits, since it is in us before all habits; (4) the conversion of life follows grace. Therefore the habits and qualities which consist in the conversion of life are effects of grace and come from grace. From all these things it is clear that the grace which the Papists have lately devised for us was utterly unknown to Origen.

units.la: Basilius sic docet: {c}Gratia immensę humanitatis Dei nos in dilectione Christi Iesu Domini nostri prævenit, cuius nobis ad mortē usq; obedientia, sicut scriptum est, facta est redemptio. Basilius ergo gratiam Dei posuit in dilectione Christi, nō in dilectione nostra. {d}Idemq;: Non in virtute, nō in sapientia humana, sed in Dei gratia est salus. Chrysostomu titur ea la fide tum fide seruat, cet. & Vincit qui mi gratia gratia Dei q tia do missio qui h pecca nē Id clefia pende iustit sertiu que propu ne no phyl ger perri tinet bitib catio tur bat ipse mos,
units.tr: Basil teaches thus: The grace of the immense goodness of God anticipated us in the love of Christ Jesus our Lord, whose obedience unto death, as it is written, became our redemption. Basil therefore placed God's grace in the love of Christ, not in our love. Again the same man: Salvation lies not in virtue, not in human wisdom, but in the grace of God. Chrysostom [the Greek text of this passage is too garbled in the scan to be recovered with certainty: the legible fragments speak of faith, of conquering, of the grace of God, of the remission of sins and of the purging of sin.]

units.la: {d} In psal. 33. stomus: {a}Illi (Galat. sc.) dicebant, qui sola fide nitur exccrabilis est. Apostolus cōtra demōstrat, qui sola fide nititur eū benedictū esse, & postea Lex nō tantum fide requirit, sed opera quoq; gratia vero ex fide seruat, & iustificat. {a}Quid est gratia remissio videlicet, & purgatio peccatorum. Cyrillus Alexādrinus {b} Vincit gratia quae iustificat impium, & omni labe eos qui misericordia consecuti sunt, liberat, atq; alibi gratiam sanctū dari a patre per filiū. Paulus testatur gratias ago Deo meo semper de vobis propter gratiam Dei q vobis data est in Christo. Theodoretus:{c} Gratia donat peccatorū remissione hæc cōfirmat Deipromissione, donans gentibus benedictionē, hæc ille, atqui habitus ille, & nitor pontificius, nec donat peccatorū remissionē, nec apprehēdit pmissionē Idemq; {d} Gratia concepit me per fidē hæc est Ecclesia vox. {e}Salus hominū ex sola misericordia Dei pendet, neq; n. hanc adipiscimur pramiū & mercedē iustitiæ, sed Dei bonitatis donū est, hæc ille, quid disertius dici potest contra habi ū inhærentē? Idēque sic habet e Dominus Christus; & Deus est, & propitiatorū & pontifex, & agnus, & in suo sanguine nostra salute procurauit, sola fide exiges. Theophylactus: Iustitia Dei est, g ex fide est, hæc nō indiget laborib operib. vt nostris vero tota ad gratiā Dei pertinet, hæc illi. Si tota iustitia Dei ad gratiā pertinet, nec laborib. nostris indiget: certe nec habitibus nostris indigebit. Idēq; gratiam iustificationis egregie exponit hīs verbis. Iustificantur omnes gratis gratia Dei, qua per redemptionē fit, hoc est per fectiā libertate, quam operatus est Christus ipse enim seipsum in pretiū redemptionis dans, iustificauit nos, Sic docuerunt Graeci.
units.tr: {d} On Psalm 33. Chrysostom: Those (in Galatians) who said that the one who rests on faith alone is accursed. The Apostle on the contrary shows that the one who rests on faith alone is blessed; and afterwards: the Law requires not only faith but works also, but grace saves and justifies through faith. {a} What is grace? Namely the remission and purging of sins. Cyril of Alexandria: {b} Grace which justifies the impious, and frees from every stain those who have obtained mercy, and elsewhere: the Holy Spirit is given by the Father through the Son. Paul testifies: "I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which has been given to you in Christ." Theodoret: {c} Grace gives the remission of sins; this confirms the promise of God, granting to the Gentiles the blessing; these are his words. But that inherent habit and Papist striving neither grants the remission of sins nor lays hold of the promise. Likewise: {d} "Grace conceived me through faith"; this is the voice of the Church. {e} The salvation of men depends on the sole mercy of God; for we do not obtain it as the reward and wage of righteousness, but it is a gift of God's goodness; these are his words. What could be said more plainly against an inherent habit? Likewise he has this: "The Lord Christ is both God and propitiator and high priest and lamb, and he procured our salvation by his own blood; you shall obtain it by faith alone." Theophylact: The righteousness of God is from faith; this needs none of our labours or works, but the whole belongs to the grace of God; these are his words. If the whole righteousness of God pertains to grace and needs none of our labours, then surely it will not need our habits either. Likewise he expounds the grace of justification excellently in these words: "All are justified freely by the grace of God, which comes through the redemption, that is, through the free gift which Christ worked; for he himself, giving himself as the price of redemption, justified us." Thus the Greeks taught.
