units.tr: The Latins follow: "In me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good thing" (Rom. 7). The good is not from us but from God, as is excellently argued against the Pelagian. Some think that [?] ... and they make [?] the grace of God, [?] salvation is not [?] which he received, [?] to repair what he lost? [?] whatever is proclaimed to remain not to the virtue of man but to God, [?] we are able; how great [?] confidence [?] from grace [?] by day and by night we ask [?] that it may be sanctified, by which grace of God [?] may be preserved. We pray that it may be done in us, [?] work [?] by his protection, because [?] but by the indulgence and mercy of God [?]. It is clear that not a due reward is given to works, [?] mercy intervening [?] to pardon sinners, not otherwise [?] where, against the Pelagians, [?] that God alone is wise [?] but nature: all [?].

units.la: renæus: a Paulus infir- nuntians ait, scio quoniam bonum, significans quod nō in salutem nostra, hæc ille de congruo Tertul-lianus, mantur, quasi Deus nec esse gnus & suspondit, & libe- ritatem. c Quum sine ofsu custodire natura hu- modo sine Dei gratia poterit Cyprianus d Gratum num ascribitur, sed de Dei quam, Dei est omne quod dei capacis adferimus, tan- tum haurimus. e Hoc die- , ut sanctificatio & vivi- mitur, ipsius protectione at in nobis voluntas Dei, Dei voluntate, id est ope emo sine viribus fortius est, ricordia tutus est. Ambro-ius gratia donum Dei est, sed gratuita ratione, mi- ncessa, & moxt veniam quam gratia est. Hiero-gianos prius docuerat, tem, non gratia, ut cc- homines esse peccato- res,
units.tr: Irenaeus, speaking of Paul pointing out our weakness, says: "I know that no good dwells in me" (that is, in our flesh), and so on. Tertullian says these things in agreement with it, as if God could neither be nor be known apart from grace; and he added and granted that the human nature could not keep its freedom of will without the grace of God. Cyprian: "Nothing can keep nature harmless without the grace of God." Cyprian: "The grace of God is not ascribed to our merit, but whatever we bring as a vessel of God's capacity, we draw only so much as we bring." Cyprian: "Thus sanctification and life are not from ourselves, but by the protection of God, and in us the will of God is ours by the will of God, that is, by his help." Cyprian: "Nothing is stronger without strength, and nothing is safer without the mercy of God." Ambrose: "Grace is the gift of God, but in a gratuitous manner, and it is a free gift, and it is by grace that we are forgiven." Jerome had earlier taught the Pelagians that men are sinners by nature, not by grace, so that...

units.la: A con imc cet: ftun vt e ille res;ex Apostolo: & fide iustificari sine operibus legis, tandem hæc subiungit {a}Maxime ostendit Apostolus, non in hominis merito, sed in Dei gratia esse iustitiam, quæ sint legis operibus credentium suscipit fidem. {b}Tunc iusti sumus, quando nos peccatores esse fatemur, & iustitia nostra non ex proprio merito, sed ex Dei confissis misericordia.
units.tr: From the Apostle: "...that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law." Finally he adds this: The Apostle chiefly shows that righteousness lies not in man's merit but in God's grace, which receives faith, and not the works of the law, of believers. {b} We are then righteous when we confess that we are sinners, and our righteousness comes not from our own merit but from the mercy of God's pardon.

units.la: Quid interest inter Pelagianos, & pontificios? Pelagius docuit, homines iustificari non gratia, sed meritis: patres contra probant, non meritis, sed gratia. Pelagius admonitus, hęc inter se pugnantia coniungere voluit, & gratia, & meritis, hoc est, gratiam Dei verbis concedere, reipsa tollere. Testantur patres, Pelagium admonitum, gratiam verbis saltem concessisse sub ambigua generalitate, quod sentiret, abscondentem, ut gratiæ vocabulo frangeret invidiam, offensionemque declinaret, hoc faciunt etiam Pontificii, qui gratiæ acceptionem novam, & antiquæ Ecclesiæ inauditam excogitarunt: ut gratia sit in habitibus nostris inhærentibus, ut comparari possit merito de congruo, ut conferatur ex opere operato, quicquid ergo patres disputarunt contra Pelagium valet contra Pontificios.
units.tr: What is the difference between the Pelagians and the Papists? Pelagius taught that men are justified not by grace but by merits; the Fathers, on the contrary, prove that they are justified not by merits but by grace. Pelagius, when admonished, wanted to join these contradictory things together, both grace and merits; that is, to concede grace in words while in fact removing it. The Fathers testify that Pelagius, when admonished, conceded grace at least in words, under an ambiguous generality, concealing what he really thought, so that by the word "grace" he might blunt the hatred and avoid the offence. The Papists do the same, who have devised a new understanding of grace, unheard of in the ancient Church: that grace is in our inherent habits, that it can be obtained by congruous merit, that it is conferred by the work wrought. Therefore whatever the Fathers argued against Pelagius holds equally against the Papists.

units.la: Augustinus omnium ac[illegible, ~2 letters]ratissime tractat controversiam de gratia contra Pelagianos, imo vero & contra Pontificios. Nam sic docet: {c}Gratia per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, in qua nos sua, non nostra iudicia iustos facit, ut ea sit vera nostra iustitia, quæ nobis ab illo est, hæc ille, non minus contra Pelagianos quam contra Tridentinos:qui negant cum Pelagianis imputatione iustitiæ Christi. Idéoq; [?] intelligãt homi-nes per eandē gratiam se iustificari à peccatis, per quæ factum, vt homo Christiũ [?] nullum habere posset pec-catum. {b}Gratia est quæ gratis datur sine meritis operantibus, sed misericordia donantis, {c}Gratia Dei per Do-minū nostrum Iesum Christum, quare gratia, quia gratis datur, quare gratis datur? quia merita tua non præ-cesserunt, sed beneficia Dei te prænenerunt. {d}Quid sit gratis datur? gratis cæstat [?], nihil boni, f. cisti [?] & datur tibi remissio peccatorum. Attenduntur opera tua & inueniuntur omnia mala, si ap [?] debetur ipsi reperis [?]. Deus redderet, vt iam damnaret, nam tibi reddit Deus debitam pœnam, sed donat indebita gratia. {e}Qui ergo inde per gratiam liberantur, nam vasa meritorum suorum, sed vasa misericordiæ nominatur, cuius misericordiæ misit illius qui Iesum Christum misit in hunc mundum peccatores saluos facere {f}viuifica me secundum verbum tuum, bene autem non ait, viuifica me secundum meritum meum, sed secundum verbum tuum, quod quid est aliud, nisi secun-dum promissum tuum, filius promissionis vult esse, nō filius elationis, vt secundum gratiam firma sit promissio omni semini, hæc ille, quā acriter pontificios etiā pungit, quos filios pbaræ [?] elationis, quia negant promissionē gratiæ fide suscipiendā ad iustitiā, nam imputationē iustitiæ Christi, q [?] Tridētini pertinaciter reiiciunt, Augustinus pertinaciter retinet. {g}Ergo in tua iustitia, non in mea, quia mea quidē præcessit iniquitas, & quum ero iustus, tua iu-stitia erit, quia iustitia mihi abste data iustus ero, & sic erit mea, vt tua sit, id est, abs te mihi data, in eum enim credo, qui iustificat impium, vt deputetur fides quæ ad iustitiam. {a} Inter gratiam, & prædestinatio-nem hoc tantum interest: quod prædestinatio est gratiæ præparatio, gratia vero iam ipsa donatio. Hæc, & plura in hanc sententiam Augustinus, vbi tunc fuerunt figmenta illa, de merito congrui de opere operato, de pictore & habituali quali-tate inhærêre? Prosper {b} Sicut nulla sunt tam de-testanda facinora quæ possunt gratia excere donū: ita nulla possunt tam præclara opera exstere, quib. hoc gratis tribuitur, præsumptionis indicium [?] esse debeatur. Vbi pœna præscribitur {c} debet esse pœnitentia, vbi remis-sio donatur, gratia est præcedat pœnitentia sequitur gratia, neq; pœnitentia ergo sine gratia, neq; gratia sine pœnitentia, debet enim pœnitentia prius dānare peccatū, vt gratia possit abolere. {d}De primi hominis pœna nemo liberatur, nisi per gratiam Domini nostri præparatam & prædestinatam in æterno consilio Dei ante constitutionem mundi. hæc ille. Quam longe sunt ista {e} à sensu pontificiorum. Sedulius e Gra-tia Dei aut filius Dei dicitur, quia per suâ gratiâ gra-tis peccata dimisit, num hæc pontificii ad suum ni-torem & habitum inhærentē trahere possunt. {f} Leo I. f Causa reparationis nostræ non est nisi misé-ricordia Dei, quam non diligeremus nisi prius nos ipse diligeret. {g} Isychius: g Gratia ex misericordia & cō-passione præbetur, & fide comprehenditur sola, non ex operibus. {h} Primatius h sola fide salvati estu per gra-tiam. {i} Christus pro peccatoribus & pro impiis mortuus est, vt ad credendum non merito, sed gratia vocaremur. Fulgentius. Postquam gratiæ di-vinæ catenam explicasset, sic {k} subiecit: Hæc omnia, id est, & vocationis nostræ initia, & iustificationis augmenta, & glorificationis præmia in prædestinatione semper Deus habuit, quia & inuocatione, & iustificatione, & in glorificatione sanctorum gratia sua futura opera præsciuit.
units.tr: Augustine treats the controversy about grace most fully and most carefully against the Pelagians, indeed also against the Papists. For he teaches thus: {c} Grace through our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he makes us righteous not by our own judgements but by his, so that that is our true righteousness which is from him; so he speaks, no less against the Tridentines than against the Pelagians, who with the Pelagians deny the imputation of Christ's righteousness. Therefore...let men understand that they are justified from sins by that same grace, through which it has come about that a man in Christ could have no sin. {b} Grace is that which is given freely, without works producing merit, but by the mercy of the giver. {c} The grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ: why grace? Because it is given freely. Why is it given freely? Because your merits did not go before, but God's benefits went before you. {d} What is meant by "given freely"? It is given freely, nothing good preceding; and forgiveness of sins is given to you. Your works are examined and all are found evil; if reward were owed to them, God would render it, so that he would condemn; for to you God renders the punishment you deserve, but he gives undeserved grace. {e} Those who are therefore freed through grace are not called vessels of their own merits, but vessels of mercy, of that mercy which sent his Son Jesus Christ into this world to save sinners. {f} "Quicken me according to your word": he does not say, "quicken me according to my merit," but "according to your word." What is this but "according to your promise"? He wishes to be a son of the promise, not a son of pride, so that the promise may stand firm for all the seed by grace. So he speaks; and he sharply stings the Papists also, whom he calls sons of pride, because they deny that the promise of grace is to be received by faith unto righteousness; for the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which the Tridentines stubbornly reject, Augustine stubbornly retains. {g} Therefore in your righteousness, not mine, because my iniquity went before; and when I am righteous, it will be your righteousness, because I shall be righteous by righteousness given to me from you, and so it will be mine in that it is yours, that is, given to me by you; for I believe in him who justifies the ungodly, so that faith is reckoned for righteousness. {a} Between grace and predestination there is only this difference: predestination is the preparation of grace, while grace is already the giving itself. Augustine says these things and more to this effect. Where then were those fictions about merit of congruity, about work wrought, about the habitual quality inhering in the soul? Prosper: {b} Just as there are no crimes so detestable that they can exclude the grace of God, so there can be no works so splendid that, when this is granted freely, they should be taken as a sign of presumption. Where punishment is prescribed, {c} there must be repentance; where remission is given, grace is. Repentance goes before, grace follows; so there is no repentance without grace, nor grace without repentance, for repentance must first condemn sin so that grace may abolish it. {d} No one is freed from the punishment of the first man except through the grace of our Lord, prepared and predestined in the eternal counsel of God before the foundation of the world. So he speaks. How far these things are from the sense of the Papists! Sedulius: {e} The grace of God or the Son of God is so called because by his grace he freely dismissed sins; can the Papists drag these words to their own effort and inherent habit? Leo I: {f} The cause of our restoration is nothing but the mercy of God, which we would not love unless he had first loved us. {g} Hesychius: {g} Grace is offered out of mercy and compassion, and is apprehended by faith alone, not from works. {h} Primasius: {h} You are saved by grace through faith alone. {i} Christ died for sinners and for the ungodly, so that we are called to believe not by merit but by grace. Fulgentius: after he had unfolded the chain of divine grace, he added thus: {k} All these things, that is, the beginnings of our calling, the increases of our justification, and the rewards of our glorification, God always had in predestination, because in the invocation, justification and glorification of the saints he foreknew his own future works of grace.

units.la: Gregorius I. Gratia redemti sumus, illa namque sola opera male viuendo dedimus, quibus si iusta retributio seruaretur, non Christus, sed supplicia redderentur, sed aliud homo per iustitiam meruit, aliud per gratiam accepit. Quam sincere Gregorius Papa contra Pontificios, figmentum vero illud Tridentinorum, de præparationibus nostris, & merito congrui, sic radicibus conuellit Gregorius, in illa verba Iob. Quis ante dedit mihi vt reddam ei. {b}Nemo, inquit, quippe vt diuina illum gratia subsequatur, prius aliquid contulit Deo, nam si nos Deum bene operando prævenimus, vbi est quod Propheta ait, misericordia eius præueniet me? Si quid nos bonæ operationis dedimus, vel eius gratiâ mereremur, vbi est quod Apostolus dicit. Gratia salvati estis per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Si nostra dilectio Deum prævenit, vbi est, quod Iohannes Apostolus ait, non quia nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quia ipse prior dilexit nos? vbi etiam plura habet Gregorius in hanc sententiam, & mox: si saltem dona bonorum operum virtute nostra bene cogitando prævenimus, vbi est quod cum super Paulus tam salubriter dictum, vt omnis de se humanæ mentis fiducia ab ipsa cordis radice succidatur, cum ait: non quia sufficientes simus aliquid cogitare à nobis quasi ex nobis, sed sufficientia nostra ex Deo est. Hæc Gregorius. Romani igitur Pontifices antiqui omnes no-
units.tr: Gregory I: We are redeemed by grace, for by living badly we have given only those works which, if a just retribution were kept, would bring not Christ but punishments in return; a man merits one thing by justice, and receives another by grace. How sincerely Gregory the Pope argues against the Papists! The fiction of the Tridentines about our preparations and merit of congruity he tears up by the roots, on those words of Job, "Who first gave to me, that I should repay him?" {b} "No one," he says, "for in order that divine grace should follow, he first contributed something to God. For if we anticipate God by doing good, where is what the Prophet says, 'his mercy shall prevent me'? If we have given anything of good work, or merited it by his grace, where is what the Apostle says, 'By grace you are saved through faith, and this not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast'? If our love anticipates God, where is what the Apostle John says, 'Not that we loved God, but that he first loved us'?" Gregory has more to this effect, and soon after: if at least by our own power and good thinking we anticipate the gifts of good works, where is what Paul said so wholesomely, that all confidence of the human mind in itself be cut out from the very root of the heart, when he says: not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God? So Gregory. Therefore all the ancient Roman pontiffs...

units.la: {b} In Iob. lib. 33. cap. 20. atri sunt, imo Christi sunt: & cum Ecclesia Christi consentiunt contra Tridentinos.
units.tr: ...are theirs, indeed they are Christ's, and they agree with the Church of Christ against the Tridentines. In Job, book 33, chapter 20.

units.la: Cassiodorus: {a}Est quidem in mala parte execrabilis libertas arbitrii, vt praevaricator creatorem deserat, & ad vitia se nefanda convertat: in bona vero parte arbitrium liberum Adam peccante perdidimus, ad quod nisi per gratiam Christi redire non possumus: dicente Apostolo: Deus est, qui operatur in nobis, & velle, & perficere pro bona voluntate. Olympiodorus: {b}Summa salutis in misericordiis domini, ac benignitate iudicis repetita {c}est. Fortunatus: hominis voluntas non habet bonum, nisi dominus inspiret, iuxta illud. Deus meus, misericordia eius praeueniet me. Maxentius Iohannes. Nullum {d}ab Adamo nunc vsque per naturae vigorem credimus esse salvatum, nisi dono gratiae Spiritus sancti in fide nominis Iesu. Liberum vero naturale arbitrium ad nihil aliud valere credimus nisi ad deserenda tantum, & desiderenda carnalia, siue secula-ria. & mox: Quapropter anathematizamus eos, qui contra vocem Apostoli audent dicere nostrum est velle Dei autem perficere, quum idem Doctor, & velle & perficere testetur donum divinum. Beda. {e}Datur a patre credentibus fides, vt nemo glorietur in fi-de sua, quae a se non est, quasi propria, sed a Deo datur quasi gratia. {f}Talis accipiet benedictionem, id est, multiplicationem a Domino hanc scilicet, vt in praesenti bene praemoueamur, & in futuro bene remoueretur, & hoc non ex meritis, sed ex sola gratia, quia accipiet misericordiam a Deo, id est, quia praecedit bona voluntas Dei in eo, & gratia eius, qua non ex meritis est, sed a Deo. Haec Beda noster, multa paucis,
units.tr: Cassiodorus: There is indeed a wretched freedom of the will in the bad sense, so that the transgressor forsakes the Creator and turns himself to unspeakable vices. In the good sense, however, we lost free will when Adam sinned, and we cannot recover it except through the grace of Christ, as the Apostle says: "It is God who works in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Phil. 2:13). Olympiodorus: The sum of salvation is sought again in the mercies of the Lord and the kindness of the Judge. Fortunatus: The human will has no good unless the Lord inspires it, according to that text: "My God, his mercy shall go before me" (Ps. 59:10). Maxentius John: We believe that no one since Adam has been saved by the strength of nature, except by the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit in faith in the name of Jesus. We believe that free natural choice is good for nothing except for forsaking and desiring carnal, or worldly, things. And soon after: Therefore we anathematize those who against the voice of the Apostle dare to say that "to will is ours, but to perform is of God," since the same Doctor testifies that both the willing and the performing are a divine gift. Bede: Faith is given by the Father to believers, so that no one may boast in his faith as if it were his own and not from himself, but it is given by God as grace. "Such a one shall receive a blessing," that is, multiplication from the Lord, namely that in the present he may be well moved and in the future well removed; and this not from merits but from grace alone, because he shall receive mercy from God, that is, because God's good will goes before him, and his grace, which is not from merits but from God. So far Bede, our author, saying much in few words.

units.la: [illegible, ~20 letters][illegible, ~20 letters][illegible, ~20 letters][illegible, ~20 letters] paucis, quæ sunt obseruatione digna: 1. fidem nemo habet à se, contra Pelagianos 2. fides est gratia: ergo gratia non oritur ex operibus, contra pontificios 3. hanc gratiam habent fideles, vt possint benepromereri in præsenti, ergo voluntas promerendi efficitur gratia, non autem gratia ex voluntate, & dispositione promerendi, sicut dicunt pontifici 4. gratiam facit, vt promereamur, sed non ex meritis: locutio Bedæ obseruanda, qua luculenter ostendit, antiquos patres quum merendi, & promerendi verbis vtterentur, non illud voluisse, quod volunt Pontificii, quia merendi & promerendi verba retinent; patres & merita reiiciunt, mereri significat antiquis sine merito obtinere. Sic Gregorius a 6 necessarium Adæ peccatum, o felix culpa, quæ talem ac tantum meruit habere redemptorem, hæc ille. Frustra igitur, & futiliter ex merendi verbo patrum sententiam de merito concludunt pontificii, quia mereri nos docent patres sine merito, quia & peccatum dicunt meruisse.
units.tr: ...few things, worth observing: (1) no one has faith from himself, against the Pelagians; (2) faith is grace; therefore grace does not arise from works, against the Papists; (3) the faithful have this grace so that they may merit well in the present; therefore the will to merit is made grace, but grace is not made from the will and disposition to merit, as the Pontiffs say; (4) he makes grace so that we may merit, but not from merits. Bede's phrasing is to be observed, which clearly shows that the ancient Fathers, when they used the words "merit" and "to merit," did not mean what the Papists want, for they retain the words "merit" and "to merit" while rejecting merits. To merit, for the ancients, meant to obtain without merit. So Gregory, on the sixth [homily]: the sin of Adam was necessary; O happy fault, which deserved to have such and so great a Redeemer, so he. Therefore the Papists conclude in vain and frivolously from the word "merit" in the Fathers that they teach merit, since the Fathers teach that we merit without merit, for they even say that sin "merited."

units.la: Alcuinus b Ex quo primum homo libero arbitrio venundatus est sub peccato, inde mala cœpit esse libertas hominis, quia ipsi libero, ablata est bonitas voluntatis, quam exinde nemo à se habere potuit, nisi gratia diuinæ misericordiæ adiutus habuisset. c Ranus: Homo non tam aliter saluari potest, nisi per gratiam Iesu Christi, videlicet sui redemptoris. Hactenus testimonia patrum posuimus, sequuntur quos pontificii inter suos numerant, quitamen cum illis in hac re nihil habent commune.
units.tr: Alcuin: From the time when man was first sold under sin by free choice, the freedom of man became evil, because the goodness of the will was taken away from the free will itself, which afterwards no one could have from himself unless he had been helped by the grace of divine mercy. Ranulf: Man cannot be saved in any other way except through the grace of Jesus Christ, that is, of his own Redeemer. So far we have set out the testimonies of the Fathers; there follow those whom the Papists count among their own, who nevertheless have nothing in common with them in this matter.

units.la: Remigius: c Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei hanc scilicet, quod non ex operibus, quæ fecimus
units.tr: Remigius: "The heavens declare the glory of God," namely that not by the works which we have done, but according to his mercy, he has saved us.

units.la: [Right page strip, fragments only: hos, / cit. / iusti / cred / fitifi / nisi / qua / qua / lefa / ftum / iusti / ria D / Gif / ficat / e Iuf / iusti / impi / prop / dia, / Gbri / num, / mul / Nan / bis r / ratg / Han / mon / phic / qua / nite / grat / B] nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvos nos fe-cit. Haymo {a}Iustitia Dei, hoc est iustificatio qua iustificat in credentes, hoc est iustitia, qua omnes credentes dono patris, & filii, & Spiritus sancti iustificantur. {b}In praesenti tempore iustitia Dei manifesta est, non eo solummodo, qua ipse iustus est, aut qua iustos facit, qui essentialiter ipsa iustitia est, sed qua induit impium, quando misericorditer [?] de infidelì facit fidelem, de adultero & fornicatore facit castum, & continentem, de iniusto, & peccatore facit iustum, & oratorem virtutum. Hincmarus {c}Gratia Dei iustificat impios, hoc est ex impiis facit iustos. Gilbertus {d}Gratia Dei est, ut homo fide iustificatus per ipsam aliquo modo posset, quod non esset. {e}Iustitiae Dei quid? iustitiam Dei dico, non qua Deus iustus est, sed qua induit hominem, qua gratis iustificat impium, huic iustitiae testimonium perhibent lex, & prophetae. Anselmus {f}Nihil sumus: nisi misericordia, & gratia Dei regamur. {g}Ab Adam vitio sola Christi gratia liberat, quae non secundum merita hominum, sed gratu [?] datur, quoniam Deus index est. quā multa, quam paucis Anselmus connectit? Nam & Pelagianos, & Tridentinos paucis verbis refutavit, Pelagianos quidem qui docuerat gratiam dari secundum merita hominis. Hanc fuisse summam Pelagiani veneni saepius monet Augustinus, pontificios vero, qui & ipsi idem docent, nempe per suas illas, nescio quas dispositiones, praeparationes opera poenitentiae, opera operata, & merita de congruo gratiam acquiri.
units.tr: [Fragments of the right-hand page, illegible] ...saved us. Haymo: The righteousness of God, that is, justification, by which he justifies believers, that is, the righteousness by which all believers are justified by the gift of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. At the present time the righteousness of God is manifest, not only in that by which he himself is righteous, or by which he makes men righteous, he who is essentially righteousness itself, but in that by which he clothes the ungodly, when he mercifully makes the unfaithful faithful, makes the adulterer and fornicator chaste and continent, and makes the unrighteous and sinner righteous and a doer of virtues. Hincmar: The grace of God justifies the ungodly, that is, from the ungodly he makes righteous men. Gilbert: It is the grace of God that a man justified by faith might in some way become through it what he was not. What is the righteousness of God? I call it the righteousness of God, not that by which God is righteous, but that by which he clothes man, by which he freely justifies the ungodly; the law and the prophets bear witness to this righteousness. Anselm: We are nothing unless we are ruled by the mercy and grace of God. From the sin of Adam only the grace of Christ delivers, which is given not according to the merits of men but freely, since God is the judge. How much, and how briefly, Anselm connects! For he refuted both the Pelagians and the Tridentines in a few words: the Pelagians, who had taught that grace is given according to the merits of man. Augustine often warns that this was the sum of the Pelagian poison; and the Papists, who teach the same thing, namely that grace is acquired through those dispositions, preparations, and works of penance of theirs, I know not what, and through works wrought, and through merit of congruity.

units.la: {h}Bernardus Sufficit mihi ad omnem iusti-tiam ciam solum habere propitium, cui soli peccavi, omne quod mihi ipse non imputare decreverit, sic est, quasi non fuerit, non peccare Dei iustitia est, hominis iustitia indulgentia Dei. {a}Mihi certe meritum deest, sed non illi miseratio, {b}Horreo quicquid de meo est, ut sim meus; nisi quod illud magis forsitan meum est, quod me meum facit, gratia reddit me mi-hi [?]iustificatum gratis, & sic liberatum a servitute peccati. Multa praeterea in hanc sententiam, ab hoc sanctoviro perscripta, haec sufficiant ad inhaerentem Tridentinorum iustitiam refutan- dam. Rupertus: {c}Spiritus sancti gratia vera, & sola peccatorum remissio est. {d}Accepimus gratiam pro gratia: scilicet gratiam aeternae salutis pro gratia fidei praesentis, ad quam nos gratis, id est, nullis nostris praecedentibus meritis, per praedicatores suos ipse vocavit, & gratuita peccatorum remissione iustificavit. Hugo de S. Victore: {e}Velle non possum nisi gratia Dei fuerit mecum, nulla enim humana industria sine gratia Dei, ex quo primus homo peccavit natura bonum perdidimus pariter & arbitrii.
units.tr: Bernard: It is enough for me, for all righteousness, to have only a merciful one, against whom alone I have sinned; whatever he has decided not to impute to me is as if it had not been, and not to sin is the righteousness of God, while the righteousness of man is the indulgence of God. Certainly I lack merit, but not mercy. I shudder at whatever is mine, so that I may be mine; but perhaps that is rather mine which makes me mine; grace restores me to myself, justified freely, and thus freed from the servitude of sin. Much else written by this holy man to the same effect is enough to refute the inherent righteousness of the Tridentines. Rupert: The grace of the Holy Spirit is true and the sole remission of sins. We have received grace for grace: namely the grace of eternal salvation for the grace of present faith, to which he called us freely, that is, without any of our preceding merits, through his preachers, and justified us by the gratuitous remission of sins. Hugh of St Victor: I cannot will unless the grace of God is with me, for no human effort without the grace of God; since the first man sinned, we have lost the good of nature together with the good of the will.

units.la: Hactenus gratia Dei recte, & sincere a patribus suscepta est, & expolita, nec habitualis qualitas, aut inhaerens nobis iustitia, aut meritum congrui, aut opus operatum, aut reliqua huius generis portenta Tridentina, scripta fuerunt, praedicata, vel omnino audita in Ecclesia ante annum Christi millesimum, hoc est ante solutionem Satanae, deinceps mutatio doctrinae de gratia in Ecclesia Romana inchoata est. Patres igitur egregie fidem propugnarunt contra haereticos, maxime contra Pelagium, gratiam Dei sic explicant, vt nihil aliud intelligant per gratiam, quam fauorem Dei, & acceptationem. Gratia est remissio peccatorum; gratia ex fide iustificat, gratiæ mensura pro mensura fidei; gratia ex miseri-cordia præbetur, in misericordia consistit; gratia est prædestinationis præparatio; gratia est in imputatione; gratia iustitiam Dei illustrat qua nos iustificat, qua impium induit. Hæc atque his similia magna fide, ac diligentia prædicata à veteribus, quid aliud demonstrant, quam gratiam ab istis omnibus pro fauore Dei tantummodo habitam fuisse? nec tunc in Ecclesia Tridentinis figmentis locum fuisse; ac proinde omnes patres qui scripserunt ante annum Christi millesimum, anathemate Tridentino esse percussos.
units.tr: Thus far grace has been rightly and sincerely received and set forth by the Fathers, and neither a habitual quality, nor an inherent righteousness in us, nor merit of congruity, nor the work wrought, nor the other monsters of this kind of the Tridentines, were written, preached, or at all heard in the Church before the year of Christ one thousand, that is, before the loosing of Satan; afterwards the change of doctrine concerning grace began in the Roman Church. The Fathers therefore nobly defended the faith against heretics, especially against Pelagius, and explained grace so that they understood nothing else by grace than the favour and acceptance of God. Grace is the remission of sins; grace justifies through faith; the measure of grace is according to the measure of faith; grace is given out of mercy, and consists in mercy; grace is the preparation of predestination; grace is in imputation; grace illuminates the righteousness of God by which he justifies us, by which he clothes the ungodly. What do these and similar things, taught with great faith and diligence by the ancients, show, other than that all these took grace only as the favour of God? Nor was there then room in the Church for the Tridentine fictions; and therefore all the Fathers who wrote before the year of Christ one thousand were struck by the anathema of Trent.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CAPUT VIII.

units.la: De erroris origine.
units.tr: On the origin of the error.

units.la: IAm, vt erroris huius origo aperiatur: Petrus Lumbardus in hac re primus delecuit veterum vestigia Patrum, & venenum sequentibus Theologis propinauit.
units.tr: Now, so that the origin of this error may be laid open: Peter Lombard was the first in this matter to depart from the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, and he gave the poison to the Theologians who followed him.

units.la: Quærit enim{a}, An gratia sit virtus, Et sic concludit: Gratia illa (qua liberat voluntatem) virtus non incongrue nominatur, quia voluntatem hominis confirmat, atque adiuuat. Aquinas deinde docet. {b}Gratiam animæ qualitatem esse, sed articulo proximo negat esse virtutem. Qualitatem autem huiusmodi describit, quæ animæ inhæreat, atque vt illius verbis vtar, {a}secundum quod est qualitas, dicitur agere in animam, non per modum causæ efficientis, sed per modum causæ formalis, sicut albedo facit album, & iustitiæ ipsum. Hæc ille. Ex quo fonte celebris illa inter pontificios doctrina recepta est: iustitiam hominis qua iustificatur coram Deo, esse qualitatem inhærentem, & charitatem, siue opera iustificare formaliter. Sed hæc docendi forma ante hæc sæcula inaudita fuerat in Ecclesia.
units.tr: For he asks whether grace is a virtue, and concludes thus: That grace (which frees the will) is not inappropriately called a virtue, because it strengthens and helps the will of man. Aquinas then teaches: Grace is a quality of the soul, but in the next article he denies that it is a virtue. He describes this quality as inhering in the soul, and, to use his own words, insofar as it is a quality, it is said to act upon the soul not by way of an efficient cause but by way of a formal cause, just as whiteness makes a thing white and justice makes a man just. So he says. From this source has come that famous doctrine received among the Papists: that the righteousness of a man by which he is justified before God is an inherent quality, and that charity, or works, justify formally. But this way of teaching was unheard of in the Church before these ages.

units.la: Nec prætereundum nobis est, Aquinatem de eadem re, non eadem proferre, sed pugnantia. Nam in commentariis in Epistolas, hanc de iustificationis gratia doctrinam integram retinuit, ita vt solius fidei iustificatione sæpenumero confirmet. In summa vero (quo scripto Aquinas videtur ingenium suum ad Rom. Pontificis præscriptum, & mandatu accommodasse, quod de aliis etiam fraterculis constat, maxime vero de Augusti Triumpho Anconitano, qui fatetur, sed ad præscriptum Romæ Pontificis docuisse) iustificationis doctrinæ vehementer obscurat, atque hanc doctrinæ partem immutat. Iustificatione enim statuit in remissione peccatorum, & in acquisitione iustitiæ. {b}Iustificatio impii, inquit, est re-missio peccatorum, cum acquisitione iustitiæ. Itaq; quod veteres scripturis docuerunt de imputata iustitia Christi, ab Aquinate vel omissum, vel reiectum videmus, qui loco imputationis acquisitionem[?] reposuit. Exin de imputationis lius diffilbeEx doiuhzcare hæc inapulas, nteone quo ad aculis pho tum doariflanisiretaq; puum, onis onis tridoctrinis missa est, à Tridentinis penitus reie-cta. De præparatione sit docuit Aquinas. {a}Quia non vita æterna omnem naturæ facultatem excedit, non potest homo meritò, in statu naturæ integræ, neque in statu naturæ corruptæ ipsam absque gratia promereri. Hæc ille. Quam sententiam confirmat etiam, ibid. q. 114 artic. 2. nullum, inquit, meritum potest esse sine gratia. Docet igitur Aquinas contra Tridentinos, nullum esse meritum congrui, quo nondum reconciliatus mereri possit gratiam iustificationis. Huic opinioni repugnat Scotus: Tridentini sequuntur Scotū. Atq; istos errores Aquinas, & Scotus, tanquam duas Antichristi prouincias, sortiri videntur, vt Aquinas meritum de condigno inferret, Scotus vero meritum de congruo. Ita tamen Aquinas priorem errorem confirmat, vt & secundo fundamenta quædam posuerit. Sic enim docet: {b}Opus meritorium hominis dupli-citer considerari potest: vno modo secundum quod procedit ex libero arbitrio: alio modo, secundum quod procedit ex gratia Spiritus Sancti. Si consideretur secundum substantiam operis, & secundum quod procedit ex libero arbitrio, sic non potest esse ibi condignitas propter maximam inaequalitatem; sed est ibi congruitas propter quandam aequalitatem proportionis. Videtur enim congruum, vt homini operanti, secundum suam virtutem, Deus recompenset secundum excellentiam virtutis suæ. Si autem loquamur de opere meritorio, secundum quod procedit ex gratia Spiritus sancti, sic est meritorium vitæ æternæ ex condigno, hæc ille quibus verbis doctrinam de gratia Dei è scripturis & patribus traditam plane subuertit.
units.tr: Nor must we pass over the fact that Aquinas does not say the same things about the same matter, but contradictory things. For in his commentaries on the Epistles he kept this doctrine of justification by grace whole, so that he very often confirms justification by faith alone. But in the Summa (a work in which Aquinas seems to have adapted his talent to the prescription and command of the Roman Pontiff, as is known also of other little friars, and especially of Augustine Triumphus of Ancona, who admits that he taught according to the prescription of the Roman Pontiff) he greatly obscures the doctrine of justification and alters this part of the teaching. For he locates justification in the remission of sins and in the acquisition of righteousness: The justification of the ungodly, he says, is the remission of sins together with the acquisition of righteousness. Therefore, what the ancients taught from Scripture about the imputed righteousness of Christ we see either omitted or rejected by Aquinas, who put acquisition in place of imputation. Thereafter the doctrine of imputation [unclear] has been wholly rejected by the Tridentines. Concerning preparation Aquinas taught thus: Because eternal life exceeds every faculty of nature, man cannot merit it, either in the state of integral nature or in the state of corrupted nature, without grace. So he says. He also confirms this opinion in the same place, question 114, article 2: No merit, he says, can exist without grace. Aquinas therefore teaches, against the Tridentines, that there is no merit of congruity by which a man not yet reconciled could merit the grace of justification. Scotus opposes this opinion; the Tridentines follow Scotus. And these errors seem to have been allotted, like two provinces of Antichrist, to Aquinas and Scotus: Aquinas introduced merit of condignity, and Scotus merit of congruity. Yet Aquinas confirms the former error in such a way that he also laid down certain foundations for the second. For he teaches thus: The meritorious work of a man can be considered in two ways: in one way insofar as it proceeds from free will; in another way insofar as it proceeds from the grace of the Holy Spirit. If it is considered according to the substance of the work, and insofar as it proceeds from free will, then there can be no condignity there, on account of the very great inequality; but there is congruity there, on account of a certain equality of proportion. For it seems fitting that God, to a man working according to his own power, should recompense according to the excellence of his virtue. But if we speak of a meritorious work insofar as it proceeds from the grace of the Holy Spirit, then it is meritorious of eternal life by condignity. So he says; with these words he plainly overturns the doctrine of the grace of God handed down from Scripture and the Fathers.

units.la: Bonaventura Aquinati σύν[?] ξεον&[?] λόγε[?] aliter docuit, de merito enim sic habet. {a}Gratiam iam habitam, per gratiae usum non contingit mereri, nec quantum ad meritum congrui nec quantum ad meritum condigni. De gratia vero sic disputat, ut vix reperias[?] inter Scholasticos quenquam qui magis illustret hanc doctrinam, nam sic scribit: {b}Gratia respectu principii à quo, diuiditur in gratiam praedestinationis, vocationis, sufficatio-nis, & magnificationis, primo enim Deus gratiam proposuit, secundo offert, tertio confert, quarto complet. Itemque sic subiicit: ut comparatur ad effectum, diuiditur, in praevenientem, & subsequentem, siue operantem, & cooperantem. Quum itaque P. Lumbardus gratiam definiuisset virtutem, Bonaventura non sequitur magistrum, tanquam seruum pecus, sicut plerique solebant, sed tanquam grauis censor {c}Dicendum, inquit, quod Magister (vbi dicit gratiam esse virtutem) non intendit in illo verbo notificare gratiam gratum facientem, quantum ad suam essentiam, sed quasi per posterius & quodammodo per effectus, quia in illos actus non exit gratia, nisi mediantibus habitibus virtutum, videlicet fidei, & charitatis, ideo notificans gratiam, dicit quod gratia nihil aliud sit quam fides cum dilectione, pro eo, quod per illos habitus dicitur gratia in actum exire, per quos innotescit nobis quo loco plura in hanc sententiam habet Bonaventura. Et quamvis nonnunquam ex seculi sui tenebris loquitur[?], tamen plura, & meliora
units.tr: Bonaventure taught otherwise than Aquinas, for he says this about merit: Grace already possessed cannot be merited through the use of grace, either as to merit of congruity or as to merit of condignity. And he disputes about grace in such a way that you would hardly find among the Scholastics anyone who illuminates this doctrine more; for he writes thus: Grace, with respect to its principle from which it comes, is divided into the grace of predestination, of calling, of sufficiency, and of magnification: for first God purposes grace, second he offers it, third he confers it, fourth he completes it. And likewise he adds: As it is compared to its effect, it is divided into prevenient and subsequent, or operating and co-operating. Since Peter Lombard had defined grace as a virtue, Bonaventure did not follow the Master like a servile flock, as most were accustomed to do, but judged him like a weighty critic: It must be said, he says, that the Master (where he says that grace is a virtue) did not intend by that word to make known grace which makes one acceptable, as to its essence, but as it were by what comes later and in some way through its effects, because grace does not issue into those acts except through the habits of the virtues, namely faith and charity; therefore, in making grace known, he says that grace is nothing other than faith with love, because grace is said to issue into act through those habits, by which it becomes known to us. In this passage Bonaventure has much more to say to this effect. And although at times he speaks from the darkness of his age, nevertheless he says more and better things

units.la: pau[?] apes[?] qui[?] con[?] cilio[?] con[?] enim[?] debe[?] tur. Cle[?] pars[?] conf[?] pac[?] ferm[?] pro[?] Cle[?] tis C[?] imm[?] tem[?] info[?] prob[?] mod[?] dem[?] dam[?] ( dor[?] qui[?] con[?] con[?] san[?] der[?] &u[?] paucis attulit, ad gratiæ naturâ distinctionib-[?] aperiendam, quam Cardinalis Bellarminus, qui gratiæ distinctionib. duo fere integra folia consumpsit. Postea hæc res agitata fuit in Concilio Viennensi, sub Clemente quinto, sicut constare potest ex Clementina prima. Quum enim ex Theologorum disputationibus variæ de hac re, & incertæ sententiæ circumferrentur. {a}quibusdam ex ipsis dicentibus (ut Clementinæ verbis utar) per virtutem baptismi parvulis quidem culpam remitti, sed gratiam non conferri; aliis è contra asserentibus; quod & culpa eisdem in baptismo remittitur, & virtutes, ac informans gratia infunduntur, quoad habitum, etsi non pro tempore, quoad usum. Nos autem (inquit Papa Clemens) attendentes generalem efficaciam mortis Christi, quæ per baptismum applicatur pariter omnibus baptizatis: opinionem secundam (quæ dicit, tam parvulis, quam adultis conferri in baptismo informantem gratiam, & virtutes) tanquam probabiliorem, & dictis sanctorum, ac doctorum modernorum Theologia magis consonam, & concordem, sancto approbante Concilio, duximus eligendam. Hactenus Clementina.
units.tr: [unclear] ... Bonaventure brought forward only a few things to explain the distinctions of the nature of grace, whereas Cardinal Bellarmine spent almost two full folios on the distinctions of grace. Afterwards this matter was debated at the Council of Vienne, under Clement V, as can be established from the first Clementine. For since various and uncertain opinions about this matter were being circulated from the disputations of the Theologians, some of them saying (to use the words of the Clementine) that through the virtue of baptism the fault is indeed remitted to little children, but grace is not conferred; others, on the contrary, asserting that both the fault is remitted to them in baptism, and the virtues and informing grace are infused, as to the habit, though not as to the use at the time. But we (says Pope Clement), attending to the general efficacy of the death of Christ, which is applied equally to all the baptized through baptism: have judged that the second opinion (which says that informing grace and the virtues are conferred in baptism both on little children and on adults), as the more probable, and more consonant and in agreement with the sayings of the saints and of the modern doctors of Theology, should be chosen, with the holy Council approving. Thus far the Clementine.

units.la: O quam disparibus dominis antiqua hæc domus, (Ecclesiam intelligo) regitur. In antiquis Conciliis fidem é scripturis constanter confirmare solebant veteres: In hoc autem conventu nulla est scripturæ mentio, sed sanctorum, & doctorum tantummodo modernorum. Per sanctos hic intelligunt sanctum scilicet Thomam Aquinatem; Bonauennaventuram, aliosve eius fermenti: nam an-te Lumbardi sæcula nemo sanctorum sic do-cuit. Porro hanc conclusionem, non tanquam cœlestem doctrinam, sed ut opinio-nem probabiliorem eligendam statuunt. Novo plane & peregrino instituto. Nam quum de fide Catholica tractat Ecclesia Christi, non solet fluctuando ad probabiliores opi-niones, nescio quas, dubitanter accedere: sed certam veritatem è scripturis definitam tradere. Viennense hoc Concilium celebratum est sub Clemente quinto, Anno Christi 1311.
units.tr: O how this ancient house (I mean the Church) is ruled by unequal lords! In the ancient Councils the ancients were accustomed to confirm the faith constantly from Scripture; but in this assembly there is no mention of Scripture, only of the saints and of the modern doctors. By the saints they mean here, namely, Saint Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, or others of that leaven; for before the ages of Lombard no one among the saints taught in this way. Furthermore, they determine that this conclusion is to be chosen not as heavenly doctrine but as a more probable opinion. This is a wholly new and strange arrangement. For when the Church of Christ treats of the Catholic faith, it is not accustomed to incline hesitantly toward I know not what more probable opinions, by wavering; but to hand down the certain truth defined from Scripture. This Council of Vienne was held under Clement V, in the year of Christ 1311.

units.la: Ex hoc fonte manarunt Scholasticorum subsequentium disputationes, de habitu infuso, & virtute inhærente: de opere operato in sacramentis de merito congrui extra sacramenta. Itaq; Iohannes Scotus sic docet: {a}Gratia formaliter est virtus quæ est charitas. Hæc ex Aquinate: quædam ipse adiecit, quæ doctrinam meriti de congruo fœculentam Tridentinis pararunt. Sic enim docet: {b}peccator potest ex naturalibus, cum communi influentia considerare peccatum commissum, ut offensivum Dei. Potest voluntas peccatum sic consideratum detestari, & ille motus potest continuari, & intendi ante infusionem gratiæ: ille autem motus dicitur attritio. Et est dispositio, siue meritum de congruo. Si manet idem motus contra peccatum in esse naturæ & mori[?], qui prius fuit attritio, in illo stante fit contritio. Hæc doctrina à Scoto vel inventa, vel sedulo retenta est. Scotus ergo meritum congrui sic describi-tur, ut invt int[?] mori[?] Au[?] tur et[?] dilp[?] pont[?] quis[?] telig[?] grat[?] te me[?] atqu[?] volu[?] tus. tini[?] reco[?] mer[?] E[?] cam[?] que[?] xim[?] ri se[?] I.ca[?] Co[?] grà[?] Pel[?] gau[?] ta[?] tifi[?] dic[?] ta[?] ort[?] an[?] vt intelligatur ante infusionem gratiæ in esse moris, & naturæ, atque in naturalibus.
units.tr: From this source flowed the subsequent disputations of the Scholastics, concerning the infused habit and inherent virtue, concerning the work wrought in the sacraments, and concerning merit of congruity outside the sacraments. Thus John Duns Scotus teaches: Grace is formally a virtue, which is charity. These things are from Aquinas; he added certain points which prepared for the Tridentines a doctrine of merit of congruity befouled with dregs. For he teaches thus: A sinner can, from natural powers, with common influence, consider sin committed as offensive to God. The will can detest sin so considered, and that movement can be continued and intensified before the infusion of grace; that movement is called attrition. And it is a disposition, or merit of congruity. If the same movement against sin remains in being of nature and [unclear], which was first attrition, then in that state contrition comes about. This doctrine was either invented by Scotus or diligently retained by him. Scotus therefore describes merit of congruity thus: [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] [unclear] [unclear], so that it is understood as before the infusion of grace, in the state of morals and of nature, and in natural things.

units.la: Atque hæc est fides illa quam hodie sequi- tur curia Rom. hæc est illa præparatio, atque dispositio, quam solius fidei iustificationi op- ponunt Tridentini: quum sic dicant: {a} Si quis dixerit, sola fide impium iustificari, ita vt intelligat nihil aliud requiri, quod ad iustificationis gratiam consequendam cooperetur, & nulla ex parte necesse esse, tantum suæ voluntatis motu præparari atque disponi, anathema sit. Hic est ille motus voluntaris, quem supra descripserat Scotus. Itaque Bellarminus ex Concilii Tridentini decreto sic docet. {b} Potest homo nondum reconciliatus per opera pœnitentiæ impetrare, & mereri ex congruo gratiam iustificationis.
units.tr: And this is that faith which the Roman court now follows; this is that preparation and disposition which the Tridentines set against justification by faith alone, since they say: "If anyone says that the impious man is justified by faith alone, in such a way that he understands nothing else to be required which cooperates to obtain the grace of justification, and that it is in no way necessary that he be prepared and disposed by the motion of his own will, let him be anathema." This is that voluntary motion which Scotus described above. Accordingly, Bellarmine, following the decree of the Council of Trent, teaches thus: "A man not yet reconciled can, through the works of penance, obtain and merit by congruity the grace of justification."

units.la: Ergo Pelagii errorem ex inferis plane revocant Tridentini: Nam quod Augustinus, aliique patres in Pelagio damnarunt, in eo maxime erat, quod docebat Pelagius, gratiam dari secundum merita. de qua re Augustinus lib. 1.cap. 6. de gratia Christi, contra Pelagium, & Cœlestinum, qua sententia restancur [?] veteres, gratiam Dei penitus euersam [?]. Itaque affirmat Pelagium negasse gratiam. Quod si gratiâ negauerit, qui docuit illam dari secundum merita: profecto non magis Pelagius, quam Pontificii gratiam negant, quid enim interest, dicas ne, gratiam dari secundum merita, quod in Pelagio hæretico damnarunt orthodoxi patres: an sic doceas, opera ante reconciliationem, & gratiam facta, mereri gratiam iustificationis? quod docent hodie Tridentini.
units.tr: Therefore the Tridentines plainly bring back from the dead the error of Pelagius. For what Augustine and the other Fathers condemned in Pelagius was chiefly this: that he taught grace to be given according to merits. Augustine speaks of this matter in book 1, chapter 6 of On the Grace of Christ, against Pelagius and Coelestius, where he says that by this opinion the ancients held the grace of God to be utterly overthrown. Thus he asserts that Pelagius denied grace. But if someone who taught that grace is given according to merits denied grace, then surely Pelagius denied grace no more than the Papists do. For what difference is there between saying that grace is given according to merits, which the orthodox Fathers condemned in the heretic Pelagius, and teaching that works done before reconciliation and before grace merit the grace of justification? This is what the Tridentines teach today.

units.la: Verbis videri volunt à Pelagio discedere, reuera consentiunt. Pelagius gratiam apertius expugnabat, quod isti occultius faciunt. Pelagius primo docuit, non gratia, sed meritis nostris nos saluari. Patres è scripturis docuerunt, non meritis nostris, sed gratia Dei. Tridentini hæc [illegible, ~5 letters] coniungunt, sicut & Pelagius, admonitus coniunxit & verumque retinere volunt, & gratia, inquiunt, & meritis. Sed quia in iustificatione impii gratia & merita simul stare non possunt: Sicut gratia, iam non ex operibus alioquin gratia iam[?] non est gratia: iccirco Tridentini quum in hac re duobus seruire non possint tam contrariis mandantibus, alterum abiiciant necesse est, vel gratiam, vel meritum. Sicut enim qui verum Dei cultum simul cum Baalim retinere volunt, verumque verbis profitentur, reuera Dei cultum conculcant: Sic qui gratiam & merita coniungunt in iustificatione, quæ, si scripturis fides habeatur, coniungi non possunt, gratiam Dei penitus reiiciunt, verumque verbis frigidis admittere videantur. Venenum Pelagianum intus conditur Tridentinis, quod si vna interrogatiuncula vrgeas istos, erumpet protinus, quod conditum erat. Quærimus ergo (quoniam multa garriunt isti de auxilio gratiæ) verum ideo adiuuetur voluntas, quia voluit: an ideo voluerit, quia adiuuatur? dicunt isti, ideo ad-iuuari voluntatem, quia voluit, auxilium gra-
units.tr: In words they wish to seem to depart from Pelagius; in reality they agree with him. Pelagius attacked grace more openly; these men do it more covertly. Pelagius first taught that we are saved not by grace but by our merits. The Fathers, from the Scriptures, taught that we are saved not by our merits but by the grace of God. The Tridentines join these two together, as Pelagius did when he was admonished, and they say they want to retain both, grace and merits. But since grace and merits cannot stand together in the justification of the impious: "If by grace, it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace", therefore the Tridentines, since they cannot serve two such contrary masters in this matter, must cast off one of them, either grace or merit. For just as those who wish to keep the true worship of God together with Baal, and profess the true worship in words, in fact trample the worship of God underfoot, so those who join grace and merits in justification, which cannot be joined if faith is given to Scripture, utterly reject the grace of God, while seeming to admit it in cold words. The Pelagian poison lies hidden within the Tridentines; if you press them with a single little question, what was hidden will at once burst forth. We ask, then (since these men chatter much about the help of grace): is the will helped because it willed, or did it will because it was helped? These men say that the will is helped because it willed, the help of grace

units.la: tig lag lan vol pra Sco mi vit per tre tia an in gio uel giu qu bir glo aut no in Re qu hu ne fe ue re mi tiæ[?], verbis concedunt, reipsa tollunt cum Pe-lagianis, hanc enim Pelagianę hæresis summu-lam fuisse obseruat {4} Prosper. Si dicant, ideo voluntatem velle, quia adiuuatur, tollitur illa præparatio, & meritum de congruo, quod ex Scoto exceperunt Tridentini.
units.tr: (the scan of this unit is too garbled to translate) …they concede in words, but in fact remove, along with the Pelagians, for Prosper observes that this was the chief point of the Pelagian heresy. If they say that the will wills because it is helped, that preparation is removed, and the merit of congruity, which the Tridentines took from Scotus.

units.la: Nec Tridentinos inuabit, si dixerint, ho-minem non reconciliatum mereri posse, non vitam æternam, sed gratiam iustificationis, & per gratiam tandem vitam æternam. Nam Patres, qui Pelagium execrantur, tantum de gratia Dei dimicant. Neque enim quæstio erat, an per gratiam vita æterna sit comparanda: sed in eo controuersia veteribus fuerat cum Pelagio, quomodo quispiam ad gratiæ statum prouehi possit. Contendunt Patres contra Pelagium, ad gratiam, & reconciliationem consequendam, non nostra opera, non liberum arbitrium, non merita valere. Concedunt nos gloriam consequi posse per gratiam, negant autem gratiam nos consequi posse per opera nostra. Quod quum profiteantur Pontificii, in manifesto Pelagianismi luto hærent, & cum Pelagio, vt gratiæ diuinæ hostes à patribus, atque ab Ecclesia Dei damnantur.
units.tr: Nor will it please the Tridentines if they say that a man not yet reconciled can merit not eternal life but the grace of justification, and through grace at last eternal life. For the Fathers, who execrate Pelagius, contended only about the grace of God. The question was not whether eternal life is to be obtained through grace; the controversy with Pelagius was rather over how anyone can be advanced to the state of grace. The Fathers contend against Pelagius that our works, our free will and our merits avail nothing toward obtaining grace and reconciliation. They concede that we can obtain glory through grace, but deny that we can obtain grace through our works. Since the Papists profess the opposite, they cling to a manifest Pelagian mire, and together with Pelagius they are condemned by the Fathers and by the Church of God as enemies of divine grace.

units.la: Iam igitur constare potest, quod originem huius erroris attiner[?], ante annum millesimum neminem in Ecclesia Romana inuentum suis-se, qui de gratia Dei aliter disputarit senserit-ue[?], quam sacræ scripturæ tradunt. Nam & patres Græci, & Latini, & quicunque cum Romana Ecclesia consensum habuerunt, contra Pelagianos errores semel exortos fortiter dimicarunt; ita ut praeter Pelagianos, de hac re nemo dubitauerit, Ecclesia Romana integra perstiterit. Id quod luculenter constare potest ex scriptis Cælestini, & Leonis, Pontificum Romanorum contra Pelagianos in Galliis. Cælestinus multa etiam Romanorum Pontificum testimonia contra Pelagianam hæresim congesit, Augustini scripta contra Pelagianos Catholica probat, & (quod plus valet apud Tridentinos) testatur Cælestinus Rom. Episcopus eiusdem Augustini scripta à Sede {a}Apostolica maxime semper fuisse probata: a ut Augustinus inter magistros optimos, inquit, etiam à meis semper decessoribus haberetur. Leo vero de eodem negotio Concilium Arausicanum II. contraxit adversus reviviscentes per Gallias Pelagianæ hæreseos errores. In quo Concilio renovata, & confirmata est Catholica, & Apostolica, eademque Augustini de gratia, & libero arbitrio, doctrina, canonibus ipsis ex beati Augustini libris passim decerptis. Romanæ Ecclesiæ fides integra in istorum Pontificum vestigiis permansit, usque ad annum Christi millesimum. Post annum millesimum, soluto Satana, opinionibus incertis, & novis fictionibus fides antiqua apud plurimos fluctuare cœpit, donec Concilio Viennensi Clemens PP. V. non fidem Catholicam, sed fluctuantem inter probabilitates opinionem elegit; sacramenta conferre gratiâ. Hinc Theologorum tenebrosæ disputationes de qualita-te inte inhærente, de opere operato, de merito congrui: sed hæc inter priuatas opiniones fraterculorum circumferebantur, donec tandem in Concilio Tridentino perniciosæ istæ speculationes pro Ecclesiasticis dogmatibus statuerentur.
units.tr: It can now be established that, as regards the origin of this error, before the year one thousand no one was found in the Roman Church who taught or thought about the grace of God otherwise than the Holy Scriptures hand it down. For both the Greek and the Latin Fathers, and all who were in agreement with the Roman Church, fought bravely against the Pelagian errors once they had arisen; so that, apart from the Pelagians, no one doubted about this matter, and the Roman Church remained whole. This can be made abundantly clear from the writings of Coelestine and Leo, Popes of Rome, against the Pelagians in Gaul. Coelestine also gathered many testimonies of the Roman Pontiffs against the Pelagian heresy, and he proves the writings of Augustine against the Pelagians to be Catholic; and (which carries more weight with the Tridentines) Coelestine, Bishop of Rome, testifies that the writings of this same Augustine had always been most highly approved by the Apostolic See: "so that Augustine," he says, "was always held by my predecessors too as one of the best teachers." Leo, moreover, concerning this same business, convened the Second Council of Orange against the errors of the Pelagian heresy that were reviving throughout Gaul. In that Council the Catholic and Apostolic doctrine was renewed and confirmed, and likewise the doctrine of Augustine on grace and free will, with canons drawn here and there from the books of the blessed Augustine himself. The faith of the Roman Church remained intact in the footsteps of these Pontiffs until the year of Christ one thousand. After the year one thousand, once Satan had been loosed, the ancient faith began to waver among many through uncertain opinions and new fictions, until at the Council of Vienne Clement V chose, not the Catholic faith, but an opinion wavering among probabilities, that the sacraments confer grace. Hence came the murky disputations of the theologians about the inherent quality, about the work worked, and about merit by congruity; but these were circulated among the private opinions of the friars, until at last, at the Council of Trent, these pernicious speculations were established as ecclesiastical dogmas.
